The stalks are Polygala about five or six inches long, several arising from the same root: the leaves are firm, smooth, entire, and grow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> upon the stalks, which are terminated with spikes of flowers, most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> blue, but often red or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>: the calyx consists of five leaves, three of which are small and green, two below, and one above the corolla; the other two intermediate ones are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, oval, flat, coloured, veined, and resemble petals, which at length turn greenish, and remain a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> to the seed-vessel; the corolla consists of three petals folded together, and forming a tube: the carina is terminated by a kind of heart-shaped, concave appendage, fringed at the extremity. The root of this plant has a bitter <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and has been found to possess the virtues of the American rattlesnake-root. It purges without danger, and is also emetic and diuretic; sometimes operating all the three ways at once. A spoonful of the decoction made by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> an ounce of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> in a pint of water till one half has exhaled, has been found serviceable in pleuritis and fevers, by promoting a diaphoresis and expectoration; and three spoonfuls of the same, taken once an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, has proved beneficial in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a> and anaerca. It has also been found serviceable in consumptive complaints. 2. The senega, or seneka, rattlesnake-wort, grows naturally in most parts of North <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. This hath a perennial root composed of several fleshy fibres, from which arise three or four branching stalks which grow erect, garnished with spear-shaped leaves placed alternately. The flowers are produced in loose spikes at the end of the branches: they are small, white, and shaped like those of the common fort. It flowers here in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, but the plants do not produce seeds. The root of this species operates more powerfully than the last; but besides the virtues of a purgative, emetic, and diuretic, it has been recommended as an antidote against the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a> of a rattlesnake; tho' how precarious every remedy in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> must be, will appear from what is said under the article Poison. As the seeds of the rattlesnake-wort seldom succeed even in the countries where the plant is a native, the best method of propagating it is to procure the roots from America, and plant them in a bed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> in a sheltered situation, where they will thrive without any other culture than keeping them free from weeds. But though the plant will stand our ordinary winters, it will be proper to cover it during that season with old tanner's bark, or other mulch, to keep out the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a>.

POLLYSYLLABLE

Pages 51-51

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, a word consisting of more than three syllables; for when a word consists of one, two, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> three syllables, it is called a monosyllable, a disyllable, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRISYLLABLE">trisyllable</a>. POLYSYNDETON. See Oratory, n° 65.

POLYGAMIA

Pages 50-50

(πολύς, "many;" and γάμος, "<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>.") This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, expressing an intercommunication of sexes, is applied, by Linnæus, both to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. A polygamous plant is that which bears both hermaphrodite flowers and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, or both.

POLYGLOTT

Pages 50-50

among divines and critics, chiefly denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a> printed in several languages. See BIBLE, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">PRINTING</a>.

POLYGON

Pages 50-50

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> with many sides, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> whose perimeter consists of more than four sides at least; such are the pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, &c.

POLYGONUM

Pages 50-51

knot-grass; a genus of the trigynia order, belonging to the octandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are 27 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; but the most remarkable are, 1. The bistorta, bistort, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> greater snakeweed, hath a thick oblique intorted root, blackish without and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> within; a simple round slender stem near two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; oval leaves, having decurrent foot-stalks, and the stalk terminated by thick short spikes of whitish-red <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. 2. The vivaparum, or smaller bistort, hath a thickish root, a simple slender stem half a foot high, spear-shaped leaves, and the stalks and branches terminated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> spikes of whitish-red flowers. Both these perennials flower in May and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, succeeded by ripe seeds in August. They grow wild in England, &c. the first in moist places, the other in mountainous situations. 3. Oriental polygonum, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called persicaria, hath <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> roots; an upright, robust, strong, jointed stem, rising eight or ten feet high, dividing at top into several branches; very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> oval-lanceolate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> leaves, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> foot-stalks half surrounding the stem; and all the branches terminated by long, slender, hanging spikes of reddish-purple heptandrous and digynious flowers, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> till October. 4. Fagopyrum, buckwheat, or brack, rises with an upright smooth branchy stem, from about a foot and a half to a yard high, heart-shaped sagittated leaves, and the branches terminated by clusters of whitish flowers, succeeded by large angular seeds; excellent for feeding pigeons, and most sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>. All these plants are hardy, and succeed in almost any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and situation; the two first are perennial in root; and the third and fourth are annual, wholly decay at the end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, or early in winter. The first two sorts are retained in some curious gardens for variety; but their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> merit is for medical purposes: they are powerful astringents, and are used both internally and externally; esteemed very efficacious in haemorrhages, and other fluxes; and good to heal sore mouths. Third sort, Oriental polygonum, or persicaria, is a most elegant annual for the embellishment of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>-ground; assuming a majestic tree-like growth by its erect luxuriant stem, and branchy head; which being garnished with noble large foliage, and numerous pendulous spikes of flowers, in constant succession three or four months, exhibits a very ornamental appearance from June or July until October, and is so easy of culture, that from its scattered seeds in autumn, young plants rise spontaneously in abundance the ensuing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and shoot up so rapidly as to attain six or eight feet stature by July, when they generally begin flowering, and continue till attacked by the frosts, then totally perish; so that a fresh supply must be raised from seed annually. The fourth sort (buck-wheat) is a sort of corn, and is frequently cultivated both by way of fodder, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> its stalks while young and green to feed Polygonum feed cattle; and for its grain to feed pigeons, poultry, hogs, &c. It flourishes in any soil and situation, but generally thrives best in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and the driest seasons seldom retard its growth. The first and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sort are easily propagated in plenty, by parting the roots in autumn. The third sort, Oriental polygonum, being annual, is always propagated from seed annually, either in the full ground, or by aid of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOT_BEDS">hot-beds</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">Use</a>. The root of a kind of bistort, according to Gmelin, is used in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> for ordinary food. This species is by Haller called *biflora foliis <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> oram nervosis*, and by some other botanists *biflora montana <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>*. The natives call it *mouka*; and so indolent are they, that, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> themselves the trouble of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> it out of the earth, they go in spring and pillage the holes of the mountain rats, which they find filled with these roots. In our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, bistort is used in medicine. All the parts of bistort have a rough astringent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, particularly the root, which is one of the strongest of the vegetable astringents. It is employed in all kinds of immoderate hemorrhages and other fluxes, both internally and externally, where astringency is the only indication. It is certainly a very powerful astringent, and is to be looked on simply as such; the sudorific, antipellitential, and other like virtues ascribed to it, has no other claim to, than in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of its astringency, and of the antiseptic power which it has in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with other vegetable astringents. The largest dose of the root in powder is one dram.

POLYGRAPHY

Pages 51-51

POLYGRAPHIA, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Polygraphice, the art of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> in various unusual manners or cyphers; as also of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECIPHERING">deciphering</a> the same. The word is formed from the Greek, πολύ, multum, and γραφή, *scriptura*, "writing." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> seem to have been very little acquainted with this art; nor is there any mark of their having gone beyond the Lacedemonian scytals. Trithemius, Porta, Vigenere, and father Niceron, have written on the subject of polygraphy or ciphers. See Cipher.

POLYHEDRON

Pages 51-51

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, denotes a body <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> comprehended under many sides or planes. Polyhedron, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, is a multiplying glass or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENS">lens</a>, consisting of several <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> surfaces disposed into a convex form. See Optics, p. 5575.

POLYHYMNIA

Pages 51-51

in the pagan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, thus named from the Greek words πολύς, "much;" and ὑμνός, "<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>." She presided over <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> rather <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>; and is represented with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of pearls and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> robe; her <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> haranguing, and holding in her left a caduceus or sceptre to shew her power.

POLYMATHY

Pages 51-51

denotes the knowledge of many arts and sciences. The word is derived from the Greek, πολύς, multum, and μάθημα, disco.

POLYPETALOUS

Pages 51-51

among botanists, an epithet applied to such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> as consist of several petals <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> flower-leaves.

POLYPODIUM

Pages 51-51

POLYPODY; a genus of the order of filices, belonging to the cryptogamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are 65 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, of which the most remarkable is the filix mas, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> fern. This grows in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty throughout <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> in woods and stony soils. The leaves are a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and grow in circular tufts. They are at first alternately pinnate, the pinnae increasing in size from the base towards the middle, and afterwards gradually decreasing upwards to the summit of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>. These pinnae are again pinnatifid, or subdivided almost to the nerve into obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> lobes, crenated on the edges. The stalks are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> silky scales. The fructifications are kidney-shaped, and covered with a permanent scaly shield or involucrenum. The capsules are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> brown, surrounded with a saffron-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>. This fern has nearly the same qualities, and is used for most of the same intentions as the pteris aquilina. They are both burnt together for the sake of their ashes, which are purchased by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> and glaze-makers. In the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURA">Jura</a> are exported annually 150l. worth of these ashes. Gunner relates, in his Flor. Novaez., that the young curled leaves, at their first appearance out of the ground, are by some boiled and eaten like asparagus; and that the poorer Norwegians cut off those succulent laminae, like the nails of the finger at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of the root, which are the bases of the future stalks, and brew them into beer, adding thereto a third portion of malt, and in times of great scarcity mix the same in their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. The same author adds, that this fern cut green and dried in the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, affords not only an excellent litter for cattle, but, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> infused in hot <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, becomes no contemptible fodder for goats, sheep, and other cattle, which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> readily eat, and sometimes grow fat upon it: a circumstance well worth the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the inhabitants of the Highlands and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>, as great numbers of their cattle, in hard winters, frequently perish for want of food. But the anthelmintic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the root of the male fern is that for which it is chiefly to be valued, and of which an account is given under the article Medicine, n° 493.

POLYPUS

Pages 51-51

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRA">Hydra</a>; which, though cut in a thousand pieces, and in every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, still exists, and each <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECTION">section</a> becomes a complete animal. Polypus of the Heart. See Medicine, n° 209, 383.

POLYTHEISM

Pages 51-51

in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, the doctrine <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of a plurality of gods.

POMACE

Pages 52-52

(pomum, an "apple,") the name of the 36th order in Linnæus's Fragments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Pomaceous Method, the genera of which have a pulpy succulent fruit of the apple, berry, and cherry kind. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, pompeys. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. vi. 36. POMEGRANATE. See Punica.

POMERANIA

Pages 52-52

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Germany, in the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Baltic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, on the south by the margraviate of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, and on the west by the duchy of Mecklenburg; and is about 250 miles in length, and in some places 75 miles and in others 50 in breadth. It is watered by several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, the most considerable of which are the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>, the Pene, the Rega, the Perfant, the Wipper, the Stolp, the Lupo, and the Lobo. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> abounds in pastures, and produces corn, of which a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> is exported. It is a flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; containing many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, woods, and forests, and has several good harbours. It is divided into the Hither and Farther Pomerania, and the territories of the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> and Prussia in this duchy are divided by the river Pene.

POMET

Pages 52-52

an able druggist at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, was born in 1658. He collected at a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> expense from all countries drugs of every kind, and rendered himself celebrated by his book intitled Histoire Generale des Droguers, which is the most complete book on the subject that has yet been printed. He gave demonstrations with respect to his drugs in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s garden, and a catalogue of all the drugs contained in his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of all the rarities of his cabinet, which he proposed to publish by subscription; but was prevented by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1699, upon the very <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> when the patent for a pension granted him by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. was made out.

POMFRET

Pages 52-52

an English poet, son of the rector of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUTON">Luton</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>, was born in 1667, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. He entered into orders, and obtained a living in Bedfordshire, but died of the smallpox at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 35. He published a small volume of tolerable poems; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are not to be extolled for their sublimity, have a moral and pious turn, which recommended them to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> readers; so that Pomfret's poems still continue to be a very popular book among those whose <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> is not very extensive either in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> prose.

POMME'

Pages 52-52
or POMMETTE', in heraldry, is a cross with one or more balls or knobs at each of the ends.

POMMEL

Pages 52-52
or PUMMEL, in the manege, a piece of brats or other matter at the top and in the middle of the saddle-bow.

POMONA

Pages 52-52

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the tutelar deity of orchards and fruit-trees. See Vertumnus.

POMPEII

Pages 52-52

(anc. geog.), a town of Campania near Herculaneum, and destroyed along with it by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> eruption of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Titus. POMPEY the Great, (Cneius Pompeius Magnus), the renowned rival of Julius Caesar. Being defeated by him at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a>, owing to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFECTION">defection</a> of his cavalry, he fled to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, where he was basely assassinated by order of Theodotus, prime minister to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> the Younger, then a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>, 48 B.C. See Rome.

POMPEYS

Pages 52-53

his sons, commanded a powerful <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> when they lost their illustrious father. Julius Caesar pursued them into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and defeated Pomponius feated them at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Munda, in which Cnecius was slain, 45 B.C. Sextus made himself <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; but being defeated in the celebrated naval engagement at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIUM">Actium</a>, by Augustus and Lepidus, he fled to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, with only 7 ships, the remains of his fleet, which consisted of more than 350; and from thence, unable to continue the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, he was obliged to retire to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>, where renewing the war by raising an army, and seizing on some considerable cities, Marcus Titius, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Marc Anthony, gave him battle, defeated him, took him prisoner, and basely put him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, 35 B.C. See Rome. POMPONIUS MELA. See Mela.

POMUM

Pages 53-53

an Apple; a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of seed-vessel, composed of a succulent fleshy pulp; in the middle of which is generally found a membranous <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cells, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> cavities, for containing the seeds. Seed-vessels of this kind have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> opening, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VALVE">valve</a>. At the end opposite to the foot-stalk is frequently a small cavity, called by the gardeners the eye of the fruit, and by botanists umbilicus, the "navel," from its fancied resemblance to the navel in animals. Gourd, cucumber, melon, pomegranate, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, and apple, furnish instances of the fruit or seed-vessel in question.

PONDICHERY

Pages 53-53

a town of the East Indies, on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Coromandel on this side the Ganges; the best French settlement in these parts. It was taken by the Dutch in 1693; but rendered back by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Ryfwick. It was taken by the British in the last <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and the fortifications were demolished. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on which it stands is low, and the vessels are obliged to come to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half from it; not even boats <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> canoes could come within musket-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> of it, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> Indians were obliged to carry their merchandizes and other things to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> in flat-bottomed boats. The factory stood on a barren spot, insomuch that there is hardly a worse on the whole coast; but it was chosen because it is difficult to be attacked on the side of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80. 14. N. Lat. 12. 26.

PONIARD

Pages 53-53

a little pointed dagger, very sharp edged; borne in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> at the girdle, or hid in the pocket. The word is formed from the French poignard, and that from poigne, "handful."—The poniard was anciently in very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; but it is now in good <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> set aside, except among assassins.—<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">Sword</a> and poniard were the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> arms of duelists; and are said to continue still to among the Spaniards. The practice of sword and poniard still make a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> taught by the masters of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>.

PONTEFRACT

Pages 53-53
or Pomfret, a town of the West Riding of Yorkshire in England, situated on the river Aire. It is said to take its name from a broken bridge, which is supposed to have been laid anciently over that marshy spot called the Wash. Here are the ruins of a noble old castle, where Richard II. was barbarously murdered, and two of Edward V.'s uncles. The collegiate chapel of St. Clement, which had a dean, three prebendaries, &c., is still distinguishable in it. This town has a good market, and fairs for horses, sheep, and other cattle. It is a corporation, governed by a mayor, recorder, aldermen, and burgesses, and gives title of earl to the family of Ferman. Pontifex In the reign of queen Elizabeth, 200 l. was left by George Talbot, earl of Shrewsbury, to be lent for ever, at 5 l. a time, on proper security, for three years, to the poor artificers of the town; and Thomas Wentworth, esquire, ancestor to the marquis of Rockingham, left 200 l. to the charity-school. A branch of the great Roman military way, called Erminstreet, which passed from Lincoln to York, may be traced betwixt this town and Doncaster. The adjacent country yields plenty of limestone, together with liquorice and skirrets. W. Long. 1. 5. N. Lat. 53. 42.

PONTIFEX

Pages 53-53

Pontif, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, a person who has the superintendence and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of divine worship, as the offering of sacrifices and other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> solemnities. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of pontiffs; and over these a sovereign pontiff, or pontifex maximus, instituted by Numa, whose <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> it was to preside over the ceremonies each god was to be worshipped withal, compose the rituals, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the vestals, and for a good while to perform the business of augury, till, on some superstitious occasion, he was prohibited intermeddling therewith. The office of the college of pontiffs was to assist the high-priest in giving judgment in all causes relating to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, inquiring into the lives and manners of the inferior priests, and punishing them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> occasion, &c. The Jews too had their pontiffs; and among the Romanists, the pope is still styled the sovereign pontiff.

PONTIFICATE

Pages 53-53

is used for the state <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a pontiff or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>; but more particularly in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers, for the reign of a pope.

PONTON

Pages 53-53
or Pontoon, in war, a kind of flat-bottomed boat, whose carcass of wood is lined within and without with tin: they serve to lay bridges over rivers for the artillery and army to march over. The French pontoons, and those of most other powers, are made of copper on the outside: though these cost more at first, yet they last much longer than those of tin; and when worn out, the copper falls nearly for as much as it cost at first; but when ours are rendered useless, they fall for nothing. Our pontoons are 21 feet long, 5 feet broad broad, and depth within 2 feet 1.5 inches. Pontoon-Carriage, is made with two wheels only, and two long side-pieces, whose fore ends are supported by a limber; and serves to carry the pontoon, boards, cross timbers, anchors, and every other thing necessary for making a bridge. Pontoon-Bridge, is made of pontoons shipped into the water, and placed about five or six feet asunder; each fastened with an anchor, when the river has a strong current; or to a strong rope that goes across the river, running through the rings of the pontoons. Each boat has an anchor, cable, baulks, and chests. The baulks are about five or six inches square, and 21 feet long. The chests are boards joined together by wooden bars, about three feet broad, and 12 feet long. The baulks are laid across the pontoons at some distance from one another, and the chests upon them joined close; which makes a bridge in a very short time, capable of supporting any weight.

PONTUS

Pages 53-70

the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a>, on the west by the river <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-HALYS">Halys</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Euxine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, and Pontus. on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. Some derive the name of Pontus from the neighbouring sea, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called by the Latins Pontus Euxinus; others from an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> named Pontus, who imparted his name both to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and the sea; but Bochart deduces it from the Phoenician word bōno, signifying a fishery, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> abounded remarkably in this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. But this derivation seems to be very far fetched; and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the country derived its name from the sea, seems by far the most probable. The kingdom was divided into three parts; the first, named Pontus Galaticus, extending from the river Halys to the Thermodon; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, named Pontus Polemoniacus, extended from the Thermodon to the borders of Pontus Cappadocicus; and this last extended from Pontus Polemoniacus to Colchis, having Armenia Minor and the upper stream of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> for its southern boundary. It is commonly believed, that the first inhabitants of Pontus were descended from Tubal; but in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> mixed with Cappadocians, Paphlagonians, and other foreign nations, besides many Greek colonies which settled in those parts, and maintained their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> till the time of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> and Pharnaces. The first king of this country whom we find mentioned in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is Artabazes, who had the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> bestowed on him by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> Hystaspes. The next was Rhodobates, who reigned in the time of Darius Nothus. After him came Mithridates, who, refusing to pay the usual tribute to the Persians, was defeated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> Memon; but a peace was soon after concluded by the mediation of Tissaphernes. Besides this, we hear nothing of him farther than that he was treacherously taken prisoner by Clearchus afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERACLEA">Heraclea</a>, and obliged to pay a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>. Mithridates I. was succeeded by Ariobarzanes, who being appointed by Artaxerxes governor of Lydia, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, employed the forces that were under his care in the extending of his own dominions, and subduing those of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. The king of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> sent one Autophrodes against him; but Ariobarzanes, having with great promises prevailed on <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGESILAUS">Agesilaus</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMOTHEUS">Timotheus</a> the Athenian to come to his assistance, obliged Autophrodes to retire. He then rewarded Agesilaus with a great sum of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and bestowed on Timotheus the cities of Settos and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYDOS">Abydos</a>, which he had lately taken from the Persians. He used his utmost endeavours to reconcile the Lacedemonians and Thebans; but, not being able to bring the latter to any reasonable terms, he afflicted the Lacedemonians with vast sums of money. The Athenians shewed so much respect for this prince, that they not only made him free of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, but granted both him and his children whatever they asked of them. He was murdered in the 28th year of his reign by one Mithridates, whom authors suppose to have been his son. This happened at the time that Alexander the Great invaded Asia, so that Pontus for a time fell under the power of the Macedonians. In the reign of Antigonus, Mithridates the son of Ariobarzanes shook off the Macedonian yoke, the particulars of which event are related as follows: Antigonus having dreamed that he had a field in which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> grew after the manner of corn, and that Mithridates cut it <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and carried it into Pontus, began to be very jealous of him, and ordered him to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> privately. But Mithridates, having got notice of the king's intention, withdrew into Paphlagonia, attended only by six horsemen. Here, being joined by many others, he possessed himself of Ciniatium; a strong hold situated near mount Olgafts; from whence, as his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> continually increased, he made an irruption into Cappadocia; and, having driven the commanders of Antigonus from that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> which borders upon Pontus, he entered his paternal kingdom, which, in spite of the utmost efforts of Antigonus, he held for the space of 26 years, and transmitted to his posterity. Under the reigns of Mithridates III., Ariobarzanes II., and Mithridates IV., the immediate successors of Mithridates III., nothing remarkable happened. But Mithridates V. made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> on the inhabitants of Sinope, a city on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Paphlagonia. He made himself <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all the adjacent places; but finding the whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on which Sinope itself stood well fortified and garrisoned, not only by the inhabitants, but by their allies the Rhodians, he abandoned the enterprise. He afterwards proved a great friend to the Rhodians, and assisted them with money to repair the losses they had sustained by an earthquake. He entered also into a strict <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with Antiochus the Great, who married one of his daughters named Laodicice. After the death of Mithridates V. his son Pharnaces I. attacking the city of Sinope, unexpectedly took it by storm. On this the Rhodians sent ambassadors to Rome, complaining of the behaviour of the king of Pontus; but Pharnaces was so far from being intimidated by their threats, that he invaded the territories of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUMENES">Eumenes</a> their great ally. The latter sent ambassadors to Rome, and entered into an alliance with Ariarathes king of Cappadocia. Pharnaces in his turn sent ambassadors to Rome, complaining of Eumenes and Ariarathes; upon which some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were sent into Asia to inquire into the state of matters. These found Eumenes and his associates willing to accommodate the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, but Pharnaces in a quite opposite disposition, which they accordingly reported at Rome. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time a war was commenced between Eumenes and Pharnaces; but the latter, being disappointed of assistance from Seleucus king of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, whom the Romans would not allow to join him, was at last forced to sue for peace, which was granted him upon the following conditions: That he should forthwith withdraw his forces from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a>, and disannul all engagements and alliances with the inhabitants of that country; that he should in like manner evacuate Paphlagonia, and send back such as he had from thence carried into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>; that he should restore to Ariarathes all the places which he had taken during the war, the hostages of both kings, all their prisoners without ransom, and moreover should deliver up to them such of their subjects as from the first breaking out of the war had fled to him; that he should return to Morzius, a petty king in these parts, and to Ariarathes, 900 talents which he had seized in the war, and pay down 300 more to Eumenes as a fine for invading his dominions without provocation. Mithridates dates, king of Armenia, having in this war joined Pharnaces, was, by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, obliged to pay 300 talents to Ariarathes for having assisted his enemy contrary to an alliance at that time subsisting between them. Soon after, Pharnaces died, and left the kingdom to his son Mithridates VI. more weakened by this peace than by the most destructive war. The new king entered into an alliance with the Romans, and proved such a faithful friend, that he was rewarded by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> with Phrygia <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>, and honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the friend and ally of the people of Rome. After a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and prosperous reign, he was murdered by some of his intimate acquaintance, and was succeeded by his son Mithridates VII. surnamed the Great. The new prince, though not exceeding 13 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, began his reign with most inhuman acts of cruelty to his mother and nearest relations. His father, by his last <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, had appointed him and his mother <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>-heirs to the kingdom; but he, claiming the whole, threw her into prison, where she soon died through the hard usage she met with. Those to whom the care of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> was committed, observing him to be of a cruel and unruly temper, made various attempts on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, but could never effect their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, as the king was always on his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and armed, in that tender age, against all kind of treachery, without showing the least difference. In his youth Mithridates took care to inure himself to hardships, passing whole months in the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of hunting, and often taking his rest amidst the frozen snow. When he came of age he married his sister named Laodice, by whom he had a son named Pharnaces. After this he took a journey through many different kingdoms of Asia, having nothing less in view than the whole continent. He learned their different languages, of which he is said to have spoken 22; took an estimate of their strength; and above all viewed narrowly their strong holds and fortified <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. In this journey he spent three years; during which time, a report being spread abroad that he was dead, his wife Laodice had a criminal conversation with one of the lords of her <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and had a son by him. When her husband returned, she presented him with a poisoned bowl; but Mithridates had accustomed himself to take <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a> from his infancy, so that it had now no other effect than to hasten the destruction of his wife, which very soon took place, together with all those who had been any way <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a> to her disloyalty and incontinence. The king now began to put in execution his schemes of conquest. However, he certainly took the wrong method by attacking first those nations which were immediately under the protection of Rome, and thus at once provoking that powerful people to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon him. He began with Paphlagonia, which the Romans had declared a free state. This country he easily reduced, and divided between himself and Nicomedes king of Bithynia, at that time his ally. The Romans remonstrated; but Mithridates, instead of paying any regard to their remonstrances, invaded Galatia, which was immediately under their protection. This he also reduced, and then turned his eyes on Cappadocia. But as the kingdom of Cappadocia was at that time held by Ariarathes, who was a great favourite of the Romans, and married to the sister of Mithridates, the latter hired an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSASSIN">assassin</a> to dispatch Ariarathes, after which he thought he might succeed better in his designs. After the death of Ariarathes, king of Cappadocia was invaded by Nicomedes king of Bithynia, who drove out the son, and married the widow of Ariarathes. This gave Mithridates a plausible pretence for invading Cappadocia; which he instantly did, and drove Nicomedes quite out of the country. Thus Mithridates gained considerable reputation, not only as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>, but as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> and good-natured prince; for as it was not known that he had any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of Ariarathes, every one imagined that he had undertaken the war against Nicomedes, merely to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the quarrel of his nephew, and to restore him to his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. To keep up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> a little longer, Mithridates actually withdrew his troops out of the country, and left the young prince master of the kingdom. In a short time, however, he began to press the young king of Cappadocia to recall the assassin Gordius, who had murdered his father; but this the king of Cappadocia refused with indignation; and Mithridates, being determined on a quarrel at all events, took the field with an army of 80,000 foot, 10,000 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and 600 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> armed with scythes. With this force he imagined he should carry all before him; but, finding the king of Cappadocia ready to oppose him with a force no way inferior to his own, he had recourse to treachery; and inviting his nephew to a conference, stabbed him, in the sight of both armies, with a dagger he had concealed in the plait of his garment. This barbarous and unexpected piece of treachery had such an effect on the Cappadocians that they threw down their arms, and suffered Mithridates, without opposition, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> upon all their strong holds. He resigned the kingdom, however, to his son, a child of eight years of age. The care of the young prince, and of the whole kingdom, he committed to Gordius; but the Cappadocians, disdaining to be ruled by such a scandalous assassin, placed on the throne the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Ariarathes, who had kept himself concealed in some part of Asia. His reign, however, was of short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; he being soon after driven out by Mithridates, and the Cappadocians again reduced. The unhappy prince died of grief; and in him ended the family of Pharnaces, who had ruled Cappadocia from the time of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> the Great. Nicomedes, king of Bithynia, being now greatly afraid of Mithridates, and supposing that his own dominions would next fall a prey to the ambitious conqueror, suborned a youth of a comely and majestic aspect to pretend that he was a third son of Ariarathes, Romans, to go to Rome, and demand the kingdom of Cappadocia as his just right. He was received by the senate with the greatest kindness, and Laodice the wife of Nicomedes even confirmed the deceit by her oath. But in the mean time Mithridates having got intelligence of the plot, sent notice of it by Gordius to the exposed by Romans, so that the imposture was soon known at Rome also. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this was, that the senate commanded Mithridates to relinquish Cappadocia, and Nicomedes that part of Paphlagonia which he possessed; declaring both these countries free. The Cappadocians protested that they could not live with- Pontus. out a king; upon which they were allowed to choose one of their own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Mithridates used all his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in favour of Gordius; but he being excluded by the Romans, one Ariobarzanes was chosen by the majority of votes. To enforce this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, Sylla was sent into Cappadocia. He had the character of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, but the real intent of his coming was to disappoint the ambitious designs of Mithridates. With an handful of forces he defeated a numerous army of Cappadocians and Armenians commanded by Gordius, and settled Ariobarzanes on the throne. But no sooner was Sylla gone, than Mithridates stirred up Tigranes king of Armenia against Ariobarzanes, who without making any resistance fled to Rome, and Tigranes restored the kingdom to Ariarathes the son of Mithridates. At the same time died the king of Bithynia; upon which Mithridates immediately invaded that country, and drove out Nicomedes the natural son of the late king. But the expelled prince, having fled to Rome, and being assisted by that powerful republic, the king of Pontus was soon obliged to abandon Bithynia and Cappadocia. The Romans now being exceedingly jealous of the power and ambition of Mithridates, resolved to humble him at all events. For this purpose they sent ambassadors to the kings of Bithynia and Cappadocia, desiring them to make frequent inroads into the neighbouring territories of Mithridates, and behave there as they pleased; assuring them of powerful assistance in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> they should have occasion. Ariobarzanes could not by any means be induced to provoke so powerful a neighbour; but Nicomedes being induced, partly by promises, and partly by menaces, to comply, entered Pontus, where he laid waste whole provinces with fire and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. Mithridates complained to the Roman legate; but they replied, that he himself had been the first aggressor; that Nicomedes had only paid him in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, and that they would not allow him to hurt their friend and ally. Upon this, Mithridates, entering Cappadocia with a numerous army, put to flight the united forces of Ariobarzanes and Altinuse the Roman legate; thus making himself once more master of this kingdom. In the mean time he sent ambassadors to Rome, complaining of the proceedings of Nicomedes; but his ambassadors met with a very indifferent reception; being enjoined to tell their master, that he must either restore the kingdom of Cappadocia to Ariobarzanes, and make peace with Nicomedes, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> be accounted an enemy of the Roman people. With this answer they were commanded to depart the city that very <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and told that no more ambassadors could be admitted till such time as their commands were obeyed. In the mean time both parties prepared for war. The Roman legates in Asia drew together all the forces they could muster in Bithynia, Cappadocia, Pamphylia, and Galatia; and, being joined by Cassius governor of Asia, took the field against Mithridates in the year 89 B.C. They divided their army into several small bodies: Cassius encamped on the confines of Bithynia and Galatia; Manius Aquilius with his body possessed himself of the avenues leading from Pontus into Bithynia; Quintus Oppius secured the entrance into Cappadocia; and the admirals Minucius Rufus and C. Popilius lay with a fleet of 300 sail at Byzantium, to prevent the enemy from entering the Euxine sea. Each of the generals had under his command an army of 40,000 men; besides a body of 50,000 foot and 6000 horse brought to their assistance by Nicomedes. On the other hand, Mithridates having invited several of the neighbouring nations to join him, collected an army of 250,000 foot, 50,000 horse, 130 chariots armed with scythes; besides 300 ships and 100 galleys. Part of this force he detached against Nicomedes; and utterly defeated him, though much superior in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, as he was taking possession of an advantageous <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a> by order of Cassius. Another part he detached against Manius Aquilius, whom he also defeated with the loss of 10,000 killed on the spot, and 3000 taken prisoners; on which the other Roman generals abandoned their posts, the fleet also dispersed, and most of the ships were either taken or sunk by the admirals of Mithridates. The king of Pontus now resolving to improve the opportunity, and drive the Romans entirely out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia Minor</a>, over-ran all Phrygia, Myria, Asia Proper, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, Lycia, Pamphylia, Pamphylia, and Bithynia, with all the rest of the countries which had either belonged to or sided with the Romans, as far as Ionia. He was received everywhere with the greatest demonstrations of joy; the inhabitants flocking to him in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> garments, and calling him their father, deliverer, their god, and the great and sole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of all Asia. What gained him the affections of the people was his kind usage to the prisoners he had taken in the two engagements above-mentioned; for he not only sent them all home without ransom, but furnished them with plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and money sufficient to defray their expenses by the way. Ambassadors flocked to him from all parts; and among others, from Laodicea on the Lycus, to whom the king promised his protection, provided they delivered up to him Q. Oppius governor of Pamphylia, who had fled thither for protection. This request was readily complied with; Oppius was sent to him in chains, with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LICTORS">lictors</a> walking before him in derision of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and ostentation. Mithridates was overjoyed to see a Roman general and proconsul in his power; and his joy was soon after increased by the arrival of Manius Aquilius, whom the Lesbians, revolting from the Romans, sent to him in fetters, together with many other Romans of distinction who had taken shelter among them. As he had been the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> author of the war, Mithridates led him about with him wherever he went, either bound on an ass, or on foot coupled with one Balternas a public malefactor, compelling him to proclaim to the crowds who came to see him, that he was Manius Aquilius the Roman legate. When he came to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a>, he caused him first to be publicly whipped, then to be put on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACK">rack</a>, and lastly melted gold death to be poured down his throat. Mithridates being now looked upon as invincible, all the free cities of Asia received him as their sovereign, contributing large sums towards the defraying the expenses of the war; by which means he became possessed of such treasures as enabled him to keep several numerous armies in the field for five years without levying any taxes on his subjects. As many Ro- Pontus. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> citizens were dispersed in the provinces which Mithridates had subdued, he considered these as so many spies who would not fail to send an account of his proceedings to Rome; for which reason he resolved to cut them all off at once by a general massacre; which barbarous policy, it is said, had never been heard of till his time, but has been since practised by other nations. He dispatched private letters to all the governors and magistrates of the cities where the Romans resided, enjoining them on pain of death, and the entire destruction of their country, to cause all the Italian <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a>, women and children not excepted, to be murdered on the 30th day from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a> of his letters, and to let their bodies <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> unburied in the open fields. One moiety of their goods was to be forfeited to the king, and the other bestowed as a reward on the assassins. Whatever slave murdered his master was to receive his liberty, and one half of the debt was to be remitted to the debtor that should kill his creditor. Whoever concealed an Italian, under any pretence whatever, was to be punished with immediate death. On the fatal day, all the gates of the cities being shut, and the avenues kept with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, the king's orders were proclaimed, which caused an universal horror, not only among the unhappy victims themselves, but among those who had any feelings of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, at seeing themselves obliged either to betray and murder their innocent guests, friends, and relations, or to become liable to a cruel death. However, as most of the Asiatics bore a mortal hatred to the Romans, and were moreover animated by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of an ample reward, the orders were without delay put into execution. The inhabitants of Ephesus, where Mithridates then resided, dragged such as had taken sanctuary in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> from the very statue of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, and put them to the sword. The Pergamenes discharged showers of darts upon them as they embraced the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> in the temple of Esculapius. At Adramyttium in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MYSIA">Mysia</a> many were murdered in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, while they were attempting, with their children on their backs, to swim over to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>. The Caunians, who not long before had been delivered from the yoke of the Rhodians, and restored to their ancient privileges, excelled all the rest in cruelty; for, as if they had apostatized from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, they took <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in tormenting and butchering the innocent children before their mothers' eyes; some of them running distracted, and others dying with grief at a sight which nature could not bear. The Trallians were the only people on the continent who could not have the cruelty to imbue their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> in the blood of the innocent Italians. However, as the king's orders were peremptory, they hired one Theophilus a Paphlagonian to dispatch the few Romans that lived among them. He, having shut them all up together in the temple of Concord, first cut off their hands as they embraced the statues of the gods, and then hacked them in pieces. Many Romans were saved on the floating <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Lydia called Calamine, where they concealed themselves till such time as they found an opportunity of escaping out of Asia. Nevertheless, according to Plutarch and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DION">Dion</a>, 150,000 Roman citizens were massacred on that day; but, according to others, only 80,000. Mithridates having now got rid of those whom he was in dread of on the continent, embarked great part of his forces in order to reduce the islands of the Archipelago. At Cos he was gladly received, and had delivered up to him the young Alexander, son of Alexander king of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, who, being driven out of Cos, that country, was killed by Charaxa, a sea-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> as he was retiring in a small vessel to Cyprus. With the young prince, they put into the king's hands vast sums of money, with all the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> vessels and jewels, to an immense value, which his grandmother Cleopatra had been amassing for many years. To the young prince Mithridates gave an education suitable for a king's son, but kept the treasures for himself. Here likewise he found 800 talents in ready money, which, at the first breaking out of the war, had been deposited by the Jews of Asia, and were designed for the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. From Cos Mithridates steered his course for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, where at that time all the Romans, who had escaped the massacre above-mentioned, found a sanctuary, and amongst others, L. Cassius the proconsul. The Rhodians, however, being very expert in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs, Mithridates did not think proper to venture an engagement. As the enemy's fleet advanced, therefore, he retired; but six of the Rhodian ships coming up with 25 of his, a sharp <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> ensued, in which the Rhodians sunk two of the king's ships, and put the rest to flight. In this encounter, though Mithridates had never seen a sea-fight before, he behaved with great intrepidity; but one of the ships of his own squadron falling foul of that which carried him, he was very near being taken prisoner. From this time forth he abhorred the sea, and took an aversion to all the Chians, because the pilot of that ship was a Chian. However, he again appeared before the island; but was forced anew to leave it with disgrace, and to give over all thoughts of reducing it. Mithridates now retired into Asia, with a design to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the civil <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the countries which he had conquered, committing the care of the war to his generals. Archelaus, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERALISSIMO">generalissimo</a>, was sent into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> with an army of 120,000 men; where, by treachery, he made himself master of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and either put to the sword or sent to Mithridates all those who favoured or were suspected to favour the Romans. From Athens he dispatched parties to reduce the neighbouring castles and the island of Delos, which they did accordingly; but Orobius, a Roman general, hearing that the enemy kept no guards, but passed their time in carousing and debauchery, fell upon them unexpectedly, and cut off the whole party, except Apellicon the comander. In the mean time, Metrophanes, another of the king's generals, entering Euboea, laid waste the whole country, exerting his rage chiefly against the cities of Demetrias and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNESIA">Magnesia</a>, which refused to open their gates to him. But as he was failing off with a great booty, Brytius, the praetor or governor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, coming up with him, sunk some of his ships, and took others, putting all the prisoners to the sword. Mithridates, upon the news of this loss, sent his son Ariarathes with a powerful army to invade Macedonia; which he soon reduced, together with the kingdom of Thrace, driving the Romans everywhere before him. The generals whom he sent into other Pontus, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> were no less successful; so that Mithridates had, according to Aulus Gellius, 25 different nations who paid him homage. The same author adds, that he was skilled in every one of their various languages, so that he could <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with the natives without an interpreter. Among these nations we find the Rhoxani, now the Russians or Muscovites, whom Deiphontes, one of the king's generals, brought under subjection, after having slain in an engagement 50,000 of the barbarians. All this time the Romans had been too much taken up with their own <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> quarrels to take such effectual <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> as they otherwise would have done for checking the progress of Mithridates. But at last, having received certain advice that the king designed to invade <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and that he had even been solicited to do so by some of the revolted Italians, they sent against him Lucius Sylla, who had already given sufficient proofs of his courage, conduct, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> in war. He had with him only five legions and a few cohorts. With this inconsiderable force he landed in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, and in a short time made himself master of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>; Archelaus not daring, or, according to others, through treachery, not caring to engage him. As Sylla had but a few frigates, he sent Lucullus to the island of Rhodes, with orders to the Rhodians to join him with their fleet. The undertaking was very dangerous, as the king's fleet in a manner covered the sea. However, Lucullus, despising all danger, ventured out, and sailed, without meeting with any perverse accident, to Syria, Egypt, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, and Cyprus; from whence he returned with such supplies of ships and experienced mariners, as enabled Sylla, after their conjunction with the Rhodians, to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> offensively by sea also. Archelaus now dispatched messengers to Taxiles, who commanded in Thrace and Macedon, desiring him to join him with all his forces; which the other readily did, and between both mustered an army of 120,000 men. Sylla met them near Cheronea, with only 15,000 foot and 1500 horse; but gave them a most dreadful overthrow, no fewer than 110,000 of the Asiatics being slaughtered, while the Romans lost only 12 men. This success having raised envy and jealousy against Sylla in Rome, the senate sent Lucius Valerius Flaccus, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> of that year, with two legions into Asia, in appearance to attack Mithridates on that side, but with private instructions to fall upon Sylla himself, if they found him dilated against the senate. As Flaccus was a man of no experience in war, C. Fimbria, a senator of great repute among the soldiery, was appointed to attend him with the character of legate and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general. Sylla was at that time in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>; but, hearing what had happened at Rome, he marched with all expedition into Thessaly, with a design to meet Flaccus, who, he expected, was to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. But no sooner had he left Boeotia, than the country was overrun by an army of Asiatics, under the command of Dorylaus the king's chief favourite. On this advice Sylla returned into Boeotia, where he gained two signal victories, which put an end to the war in Greece. In the first of these Dorylaus lost 15,000 of his men according to some, or 200,000 according to others; and in the next all the rest. In this last engagement 20,000 were driven into a river, Pontus, where they all perished; an equal number were pursued into a marsh, and entirely cut off; the rest were killed in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, the Romans giving no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> to men who had treated their fellow-citizens after such a barbarous manner in Asia. Plutarch tells us, that the marshes were dyed with blood; that the course of the river was stopped by the dead bodies; and that even in his time, that is, near 200 years after, a great number of bows, helmets, coats of mail, and swords, were found buried in the mud. Archelaus, who had joined Dorylaus with a body of 10,000 men a few days before the battle, lay three days stripped among the slain till he found a small vessel which carried him to Euboea, where he gathered what forces he could, but was never again able to appear in the field. Indeed Livy tells us, that Archelaus betrayed the king's cause; and Aurelius Victor, that the king's fleet was intercepted by Sylla through the treachery of Archelaus: adding, that there was a good understanding between these two commanders, as was plain from Sylla's bestowing upon Archelaus 10,000 acres of land near the city of Chalcis in Euboea. Strabo also informs us, that Archelaus was afterwards greatly esteemed and cared for by Sylla and the senate; but Sylla himself in his commentaries, and Dio, endeavour to clear Archelaus from all suspicion of treachery. In the mean time, Sylla having given up Boeotia to be plundered by his soldiers, marched into Thessaly, where he took up his winter-quarters, caused his old ships to be refitted and several new ones built, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over into Asia in the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, that he might drive from thence not only Mithridates but his rival Flaccus also, whom the senate, out of opposition to him, had appointed governor of that province. But before he arrived, some differences having arisen between Flaccus and Fimbria, the latter was by the consul deprived of his command. Up-Fimbria on this Fimbria, having gained over the soldiery to put Flaccus his side, made war on the consul, took him prisoner, put him to death, and assumed the command of all the Roman forces in Asia. In this station he behaved with the greatest cruelty, insomuch that his name became more odious than even that of Mithridates itself. This hatred the king of Pontus endeavoured to improve to his own advantage; and therefore commanded his son, by name also Mithridates, to join Taxiles, Diophantes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MENANDER">Menander</a>, three of his most experienced commanders, to return at the head of a numerous army into Asia; not doubting, but the inhabitants, thus harassed by Fimbria, would shake off the Roman yoke when they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> such a powerful army in the field ready to protect them. But Fimbria, distrusting the Asiatics, marched out to meet the enemy, and offered them battle before they entered the province. As the king's army was greatly superior to the Romans in number, the latter suffered greatly in the engagement, but held out till night parted them, when they withdrew to the opposite side of a river, which was at a small distance from the field of battle. Here they designed to intrench themselves; but in the mean time a violent storm arising, Fimbria laid hold of that opportunity to repulse the Pontus. the river and surprise the enemy; of whom he made such havoc as they lay in their tents, that only the commanders and some few troops of horse escaped. Among these was the king's son; who, attended by a few horse, got safe to Pergamus, where his father resided. But Fimbria, pursuing him night and day without intermission, entered Pergamus sword in hand; and hearing that both Mithridates and his son had fled from thence a few hours before, he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his pursuit, and would have taken the king himself, had he not entered Pitane with a considerable body of horse. The place was closely invested by Fimbria; but as he had no ships to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> it up by sea also, he sent a messenger to Lucullus, who commanded the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> in Asia, intreating him, as he tendered the welfare of the republic, to make what haste he could to Pitane, and assist him in taking the most inveterate enemy the Romans had. But Lucullus, preferring the gratification of a private pique to the good of his country, refused to come; and thus allowed the fleet of Mithridates to carry him in safety to Mitylene. Soon after the king's departure Fimbria took Pitane by storm, and reduced most of the cities of Asia, particularly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, which he took by storm in eleven days, and put most of the inhabitants to the sword, because they had sent an embassy to Sylla, offering to submit to him rather than to Fimbria.—To add to the misfortunes of Mithridates, his fleet was entirely defeated in two engagements by Lucullus; so that he began to be weary of the war, and therefore desired Archelaus to conclude a peace upon as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> terms as he could. The king himself had afterwards also a conference with Sylla, and a peace was concluded in 85 B.C. on the following terms, viz. That Mithridates should relinquish all his conquests, and content himself with his paternal dominions which were confined within the limits of Pontus: that he should immediately resign Bithynia to Nicomedes, and Cappadocia to Ariobarzanes, and release without ransom all the prisoners he had taken during the war: that he should pay to the Romans 2000, or as others will have it 3000 talents, and deliver up to Sylla 80 ships with all their arms and ammunition, and 500 archers; and lastly, that he should not molest such cities or persons as had during the war revolted to him and sided with the Romans. Sylla, having thus concluded the war with great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> to himself and advantage to the republic, turned his army against Fimbria; but the latter, finding himself in no condition to oppose his rival by force, had recourse to treachery, and attempted to get Sylla murdered. The plot miscarried, and Fimbria put an end to his own life; upon which Sylla, having now an uncontroled power in Asia, declared the Chians, Rhodians, Lycians, Magnesians, and Trojans, free, and friends of the people of Rome, by way of reward for their having sided with the Romans: but on the other cities he laid heavy fines; condemning them in one year to pay 20,000 talents, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERING">quartering</a> his soldiers in the houses of those who had shewn disaffection to the Romans. Each private man was to receive of his landlord 16 drachmas a day, and each officer 50; and besides, both were to be supplied with provisions, not only for themselves, but for such of their friends as they thought proper to invite. By these impositions most of the people of Asia were reduced to beggary; especially the inhabitants of Ephesus, who had above all others shown their hatred to the Romans. Sylla then, having collected immense treasures, set sail for Italy; leaving behind him Lucullus with the character of quaestor, and Muræna with that of praetor.
