Sedochus at first refused to deliver him up to the Romans; but was soon prevailed upon, partly by threats, partly by presents, to surrender both him and all the other fugitives who had taken sanctuary in his dominions. Thus ended that servile war; and the kingdom of Pontus continued to be a province of the empire till the time of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALEXIS">Alexis</a> Comneni, who being driven from Constantinople by the French and Venetians, under the command of Baldwin <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, settled, the one at Haraclea, the other at Trebifond. The troubles that arose among the Latins gave Alexus Commenus an opportunity of erecting here a new empire, which comprehended great part of Pontus, and was known by the name of the empire of Trebifond. The Comneni held it about 250 years, till the time of Mohamed II., who carried David Commenus, the last emperor of Trebifond, prisoner to Constantinople, with all his family, and subjected his empire to that of Constantinople; in which abject slavery Trebifond and all Pontus have continued ever since.

PONTYPOOL

Pages 70-70

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a> in England, seated between two hills. It is but a small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, though noted for its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> manufacture of japanned mugs, &c. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 3. c. N. Lat. 51. 45.

PONZA

Pages 70-70
or PONTIA, a small island in the Tuscan sea, being the place to which many illustrious Romans were formerly banished. E. Long, 13. 50. N. Lat. 41. 15.

POOL

Pages 70-70

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a> in England. It is surrounded on all sides by the sea, except on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, where there is an entrance through a gate. It was formerly nothing but a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where a few fishermen lived: but in the reign of Henry VI. it was greatly enlarged, and the inhabitants had the privilege to wall it round; it was also made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of itself, and sent two members to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It is governed by a mayor, a senior <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, four other justices, and an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of burgesses. The town consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and about 600 houses, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> paved streets; and has a manufactory of knit hose. It is 47 miles west south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, and 110 west by south of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 6. N. Lat. 50. 45.

POOLE

Pages 70-70

a very learned writer in the 17th century, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a> in 1624. He was educated at Emanuel-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and afterwards incorporated in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. He succeeded Dr Anthony Tuckney in the rectory of St Michael de Quern, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, about 1648. In 1658 he set on foot a project for maintaining youths of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> parts at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and had the approbation of the heads of houses in both of them. He solicited the affair with so much vigour, that in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> good per annum was procured for that purpose; but this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was laid aside at the Restoration. In 1662, he was ejected from his living for nonconformity. Ten years was he employed in composing his Synopsis Criticorum Bibliorum. Besides this great <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> he published several other pieces. When Dr Oates's depositions concerning the Popish plot were printed, our author found his name in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of those who were to be cut off, on the account (as was supposed) of what he had written against the Papists in his Nullity of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a>. So that he was obliged to retire into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where he died in 1679, and left behind him the character of a very able critic and casuist.

POPAYAN

Pages 71-71

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of that name in South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, with a bishop's see, a Spanish governor, and where the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> are held. The inhabitants are almost all Creoles. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 73° 5' N. Lat. 2° 25'.

POPE

Pages 71-73

a late celebrated English poet, was descended from good families, and born the 8th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1688, at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where his father was then a considerable merchant. He was taught to read very early by an aunt; and learned to write without any assistance, by copying printed books. The family being of the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, he was put, at eight years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, under one Taverner, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, who taught him the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the Latin and Greek tongues together; and soon after was sent to a Popish seminary at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, from whence he was removed to a school at Hyde-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARK">Park</a> Corner. He discovered early an inclination to versifying; and the translations of Ogilby and Sandys from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> and Ovid first falling in his way, these were his favourite authors. At 12, he retired with his parents to Binfield, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> Forest; and there became acquainted with the writings of Spenser, Waller, and Dryden. Dryden struck him most, probably because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of that poet was most congenial with his own; and therefore he not only studied his works intensely, but ever after mentioned him with a kind of rapturous veneration. He once obtained a sight of him at a coffee-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, but never was known to him: a misfortune which he laments in these pathetic words, *Virgilium tantum vidi.* Though Pope had been under more tutors than one, yet it seems they were so insufficient for the purpose of teaching, that he had learned very little from them: so that, being obliged afterwards to begin all over again, he may justly be considered as one of the *autoctonus,* <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> "self-taught." At 15 he had acquired a readiness in the two learned languages; to which he soon after added the French and Italian. He had already scribbled a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> in various ways; and this year set about an epic poem, called *Alexander.* He <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after communicated it to Atterbury, with a declared intention to burn it; and that friend concurred with him: "Though (adds he) I would have interceded for the first page, and put it, with your leave, among my curiosities." What the poet himself observes upon these early pieces is agreeable enough; and shows, that tho' at first a little intoxicated with the waters of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HELICON">Helicon</a>, he afterwards arrived to great sobriety of thinking. "I confess (says he) there was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> when I was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with myself; and my first productions were the children of Self-love upon Innocence. I had made an epic poem, and panegyrics on all the princes, and I thought myself the greatest genius that ever was. I cannot but regret these delightful visions of my childhood, which, like the fine colours we see when our eyes are shut, are vanished for ever." His pastorals, begun in 1704, first introduced him to the wits of the time; among which were Wycherly and Walsh. This last <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> proved a sincere friend to him; and soon discovering that his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> lay, not so much in striking out new thoughts of his own, as in improving those of other men, and in an easy versification, told him, among other things, that there was one way left open for him to excel his predecessors in, which was correctness: observing, that though we had several great poets, yet none of them were correct. Pope took the hint, and turned it to good account; for no doubt the distinguishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of his numbers was in a great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> owing to it. The same year, 1704, he wrote the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his Windsor Forest, though the whole was not published till 1710. In 1708, he wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Criticism: which production was justly esteemed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-piece in its kind, and showed not only the peculiar turn of his talents, but that those talents, young as he was, were ripened into perfection. He was not yet 20 years old; and yet the maturity of judgment, the knowledge of the world, and the penetration into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, displayed in that piece, were such as would have done <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the greatest abilities and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. But whatever may be the merit of the Essay on Criticism, it was still surpassed, in a poetical view, by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAPE">Rape</a> of the Lock, first completely published in 1712. The former excelled in the didactic way, for which he was peculiarly formed; a clear head, strong <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> judgment, being his characteristic qualities: but it is the creative power of the imagination that constitutes what is properly called a poet; and therefore it is in the Rape of the Lock that Pope principally appears one, there being more *vis imaginandi* displayed in this poem than perhaps in all his other works put together. In 1713, he gave out proposals for publishing a translation of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s Iliad, by subscription; in which all parties concurred so heartily, that he acquired a considerable fortune by it. The subscription amounted to 6000l. besides 1200l. which Lintot the bookseller gave him for the copy. Pope's finances being now in good condition, he purchased a house at Twickenham, whither he removed with his father and mother in 1715: where the former died about two years after. As he was a Papist, he could not purchase, nor put his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> on real security; and as he adhered to the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> James, he made it a point of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> not to lend it to the new <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>: so that, though he was worth near 20,000l. when he laid aside business, yet, living afterwards upon the quick stock, he left but a slender substance to his family. Our poet, however, did not fail to improve it to the utmost: he had already acquired much by his publications, and he was all <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to acquire more. In 1717, he published a collection of all he had printed separately; and proceeded to give a new edition of Shakespeare, which, being published in 1721, discovered that he had consulted his fortune more than his fame in that undertaking. The Iliad being finished, he engaged upon the like footing to undertake the Odyssey. Mr Broome and Mr Fenton did part of it, and received 500l. of Mr Pope for their labours. It was published in the same manner, and on the same conditions to Lintot; excepting that, instead of 1200l., he had but 600l. for the copy. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> being finished in 1725, he was afterwards employed with Swift and Arbuthnot in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> some volumes of Miscellanies. About this time he narrowly escaped losing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, as he was returning home in a friend's chariot; which, on passing a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, happened to be overturned, and thrown with the horses into the river. The glasses were up, and he not able to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> them; so that he had immediately been drowned, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the poilion had not broke them, and dragged him out to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a>. A fragment of the glass, however, cut him so desperately, that he ever after lost the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of two of his fingers. In 1727, his Dunciad appeared in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; and the year after in England, with notes by Swift, under the name of Scriblerus. This edition was presented to the king and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> by Sir Robert Walpole; who, probably about this time, offered to procure Pope a pension, which however he refused, as he had formerly done a proposal of the same kind made him by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>. He greatly cultivated the spirit of independence; and "Unplac'd, unpension'd, no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s heir or slave," was frequently his boast. He somewhere observes, that the life of an author is a state of warfare: he has shown himself a complete general in this way of warring. He bore the insults and injuries of his enemies long; but at length, in the Dunciad, made an absolutely universal slaughter of them: for even Cibber, who was afterwards advanced to be the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of it, could not forbear owning, that nothing was ever more perfect and finished in its kind than this poem. In 1729, by the advice of Lord Bolingbroke, he turned his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a> to subjects of morality; and accordingly we find him, with the assistance of that noble friend, who furnished him with the materials, at work this year upon the Essay on Man. The following extract of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Swift discovers the reason of Lordship's advice: "Bid him (says Bolingbroke) talk to you of the work he is about, I hope, in good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a>; it is a fine one, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be, in his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, an original. His sole complaint is, that he finds it too easy in the execution. This flatters his laziness; it flatters my judgment; who always thought, that, universal as his talents are, this is eminently and peculiarly his, above all the writers I know, living or dead; I do not except Horace. Pope tells the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> in the next letter, that "the work, Lord Bolingbroke speaks of with such abundant partiality, is a system of ethics, in the Horatian way." In pursuing the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, he wrote his Ethic Epistles: the fourth of which, Upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">Taste</a>, giving great offence, as he was supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Chandos under the character of Timon, is said to have put him upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> satires, which he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till 1739. He ventured to attack persons of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and set no bounds to his satirical rage. A genuine collection of his letters was published in 1737. In 1738, a French translation of the Essay on Man, by the Abbé Refnel, was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; and Mr Crousaz, a German professor, animadverted upon this system of ethics, which he represented as nothing else but a system of naturalism. Mr Warburton, afterwards bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> upon the Essay; in which he defends it against Crousaz, whose objections he supposes owing to the faults of the Abbé Refnel's translation. The poem was republished in 1740, with the commentary. Our author now added a fourth book to the Dunciad, which was first printed separately in 1742; but the year after, the whole poem came out together, as a specimen of a more correct edition of his works. He had made some progress in that design, but did not live to complete it. He had all his life long been subject to the head-ach; and that complaint, which he derived from his mother, was now greatly increased by a drop in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, under which he expired the 30th of May 1744, in the 56th year of his age. In his will, dated <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 12, 1743, Miss Blount, a lady to whom he was always devoted, was made his heir during her life: and among other legacies, he bequeathed to Mr Warburton the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of all such of his works, already printed, as he had written or should write commentaries upon, and had not otherwise been disposed of or alienated; with this condition, that they were published without future alterations. In discharge of this trust, that gentleman gave a complete edition of all Mr Pope's works, 1751, in 9 vols., 8vo. A work, entitled, An Essay on the Writings and Genius of Pope, by Mr Warton, 2 vols., 8vo, will be read with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> by those who desire to know more of the person, character, and writings of this excellent poet. In the meantime, the following account of him by Lord <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORRERY">Orrery</a> may suffice: "If we may judge of him by his works, (says this noble author) his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> aim was to be esteemed a man of virtue. His letters are written in that style; his last volumes are all of the moral kind; he has avoided trifles, and consequently has escaped a rock which has proved very injurious to Swift's reputation. He has given his imagination full scope, and yet has preserved a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> upon his conduct. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of his body and mind might really incline him to the habits of caution and reserve. The treatment which he met with afterwards, from an innumerable tribe of adversaries, confirmed this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; and made him slower than the dean, in pronouncing his judgment upon persons and things. His prose-writings are little less harmonious than his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; and his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> conversation, was so naturally musical, that I remember honest Tom Southern used to call him the little nightingale. His manners were delicate, easy, and engaging; and he treated his friends with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> that charmed, and a generosity that was much to his honour. Every guest was made happy within his doors; pleasure dwelt under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, and elegance presided at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>." Pope's Dominions, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> States; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the gulph of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> and the Venetian dominions, on the south by the Mediterranean, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> and the Adriatic, and on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>. Its length is about 240 miles, but its breadth varies from 20 to 120 miles. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, in general, of the pope's dominions is very fertile, but ill cultivated; and there are many fens and marshy grounds, which are very prejudicial to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. That the lands are badly cultivated and inhabited, the air bad, and the inhabitants <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, idle, lazy, and grossly superstitious, is owing to their being governed by priests, who may justly be said not only to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a> them, but fleecing them. This country, with respect to the accommodations of life, is but in a very indifferent condition; for, notwithstanding the fertility of its soil, its advantageous situation for traffic, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums spent in it by travellers, or remitted to it from foreign countries, and its having, for its ruler, the successor of St <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the apostles, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, yet it is poor and thin of inhabitants, ill cultivated, and without trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. This is partly owing to the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of holidays, of sturdy beggars called pilgrims, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, with the amazing but useless wealth of churches and convents, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>; but the chief cause is the severity of the government, and the grievous exactions and hardships to which the subjects are exposed. The legates, tho' mostly clergymen, whose thoughts should be chiefly employed about laying up treasures in heaven, and who ought to set an example to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> of disinterestedness and a contempt of this world, yet, in fact, scruple no kind of rapaciousness: even the holy father himself, and the cardinals, make the enriching of their nephews and other relations, and the aggrandizing their families, the great business of their lives. The extravagant claims and pretensions of the pope are well known, and by all the rational part of Christendom now treated with contempt and mockery. The Reformation gave a great blow to his spiritual power; but as to his temporal dominions, he still possesses them entire; tho' it is not likely that will long be the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, considering how much he hath lost, and is daily losing, of his ghostly empire, and the veneration in which he was formerly held. The Papal dominions were originally procured, partly by the voluntary gift of bigotted princes, and partly by other methods. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> of Rome is under the pope's immediate government; but the other provinces are governed by legates and vice-legates, and there is a commander-in-chief of the pope's forces in every <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. The pope is chosen by the cardinals in the conclave, who are 70 in number when complete, and consist of three classes, namely, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, priests, and deacons: they look upon themselves as on a footing with crowned heads, and have the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of eminentissimi. The pope holds a confessor of cardinals on ecclesiastical affairs; but the cardinals do not meddle with his civil government. The pope's chief minister is the cardinal-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, usually his nephew, who amasses an immense estate, if the reign be of any long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. The cardinal that is chosen pope must be an Italian, and at least 55 years of age. The spiritual power of the pope, though far short of what it was before the Reformation, is still considerable. It is computed that the monks and regular clergy, who are absolutely at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, do not amount to less than 2,000,000 of people dispersed through all the Roman Catholic countries, to assert his supremacy over princes, and promote the interest of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The revenues of these monks do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> short of L. 20,000,000 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>, besides the casual profits arising from offerings, and the people's bounty to the church, who are taught that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> depends on this kind of benevolence. The pope's revenues, as a temporal prince, may amount to about L. 15,000,000 Sterling per annum, arising chiefly from the monopoly of corn, the duties on wine and other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. Over and above these, vast sums are continually flowing into the papal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> from all the Roman Catholic countries, for dispensations, indulgences, canonizations, annates, the pallia, and investitures of archbishops, bishops, &c. The pope has a considerable body of regular forces, well clothed and paid; but his fleet consists only of a few galleys. His life-guards are 40 Switzers, 75 cuirassiers, and as many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>.

POPHAM

Pages 73-73
lord chief justice of the common pleas in the reign of queen Elizabeth, was the eldest son of Edward Popham, esq., of Huntworth in Somersetshire, and born in the year 1531. He was some time a student of Balliol college in Oxford; "being then," says Ant. Wood, "given at leisure hours to many sports and exercises." After quitting the university, he fixed in the Middle Temple; where, during his novitiate, he is said to have indulged in that kind of dissipation to which youth and a vigorous constitution more naturally incline than to the study of voluminous reports: but, fatigued at length with what are called the pleasures of the town, he applied sedulously to the study of his profession, was called to the bar, and in 1568 became summer or autumn reader. He was soon after made serjeant at law, and solicitor-general in 1579. In 1581, he was appointed attorney-general, and treasurer of the Middle Temple. In 1592, he was made lord chief justice of the king's bench, and the same year received the honour of knighthood. In the year 1601, his lordship was one of the council detained by the unfortunate earl of Essex, when he formed the ridiculous project of defending himself in his house; and, on the earl's trial, he gave evidence against him relative to their detention. He died in the year 1607, aged 76; and was buried in the south aisle of the church at Wellington in Somersetshire, where he generally resided as often as it was in his power to retire. He was thought somewhat severe in the execution of the law against capital offenders; but his severity had the happy effect of reducing the number of highway robbers. He wrote, 1. Reports and cases adjudged in the time of queen Elizabeth. 2. Resolutions and judgments upon cases and matters agitated in all the courts at Westminster in the latter end of queen Elizabeth.

POPLITEUS

Pages 73-73

in anatomy, a small muscle obliquely pyramidal, situated under the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAM">ham</a>. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

POPLUS

Pages 73-74

the poplar; a genus of the ocotandra order, belonging to the dioecia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">Species</a>. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> abele-tree, grows naturally in the temperate parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Its leaves are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. Populus, large, and divided into three, four, or five lobes, indented on their edges, of a very dark <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> on their upper side, but very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and downy on the under side; standing upon footstalks an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. The young branches have a purple bark, and are covered with a white <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; but the bark of the stem and older branches is grey. In the beginning of April, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> or catkins appear, which are cylindrical, and about three inches long. About a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> after come out the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> flowers on catkins, which have no stamina like those of the male. Soon after these come out, the male catkins <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off; and in five or six weeks after, the female flowers <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have ripe seeds inclosed in a hairy covering. The catkins will then drop, and the seeds be wafted by the winds to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, or white poplar, has its leaves rounder than the first, and not much above half their size; they are indented on their edges, and are downy on their under side, but not so white as those of the former, nor are their upper surfaces of such a deep green colour. 3. The nigra, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> poplar, has oval heart-shaped leaves, slightly crenated on their edges; they are smooth on both sides, and of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> green colour. 4. The tremula, or aspen-tree, has roundish, angularly-Indented leaves: they are smooth on both sides, and stand on long footstalks; so are shaken by the least <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; from whence it has the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the trembling poplar, or aspen-tree. 5. The balsamifera, or Carolina poplar, is a native of Carolina, where it becomes a large tree. The shoots of this sort grow very strong in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and are generally angular; with a light green bark like the willow. The leaves on young trees, and also those on the lower shoots, are very large, almost heart-shaped and crenated; but those upon the older trees are smaller: as the trees advance, their bark becomes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>, approaching to a greyish colour. 6. The tacamahaca grows naturally in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. This is a tree of a middling growth, sending out on every side many short thick shoots, which are covered with a light <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> bark, garnished with leaves differing from one another in shape and size; most of them are almost heart-shaped; but some are oval, and others nearly spear-shaped; they are whitish on their under side, but green on their upper. Culture. These trees may be propagated either by layers or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>, as also from suckers which the white poplars send up from their roots in great plenty. The best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> for transplanting these suckers is in October, when their leaves begin to decay. These may be placed in a nursery for two or three years to get strength before they are planted out where they <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to remain; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are propagated from cuttings, it is better to defer the doing of that until February, at which time truncheons of two or three feet long should be thrust about a foot and a half into the ground. These will readily take root; and if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in which they are planted be moist, they will arrive at a considerable bulk in a few years. The black poplar is less apt to take root from large truncheons; therefore it is a better method to plant cuttings of it about a foot and a half in length, thrusting them a foot deep in the ground. This sort will grow almost on any soil, but will thrive best in moist places. The Carolina poplar may also be propagated by cuttings or layers; but the last is the method generally practised, and the plants raised by it are less moist than others. The shoots of this tree while young are frequently killed down to a considerable length by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a> in winter; but as the trees grow older, their shoots are not so vigorous, and become more ligneous, so are not liable to the same disaster. But the trees should be planted in a sheltered situation; for, as their leaves are very large, the wind has great power over them; and the branches being tender, they are frequently broken or split by the winds in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, when they are much exposed. The tacamahaca sends up a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of suckers from its roots, by which it multiplies in plenty, and every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> which is planted will take root. Uses. The wood of these trees, especially of the abele, is good for laying floors, where it will last for many years; and on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> whiteness is by many preferred to oak; yet, on account of its soft contexture, being very subject to take the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of nails, &c., it is less proper on this account than the harder woods. The inner bark of the black poplar is used by the inhabitants of Kamtchatka as a material for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> has sometimes been made of the cottony down of the seeds. The roots have been observed to dissolve into a kind of gelatinous substance, and to be coated over with a tubular crustaceous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>, called by naturalists gneocolla, formerly imagined to have some virtue in producing the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALCULUS">calculus</a> of a fractured bone. The buds of the fifth species are covered with a glutinous resin which smells very strong, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a> tacamahaca of the shops. The best, called, from its being collected in a kind of gourd-shells, tacamahaca in shells, is somewhat unctuous and softish, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> yellowish or greenish colour, an aromatic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and a fragrant delightful smell, approaching to that of lavender or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a>. This sort is very rare; that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> found in the shops is in semitransparent globes or grains, of a whitish, yellowish, brownish, or greenish colour, of a less grateful smell than the foregoing. This resin is said to be employed externally by the Indians, for dissolving and maturing tumours, and abating pains in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>. It is an ingredient in some anodyne, hypnotic, cephalic, and stomachic plasters; but the fragrance of the finer sort sufficiently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out its being applicable for other purposes.

PORCELAIN

Pages 74-79

a fine kind of earthen <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, chiefly manufactured in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, and thence called China-ware. All earthen wares which are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and semi-transparent are generally called porcelains; but amongst these, so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> differences may be observed, that notwithstanding the similarity of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance, they cannot be considered as matters of the same kind. These differences are so evident, that even persons who are not connoisseurs in this way prefer much the porcelain of some countries to that of others. The art of making porcelain is one of those in which <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> has been excelled by oriental nations. The first porcelain that was seen in Europe was brought from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> and China. The whiteness, transparency, fineness, neatness, elegance, and even the magnificence of this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a>, which soon became the ornament of sumptuous tables, did not fail to excite the admiration Porcelain. ration and industry of Europeans; and their attempts have succeeded so well, that in different parts of Europe, earthen wares have been made so like the oriental that they have acquired the name of porcelain. The first European porcelains were made in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> and in France; and afterwards in England, Germany, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; but as all these were different from the Japanese, so each of them had its peculiar character. The illustrious Reaumur first attended to the manufacture of porcelain as a science, and communicated his researches in two <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> before the Academy of Sciences in 1727 and 1729. He did not satisfy himself with considering the external appearance, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and gilding, which are only ornaments not essential to the porcelain, but he endeavoured to examine it internally: and having broken pieces of the Japanese, Saxon, and French porcelains, he examined the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of their grains (which name is given to their internal structure). The grain of the Japanese Porcelain appeared to him to be fine, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, moderately smooth, and somewhat shining. The grain of the Saxon porcelain was found to be still more compact, not granulous, smooth, shining like enamel. Lastly, the porcelain of St Cloud had a grain much less close and fine than that of Japan; nor, but little, shining; and resembling the grain of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. From these first observations Mr Reaumur perceived that porcelains differed considerably. That he might examine them further, he exposed them to a violent <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. More essential differences than those of the grain appeared upon this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>; for the Japanese porcelain was unaltered by the fire, and all the European were melted. This essential difference betwixt the Japanese and European porcelains suggested to Mr Reaumur a very ingenious thought, and in many respects true, concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of porcelain in general. As all porcelains somewhat resemble glass in consistence and transparency, though they are less compact and much less transparent, Mr Reaumur considered them as semivitrifications. But every substance may appear, and may actually be, in a semivitrified state in two ways: for, first, it may be entirely composed of vitrifiable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> fusible matters; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> it to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of fire, it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be actually melted or vitrified, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the heat be sufficiently strong and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>. But as this change is not made instantly, especially when the heat is not very violent; and as it passes through different stages or degrees, which may be more easily observed as the heat is better managed; hence, by stopping in proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the application of heat to porcelain made in this manner, we may obtain it in an intermediate state betwixt those of crude earths and of completely vitrified substances, and also possessed of the semitransparency and of the other sensible qualities of porcelain. We know also, that if such porcelain be exposed to a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fire, it will then be completely fused and entirely vitrified. But the European porcelains tried by Mr Reaumur had this fusibility; from which he concluded, that their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is founded upon the abovementioned principle. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, a paste of porcelain may be composed of fusible and vitrifiable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, mixed with a certain proportion of another matter which is absolutely unfusible in the fires of our furnaces. We may easily perceive, that if such a mixture be exposed to a heat sufficient to melt entirely the vitrifiable ingredient, that this matter will actually melt; but as it is intermixed with another matter which does not melt, and which consequently preserves its consistence and opacity, the whole must form a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> partly opake and partly transparent; or rather a semitransparent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>; that is, a semi-vitrified substance, or porcelain, but of a kind very different from the former; for as the fusible <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of this latter has produced all its effect, and as it has been as much fused as it can be during the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAKING">baking</a> of the porcelain, the compound may be exposed a second time to a more violent fire, without approaching nearer to a complete vitrification, or without departing from its state of porcelain. But as oriental porcelain has precisely these appearances and properties, Mr Reaumur concludes with reason, that it is composed upon this principle; and he afterwards confirmed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> by undeniable facts. Father Entrecelles, missionary at China, had sent from thence a summary <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> by which the inhabitants of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> make their porcelain, and also a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the materials which they employ in its composition. He said that the Chinese composed their porcelain of two ingredients; one of which is a hard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or rock, called by them petuntse, which they carefully grind to a very fine powder; and the other, called by them kaolin, is a white, earthy substance, which they mix intimately with the ground petuntse. Mr Reaumur examined both these matters, and having exposed them separately to a violent fire, he discovered that the petuntse had fused without addition, and that the kaolin had given no sign of fusibility. He afterwards mixed these matters, and formed cakes of them, which by baking were converted into porcelain similar to that of China. Mr Reaumur easily found, that the petuntse of the Chinese was a hard stone of the kind called vitrifiable, but much more fusible than any of those which were known in Europe; and that the kaolin was a talc matter, reduced to a very fine powder. From that time he hoped to make a porcelain of the same kind as the Chinese with materials found in France. Whether he could not find any materials equal to those of China, particularly that material analogous to the petuntse of the Chinese, or because other occupations prevented the continuance of his researches, we do not know; but we find, from his second memoir upon porcelain, that he afterwards attempted to make an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> petuntse, by mixing our vitrifiable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> with salts capable of rendering them fusible, or even by substituting for it glass ready formed, and by adding to these such substances as he thought might be substituted for kaolin. But he probably found he could not execute these intentions; for he did not resume this subject from the year 1729 to 1730, when he gave a report by process for converting <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> glass to a singular kind into a kind of porcelain, to which he has given his name, and of which an account is given under the article <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, No. 92. Although Mr Reaumur has surmounted many difficulties, and has given <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> notions concerning this subject, yet he has been mistaken, or rather misled, in particular, two important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. His first <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> concerns the Saxon Porcelain. Saxon porcelain, which he confounds with the other fusible porcelains made in Europe. Formerly, indeed, a porcelain might be made in Saxony, composed entirely of fusible or vitrifiable materials, the vitrification of which was stopped in proper time, and which Mr Reaumur had examined. But now we are certainly informed, that all of that country is capable of resisting the most violent fires without fusion, as well, at least, as those of China and Japan. Mr Reaumur might have been misled by the appearance of the internal texture of this porcelain. For when a piece of it is broken, its internal surface does not appear granulous, but compact, uniform, smooth, shining, and much resembling white enamel. But this appearance, so far from showing that Saxon porcelain is a fused or vitrified substance, proves that it is not entirely composed of fusible matters. All who have considered attentively this subject know, that the internal surface of the most fusible porcelains is also the least dense and least compact; the reason of which is, that no vitreous matter can be smooth and dense internally, unless it has been completely fused. But if the density and shining appearance of the internal surface of the Saxon porcelain were only the effects of the fusion of a vitreous matter, how could we conceive that vessels formed of that matter should have sustained the necessary fusion for giving this density and shining appearance, without having entirely lost their shape? The impossibility of this is evident to any persons who have been conversant in these matters and in the fusion of glazes. This <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the Saxon porcelain must therefore, proceed from another cause. It does indeed contain, as every porcelain does, particularly those of China and Japan, a fusible substance, which has been even completely fused during the baking. Its density also and its internal lustre proceed chiefly from this fused matter: but we are also certain, that it contains a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of a substance absolutely unfusible, from which it receives its admirable whiteness, its firmness and solidity, during the baking; in a word, which supplies the place of the oriental kaolin, and which has the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of contracting its dimensions considerably while it incorporates with the fusible substance. If it be subjected to the most decisive trial, namely, the action of a violent fire, capable of melting every porcelain composed of fusible matters alone, Chem. Diff. "I affirm," says Mr Macquer, "after many experiments, that it cannot be fused, unless by a fire capable also of melting the best Japanese porcelain." The Saxon porcelain is therefore not to be confounded with those which are vitreous and fusible; but is in its kind as excellent as that of Japan, and perhaps superior, as we shall see when we enumerate the qualities which constitute the excellence of porcelain. The subject of Mr Reaumur's second error, or at least that which he has not sufficiently explained, is the kaolin of China. According to him, this matter is a fine talc powder, from the mixture of which with petuntse the oriental porcelain is formed. Possibly a very finely-ground talc substance mixed with petuntse might form a porcelain similar to the oriental; but persons acquainted with the manufacture of any porcelain, must perceive the impossibility of forming vessels, unless the paste of which they are made be so ductile and tenacious, that it may be worked upon a potter's lathe, or at least that it may be moulded. But talc, porcelain, or any kinds of stones, however finely-ground, cannot acquire the requisite tenacity, which clays only, of all known earthy substances, possess. The Chinese porcelain vessels evidently appear to be turned upon the lathe, since they retain the marks of it; hence they must have been formed of a very tenacious paste, and consequently the kaolin is not a purely talc matter, but is mixed with clay; or else the petuntse and kaolin are not, as Mr Reaumur supposes, the only ingredients of the paste of which Chinese porcelain is formed, but a sufficient quantity of some binding matter, unknown to father d'Entrecolles and Mr Reaumur, must be also added. Although, since Mr Reaumur, no scientific person has written concerning porcelain, many have attempted to make it. Manufactories have been established in almost all the states of Europe. Besides that of Saxony, which has been long established, porcelain is also made at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, at Frankendal, and lately in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>. All these German porcelains are similar to the Saxon; and are made of materials of the same kind, although they differ somewhat from each other. England and Italy also have their porcelains, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which are those of Chelsea and of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. Mr de la Condamine, in his last journey into Italy, visited a manufacture of porcelain established at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> by the marquis de la Ginori, then governor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>. Mr de la Condamine observed particularly the large size of some pieces of this porcelain. He says he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and groups half as large as nature, modelled from some of the finest antiques. The furnaces in which the porcelain was baked were constructed with much art, and lined with bricks made of the porcelain materials. The paste of this porcelain is very beautiful; and from the grain of broken pieces it, appears to have all the qualities of the best Chinese porcelain. A whiter glazing would be desirable, which they might probably attain, if the Marquis Ginori was not determined to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> those materials only which were found in that country. But in no state of Europe have such attempts been made to discover porcelain, or so many manufactories of it been established, as in France. Before even Mr Reaumur had published on this subject, porcelain was made at Saint Cloud, and in the suburb of St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTOINE">Antoine</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, which was of the vitreous and fusible kind, but considerably beautiful. Since that time, considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of it have been established at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANTILLY">Chantilly</a>, at Villeroy, and at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>; the porcelains of which have a distinguished merit. But the porcelain produced in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s manufacture at Sevres holds at present the first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, from its shining white, its beautiful glazing, and coloured grounds, in which no porcelain has ever equalled it. The magnificence of the gilding, the regularity and elegance of its forms, surpass every thing of the kind. Mr Guettard has published an account of his discoveries on this subject, in the Memoirs of the Academy of Sciences for the year 1765. The kaolin which he employed was a white argillaceous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, filled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICA">mica</a>, which he found in the neighbourhood of Alençon; and his petuntse is a hard, quartzose grit stone, found abundantly in the same country, with which the streets of Alençon are paved. We al- Porcelain so know that Mr Guettard had begun to make his experiments on porcelain with these materials in the year 1751, together with the late <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Orleans, to whom he was attached. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> de Lauraguais, of the Academy of Sciences, engaged in the pursuit of porcelain for several years with uncommon ardour and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>. He spared no trouble nor expense to attain his purpose, which was to make porcelain equal in all respects to that of China and Japan. He showed some pieces made by him, in the year 1766, to the members of the Academy of Sciences. The persons appointed by them to examine it gave their opinion, "that of all the porcelains made in the country, that of the Count de Lauraguais most resembles the porcelain of China and Japan in solidity, grain, and unfusibility." It were to be wished that it possessed equally the other qualities essential to the excellence of porcelain, namely, the whiteness and lustre observable in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Japanese porcelain. See Chemistry, p. 91. We shall now show what those qualities are which constitute the perfection of porcelain. We must first carefully distinguish the qualities which only contribute to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and external appearance, from the intrinsic and essential properties in which the goodness and solidity of porcelain consist. All persons who have made experiments in this way have soon discovered the possibility of making compounds very white, beautifully semi-transparent, and covered with a shining glazing; but which cannot be worked for want of tenacity, are not sufficiently compact, are essentially fusible, are subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> by sudden application of heat and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; and lastly, the glazing of which cracks, becomes rough, and consequently loses its lustre by use, because it is too soft. On the other side, we shall also find it not difficult to compose very tenacious pastes, which shall be capable of being easily worked and well baked; which in the baking shall acquire the desirable <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and density; which are fusible, and capable of sustaining very well the sudden change of heat and cold; and, in a word, which shall have all the qualities of the most excellent porcelain, excepting whiteness and beauty. We shall soon see that the materials fit for the composition of such porcelains may be found abundantly in every country. The only difficulty, then, in this inquiry concerning porcelain, is to unite beauty and goodness in one composition; and indeed nature seems to be very sparing of materials fit for this purpose, and therefore perfect porcelain will always be a dear and valuable commodity. Those potteries which we call stone-ware are not of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, and have all the essential qualities of the best Japanese. For if we except whiteness, on which alone the semi-transparency depends, and compare all the properties of Japanese porcelain with those of our stone-ware, no difference can be found between them. The same grain appears internally in both; the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> is produced by striking them when properly suspended; the same density, the same hardness by which they strike fire with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of sustaining the heat of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> liquors without breaking, and the same unfusibility in fire, are observable. Lastly, if the earths of which stone-ware is made were free from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> colouring matters, which prevent their whiteness and semitransparency; if vessels were carefully formed; if all the proper attentions were given; and if these vessels were covered over with a fine glazing; they would be as perfect porcelain as that of Japan. The most perfect porcelain, therefore, is nothing else than a fine white stone-ware. Earths of this kind are probably more rare in Europe than in Japan and China. And probably also the want of these earths was the cause that the first makers of porcelain in this country confined themselves to an external <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>, by employing nothing but vitrifiable matters with fusible salts and a small quantity of white earth, from which fusible and vitreous porcelains were composed, which might be called false porcelains. But things are much changed since their first attempts. Besides the discoveries of the count de Lauraguais and genuine porcelain of Mr Guettard, genuine white porcelains have been made a long time ago in Germany, especially in Saxony and at Frankendal. These porcelains are not inferior in any respect to rope. The oriental; they are even much superior in beauty and whiteness to the modern oriental porcelain, which has much degenerated in these respects; they seem even to excel the oriental in the most valuable quality of porcelain, namely, the property of sustaining the sudden change of heat and cold. We cannot judge of the quality of porcelain by a flight trial; for so many circumstances concur to make a piece of porcelain capable or incapable of sustaining the sudden application of heat and of cold, that if at the same time boiling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> be poured into two vessels, one of which is good porcelain and the other bad, the former may possibly break and the latter remain entire. The only true method of discovering good porcelain in this respect is, to examine several pieces of it which are daily used; for instance, a set of coffee-cups. But it has been observed, that in many such pieces of oriental porcelain, which have been long and daily used, cracks in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of their height may be always perceived, which are never seen in the good European porcelains. Every one talks of porcelain, and yet few are connoisseurs of it. None can be considered as such but those who have long made it an object of their inquiries. That the ancient Japanese porcelain is the most perfect, is a general opinion. This porcelain is indeed very beautiful, and we must also acknowledge that its quality is excellent. It has been our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, and has long been the object of our admiration and emulation; but which we have been never able to equal, and which many persons believe never can be equalled. Some persons even decry the Saxon porcelain for a quality which really gives it a superiority to the Japanese, namely, the greater smoothness, lustre, and less granulous appearance of its internal surface than the oriental. The resemblance of this surface to that of glass has evidently suggested this notion; and it would be well founded, if the density and lustre of this porcelain proceeded only from a fusible and vitreous quality; but as they do not, and as this porcelain is as fixed and as unfusible as the Japanese, its density, so far from being a fault, is a valuable quality. For we must allow, that of porcelains equal in other respects, those are best which are most firm and compact. Hence the interior substance of the Japanese porcelain is esteemed for its great- Porcelain, or density, compactness, and lustre, than our vitreous sand or frit porcelain, because these qualities indicate greater <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a>, and more intimate incorporation of its parts. For the same reason also the superior density of the Saxon porcelain ought to give it the preference to the Japanese. Besides, nothing would be easier than to give the Saxon porcelain the granulous texture of the Japanese, by mixing with the paste a certain quantity of sand. But the persons who perfected that manufacture were certainly sensible, that such a conformity to the Japanese porcelain would lessen the merit of theirs. For we know, that in general porcelains are better in proportion as they contain a larger proportion of clay or earth, and less of sand, flints, or other matters of that kind. What we have said concerning porcelain in general, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> kinds of it, seems sufficient to give just notions of it, if not to persons who without considering the subject are determined to prefer the most ancient, to those, at least, who have made experiments on this subject, or who, having a sufficient knowledge of chemistry, are capable of studying and examining it thoroughly. We shall finish this article by giving a short description of the method of manufacturing porcelain. The basis of the porcelains which we have called fusible or vitreous, or false porcelains, is called by artists a frit; which is nothing else than a mixture of sand or powdered flints, with salts capable of dissolving them to fusion, and of giving them a great whiteness by means of a sufficient heat. This frit is to be then mixed with as much, and no more, of a white tenacious earth of an argillaceous or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARLY">marly</a> nature, than is sufficient to make it capable of being worked upon the wheel. The whole mixture is to be well ground together in a mill, and made into a paste, which is to be formed, either upon the wheel or in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>, into pieces of such forms as are required. Each of these pieces, when dry, is to be put into a case made of earthen ware (A); which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> are to be ranged in piles one upon another, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KILN">kiln</a>, which is to be filled with these to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>. The furnaces are chambers or cavities of various forms and sizes; and are disposed, that their fire-place is placed on the outside opposite to one or more openings, which communicate within the furnace. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> is drawn within the furnace, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> of which raising, determines a current of air from without inwards, as in all furnaces. At first a very little fire is made, that the furnace may be heated gradually, and is to be increased more and more till the porcelain is baked, that is, till it has acquired its proper hardness and transparency; which is known by taking out of the furnace from time to time, and examining, small pieces of porcelain, placed for that purpose in cases which have lateral openings. When these pieces show that the porcelain is sufficiently baked, the first is no longer to be supplied with fuel, the furnace is to be cooled, and the porcelain taken out, which in this state resembles white marble not having a shining surface, which is afterwards to be given by covering them with a vitreous composition called the glazing. The porcelain when baked and not glazed is called biscuit, which is more or less beautiful according to the nature of the porcelain. The manufacture of Sévres sculptures excels all others in this respect, and it is therefore the only one which can produce very fine pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>; that is, in which all the fineness of the workmanship is preserved, and which are preferable in smoothness and whiteness to the finest marble of Italy. As no piece of sculpture of this kind can preserve all the delicacy of its workmanship when covered with a glazing; and as sculptors avoid polishing their marble figures, because the lustre of the polish is disadvantageous; therefore, in the manufactures at Sévres, all figures, or little statues, and even some ornamental vases, are left in the state of biscuit. The other pieces of porcelain are to be glazed in the following manner. A glaze is first to be composed suited to the nature of the porcelain to which it is to be applied; for every glazing and glaze is not fit for this purpose. We frequently find colouring that a glaze which makes a fine glazing for one porcelain shall make a very bad glazing for another porcelain; shall crack in many places, shall have no lustre, or shall contain bubbles. The glazing then must be appropriated to each porcelain, that is, to the hardness and density of the ware, and to the ingredients of its composition, &c. These glazings are prepared by previously fusing together all the substances of which they consist, so as to form vitreous masses. These masses are to be ground very finely in a mill. This vitreous powder is to be mixed with a sufficient quantity of water, or other proper liquor, so that the mixture shall have the consistence of cream of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. The pieces of porcelain are to be covered with a thin stratum of this matter; and when very dry, they are to be again put into the furnace in the same manner as before for the forming of the biscuit, and to be continued there till the glazing be well fused. The necessary degree of fire for fusing the glazing is much less than that for baking the paste. The pieces of porcelain which are intended to remain white are now finished; but those which are to be painted and gilded must undergo further operations. The colours to be applied are the same as those used for enamel painting. They all consist of metallic calxes bruised and incorporated with a very fusible glaze. Crocus of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> furnishes a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> + precipitated by tin makes the purple and violet; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> calcined by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> and precipitated by an alkali gives a fine green; zaffire makes the blue; earths slightly <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> produce a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; and, lastly, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> colours are produced by calcined iron, together with a deep blue of zaffire. These colours being ground with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-water, or with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of spike, are to be employed for the painting of the porcelain with designs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and other figures. For gilding, a powder or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> of gold is to be applied in the same manner as the coloured enamels. The painted and gilded porcelains are to be then exposed to a fire capable of fusing the glaze, with which the metallic colours are mixed. Thus (a) The cases are called by English potters, Seggers. They are generally formed of coarser clays, but which must be also capable of sustaining the heat required without fusion. By means of these cases, the contained porcelain is preserved from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> fuel. The whiteness of the porcelain depends much on their compactness of texture by which the smoke is excluded, and on the purity of the clay of which they are made. Thus the colours are made to adhere, and at the same time acquire a gloss equal to that of the glazing. The gold alone has not then a shining appearance, which must be afterwards given to it by burnishing with a blood stone. The operations for the unfusible porcelains, and also for such as are of the nature of stone-ware, are somewhat more simple. The sands and stones which enter into their composition are to be ground in a mill; the earths or clays are to be washed; the materials are to be well mixed, and formed into a paste; the pieces are first rudely formed upon a potter's wheel; and when dry, or half dry, they are turned again upon the wheel, and their form is made more perfect; they are then placed in the furnace, not to bake them, but only to apply a sufficient heat to give them such a solidity that they may be handled without breaking, and may receive the glazing. As the pieces of porcelain after this slight heat are very dry, they imbibe water readily. This disposition affords the application of the glazing. The vitrifiable or vitrified matter of this glazing, which has been previously ground in a mill, is to be mixed with such a quantity of water, that the liquor shall have the consistence of milk. The pieces of porcelain are hastily dipped in this liquor, the water of which they imbibe, and thus on their surface is left an uniform covering of the glazing materials. This covering, which ought to be very thin, will soon become dry, that it cannot stick to the fingers when the pieces are handled. The pieces of this porcelain are then put into the furnace to be perfectly baked. The heat is to be raised to such a height, that all within the furnace shall be white, and the cases shall be undistinguishable from the flame. When, by taking out small pieces, the porcelain is known to be sufficiently baked, the fire is discontinued, and the furnace cooled. If the baking has been well performed, the pieces of porcelain will be found by this single operation to be rendered compact, sonorous, close-grained, moderately glossy, and covered externally with a fine glazing. The painting and gilding of this porcelain are to be executed in a manner similar to that already described. Porcelain Shell, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Cypraea.

PORCH

Pages 79-79

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a kind of vestibule supported by columns; much used at the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, halls, churches, &c. A porch, in the ancient architecture, was a vestibule, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a disposition of insulated columns usually crowned with a pediment, forming a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> door of a temple or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Such is that before the door of St Paul's, Covent-Garden, the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Inigo Jones. When a porch had four columns in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, it was called a tetrastyle; when five, hexastyle; when eight, octastyle, &c.

PORK

Pages 79-79

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of swine killed for the purposes of food. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUS">Sus</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a> is the only <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animal that we know of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> when alive, and therefore seems properly designed for food. Besides, as loathsome and ugly to every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> eye, it is killed without reluctance. The Pythagoreans, whether to preserve <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> on account of compassion, generally forbade the use of animal food; and yet it is alleged that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> reserved the use of hogs' flesh for himself. The Jews, the Egyptians, &c., and others in the warm countries, and all the Mahometans at present, reject the use of pork. It is difficult to find out the reason of this, or of the precept given to some of them, though <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> such as are not given without a particular one. The Greeks gave <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> commendations to this food; and Galen, though indeed that is suspected to be from a particular fondness, is everywhere full of it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> considered it as one of their delicacies; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> some of the inhabitants of the northern climates have taken an aversion to it, that probably arose from the unculivated state of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> not being able to rear it. Pork is of a very tender structure; increased perhaps from a peculiarity in its economy, viz., taking on fat more readily than any other animal. Pork is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> meat even in its adult state, and then gives out a jelly in very great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>.
