On account of its little perishability and tenderness, it is very nutritious, and was given for that intention to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol2.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a>. With regard to its alkalinity, no proper experiments have yet been made; but as it is of a gelatinous and succulent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, it is probably less than many others. Upon the whole, it appears to be a very valuable nutriment, and the reason is not very obvious why it was in some countries forbidden. It is said that this animal is apt to be diseased; but why were not inconveniences felt on that account in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>? Again, it has been alleged, that as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> would not rear these animals, and as the Jews had learned the use of them in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, it was necessary they should have a precept to avoid them. But the Egyptians themselves did not use this meat; and this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> precept, indeed, as well as many others, seems to have been borrowed from them. Possibly, as pork is not very perishable, it might increase the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>, which was said to be epidemic in Palestine; though this is far from being certain.

PORPHYRIUS

Pages 79-79

a famous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a> in 233, in the reign of Alexander Severus. He was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Longinus, and became the ornament of his school at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; from thence he went to Rome, and attended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOTINUS">Plotinus</a>, with whom he lived six years. After Plotinus's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he taught <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at Rome with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause; and became well skilled in polite literature, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and music. He lived till the end of the third century, and died in the reign of Diocletian. There are still extant, his book on the Categories of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>; a Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTINENCE">Abstinence</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">Flesh</a>; and several other pieces in Greek. He also composed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> treatise against the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>, which is lost. That <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> was answered by Methodius bishop of Tyre, and also by Eusebius, Apollinaris, St Augustine, St Jerome, St Cyril, and Theodoret. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius the Great caused Porphyrius's book to be burned in 338. Those of his works that are still extant, were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> in 1655, 8vo., with a Latin version.

PORPHYRY

Pages 79-80

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of a plain uniform <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, spotted with separate concretions, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>, giving fire with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, not fermenting with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, and very slowly and difficultly calcining in a strong fire. Porphyry is of several sorts; as, 1. The porphyry Porphyry of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, which is a most elegant mass of an extremely firm and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> structure, remarkably heavy, and of a fine strong purple, variegated more <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> less with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; its purple is of all degrees, from the claret-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to that of the violet; and its variegations are rarely disposed in veins, but spots, sometimes very small, and at others running into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> blotches. It is less fine than many of the ordinary marbles; but it excels them all in hardness, and is capable of a most elegant polish. It is still found in immense <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. 2. The hard red-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> coloured porphyry, variegated with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, white, and green. This is a most beautiful and valuable substance. It has the hardness and all the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the oriental porphyry; and even greatly excels it in brightness, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and variegation of its colours. It is found in great plenty in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINORCA">Minorca</a>; and is extremely worth importing, for it is greatly superior to all the Italian marbles. 3. The hard, pale-red porphyry, variegated with black, white, and green. This is of a pale <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-colour; often approaching to white. It is variegated in blotches from half an inch to an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. It takes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> polish, and emulates all the qualities of the oriental porphyry. It is found in immense strata in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea, and in the Upper Egypt; and in separate nodules in Germany, England, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. Porphyry-Shell, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Murex.

PORRUM

Pages 80-80

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEEK">Leek</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the genus of Allium. There are two species known in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; the sativum, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> leek, and the ampeolopraenum. The first is the kind <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> cultivated; and of it there have been supposed two varieties: but Mr Miller observes, that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> has been occasioned by some persons saving the seeds from old leeks, and not from the seedling leeks; whereby they have degenerated, and become smaller and narrower-leaved; but may be recovered again by proper care. The other species is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>; its leaves are narrower than the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sort; the stalks are smaller, and do not rise near so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; the heads of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are also smaller, and of a purplish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; the stamens stand out beyond the flower. Leeks are cultivated in the same manner as onions, and commonly sown along with them; their qualities as food are also the same.

PORT

Pages 80-80

a harbour, river, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> haven, formed either by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> or art, to receive and shelter shipping from the storms and waves of the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> ports are those which are either formed by throwing a strong mound or rampire across the harbour's mouth to some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> or rock, or erecting two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> barriers, which stretch from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> on each side like arms or the horns of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, and nearly inclose the haven; the former of these are called <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOLE">mole</a>-heads, and the latter piers. Port, is also a name given on some occasions to the larboard or left side of the ship, as in the following instances. Thus it is said, "the ship heels to port," i.e., floops or inclines to the larboard side. "Top the yard to port!" the order to make the larboard extremity of a yard higher than the other. "Port the helm!" the order to put the helm over to the larboard-side of the vessel. In all these senses this phrase appears intended to prevent any mistakes happening from the similarity of sounds in the words larboard and larboard, particularly when they relate to the helm, where a misapprehension might be attended with very dangerous consequences. Ports, the embrasures or openings in the side of a ship of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> is ranged in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> upon the decks above and below. The ports are formed of a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> to point and fire the cannon, without injuring the ship's side by the recoil; and as it serves no end to enlarge them beyond what is necessary for that purpose, the shipwrights have established certain dimensions, by which they are cut in proportion to the size of the cannon. The ports are shut in at sea by a fort of hanging-doors, called the port-lids; which are fastened by hinges to their upper-edges, so as to let <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> when the cannon are drawn into the ship. By this means the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> is prevented from entering the lower-decks in a turbulent sea. The lower and upper edges of the ports are always <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the deck, so that the guns, when levelled in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, are all equally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> above the lower extremity of the ports, which is called the port-cells. Port, is also a strong wine brought from Port-a-port, and also called Porto and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-OPORTO">Oporto</a>. Port of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">Voice</a>, in music, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of making the shakes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, and diminutions, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of a song or piece of music consists. Port-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRAYON">Crayon</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, which is usually four or five inches long, and contrived so as that the pencil may slide up and down. Its inside is round, and its outside is sometimes filed into eight sides or faces, on which are drawn the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECTOR">sector</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; sometimes it is made round both without-side and within, and has its length divided into inches and parts of inches.

PORT-GREVE

Pages 81-81
or Portgrave, was anciently the principal magistrate in ports and other maritime towns. The word is formed from the Saxon port, "a port or other town;" add geref, a "governor."—It is sometimes also written port-reve. Camden observes, that the chief magistrate of London was anciently called port-greve: instead of whom, Richard I. ordained two bailiffs; and soon afterwards king John granted them a mayor for their yearly magistrate.

PORTA

Pages 81-81
or Vena Porta, in anatomy, a large vein distributed through the liver in the manner of an artery. See Anatomy, no 357, d.

PORTAL

Pages 81-81

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a little gate where there are two gates of a different bigness; also a little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> corner of a room cut off from the rest by the wainscot, and forming a short passage into the room. The same name is also sometimes given to a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of joiners <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> before a door.

PORTATE

Pages 81-81
or a Crois Portate, in heraldry, a cross which does not stand upright, as crosses generally do; but lies across the escutcheon in bend, as if it were carried on a man's shoulder.

PORTCULLICE

Pages 80-81

in fortification, is an assemblage of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pieces of wood, joined across one another like a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARROW">harrow</a>, and each pointed with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> at the bottom. They are sometimes hung over the gate-way of old fortified <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, ready to let <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of surprise, when the gates could not be shut. Port-Fire, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> for setting fire to powder, &c. Port-fires are frequently used by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> people in preference to matches; and they are distinguished into wet and dry port-fires. The composition of the former is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a> four, sulphur one, and mealed powder four. When these materials are thoroughly mixed and fitted, the whole is to be moistened with a little linseed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and rubbed between the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> till all the oil is imbibed by the composition. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for dry port-fires is saltpetre four, sulphur one, mealed powder two, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a> one. These compositions are driven into small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, to be used whenever necessary. Port-aux-Prune, so called by the French, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Madagascar. It is a rich country, and fertile in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and pastures; it is inhabited only by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a>, who are industrious, good sort of people, but very superstitious. There are no towns, but several villages, and they have some customs which seem to incline to Judaism. Port-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in the island of Jamaica. It was once one of the finest sea-port towns in America, abounding in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and trade; but but in 1692 it was destroyed by an earthquake, in 1702 by fire, in 1722 by an inundation of the sea, and in 1744 it suffered greatly by a hurricane. It is now but a small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and yet it consists of three handsome streets, with several croes lanes, and a fine <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Not many years ago there was a yard built here for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s naval stores, and for workmen employed about men of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>. It is built on a small neck of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> which jets out several miles into the sea, and is guarded by a very strong fort, which has a line of near 100 pieces of cannon, and a garrison of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. The harbour is one of the best in the world, and 1000 ships may ride therein, secure from every <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> that can blow. It is five miles east of Spanish-town, and as much by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 77° O. N. Lat. 17° 30'. Port-Royal, an island in North America, on the coast of South Carolina, which, with the neighbouring continent, forms one of the most commodious harbours in the British plantations. It is 15 miles in length; and the town on the north shore is called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUFORT">Beaufort</a>. W. Long. 80° 10'. N. Lat. 31° 45'. Port-Royal, the name of two monasteries of Cistercian nuns in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; the one near Chevreuse, at the distance of five leagues from Paris, called Port-Royal of the Fields; and the other in Paris, in the suburbs of St James. The nuns of the former of these monasteries proving refractory, were dispersed; when many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, and others, who were of the same sentiments as these <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, retired to Port-Royal, took apartments there, and printed many books. Hence the name of Port-Royalists was given to all of their party, and their books were called books of Port-Royal: from hence we say the writers of Port-Royal, Messieurs de Port-Royal, and the translations and grammars of Port-Royal.

PORTER

Pages 81-81

a kind of malt-liquor which differs from ale and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> beer in its being made with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> dried malt. See Ale, Beer, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BREWING">Brewing</a>.

PORTICI

Pages 81-81

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, four miles from that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. It has a charming situation, on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-side, near mount <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>. It is enriched with a vast <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fine <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and other remains of antiquity, taken out of the ruins of Herculaneum, which is not far from thence, and was swallowed up by an earthquake which attended an eruption of mount Vesuvius in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Titus.

PORTICO

Pages 81-81

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a kind of gallery on the ground; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIAZZA">piazza</a> encompassed with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> supported by columns, where people walk under <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COVERT">covert</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is usually vaulted, sometimes flat. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> called it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LACUNAR">lacunar</a>. Though the word portico be derived from porta, "gate, door;" yet it is applied to Porto-bello, to any disposition of columns which form a gallery, without any immediate relation to doors or gates. The most celebrated porticos of antiquity were, those of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>'s temple, which formed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATRIUM">atrium</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and encompassed the sanctuary: that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, built for the people to divert themselves in, and wherein the philosophers held their disputes and conversations; which occasioned the disciples of Zeno to be called Stoics, from the Greek root, porticus: and that of Pompey at Rome, raised merely for magnificence, consisting of several rows of columns supporting a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; a draught whereof, Serlio gives us in his antique buildings. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> porticos, the most celebrated is the piazza of St <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> of the Vatican.—That of Covent-Garden, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Inigo Jones, is also much admired.

PORTLAND

Pages 81-81

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength both by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art, being surrounded with inaccessible rocks, except at the landing-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, where there is a strong castle, called Portland castle, built by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Henry VIII. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; and that stands so near the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, that it is often in danger from it. But this peninsula is chiefly noted for the free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> which is got here, and greatly employed in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the finest structures, and particularly St Paul's church was built therewith. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 35'. N. Lat. 50° 30'.

PORTO-BELLO

Pages 81-82

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, situated in N. Lat. 9° 34' 35", <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the declivity of a mountain, which surrounds the whole harbour. This harbour is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, deep, and safe, that Columbus, who first discovered it, gave it the name of Porto-Bello, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the "Fine Harbour," which is now <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used to denote the town. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the houses is about 130; most of them of wood, large and spacious, forming one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> street along the strand, with other smaller ones crossing it. The governor of the town is always a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, subordinate to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a>; but having under him the commandants of the forts that defend the harbour. At the east end of the town, on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Panama, is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, where all the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> of both sexes, whether slaves or free, have their habitations. This place is very much crowded when the galleons are here: most of the inhabitants of the town quitting their houses entirely, for the sake of letting them; while others content themselves with a small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, in order to make <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of the rest. The Mulattoes, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> families also, remove either to Guinea, or to cottages already erected near it, or built on the occasion. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> numbers of artificers likewise, who flock to Porto-Bello from Panama to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> at their respective callings during the fair, lodge in Guinea for cheapness. Towards the sea, in a large tract bet- Porto-Bello between the town and Gloria castle, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a> are erected, in most of which the ships crews keep stalls of sweetmeats, and other kinds of eatables, brought from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; but at the conclusion of the fair, when the ships put to sea, all these buildings are taken <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and the town returns to its former tranquillity and emptiness. In 1739, the harbour was defended by a castle and two forts; which were all demolished by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VERNON">Vernon</a>, who, with six ships only, made himself <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of this port. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about Porto-Bello is over-run with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and impenetrable forests, except a few valleys, in which are some scattered farms. Among the mountains that surround the harbour, one distinguished by the name of Capiro and by its superior loftiness, is a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a> to the country, by foretelling every change of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Its top is always covered with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, of a density and darkness seldom seen in those of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. When these clouds thicken, increase their blackness, and sink below their usual station, it is a sure sign of a tempest; while, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, their clearness and ascent as certainly indicate the approach of fair weather. These changes are very sudden and frequent here. The summit of the mountain is scarce ever clear from clouds; and when it happens, it is only, as it were, for an instant. Except in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the fair, all the inhabitants of Porto-Bello do not amount to 3000; half of whom are Indians, Mulattoes, or negroes; the Spaniards of any substance not choosing to reside in a place so extremely unhealthy, and fatal even to the lives of the natives. Ulloa tells us, that the cattle brought hither from Panama or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>, lose their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> so fast in the hot pastures, as to become scarce eatable: he assures us also, that neither horses nor asses are bred here. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, indeed, is excessive; and the torrents of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> are so dreadful, sudden, and impetuous, that one not accustomed to them would imagine a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> deluge was coming. These torrents are also accompanied with frightful tempests of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, the awfulness of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> being heightened by the reverberations from the mountains, and the shrieks and howlings of multitudes of monkeys of all kinds which inhabit the surrounding woods. Fresh <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> pours down in streams from the mountains, some running without the town, and others crossing it. These waters are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGESTIVE">digestive</a>; qualities, which in other countries would be very valuable, but are here pernicious, producing dysenteries, which the patient seldom survives. However, these rivulets, formed into reservoirs, serve the purposes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>, which is here found to be very conducive to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. As the forests almost border on the houses of the streets, tygers often make incursions into the streets during the night, carrying off fowls, dogs, and other <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals, and sometimes even children have fallen a prey to them. Besides the snares usually laid for them, the negroes and mulattoes, who fell wood in the forests of the mountains, are very dextrous in encountering them; and some, for a slender reward, even seek them in their retreats. The town of Porto-Bello, which is thinly inhabited by reason of its noxious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, the scarcity of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and the barrenness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, becomes, after the arrival of the galleons, one of the most populous <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in the world. He who had seen it quite empty, and Porto-Bello every place wearing a melancholy aspect, would be filled with astonishment, to see the bustling multitudes in the time of the fair, when every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is crowded, the squares and streets encumbered with bales of merchandise and chests of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, the harbour full of ships and vessels, some loaded with provisions from Carthagena, and others with the goods of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, as cocoa, Jesuits bark, Vicuna <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEZOAR">bezoar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; and this town, at all other times detested for its deleterious qualities, becomes the staple of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of the Old and New World, and the scene of one of the most considerable branches of trade in the universe. Formerly the fair was limited to no particular time; but as a long stay in such a sickly place extremely affected the health of the traders, his Catholic majesty transmitted an order that the fair should not last above 40 days; and that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> in that time the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> could not agree on their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RATES">rates</a>, those of Spain should be allowed to carry their goods up the country to Peru; and accordingly, the commodore of the galleons has orders to re-embark them, and return to Carthagena; but otherwise, by virtue of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> between the merchants of both kingdoms, and ratified by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, no Spanish trader is to send his goods, on his own account, beyond Porto-Bello. The English were formerly allowed to send a ship annually to this fair, which turned to great account; and, whilst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSIENTO">assiento</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> subsisted, either with the English or the French, one of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> factories was at Porto-Bello. Porto-Ferralo, a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBA">Elba</a>, with a good citadel. It is very strong, and seated on a long, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, steep point of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, to the west of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name, which has two forts. It belongs to the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, who always keeps a good garrison there. E. Long. 10. 37. N. Lat. 48. 55. Porto-Longone, a small but very strong town of Italy, and in the isle of Elba, with a good harbour, and a fortress upon a rock almost inaccessible. The king of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> has a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to put a garrison therein, though the place belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIOMBINO">Piombino</a>. It is seated on the east end of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, eight miles southwest of Piombino. E. Long. 10. 40. N. Lat. 42. 45. Porto-Santo, an island of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic Ocean</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and the least of those called the Madeiras. It is about 15 miles in circumference, and produces but little corn; however, there are oxen and wild hogs, and a vast number of rabbits. There are trees which produce the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a> or rosin called dragon's blood; and there is likewise a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and wax, which are extremely good. It has no harbour, but good mooring in the road. It belongs to the Portuguese, and is 300 miles west of the coast of Africa. W. Long. 15. 5. N. Lat. 32. 30. Porto-Seguro, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of South America, on the eastern coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>; bounded on the north by the government of Rio-dos-Hilios, on the east by the North Sea, on the south by the government of Spiritu-Santo, and on the west by the Tupicks. It is a very fertile country, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town is of the same name. It is built on the top of a rock, at the mouth of a river, on the coast of the North Sea, and is inhabited by Portuguese. W. Long. 35. 50. S. Lat. 17. 0.

PORTRAIT

Pages 82-83

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, the representation of a person, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a> person, and especially of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>, done from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> portrait-painting, in contradistinction to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>-painting, where a resemblance of person is usually disregarded. Portraits, when as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as the life, are usually painted in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-colours; sometimes they are painted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-colours, crayons, pastels, &c. See Painting, § 39.

PORTSMOUTH

Pages 83-83

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, with one of the most secure and capacious harbours in England, being defended by a numerous <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, both on the sea and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-side, and very good fortifications. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> is built here; and here are some of the finest docks, yards, and magazines of naval stores, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It is seated in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Portsea, being surrounded by the sea except on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side, where there is a river which runs from one arm of it to the other. It is much resorted to on account of the royal navy, whose usual rendezvous is at Spithead, which is at the east end of the isle of Wight, and opposite to Portsmouth. There is a draw-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river, and it has always a good garrison. It is governed by a mayor, 12 aldermen and burgesses, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It has one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and two chapels, one in the garrison, and one in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">Common</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOCK">dock</a>, and others, besides several meeting-houses of the dissenters. The houses of Portsmouth amount to about 2000, and the inhabitants to about 12,000. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 6. N. Lat. 50° 48'. The town is supposed to receive its name from Port, a famous Saxon chieftain, who, A.D. 501, landed here with his two sons. It made a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Saxons; and from the utility of its situation, was highly favoured by all our monarchs of the Norman line. It was incorporated, and became also a parliamentary borough. In the reign of Edward III., it was in a very flourishing state; but, A.D. 1338, in the very same reign, was burned by the French, when that monarch, which was afterwards ratified by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Richard II., forgave the inhabitants a debt, and remitted their fee-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FARM">farm</a> for 10 years; within which space they so recovered themselves, as to equip a squadron, which sailed into the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, sunk two ships, and brought away a great booty. The singular excellence of its port, and the convenience of fitting out fleets from thence in the time of a French <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, induced Edward IV. to think of fortifying it, as he actually, in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, did; which fortifications were farther carried on by Richard III. But king Henry VII. was the first who settled a garrison therein; which was increased, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> made still stronger, in the reign of Henry VIII., who had a great dock there, wherein was built the Henry <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a> de Dieu, which was the largest ship in the navy of his time. The same monarch, remarkably attentive to the security of all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> places, built what is now called South-Sea Castle, for the protection of this. The improvements made here in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, were much superior to all these. King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., after his restoration, directed great alterations, established new docks and yards, raised several forts, and fortified them after the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> manner; which works were augmented under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>'s reign. Notwithstanding this, king William directed likewise fresh alterations and additions; and succeeding princes, following his example, have, at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> expense, extended these fortifications, and taken in a vast <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of ground; so that it is at present, as the importance of the place deserves, the most regular fortress in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; and, as it cannot be effectually attacked by sea, may be justly esteemed impregnable.

PORTUGAL

Pages 83-95

the most westerly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, bounded on the west and south by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic Ocean</a>, and on the east and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; extending about 310 miles in length, and 150 in breadth. By <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers, we find this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> constantly styled in Latin, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUSITANIA">Lusitania</a>; and it is certain, that anciently a country of Spain went by that name; but it does not by any means appear that the country called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> Lusitania, had the same boundaries with the modern kingdom of Portugal. Before Augustus Caesar, Lusitania seems to have been bounded on the north by the ocean, and on the south by the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>; by which means it comprehended all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, and excluded two of the six provinces of Portugal. But in the more strict and restrained <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, it was bounded on the north by the Durius, now the Douro, and on the south by the river <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANAS">Anas</a>, now the Guadiana; in which sense it was not quite so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as modern Portugal, but considerably broader. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> received <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> with regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the word Portugal is, that a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the name, of the number of Gauls landed at Porto, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-OPORTO">Oporto</a>, whence it received the name of Portus Gallorum, or the Port of the Gauls; and in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> that name gradually extended over the whole country, being softened, or rather shortened, into Portugal. But the time when this event happened, the reason why these Gauls came thither, and what became of them afterwards, are all particulars which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> buried in oblivion. It is alleged, however, that, upon an eminence which overlooks the mouth of the river Douro, there stood an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town called Cale, strong and well peopled, but ill fitted for trade; and this occasioned the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of a lower town or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a>, which was called Portus Cale, that is, the haven of Cale; and, in process of time, Portucalia. At length becoming so considerable as to merit an episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, these <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> subscribed themselves, as the records of ancient councils testify, Portucalenses, and the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> was transferred to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>. It is true, that these bishops afterwards changed their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, and subscribed themselves Portuenses, that is, bishops of Porto. But the facts <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned are actually recorded in authentic histories; and as the diocese of Portucalia contained in a great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> that little country in which the sovereignty originally began, the name extended itself, together with the acquisitions of the sovereigns, and has remained to the kingdom, tho' the diocese itself has changed its name, and possibly on that very account. Portugal, though even yet but a small kingdom, was originally much smaller. The Spanish and Portuguese historians agree, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> Alonso, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Leon and Castile, and son to Don Ferdinand the Great, bestowed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Donna Theresa in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> upon an illustrious stranger, Don Henry, and gave him with her the frontier <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> which he had conquered from the Moors, small indeed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, but Portugal, but excellently situated, and so pleasant and fertile, that it has sometimes been styled Medulla Hispanica, or the marrow of Spain. To this territory was added the title of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">Count</a>; but authors are much divided about the time that this stranger came into Spain, and who he was. However, the authors of the Universal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> make it pretty evident, that he was a grandson of Robert the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>. The manner in which he obtained the principality abovementioned is related as follows. The king, Don Alonzo, apprehensive that his success in taking the city of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a> would bring upon him the whole force of the Moors, sent to demand assistance from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> I. of France, and the duke of Burgundy, whose daughter he had married. His request was granted by both princes; and a numerous body of troops was speedily collected for his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, at whose head went Raymond count of Burgundy, Henry younger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Hugh duke of Burgundy, Raymond count of Thoulouse, and many others. They arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Don Alonzo in the year 1087, where they were received and treated with all possible marks of esteem; and having in the course of two or three years given great proofs of their courage and conduct, the king resolved to bestow his only daughter named Urraca, then a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> child, being at most in her ninth year, upon Raymond count of Burgundy, and assigned them the province of Galicia for the support of their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. About four years after, Don Alonzo being very desirous to express his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to Henry of Burgundy, gave him in marriage a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> daughter of his, born while he remained in exile at Toledo, whose name was Donna Theresa; and upon this marriage, he gave up in full <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> the country which has been already mentioned. The new sovereign, with his consort, fixed their residence in the town of Guimarães, pleasantly situated on the banks of the river Ave. The remains of an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> belonging to their successors are still to be seen; and on account of its having been anciently the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, the king Don Denis granted the inhabitants an immunity from taxes, which they still enjoy. The Portuguese, now finding themselves independent, immediately began, like other nations, to attempt the subjection of their neighbours. Henry is said to have performed great exploits against the Moors; but the accounts of them are so indistinct, that they cannot be taken notice of here. He died in 1112; and was succeeded by his son Don Alonzo, then an infant in the third year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. In his minority, the kingdom was governed by his mother Donna Theresa, assisted by two able ministers. During the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years of their administration nothing remarkable happened; but after that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, some differences took <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> regent (for she had assumed the title of queen after her father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and Urraca queen of Castile.) Theresa insisted, that some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Galicia belonged to her in virtue of her father's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>; and therefore seized on Tuy an episcopal town, and a place of some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. Urraca, having assembled a numerous <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, went in person into Galicia; upon which Theresa was obliged to abandon Tuy, and take shelter in one of her own fortresses. The consequences, in all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, would have been fatal to the new kingdom, had not the archbishop of Portugal, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOSTELLA">Compostella</a>, without whose assistance Urraca could do nothing, demanded leave to retire with his vassals. This offended the queen to such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that she threw him into prison; which <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of violence excited such a commotion among her own subjects, that the Portuguese were soon delivered from their apprehensions. Queen Theresa fell immediately after into a similar <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, by throwing into prison the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRAGA">Braga</a>, who had not espoused her cause so warmly as she had expected. The bishop, however, was quickly delivered by a bull from the pope, who also threatened the kingdom with an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERDICT">interdict</a>; and this was the first remarkable offence which Theresa gave her subjects. Soon after this, queen Urraca died, and all differences were amicably settled at an interview between Theresa and Don Alonzo Raymond, who succeeded to the kingdom of Castile. But, in 1126, the king of Castile being obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a> with the whole strength of his dominions against his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> the king of Navarre and Arragon, Theresa took the opportunity of again seizing upon Tuy; but the king soon returning with a superior army, she was again obliged to abandon her conquest. But the greatest misfortune which befell this princess, was a quarrel with her own son Don Alonzo Enriquez. It does not appear indeed that Theresa had given him any just cause of offence; but it is certain that a civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> ensued, in which the queen's forces were totally defeated, and she herself made prisoner, in which situation she <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> during the remainder of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Enriquez having thus attained to the free and Don Alonso full possession of his dominions, made several attempts to make peace with the king of Castile, and that he was at last constrained to make peace with the Moors, who had affluence. He received the title of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> of the Spains; the more especially as his dominions happened to be at that time invaded by the Moors. The number of infidels was so great, that the count of Portugal had little hopes of subduing them; but a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> breaking out in the Moorish army, they were obliged to retreat; after which he reduced several places belonging to that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. But in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time the emperor Don Alonzo, breaking into the Portuguese territories, destroyed every thing with fire and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The king of Portugal surprized and cut off a considerable part of his army; which, however, did not hinder the emperor from marching directly towards him. But, at the intercession of the pope's legate, all differences were accommodated, and a peace concluded; all places and prisoners taken on both sides being delivered up. In the mean time, the progress of the Christian arms in Spain being reported to Abu-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALI">Ali</a> Teshen the miramamolin or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> monarch of the Moors in Barbary, he directed Ifmar, or Ishmael, his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> in Spain, to assemble all the forces in the southern provinces, and drive the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> beyond the Douro. Ishmael immediately began to prepare for putting these orders in execution; and having added a considerable body of troops brought from Barbary to those whom he had raised in Spain, the whole army was very numerous. He was met by Don Alonzo of Portugal in the plains of Ourique on the banks of the river Tayo; and Victory of Ourique. Ishmael took all possible means to prevent the Christians from passing that river, because his own cavalry, in which the strength of his army chiefly consisted, had thus more room to act. The Portuguese forces were very inconsiderable in number in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of the Moors; but Ishmael, being too confident of victory, divided his army into 12 bodies, and disposed them in such a manner as might best prevent the flight, not sustain the attack, of the Christians. The consequence was, that his army was overthrown with incredible slaughter, and a vast number of prisoners taken, among whom were 1000 Christians, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> styled Mozarabians, whom, at the request of Theotonus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">Cross</a>, Don Alfonso set at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> with their wives and children, and procured them settlements in his own dominions. After this signal victory, gained in the year 1139, Don Alfonso was proclaimed king by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, and ever after retained that title, renouncing all kind of subjection to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Spain. Being very desirous, however, of bringing <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the power of the emperor, he entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> with Raymond count of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a> and regent of the kingdom of Arragon, against that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. In consequence of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, he entered Galicia with a considerable force on one side, while Don Raymond did the same on the other. Neither of these enterprises, however, succeeded. The Portuguese monarch met with a severe check in his expedition into Galicia, where he received a dangerous wound, and had some of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> who attended him taken prisoners. At the same time he received intelligence that the Moors had invaded his dominions, so that he was obliged to retire; which, however, was not done in time sufficient to prevent the strong fortresses of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEYRIA">Leyria</a> from falling into their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. These fortresses demolished, and put all the garrison to the sword; but the king caused it to be rebuilt stronger than before, and put a more numerous garrison into it; however, he undertook nothing farther this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>. The war continued with various successes till the year 1145, when the king projected an enterprise against Santaren, a strong city about 12 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>. In this he luckily succeeded; and by that means gained a considerable track of country, and a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to his dominions. After this success Don Alfonso caused himself with much <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> to be chosen and crowned king of Portugal before an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the states, where he also solemnly renounced all dependence on the crown of Spain, declaring, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any of his successors should consent to pay tribute or to do homage to that crown, he was unworthy of enjoying the kingdom of Portugal. The next year the king undertook the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of Lisbon out of the hands of the Moors; and concerning this expedition there are such numbers of fables, that it is almost impossible to come at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. What can be gathered from these accounts is, that he undertook the siege with a small army, and was able to make but little progress in it, partly from the strength of the place, and partly from the numerous garrison by which it was defended. At length, fortunately for Don Alfonso, a fleet of adventurers, French, English, Germans, and Flemings, that were going to the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">Land</a>, anchored at the mouth of the river Tagus, whose assistance he demanded, as not altogether fo- reign to their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of making war on the infidels. Portugal. His request was readily granted; and, with their assistance, Lisbon was speedily reduced; which conquest so much raised the reputation of this monarch, and brought such numbers to recruit his army, that before the end of the year 1147 he had reduced 12 other considerable cities. For many years after this, Don Alfonso was successful in all his undertakings. He settled the internal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of his kingdom; procured a bull from pope Alexander III., confirming his regal dignity, undertook many successful expeditions against the Moors, and became <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of four of the six provinces which compose the present kingdom of Portugal. In all his undertakings, he was assisted by the counsels of his queen Matilda, who was a woman of great capacity, and sufficient for the government of the kingdom in her husband's absence. By her he had a numerous offspring, particularly three daughters; the eldest of whom, Donna Matilda, or Mathilda, was married to the king of Arragon; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, Urraca, to Don Ferdinand king of Leon; and the third, Theresa, to Philip <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. In 1166, however, the king His unselfish thought proper, from what provocation we know not, ceased war to invade the dominions of his son-in-law Don Ferdinand; and possessed himself of Limia and Turon, two cities of Galicia, in which he put strong garrisons. The next year, elated with his success, he marched with a numerous army towards Badajos, which he invested; on the news of which, Don Ferdinand, who had assembled a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> army at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CIUDAD_RODRIGO">Ciudad Rodrigo</a>, marched to its relief. Yet before he could come within sight of it, it had surrendered to the king of Portugal; upon which Don Ferdinand came to a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of besieging his antagonist in his newly conquered city; which Don Alfonso perceiving, endeavoured to draw out his forces into the field. Though he was at that time upwards of 70 years of age, he was himself on horseback, and pushing forwards at the head of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> to get out at the gate, he struck his leg against one of the bolts with such violence that the bone was shattered to pieces. This accident occasioned such confusion, that the Portuguese troops were easily beaten, and Don Alfonso was taken prisoner. He was exceedingly mortified by this disgrace, especially as he had no great reason to expect very kind treatment from his son-in-law. However, the king of Leon behaved towards him with the greatest respect and affection. He desired him to lay aside all thoughts of buffets, and attend to his cure; but finding him restless and impatient, he assured him that he expected nothing more than to have things put into the same condition as before the war, and that they might live in peace and friendship for the future: to which the king of Portugal most readily assented; but returned to his dominions before his cure was perfected, which was the cause of his being lame all the rest of his life. However, this did not abate his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> ardour; for notwithstanding this inconvenience, his courage transported him into the field wherever he was called by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his subjects. Towards the end of his reign, an opportunity seemed to present itself of obtaining once for all an entire release from the disagreeable pretensions of the king of Leon, who, it seems, had insisted on the king of Portugal's doing homage for his kingdom. The opportunity which now presented itself was a quarrel between the king of Leon and his nephew Don Alonfo king of Castile. The latter asked assistance from the king of Portugal, which was readily granted. But Don Ferdinand, having received intelligence that the infant Don Sancho (the king's eldest son) was advancing towards Ciudad Rodrigo, assembled his troops on that frontier with such diligence, that he was enabled to attack him unexpectedly, and entirely defeated him. Understanding, however, that Don Sancho was recruiting his forces with great diligence, he let him know that they might be much better employed against the infidels, who remained careless and unprepared, expecting the issue of the war. Don Sancho made a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this advice; and, after making some motions to amuse the enemy, made a sudden irruption into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, penetrating as far as Triana, one of the suburbs of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>. The Moors assembled their forces in order to attack him on his retreat; but Don Sancho having first fatigued them by the celerity of his march, at length chose a strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, and, having given his troops time to repose, drew them out and offered the enemy <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The Moors accepted the challenge, but were entirely defeated; and Don Sancho returned into Portugal with spoils to an immense value. For some years after, the war was continued without any remarkable event; but, in 1184, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> king of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, having already transported multitudes of men from Barbary, at length followed in person with a prodigious army, and carried all before him as far as the Tagus. He appeared before the city of Santarem; but having wearied and reduced his army by unsuccessful assaults on that place, he was attacked by the Portuguese forces assisted by Ferdinand of Leon, entirely defeated, and himself killed. By this victory, the Portuguese were left at liberty to improve the interior part of their country, and fortify their frontiers; and during this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, the king died in the 76th year of his age, in the year 1185. Don Alonfo was succeeded by his son Don Sancho I. Of this prince it is remarkable, that, before he ascended the throne, he was of a restless and warlike disposition; but no sooner did he come to the possession of the kingdom, than he became a lover of peace, and began with great assiduity to repair the cities that had suffered most by the war, and to repeople the country around them. By his steady <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to this, he in a very short time quite altered the appearance of his territories, and procured to himself the glorious title of The restorer of cities, and father of his country. In the year 1189, a fleet composed for the most part of English vessels, but having on board a great number of adventurers of other nations, bound to the Holy Land, entered the river of Lisbon. They were very kindly received, and supplied with all kinds of refreshments by Don Sancho, who took this opportunity of soliciting them to assist him in a design he had formed of attacking the city of Silves in Algarve, to which they readily yielded. Having joined a squadron of his own galleys, and marched a body of troops by land, the place was reduced, and the English, according to agreement, rewarded with the plunder. But, in a short time, the Moors from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> having again invaded Portugal, the town was several times taken and retaken, till at last, Don Sancho, being sensible of the difficulties that would attend the keeping of it, caused it to be demolished. His last enterprise was the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Elvas; soon after which he died with the reputation of the best economist that ever sat on the throne of Portugal. With the character of being rather liberal than avaricious, he had amassed a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of more than 700,000 crowns in ready <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, besides 1400 merks of silver, and 100 of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> plate, which he disposed of some time before his death. He was interred by his own command with much less pomp than his father, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>; and when his body was taken up 400 years after by order of the king Don Emanuel that it might be laid in a new <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, it was found uncorrupted. The history of Portugal affords scarce any event of importance till the year 1289; when, in the reign of Don Denis, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> commenced with Castile, which subsisted for a long time. Frequent reconciliation took place; but these were either of very short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, or never sincere. At length, in the reign of John I., Don Juan of Castile, who had also pretensions to the crown of Portugal, invaded that kingdom at the head of the whole force of his dominions, and with the flower of the Castilian nobility entered the province of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALENTEJO">Alentejo</a>. According to the Portuguese historians, he besieged the city of Elvas without effect; which disappointment enraged him to such a degree, that he determined next year to invade Portugal a second time, and ruin all the country before him. Accordingly, having collected an army of 30,000 men, he invaded Portugal, took and ruined several places, while king John lay inactive, with a small army, waiting for some English succours, which he expected. At last he ventured an engagement with the forces which he had; and, notwithstanding the great superiority of the enemy, obtained a complete victory; by defeated, after which he made an irruption into Castile, and had the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> another battle, which fixed him firmly on the throne of Portugal. The Castilians were obliged to consent to a truce of three years, which was soon after improved into a lasting peace. In 1214, king John undertook an expedition against the Moors in Barbary, where he commanded the city of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEUTA">Ceuta</a> taken from the Moors. But before he set out, his queen (Philippa the daughter of John duke of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>) died of grief at the thoughts of his absence. The expedition, however, proved successful, and the city of Ceuta was taken from the Moors almost at the first assault; but fearce had the king left that country, when the princes of Barbary formed a league for the recovery of it; and though they were defeated by the young princes of Portugal, whom John again sent into Barbary, yet the trouble of keeping it was so great, that some of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> were of opinion that the town should be demolished. But John, having considered the arguments on both sides, determined to keep the city; and therefore enlarged and strengthened the fortifications, augmenting his forces there to 6000 foot and 2500 horse, which he hoped would be sufficient for keeping off the attacks of the Moors. King John died in 1228, and was succeeded by his eldest son Edward. He undertook an expedition against <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TANGIER">Tangier</a> in Barbary; but the event proved very unfor- unfortunate; the Portuguese being so shut up by the Moors, that they were obliged to offer Ceuta back again, in order to obtain leave to return to Portugal. The king's son, Don Ferdinand, was left as a hostage for the delivery of Ceuta; but was, with the utmost cruelty and injustice, left in the hands of the infidels, by the king and council of Portugal, who constantly refused to deliver up the place. Many preparations indeed were made for recovering the prince by force; but before anything could be accomplished the king died in 1430, which put an end to all these designs. The war with Barbary continued at intervals, but with little success on the part of the Portuguese; and till the year 1497, there is no event of any consequence recorded in the history of Portugal. This year was remarkable for the discovery of the passage to the East Indies by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope. The enterprising spirit of the Portuguese had prompted them to undertake voyages along the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Africa for a considerable time before; but none of the voyagers had the good fortune to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the Cape of Good Hope, before Vasco da Gama, in the year abovementioned. He performed his voyage in two years, but with a great loss of men; for out of 148 persons whom he took out with him, only 55 returned. The king received him with all possible testimonies of respect and kindness; created him count of Vidigueira; and not only declared him <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of the Indies, but made that office <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> in his family. This discovery tended greatly to enrich the kingdom; but at the same time it proved detrimental, by inducing the most bold and enterprising adventurers to leave their country for the Indies, whence very few of them returned. The introduction of foreign luxuries also proved detrimental by corrupting the manners of the people, and producing an effeminacy unknown before. The settlements on the western coasts of Africa, of which there were now a great number, contributed also to produce the same effect. However, the king had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of beginning a correspondence with the emperor of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, and of gaining some advantages over the Moors in Barbary; but neither of these turned out to be of any service to the kingdom; for jealousy, envy, rapine, and every kind of vice, had diffused itself thro' the whole nation, inasmuch that the Portuguese could neither be unanimous among themselves, nor behave with propriety to any other nation. In September 1522, king Emanuel died of an epidemic fever, and was succeeded by his son John III. The most remarkable transaction of this prince's reign was the introduction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> into his dominions. This happened in the year 1525, or, as some say, in 1535. A famine happening to cease in a short time after it was introduced, the priests persuaded the ignorant multitude that it was a blessing from heaven on account of the erecting such an holy tribunal. However, it was not long before the bulk of the nation perceived what kind of a blessing the inquisition was; but their discernment came too late; for by that time the inquisitors had acquired such power, that it became equally dangerous and ineffectual to attempt disclosing any of their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>. In the mean time the Mohammedans, provoked at the continual depredations and arbitrary behaviour of the Portuguese in the East Indies, resolved to drive them all out at once. This scheme had been proposed by Campson <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of the Mamalukes in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, but Soliman at his affairs not allowing him to put it in execution, tempted to Soliman II., emperor of the Turks resolved to take drive the up the quarrel against the Portuguese; and accordingly sent orders to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BASHAW">bashaw</a> of Egypt to employ from their his whole strength against the Christians in the East Indies. The bashaw, into obedience to these orders, but in vain, failed out from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> with a greater naval force than ever the Mohammedans had employed before; having 4000 Janissaries, and 16,000 other land troops on board. Yet, by the courage and conduct of the Portuguese officers and soldiers, all this mighty armament was defeated, and their East <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> possessions saved from the danger which threatened them. In Africa likewise the king of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a> was baffled before the town of Safi, and fresh quarrels breaking out among the princes gave great relief to the Christians, who had long been obliged to carry on a defensive war, and had more than once been on the very brink of ruin.
