For a long time indeed their safety had been derived only from the quarrels of the Moors among themselves; for such was the envy and jealousy which reigned among the Portuguese, that they could never unite heartily in opposing the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> enemy, and therefore had their enemies united against them, they must certainly have been cut off. But whenever the sheriffs quarrelled with each other, one party was sure to have recourse to the Portuguese; who, by sending them a small supply, secured quiet to themselves, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of seeing their enemies destroy one another. Yet in the end even this had bad effects; for, on one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it kept up a martial spirit among the Moors, and on the other it made them acquainted with the Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; so that after every short interval of repose they not only found them as much enemies as before, but much more formidable than ever. The consequence of all was, that king John began to apprehend that the conquest of Barbary was impossible, and therefore began to limit his desires to the keeping of those few fortresses which he had already; which, though a necessary and prudent measure, displeased the generality of his subjects. King John exerted himself much in the settlement of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, which he brought into a very good state, caused several strong <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> to be erected there, and took all possible methods to encourage the conversion of the natives to Christianity. He also made many regulations for the welfare and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of his subjects. The disputes of the nobility about precedence were frequently attended with very disagreeable consequences, which made the king resolve once for all to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> them by established rules, and the rules established by him on this occasion have subsisted ever since, and in a great measure prevent these alterations. He had other great designs in his mind, particularly with regard to the reformation, which he had pushed very far with respect to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> persons of both sexes; but, on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of his affairs, he found his subjects in general to have been so much injured by his leaving their concerns to the inspection of his council, that he was thrown by the grief of it into a kind of apoplexy, from which he never recovered. His death happened in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1557; and he was succeeded by his son Don Sebastian III., an infant of three years of age. After the death of King John, the administration remained in the hands of the queen, grandmother to Sebastian, who behaved with great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and circumspection. The Moors, however, supposing that under a minority they might be able to dispossess the Christians of such places as they held in Barbary, laid close siege to Masagnan. But the queen-regent sent such speedy succours, and promised such rewards to those who distinguished themselves, that the Moors, though they brought 80,000 men into the field, were obliged to abandon the enterprise. This was at first magnified as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> instance of the queen's capacity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>; but in a short time the natural aversion which the Portuguese had to the government of women, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> they had against her country, as being a Castilian, appeared so plainly, and gave her so much uneasiness, that of her own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> she resigned her authority into the hands of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> Don Henry the king's brother. By him Don Alexius de Meneses was appointed the king's governor, and Gonçales de Gomera with two other prelates his preceptors. By means of these instructors young king the king's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> was totally marred. His governor affluently inculcated upon him that the chief virtue of a king was courage; that danger was never to be avoided, but always furtively, let the occasion be what it would. His other tutors, instead of instructing him in the true <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, only inspired him with an abhorrence of professed infidels: the consequence of all which was, that he became rash, inconsiderate, and obstinate; all which qualities conspired to draw upon him the catastrophe which ruined both him and the kingdom. After the king was grown up to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s estate, his desire was to distinguish himself against the infidels. He himself chose an expedition to the East Indies; but the prime minister Alceçova, who did not choose to attend his monarch to such a distance, substituted Africa in its stead. This expedition the king entered into in the most inconsiderate and absurd manner. He first sent over Don Antonio prior of Crato, with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of soldiers; carried his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> courtiers over with him from a hunting <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATCH">match</a>, and without equipages; he then sent for the duke of Aveyro, with such troops as he could collect on the short warning he had got; and when all these were assembled, the king spent his time in hunting, and flight excursions against the enemy, without doing anything of consequence, except <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> his person upon all occasions. At length he returned to Portugal in such tempestuous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, that his subjects had given him up for lost; when they were agreeably surprised by his unexpected arrival in the river of Lisbon, which they celebrated with the greatest rejoicings. The little success which attended the king in this expedition served only to inflame him more with desire for another; so that from the time he returned, he seemed to think on nothing else. He was highly delighted also with an accident which at this time furnished him with a pretence for war, though of that he stood in no great need. Muley Hamet, king of Fez and Morocco, had been dispossessed of his dominions by his uncle Muley Moloch. At the beginning of this war Don Sebastian had offered him his troops in Africa, which offer was rejected with contempt; but now being a fugitive, and having in vain applied for assistance to Philip of Spain, Muley Hamet applied to the king of Portugal; and, that he might the more easily succeed, caused the fortresses of Arzila, which his father had recovered, to be restored to the Portuguese. The king was in a rapture at this event, and fancied that his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> would exceed that of all his predecessors. He was advised against this expedition, however, by all his friends. King Philip of Spain having done every thing to dissuade him from it in a personal conference, sent Francisco Aldana, an old and experienced officer, to Morocco; and at his return ordered him to attend Don Sebastian, in order to give him an account of the state of affairs in that country. This he performed with the greatest fidelity, but without any effect. The queen dowager and cardinal united in their endeavours to divert him from this unfortunate enterprise; but he treated them both with so little respect, that his grandmother broke her heart, and the cardinal, to shew his distaste to the measure, retired to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVORA">Evora</a> without coming either to court or council; which example was followed by many of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>. Many of these, however, sent very free remonstrances to the king on the impropriety of his conduct; and king Philip sent to him the duke de Medina Celi, once more to lay before him the reasons why he thought his scheme impracticable, and to put him in mind that he had no hand in pushing him upon his destruction, or of concealing from him the dangers into which he seemed determined to plunge himself and his subjects. Lastly, he received a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> on the subject from Muley Moloch himself, wherein that prince explained to him his own <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the crown of Fez, and shewed that he had only dispossessed a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> and a murderer, who had therefore no right to his friendship or assistance. He next assured him that he had no reason to fear either the power or neighbourhood of the Portuguese; as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of which, and as a mark of his esteem, he was content to make him a present of ten miles of arable ground round each of the fortresses he possessed in Africa, and which indeed were no more than four, viz. Tangier, Ceuta, Masagan, and Arzila. At the same time he addressed himself to king Philip of Spain, with whom he was on good terms, desiring him to interpose with his nephew Sebastian, that things might be yet adjusted without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> blood. But the king of Portugal was deaf to all salutary advice; and therefore paid no regard to this letter, nor to the remonstrances of his uncle. On the 24th of June 1577, therefore, he set sail from the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of Lisbon with a fleet of 50 ships and five galleys, twelve pieces of cannon, and transports and tenders, making up near 1000 sail. His troops consisted of 9000 Portuguese foot; 3000 Germans; 700 Italians commanded by Sir Thomas Stukeley, an English exile, but remarkably brave; 2000 Castilians and 300 volunteers, commanded by Don Christopher de Tuvara master of the horse, a man of courage, but without either conduct or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. He touched first at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAGOS">Lagos</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> in the kingdom of Algarve, where he remained for four days; thence he proceeded to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>; where he was magnificently feasted. Portugal feasted for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> by the duke de <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-MEDINA_SIDONIA">Medina Sidonia</a>, who took the opportunity once more, by order of Philip, of dissuading him from proceeding further in person. But this exhortation proved as fruitless as the rest; and the king having failed with a strong <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> for Tangier, ordered Don Diego de Sousa, his commander in chief, to follow with the remaining part of the army. The troops landed on the coast of Africa without any bad accident, and joined at Arzila. Here the king was met by the sherif Muley Hamet, on whose account he had undertaken the war, who delivered him his son Muley, a boy of 12 years of age, as a hostage, and brought a reinforcement of 300 Moors. The boy was sent to Safagran under a strong <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>; but the father remained in the Portuguese camp. Here it was resolved in a council of war to reduce the town of Larache, but it was disputed whether the troops should proceed thither by land or sea. Don Sebastian, who espoused the former opinion, finding himself opposed by Muley Hamet, gave him such a rude answer, that he left his presence in discontent; after which the king's opinion prevailed, and the army began its march on the 29th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. As they proceeded, the king received a letter from the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a>, requesting him to attempt nothing beyond the taking of the town of Larache. Along with this letter was sent an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a> which had been worn by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. On the other hand Muley Moloch, having intelligence of this formidable invasion, took the field, though at that time so ill of a fever that he could not fit on horseback, with 40,000 foot and 60,000 horse. He conducted every thing, notwithstanding his distressed situation, with the greatest prudence. Finding some reason to suspect that part of his army were disposed of going over to his rival, he proclaimed that such as inclined to join their old master were at liberty to do it. This at once put a stop to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFECTION">defection</a>, and only a very few made use of the liberty which was granted them. Standing in doubt likewise of the fidelity of a body of 3000 horse, he sent them to reconnoitre the enemy, by which act of confidence he secured them. Still, however, he feared that his officers might be corrupted by the Portuguese gold; for which reason he changed the disposition of his army entirely, so that none of his officers commanded the corps to which they had been accustomed; and therefore, having new men to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> with, had none whom they could trust. Having taken these precautions, he advanced against the Portuguese army with such celerity, that he came in sight of them on the 3rd of August. On this Don Sebastian called a council of war; in which many who out of complaisance had given their opinions for this march, were now for returning. They were separated from the enemy by a river, and the Moors were masters of the ford, so that it was impossible to force them immediately in their posts; neither was it practicable for them to wait for a more favourable opportunity, because they had no <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. The foreign officers, on the contrary, were of opinion that fighting was now become necessary, and a retreat dangerous. This, however, was violently opposed by the sherif, who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> plainly that they ran a great risk of being defeated and of losing all, while at the same time they were not certain of gaining anything of consequence though they should be victorious; whereas, if they drew down towards the sea, they might entrench themselves till they were relieved by their fleet; during which interval if Muley Moloch should die, he looked upon it as certain that a great part of the army would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> to him, which would render him master not only of the kingdom, but of the fate of the Christians also. When he found that the king was bent on fighting, he only requested that the engagement might be delayed till 4 o'clock in the afternoon, that, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a defeat, they might have some chance of escaping; but even in this he could not prevail; for the king having disposed of every thing for a battle the next <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, was impatient to begin the onset as soon as it was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. In the mean time Muley Moloch was so sensible of the advantages of his situation, that he was inclined to take the whole Portuguese army prisoners; but finding his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> increase, so that he had no hopes of recovery, he came to a resolution to fight, that his antagonist might not avail himself of his death. The disposition of the Christian army was very regular and correct, through the care of some old officers in Don Sebastian's service: the infantry were disposed in three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; the battalion of volunteers made the vanguard; the Germans commanded by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBERG">Amberg</a>, and the Italians by Sir Thomas Stukeley, were on the right; the Castilian battalions on the left; the Portuguese in the centre and rear; the cavalry, consisting of about 1500 men, partly on the right under the command of the duke d'Avegro, to whom the sherif joined himself with his horse: on the left was the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> standard, with the rest of the cavalry, under the command of the duke of Barcelos eldest son to the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRAGANZA">Braganza</a>, Don Antonio prior of Crato, and several other persons of great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The king took <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a> at first with the volunteers. Muley Moloch disposed also his troops in three lines: the first consisted of the Andalusian Moors, commanded by three officers who had distinguished themselves in the wars of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>; the second of renegadoes; and the third of the natives of Africa. They moved in a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, with 10,000 horse on each wing, and the rest in the rear, with orders to extend themselves in such a manner as to encompass the Christian army. Muley Moloch, though extremely weak, was taken out of his litter, and set on horseback, that he might see how his commands had been obeyed; and being perfectly satisfied with the situation of his troops, he directed the signal of battle to be given. The Christians advanced with the greatest resolution; broke the first line of the Moorish infantry, and disordered the second. On this Muley Moloch drew his sword, and would have advanced to encourage his troops, but that his guards prevented him; on which his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a> of mind was so great, that he fell from his horse. One of his guards caught him in his arms, and conveyed him to his litter; where he immediately expired, having only time to lay his finger on his lips by way of enjoining them to conceal his death. But by this time the Moorish cavalry had wheeled quite round, and attacked the Christian army in the rear: upon which the cavalry in the left wing made such a vigorous effort that they broke the Portuguese on the right; and at this time the sherif, in passing a rivulet Portugal. rivulet was drowned. In this emergency, the Germans, Italians, and Castilians, did wonders; but the Portuguese, according to their own historians, behaved indifferently. Attacked on all sides, however, they were unable to resist; and the whole army, except about 50 men, were killed or taken prisoners. The fate of the king is variously related. According to some, he had two horses killed under him, and then mounted a third. His bravest officers were killed in his defense; after which the Moors surrounding him, seized his person, stripped him of his sword and arms, and secured him. They immediately began to quarrel about whose prisoner he was; upon which one of the generals rode in among them, crying, "What, you dogs, when God has given you so glorious a victory, would you cut one another's throats about a prisoner?" at the same discharging a blow at Sebastian, he brought him to the ground, when the rest of the Moors soon dispatched him. Others affirm, that one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> de Brito meeting the king with his standard wrapped round him, Sebastian cried out, "Hold it fast, let us die upon it!" upon which charging the Moors, he was seized, rescued by Brito, who was himself taken with the standard, and carried to Fez. He affirmed, that after he was taken, he saw the king at a distance, and unpursued. Don Lewis de <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a> met him afterwards making towards the river, and this is the last account we have of his being seen alive. Muley Hamet, the brother of Muley Moloch, was proclaimed king by the Moors immediately after the battle. Next day, having ordered all the prisoners to be brought before him, the new sovereign gave orders to search for the body of Don Sebastian. The king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VALET">valet</a>-de-chambre brought back a body, which he said was that of his master, but so disfigured with wounds, that it could not well be known; so that notwithstanding the most diligent search, this monarch's death could never be properly authenticated. This body, however, was preferred by Muley Hamet, who delivered it up as the body of Don Sebastian, to king Philip of Spain. By him it was sent to Ceuta, from whence it was transported to Portugal, and buried among his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> at Belem, with all possible solemnity. By this terrible disaster, the kingdom of Portugal, from being the most eminent, sunk at once into the lowest rank of the European states. All the young nobility were cut off, or carried into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>: the kingdom was exhausted of men, money, and reputation; so that Don Henry, who assumed the government after the death of his brother Don Sebastian, found himself in a very disagreeable situation. The transactions of his reign were quite trifling and unimportant; but after his death a great revolution took place. The crown of Portugal was claimed by three different competitors; viz. the prince of Parma, the duchess of Braganza, and king Philip of Spain. Whatever might have been the merits of their respective claims, the power of Philip quickly decided the contest in his favour. He found his schemes facilitated by the treachery of the regents, who took the most scandalous methods of putting the kingdom into his hands. Under pretence of inspecting the magazines, they took out some of the powder, and mixed the rest with sand: they appointed an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> to go to France for succours, from whence they knew that they could not arrive in time; they dissolved the states as soon as they discovered that they were bent on maintaining the freedom of the nation; and, under a show of confidence, sent off to distant places such of the nobility as they suspected. King Philip, finding everything in his favour, commanded the duke of Alva to invade Portugal, at the head of 20,000 men. The people, perceiving that they were betrayed, exclaimed against the governors, and placed on the throne Don Antonio prior of Crato. But his forces being inexperienced, and he himself behaving in a very improper manner, he was quickly defeated by the duke of Alva, and forced to fly out of the kingdom, which he effected with great difficulty. On his flight the whole kingdom submitted; together with the garrisons in Barbary, the settlements on the western coast of Africa, of Brazil, and in the East Indies. All the Madeiras, however, except the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of St Michael, held out for Don Antonio until they were reduced, and the French <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, who came to their assistance, entirely defeated and destroyed. Philip made his entry into Lisbon as soon as the kingdom was totally reduced, and endeavoured to conciliate the affections of the people by confirming the terms which he had before offered to the states. These terms were, that he would take a solemn oath to maintain the privileges and liberties of the people; that the states should be assembled within the realm, and nothing proposed in any other states that related to Portugal; that the viceroy or chief governor should be a native, unless the king should give that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> to one of the royal family; that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> should be kept on the same footing; that the post of first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, and of all offices, civil, military, and judicial, should be filled with Portuguese; all dignities in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and in the orders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> confined to the same; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of Ethiopia, Africa, and the Indies, reserved also to them, and to be carried on only by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and vessels; that he would remit all imposts on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> revenues; that he would make no <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of any city, town, or jurisdiction royal, to any but Portuguese; that estates resulting from forfeitures should not be united to the domain, but go to the relations of the last possessor, or be given to other Portuguese for recompense of services; that when the king came to Portugal, where he should reside as much as possible, he should not take the houses of private persons for his officers lodging, but keep to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of Portugal; that wherever his majesty resided, he should have an ecclesiastic, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, two masters of requests, with under officers, all of them Portuguese, who should dispatch every thing relating to the kingdom; that Portugal should ever continue a distinct kingdom, and its revenue be consumed within itself; that all matters of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> should be decided within the realm; that the Portuguese should be admitted to charges in the households of the king and queen of Spain; that all duties on the frontiers should be taken away; and lastly, that Philip should give 300,000 ducats to redeem prisoners, repair cities, and relieve the miseries which the plague and other calamities had brought upon the people. people. All these conditions, formerly offered and rejected by the Portuguese, the king now confirmed; but whereas the duke of Ofluna, by way of security for these conditions, had promised them a law, that if the king did not adhere to them, the states should be freed from their obedience, and might defend their right by the sword, without incurring the reproach of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>, or the guilt of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>; this he absolutely refused to ratify. All these concessions, however, did not answer the purpose; nay, though Philip was to the last degree lavish of honours and employments, the Portuguese were still dissatisfied. This had also an effect which was not foreseen: it weakened the power, and absorbed the revenues, of the crown; and, by putting it out of the power of any of his successors to be liberal in the same proportion, it raised only a short-lived gratitude in a few, and left a number of malcontents, to which time was continually adding. Thus Philip, with all his policy, and endeavours to please, found his new subjects still more and more disgusted with his government, especially when they found their king treating with the utmost severity all those who had supported Don Antonio. The exiled prince, however, still styled himself king of Portugal. At first he retired to France, and there demanded succours for the recovery of his dominions. Here he found so much countenance, that with a fleet of near 60 sail, and a good body of troops on board, he made an attempt upon the Terceras, where his fleet was <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> by the Spaniards; and a great number of prisoners being taken, all the officers and gentlemen were beheaded, and a great number of meaner people hanged. Don Antonio, notwithstanding, kept possession of some places, coined money, and did many other acts of regal power; but was at length constrained to retire, and it was with some difficulty that he did this, and returned into France. He passed from thence into England, where he was well received; and many fitted out <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a> to cruise against the Spaniards under his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>. But after king Philip had ruined the naval power of Portugal as well as Spain, by equipping the armada, Queen <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> made no difficulty of owning and aiding Don Antonio, and even of sending Sir John Norris and Sir Francis Drake with a strong fleet and a great army to restore him. Upon this occasion Don Antonio sent his son Don Christopher a hostage to Muley Hamet king of Fez and Morocco, who was to lend him 200,000 ducats. But king Philip prevented this by surrendering Arzila; and this disappointment, the unseasonable enterprise upon Corunna, and the disputes that arose between Norris and Drake, rendered that expedition abortive; so that, except carrying the plague into England, it was attended with no consequences worthy of notice. He remained some time after in England; but finding himself little regarded, he withdrew once more into France, where he fell into great poverty and distress; and at length dying in the 64th year of his age, his body was buried in the church of the nuns of Ave <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a>, with an inscription on his tomb, in which he is styled king. He left several children behind him, who, on account of his being a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, and having made a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOW">vow</a> of virginity at his entrance into the order, were looked upon as illegitimate. He preserved, even to the day of his death, a great interest in Portugal; and had drawn from thence, in the course of his life, immense sums of money; which had been squandered in many fruitless negotiations, and attempts to disturb the possessions of king Philip in almost all parts of his dominions, and particularly in the Indies, where the Portuguese were rather more averse to the Castilian yoke, or at least testified their aversion more openly, than in Europe. But Don Antonio was not the only pretender to the crown of Portugal: for the people, partly through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of their prince, and partly from their hatred to the Castilians, were continually feeding themselves with the hopes that Don Sebastian would appear and deliver them; and in this respect such a spirit of credulity reigned, that it was said proverbially, they would have taken a negro for Don Sebastian. This humour put the son of a tyler at Alcobaza, who had led a profligate life, and at length turned hermit, to give himself out for that prince; and having with him two companions, one of them styled himself Don Christopher de Tavora, and the other the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARDA">Guarda</a>, they began to collect money, and were in a fair way of creating much disturbance, if the cardinal <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-duke had not caused him to be apprehended; and after leading him ignominiously through the streets of Lisbon, he who took the name of Sebastian was sent to the galleys for life, and the pretended bishop was hanged. Not long after, Gonfalo Alvarez, the son of a mason, gave himself out for the same king, and having promised marriage to the daughter of Pedro Alonso, a rich yeoman, whom he created earl of Torres Novas, he assembled a body of about 800 men, and some blood was spilt before he was apprehended; at length, being clearly proved to be an impostor, himself and his intended father-in-law were publicly hanged and quartered at Lisbon; which, instead of extinguishing this humour, farther increased it. There was, however, a person who appeared, about 20 years after the fatal defeat of Sebastian, at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, a remarkable one, who created much more trouble. He assumed the name of Don Sebastian, and gave a very distinct account of the manner in which he had passed his time from that defeat. He affirmed, that he had preserved his life and liberty by hiding himself amongst the slain; that, after wandering in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> for some time in Africa, he returned with two of his friends into the kingdom of Algarve; that he gave notice of this to the king Don Henry; that finding his life fought, and being unwilling to disturb the peace of the kingdom, he returned again among the Moors, and passed freely from one place to another in Barbary, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a penitent; that after this he became a hermit in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; but at length resolved to go to Rome, and discover himself to the pope. On the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> he was robbed by his domestics, and came almost naked to Venice, where he was known, and acknowledged by some Portuguese. Complaint being made to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, he was obliged to retire to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>. But the governor of that city ordering him also to depart, he, not knowing what to do, returned again to Venice; where, at the request of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, who <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> him not only with being an impostor, but also with many <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and atrocious crimes, he was seized, and thrown into prison. He underwent 28 examinations before a committee of noble and... and impartial persons; in which he not only acquitted himself clearly of all the crimes that had been laid to his charge, but entered also into so minute a detail of the transactions that had passed between himself and the republic, that the commissioners were perfectly astonished, and shewed no disposition to declare him an impostor; moved more especially by the firmness of his behaviour, his singular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, the sobriety of his life, his exemplary piety, and his admirable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> under his afflictions. The noise of this was diffused throughout Europe, and the enemies of Spain endeavoured everywhere to give it <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. The state, however, refused to discuss the great point, whether he was or was not an impostor, unless they were requested to do so by some prince or state in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with them. Upon this the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> sent Don Christopher, the son of the late Don Antonio, to make that demand; and at his request an examination was made with great solemnity: but no decision followed; only the senate set him at liberty, and ordered him to depart their dominions in three days. He went therefore, by the advice of his friends, to Padua, but in the disguise of a monk, and from thence to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>; where he was arrested by the command of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> duke, who delivered him to the viceroy of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. The count de Lemos, then in possession of that dignity, died soon after, before whom he was first brought; this man assured, he must know him to be Don Sebastian, since he had been twice sent to him from the king of Spain. He remained prisoner several years in the castle of Ovo, where he endured incredible hardships. At length he was brought out, led with infantry through the streets of the city, and declared to be an impostor, who assumed the name of Sebastian: at which words, when proclaimed before him, he said gravely, And so I am. In the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> it was affirmed, that he was in truth a Calabrian; which as soon as he heard, he said, It is false. He was next shipped on board a galley as a slave; then carried to St Lucar, where he was some time confined; from thence he was transferred to a castle in the heart of Castile, and never heard of more. Some persons were executed at Lisbon for their endeavours to raise an insurrection on his behalf; but it was thought strange policy, or rather a strange want of policy, in the Spaniards, to make this affair so public without proofs; and the attempt to silence this objection, by affirming him to be a magician, was justly looked upon as ridiculous. The administration of affairs in Portugal, during the reign of Philip, was certainly detrimental to the nation; and yet it does not appear that this flowed so much from any ill intention in that monarch, as from errors in judgment. His prodigious preparations for the invasion of England impoverished all his European dominions; but it absolutely exhausted Portugal. The pretensions of Don Antonio, and the hopes of despoiling their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> fleets, exposed the Portuguese to the resentment of the English; from which the king having granted away all his domains, wanted power to defend them. Their clamours were not at all the less loud for their being in some measure without cause. The king, to pacify them, borrowed money from the nobility upon the customs, which were the only sure remedy he had still left; and this was attended with fatal consequences. The branches, thus mortgaged, became, and continue to this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, fixed and hereditary; so that the merchant was oppressed, and the king received nothing. This expedient failing, a tax of three per cent. was imposed, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of ship-money, for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the coasts and the commerce, which for some years was properly applied; but then made a part of the ordinary revenue, and went into the king's exchequer without account. This made way for diverting other appropriated branches; as for instance, that for the repair of fortifications, the money being strictly levied, and the works suffered to decay and tumble down; and for the maintenance of the conquests in Africa, by which the garrisons mouldered away, and the places were lost. Upon the whole, in the space of 18 years, the nation was visibly impoverished: and yet the government of Philip was incomparably better than that of his successors; so that his death was justly regretted; and the Portuguese were taught by experience to confess, that of bad matters he was the best. His son Philip, the second of Portugal and the third of Spain, sat 20 years upon the throne before he made a visit to Portugal, where the people put themselves to a most enormous expense to receive him; for which they received little more than the compliment, that, before his entry into Lisbon, he knew not how great a king he was. He held an assembly of the estates, in which his son was sworn successor. Having done all that he wanted for himself, he acquired a false idea of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of the nation from an immoderate and foolish display of them during his short stay at Lisbon; and having shown himself little, and done less, he returned into Spain; where he acted the part of a good king upon his deathbed, in deploring bitterly that he never thought of acting it before. The reign of Philip III., Great losses and IV. was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of worse <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, and worse fortune: all his dominions suffered greatly; Portugal most of all. The loss of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a> in the East, of Brazil in the West Indies, together with the shipwreck of a fleet sent to escort that from Goa, brought the nation incredibly low, and encouraged the conde duke to hope they might be entirely crushed. These are the heads only of the transactions for 40 years: to enter in any degree into the particulars, is, in other words, to point out the breaches made by the Spanish ministers on the conditions granted by king Philip; which, with respect to them, was the original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, and unalterable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of Portugal while subject to the monarchs of Castile; and which, notwithstanding, they so often and so flagrantly violated, that one would have imagined they had studied to provoke the wrath of heaven, and insult the patience of men, instead of availing themselves, as they might have done, of the riches, power, and martial spirit of the Portuguese people. It was the very basis and foundation of their privileges, that the kingdom should remain separate and independent, and consequently that Lisbon should continue as much its capital as ever, the several supreme councils and courts residing; so that the natives of this realm might not be obliged to travel in search of justice. So little, or at least so short a time was this observed, that neither promotion nor justice was to be obtained without journeys, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> was not more the capital of Castile than of Portugal. The general assembly of estates was to be held frequently, and they were held thrice in the space of 60 years; and of these twice twice within the first three. The king was to reside in this realm, as often and as long as possible; in compliance with which, Philip I. was there but once, Philip II., but four months, and Philip III. was never there at all. The household establishment was suppressed through all their reigns. The viceroy was to be a native of Portugal, or a prince or princess of the blood; yet when any of the royal family bore the title, the power was in reality in the hands of a Spaniard. Thus, when the princess of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a> was vice-queen, the marquis de la Puebla was to assist in council, and in all dispatches; and she was to do nothing without his advice. The council of Portugal, which was to be composed entirely of natives, was filled with Castilians, as the garrisons also were, though the contrary had been promised. The presidents of provinces, or corregidors, were to be natives; but by keeping those offices in his own hands, the king eluded this article. No city, town, or district, were to be given but to Portuguese; yet the duke of Lerma had <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEJA">Beja</a>, Serpa, and other parts of the demesnes of the crown, which were formerly appanages of the princes of the blood. None but natives were capable of offices of justice, in the revenue, in the fleet, or of any post civil or military; yet these were given promiscuously to foreigners, or sold to the highest bidder; not excepting the governments of castles, cities, and provinces. The natives were so far from having an equal chance in such <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, that no posts in the presidials were ever given to them, and scarce any in garrisons; and whenever it happened, in the case of a person of extraordinary merit, whose pretensions could not be rejected, he was either removed, or not allowed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> his charge; as fell out to the marquis of Marialva and others. The forms of proceeding, the jurisdiction, the ministers, the secretaries, were all changed, in the council of Portugal; being reduced from five to three, then two, and at last to a single person. By reason of these and many other grievances too tedious to be mentioned here, the detestation of the Spanish government became universal; and in 1640 a revolution took place, in which John duke of Braganza was declared king, by the title of John IV. This revolution, as being determined by the almost unanimous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of the nation, was attended with very little effusion of blood; neither were all the efforts of the king of Spain able to regain his authority. Several attempts indeed were made for this purpose. The first battle was fought in the year 1644, between a Portuguese army of 6000 foot and 1100 horse, and a Spanish army of nearly the same number. The latter were entirely defeated; which contributed greatly to establish the affairs of Portugal on a firm basis. The king carried on a defensive war during the remainder of his life; but after his death, which happened in 1655, the war was renewed with great vigour. The marquis of Marialva gained another battle at Elvas; and in 1665 the fortune of the war was finally decided in favour of the Portuguese by the victory of Monteflores, which entirely broke the power of the Spaniards, and since that time they have never been able to undertake any thing of moment against Portugal. But though the Portuguese had recovered their liberty, they have entirely lost their consequence in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of Europe; and had not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, for commercial reasons, constantly kept their powerful neighbours in awe, it is more than probably that the country would long since have again become a province of Spain; of which the last invasion of Portugal by the Spaniards affords a convincing proof. See BRITAIN, no. 449. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> of Portugal, in the southern provinces, would be excessive hot, if it were not refreshed by the sea breezes; but in the northern, it is much cooler, and the weather more subject to rains. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> is extremely delightful here; and the air, in general, more temperate than in Spain. Lisbon has been much reported to be late by valetudinarians, and consumptive persons, from Great Britain, on account of its air. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very fruitful in wine, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, lemons, oranges, pomegranates, figs, raisins, almonds, chestnuts, and other fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; but there is a want of corn, owing, it is said, in a great measure to the neglect of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. There is plenty of excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> here; and also of sea and river-fish, and sea-fowl. The horses in Portugal are brisk lively animals, as they are in Spain, but of a slight make; but mules being surer-footed, are more used for carriage and draught. By reason of the scarcity of pasture, there are not many herds of cattle or flocks of sheep; and what they have are small and lean, though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is tolerably good: their beef meat is said to be that of hogs and kids. The country in many parts is mountainous: but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> contain all kinds of ores; particularly of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, tin and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, with a variety of gems, beautifully variegated marble, mill-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and many curious fossils. Not far from Lisbon is a mine of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-petre; but none of the metal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> are here worked, the inhabitants being supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> of all kinds from their foreign settlements. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Minho, in Latin Minius; the Limia, anciently the famed Lethe; the Cavado; the Douro; the Guadiana, anciently Anas; and the Tajo, or Tagus, which is the largest river in the kingdom, carrying some gold in its sands, and falling into the sea a little below Lisbon. There are several mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> in the kingdom, both hot and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, which are much frequented. The only religion tolerated in Portugal is that of the church of Rome; yet there are many concealed Jews, and those too even among the nobility, bishops, prebends, monks, and nuns, and the very inquisitors themselves. If a Jew pretends to be a Christian and a Roman catholic, while he is really a Jew, by going to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, confession, &c. or if after being converted, or pretending to be converted and pardoned, he relapses in Judaism and is discovered, the inquisition lays hold of him. In the first case, if they renounce Judaism, they are only condemned to some corporal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> or public shame, and then ordered to be instructed in the Christian religion. In the second, they are condemned to the flames without mercy. Besides Jews and heretics, who <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BROACH">broach</a> or maintain any doctrines contrary to the religion of the country, the inquisition punishes all sodomites, pretenders to sorcery and the black art, apostates, blasphemies, perjured persons, impostors, and hypocrites. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of those condemned by the inquisition, is called an auto da fé, or "act of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>." There are several tribunals of the inquisition, one of which is at Goa in the East Indies; but there are none in Brazil. The number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> in Portugal in Portugal is said to be 900. The order of Jesuits hath been suppressed in this country, as they have been in others. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, several archbishops and bishops; the patriarch is always a cardinal, and of the royal family. The archbishops rank with marquises, and the bishops with counts. The Portuguese have archbishops and bishops in the other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the world, as well as in Europe. The sums raised by the popes here, by virtue of their prerogatives, are thought to exceed the revenues of the crown, and the nuncios never fail of acquiring vast fortunes in a short time. Though there are two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> and several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>, yet while the papal power, and that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, continues at such a height, true learning is like to make but a small progress. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the Portuguese does not differ much from that of Spain: Latin is the ground-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of both; but the former is more remote from it, and harsher to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, than the latter. The Portuguese tongue is spoken on all the coasts of Africa and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> as far as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, but mixed with the languages of the several nations in those distant regions. With regard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, there are very few in Portugal, and those chiefly coarse silks, woollen cloths, and some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>; but their foreign trade is very considerable, especially with England, which takes a great deal of their wine, salt, foreign commodities, and fruits, in return for its woollen manufactures, with which the Portuguese furnish their colonies and subjects in Asia, Africa, and America. Their plantations in Brazil are very valuable, yielding gold, diamonds, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, copper, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, ginger, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, drugs, dying woods, &c. From their plantations in Africa, they bring gold and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, and slaves to cultivate their sugar and tobacco plantations in Brazil. They have still several settlements in the East Indies, but far less considerable than formerly, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AZORES">Azores</a> or Western Isles, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a> and the Cape de Verde <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> also belong to them; but a great part of the riches and merchandize brought from these distant countries becomes the property of foreigners, for the goods they furnish the Portuguese with to carry thither. The king's fifth of the gold brought from Brazil amounts commonly to about 300,000 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>; so that the whole annual produce of gold in Brazil may be estimated at near 2,000,000 Sterling. Lisbon is the greatest port in Europe next to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>. As to the constitution of Portugal, it is an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> hereditary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>. Both here and in Spain, there were anciently cortes, states, or parliaments; but they have long since entirely lost their share in the legislature. For the administration of the civil government, there is a council of state, and several secretaries; for military affairs, a council of war; for the finances, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>-court; and, for the distribution of justice, several high tribunals, with others subordinate to them, in the several districts into which the kingdom is divided. The cities have their particular magistracy. The proceedings of the courts are regulated by the Roman law, the royal edicts, the canon law, and the pope's mandates. Like the Spaniards, they transact most of their business in the mornings and evenings, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> at noon. The nobility are very numerous, and many of them are descended from natural sons of the royal family. They are divided into high and low. The high consists of the dukes, marquises, counts, viscounts, and barons, who are also grandees, but of different classes, being suffered to be covered in the king's presence, and having the title of dons, with a pension from the royal treasury, to enable them the better to support their dignity: the king styles them illusirious in his letters, and treats them as princes. A duke's sons are also grandees and his daughters rank as marchionesses. The inferior nobility or gentry are termed Hidalgos, i.e., gentlemen; they cannot assume the title of don, without the king's licence. The revenues of the crown, since the discovery of the Brazilian mines are very considerable; but the real amount can only be guessed at. Some have said that it amounts, clear of all salaries and pensions, to upwards of 3,000,000 Sterling; others make it a great deal less. Thus much is certain, that the customs and other taxes run excessively high. Besides the royal demesnes, the hereditary estates of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Braganza, the monopoly of Brazil snuff, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COINAGE">coinage</a>, the money arising from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of indulgences granted by the pope, the fifth of the gold brought from Brazil, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FARM">farm</a> of the Brazil diamonds, the masterships of the orders of knighthood, and other sources, yield very large sums. The forces, notwithstanding, of this nation, both by sea and land, are very inconsiderable; their land-forces being the worst <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> in Europe, and their navy of little importance. They would be an easy conquest to the Spaniards if they were not under the protection of Britain. There are several orders of knighthood here, viz. Orders of the order of Christ, the badge of which is a red cross within a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> one, and the number of the commanderies 454. 2. The order of St James, the badge of which is a red sword in the shape of a cross. A great number of towns and commanderies belong to this order. 3. The order of Aviz, whose badge is a green cross in form of a lily, and the number of its commanderies 49. Though these three orders are religious, yet the knights are at liberty to marry. 4. The order of St John, which has also several commanderies. The king's titles are, King of Portugal and the Algarves, on this side and the other side the sea of Africa; titles, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, conquests, and commerce, in Ethiopia, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, India, &c. The king's eldest son is styled Prince of Brazil. In the year 1749, pope Benedict XIV. dignified the king with the title of His most faithful majesty. The Portuguese are represented as inferior to the character Spaniards both in person and genius; as extremely haughty, treacherous, and crafty in their dealings, much given to avarice and fury; and vindictive, malicious, and cruel. The meaner sort are said to be extremely addicted to thieving; notwithstanding, it must be owned, that they have shown themselves on many occasions a brave and warlike people. They are justly famed for their skill in navigation; and for the many discoveries they have made, both in the East and West Indies. The women here, and in other countries of the same degree of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, are not so prolific as in the colder climates; but they are said to be very beautiful whilst young, though their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>... Portugalica is somewhat upon the olive. Their eyes are very black and sparkling, and retain their brilliancy after all their other charms are gone. It is the fashion here, at present, as in most other countries, for the ladies to spoil and disfigure their skins and complexions with paints and washes; but, though lively and witty, they are said to have a nice sense of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> honour. Both men and women make great use of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a>; often not so much to aid their sight, as to denote their wisdom and gravity. Their dress, like that of the Spaniards, never used to vary till of late, especially among the men; but of late years, both men and women have given much into the French modes. The women, when they go abroad on foot, are wont to use long veils, which cover their heads, but leave their faces bare.

PORTUGALLICA TERRA

Pages 95-95
earth of Portugal; the name of a fine alluring bole, dug in great plenty in the northern part of Portugal.

PORTULACA

Pages 95-95

purslane; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the dodecandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, but the two following are the most remarkable. 1. The oleracea, annual <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> culinary purslane, rises with herbaceous, low, succulent, branchy stalks, six or eight inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, garnished with wedge-shaped, thick, succulent-leaves, and small clove-setting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. There are two varieties; one with deep green leaves, the other with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> leaves; both of which rise from the same seed. 2. The anacampferos, perennial or shrubby <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> purslane, rises with a shrubby branchy stalk, about six inches high, with oval, gibbous, succulent leaves, and the stalks terminated by small clusters of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> flowers. Both these plants are of a succulent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: the first is an herbaceous annual, for culinary uses; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> a shrubby perennial, raised by the curious for variety. They are both exotics of a tender <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, of the temperature of greenhouse or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STOVE">stove</a>-plants. The common culinary purslane is raised annually from seed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, and is an excellent ingredient in summer salads, but improper for winter on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> moist nature. The plant being tender, must be raised either on a hot-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>, or in a warm border; in which last it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not succeed before April or May. The shrubby form must be kept in the hot-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, in pots of dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>.

POSITIVE

Pages 95-95

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> of relation, opposed to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>. It is also used in opposition to relative <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> arbitrary: thus we say, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">Beauty</a> is no positive thing, but depends on the different tastes of people. Positive <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">Degree</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, is the adjective in its simple signification, without any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>. Positive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>. In the Franklinian system all bodies supposed to contain more than their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of electric <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, are said to be positively electrified; and those from whom some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their electricity is supposed to be taken away, are said to be electrified negatively. These two electricities being first produced, one from glass, the other from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> or resin, the former was called vitreous, the latter resinous electricity.

POSSE COMITATUS

Pages 95-95

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies the power of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the aid and assistance of all the knights, gentlemen, yeomen, labourers, servants, apprentices, &c., and all others within the county that are above the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 15, except women, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> persons, and such as are decrepit and infirm. This posse comitatus is to be raised where a riot is committed, a possession kept upon a forcible entry, or any force of rescue used contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s writ, or in opposition to the execution of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; and it is the duty of all sheriffs to assist justices of the peace in the suppression of riots, &c., and to raise the posse comitatus, or to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men for that purpose.

POSSESSION

Pages 95-95

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is either actual, where a person actually enters into lands <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> tenements defended or conveyed to him; or where lands are defended to a person, and he has not yet entered into them. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> possession is much favoured by the law, as an argument of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, even tho' no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> can be shown, and it is more regarded than an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> deed without possession. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he that is out of possession of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> brings an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, he must prove an undeniable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to it; and when a person would recover any thing of another, it is not sufficient to destroy the title of the person in possession, without he can prove that his own right is better than his. In order to make possession lawful upon an entry, the former possessor and his servants are to be removed from off the premises entered on; but a person by leave and release, is in possession without making any entry upon the lands. Possession, in Scots law. See Law, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> III, No. clxii. 11, &c. Demoniacal Possession. See Demon, Demoniacs, and Demoniacal, in the Appendix.

POSSESSIVE

Pages 95-95

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRONOUNS">pronouns</a>, which denote the enjoyment <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> possession of anything either in particular, or in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>: as meus, "mine;" and tuis, "thine." Possessory <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">Action</a>, in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>. See Law, No. clxxxiii. 18.

POSSIBILITY

Pages 95-95

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is defined to be anything that is altogether uncertain, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> what may or may not be.

POSSIBILITY ALSO

Pages 95-95

y also denotes a non-repugnance to existing, in any thing that does not any way exist.

POSSIBLE

Pages 95-95

is sometimes opposed to real existence, and is understood of a thing, which, though it actually does not exist, yet may exist; as a new <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a>.

POST

Pages 95-96

a courier <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIER">carrier</a>; or one who frequently changes horses, posted or placed on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, for quicker dispatch. We find mention made of post-horses in the Theodosian Code, De curfu publica; but these were very different from the present establishment, and were only public horses first appointed by Trajan, till whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the messengers seized any horses that came in their way. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Hornigk has an express treatise on posts, whereof he makes four kinds: viz. on horseback, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>, in boats, and on foot; which last kind is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> ascribes the origin of posts to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>; but the posts instituted by those princes were no more than couriers. In effect, posts on the present footing are but a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>; though some go back as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>.—It is certain it was the policy, or rather the dissidence, of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XI. of France that they owed their rise to; that uneasy <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> first settling them by an ordonnance of the 19th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1464, to be the sooner, and the more surely, advertised of what passed in his own <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and in the neighbouring states. From France, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> propagated itself, by degrees, through the several other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In Germany, Hornigk observes, Posts were first settled by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Taxis at his own expense; in acknowledgment whereof, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Matthias, in 1716, gave him, in fact, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of post-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> under him and his successors. The duty for the carriage of letters by post in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, forms a branch of the Revenue. This useful invention owes its first legislative establishment in England to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> 1643. It is true, there existed post-masters in much earlier times: but their business was confined to the furnishing of post-horses to persons who were desirous to travel expeditiously, and to the dispatching of extraordinary packages upon special occasions. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. originally erected a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST_OFFICE">post-office</a> under the control of one Matthew de Queker or de l'Equeter for the conveyance of letters to and from foreign parts; which office was afterwards claimed by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Stanhope, but was confirmed and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to William Frizzell and Thomas Witherings by king <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. A.D. 1632, for the better accommodation of the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. In 1635, the same prince erected a letter-office for England and Scotland, under the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the same Thomas Witherings, and settled certain <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RATES">rates</a> of postage. But this extended only to a few of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, the times of carriage were uncertain, and the post-masters on each road were required to furnish him with horses at the rate of £4½ d. a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a>. Witherings was superseded, for abuses in the execution of both his offices, in 1640; and they were sequestrated into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Burlamachy, to be exercised under the care and oversight of the king's principal secretary of state. On the breaking out of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> confusions and interruptions were necessarily occasioned in the conduct of the letter-office. And, about that time, the outline of the present more extended and regular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> seems to have been conceived by Mr Edmond Prideaux, who was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a> to the commonwealth after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of king Charles. He was chairman of a committee in 1642, for considering what should be set upon inland letters; and afterwards appointed post-master by an ordonnance of both the houses, in the execution of which office he first established a weekly conveyance of letters into all parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; thereby saving to the public the charge of maintaining postmasters, to the amount of 7000 l. per annum. And, his own emoluments being probably very considerable, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> endeavoured to erect another post-office in opposition to his; till checked by a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of the commons, declaring, that the office of post-master is, and ought to be, in the sole power and disposal of the parliament. This office was afterwards farmed by one Manley in 1654. But, in 1657, a regular post-office was erected by the authority of the protector and his parliament, upon nearly the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> as has been ever since adopted, with the same rates of postage as were continued till the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>. After the restoration, a similar office, with some improvements, was established by statute 12 Car. II. c. 35; but the rates of letters were altered, and some farther regulations added, by the statutes 9 Ann. c. 10; 6 Geo. I. c. 21; 26 Geo. II. c. 12; 5 Geo. III. c. 25; & 7 Geo. III. c. 50; and penalties were enacted, in order to confine the carriage of letters to the public office only, except in some few <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>: a provision, which is absolutely necessary; for nothing but an exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> can support an office of this sort: many rival independent offices would only serve to ruin one another. Post, in war, any fort of ground, fortified or not, where a body of men can be in a condition of resisting the enemy. Advanced Post, a spot of ground, seized by a party to secure their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> and the posts behind them. Post of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">Honour</a>. The advanced <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> is a post of honour: the right of the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> is the post of honour, and is always given to the eldest regiment: the left is the next post, and is given to the next eldest, and so on. The centre of the lines is the post the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>, and is given to the youngest regiments. A centinel placed before the colours, and at the door of the commanding officer, is a post of honour. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENNY">Penny</a>-Post, a post established for the benefit of London and the adjacent parts; by which any letter or parcel not exceeding 16 ounces <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, is speedily conveyed to and from all parts within ten miles of London. POSTDAM. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-POTSDAM">POTSDAM</a>.

POSTERIOR

Pages 96-96

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> of relation, implying something behind, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> that comes after another. In which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is used in opposition to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> and anterior. The back and hips are the posterior parts of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> has given prior and posterior analytics. A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a> is posterior to another, when it is later or fresher.

POSTERN

Pages 96-96

in fortification, a small gate, usually made in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the flank of a bastion, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> in that of the curtain, or near the orillon, descending into the ditch; whereby the garrison can <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a> in and out, unperceived by the enemy; either to relieve the works, or to make private sallies, &c. The word is also used in the general for any private or back-door.

POSTHUMOUS

Pages 96-96

a child born after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> taken out of the body of a dead mother; from whence it is frequently applied to the works of an author not published till after his decease.

POSTIL
