Pages 96-96

a name anciently given to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in the margin of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a>, and afterwards to one in any other book <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> to the text.

POSTING

Pages 96-96

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, the putting an account forward from one book to another, particularly from the journal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> waste-book to the ledger. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOOK_KEEPING">BOOK-KEEPING</a>.

POSTPONING

Pages 96-97

putting any thing after <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> behind another with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

POSTULATE

Pages 97-97

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, &c., is described to be such an easy and self-evident supposition, as needs no explication <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> illustration to render it intelligible; so that a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line may be drawn from one point to another.

POSTURE

Pages 97-97

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, the situation of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> with regard to the eye, and of the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> members thereof with regard to one another, whereby its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> is expressed. A considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the art of a painter, consists in adjusting the postures; in giving the most agreeable ones to his figures, in accommodating them to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the respective figures and the part each has in the action, and in conducting and in pursuing them throughout. Postures are either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>. Natural postures are such as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> seems to have had a view to in the mechanism of the body, or rather such as the ordinary actions and occasions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to exhibit while young, and while the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, muscles, ligaments, &c., are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>. Artificial postures, are those which some extraordinary views, or studies, occasion us to learn; as those of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FENCING">fencing</a>, &c. Such also are those of our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> and posture-masters. A painter would be strangely puzzled with the figure of Clark (a late famous posture-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>) in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>-piece. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, we are told in the Phil. Trans., had such an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> command of his muscles, &c., that he could disjoint almost his whole body; so that he imposed on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> surgeon Mullens, who looked upon him as in such a miserable condition, he would not undertake his care. Though a well-made man, he would appear with all the deformities imaginable; hunch-backed, pot-bellied, sharp-breasted, &c. He disjoined his arms, shoulders, legs, and thighs; and rendered himself such an object of pity, that he has frequently extorted <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a cripple, from the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> in which he had the minute before been in quality of a comrade. He would make his hips stand a considerable way out from his loins, and so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as to invade the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his back. Yet his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> was the most changeable part about him, and showed more postures than all the rest. Of himself he could exhibit all the uncounted odd faces of a Quaker's meeting.

POT-ASH

Pages 97-101

the lixivious ashes of certain vegetables, used in making of glass, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, &c. See Glass, Soap, &c. The method of making pot-ash is directed by Dr Shaw, as follows. Burn a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILLET">billet</a>-wood to grey ashes; and taking several pounds of these ashes, boil them in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, so as to make a very strong lixivium, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> ley. Let this ley be strained through a coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, to keep out any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> parts of the half-burnt wood that might happen to remain in the ashes; then evaporate this strained ley in an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAN">pan</a> over a quick fire almost to dryness; then taking out the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> remaining at the bottom, and putting it into an iron-crucible, let it in a strong fire till the matter is melted, and then immediately pour it out upon an iron-plate, where it soon cools, and appears in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> lump of pot-ash. Much after this manner is pot-ash made in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> way of business, for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the soap-boiler, glass-maker, fuller, &c., but according to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the wood, or combustible matter employed, with the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> it, and conducting the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, different kinds of pot-ash are prepared. There are certain saline-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> that yield this pot-ash to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage, as particularly the plant kali; there are others that afford it in less plenty, and of an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, as bean-stalks, &c., but in general, all vegetable subjects afford it of one kind or other, and may most of them be made to yield it tolerably perfect after the manner of the process already laid <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, even the loppings, roots, and refuse parts of ordinary trees, vine clippings, &c. The fixed salts of all vegetables excepting the kali, and marine plants, when reduced to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> purity, or entirely separated from the other principles, appear to be one and the same thing: when it should seem, says Dr Shaw, that by a suitable management, good saleable pot-ash might be made in all places where vegetable matters abound. For <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> by examining Ruffia pot-ash, for example, we find that its superior excellence depends upon its being clear of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, or upon its containing a large proportion of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, or fixed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, these advantages may, by properly regulating the operation, be given to English pot-ashes, so as perhaps to render the latter as good as the former: but where the pot-ash of any remarkable saline vegetable is to be imitated, that of the kali, for example, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> recommends a prudent sprinkling of the subject with salt, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-water, in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>; and by these ways, properly diversified, any principle that is naturally wanting, might be artificially introduced so as to perfect the art of pot-ash. In the 70th volume of the Philosophical Transactions we have an account of a method of procuring this salt from the putrid water which runs from dung-hills. The process is very simple, consisting only in simple <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of the fluid, and calcining the impure salt till most of the foulness is burnt out. From 24 wine <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> full of this muck-water were obtained 9 Cw. 1 q. 12 lb. of saleable pot-ash, valued at 42 s. per Cw.; the expense of manufacturing them being only valued at 4l. 9s. The pot-ash thus made is of a greyish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> appearance; deliquesces a little in moist <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>; but if kept in a dry room, near the fire, acquires a powdery surface. It is hard and of a spongy texture when broken, with many small crystals in its substance. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of its internal parts is dusky and variegated. To the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> it is acid, saline, and sulphurous. It emits no smell of volatile alkali, either in a solid form, dissolved, or when added to lime-water; neither does it communicate the sapphire colour to a solution of blue vitriol. Silver is quickly tinged black by it; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that it contains much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a>. Ten grains of this pot-ash required 11 drops of the weak spirit of vitriol to separate it. The like quantity of salt of tartar required 24 drops: a strong effervescence occurred in both Pot-ashes mixtures; and a sulphureous vapour exhaled from the former. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEA">tea</a> spoonful of the syrup of violets diluted with an ounce of water, was changed into a bright green colour by five grains of the salt of tartar; but ten grains of this pot-ash were necessary to produce the same hue in a similar mixture. Half an ounce of the salt dissolved entirely in half a pint of hot-water; but when the liquor was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, a large purple sediment subsided to the bottom; and it was found that this sediment amounted to about two-thirds of the whole quantity of ashes used. These are the two processes most essentially different from one another which have appeared concerning the manufacture of this useful salt. Some indeed have attempted to compose it on the supposition that alkali consisted of an earth combined in a peculiar manner with a certain acid. But the little success of all these attempts show that they have been built on a false principle. The only method of producing alkaline salts originally is from the ashes of vegetables; and the vegetable substances which yield the largest quantity of them are tartar, and marine plants. From the former the purest and strongest vegetable alkali is obtained, and from the latter the mineral alkali. From other vegetables, as fern, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>, bean-stalks, &c., an alkaline salt is produced, but so impure, and in such small quantity, that no manufacture of it can be established in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> with any reasonable expectations of profit. The pot-ashes of different countries also vary much in quality; and the experiments of Dr Home, in his treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLEACHING">Bleaching</a>, seem to set forth their different properties in the clearest point of view. The different kinds tried by him were, 1. Blue <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>-ashes. These appear to be a pure alkaline salt, mixed with a small quantity of vitriolated tartar, and earth. Half a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of this, filtered and evaporated, yielded 5½ ounces of pure salt.—Here, however, we must observe, that though the quantity was so far diminished by this operation, yet we are not to imagine that the whole of this diminution was owing to impurities; for all salts are destroyed in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> by solution in water and evaporation. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, no. 21. 2. White pearl-ashes are nearly of the same quality with the former; half a pound of them giving five ounces and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> drams of pure salt, with some vitriolated Tartar and earth. 3. Rustic or Mucousy ashes have very much the appearance of flaked lime, and are, like it, friable between the fingers. They adhere to the tongue, and their alkaline taste soon goes away, leaving in the mouth a strong taste of lime. Some small bits of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> are observable in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, and they never turn moist in the air. Half a pound of the salt lixiviated with water and evaporated, gave only 10 drams 15 grains of very caustic salt. These consist therefore of a small quantity of alkaline salt united with a large quantity of lime. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAITHNESS">Caithness</a> ashes are of the colour of ironstone, and extremely hard, with many shining particles of charcoal in them. They have a saline taste with a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of pungency; feel gritty in the mouth, when broken in pieces by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> dissolve in water. To extract the pure salt, half a pound of the ashes were boiled in a pint of water; then that water poured off, and half a pint put on the ashes again; and so on, till the ashes taste no more salt. This <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> took 24 hours, and the last water that came off had a strong taste of sulphur and was blackish. A piece of silver put in the decoction was in a few minutes turned almost black; but though the decoction was evaporated considerably, it did not turn silver black more speedily than before. The whole, when totally evaporated, yielded only 10 drams of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> salt having a strong caustic alkaline taste. Some Caithness ashes powdered, and often washed in water so that the salts were all carried off, were infused in water. After standing some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, there was a weak lime-water, with something of a saline taste, but no pellicle. Some of this residuum was put into a reverberatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> for two hours; after which it afforded good lime-water. Caithness ashes then appear to contain an earth half vitrified, some lime, alkaline salts, and a quantity of sulphur. 5. Marcol ashes are of a paler colour than the former, with some small pieces of charcoal in their composition. They have a strong saline taste; and so great pungency, that they cannot be held <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the mouth. Half a pound dissolved in water, filtered and evaporated, yielded 11 drams one scruple and two grains of alkaline residuum. The decoction blackened silver, but not so strongly as the former, and by evaporation it quickly lost that quality. Our author next proceeds to consider the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of manufacturing these ashes in this country; on which subject he has the following observations— "The blue and white pearl-ashes we have discovered to be pure alkaline salts, without any considerable mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> bodies. Their purity shows the lixiviate to have been strained through some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> substance, such as linen or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a>. The blue ashes show, by their colour, that they have sustained the most fire. But both of them are so much alike, that the one may be substituted for the other; and therefore we shall consider them in one view. "Every one knows, that alkaline salts, such as these, are got from all plants except the alkaline, and from all trees except the most resinous, which afford them in very small quantity. These plants, or trees, when found, are pulled or felled in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, dried, and burnt to ashes. By the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of warm water the salts are dissolved, and, by straining, separated from the earth along with the water. This saline liquor, which is called a lixiviate, is evaporated over a fire; and what remains, is an alkaline salt of the same kind with the pearl-ashes. "I was informed by a skilful bleacher in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, that he practiced a more expeditious way of extracting the salts. He bought the ashes of different vegetables from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a> for 9s. a-bushel. From these a very strong ley was made, into which dry straw was dipped, until it fucked up all the ley. This straw was afterwards dried and burnt, and gave him salts which he showed me, almost as good and pure as the pearl-ashes. This method I have several times tried; but could never burn the straw to white ashes, the salts diminishing the inflammability of the straw. It is a very expeditious method, if it can be practised. But I can see no occasion for bringing the ley into a solid form, as the salts must again be dissolved in water before they can be used. The strength of the ley can easily be determined by the hydrostatic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>. "Though "Though I make no question, that the quantity of salt, in plants of the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, will vary in different soils and climates; yet it would be of advantage to have the proportion ascertained in general. Some trials of this kind I have made. "Two pounds of fern which had been pulled August 16th were dried, and burnt to white ashes. These weighed 7 dr. and tasted very salt. When lixiviated, strained, and evaporated, they gave me 49 gr. of salt, about the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ashes. If the fern had been pulled in April, it would have afforded more salt. Why then should we not prepare salts from this vegetable? There is more of it growing on our hills than would serve all our bleachfields. The Irish make great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it. "From 11 oz. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>-ashes I had 1 oz. of salt. Two oz. of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEAT">peat</a>-ashes afforded half a drachm of salt. Nettles, I am informed, afford much salt. Furz and broom, natives of this country, are very fit for this purpose. "But the kelp, as it grows in such plenty along our shore, and contains more salt than any other vegetable I know, would be the most proper, were it not for a mixture of some substance that renders it unfit for bleaching, at least of fine cloths, after they have obtained a tolerable degree of whiteness. It is observed by bleachers, that, in these circumstances, it leaves a great yellowness in the linen. As these ashes are much used in Ireland, and, as it is not uncommon to bleach coarse cloths with them in Scotland, a disqualification into their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and some attempts to purify them, may not be improper. There are no ashes sold so cheap as these; for the best gives but 2l. the 2000 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> (A). They may, therefore, allow of more labour to be expended on them, and come cheaper at long-run than the foreign salts. "I dried some sea-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, and burnt it, though I found that last operation very difficult. When I had kept them fused in the fire for two hours, they weighed 3½ oz. I poured on the ashes an English pint and a half of cold water, that I might have as little of the sulphur as possible. This ley, after it had stood for some hours, was poured off clear, and had but a slight tendency to a green colour. I made a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> infusion with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>-warm water, and poured it off from the sediment. This had a darker colour than the former; was kept separated from it, and evaporated by itself. There was a third infusion made; but having no salt taste, it was thrown away. The second infusion seemed to contain more sulphur than the first; and a piece of white linen kept in it half an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, while it was boiling, was tinged <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and could not be washed white again. The earthy part remaining, weighed, when well dried, 1 oz. 2 dr. The saline decoction, evaporated by degrees, and set at different times in a cellar to crystallize, afforded me 5 dr. 46 gr. The liquor, when entirely evaporated, left 4½ dr. of a yellow salt, which appeared to be a strong alkaline. The salts which crystallized seemed to be mostly sea-salt, with a considerable quantity of sulphur, and some alkaline salt. There appeared no signs of the bittern in these salts, as their solution did not turn turbid with the oil of tartar. Nor was any of the bittern to be expected in kelp ashes, although it probably is to be found in the recent vegetable; because the alkaline salts formed by the fire must have changed it into a neutral. The ley made warm with water, being evaporated, left 4 dr. of a black bitter salt, which, from its quantity of sulphur, appeared unfit for bleaching. These ashes, then, seem to be a composition of somewhat less than the fourth of sulphur, the same quantity of sea-salt, about a fourth of alkaline salt, and somewhat more than a fourth of earth. The alkaline salt contained in kelp ashes, amounts to one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> a pound. This cheapness makes it worth our pains to bestow some labour on them. "If the bad effects in bleaching with kelp ashes arise from the sea-salt, as some of the most knowing bleachers think, they can be freed from it in an easy manner. Let a lixiv of kelp-ashes be made with cold water, for that does not extract so much of the sulphur; it must stand but for a short time, for these salts dissolve easily; decant it, and evaporate the ley. As the boiling continues, the sea-salt will crystallize. When that is all separated, the remaining ley will contain alkaline salt with some sulphur. This operation every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a bleachfield may learn and oversee, without taking up much of his time. A similar process is carried on by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> servants in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>-works, who have by practice learned it from others. "I had some hopes that the sulphur might be carried off by long roasting; such as these salts undergo before they are fused in order to be turned into glaigs; because I had observed, that the longer time they were kept in the fire, the freer were they from this sulphureous part. "I ordered a quantity of kelp ashes to be kept in the furnace of a glaigs-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> below the vitrifying point, for 24 hours. During this time they had lost almost four-fifths of their weight. They were now much freer from their sulphur, and were of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> colour; but much of the alkaline salt had been driven off with the oils. If a ley is much impregnated with this sulphureous matter, it appears to be carried off, in a great measure, by long boiling. "We come now to explain the method of manufacturing the white Mulcovy ashes. We have shown, by undoubted experiments, that the greatest part of these ashes consists of lime; and yet we have several acts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> which forbid the use of that material under severe penalties. The parliament were in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to discharge its use, upon the disadvantageous reports which were made to them. We shall immediately see how dangerous a material it is when used improperly, or without the mixture of alkaline salts, which render it safe, and more soluble in water. But I will venture to say, that experiment will not support the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> entertained with regard to it, if carried any further. "Since bleaching, then, cannot be carried on without it; for those ashes which contain it, are quite necessary in that operation; and since we import them from foreign countries; let these prejudices against it cease, and let us only consider how we may render our own lime as safe as the foreign. If we can do that, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of the legislature will be as ready to abrogate (A) Since this treatise was written, however, the price of kelp has been advanced to 2l. or upwards the 2000 weight, so that those who would now attempt any thing of this kind, must also manufacture the kelp themselves. gate these acts, as they were to make them. "By my experiments on the white Muscovy ashes, I got about the eighth part of alkaline salts from them. This made me expect, that, by mixing in the same proportion quick-lime and alkaline salts, I should be able to produce Muscovy ashes. "To an ounce of quick-lime and a drachm of white pearl ashes, I added about a gill of water, and boiled them together till the water was all evaporated. The taste of this substance was little different from lime. To recover the salts again from the lime, I dissolved it in water, strained off the liquor, and evaporated it. Instead of the drachm of salts, I had but 2 gr. of a substance which was more earthy than saline. "To 3 dr. of quicklime, and as much potashes, I added a mutchkin of water, and kept it boiling for two hours till it was evaporated. I dissolved it again in water, which being filtered and evaporated, gave me 1/2 dr. of a caustic salt, that liquefied in the air when it had been but four minutes from the fire. It appears, then, that the alkaline salts are destroyed by lime, and that a great part of them can never be again recovered. From the remaining lime, after the salts were extracted, I got strong lime-water, but without a pellicle. This shows, that a quantity of alkaline salts, equal to the lime, boiled with it for two hours, are not able to fix all the soluble part of the lime. "From these experiments we may draw some corollaries with regard to the present subject. 1st, That evaporating the water from the lime and salts by boiling, is a most unfrugal way of preparing these white ashes. 2ndly, That these ashes ought to be kept close shut up in casks; for if exposed to the open air, though in a room, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> moisture and drought must fix their most useful parts. This I have found to be fact: for the salts that I made became less pungent by keeping; and I have observed, that the surface of the Muscovy ashes lost all pungency by being exposed to the air, while their internal parts still retained it. 3rdly, That all boiling is prejudicial to these Muscovy ashes, as it fixes, and that quickly, their most subtile, and probably their most serviceable parts. "Let us now proceed to another method of making these white ashes. I imagined, that if the salts were dissolved in water, and the quick-lime flaked with that, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> would soon dry without the assistance of fire. In this way I added equal parts of both; but the composition was so strong, that it blistered my tongue if it but touched it. When the fourth part was alkaline salt, it blistered my tongue when kept to it a few seconds. I could taste the salts plainly in the composition, when they made but the thirty-second part of the whole. "I thought, when composed with the eighteenth part of salt, it had, when fresh made, just the taste and look of the Muscovy ashes; nor could any person have distinguished them. This I once imagined was the proportion; but when I found that the saline pungency soon turned weaker by keeping, and that this composition would not afford the same quantity of salts that the Muscovy ashes did, I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that a much greater quantity of salts was necessary. The proportion appears to be one of salt to four of lime, prepared in this last way. Three drachms of ashes prepared in this way, and kept for a fortnight, gave me but 15 grains of salt; which is but the half of what the Muscovy would have afforded. I find, if the quick-lime is first quenched, it does not fix the salts so much; and therefore is better and cheaper. One drachm of potashes dissolved in a little water, and added to 3 drachms of quenched lime, gave me 44 grains of a very caustic salt. I prefer this method as the best. "The manufacturers of this salt probably pour the lixivie upon the lime, as they can know by its specific gravity what quantity of salts is in the water, and so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> themselves the expense of procuring the salts in a dry form. "The manufacture of the Marçoit and Calthub ashes remains yet to be explained. We have discovered that both of them contain sulphur, earth, alkaline salts, and lime; and differ in nothing, but in the Calthub's having more sulphur than the Marçoit ashes. We shall therefore consider them together. "Whether these two species of ashes are of any use in bleaching, may be, and has already been, disputed. I find they contain no other principles, the sulphureous part excepted, than the former ashes combined together. Why then should we expect any other effects from the same ingredients in the Marçoit and Calthub ashes, than what we have from either of the pearl and Muscovy ashes mixed together? The sulphureous principle in the former must have very bad effects; as I find by experiment, that it leaves a yellowness on cloth that is very hard to be washed out. It is owing to this sulphureous principle, that linen, after it has been washed with soap, and is pretty well advanced in whiteness, is apt to be discoloured by ley which is brought to boil; for, by boiling, the sulphureous part is extracted from these ashes, and the ley becomes of a deep brown colour. Daily practice, then, shows the disadvantage of this sulphureous principle. Besides, as sulphur unites itself, quickly and firmly, with alkaline salts, it must weaken, or altogether destroy a great quantity of these in the Marçoit and Calthub ashes, and so render them of no effect in bleaching. These two reasons seem to me sufficient to exclude them from the bleachfield; especially as, by increasing the other materials, we can attain, perhaps more speedily, the same end. "However, as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> has introduced them into general practice, we shall consider how they are to be manufactured. Dr Mitchell has, in a very ingenious and useful <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, contained in the Philosophical Transactions for the year 1748, delivered an account transmitted to him by Dr Linnæus, of the method of making potashes in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. This account was contained in an academical dissertation of one Lundmark upon this subject at Aboe in Sweden. The substance of this account is, "That birch or alder is burnt by a slow fire to ashes, and made into a paste with water. This paste is plastered over a row of green pine or fir logs. Above that is laid, transversely, another row of the same; and that likewise is plastered over. In this way they continue <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and plastering, till the pile be of a considerable height. This pile is set on fire; and whenever the ashes begin to run, it is overturned, and the melted ashes are <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> sticks, so that the ashes incrust the logs of wood, and become as hard as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>." This, in the Doctor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, is the method of making the potashes that come from Sweden, Russia, and Dantzig; and and that there is no other difference betwixt the ashes made in those different countries, but that the Russian, containing more salt, must be made into a paste with a strong ley. "There would appear, by my experiments, a greater difference than this, betwixt the Swedish ashes, if that is the true process, and those I have examined. I had discovered the greatest part of the Muscovy ashes to be lime. I suspected it might enter into the composition of the Marcolf and Cashub; and have accordingly discovered it there. Without the same grounds, none would ever have searched for it. Whence then comes this lime? It must either enter into its composition, or arise from the materials managed according as the process directs. "I have tried the birch ashes made into a paste with water. I have tried common charcoal, made into a paste with a third part of potashes, and kept them in a strong reverberatory heat for some hours, and yet no such caustic substance appeared. I have kept earth and salts of kelp-ashes fused together for 24 hours in the furnace of a glass-house, where the heat was just below the degree of vitrification; and yet no remarkable causticity appeared, afterwards, in the concreted mass. But supposing that there did, will ever this account for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of lime? These chemists do not assert that it is a calcareous causticity. The earth of vegetables kept in fusion with their salts, is so far from turning into a quick-lime, that the mass takes the opposite course, and becomes glaas. Bodies that, by the laws of nature, are vitreifiable, can never, so far as we know, become calcareous. In one or other of these two substances all bodies terminate, that are changeable by fire; and vegetables are of the former kind. Here it may be asked, Why then, since they endure such a fire, are they not vitrified? The objection would be just, did they contain nothing else but what was found in vegetables. But if we once allow, that lime is one of the materials, the difficulty is easily solved: for lime; we know, in proportion as it is mixed, hinders the vitrification of all bodies. In effect, the earthy part in these ashes is almost vitrified; and I think that I have carried the vitrification yet farther in that part; but I never was able, with the utmost heat of a reverberatory furnace, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for six hours, to produce anything like a thorough vitrification in these ashes. The heat of the fire used in the process would seem to be very great; and must, if it were not very difficult, reduce them to glaas. The inviolable nature of these salts, so far from being an objection, becomes a strong proof of my opinion. "These salts have a remarkable pungency. This we have already seen is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> effect of quick-lime on salts. "These salts are found to be the fittest for making soap, and to incorporate soonest and best with oils. Salts, we know, of themselves do not readily unite with oil; but when once mixed with quick-lime, they have a greater tendency to union. "Again, I find that these ashes are more easily fluxed than charcoal made into a paste with the third part salt; which is much more than the ashes contain. Now, it is observed, that quicklime increases the fluxing power of alkaline salts; for the common caustic made of quicklime and alkaline salts, is sooner fused than the latter alone. "From these reasons, and the experiments that discover lime in these ashes, I am led to think, that it is not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the process, but mixed with the ashes when they are made into a paste. The following experiment is a convincing proof of what I have been endeavouring to make out. "I boiled some peat-straw in a strong ley of pearl ashes burnt into a black coal, and made it into a paste with water. Another quantity of straw was boiled in a ley made of one part of quick-lime and four parts pearl salts, the ley being poured off turbid from the lime. This straw was likewise burnt when dry, and made into a paste. These two substances were put into separate crucibles, and fluxed in a reverberatory furnace. The latter appeared to resemble the Marcolf and Cashub ashes more than the former, which seemed to want their pungency." Though the only method of preparing the alkaline salt originally is by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBUSTION">combustion</a> of vegetables, yet there are some neutral salts from which if it were possible to expel the acid, we should have it in our power to procure the finest pearl-ashes in vast quantity. These are vitriolated tartar, nitre, but especially sea-salt, on account of the inexhaustible quantities of it to be met with in the waters of the ocean. Unhappily, however, there are some objections to every one of these. The vitriolated tartar, or any other salt in which the vitriolic acid enters, cannot be decomposed without converting the acid into sulphur by charcoal dust; in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> it is as difficult to get free of the sulphur as of the acid; and if we treat it by frequent solutions in water, we destroy the phlogiston of the sulphur, and have only vitriolated tartar again instead of alkali. See Chemistry, p. 225, 324. With respect to nitre, though its acid may be expelled by fire, yet it is too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-priced, and too much used in other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, to be thought of for this purpose. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a> manufacture from sea-salt has indeed been lately erected in England. The principle on which this was established is, that the acid of sea-salt may be extracted by means of lime; and accordingly we find that the saline efflorescence, which frequently appears on walls, consists chiefly of the marine alkali deprived of its acid. But this, tho' delivered on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of a very eminent chemist, we can affirm from our own observation to be a mistake. Of the many <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> in which we have examined this efflorescence, only one was found to be alkaline; the others uniformly appeared to be true Glauber's salt composed of the vitriolic acid and fossil alkali. Neither did this appear to be formed by any decomposition of salt originally in the platter, but to be a real generation of both acid and alkali where none of them existed before. See Efflorescence, in the Appendix.

POTAMOGETON

Pages 101-101

pond-weed; a genus of the tetragynia order, belonging to the tetrandria class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are 12 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, all of them floating vegetables on the surfaces of stagnant waters, affording an agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> to fish, and food to cattle.

POTATOE

Pages 101-105

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. See Solanum. These roots came first from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> where they are still very much cultivated. It was, however, 40 years after their introduction before they were much cultivated about <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and then they were con- considered as rarities, without any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of the utility that might arise from bringing them into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. At this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> they were distinguished from the Spanish by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> potatoes, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> batatas, which is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> name of the Spanish sort. At a meeting of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 18th, 1662-3, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> was read from Mr Buckland, a Somerset <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, recommending the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> of potatoes in all parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> to prevent famine. This was referred to a committee; and, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their report, Mr Buckland had the thanks of the society, such members as had lands were intreated to plant them, and Mr Evelyn was desired to mention the proposals at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of his Sylva. Since that time the plant has been so universally cultivated, that it has become a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of our food; and attempts have even been made to substitute the potatoe instead of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, or to make bread from it. See the article BREAD. For the method of cultivating potatoes, see <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a>, no 127—129. Besides what is there delivered, there are many curious experiments concerning the culture of potatoes related in the Georgical Essays. "1. On the Howard or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a> potatoe. By all the experiments that have been made, the Howard potatoe is found to produce the largest crop. On that account they are chiefly used in feeding of cattle. In two beds, four feet wide and 200 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, I planted in a common field a sufficient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of sets of this kind of potatoe, and managed them by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-hoe. The produce was 64 bushels, each bushel up-heaped, weighing about 70 lb. My cattle eat them boiled with as much eagerness as the best sorts, and came on as well with them. I have built a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, &c. on Mr Young's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and during this whole winter have boiled potatoes for my cattle. For the fattening ones, I mix ground oats with them; and for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>-cows, malt-dust; and dare venture to affirm, that they are much more profitable than either turnips or cabbages. Once, when my potatoes grew low, I desisted giving them to the milking-cows. Immediately, though fed with the best hay, they fell off amazingly in their milk. I therefore began again, and in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>'s time they gave better than one-third more <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>. I own this accidental discovery gave me much satisfaction, as it confirmed my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that potatoes boiled are an excellent winter food for cattle. Their culture is not so difficult, at least not so precarious, as either turnips or cabbages. Their value is superior, and there is no risk of their giving a disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> either to butter or milk. Add to this the vast increase of the Howard potatoe, and its equality with the best sorts when used for cattle. "2. On the increase of potatoes. My gardener cut a large potatoe into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> pieces, which he planted with dungs, in a drill, in the garden. By earthing up and laying the shoots, he produced 575 sizeable potatoes, which weighed eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> eight <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. Another of my servants produced, in the field, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> stone of good potatoes from the same number of sets. Tho' this experiment cannot always be executed in its full force in an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, it ought, notwithstanding, to be imitated as nearly as circumstances <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> allow. It shows, in the most distinguishing manner, the use of clean and careful husbandry. "3. On the increase of potatoes. On the 14th of April, I cut a large <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> potatoe into 17 sets, which were planted in as many hillocks, at the distance of four feet. In the course of growing, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> were earthed up, and on the 14th of October the crop was taken up: The produce, 10 pecks of sizeable potatoes. At the time that this experiment was made, I had several hillocks, in which I put three and four sets of the same kind of potatoe. But, upon the most careful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, I could not observe that these hillocks produced a greater crop than the others planted with a single set. Hence it is obvious, that the potatoe spreads its roots most kindly when least crowded. "4. On the method of raising seedling potatoes. Take a bunch of the apples of any sort of potatoe. Hang it up in a warm room during the winter, and in February separate the seeds from the pulp, by washing the apples in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and pressing them with the fingers. Then dry the seeds upon <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April, sow these seeds, in drills, in a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> well dug, and manured with rotten dung. When the plants are about an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, draw a little earth up to them with a hoe, in order to lengthen their main roots. When they are about three inches high, dig them up with a spade, and separate them carefully from each other, in order for planting out in the following manner. "Prepare a piece of fresh ground by trenching it well. Dig up the seedling plants as before directed; and plant them out in the ground, thus prepared, in such a manner, that there shall be 16 inches between each plant. As they advance in growth, let them receive one or two earthings up, in order to lengthen the main root, and encourage the shoots under ground. "By this management, the potatoes will, in the course of one season, arrive at the size of hen's eggs, and the haulm will be as vigorous as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> sets had been planted. But what proves the luxuriancy, in the most convincing manner, is, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and apples are produced. "In Lancashire, where the gardeners raise potatoes from seed, they are always two, and sometimes three years in bringing them to full size. By the above method of transplanting, with wide distances, many of the potatoes nearly attain their full size in one season. "It is observable, that these seedlings produce potatoes of all the different kinds; and sometimes new sorts are procured. We do not find any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> whether the apple comes from one kind or another. It is not so when we use the set, which invariably produces the same kind. "Potatoes, when propagated from sets, after a number of years, are found to decrease in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>; for which reason they should be brought back every 14 years to their original. "From a want of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to this circumstance, I have known potatoes to run out, that they hardly returned treble seed. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> complains that his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> is tired of them, but the true cause is the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the sets. "The increase of potatoes raised from seed is auto- astonishing. They continue in vigour for about 14 years; after which, the produce gradually declines. 5. On the best method of raising early potatoes. As the culture of potatoes, and particularly of the early sorts for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, has of late become an object of very general attention, I hope the following account of a new method of obtaining these (without the help of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOT_BEDS">hot-beds</a>) will be acceptable to the public. On the 2d of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1772, I made a hot-bed for the forward sort of potatoes, and on the 7th put in the sets, placing a glass and frame over them, and taking every precaution to defend them from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a>. Of these small potatoes, or sets, there remained about 40 in a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>, which was accidentally hung up in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>, and there remained unnoticed till about the 25th of April. I then accidentally observed the basket, and perceiving something green on the edge of it, took it <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and, to my <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> surprise, found that the potatoes had sprouted half a yard in length, and that there were a great number of very small potatoes formed on the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> roots which had grown out. I took them into my garden, and planted them in a rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, without any manure. The roots I put into the ground three inches deep, and laid down the stems that had sprouted, horizontally, and covered them with two inches of soil, but left the tops uncovered. Without farther attention they grew surprisingly. On the 26th of May, I took up the roots planted in the hot-bed on the 7th of January. They by no means answered my expectations, or paid for the trouble of their culture; but, at the same time, I was astonished to find the others, which were put into the ground so late, to have produced larger potatoes than the roots in the hot-bed. I took up all the roots, and picked off the large potatoes from them, which amounted to from 4 to 12 on each root, and then set the roots again in the same ground. This, indeed, I have successfully practised for many years, sometimes even twice, and have had a third good crop at Michaelmas. When this method is tried, the roots must be watered on the evenings of hot days. In January 1773, in order to make a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of this experiment with a large <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, I placed a great many potatoes of the early sorts on a thick layer of gravelly soil, close to each other, over an oven, flatted over, but open to the south-west, and covered them two inches deep with the same earth. At the end of April I took them up, and found the items about a foot long or more. For fear of injuring the fine and delicate fibres of the roots, I took great care in taking them up, and planting them in the foil. This I now manured, but in all other respects treated them in the manner above described, many of the fibrous roots having then potatoes formed upon them, nearly as large as walnuts. For a week, the plants came on surprisingly, when, by one sharp night's uncommon frost, they were nearly destroyed. However, notwithstanding this, fresh items grew up in a few days, and I actually gathered from them, on the 3d of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> following, finer potatoes than were sold at that time, at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, from 1s. to 1s. 6d. per pound, being the produce of hot-beds. After taking off the larger potatoes, I again planted the roots for a second crop, and in September obtained a very large produce. I weighed the increase of many separate roots, which amounted from four pound eight ounces to 14 pound 12 ounces, the potatoes being the largest of the forward kinds I ever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a>. 6. On a method of raising potatoes in winter. Make a compost of earth, sand, and coal-ashes. With this mixture fill a tub about 16 inches deep. Plant this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> soil with some sets of the early round potatoe, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the tub in a stable opposite to a window, taking care to water the earth now and then. In all seasons the sets will sprout, and give a tolerable increase of potatoes. Last November I planted some sets in the above manner; and, in February following, I took up a considerable number of young potatoes, clean skinned and well flavoured. 7. On transplanting potatoe tops. On the 18th of May 1772, finding some beds I had sown very early with onions, to be a milling crop, I was induced to make the following experiment. The year before, I had set some potatoes in another part of my garden, in the common way; and as it is impossible but some will remain in the ground all winter, so I found a number of sprouts about three inches high, which I nipped off close to the ground, and transplanted them into the onion-beds, without any further <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, about a foot and a half asunder, in the same manner that cabbages and cauliflowers are planted. As the season became immediately very dry, I was obliged to give my plants a little water for four or five successive nights; after which they began to flourish, and had the appearance of a promising crop during all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. At the usual time, in October, I ordered them to be taken up; and for size, quantity, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, they exceeded all I ever had in the common way. Had the ground been fresh, properly manured and prepared, and the plants put down at a proper distance from each other, I am of opinion that the success would have been still greater. 8. On feeding hogs with potatoes. From an accurate experiment made last year, I dare venture to recommend baked potatoes as an excellent food for hogs. The pork produced by this food, was equal to that from barley and beans; but at present I cannot exactly ascertain the comparative experiment with regard to expense; however, I am of opinion, that roasted potatoes, considering the improvement of the hogs, is as cheap a food, if not cheaper, than can be given them. I roasted my potatoes upon a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KILN">kiln</a>, similar to what is used by oat-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> shellers for drying their oats. The difference in expense between boiling and roasting the potatoes is prodigious, both with regard to the labour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>. A kiln that will cost £1. will roast potatoes sufficient for the maintenance of more than 20 hogs; and one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> will perform all the necessary attendance upon them, and do other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> besides. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the fire, by dissipating the crude juices that are contained in raw potatoes, reduces them into a state highly wholesome and nutritious. Boiling does this in part, but not so effectually. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a> roasted in the manner above described, partakes much of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a chestnut, and perhaps is not greatly inferior to it." There is one remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the potatoe, that when planted in water, it shoots out a great num Potatoe her of fine white roots like threads into the water; but on none of them is there to be found the least appearance of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BULB">bulb</a>; while on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the potatoes in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> always grow on the top. **Potatoe-Bread.** See Bread. **Spanish Potatoe.** See Convolvulus. **POTENT,** or **Potence,** in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> for a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, whose ends all terminate like the head of a crutch. It is otherwise called the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> cross, and is represented Plate CXLVI. fig. x. 12. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTENTIA">POTENTIA</a> (power,)** that whereby a thing is capable either of acting, or being acted upon. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTENTIAL">POTENTIAL</a>,** in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, is used to denote and distinguish a kind of qualities, which are supposed to exist in the body in potentia only; by which they are capable in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of affecting and impressing on us the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of such qualities, though not actually inherent in themselves; in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we say, potential <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, potential <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, &c. **Potential Cautery,** in medicine, denotes the consuming, or reducing to an eschar, any part of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body by a caustic alkaline or metallic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, &c., instead of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, which last is called the actual cautery. **Potential,** in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, an epithet applied to one of the moods of verbs. The potential is the same in form with the subjunctive, and is, according to Ruddiman, implied in that mood, for which reason that grammarian rejects it; but others will have it to differ from the subjunctive in this, that it always implies in it either possum, volo, or debeo. It is sometimes called the permissive mood, because it often implies a permission or concession to do a thing. See Grammar, n° 43. **POTENTILLA,** silver-weed, wild tansey, or cinquefoil; a genus of the pentagynia order, belonging to the icofandra class of plants. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The fruticosa, or shrubby potentilla, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called shrub cinquefoil. This rises with a short shrubby stem, dividing into a branchy full head, three or four feet high; closely garnished with pinnate leaves of five <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, narrow, acute-pointed, folioles, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> green above, and whitish underneath; and the branches terminated by clusters of large, spreading, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> flowers. This is a beautiful deciduous flowering shrub, worthy a place in every curious collection. It grows wild in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> and other northern parts of England, &c., but has been long cultivated in gardens as an ornamental shrub. 2. The reptans, or creeping common five-leaved potentilla, or five-leaved grasa, hath a thick fibrous root, slender, trailing, repent stalks, digitated, five-lobed, petiolated leaves, and yellow flowers singly. 3. The rupestris, or mountain upright cinquefoil, hath upright stalks, eight or nine inches high; pinnated five and three-lobed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> leaves, having oval crenated lobes, and the stalks terminated by small white flowers. 4. The recta, or erect seven-lobed yellow cinquefoil, hath erect stalks, seven-lobed leaves; having three lobes spear-shaped and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>, green and hairy on both sides, and the stalks terminated by corymbose clusters of yellow flowers. 5. The fragaroides, or strawberry-like trailing potentilla, hath a somewhat tuberous root, furnished with many long fibres, long trailing shoots, rooting at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>; pinnated, mostly three-lobed leaves, having oval lobes, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> Potentilla lobe the largest, and clusters of small white flowers. This species bears a great resemblance to the small sterile strawberry plants. 6. The argentea, silvery upright potentilla, hath upright stalks, branching a foot high; and five-lobed leaves, having the lobes wedge-shaped, cut on the edges, hoary and white underneath, and the branches terminated by small yellow flowers. All these plants flower in June and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>; the flowers are composed each of five roundish petals, and about 20 stamens. They are all very hardy, and may be employed in the different compartments of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> ground. Their propagation is very easy. The shrubby potentilla may be propagated abundantly by suckers, layers, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>; all of which will readily grow, and make plants in one year, which after having two or three years growth in the nursery will be fit for any of the shrubby compartments. All the herbaceous kinds may be propagated by parting the roots in autumn or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, or by seed in any of those seasons. **POTERIUM,** garden burnet; a genus of the polyandria order, belonging to the monoeia class of plants. The species are, 1. The sanguisorba, or common garden burnet, hath fibrous perennial roots, crowned by a large tuft of pinnated leaves, or six or seven <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of sawed lobes, terminated by an odd one; upright angular stalks, dividing, and branching a foot and a half high, terminated by oblong spikes of purplish red flowers. This species grows wild in England, in chalky soils; but has been long cultivated as a choice salad-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> for winter and spring use, it being of a warm nature; the young leaves are the useful parts. It is perennial in root, and retains its radical leaves all the year, but the stalks are annual. 2. The hybridum, hybrid agrimony-leaved Montpelier burnet, rises with upright, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a>, closely gathered stalks two feet high; pinnated odoriferous leaves of three or four pair of sawed lobes, terminated by an odd one; and the stalks terminated by long footstalks dividing into smaller, each supporting a small roundish spike of flowers. This species often proves biennial; but by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> down some of the stalks before they flower, it will cause it to multiply at bottom, and become abiding. 3. Poterium spinosum, shrubby spinous burnet of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, hath a shrubby stem and branches, rising a yard high, armed with spines; small pinnated evergreen leaves, of six or seven pair of lobes, terminated by an odd one, and the branches terminated by small heads of greenish flowers. All these three species flower in June and July, succeeded by ripe seeds in Autumn. They are all naturally perennial; but the two herbaceous ones are abiding in root only; the other in root, stem, and branches; the two former are hardy, and the third requires shelter in winter. The first sort merits culture in every kitchen-garden for winter and spring salads. Some plants, both of the first and second sorts, may be introduced in the herbaceous collection in the pleasure-garden for variety. The third sort must be kept always in pots to have shelter in winter. They are all easily propagated, the first sort by seed, and by parting the roots. The second sort may also be increased by seeds and slips off the root, as for the for- former fort. And the propagation of the third is by slips or cuttings of the branches in spring and summer, planted in pots, and placed under glasses, giving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> and water; or might be forwarded more by plunging them in a hot-bed. Burnet is of a heating drying nature, cordial, and alexipharmic; in summer, the leaves are used for cool tankards, to give the wine an agreeable flavour. The powder of the root of the first species is commended against spitting of blood, bleeding at the nose, dylen-teries, and diseases attended with violent secretions. In winter and spring, the young tender leaves are used in salads. For its uses as food for cattle, see Agriculture, p. 47—49.

POTION

Pages 105-105

a liquid medicine, consisting of as much as can be drunk at one draught.

POTOSI

Pages 105-105

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, situated at the bottom of a mountain of that name, in which is the richest silver mine ever discovered. Situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 67° S. Lat. 22°. See the article Peru, p. 5996.

POTTER

Pages 105-105

a learned English divine, was born in 1591, and bred at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. In 1623, he published his "Answer to a late Popish plot," intitled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">Charity</a> mistaken, which he wrote by special order of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., whose chaplain he was. In 1634, he was promoted to the deanery of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>; and, in 1640, was constituted vice-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the university of Oxford, in the execution of which office he met with some trouble from the members of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. Upon breaking out of the civil wars, he sent all his plate to the king, declaring, "that he would rather, like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a>, drink out of the hollow of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, than that his majesty should want;" and he afterward suffered much for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> cause. In consideration of this he was nominated to the deanery of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a> in 1646, but was prevented from being installed by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened about two months after. He was a person learned and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, exemplary in his conversation, courteous in his carriage, of a sweet and obliging <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and of a comely presence. He was remarkable in his charity to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. Potter (Dr John), archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, was the son of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>-draper at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WAKEFIELD">Wakefield</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, where he was born about the year 1674. He studied at University <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, Oxford; and at 19 published Variantes lectiones & nota <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Plutarchi librum de audiendis poetis; & ad Baffili magni orationem ad juvenes, quomodo cum fructu legere possint Graecorum libros, 8vo. 1693. In 1697, came out his edition of Lyco-phon, in folio; which is reckoned the best of that obscure writer; soon after, he published his Antiquities of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, 2 vols, 8vo. These works established his literary reputation, and engaged him in a correspondence with Gravius and other learned foreigners. In 1706, he was made chaplain to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>; in 1715, bishop of Oxford; and in 1737, he succeeded archbishop Wake in the see of Canterbury; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> station he supported with much <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> until his death in 1747. He was a learned and exemplary churchman; but not of an amiable disposition, being strongly tinctured with that sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> which usually accompanies rigid orthodoxy; nor is it to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> that he disdained his eldest son for marrying below his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. His "Theological works, containing sermons, charges, discourses on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> lectures," were printed at Oxford, in 3 vols, 8vo. 1753.

POTTERY

Pages 105-106

the manufacture of earthen <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the art of making earthen vessels. See Delft-Ware, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>-Ware, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORCELAIN">Porcelain</a>. The wheel and lathe are the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> and almost the only instruments in pottery: the first for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> works, and the last for small. The potters-wheel consists principally in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, which is a beam or axis, whose foot or pivot plays perpendicularly on a free-stone sole or bottom. From the four corners of this beam, which does not exceed two feet in height, arise four <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> bars, called the spokes of the wheel; which forming diagonal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> with the beam, descend, and are fastened at bottom to the edges of a strong wooden circle, four feet in diameter, perfectly like the felloes of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COACH">coach</a>-wheel, except that it has neither axis nor radius, and is only joined to the beam, which serves it as an axis by the iron bars. The top of the nut is flat, of a circular <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and a foot in diameter: and on this is laid the clay which is to be turned and fashioned. The wheel thus disposed, is encompassed with four sides of four different pieces of wood fastened on a wooden frame; the hind-piece, which is that on which the workman sits, is made a little inclining towards the wheel; on the fore-piece are placed the prepared <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; on the side-pieces he rests his feet, and these are made inclining to give him more or less room. Having prepared the earth, the potter lays a round piece of it on the circular head of the nut, and fitting <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> turns the wheel with his feet till it has got the proper velocity; then, wetting his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, he presses his fist or his fingers-ends into the middle of the lump, and thus forms the cavity of the vessel, continuing to widen it from the middle; and thus <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the inside into form with one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, while he proportions the outside with the other, the wheel constantly turning all the while, and he wetting his hands from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time. When the vessel is too thick, he uses a flat piece of iron, somewhat sharp on the edge, to pare off what is redundant; and when it is finished, it is taken off from the circular head, by a wire passed under the vessel. The potters-lathe is also a kind of wheel, but more simple and slight than the former; its three chief members are an iron beam or axis three feet and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and two feet and a half diameter, placed horizontally at the top of the beam, and serving to form the vessel upon: and another larger wooden wheel, all of a piece, three inches thick, and two or three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, fastened to the same beam at the bottom, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon. The beam or axis turns by a pivot at the bottom in an iron stand. The workman gives the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> to the lathe with his feet, by pushing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> wheel alternately with each foot, still giving it a greater or lesser <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of motion as his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> requires. They work with the lathe, with the same instruments, and after the same manner, as with the wheel. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a> are formed by holding a piece of wood or iron cut in the form of the moulding to the vessel, while the wheel is turning round; but the feet and handles are made by themselves and set on with the hand; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> in the work; it is usually done in wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>, and stuck on piece by piece on the outside of the vessel. For the glazing of the work, see Glazing.

POULTICE

Pages 106-106

a sort of medicine, called also a cataplasm. See CATAPLASM.

POULTRY

Pages 106-106

all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> birds brought up in yards, as cocks, hens, capons, ducks, turkeys, &c. Almost, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not all the domestic birds of the poultry kind that we maintain in our yards are of foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>; but there are others to be ranked in this class that are as yet in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and perhaps only wait till they become sufficiently scarce to be taken under the care of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> to multiply their propagation. It <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear remarkable enough, if we consider how much the tame poultry which we have imported from distant climates has increased, and how much those wild birds of the poultry kind that have never yet been taken into keeping have been diminished and destroyed. They are all thinned; and many of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, especially in the more cultivated and populous parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, are utterly unseen. Under birds of the poultry kind may be ranked all those that have <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and, comparatively to their head and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, have bulky bodies.
