They are furnished with short strong bills for picking up grain, which is their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> and often their only sustenance. Their wings are short and concave; for which reason they are not able to fly far. They lay a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many eggs; and as they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> their young abroad, the very <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> they are hatched, in quest of food, which they are shown by the mother, and which they pick up for themselves, they generally make their nests on the ground. The toes of all these are united by a membrane as far as the first articulation, and then are divided as in those of the former class. Under this class we may therefore render the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> cock, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">turkey</a>, the pintada <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Guineas hen, the pheasant, the bustard, the grouse, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUAIL">quail</a>. They all bear a strong similitude to each other, being equally granivorous, fleshy, and delicate to the palate. They are among birds what beasts of pasture are among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, peaceable tenants of the field, and shunning the thicker parts of the forest, that abounds with numerous animals who carry on unceasing hostilities against them. As nature has formed the rapacious class for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, so she seems equally to have fitted these for peace, rest, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. Their wings are but short, so that they are ill formed for wandering from one region to another; their bills are also short, and incapable of annoying their opposers; their legs are strong indeed; but their toes are made for scratching up their food, and not for holding or tearing it. These are sufficient indications of their harmless nature; while their bodies, which are fat and fleshy, render them unwieldy travellers, and incapable of straying far from each other. Accordingly, we find them chiefly in society; they live together; and though they may have their disputes, like all other animals, upon some occasions; yet, when kept in the same district, or fed in the same yard, they learn the arts of subordination; and, in proportion as each knows his strength, he seldom tries a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> where he has once been worsted. In this manner, all of this kind seem to lead an indolent voluptuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. As they are furnished internally with a very strong stomach, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called a gizzard, so their voraciousness scarce knows any bounds. If kept in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, and separated from all their former companions, they have still the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of eating left; and they soon grow fat and unwieldy in their prison. To say this more simply, many of the wilder species of birds, when cooped or caged, pine away, grow gloomy, and some refuse all sustenance whatever; none except those of the poultry kind grow fat, who seem to lose all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of their former <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, satisfied with indolence and plenty.

POUNCE

Pages 106-106

is also a little heap of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> dust, inclosed in a piece of muslin <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> some other open stuff, to be passed over holes pricked in a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, in order to mark the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> or designs thereof on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, &c. placed underneath; which are to be afterwards finished with a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INK">ink</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, or the like. This kind of pounce is much used by embroiderers, to transfer their patterns upon stuffs; by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LACE">lace</a>-makers, and sometimes also by engravers.

POUNCES

Pages 106-106

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FALCONRY">falconry</a>, the talons <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> claws of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> of prey.

POUND

Pages 106-106

a standard-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; for the proportion and subdivisions of which, see the article WEIGHT.

POUND ALSO

Pages 106-106

d also denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of account; so called, because the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of silver weighed a pound <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">troy</a>. Pound, among lawyers, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of strength, in which to keep cattle that are distrained, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> put in for trespass, until they are replevied or redeemed.

POUNDAGE

Pages 106-106

a subsidy of 12 d. in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, granted to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on all goods and merchandizes exported <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> imported; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> by aliens, one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> more.

POURPRESTURE

Pages 106-106

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is a wrongful infelicity, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> incroachment upon another person's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>.

POURSUVANT

Pages 106-106
or Pursuivant, in heraldry, the lowest order of officers at arms.—They are properly attendants on the heralds when they marshal public ceremonies. Of these in England there were formerly many; but at present there are only four, viz. blue-mantle, rouge-crofs, rouge dragon, and portcullice. In Scotland, there is only one king-at-arms, who is styled Lyon; and has under him no less than six heralds, as many pursuivants, and a great many messengers at arms. See LYON.

POURVEYANCE

Pages 106-106
or Purveyance, in law, the providing corn, fuel, victuals, &c. for the king's household; and hence the officer who did so was termed purveyor. As several offences were committed by these officers, it was enacted by stat. 12 Car. II. that no person, under colour of purveyance, shall take any timber, cattle, corn, &c. from any subject without his free consent, or without a just apprailement and paying for the same.

POUSSIN

Pages 106-107

an eminent French painter, born POW Poussin, Powder. born in 1594 at Andel, a little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> in Normandy, where his father was of noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> but born to a small estate. He was instructed for a few months by one Ferdinand Elle a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>-painter, and afterward spent a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> with L'Allemant; but finding these artists not likely to improve him suitably to his desires, he first studied the paintings of the best masters, and then hastened to finish a few pieces he was engaged in, and traveled to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Here he devoted almost his whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of antique <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and bas reliefs; which was probably the cause of his want of knowledge in, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for, the art of colouring. Being invited back to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIII., who assigned him a pension with lodgings in the Tuileries, he painted for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> Juffiani an historical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> representing Herod's cruelty; an admirable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, in which he gave such <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> to every character, as could not fail to strike the beholder with terror and pity: he then laboured for several years on the celebrated pictures of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sacraments of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. But none of Poussin's designs have been more generally admired than that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Germanicus; which would have gained him immortal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had never painted another picture. He began the labours of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> in the gallery of the Louvre; but the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> of Vouet's school railing at him and his performances, put him so out of humour with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, that he returned to Rome, where he died in 1665. He never went beyond easel pieces, for which he had a perpetual demand; and his method was to fix the price he expected on the back of the canvas, which was readily paid. Poussin (Galpar), this painter, whose real name was Duguet, was born at Paris in 1600; and was induced to travel to Rome, not only from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to the art of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, but also to visit his sister who was married to Nicholas Poussin. Sandrart says that Galpar was employed at first only to prepare the pallet, pencils, and colours, for Nicholas; but by the precepts and example of that excellent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, gradually rose to the highest reputation, and is undoubtedly one of the best landscape painters that ever appeared. It is generally thought that no painter ever studied <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to better purpose, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> represented the effects of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-storms more happily, than Galpar; all his trees shew a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of agitation, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> being in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; his scenes are all beautifully chosen, as are the sites of his buildings. He designed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> figures but very indifferently; for which reason he frequently prevailed on Nicholas to paint them for him; and they were always introduced with the utmost propriety. While he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> at Rome, he dropped his own name, and assumed that of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> and benefactor, by which only he is at present known. He died in 1662.

POWDER

Pages 107-107

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, a dry medicine well broken, either in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> by some chemical operation. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">Gun</a>-Powder. See Gun-Powder. Powder-Chests, certain small boxes <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with powder and a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of old nails or splinters of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and fastened occasionally on the deck and sides of a ship, in order to be discharged on an enemy who attempts to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> her by boarding. These <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> are usually from 12 to 18 inches in length, and about eight or ten in breadth, having their outer or upper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> terminating in an edge. They are nailed to several places of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-deck and bulk-head of the waist, having a train of powder, which communicates with the inner apartments of the ship, so as to be fired at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to annoy the enemy. They are particularly used in merchant-ships which are furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> to oppose the boarders. Powder for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">Hair</a>. The best sort is first well pounded and sifted, and generally prepared with some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a>.

POWER

Pages 107-107

the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of doing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> suffering any thing. Power therefore is two-fold, viz. considered as able to make, or able to receive, any change; the former whereof may be called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> power, and the latter <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> power. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, n° 73—80. Power, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, denotes any force, whether of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, &c. which, being applied to a machine, tends to produce <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. Power, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies in general, a particular authority granted by any person to another to represent him, or to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in his stead.

POWERS

Pages 107-107

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, are nothing but the products arising from the continual multiplications of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> into itself. See Algebra and Arithmetic.

POYNING'S LAW

Pages 107-107

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> made in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> under Henry VII. whereby all the statutes of force in England were made of force in Ireland; which before that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> they were not.—Nor are any now in force there, made in England since that time. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> took its name from Sir Edward Poyning, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> at the time of its making.

PRACTICE

Pages 107-110

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>. See there, n° 16, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">Gun</a>-Practice, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, as soon as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> permits, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> guns begins, with an intention to show the gentlemen cadets at the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> military academy at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOOLWICH">Woolwich</a>, and private men, the manner of laying, loading, pointing, and firing the guns. Sometimes instruments are used to find the centre line, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, one at the breech, the other at the muzzle, which are marked with chalk, and whereby the piece is directed to the target: then a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> is put into the mouth to give the gun the required elevation, which at first is guessed at, according to the distance the target is from the piece. When the piece has been fired, it is sponged to clear it from any dust or sparks of fire that might remain in the bore, and loaded: then the centre line is found, as before; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> went too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> or too low, to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or to the left, the elevation and trail are altered accordingly. This practice continues morning and evening for about six weeks, more or less, according as there are a greater or lesser <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of recruits. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> others are shown the motions of quick firing with field-pieces. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORTAR">Mortar</a>-Practice, generally thus. A line of 1500 or 2000 yards is measured in an open spot of ground from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the mortars stand, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> fixed at about 300 or 500 yards: this being done, the ground where the mortars are to be placed is prepared and PRÆMUNIRE, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is taken either for a writ so called, or for the offence whereon the writ is granted; the one may be understood by the other.—The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, under pretence of her supremacy and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, took on her to bestow most of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> livings of any worth in England by mandates, before they were void; pretending therein great care to see the church provided of a successor before it needed. Whence these mandates or bulls were called gratia expectativa, or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>; whereof see a learned discourse in Duarenus de beneficiis, lib. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 1. These provisions were so <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, that at last Edward III. not digesting to intolerable an encroachment, in the 35th year of his reign made a statute against papal provisions, which, according to Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, is the foundation of all the subsequent statutes of præmunire: which is ranked as an offence immediately against the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, because every encouragement of the papal power is a diminution of the authority of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. In the weak reign of Edward II. the pope again endeavoured to encroach, but the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> manfully withstood him; and it was one of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> against that unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, that he had given allowance to the bulls of the see of Rome. But Edw. III. was of a temper extremely different; and, to remedy these inconveniences first by gentle means, he and his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> wrote an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPOSTULATION">expostulation</a> to the pope: but receiving a menacing and contemptuous answer, withal acquainting him, that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> (who a few years before at the diet of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>, A.D. 1323, had established a law against provisions) and also the king of France had lately submitted to the holy see; the king replied, that if both the emperor and the French king should take the pope's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, he was ready to give <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> to them both, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the liberties of the crown. Hereupon more sharp and penal laws were devised against provisors, which enact severally, that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome shall present or collate to no bishopric or living in England; and that whoever disturbs any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> in the presentation to a living by virtue of a papal provision, such provisor shall pay fine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> to the king at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and be imprisoned till he renounces such provision; and the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> is inflicted on such as cite the king, or any of his subjects, to answer in the court of Rome. And when the holy see reflected these proceedings, and pope Urban V. attempted to revive the vassalage and annual rent to which king John had subjected his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, it was unanimously agreed by all the estates of the realm in parliament assembled, 40 Edw. III. that king John's donation was null and void, being without the concurrence of parliament, and contrary to his coronation oath; and all the temporal nobility and commons engaged, that if the pope should endeavour by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> or otherwise to maintain these usurpations, they would resist and withstand him with all their power. In the reign of Richard II. it was found necessary to sharpen and strengthen these laws, and therefore it was enacted by statutes 3 Ric. II. c. 3. and 7 Ric. II. c. 12., first, that no alien shall be capable of letting his benefice to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FARM">farm</a>; in order to compel such as had crept in, at least to reside in their preferments; and afterwards, that no alien should be capable to be presented to any ecclesiastical preferment, under the penalty of the statutes of provisors. By the statute 12 Rich II. c. 15. all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEGE">liege</a> men of the king accepting of a living by any foreign provision, are put out of the king's protection, and the benefice made void. To which the statute 13 Rich. II. st. 2. c. 2. adds banishment and forfeiture of lands and goods: and by c. 3. of the same statute, any person bringing over any citation or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a> from beyond <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on account of the execution of the foregoing statutes of provisors, shall be imprisoned, forfeit his goods and lands, and moreover suffer pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and member. In the writ for the execution of all these statutes, the words præmunire facias, being used to command a citation of the party, have denominated in common speech, not only the writ, but the offence itself of maintaining the papal power, by the name of præmunire. And accordingly the next statute we shall mention, which is generally referred to by all subsequent statutes, is usually called the statute of præmunire. It is the statute 16 Rich. II. c. 5. which enacts, that whoever procures at Rome, or elsewhere, any translations, processes, excommunications, bulls, instruments, or other things which touch the king, against him, his crown, and realm, and all persons aiding and afflicting therein, shall be put out of the king's protection, their lands and goods forfeited to the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, and they shall be attached by their bodies to answer to the king and his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; or process of præmunire facias shall be made out against them as in other <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of provisors. By the statute 2 Henry IV. c. 3. all persons who accept any provision from the pope, to be exempt from canonical obedience to their proper ordinary, are also subjected to the penalties of præmunire. And this is the last of our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> statutes touching this offence; the usurped civil power of the bishop of Rome being pretty PRAE Fraenumire, pretty well broken <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by these statutes, as his usurped <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> power was in about a century afterwards; the spirit of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> being so much raised against foreigners, that about this time, in the reign of Hen.V., the alien priories, or abbeys for foreign monks, were suppressed, and their lands given to the crown. And no farther attempts were afterwards made in support of these foreign jurisdictions. This then is the original meaning of the offence which we call praemunire; viz. introducing a foreign power into this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and creating imperium in imperio, by paying that obedience to papal process which constitutionally belonged to the king alone, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the Reformation in the reign of Henry VIII. at which time the penalties of praemunire were indeed extended to more papal abuses than before; as the kingdom then entirely renounced the authority of the see of Rome, though not all the corrupted doctrines of the Roman church. And therefore by the several statutes of 24 Hen.VIII. c.12. and 25 Hen.VIII. c.19. & 21. to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to Rome from any of the king's courts, which (though illegal before) had at times been connived at; to sue to Rome for any licence or dispensation, or to obey any process from thence, are made liable to the pains of praemunire. And, in order to restore to the king in effect the nomination of vacant bishoprics, and yet keep up the established forms, it is enacted by statute 25 Hen.VIII. c.20. that if the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> refuse to elect the person named by the king, or any archbishop or bishop to confirm or consecrate him, they shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> within the penalties of the statutes of praemunire. Also by statute 5 Eliz. c.1. to refuse the oath of supremacy will incur the pains of praemunire; and to defend the pope's jurisdiction in this realm, is a praemunire for the first offence, and high <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. So too, by statute 13 Eliz. c.2. to import any agnus Dei, crosses, beads, or other superstitious things pretended to be hallowed by the bishop of Rome, and tender the same to be used; or to receive the same with such intent, and not discover the offender; or if a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, knowing thereof, shall not within 14 days declare it to a privy counsellor, they all incur a praemunire. But importing or selling mals-books, or other Popish books, is by stat. 3 Jac. I. c.5. §25. only liable to a penalty of 40s. Lastly, to contribute to the maintenance of a Jesuit's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, or any Popish seminary whatever beyond sea, or any person in the same, or to contribute to the maintenance of any Jesuit or Popish <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in England, is by statute 27 Eliz. c.2. made liable to the penalties of praemunire. Thus far the penalties of praemunire seem to have kept within the proper bounds of their original <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, the depreffing the power of the pope: but, they being pains of no inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, it has been thought fit to apply the same to other heinous offences; some of which bear more, and some less relation to this original offence, and some no relation at all. Thus, 1. By the statute 1 & 2 Ph. and Mar. c.8. to molest the possessors of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>-lands granted by parliament to Henry VIII. and Edward VI. is a praemunire. 2. So likewise is the offence of acting as a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BROKER">broker</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in any usurious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> where above 10 per cent. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> is taken, by statute 13 Eliz. c.10. 3. To obtain any stay of proceedings, other than by praemunire-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> of judgment or writ of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, in any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> for a monopoly, is likewise a praemunire, by statute 21 Jac. I. c.3. 4. To obtain an exclusive patent for the sole making or importation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> or arms, or to hinder others from importing them, is also a praemunire by two statutes; the one 16 Car. I. c.21. the other 1 Jac. II. c.8. 5. On the abolition, by stat. 12 Car. II. c.24. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PURVEYANCE">purveyance</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of pre-emption, or taking any victual, beasts, or goods for the king's use, at a stated price, without consent of the proprietor, the exertion of any such power for the future was declared to incur the penalties of praemunire. 6. To affirm, maliciously and advisedly, by speaking or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, that both or either <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of parliament have a legislative authority without the king, is declared a praemunire by statute 13 Car. II. c.1. 7. By the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABEAS_CORPUS">habeas corpus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> also, 31 Car. II. c.2. it is a praemunire, and incapable of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, besides other heavy penalties, to send any subject of this realm a prisoner into parts beyond the seas. 8. By the statute 1 W. & M. st.1. c.8. persons of 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> refusing to take the new <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, as well as supremacy, upon tender by the proper <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, are subject to the penalties of a praemunire; and by statute 7 & 8 W. III. c.24. ferrets, counsellors, proctors, attorneys, and all officers of courts, practising without having taken the oaths of allegiance and supremacy, and subscribed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>, are guilty of a praemunire, whether the oaths be tendered or no. 9. By the statute 6 Ann. c.7. to affirm maliciously and directly, by preaching, teaching, or advised speaking, that the then pretended prince of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, or any person other than according to the acts of settlement and union, hath any right to the throne of these kingdoms, or that the king and parliament cannot make laws to limit the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the crown; such preaching, teaching, or advised speaking, is a praemunire: as writing, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, or publishing the same doctrines amounted, we may remember, to high treason. 10. By statute 6 Ann. c.23. if the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> of Scotland, convened to elect their 16 representatives in the British parliament, shall presume to treat of any other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> only the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, they incur the penalties of a praemunire. 11. The stat. 6 Geo. I. c.18. (enacted in the year after the infamous South Sea project had beggared half the nation) makes all unwarrantable undertakings by unlawful subscriptions, then <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of bubblers, subject to the penalties of a praemunire. 12. The stat. 12 Geo. III. c.11. subjects to the penalties of the statute of praemunire all such as knowingly and wilfully solemnize, assist, or are present at, any forbidden <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of such of the descendants of the body of king George II. as are by that act prohibited to contract matrimony without the consent of the crown. Having thus inquired into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of praemunire, its punishment may be gathered from the foregoing statutes, which are thus shortly summed up by Sir Edward Coke: "That, from the conviction, the defendant shall be out of the king's protection, and his lands and tenements, goods and chattels, forfeited to the king; and that his body shall remain in prison at the king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, or (as other authorities have it) during life; both which amount to PRÆNESTE (anc. geog.) a town of Latium, to the south-east of Rome, towards the territory of the Æqui; a place of great strength. Famous for the temple and oracle of Fortune, called Sortes Prænestinae, (Strabo); which Tiberius wanted to destroy, but was deterred by the awful majesty of the place. From a colony it was raised to a municipium by Tiberius, (<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a>, Florus, A. Gellius), on the consideration of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> from a dangerous illness near this place. Thither the Roman emperors usually retired, on account of the agreeableness of the situation, (Suetonius). It was a very ancient <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, with a territory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, (Livy.) The temple of Fortune was built in the most sumptuous manner by Sylla, and the pavement was mosaic <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, (Pliny). Concerning the Sortes, there is a remarkable passage in Cicero; who says, that it was all a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> contrivance, in order to deceive, either for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. The town that has succeeded it, stands low in a valley, and is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTRINA">Palestrina</a>, in the Campania of Rome. E. Long. 13. 30. Lat. 42. 0. PRÆSIDIUM, (Notitia) a town of the Cornovii in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Now thought to be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, (Camden), —Another of Coriaca (Antonine), 30 miles to the south of Aleria.—A third Præsidium farnamed Julium, in Batetia, (Pliny). PRÆTORIA AUGUSTA (<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>), a town of Dacia. Now called Brașov by the natives, and Kronstadt by the Germans, (Baudrand); a town in Transylvania. E. Long. 25°. N. Lat. 47°.—Another of the Salassi, near the two gates or defiles of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, the Grajze and Penninze, (Pliny); a Roman colony, settled by Augustus after the defeat of the Salassi by Terentius Varro, on the spot where he encamped, (Strabo, Dio Cassius, Ptolemy), situated on the river Duria <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>. The town is now called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AOSTA">Aosta</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AVA">Ava</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>. E. Long. 7. 14. N. Lat. Praetorium, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>. PRÆTORIUM (Antonine, Notitia Imperii), a town of the Brigantes. New Paterington (Camden), near the mouth of the Humber in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, (Talbot.)

PRAGUE

Pages 110-111

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, is situated 14° 40' of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>., and 50° 5' of lat. It stands on both sides the Mulda, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>; but the river, though of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> breadth here, is nevertheless shallow, and not navigable. On both sides the bridge are several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and, among others, that of St John of Nepomuck, whom <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Wenzel caused to be thrown from the bridge into the river, for venturing to reprove him upon some occasion; but in 1720 he was canonized as a saint, and is at present held in such veneration in Bohemia, that all other saints seem, on his account, to be forgotten. The houses of this city are wholly built of stone, and consist for the most of three stories. Here are near 100 churches and chapels, and about 40 cloisters. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of its Christian inhabitants is said to be 70,000, and of Jews about 12,000. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> branch of its trade consists in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a> of beer. It is divided into the Old and the New <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">Towns</a>, and that called the Small side; the former lying on the east side of the Mulda, and the latter on the west. The whole is about 12 miles in circumference, and but thinly inhabited. The fortifications are not of great importance, as it may be flanked and raked on all sides. However, the king of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> was not able to make himself <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it in the late <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, though he almost destroyed it with his bombs, &c. It stands in a pleasant and fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in the midst of gardens, fine fields, palaces, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>-houses. It hath suffered greatly by sieges, and hath been often taken and plundered. The university was founded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IV. in the year 1347. In 1409, when John Hus was rector of the university, there were no less than 44,000 students; and when the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Charles V. would have retrenched their privileges, 24,000 are said to have left it in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, and 16,000 in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> after. The Jews have the trade of this city almost entirely in their own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. They <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in all sorts of commodities, especially the precious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> found in the Bohemian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, and, by receiving all old-fashioned things in payment, quite ruin the Christian handicraftsmen. In 1744 they narrowly escaped being expelled the kingdom, having been suspected of corresponding with the Prussians, when they made themselves masters of the city. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of the order of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, for Bohemia, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, resides here; and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> of the Holy Ghost is the seat of the general and grand-masters of the holy order of knights of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a>, residing in the above-mentioned countries, and in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is dedicated to St Vit, and adorned with many magnificent tombs of great personages. On Ratschin-hill, in Upper-Prague, most of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> have houses, and the emperor a very magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, commanding one of the finest prospects in the world. Here the tribunals of the regency meet; and the halls, galleries, and other apartments, are adorned with a multitude of noble pictures. The great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, where where the coronation-feast is kept, is said to be the largest of the kind in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> next to that of Westminster. The castle stands on the above-mentioned mountain, called Ratshin <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Mountain, and is very strong. From a window of this castle the emperor's counsellors were thrown in 1618; but though they fell from a great height, yet they were not killed, nor indeed much hurt. On the same mountain stands also the archiepiscopal palace. In the New Town is an arsenal, and a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> foundation for ladies, called the Free Temporal English foundation, over which an abbess presides. In the Lesser Side or Town, the counts Colloredo and Wallenstein have very magnificent palaces and gardens. The stables of the latter are very grand; the racks being of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, and the mangers of marble, and a marble pillar betwixt each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; over each horse also is placed his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, as big as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Though the inhabitants of Prague in general are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and their shops but meanly furnished; yet, it is said, there are few cities where the nobility and gentry are more wealthy, and live in greater state. Here is much <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>, masquerading, sealing, and very splendid public balls, with an Italian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OPERA">opera</a>, and assemblies in the houses of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> every night. On the White Mountain, near the town, was fought the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> Palatine Frederic their king, were defeated. The lustres and drinking glasses made here of Bohemian crystal are much esteemed, and vended all over Europe. These crystals are also polished by the Jews, and set in rings, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>-pendants, and shirts-buttons. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> tribunal consists of twelve stadtholders, at the head of whom is the great burggrave, governor of the kingdom and city, immediately under the emperor, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> of Bohemia.

PRAME

Pages 111-111

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, a kind of floating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, being a flat-bottomed vessel, which draws little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, mounts several guns, and is very useful in covering the disembarkation of troops. They are generally made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in transplanting the troops over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>.

PRAMNION

Pages 111-111

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of a semi-pellucid gem.—This is a very singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and of a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> concealed <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Our lapidaries, when they meet with it, call it by the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>. It is of an extremely <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and firm texture, of a smooth and equal surface, and in shape very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, being sometimes round, sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, and often flat; in size it seldom exceeds two inches. It appears, on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> inspection, to be of a fine deep black; but held up against the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, it is an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> clouded by a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of subtile black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. We have it from the East Indies.

PRATIQUE

Pages 111-111
or PRATTIC, in commerce, a negotiation or communication of commerce which a merchant vessel obtains in the port it arrives in and the countries it discovers; hence to obtain a pratique, is to obtain liberty to frequent a port, to go ashore, to buy and sell, &c.

PRAXAGORAS

Pages 111-111

a native of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, at 19 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> composed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Kings of Athens, in two books: and at 22 the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Constantine the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, in which, though a pagan, he speaks very advantageously of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. He also wrote the History of Alexander the Great. He lived under Constantius, about the year 345.

PRAXITELES

Pages 111-111

a very famous Greek sculptor, who lived 330 years before Christ, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the reign of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. All the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers mention his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> commendation, especially a Venus executed by him for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Cnidos, which was so admirable a piece, that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Nicomedes offered to release the inhabitants from their tribute as the purchase of it; but they refused to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> with it. He was one of the gallants of the celebrated courtezan Phryne. PREACHING. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECLAMATION">DECLAMATION</a>, Art. I.—The word is derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> parash, expofit, "he expounded."

PRE-EMPTION

Pages 112-112

a privilege anciently allowed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s purveyor, of having the choice and first buying of corn and other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> for the king's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; but taken away by the statute 19, Car. II.

PRE-EXISTENCE

Pages 112-114

a priority of being, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the being of one thing before another. Thus a cause, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, is yet in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> pre-existent to its effect. Thus God is pre-existent to the universe. Thus a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> father is pre-existent to his son. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a>, though they maintained the eternity of the world, maintain the world was produced, actuated, and governed, by a formal, sovereign intelligence. Embarrassed, however, with the difficulty, that causation seemed to imply previous existence, as no being could operate either production or change upon another till its own existence and powers of operation had first been realized, these profound and accurate philosophers exerted all their subtlety and learning to obviate an objection so formidable. Thus, in order to extricate their system, they had recourse to a distinction which equally showed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of their genius and the depth of their erudition. They distinguished between priority in nature and priority in time. It is impossible, say they, to conceive the existence of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, for one indivisible instant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to his emission of rays. When a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> is stamped upon wax, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> must be strictly and absolutely coextensive with the impulse; thus the emanent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> or exertion of Deity in producing, moving, and superintending the universe, must be one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> and unsuccessive energy. It is unnecessary to enter into the depth or minutiae of this controversy, since we are assured by the best of all authorities, that the world was created in time; from whence it follows, that even in the course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> the existence of God must have been anterior to that of his works. The difficulty urged by them, and by other sceptical philosophers, that at whatever <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of duration creative power began to be exerted, it must have passed an eternity prior to that point in supine indolence and inactivity; though not to be solved by human divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> reason, is yet less formidable, because more easily conceivable, than the eternal coexistence of an effect with its cause. Previous to that distinguished era in endless duration, when nature at the Almighty fiat emerged from nothing, we are entirely ignorant of the motives (if it may be so expressed) which might predispose infinite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, power, and goodness, then, and not till then, to exert themselves in creating. But since, from all that we see of the divine energy and administration, nothing appears to be done without a sufficient reason, we have the best grounds to conclude, that the same conduct prevails in those divine exertions, whose nature, manner, and adjuncts, are absolutely incomprehensible by our limited powers. It is evident, that the Divine Nature, rich in its eternal and independent all-sufficiency, could never feel any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> which might be redressed or gratified by the existence or homage of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> nature. The universe therefore must be formed for itself alone; and could only be the glorious result of unconstrained wisdom and voluntary goodness. Besides, there is no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of deductions more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and congenial to the human mind, than to conclude, that what is eternal must be unproduced: That if it was produced, there must have been a period when it did not exist: if it was not produced, it must be independent; if independent, it must be self-existent; and if self-existent, it must from eternity to eternity be invested with powers sufficient for the maintenance and regulation of its own existence; so that not only the necessity, but perhaps even the possibility of a supreme <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">Agent</a> and wise Superintendent, acting upon nature, and animating or controlling her operations, is upon this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> entirely superfluous. But from the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, symmetry, and order, of nature, and from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> causes pursued in her progress and accomplished in its results, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and his followers were too wise not to perceive, and too ingenious not to acknowledge, the sacred vestiges, the conspicuous interpositions, of infinite wisdom, power, and goodness; hence his notion of an eternal world, though generally admitted among the sages of antiquity, was an incompatible or self-destructive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. The objections which have already been mentioned against a temporary <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, might perhaps be obviated, if not annihilated, were it our present business to enter deeply into the nature of space and time. But this disquisition requires a boldness and abstraction of thought, in which we might probably be followed by few, and relished by fewer readers. Such, however, as have courage, sagacity, and perseverance, to penetrate and pursue these intricacies to their ultimate conclusions, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> find their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> cheered and enlightened by the philosophical essays of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Watts, and by the chevalier Ramlay's principles of natural and revealed <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. Veracity likewise obliges us to add, that the speculations of Mr Hume on this abstruse and arduous subject, had a greater tendency to dissipate its gloom than that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> himself could imagine. The pre-existence of the human <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> to its corporeal vehicle had been from time immemorial a prevailing opinion among the Asiatic sages, and from them was perhaps transferred by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of the Greeks; but his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METEMPSYCHOSIS">metempsychosis</a>, or transmigration of souls, is too trivial either to be seriously proposed or refuted. Nevertheless, from the sentiments of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the soul, delivered in his last interview with his friends, it is obvious that the tenet of pre-existence was a doctrine of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> school. If at any period of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, say these philosophers, you should examine a boy, of how many <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, of what a number of principles, of what an extent of knowledge, will you find him possessed? These, without doubt, could neither be self-derived nor recently acquired. With what avidity and promptitude does he attain the knowledge of arts and sciences, which appear entirely new to him! These rapid and successful advances in knowledge can only be the effects of reminiscence, or of a fainter and more indistinct <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of recollection. But in all the other operations of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, we find retrospective impressions attending every object or idea which emerges to her view; nor does she ever suggest any thought, word, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, without informing us, in a manner equally clear and evident, that those impressions have been made upon our senses, mind, or intellect, on some former occasion. Whoever contemplates her progress, will easily discover, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> is her most faithful and efficacious auxiliary; and that by joining impression with impression, idea with idea, circumstance with circumstance, in the order of time, of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, of similarity or dissimilarity, she is capacitated to accumulate her treasures and enlarge her <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> even to an indefinite extent. But when intuitive principles, or simple conclusions, are elicited from the puerile understanding, by a train of easy questions properly arranged; where is the retrospective act of memory, by which the boy recognizes those truths as having formerly been perceived in his mind? Where are the crowds of concomitant, antecedent, or subsequent ideas, with which those recollections ought naturally to have been attended? In a word, where is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of personal identity, which seems absolutely inseparable from every act of memory? This hypothesis, therefore, will not support pre-existence. After the Christian religion had been considerably diffused, and warmly combated by its philosophical antagonists, the same doctrine was resumed and taught at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, by Platonist professedly, not only as a topic constituent of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s philosophy, but as an answer to those formidable objections which had been deduced from the doctrine of original sin, and from the vices which stain, and from the calamities which disturb, human life: hence they strenuously asserted, that all the human <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a> were either introduced to being prior to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, or pre-existent in his person; that they were not therefore represented by our first parents, but actually concurred in their crime, and participated their ruin. The followers of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, and such as entertained the notion of pre-Adamites, might argue from the doctrine of pre-existence with some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of plausibility. For the human beings introduced by them to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> of probation had already attained the capacity or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of moral agents; as their crime therefore was voluntary, their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> might be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a>. But those who believe the whole human race created in Adam to be only pre-existent in their germs or stamina, were even deprived of this miserable subterfuge; for in these homunculi we can neither suppose the moral nor rational <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> unfolded. Since, therefore, their degeneracy... Pre-existence was not spontaneous, neither could their sufferings be equitable. Should it be said that the evil of original sin was penal, as it extended to our first parents alone, and merely consequential as felt by their posterity, it will be admitted that the distinction between penal and consequential evil may be intelligible in human affairs, where other laws, affections, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> than those which are simply and purely moral, take place. But that a moral <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, at one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> periods of its administration, should admit gratuitous or consequential evil, seems to us irreconcilable with the attributes and conduct of a wise and just <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. Consequential evil taken as such, is misery sustained without demerit; and cannot result from the procedure of wisdom, benignity, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; but must flow from necessity, from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, from cruelty, or from caprice, as its only possible sources. But even upon the supposition of those who pretend that man was mature in all his faculties before the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of original sin, the objections against it will still remain in full force. For it is admitted by all except the Samian sage, that the consciousness of personal identity which was felt in pre-existence, is obliterated in a subsequent state of being. Now it may be demanded, whether agents thus subjected for punishment, have not the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to murmur and complain as if they had been perfectly innocent, and only created for that dreadful catastrophe? It is upon this principle alone that the effects of punishment can be either exemplary or disciplinary; for how is it possible, that the punishment of beings unconscious of a crime, should ever be reconciled either to the justice or beneficence of that intention with which their sufferings are inflicted? or how can others be supposed to become wise and virtuous by the example of those who are neither acquainted with the origin nor the tendency of their miseries, but have every reason to think themselves afflicted merely for the sake of afflicting. To us it seems clear, that the nature and rationale of original sin <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> inscrutably retired in the bosom of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>; nor can we, without unpardonable presumption and arrogance, form the most simple conclusion, or attempt the minutest discovery, either different from or extraordinary to the clear and obvious sense of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>. This sense indeed may with propriety be extracted from the whole, or from one passage collated with another; but independent of it, as reason has no premises, she can form no deductions. The boldness and temerity of philosophy, not satisfied with contemplating pre-existence as merely relative to human nature, has dared to try how far it was compatible with the glorious Persons of the Sacred Trinity. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, who allowed the subordinate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of our Saviour, believed him pre-existent to all time, and before all worlds; but the Socinians, who esteemed his nature as well as his person merely human, insisted that before his incarnation he was only pre-existent in the divine idea, not in nature or person. But when it is considered, that children do not begin to deduce instructions from nature and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, at a period so late as we are apt to imagine; when it is admitted, that their progress, tho' insensible, may be much more rapid than we apprehend; when the opportunities of sense, the ardour of curiosity, the avidity of memory, and the activity of understanding, are remarked; we need not have recourse to a pre-existent state for our account of the knowledge which young minds discover. It may likewise be added, that moral agents can only be improved and cultivated by moral <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>. Such effects therefore of any state, whether happy or miserable, as are merely <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>, may be noxious or salutary to the patient, but can never enter into any moral economy as parts of its own administration. Pre-existence, therefore, whether rewarded or punished, without the continued impression of personal identity, affords no solution of original sin.

PREADAMITE

Pages 111-111

a denomination given to the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, conceived, by some people, to have lived before <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> de la Pereyra, in 1655, published a book to evince the reality of Preadamites, by which he gained a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of proselytes to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; but the answer of Demarets, professor of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a>, published the year following, put a stop to its progress; though Pereyra made a reply. His system was this: The Jews he calls Adamites, and supposes them to have issued from Adam; and gives the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> Preadamites, to the Gentiles, whom he supposes to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> before Adam. But this being expressly contrary to the first words of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, Pereyra had recourse to the fabulous antiquities of the Egyptians and Chaldeans, and to some idle rabbins, who imagined there had been another world before that described by Moses. He was apprehended by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, and very roughly used, though in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the dauphin. But he appealed from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> to Rome; whither he went in the time of Alexander VII., and where he printed a retraction of his book of Preadamites.

PREAMBULE

Pages 111-111

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the beginning of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, &c. which serves to open the intent of the act, and the mischiefs intended to be remedied by it.

PREBEND

Pages 111-111

the maintenance a prebendary receives out of the estate of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Prebends are distinguished into simple and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITARY">dignitary</a>: a simple prebend has no more than the revenue for its support; but a prebend with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, has always a jurisdiction annexed to it.

PREBENDARY

Pages 111-111

an ecclesiastic who enjoys a prebend. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between a prebendary and a canon is, that the former receives his prebend in consideration of his officiating in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, but the latter merely by his being received into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>.

PRECARIUM

Pages 111-112

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>. See Law, No clxxiii. 9. PRECEDENCE, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to which a person is entitled. This is either of courtesy <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. The former is that which is due to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, estate, &c. which is regulated by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> and civility: the latter PRE latter is settled by authority; and, when broken in upon, gives an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> at law. For the rules of precedence in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, see <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, p. 3612.

PRECEDENT

Pages 112-112

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> which has been determined, and which serves as a rule for all of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>.

PRECENTOR

Pages 112-112

a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in cathedrals, popularly called the chantor, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the choir.

PRECEPT

Pages 112-112

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a command in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> sent by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> justice of the peace, for bringing a person, record, or other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> before him. Precept of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a> Conflat, in Scots law. See Law, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. No clxxx. 28. Precept of Selina, in Scots law. See Law, Part III. No cixiv. 16.

PRECEPTIVE

Pages 112-112

any thing which gives <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> contains precepts. Preceptive <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>. See Poetry, no 69, &c.

PRECIAE

Pages 112-112

(precius, "early,") the name of the order in Linnaeus's fragments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method; consisting of primrose, an early flowering plant, and a few genera which agree with it in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and structure, tho' not always in the character <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> circumstance expressed in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a>.

PRECIPITANT

Pages 112-112

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, is applied to any liquor, which, when poured on a solution, separates what is dissolved, and makes it precipitate, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to the bottom of the vessel.

PRECIPITATE

Pages 112-112

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, a substance which, having been dissolved in a proper menstruum, is again separated from its solvent, and thrown <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the bottom of the vessel, by pouring some other liquor upon it. PRECIPITATION. See Chemistry, no 71.

PRECOGNITION

Pages 112-112

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>. See Law, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> III. No clxxxvi. 43.

PRECORDIA

Pages 112-112

in anatomy, a general name for the parts situated about the heart, in the forepart of the thorax: as the diaphragm, pericardium, and even the heart itself, with the spleen, lungs, &c.

PREDECESSOR

Pages 112-112

properly signifies a person who has preceded <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> gone before another in the same office or employment, in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is distinguished from ancestor.

PREDESTINATION

Pages 112-112

in general, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of God, whereby, from all eternity, he ordained such a concatenation of causes as must produce every event by a kind of fatal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, and manage all opposition. In this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the Turks are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> predestinarians; and on this account are much more daring in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and willingly encounter greater dangers that they would otherwise do. Predestination, among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, is used, in a more limited sense, for a judgment <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> decree of God, whereby he has resolved, from all eternity, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> a certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons, from thence called elect; so that the rest of mankind, being left in a state of impenitence, are said to be reprobated. Nothing has occasioned more disputes than this thorny subject of predestination; the Lutherans speak of it with horror, while the Calvinists contend for it with great zeal; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOLINISTS">Molinists</a> and Jesuits preach it <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as a most dangerous doctrine, whilst the Janes assert it as an article of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMINIANS">Arminians</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REMONSTRANTS">Remonstrants</a>, and Pelagians, are all avowed enemies to predestination.

PREDIAL TITHES

Pages 112-112

are those that are paid of things arising and growing from the ground only; as corn, hay, fruit, &c.

PREDICABLE

Pages 112-112

among logicians, denotes a general <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> which may be predicated, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> asserted of several things: thus animal is predicable of mankind, beasts, birds, fishes, &c.

PREDICATE

Pages 112-112
