A dissolution of this partnership ensued in 1455; and in 1457 a magnificent edition of the Psalter was published by Fust and Schoeffer, with a remarkable commendation, in which they claimed to themselves the merit of a new invention, (viz. of metal types), ad inventionem artificiosam imprimenti ac characterizandi. This book was uncommonly elegant, and in some measure the work of Gutenberg; as it was four years in the press, and came out but 18 months after the partnership was dissolved between him and Fust. The latter continued in possession of the printing-office; and Gutenberg, by the pecuniary assistance of Conrad Humery (friend of Mentz (s)), and others, opened another office in the same city; whence appeared, in 1460, without the printer's name, the Catholicon Jo. de Janna, with a pompous colophon in praise of its beauty, and ascribing the honour of the invention to the city of Mentz. It was a very handsome book, though inferior to the Psalter which had been published in 1457 by Fust and Schoeffer. Both the Psalter and Catholicon were printed on cut metal types (r). It may not be improper to observe here, that as the Psalter is the earliest book which is known to have a genuine date, it became a common practice after that publication, for printers to claim their own performances, by adding their names to them. III. The progress of the art has been thus traced through its second period, the invention of cut metal types. But the honour of completing the discovery is due to Peter Schoeffer (g) de Gernheim. A very clear account of this final completion of the types is preferred by Trithemius (u). Post hæc inventis successerunt subtiliora, inveneruntque medium fundendi formas omnium Latini alphabeti literarum, quæ ipsi matrices nominabant: ex quibus rursum annos five fiamnes characteres fundebant, ad ommem præferræ sufficiences, quæ prius manibus sculpsent. Et sevæ fianti ante xxx ferme annos ex ore Petri Opilioni de Gernheim, civis Moguntini, qui gener erat primi artis inventoris, audet, magnæ a primo inventione fæcibus hic imperforis habuit difficulatem.—Petrus autem memora tus Opilio, tunc famulus petæa genæ, fecit diximus, inventoris primi, Johannis Fusti, homo ingeniosus et prudentis, facilem medium fundendi characteres excogitavit, et artem, ut nunc est, complevit. Another ample testimony in favour of Schoeffer is given by Jo. Frid. Faustus of Aschaffenburg, from papers preserved in his family: "Peter Schoeffer of Gernheim, perceiving his master Fust's design, and being himself ardently desirous to improve the art, found out (by the good providence of God) the method of cutting (incidenti) the characters in a matrix, that the letters might easily be singly cast, instead of being cut. He privately cut matrices for the whole alphabet; and when he showed his master the letters cast from these matrices, Fust was so pleased with the contrivance, that he promised Peter to give him his only daughter, Christine, in marriage; a promise which he soon after performed. But there were as many difficulties at first with these letters, as there had been before with wooden ones; the metal being too soft to support the force of the impression: but this defect was soon remedied, by mixing the metal with a substance which sufficiently hardened it (i)." Fust and Schoeffer concealed this new improvement, by administering an oath of secrecy to all whom they intrusted, till the year 1462; when, by the dispersion of their servants into different countries, at the lacking of Mentz by the archbishop Adolphus, the invention was publicly divulged. The first book printed with these improved types was Durandi Rationale, in 1459; at which time, however, they (n) Many writers have supposed that this was the edition of which some copies were sold in France, by Fust, as manuscripts, for the great price of 500 or 600 crowns, which he afterwards lowered to 60, and at last to less than 40. But it was the second and more expensive edition of 1462, that was thus disposed of, when Fust went to Paris in 1466, and which had cost 4000 florins before the third quaternion (or quire of four sheets) was printed. Meerman, vol. I. p. 6, 151, 152. (s) At death of Gutenberg, Conrad Humery took possession of all his printing materials; and engaged to the archbishop Adolphus, that he never would sell them to any but a citizen of Mentz. They were, however, soon disposed of to Nicholas Bechtermunz of Altavilla, who, in 1469, published Vocabularium Latino-Teutonicum, which was printed with the same types which had been used in the Catholicon. This very curious and scarce Vocabulary was known to Mr Meerman, by Mr Bryant, in the duke of Marlborough's valuable library at Blenheim. It is in quarto, 35 lines long, contains many extracts from the Catholicon, and is called Ex quo, from the preface beginning with those words. Meerman, vol. II. p. 95. (r) Gutenberg never used any other than either wooden or cut metal types till the year 1462. In 1465 he was admitted inter fulices by the elector Adolphus, with an annual pension; and died in February 1468. His elder brother Geimallech died in 1462. Their epitaphs are printed by Mr Meerman, vol. II. p. 154, 295. (g) In German, Schöffer; in Latin, Opilio; in English, Shepherd.—He is supposed by Mr Meerman to have been the first engraver on copper-plates. (u) Annales Hieronymianæ, tom. ii. ad ann. 1450.—As this book was finished in 1514, and Trithemius tells us he had the narrative from Schoeffer himself about 30 years before; this will bring us back to 1484, when Schoeffer must have been advanced in years, and Trithemius about 22 years old, who died in 1516. See Voß, Hist. Lat. l. i. c. 10. (f) See Meerman, vol. I. p. 183, who copied this testimony from Wolfius, Monument. Typograph. vol. I. p. 468.

PRIORITY

Pages 143-143

the relation of something considered as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to another. **Priority**, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, denotes an antiquity of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of another less <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>.

PRISCANUS

Pages 143-143

an eminent grammarian, born at Caesarea, taught at Constantinople with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation about the year 525. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAURENTIUS">Laurentius</a> Valla calls Priscian, Donatus, and Servius, *triumviri in re grammatica*; and thinks none of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> who wrote after them, fit to be mentioned with them. He composed a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> *De arte grammatica*, which was first printed by Aldus at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1476; and another *De naturalibus quaestionibus*, which he dedicated to Chosroes <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>; beside which he translated Dionysius's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the world into Latin <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. A person who writes false Latin is proverbially said to "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> Priscian's head."

PRISCILLIANISTS

Pages 143-143

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, Christian heretics, so called from their leader Priscillian, a Spaniard by birth, and bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AVILA">Avila</a>. He is said to have practised <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>, and to have maintained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> errors of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANICHEES">Manichees</a>; but his peculiar tenet was, That it is lawful to make false <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> in order to support one's cause and interests.

PRISM

Pages 143-143

an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, contained under more than four planes, whose bases are equal, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>, and alike situated. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>.

PRISON

Pages 143-143

a goal, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of confinement. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> observes, that a prison is only a place of safe custody, *salva custodia*, not a place of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. Any place where a person is confined may be said to be a prison; and when a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is issued against one, he must, when arrested thereon, either be committed to prison, or be bound in a recognizance with sureties, or else give bail, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, to appear at a certain <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, there to make answer to what is alleged against him. Where a person is taken and sent to prison, in a civil case, he may be released by the plaintiff in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> or felony, he may not regularly be discharged, until he is indicted of the fact and acquitted. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INDICTMENT">Indictment</a>, and the next article.

PRISONER

Pages 143-143

a person restrained <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> kept in prison upon an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> civil or criminal, or upon commendment; and one may be a prisoner on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of record or matter of fact. A prisoner upon matter of record, is he who, being present in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, is by the court committed to prison; and the other is one carried to prison upon an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a>, whether it be by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a>, or other officer.

PRIVATEERS

Pages 143-143

are a kind of private men of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the persons concerned wherein administer at their own costs a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a war, by fitting out these ships of force, and providing them with all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> stores; and they have instead of pay, leave to keep what they take from the enemy, allowing the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> his share, &c. Privateers may not attempt anything against the laws of nations; as to assault an enemy in a port <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> haven, under the protection of any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or republic, whether he be friend, ally, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEUTER">neuter</a>; for the peace of such places must be inviolably kept: therefore, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> made by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> William and the States of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, before a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> shall be granted to any privateer, the commander is to give security, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the ship be not above 150 tons, in L. 1500, and if the ship exceeds that burden, in L. 3000, that they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> make satisfaction for all damages which they shall commit in their courses at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, contrary to the treaties with that state, on pain of forfeiting their commissions; and the ship is made liable. Besides these private commissions, there are special commissions for privateers, granted to commanders of ships, &c. who take pay; who are under a marine <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; and if they do not obey their orders, may be punished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>: and the wars in later ages have given occasion to princes to issue these commissions, to annoy the enemies in their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and hinder such supplies as might strengthen them or lengthen out the war; and likewise to prevent the separation of ships of greater force from their fleets or squadrons. Ships taken by privateers, were to be divided into five parts; four parts whereof to go to the persons interested in the privateer, and the fifth to his Majesty: and as a farther encouragement, privateers, &c. destroying any French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of war or privateer, shall receive, for every piece of ordnance in the ship so taken, L. 10 reward, &c. By a particular statute lately made, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> admiral, or commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, may <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> commissions to commanders of privateers, for taking ships, &c. which being adjudged <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>, and the tenth part paid to the admiral, &c. wholly belong to the owners of the privateers and the captors, in proportions agreed on between themselves.

PRIVATION

Pages 143-143

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes the absence <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> want of something; in which sense darkness is only the privation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>.

PRIVATIVE

Pages 143-143

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, a particle, which, prefixed to a word, changes it into a contrary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Thus, among the Greeks, the α is used as a privative; as in α-ποτελος, atheft, ακεφαλος, &c.—The Latins have their privative in: ας, incorrigibilis, indeclinabilis, &c.—The English, French, &c. on occasion, borrow both the Latin and Greek privatives.

PRIVERNUM

Pages 143-143

(Livy, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>); a town of the Volsci, in Latium, to the east of Setia. Privernates, the people. Whose ambassadors being asked, What <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> they deserved for their revolt? answered, What those deserve who deem themselves worthy of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. And again, being asked by the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, should the punishment be remitted, What peace was to be expected with them? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> you <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> a good peace, you may hope to have it sincere and lasting; but if a bad one, you may well expect it of short continuance. At which answer, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were so far from being displeased, that by a vote of the people they had the freedom of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> granted them. Privernas, attis, the epithet. The town is now called Piperno Vecchio, situate in the Campania of Rome. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 0. N. Lat. 41. 30. **PRIVET,**

PRIVILEGE

Pages 144-144

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, some peculiar benefit granted to certain persons <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> places, contrary to the usual course of the law. Privileges are said to be personal or real. Personal privileges are such as are extended to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>, ambassadors, members of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>, &c. See LORDS, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">AMBASSADOR</a>, PARLIAMENT, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARREST">ARREST</a>. A real privilege is that granted to some particular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, the courts at Westminster, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">PRIVY <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">COUNCIL</a>. See COUNCIL. PRIVY <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">SEAL</a>. See SEAL.

PRIZE

Pages 144-144
or PRAISE, in maritime affairs, a vessel taken at sea from the enemies of a state, or from pirates; and that either by a man of war, a privateer, &c. having a commission for that purpose. Vessels are looked on as prize, if they fight under any other standard than that of the state from which they have their commission; if they have no charter-party, invoice, or bill of lading aboard; if loaded with effects belonging to the king's enemies, or with contraband goods. In ships of war, the prizes are to be divided among the officers, seamen, &c. as his Majesty shall appoint by proclamation; but among privateers, the division is according to the agreement between the owners. By Stat. 13 Geo. II. c. 4.; judges and officers, failing of their duty in respect to the condemnation of prizes, forfeit L. 500, with full costs of suit; one moiety to the king, and the other to the informer.

PRO RATA

Pages 164-164

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> sometimes used by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> for in proportion; as each person must reap the profit <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> sustain the loss, pro rata to his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, that is, in proportion to his stock.

PROBABILITY

Pages 144-144

is nothing but the appearance of the agreement <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> disagreement of two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> by the intervention of proofs, whose connection is not constant and immutable; or is not perceived to be so; but is, or appears for the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> to be so; and is enough to induce the mind to judge the proposition to be true or false, rather than the contrary. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>, p. 246-265. PROBATE of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is the exhibiting and proving of last wills and testaments before the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> judge delegated by the bishop who is ordinary of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the party died.

PROBATION

Pages 144-144

in a monastic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies the year of a novitiate, which a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> in a convent, to prove his virtue and vocation, and whether he can bear the severities of the rule.

PROBATIONER

Pages 144-144

in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Scotland, a student in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, who bringing a certificate from a professor in an university of his good morals, and his having performed his exercises to approbation, is admitted to undergo several trials; and, upon his acquitting himself properly in these, receives a licence to preach.

PROBATUM EST

Pages 144-144

(It is proved,) a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> frequently subjoined to a receipt for the cure of some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>.

PROBE

Pages 144-144

a surgeon's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for examining the circumstances of wounds, ulcers, and other cavities, searching for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> in the bladder, &c.

PROBLEM

Pages 144-144

in logic, a proposition that neither appears absolutely true <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> false; and, consequently, may be asserted either in the affirmative or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>. Problem, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, is a proposition, wherein some operation or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> is required; as to divide a line or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>, erect or let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> perpendiculars, &c. See GEOMETRY.

PROBOSCIS

Pages 144-144

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> snout of an elephant, and some other animals and insects. Flies, gnats, &c. are furnished with a proboscis or trunk; by means of which they suck the blood of animals, the juice of vegetables, &c. for their food.

PROBUS

Pages 144-144

from the son of a gardener, became, by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> valour as a soldier, and his eminent virtues, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Rome, to which <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> he was raised by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. After having subdued the barbarous nations that had made incursions into different parts of the empire where they committed horrid cruelties, and governed with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>, he was massacred in the 7th year of his reign, by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> who were weary of the public works at which he made them labour, in 282.

PROCATARCIC CAUSE

Pages 144-144

in medicine, the pre-existing, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> predisposing cause or occasion of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>.

PROCELEUSMATICUS

Pages 144-144

in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a foot consisting of four short syllables, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> two pyrrhichius; as hominibus.

PROCELLARIA

Pages 144-145

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>; a genus of birds, belonging to the order of anseres. The beak is somewhat compressed, and without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; the mandibles are equal, the superior one being crooked at the point; the feet are palmated, the hind claw being sessile, without any toe. There are six <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, principally distinguished by their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The most remarkable are: 1. The cinerea, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> fulmar. The size of this <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> is rather superior to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> gull; the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> very strong, much hooked at the end, and of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour. The nostrils are composed of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tubes, lodged in one sheath; the head, neck, whole under side of the body, and tail, are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; the back and coverts of the wings ash-coloured; the quill-feathers dusky; the legs yellowish. In lieu of a back toe, it has only a sort of spur, or sharp straight nail. These birds feed on the blubber or fat of whales, &c. which, being soon convertible into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, supplies them constantly with means of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, as well as provision for their young, which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> up into their mouths. They are likewise said to feed on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>, which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to qualify the unctuous diet they live on. This species inhabits the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of St Kilda; makes its appearance there in November, and continues the whole year, except September and October; it lays a large, white, and very brittle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>; and the young are hatched the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. No bird is of such use to the islanders as this: the fulmar supplies them with oil for their lamps, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> for their beds, a delicacy for their tables, a balm for their wounds, and a medicine for their distempers. The fulmar is also a certain prognosticator of the change of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it comes to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, no west wind is expected for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and the contrary when it returns and keeps the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The whole genus of petrels have a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of spouting from their bills, to a considerable distance, a large <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of pure pure oil; which they do, by way of defense, into the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of any that attempts to take them; so that they are, for the sake of this panacea, seized by surprise; as this oil is subservient to the abovementioned medical uses. Martin tells us, it has been used in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> with success in rheumatic <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. Frederick Martens, who had opportunity of seeing vast numbers of these birds at Spitzbergen, observes, that they are very bold, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> after the whale-fishers in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> flocks; and that, when a whale is taken, they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, in spite of all endeavors, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on it and pick out large lumps of fat, even when the animal is alive: That the whales are often discovered at sea by the multitudes of mallemucks <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>; and that when one of the former are wounded, prodigious multitudes immediately follow its bloody track. He adds, that it is a most glutinous bird, eating till it is forced to disgorge itself. 2. The puffinus, or shear-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, is 15 inches in length; the breadth 31; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> 17 ounces: the bill is an inch and three-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; nostrils tubular, but not very prominent: the head, and whole upper side of the body, wings, tail, and thighs, are of a footy blackness; the under side from chin to tail, and inner coverts of the wings, white: the legs weak, and compressed sidewise; dusky behind, whitish before. These birds are found in the Calf of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">Man</a>; and, as Mr Ray supposes, in the Scilly-isles. They resort to the former in February; take a short possession of the rabbit burrows, and then disappear till April. They lay one egg, white and blunt at each end; and the young are fit to be taken the beginning of August; when great numbers are killed by the person who farms the isle: they are salted and barrelled; and when they are boiled, are eaten with potatoes. During the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> they keep at sea, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>; and towards evening return to their young; whom they feed, by discharging the contents of their stomachs into their mouths; which by that time is turned into oil: by reason of the backward situation of their legs, they sit quite erect. They quit the isle the latter end of August, or beginning of September; and, from accounts lately received from navigators, we have reason to imagine, that like the storm-finches, they are dispersed over the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>. This species inhabits also the Orkney isles, where it makes its nest in holes on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> near the shelves of the rocks and headlands: it is called there the lyre; and is much valued, both on account of its being a food, and for its feathers. The inhabitants take and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> them in August for winter <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, when they boil them with cabbage. They also take the old ones in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>; but they are then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and not so well tasted as the young: they appear first in those <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in February. 3. The pelagica, or stormy petrel, is about the bulk of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-swallow: the length six inches; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of wings, 13. The whole bird is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, except the coverts of the tail and vent-feathers, which are white: the bill is hooked at the end: the nostrils tubular: the legs slender, and long. It has the same faculty of spouting oil from its bill as the other species: and Mr Brunnich tells us, that the inhabitants of the Ferroe isles make this bird serve the purposes of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> a wick through the mouth and rump, which being lighted, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> is fed by the fat and oil of the body. Except in breeding-time, it is always at sea; and is seen all over the vast Atlantic ocean, at the greatest distance from land; often following the vessels in great flocks, to pick up anything that falls from on board: for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> sake, chopped straw has been flung over, which they would stand on with expanded wings; but were never observed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> on or swim in the water: it presages bad <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and cautions the seamen of the approach of a tempest, by collecting under the stern of the ships: it braves the utmost fury of the storm, sometimes skimming with incredible velocity along the hollows of the waves, sometimes on the summits: Clusius makes it the Camilla of the sea. Vel mare per medium fluita suspensa tumenti Ferret iter, celere nec singere aquae plantas. Virg. She swept the seas, and as she skim'd along, Her flying feet unbarb'd on billows hung. Dryden. These birds are the cypseli of Pliny, which he places among the apodes of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>; not because they wanted feet, but were kaxonota, or had bad or useless ones; an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> he gives to these species, on a supposition that they were almost always on the wing. In August 1772, Mr Pennant found them on the rocks called Macdonald's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>, off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> end of the isle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SKYE">Skye</a>; so conjectures they breed there. They lurked under the loose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, but betrayed themselves by their twittering noise.

PROCESS

Pages 145-150

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, denotes the proceedings in any cause, real <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> personal, civil or criminal, from the original writ to the end thereof. In a more limited <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, process denotes that by which a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> is called first into any temporal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>. It is the next step for carrying on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, after suing out the original writ. See SUIT AND WRIT. It is the method taken by the law to compel a compliance with the original writ, of which the primary step is by giving the party notice to obey it. This notice is given upon all real preceps; and also upon all personal writs for injuries not against the peace, by summons; which is a warning to appear in court at the return of the original writ, given to the defendant by two of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s messengers called summoners, either in person, or left at his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>; in like manner as in the civil law the first process is by personal citation, in jus vocando. This warning on the land is given, in real actions, by erecting a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> stick or wand on the defendant's grounds, (which stick or wand among the northern nations is called the baculus nuntiatorius), and by statute 31 Eliz. c. 3, the notice must also be proclaimed on some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> before the door of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the defendant disobeys this verbal monition, the next process is by writ of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>, or pone; so called from the words of the writ, pone per vadum et salvo plegio, "put by gage and safe pledges A.B. the defendant, &c." This is a writ not issuing out of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, but out of the court of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-pleas, being grounded on the non-appearance of the defendant at the return of the original writ; and thereby the sheriff is commanded to attach him, by taking gage, that is, certain of his goods, which he shall forfeit if he doth not appear; or by making him find safe pledges or sureties, which shall be amerced in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of his non-appearance. This is also the first and immediate process, without any previous summons, upon actions of tre- Process. pali vi et armis, or for other injuries, which, though not forcible, are yet trespasses against the peace, as deceit and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a>; where the violence of the wrong requires a more speedy remedy, and therefore the original writ commands the defendant to be at once attached, without any precedent warning. If, after attachment, the defendant neglects to appear, he not only forfeits this security, but is moreover to be farther compelled by writ of distringas, or distress infinite; which is a subsequent process issuing from the court of common-pleas, commanding the sheriff to detain the defendant from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, and continually afterwards, by taking his goods and the profits of his lands, which are called illius, and which he forfeits to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> if he doth not appear. But the issues may be sold, if the court shall so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, in order to defray the reasonable costs of the plaintiff. In like manner by the civil law, if the defendant absconds, so that the citation is of no effect, mittitur adversarius in possessionem bonorum ejus. And here, by the common as well as the civil law, the process ended in case of injuries without force: the defendant, if he had any substance, being gradually stripped of it all by repeated distresses, till he rendered obedience to the king's writ; and, if he had no substance, the law held him incapable of making satisfaction, and therefore looked upon all farther process as nugatory. And besides, upon feudal principles, the person of a feudatory was not liable to be attached for injuries merely civil, lest thereby his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> should be deprived of his personal services. But, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of injury accompanied with force, the law, to punish the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of the peace and prevent its disturbance for the future, provided also a process against the defendant's person, in case he neglected to appear upon the former process of attachment, or had no substance whereby to be attached; subjecting his body to imprisonment by the writ of capias <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> respondendum. But this immunity of the defendant's person, in case of peaceable though fraudulent injuries, producing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> contempt of the law in indigent wrongdoers, a capias was also allowed, to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> the person in actions of account, though no breach of the peace be suggested, by the statutes of Marlbridge, 52 Hen. III. c. 23. and Westm. 2. 13 Edw. I. c. 11. in actions of debt and detinue, by statute 25 Edw. III. c. 17. and in all actions on the case, by statute 19 Hen. VII. c. 9. Before which last statute a practice had been introduced of commencing the suit by bringing an original writ of trespass quare clausum fregit, by breaking the plaintiff's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, vi et armis; which by the old common law subjected the defendant's person to be arrested by writ of capias: and then afterwards, by connivance of the court, the plaintiff might proceed to prosecute for any other less forcible injury. This practice (through <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> rather than <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, and for saving some trouble and expense, in suing out a special original adapted to the particular injury) still continues in almost all cases, except in actions of debt; though now, by virtue of the statutes above cited and others, a capias might be had upon almost every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of complaint. If therefore the defendant, being summoned or attached, makes default, and neglects to appear; or if the sheriff returns a nihil, or that the defendant hath nothing whereby he may be summoned, attached, or distrained, the capias now usually issues: being a writ commanding the sheriff to take the body of the defendant, if he may be found in his bailiwick or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, and him safely to keep, so that he may have him in court on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the return, to answer to the plaintiff of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> of debt, or trespass, &c. as the case may be. This writ, and all others subsequent to the original writ, not issuing out of chancery, but from the court into which the original was returnable, and being grounded on what has passed in that court in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the sheriff's return, are called judicial, not original, writs; they issue under the private <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of that court, and not under the great seal of England; and are called, not in the king's name, but in that of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> only. And these several writs being grounded on the sheriff's return, must respectively bear <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a> the same day on which the writ immediately preceding was returnable. This is the regular and orderly method of process. But it is now usual in practice, to sue out the capias in the first instance, upon a supposed return of the sheriff; especially if it be suspected that the defendant, upon notice of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> abscond; and afterwards a fictitious original is drawn up, with a proper return thereupon, in order to give the proceedings a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of regularity. When this capias is delivered to the sheriff, he by his under-sheriff grants a warrant to his inferior officers or bailiffs to execute it on the defendant. And, if the sheriff of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a> (in which county the injury is supposed to be committed and the action is laid) cannot find the defendant in his jurisdiction, he returns that he is not found, non est inventus, in his bailiwick: whereupon another writ issues, called a teftatum capias, directed to the sheriff of the county where the defendant is supposed to reside; as of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, reciting the former writ, and that it is testified, teftatum eft, that the defendant lurks or wanders in his bailiwick, where he is commanded to take him, as in the former capias. But here also, when the action is brought in one county and the defendant lives in another, it is usual, for saving trouble, time, and expense, to make out a teftatum capias at the first; supposing not only an original, but also a former capias, to have been granted; which in fact never was. And this fiction, being beneficial to all parties, is readily acquiesced in, and is now become the settled practice; being one among many instances to illustrate that maxim of law, that in fictione juris consistit æquitas. But where a defendant absconds, and the plaintiff would proceed to an outlawry against him, an original writ must then be sued out regularly, and after that a capias. And if the sheriff cannot find the defendant upon the first writ of capias, and returns a non est inventus, there issues out an aliter writ, and after that a pluribus, to the same effect as the former: only after these words "we command you," this clause is inserted, "as we have formerly," or, "as we have often, commanded you;"— "sic ut alius," or, "sic ut pluribus, præceptum." And if a non est inventus is returned upon all of them, then a writ of exigent or exigi facias may be sued out, which requires the sheriff to cause the defendant to be proclaimed, required, or exacted, in five county-courts successively, to render himself; and if he does, then to take him, as in a capias; but if he does not appear, and is returned. turned quinto exactus, he shall then be outlawed by the coroners of the county. Also by statute 6 Hen. VIII. c. 4. and 31 Eliz. c. 3. whether the defendant dwells within the same or another county than that wherein the exigent is sued out, a writ of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> shall issue out at the same time with the exigent, commanding the sheriff of the county, wherein the defendant dwells, to make three proclamations thereof in places the most notorious, and most likely to come to his knowledge, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> before the outlawry shall take <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Such outlawry is putting a man out of the protection of the law, so that he is incapable to bring an action for redress of injuries; and it is also attended with a forfeiture of all one's goods and chattels to the king. And therefore, till some time after the conquest, no man could be outlawed but for felony: but in Bracton's time, and somewhat earlier, process of outlawry was ordained to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in all actions for trespasses vi et armis. And since, by a variety of statutes (the same which allow the writ of capias before-mentioned) process of outlawry doth lie in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> actions that are merely civil; providing they be commenced by original and not by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a>. If after outlawry the defendant appears publicly, he may be arrested by a writ of capias uitlagatum, and committed till the outlawry be reversed. Which reversal may be had by the defendant's appearing personally in court (and in the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> without any personal appearance, so that he appears by attorney, according to statute 4 & 5 W. & M. c. 18.) and any plausible cause, however slight, will in general be sufficient to reverse it, it being considered only as a process to compel an appearance. But then the defendant must pay full costs, and put the plaintiff in the same condition as if he had appeared before the writ of exigii facias was awarded. Such is the first process in the court of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS">common pleas</a>. In the king's bench they may also (and frequently do) proceed in certain causes, particularly in actions of ejectment and trespasses, by original writ, with attachment and capias thereon; returnable, not at Westminster, where the common pleas are now fixed in consequence of magna carta, but ubiunque fuerimus in Anglia, wherefover the king shall then be in England; the king's bench being removable into any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of England at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. But the more usual method of proceeding therein is without any original, but by a peculiar species of process entitled a bill of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>; and therefore so intitled, because the court now sits in that county; for if it sat in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, it would then be a bill of Kent. For though, as the justices of this court have, by its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, power to determine all offences and trespasses, by the common law and custom of the realm, it needed no original writ from the crown to give it cognizance of any misdemeanor in the county wherein it resides; yet as, by this court's coming into any county, it immediately superseded the ordinary administration of justice by the general commissions of eyre and of eyre and terminer, a process of its own became necessary, within the county where it sat, to bring in such persons as were accused of committing any forcible injury. The bill of Middlesex (which was formerly always founded on a plaint of trespass quare clausum fregit, entered on the records of the court) is a kind of capias, directed to the sheriff of that county, and commanding him to take the defendant, and have him before our lord the king at Westminster on a day prefixed, to answer to the plaintiff of a plea of trespass. For this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of trespass it is that gives the court of king's bench jurisdiction in other civil causes, as was elsewhere observed; since, when once the defendant is taken into custody of the marshal, or prison keeper of this court, for the supposed trespass, he, being then a prisoner of this court, may here be prosecuted for any other species of injury. Yet, in order to found this jurisdiction, it is not necessary that the defendant be actually the marshal's prisoner; for, as soon as he appears, or puts in bail, to the process, he is deemed by so doing to be in such custody of the marshal, as will give the court a jurisdiction to proceed. And, upon these accounts, in the bill or process, a complaint of trespass is always suggested, whatever else may be the real cause of action. This bill of Middlesex must be served on the defendant by the sheriff, if he finds him in that county: but if he returns, non est inventus, then there issues out a writ of latitat, to the sheriff of another county, as Berks; which is similar to the teffatum capias in the common pleas, and recites the bill of Middlesex and the proceedings thereon, and that it is testified that the defendant latitat et discurrit, lurks and wanders about in Berks; and therefore commands the sheriff to take him, and have his body in court on the day of the return. But as in the common pleas the teffatum capias may be used upon only a supposed, and not an actual, preceding capias; so in the king's bench a latitat is usually used out upon only a supposed, and not an actual, bill of Middlesex. So that, in fact, a latitat may be called the first process in the court of king's bench, as the teffatum capias is in the common pleas. Yet, as in the common pleas, if the defendant lives in the county wherein the action is laid, a common capias suffices; so in the king's bench likewise, if he lives in Middlesex, the process must still be by bill of Middlesex only. In the exchequer the first process is by writ of quo minus, in order to give the court a jurisdiction over pleas between party and party. In which writ the plaintiff is alleged to be the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> or debtor, and that the defendant hath done him the injury complained of, qua minus sufficiens existit, by which he is the less able to pay the king's his rent or debt. And upon this the defendant may be arrested as upon a capias from the common pleas. Thus differently do the three courts set out at first, in the commencement of a suit, in order to entitle the two courts of king's bench and exchequer to hold plea in subjunctive causes, which by the original constitution of Westminster-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> they were not empowered to do. Afterwards, when the cause is once drawn into the respective courts, the method of pursuing it is pretty much the same in all of them. If the sheriff had found the defendant upon any of the former writs, the capias latitat, &c. he was anciently obliged to take him into custody, in order to produce him in court upon the return, however small and minute the cause of action might be. For, not having obeyed the original summons, he had shown a contempt of the court, and was no longer to be trusted. Process at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. But when the summons fell into disuse, and the capias became in fact the first process, it was thought hard to imprison a man for a contempt which was only supposed; and therefore, in common cases by the gradual <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> of the courts (at length authorized by statute 12 Geo. I. c. 29, which was amended by statute 5 Geo. II. c. 27, and made perpetual by statute 21 Geo. II. c. 3,) the sheriff or his officer can now only personally serve the defendant with the copy of the writ or process, and with notice in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to appear by his attorney in court to defend this action; which in effect reduces it to a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> summons. And if the defendant thinks proper to appear upon this notice, his appearance is recorded, and he puts in sureties for his future attendance and obedience; which sureties are called common bail, being the same two imaginary persons that were pledges for the plaintiff's prosecution, John Doe and Richard Roe. Or, if the defendant does not appear upon the return of the writ, or within four (or in some cases eight) days after, the plaintiff may enter an appearance for him, as if he had really appeared; and may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILE">file</a> common bail in the defendant's name, and proceed thereupon as if the defendant had done it himself. But if the plaintiff will make affidavit, or assert upon oath, that the cause of action amounts to ten pounds or upwards, then in order to arrest the defendant, and make him put in substantial sureties for his appearance, called special bail, it is required by statute 13 Car. II. stat. 2. c. 2, that the true cause of action should be expressed in the body of the writ or process; else no security can be taken in a greater sum than L. 40. This statute (without any such intention in the makers) had like to have ousted the king's bench of all its jurisdiction over civil injuries without force; for, as the bill of Middlesex was framed only for actions of trespass, a defendant could not be arrested and held to bail thereupon for breaches of civil contracts. But to remedy this inconvenience, the officers of the king's bench devised a method of adding what is called a clause of ac etiam to the usual complaint of trespass; the bill of Middlesex commanding the defendant to be brought in to answer the plaintiff of a plea of trespass, and also to a bill of debt: the complaint of trespass giving cognizance to the court, and that of debt authorising the arrest. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of which, lord chief justice <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a>, a few years afterwards, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the suitors of his court the trouble and expense of suing out special originals, directed, that in the common pleas, besides the usual complaint of breaking the plaintiff's close, a clause of ac etiam might be also added to the writ of capias, containing the true cause of action; as, "that the said <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the defendant may answer to the plaintiff of a plea of trespass in breaking his close: and also, ac etiam, may answer him, according to the custom of the court, in a certain plea of trespass upon the case, upon promises, to the value of twenty pounds, &c." The sum sworn to by the plaintiff is marked upon the back of the writ; and the sheriff, or his officer the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, is then obliged actually to arrest or take into custody the body of the defendant, and, having so done, to return the writ with a copia corpus endorsed thereon. See Arrest. When the defendant is regularly arrested, he must either go to prison, for safe custody; or put in special bail to the sheriff. For, the intent of the arrest being only to compel an appearance in court at the return of the writ, that purpose is equally answered, whether the sheriff retains his person, or takes sufficient security for his appearance, called bail, (from the French word bailer, to deliver), because the defendant is bailed, or delivered, to his sureties, upon their giving security for his appearance; and is supposed to continue in their friendly custody instead of going to gaol. See Bail. The method of putting in bail to the sheriff is by entering into a bond or obligation, with one or more sureties, (not fictitious persons, as in the former case of common bail, but real, substantial, responsible bondmen), to insure the defendant's appearance at the return of the writ; which obligation is called the bail-bond. The sheriff, if he pleases, may let the defendant go without any sureties; but that is at his own peril: for, after once taking him, the sheriff is bound to keep him safely, so as to be forthcoming in court; otherwise an action lies against him for an escape. But, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, he is obliged, by statute 23 Hen. VI. c. 10, to take (if it be tendered) a sufficient bail-bond; and, by statute 12 Geo. I. c. 29, the sheriff shall take bail for no other sum than such as is sworn to by the plaintiff, and endorsed on the back of the writ. Upon the return of the writ, or within four days after, the defendant must appear according to the exigency of the writ. This appearance is effected by putting in and justifying bail to the action; which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called putting in bail above. If this be not done, and the bail that were taken by the sheriff below are responsible persons, the plaintiff may take an assignment from the sheriff of the bail-bond (under the statute 4 & 5 Ann. c. 16,) and bring an action thereupon against the sheriff's bail. But if the bail so accepted by the sheriff, be insolvent persons, the plaintiff may proceed against the sheriff himself, by calling upon him, first to return the writ (if not already done), and afterwards to bring in the body of the defendant. And if the sheriff does not then cause sufficient bail to be put in above, he will himself be responsible to the plaintiff. The bail above, or bail to the action, must be put in either in open court, or before one of the judges thereof; or else, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, before a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> appointed for that purpose by virtue of the statute 4 W. & M. c. 4, which must be transmitted to the court. These bail, who must at least be two in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, must enter into a recognizance in court, or before the judge or commissioner, whereby they do jointly and severally undertake, that if the defendant be condemned in the action, he shall pay the costs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a>, or render himself a prisoner, or that they will pay it for him: which recognizance is transmitted to the court in a slip of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, intitled a bail-piece. And, if required, the bail must justify themselves in court, or before the commissioner in the country, by swearing themselves housekeepers, and each of them to be worth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the sum for which they are bail, after payment of all their debts. This answers in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to the stipulatio or satisfactio of the Roman laws, which is mutually given by each litigant party to the other: by the plaintiff, that he will prosecute his suit, and pay the costs if he loses his cause; in like manner as our law still requires nominal pledges of prosecution from the plaintiff: by the defendant, that he shall continue in court, and abide the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of the judge, much like our special bail; but with this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the fidejussores were there absolutely bound judicatum solvere, to see the costs and condemnation paid at all events: whereas our special bail may be discharged, by surrendering the defendant into custody within the time allowed by law; for which purpose they are at all times entitled to a warrant to apprehend him. Special bail is required (as of course) only upon actions of debt, or actions on the case in trover, or for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> due, where the plaintiff can swear that the cause of action amounts to ten pounds: but in actions where the damages are precarious, being to be assessed ad libitum by a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, as in actions for words, ejectment, or trespass, it is very seldom possible for a plaintiff to swear to the amount of his cause of action; and therefore no special bail is taken thereon, unless by a judge's order, or the particular directions of the court, in some peculiar species of injuries, as in cases of mayhem or atrocious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>; or upon such special circumstances as make it absolutely necessary that the defendant should be kept within the reach of justice. Also in actions against heirs, executors, and administrators, for debts of the deceased, special bail is not demandable; for the action is not so properly against them in person, as against the effects of the deceased in their possession. But special bail is required even of them, in actions for a devolavit, or waiving the goods of the deceased; that wrong being of their own committing. Thus much for process; which is only meant to bring the defendant into court, in order to contest the suit, and abide the determination of the law. When he appears either in person as a prisoner, or out upon bail, then follow the pleadings between the parties. See Pleadings. Process upon an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INDICTMENT">Indictment</a>. See Prosecution. The proper process on an indictment for any petty misdemeanor, or on a penal statute, is a writ of venire facias, which is in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a summons to cause the party to appear. And if by the return to such venire it appears, that the party hath lands in the county whereby he may be distrained, then a diffret infinitae shall be issued from time to time till he appears. But if the sheriff returns, that he hath no lands in his bailiwick, then (upon his non-appearance) a writ of capias shall issue, which commands the sheriff to take his body, and have him at the next assizes; and if he cannot be taken upon the first capias, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and a third shall issue, called an alias, and a pluries capias. But, on indictments for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> or felony, a capias is the first process; and, for treason or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a>, only one shall be allowed to issue, or two in the case of other felonies, by statute 25 Edw. III. c. 14, though the usage is to issue only one in any felony; the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of this statute being in most cases found impracticable. And so, in the case of misdemeanors, it is now the usual practice for any judge of the court of king's bench, upon certificate of an indictment found, to award a writ of capias immediately, in order to bring in the defendant. But if he absconds, and it is thought proper to pursue him to an outlawry, then a greater exactness is necessary. For, in such case, after the several writs have issued in a regular number, according to the nature of the respective crimes, without any effect, the offender shall be put in the exigent in order to his outlawry: that is, he shall be exacted, proclaimed, or required, to surrender, at five county-courts; and if he be returned quinto exactus, and does not appear at the fifth exaction or requisition, then he is adjudged to be outlawed, or put out of the protection of the law; so that he is incapable of taking the benefit of it in any respect, either by bringing actions or otherwise. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, for outlawries upon indictments for misdemeanors, is the same as for outlawries upon civil actions; viz. forfeiture of goods and chattels. But an outlawry in treason or felony, amounts to a conviction and attainder of the offence <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> in the indictment, as much as if the offender had been found guilty by his country. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is, however, still under the protection of the law, as hath elsewhere been observed; (see Homicide:) that though anciently an outlawed felon was said to have caput lupinum, and might be knocked on the head like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>, by any one that should meet him; because, having renounced all law, he was to be dealt with as in a state of nature, when every one that should find him might slay him: yet now, to avoid such inhumanity, it is holden that no man is entitled to kill him wantonly or wilfully; but in so doing is guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, unless it happens in the endeavour to apprehend him. For any person may arrest an outlaw on a criminal prosecution, either of his own head, or by writ or warrant of capias utlagatum, in order to bring him to execution. But such outlawry may be frequently reversed by writ of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>; the proceedings therein being (as it is fit they should be) exceedingly nice and circumstantial; and if any single minute point be omitted or misconducted, the whole outlawry is illegal, and may be reversed: upon which reversal the party accused is admitted to plead to, and defend himself against, the indictment. Thus much for process to bring in the offender after indictment found; during which stage of the prosecution it is that writs of certiorari facias are usually had, though they may be had at any time before <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, to certify and remove the indictment, with all the proceedings thereon, from any inferior court of criminal jurisdiction into the court of king's bench; which is the sovereign ordinary court of justice in causes criminal. And this is frequently done for one of these four purposes; either, 1. To confer and determine the validity of appeals or indictments and the proceedings thereon; and to quash or confirm them as there is cause: or, 2. Where it is furnished that a partial or insufficient trial will probably be had in the court below, the indictment is removed, in order to have the prisoner or defendant tried at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of the court of king's bench, or before the justices of nisi prius: or, 3. It is so removed, in order to plead the king's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> there: or, 4. To issue process of outlawry against the offender, in those counties or places where the process of the inferior judges will not reach him. Such writ of certiorari, when issued and delivered to the inferior court for removing any record or other proceed- ceeding, as well upon indictment as otherwise, supersedes the jurisdiction of such inferior court, and makes all subsequent proceedings therein entirely erroneous and illegal; unless the court of king's bench remands the record to the court below, to be there tried and determined. A certiorari may be granted at the instance of either the prosecutor or the defendant; the former as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, the latter as a matter of discretion; and therefore it is seldom granted to remove indictments from the justices of goal-delivery, or after issue joined, or confession of the fact in any of the courts below. At this stage of prosecution also it is, that indictments found by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> jury against a peer, must, in consequence of a writ of certiorari, be certified and transmitted into the court of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, or into that of the lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; and that, in places of exclusive jurisdiction, as the two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, indictments must be delivered (upon challenge and claim of cognizance) to the courts therein established by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, and confirmed by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament, to be there respectively tried and determined. See Plea. Process, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, the whole course of an experiment or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of operations, tending to produce something new. Process, in anatomy, denotes any protuberance or eminence in a bone. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">Procession</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> in the Romish church, consisting of a formal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a> of the clergy and people, putting up prayers, &c. and in this manner visiting some church, &c. They have also processions of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOST">host</a> or sacrament, &c. See Host. Prochein Amy, in law, the person next akin to a child in non-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and who, in that respect, is allowed to act for him, and be his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a>, &c. if he hold land in socage. To sue, an infant is not allowed to make an attorney; but the court will admit his next friend as plaintiff, or his guardian as defendant. Proclamation, a public notice given of anything of which the king thinks proper to advertise his subjects. Proclamations are a branch of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>*; and have then a binding force, when (as Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> observes) they are grounded upon and enforce the laws of the realm. For, though the making of laws is entirely the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of a distinct part, the legislative branch of the sovereign power, yet the manner, time, and circumstances of putting those laws in execution, must frequently be left to the discretion of the executive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. And therefore his constitutions or edicts, concerning those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> which we call proclamations, are binding upon the subject, where they do not either contradict the old laws, or tend to establish new ones; but only enforce the execution of such laws as are already in being, in such manner as the king shall judge necessary. Thus the established law is, that the king may prohibit any of his subjects from leaving the realm: a proclamation therefore forbidding this in general for three weeks, by laying an embargo upon all shipping in time of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, will be equally binding as an act of parliament, because founded upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> law. But a proclamation to lay an embargo in time of peace upon all vessels laden with wheat, (though in the time of a public scarcity), being contrary to law, and particularly to statute 22 Car. II. c. 13., the advisers of such a proclamation, and all persons acting under it, found it necessary to be indemnified by a special act of parliament, 7 Geo. III. c. 7. A proclamation for disarming Papists is also binding, being only in execution of what the legislature has first ordained; but a proclamation for allowing arms to Papists, or for disarming any Protestant subjects, will not bind; because the first would be to assume a dispensing power, the latter a legislative one; to the vesting of either of which in any single person the laws of England are absolutely strangers. Indeed, by the statute 31 Hen. VIII. c. 8. it was enacted, that the king's proclamations should have the force of acts of parliament: a statute, which was calculated to introduce the most despotic tyranny; and which must have proved fatal to the liberties of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, had it not been luckily repealed in the minority of his successor, about five years after. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLUS">Proclus</a>, surnamed Diadocus, a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and mathematician, was born in Lycia, and lived about the year 500. He was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Syrianus, and had a great share in the friendship of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Anastasius. It is said, that when Vitalian laid siege to Constantinople, Proclus burnt his ships with large brazen speculums. This philosopher was a pagan, and wrote against the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. There are still extant his Commentaries on some of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>'s books, and other of his works written in Greek. Proconsul, a Roman magistrate, sent to govern a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> with consular authority. The proconsuls were appointed out of the body of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>; and usually as the year of any one's consulship expired, he was sent proconsul into some province. The proconsuls decided cases of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> and justice, either privately in their praetorium or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, where they received petitions, heard complaints, granted writs under their seal, and the like; or else publicly, in the common hall, with the usual formalities observed in the court of judicature at Rome. They had besides, by virtue of their edicts, the power of ordering all things relating to the tribunes, taxes, contributions, and provisions of corn and money, &c. Their office lasted only a year. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSUL">Consul</a>. Procopius, a famous Greek historian, born in Cæsaria, acquired great reputation by his works in the reign of Juttimian, and was secretary to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELISARIUS">Belisarius</a> during all the wars carried on by that general in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. He at length became senator, obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of illustrious, and was made pretor of Constantinople. Procreation, the begetting and bringing forth children. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">Generation</a>. Proctor, a person commissioned to manage another person's cause in any court of the civil or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> law. Procuration, an act or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> by which a person is empowered to treat, transact, receive, &c. in another person's name. Procator, a person who has a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> committed to him to act for another. Product, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, the factum of two or more numbers, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, &c. into one another; thus $5 \times 4 = 20$ the product required.

PROFANE

Pages 151-151

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in opposition to holy; and in general is applied to all persons who have not the sacred character, and to things which do not belong to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>.

PROFESSION

Pages 151-151

among the Romanists, denotes the entering into a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order, whereby a person offers himself to God by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOW">vow</a> of inviolably observing obedience, chastity, and poverty.

PROFESSOR

Pages 151-151

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, a person who teaches <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> reads public lectures in some art or science from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> for the purpose.

PROFILE

Pages 151-151

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, the draught of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, fortification, &c. wherein are expressed the several heights, widths, and thicknesses, such as they would appear were the building cut <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> perpendicularly from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> to the foundation. Whence the profile is also called the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECTION">section</a>, sometimes orthographical section, and by Vitruvius also scagiography. Profile, in this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, amounts to the same with elevation; and (stands opposed to a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> ichnography. Profile is also used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTOUR">contour</a> or outline of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, building, member of architecture, or the like; as a base, a cornice, &c.
