Hence profiling is sometimes used for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a>, or describing the member with rule, compass, &c. thus \( \{a_1, a+d, a+2d, a+3d, \ldots\} \) increasing by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> \( d \). In numbers \( \{2, 4, 6, 8, 10, \ldots\} \) increasing by the difference \( 2 \). Geometric Progression, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">Continued</a> Geometric Proportion, is when the terms do increase or decrease by equal ratios: thus, \[ a, ar, arr, arrr, \ldots \] increasing \[ a, \frac{a}{r}, \frac{a}{rr}, \frac{a}{rrr}, \ldots \] decreasing \[ 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, \ldots \] increasing \[ 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, \ldots \] decreasing See the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLUXIONS">Fluxions</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">Series</a>.

PROJECTILES

Pages 151-157

are such bodies as, being put in a violent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> by any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force, are then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> off <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> let go from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where they received their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of motion: as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> thrown from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLING">sling</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> from a bow, a bullet from a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, &c. It is usually taken for granted, by those who treat of the motion of projectiles, that the force of gravity near the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>'s surface is everywhere the same, and acts in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> directions; and that the effect of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>'s resistance upon very heavy bodies, such as bombs and cannon-balls, is too small to be taken into consideration. The famous Sir <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton has shown, that the gravity of bodies which are above the superficies of the earth, is reciprocally as the squares of their distances from its centre; but the theorems concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of heavy bodies, demonstrated by Galileo, Huygens, and others, are built upon this foundation, that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of gravity is the same at all distances; and the consequences of this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> are found to be very nearly agreeable to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. For it is obvious, that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> arising from the supposition of gravity's acting uniformly, and in parallel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, must be exceeding small; because even the greatest distance of a projectile above the surface of the earth, is inconsiderable in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of the distance from the centre to which the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a> tends. But then, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it is very certain, that the resistance of the air to very swift motions, is much greater than it has been <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> represented. Nevertheless, (in the application of this doctrine to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUNNERY">gunnery</a>), <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the amplitude of the projection, answering to one given elevation, be first found by experiment, (which we suppose), the amplitudes in all other <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, where the elevations and velocities do not very much differ from the first, may be determined, to a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of exactness, from the foregoing hypothesis: because, in all such cases, the effects of the resistance <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be nearly as the amplitudes themselves; and were they accurately so, the proportions of the amplitudes, at different elevations, would then be the very same as in vacuo. Now, in order to form a clear idea of the subject here proposed, the path of every projectile is to be considered as depending on two different forces: that is to say, on the impellant force, whereby the motion is first begun, (and would be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line); and Projectiles, and on the force of gravity, by which the projectile, during the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of its flight, is continually urged downwards, and made to deviate more and more from its first <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. As whatever relates to the track and flight of a projectile or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a> (neglecting the resistance of the air) is to be determined from the action of these two forces, it will be proper, before we proceed to consider their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> effect, to premise something concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the motion produced by each, when supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> alone, independent of the other; to which end we have premised the two following lemmata. Lem. I. Every body, after the impressed force whereby it is put in motion ceases to act, continues to move uniformly in a right line; unless it be interrupted by some other force or impediment. This is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nature, and has its demonstration from experience and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of fact. Corollary. It follows from hence, that a ball, after leaving the mouth of the piece, would continue to move along the line of its first direction, and describe spaces therein <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the times of their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, were it not for the action of gravity, whereby the direction is changed, and the motion interrupted. Lem. II. The motion or velocity acquired by a ball, in freely descending from rest, by the force of an uniform gravity, is as the time of the descent; and the space fallen through, as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of that time. The first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of this lemma is extremely obvious: for since every motion is proportional to the force whereby it is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a>, that generated by the force of an uniform gravity must be as the time of the descent; because the whole effort of such a force is proportional to the time of its action; that is, as the time of the descent. To demonstrate that the distances descended are proportional to the squares of the times, let the time of falling through any proposed distance <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a>, be represented by the right line PQ; which conceive to be divided into an indefinite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of very small, equal particles, represented each by the symbol $m$; and let the distance descended in the first of them be Ac; in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> cd; in the third de; and so on. Then the velocity acquired being always as the time from the beginning of the descent, it will at the middle of the first of the said particles be represented by $\frac{1}{2}m$; at the middle of the second, by $\frac{1}{2}m$; at the middle of the third, by $\frac{1}{2}m$, &c. which values constitute the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> $\frac{m}{2}, \frac{3m}{2}, \frac{5m}{2}, \frac{7m}{2}, \frac{9m}{2}$, &c. But since the velocity, at the middle of any one of the said particles of time, is an exact <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> between the velocities of the two extremes thereof, the corresponding particle of the distance AB may be therefore considered as described with that mean velocity: and so the spaces Ac, cd, de, ef, &c. being respectively equal to the abovementioned quantities $\frac{m}{2}, \frac{3m}{2}, \frac{5m}{2}, \frac{7m}{2}, \frac{9m}{2}$, &c. it follows, by the continual addition of these, that the spaces Ac, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">Ad</a>, Ae, Af, &c. fallen thro' from the beginning, will be expressed by $\frac{m}{2}, \frac{4m}{2}, \frac{9m}{2}, \frac{16m}{2}, \frac{25m}{2}$, &c. which are evidently to one another in proportion, as 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, &c. that is, as the squares of the times. Corol. Seeing the velocity acquired in any number (n) of the aforesaid equal particles of time (measured in the space that would be described in one single particle) is represented by (n) times m, or nm; it will therefore be as one particle of time is to n such particles, so is nm, the said distance answering to the former time, to the distance, nm, corresponding to the latter, with the same celerity acquired at the end of the said n particles. Whence it appears, that the space $\frac{n^2m}{2}$ (found above) through which the ball falls in any given time n, is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> the half of that time ($\frac{n^2m}{2}$) which might be uniformly described with the last, or greatest celerity in the same time. Schol. It is found by experiment, that any heavy body near the earth's surface (where the force of gravity may be considered as uniform) descends about 16 feet from rest, in the first second of time. Therefore, as the distances fallen through are proved above to be in proportion as the squares of the time, it follows, that as the square of one second is to the square of any given number of seconds, so is 16 feet to the number of feet a heavy body will freely descend in the said number of seconds. Whence the number of feet descended in any given time will be found, by multiplying the square of the number of seconds by 16. Thus the distance descended in 2, 3, 4, 5, &c. seconds, will appear to be 64, 144, 256, 400 feet, &c. respectively. Moreover, from hence, the time of the descent through any given distance will be obtained, by dividing the said distance in feet by 16, and extracting the square root of the quotient; or, which comes to the same thing, by extracting the square root of the whole distance, and then taking $\frac{1}{2}$ of that root for the number of seconds required. Thus, if the distance be supposed 2640 feet; then, by either of the two ways, the time of the descent will come out 12.84, or 12.50 seconds. It appears also (from the corol.) that the velocity per second (in feet) at the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, will be determined by multiplying the number of seconds in the fall by 32. Thus it is found, that a ball, at the end of 10 seconds, has acquired a velocity of 320 feet per second. After the same manner, by having any two of the four following quantities, viz. the force, the times, the velocity, and distance, the other two may be determined; for let the space freely descended by a ball, in the first second of time (which is as the accelerating force) be denoted by F; also let T denote the number of seconds wherein any distance, D, is descended; and let V be the velocity per second, at the end of the descent: then will $V = 2FT = 2\sqrt{FD} = 2DT = \sqrt{D} = V = \frac{T}{F} = \frac{2F}{V}$. All which equations are very easily deduced from the two original ones, \(D = FT\), and \(V = 2FT\), already demonstrated; the former in the proposition itself, and the latter in the corollary to it; by which it appears, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the velocity at the end of the first second is \(2F\); whence the velocity \((V)\) at the end of \((T)\) seconds must consequently be expressed by \(2FT\) or \(2TT\). **Theorem 1.** A projected body, whose line of direction is parallel to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the horizon, describes by its fall a parabola. If the heavy body is thrown by any extrinsical force, as that of a gun or the like, from the point \(A\) (fig. 2, n° 1.) so that the direction of its projection is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> line \(AD\); the path of this heavy body will be a semi-parabola. For if the air did not resist it, nor was it acted on by its gravity, the projectile would proceed with an equable motion, always in the same direction; and the times wherein the parts of space \(AB, AC, AD, AE\), were passed over, would be as the spaces \(AB, AC, AD, &c.\) respectively. Now if the force of gravity is supposed to take place, and to act in the same tenour as if the heavy body were not impelled by any extrinsical force, that body would constantly decline from the right-line \(AE\); and the spaces of descent, or the deviations from the horizontal line \(AE\), will be the same as if it had fallen perpendicularly. Wherefore if the body falling perpendicularly by the force of its gravity, passed over the space \(AK\) in the time \(AB\), descended through \(AL\) in the time \(AC\), and through \(AM\) in the time \(AD\); the spaces \(AK, AL, AM\), will be as the squares of the times, that is, as the squares of the right-lines \(AB, AC, AD, &c.\) or \(KF, LG, MH\). But since the impetus in the direction parallel to the horizon always remains the same, (for the force of gravity, that only solicits the body downwards, is not in the least contrary to it,) the body will be equally promoted forwards in the direction parallel to the plane of the horizon, as if there was no gravity at all. Wherefore, since in the time \(AB\), the body passes over a space equal to \(AB\); but being compelled by the force of gravity, it declines from the right-line \(AB\) through a space equal to \(AK\); and \(BF\) being equal and parallel to \(AK\), at the end of the time \(AB\), the body will be in \(F\); so in the same manner, at the end of the time \(AE\), the body will be in \(I\), and the path of the projectile will be in the curve \(AFGH\); but because the squares of the right lines \(KF, LG, MH, NI\), are proportionable to the abscissas \(AK, AL, AM, AN\). The curve \(AFGH\) will be a semi-parabola. The path, therefore, of a heavy body projected according to the direction \(AE\), will be a semi-parabolical curve. **Theorem 2.** The curve line that is described by a heavy body projected obliquely and upwards, according to any direction, is a parabola. Let \(AF\) (ibid. n° 2.) be the direction of projection, any ways inclined to the horizon, gravity being supposed not to act, the moving body would always continue its motion in the same right-line, and would describe the spaces \(AB, AC, AD, &c.\) proportional to the times. But by the action of gravity it is compelled continually to decline from the path \(AF\), and to move in a curve, which will be a parabola. Let us suppose the heavy body falling perpendicularly in the time \(AB\), through the space \(AQ\), and in the time \(AC\), through the space \(AR\), &c. The spaces \(AQ, AR, AS\), will be as the squares of the times, or as the Projection-squares of \(AB, AC, AD\). It is manifest from what was demonstrated in the last theorem, that if in the perpendicular \(BG\), there is taken \(BM = AQ\), and the parallelogram be completed, the place of the heavy body at the end of the time \(AB\), will be \(M\), and so of the rest; and all the deviations \(BM, &c.\) from the right-line \(AF\), arising from the times, will be equal to the spaces \(AQ, AR, AS\), which are as the squares of the right-lines \(AB, AC, AD\). Through \(A\) draw the horizontal right-line \(AP\), meeting the path of the projectile \(P\). From \(P\) raise the perpendicular \(PE\), meeting the line of direction in \(E\); and by reason the triangles \(ABG, ACH, &c.\) are equiangular, the squares of the right-lines \(AB, AC, &c.\) will be proportionable to the squares of \(AG, AH, &c.\) so that the deviations \(BM, CN, &c.\) will be proportionable to the squares of the right-lines \(AG, AH, &c.\). Let the line \(L\) be a third proportional to \(EP\) and \(AP\); and it will be (by 17 El. 6.) \(L \times EP = APq\), but \(APq : AGq :: EP : BM :: L \times EP : L \times BM\); whence since it is \(L \times EP = APq\), it will be \(L \times BM = AGq\). In like manner it will be \(L \times CN = AHq, &c.\). But because it is \(BG : AG :: (EP : AP :: by hypothesis) AP : L\); it will be \(L \times BG = AG \times AP = AG \times AG + AG \times GP = AGq + AG \times GP\). But it has been shown that it is \(L \times BM = AGq\), wherefore it will be \(L \times BG - L \times BM = AG \times GP\), that is, \(L \times MG = AG \times GP\). [By the same way of reasoning it will be \(L \times NH = AH \times HP, &c.\). Wherefore the rectangle under \(MG\) and \(L\), will be equal to the square of \(AG\), which is the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the parabola; and so the curve \(AMNOPK\) wherein the projectile is moved will be a parabola. **Cor. 1.** Hence the right line \(L\) is the latus rectum or parameter of the parabola, that belongs to its axis. **Cor. 2.** Let \(AH = HP\), and it will be \(L \times CN = AHq = L \times NH\), whence it will be \(NH = CN\); and consequently the right-line \(AF\) being the line of direction of the projectile, will be a tangent to the parabola. **Cor. 3.** If a heavy body is projected downwards, in a direction oblique to the horizon, the path of the projectile will be a parabola. **Theorem 3.** The impetus of a projected body in different parts of the parabola, are as the portions of the tangents intercepted betwixt two right-lines parallel to the axis; that is, the impetus of the body projected in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> \(A\) and \(B\), (ibid. n° 3.) to which \(AD\) and \(BE\) are tangents, will be as \(CD\) and \(EB\), the portions of the tangents intercepted betwixt two right-lines, \(CB\) and \(DE\), parallel to the axis. These calculations and demonstrations, however, are all founded on a supposition that the projectiles move in an unresisting medium, or in one whose resistance is but small. Hence they answer with tolerable exactness where the motions are not very quick; but in those cases where the projectiles are moved with immense velocity, the resistance of the air occasions errors of such enormous magnitude, that a musket-ball, which, by calculation, ought to fly 17 miles, seldom exceeds three <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a>. See the article Gunnery, paffin. **PROJECTION,** in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, the act of communicating motion to a body, from thence called projectile. See the preceding article. Projection. Projection, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, the appearance or representation of an object on the perspective plane. See Perspective. Projection of the Sphere, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, signifies the laying <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> those imaginary circles of the sphere by which the degrees of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> and latitude are counted on celestial and terrestrial maps. Projection of the sphere is either orthographic or stereographic. The orthographic projection supposes the eye placed at an infinite distance; whereas, in the stereographic projection, it is supposed to be only 90° distant from the primitive circle, or placed in its pole, and thence viewing the circles on the sphere. The primitive circle is that great circle which limits or bounds the representation or projection; and the place of the eye is called the projecting point. See Geography, n° 13, &c. The laws of the orthographic projection are these: 1. The rays by which the eye, placed at an infinite distance, perceives any object are parallel. 2. A right-line, perpendicular to the plane of the projection, is represented by a point, where it cuts the plane of the projection. 3. A right-line, as AB, or CD, (fig. 3, n° 1,) not perpendicular, is projected into a right-line, as FE and GH, and is always comprehended between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> perpendiculars AF and BE, and CG and GH. 4. The projection of the right-line, AB, is the greatest when it is parallel to the plane of projection; being projected in a right-line equal to itself. 5. But an oblique line is always projected into one less than itself; and the more so, the nearer it approaches to a perpendicular, which, as already observed, is projected into a point. 6. A plane surface, as ABCD, (ibid. n° 2,) at right <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> to the plane of the projection, is projected into the right line AB, in which it cuts the plane of the projection; and any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, as BC, CC, or CA, is projected into the corresponding lines BO, OO, or OA. 7. A circle parallel to the plane of projection, is represented by a circle equal to itself; and a circle oblique to the plane of projection, is represented by an ellipse. As to the stereographic projection, its laws are these: 1. The representations of all circles, not passing thro' the projecting point, will be circles. Thus, let ACEDB (fig. 4, n° 1, 2, 3) represent a sphere, cut by a plane RS, passing thro' the centre I, at right angles to the diameter EH, drawn from E the place of the eye; and let the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of the sphere by the plane RS, be the circle CFDL, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> are H and E. Suppose now AGB is a circle on the sphere to be projected, whose pole most remote from the eye is P; and the visual rays from the circle AGB meeting in E, form the cone AGBE, whereof the triangle AEB is a section thro' the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERTEX">vertex</a> E, and diameter of the base AB; then will the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> agbf, which is the projection of the circle AGB, be itself a circle: for if the plane RS is supposed to revolve on the line CD, till it coincides with the plane of the circle ACEB; then will the circle CFDL coincide with the circle CEDH, and the projected circle agbf with the circle anbk. Hence, the middle of the projected diameter is the centre of the projected circle, whether it be a great circle or a small one; the poles and centres of all circles, parallel to the plane of projection, fall in the centre of the projection; and all oblique great circles cut the primitive circle in two points diametrically opposite. 2. The Projection, projected diameter of any circle subtends an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> at the eye equal to the distance of that circle from its nearest pole, taken on the sphere; and that angle is bisected by a right line, joining the eye and that pole. Thus let the plane RS (ibid. n° 4.) cut the sphere HFEG through its centre I; and let ABC be any oblique great circle, whose diameter AC is projected in ac; and KOL, any small circle parallel to ABC, whose diameter KL is projected in kl. The distances of those circles from their pole P, being the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> AHP, KHP; and the angles aEc, kEl, are the angles at the eye, subtended by their projected diameters, ac, kl. Then is the angle aEc measured by the arch AHP, and the angle kEl measured by the arch KHP, and those angles are bisected by EP. 3. Any point of a sphere is projected at the distance of the tangent of half the arch intercepted between that point and the pole opposite to the eye, from the centre of projection; the semi-diameter of the sphere being radius. Thus, let CbEB (ibid. n° 5.) be a great circle of the sphere, whose centre is c; GH the plane of projection <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the diameter of the sphere in b, B; E, C, the poles of the section by that plane; and a, the projection of A. Then is ca = the tangent of half the arch AC, as is evident by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> CF = the tangent of half that arch, and joining cF. 4. The angle made by two projected circles, is equal to the angle which these circles make on the sphere. For let IACE and ABL (ibid. n° 6.) be two circles on a sphere intersecting in A; E, the projecting point; and RS, the plane of projection, wherein the point A is projected in a, in the line IC the diameter of the circle ACE. Aflb led DH, FA, be tangents to the circles ACE, ABL. Then will the projected angle daf be equal to the spheric angle BAC. 5. The distance between the poles of the primitive circle and an oblique circle, is equal to the tangent of half the inclination of those circles; and the distance of their centres is equal to the tangent of their inclination, the semi-diameter of the primitive being radius. For let AC (ibid. n° 7.) be the diameter of a circle, whose poles are P and Q, and inclined to the plane of projection in the angle AIF; and let a, c, p, be the projections of the points A, C, P; also let HaE be the projected oblique circle, whose centre is q. Now when the plane of projection becomes the primitive circle, whose pole is I; then is IP = tangent of half the angle AIF, or of half the arch AF; and Ig = tangent of AF, or of the angle FHa = AIF. 6. If through any given point in the primitive circle, an oblique circle be described; then the centres of all other oblique circles passing through that point, will be in a right line drawn through the centre of the first oblique circle at right angles to a line passing through that centre, the given point, and the centre of the primitive. Thus let GACE (ibid. n° 8.) be the primitive circle, ADEI a great circle described through D, its centre being B. HK is a right line drawn through B perpendicular to a right line, CI, passing through D, B, and the centre of the primitive circle. Then the centres of all other great circles, as FDG, passing through D, will fall into the line HK. 7. Equal arches of any two great circles of the sphere, will be intercepted between two other circles drawn on the sphere through the remotest poles of those great circles. For let PBEA PBEB (ibid. n° 9.) be a sphere, whereon AGB, CFD, are two great circles, whose remotest poles are E, P; and through these poles let the great circle PBEC, and the small circle PGE, be drawn, intersecting the great circles AGB, CFD, in the points B, G, and D, F. Then are the intercepted arches BG, and DF equal to one another. 8. If lines be drawn from the projected pole of any great circle, cutting the peripheries of the projected circle and plane of projection, the intercepted arches of those circumferences are equal; that is, the arch GB = f/d, (ibid.) 9. The radius of any small circle, whose plane is perpendicular to that of the primitive circle, is equal to the tangent of that lesser circle's distance from its pole; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECANT">secant</a> of that distance, is equal to the distance of the centres of the primitive and lesser circle. For let P (ibid. n° 10.) be the pole, and AB the diameter of a lesser circle, its plane being perpendicular to that of the primitive circle, whose centre is C: then d being the centre of the projected lesser circle, da is equal to the tangent of the arch PA, and dC = secant of PA.

PROJECTURE

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, the outjetting and promiscuity, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> embossing, which the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a> and other members have beyond the naked wall, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, &c.

PROLAPSUS

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, a prolapsion <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> falling out of any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> situation: thus we say, prolapsus intestini, a prolapsion of the intestine, &c. See Surgery.

PROLATE

Pages 157-157

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, an epithet applied to a spheroid produced by the revolution of a semi-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELLIPSIS">ellipsis</a> about its larger diameter.

PROLEGOMENA

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOLOGY">philology</a>, certain preparatory observations <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> discourses prefixed to a book, &c. containing something necessary for the reader to be apprised of, to enable him the better to understand the book, or to enter deeper into the science, &c.

PROLEPSIS

Pages 157-157

a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, by which we anticipate <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> prevent what might be objected by the adversary. See Oratory, n° 80.

PROLEPTIC

Pages 157-157

an epithet applied to a periodical <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> which anticipates, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> whose paroxysm returns sooner and sooner every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; as is frequently the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> in agues. PROLIFER FLOS; (prolet, an "offspring;" and fero, to "bear;") a prolific flower, or flower which from its own substance produces another; a singular <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of luxuriance, to which full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are chiefly incident.

PROLIXITY

in discourse, the fault of entering into too minute a detail, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> being too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, precise, and circumstantial, even to a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of tediousness.

PROLOGUE

Pages 157-157

in dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a discourse addressed to the audience before the drama <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> play begins. The original intention was to advertize the audience of the subject of the piece, and to prepare them to enter more easily into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and sometimes to make an apology for the poet.

PROMETHEUS

Pages 157-157

the son of Japhet, supposed to have been the first discoverer of the art of striking fire by flint and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>; which gave rise to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of his stealing fire from heaven; A renowned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>; but whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is involved in fable. He flourished about 1687 B.C. The poetical account is, that he formed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of clay of such exquisite workmanship, that Palas, charmed with his ingenuity, offered him whatever in heaven could contribute to finish his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; and for this purpose took him up with her to the celestial mansions, where he stole some fire from the chariot of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, which he used to animate his image. At this theft <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> was so enraged, that he ordered Vulcan to chain him <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on mount <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, and sent an eagle <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> vulture to prey on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>; which every night was renewed, in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> eaten up in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, until at last he was delivered by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, who killed the vulture.

PROMISE

Pages 157-157

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is, when upon any valuable consideration one binds himself by word of mouth to another, to perform a thing agreed on. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSUMPSIT">Assumpsit</a>.

PROMONTORY

Pages 157-157

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> point of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> rock projecting out into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; the extremity of which towards the sea is called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> or headland. See 2d Plate CXVI.

PROMPTER

Pages 157-157

in the drama, an officer posted behind the scenes, whose business it is to watch attentively the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> speaking on the stage, in order to suggest and put them forward, when at a stand, to correct them when amiss, &c. in their parts.

PROMULGATED

Pages 157-157
or PROMULGED, something published or proclaimed, and generally applied to a law, to denote the publishing or proclaiming it to the people.

PRONAOS

Pages 157-157

in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a porch to a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other spacious <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. See the article Porch.

PRONATION

Pages 157-157

among anatomists. The radius of the arm has two kinds of motions, the one called pronation, the other supination. Pronation is that whereby the palm of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> is turned downwards; and supination, the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> thereto, is that whereby the back of the hand is turned downwards. The peculiar muscles whereby pronation is performed are called pronators; as those by which supination is performed are termed supinators. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles, and Plates.

PRONOUN

Pages 157-157

PRONOMEN, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, a declinable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of speech, which being put instead of a noun, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out some person <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> thing. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRONOUNS">Pronouns</a> are divided into the six following classes, viz. Demonstrative pronouns; relative pronouns; possessive pronouns; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENTILE">gentile</a> pronouns, or such as denote a person's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, as nostras, vestras, and cujas; interrogative pronouns; and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> pronouns.

PRONUNCIATION

Pages 157-159

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, the manner of articulating <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> sounding the words of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Pronunciation makes the most difficult <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of written grammar; in regard that a book expressing itself to the eyes, in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> that wholly concerns the ears, seems next akin to that of teaching the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> to distinguish colours: hence it is that there is no part so defective in grammar as that of pronunciation, as the writer has frequently no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> whereby to give the reader an idea of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> he would express; for want of a proper term, therefore, he substitutes a vicious and precarious one. To give a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> idea of the pronunciation of a language, it seems necessary to fix as nearly Pronunciation as possible all the several sounds employed in the pronunciation of that language. Cicero tells us, that the pronunciation underwent several changes among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and indeed it is more precarious in the living languages, being, as Du <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOS">Bos</a> tells us, subservient to fashion in these. The French language is clogged with a difficulty in pronunciation from which most others are free; and it consists in this, that most of their words have two different pronunciations, the one in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> prose, the other in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. As to the pronunciation of the English language, the ingenious Mr Martin, in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPELLING">Spelling</a>-Book of Arts and Sciences, lays <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the following rules: 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> (e) lengthens the sound of the foregoing vowel; as in can, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANE">cane</a>; rob, robe; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TUN">tun</a>, tune, &c. 2. The final (e) in words ending in re, is sounded before the r like u; as massacre, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASSA">massa</a>-cur; lucre, lu-cur, &c. 3. The Latin diphthongs ae, oe are sounded like e; as Etina, Etina; economy, economy, &c.; but at the end of the words oe sounds like o; as in toe, foe, &c. 4. Also the English improper diphthongs, ea, eo, eu, ue, found only the e and u; as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEA">tea</a> and te; jeoffre or jeffre due or tru; true or tru, &c. though sometimes eo and ea are pronounced like ae, as in people, fear, near, &c. 5. Sometimes the diphthong (ie) is pronounced like e in ceiling, like ee in field, and, at the end of words, always like g, as in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a>, &c.; and ei is pronounced either like e or ai, as in deceit, reign, &c. 6. The triphthong eau is pronounced like o, in beau and jet d'eau; and ieu sounds like u in lieu, adieu, &c. 7. The sound of c hard before the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a> a, o, u, as in call, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, cup, &c.; also sometimes before b, as in chart, cold, &c.; and before l and r, as in clear, creep, &c. It is otherwise generally soft, as in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, cyder, child, &c. 8. In French words ch, is sounded like sh, as in chagreen, machine; and sometimes like qu, as in choir. 9. The sound of g is hard before a, o, u, l, r, as in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALL">gall</a>, go, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a>, glean, grope; also before ui, as in guilt, guild, &c.; and before h, as in ghoul; sometimes before i, as in gibbous, gibberish. It is also generally hard before e, as in get, geld, &c.; but soft in many words derived from the Greek and Latin, as in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, genealogy, genius, &c. Two gg are always hard, as in dagger, &c. The sound of g, when soft, is like that of j. 10. In any part of a word, ph sounds like f, as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, &c. 11. The sound of gu, at the end of French words, is like k, as in risque, &c. 12. The syllables ti and ci, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> followed by a vowel, sound like si or shi; as in fiction, logician, &c. 13. When cc occurs before i, the first is hard and the latter is soft; as in flaccid, &c. 14. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> p is not pronounced at the beginning of syllables, before f and t; as in psalm, ptarmics, &c. As to other peculiarities, regarding the pronunciation of single letters, many of them have been taken notice of at the beginning of each, in the course of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. But it is not enough to know the just pronunciation of single letters, but also of words: in order to which, the accenting of words ought to be well understood; since nothing is more harsh and disagreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, than to hear a person speak or read with wrong accents. And, indeed, in English, the same word is often both a noun and a verb, distinguished only by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCENT">accent</a>, which is on the first <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> of the noun, and on the last of the verb; as ferment and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, record and recording, &c. We are to observe also, that in order to a just <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of words, some require only a single accent on the syllable, as in torment, &c.; but in others it should be marked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, as in animal, because it is pronounced as if the letter was wrote double, viz. animal. The best directory in this matter is the excellent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> of Mr Sheridan, lately published. Pronunciation is also used for the fifth and last part of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, which consists in varying and regulating the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> agreeably to the matter and words, so as most effectually to persuade and touch the hearers. See Oratory, Part II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">Proof</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, &c., denotes the mediums or arguments used to evince the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of any thing. Proof of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">Artillery</a> and Small Arms, is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> whether they stand the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of powder allotted for that purpose. The rule of the board of ordnance is, that all guns, under 24-pounders, be loaded with powder as much as their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> weighs; that is, a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> 24-pounder with 21 lb., a brass 32-pounder with 26 lb., 12 oz. and a 42-pounder with 31 lb., 8 oz.; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> 24-pounder with 18 lb., the 32-pounder with 21 lb., 8 oz. and the 42-pounder with 25 lb. The brass <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> field-pieces are proved with powder that weighs half as much as their shot, except the 24-pounder, which is loaded with 10 lb. only. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">Government</a> allows 11 bullets of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> for the proof of muskets, and 14½, or 29 in two-pounds, for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; 17 in the pound for the proof of carbines, and 20 for service; 28 in the pound for the proof of pistols, and 34 for service. When guns of a new metal, or of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, are proved; then, besides the common proof, they are fired 200 or 300 times, as quick as they can be, loaded with the common <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> given in actual service. Our light 6 pounders, were fired 300 times in 3 hours 27 minutes, loaded with 1 lb. 4 oz. without receiving any damage. Proof of Powder, is in order to try its goodness and strength. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">Gun</a>-Powder. Proof of Cannon, is made to ascertain their being well <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, their having no cavities in their metal, and, in a word, their being fit to resist the effort of their charge of powder. In making this proof, the piece is laid upon the ground, supported only by a piece of wood in the middle, of about 5 or 6 inches thick, to raise the muzzle a little; and then the piece is fired against a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> butt of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Tools used in the Proof of Cannon are as follows: Searcher, an iron socket with branches, from 4 to 8 in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> outwards a little, with small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> at their ends: to this socket is fixed a wooden handle, from 8 to 12 feet-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 1½ inch in diameter. This searcher is introduced into the gun after each firing, and turned gently round to discover the cavities within: if any are found, they are marked on the outside with chalk; and then the Searcher with one point is introduced: about which point a mixture of wax and tallow is put, to take the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of the holes; and if any are found of ¼ of an inch deep, or of any considerable length, the gun is rejected as unserviceable to the government. Reliever, is an iron <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> fixed to a handle, by means of a socket, so as to be at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>: it serves to disengage the first searcher, when any of its points are retained in a hole, and cannot otherwise be got out. When guns are rejected by the proof-masters, they order them to be marked thus, which the contractors generally alter WP thus; and after such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>, dispose of them to foreign powers for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOOLWICH">Woolwich</a> proof. The most curious <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for finding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> defects in pieces of artillery, was lately invented by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general Desguliers, of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> regiment of artillery. This instrument, grounded on the truest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> principles, is no sooner introduced into the hollow <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> of the gun, than it discovers its defects, and more particularly that of the piece not being truly bored; which is a very important one, and to which most of the disasters happening to pieces of artillery are in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to be imputed; for, when a gun is not truly bored, the most expert artillerist <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be able to make a good shot. Proof of Mortars and Howitzers, is made to ascertain their being well cast, and of strength to resist the effort of their charge. For this purpose the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> or howitzer is placed upon the ground, with some part of their trunions or breech sunk below the surface, and resting on wooden billets, at an elevation of about 70 degrees. The mirror is generally the only instrument to discover the defects in mortars and howitzers. In order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> must shine; the breech must be placed towards the sun, and the glass over-against the mouth of the piece: it illuminates the bore and chamber sufficiently to discover the flaws in it. Proof of Foreign Brass-Artillery. 1st. The Prussians. Their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTERING">battering</a>-train and garrison-artillery are proved with a quantity of powder equal to \( \frac{1}{2} \) the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the shot, and fired 75 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a> as fast as in real service; that is, 2 or 3 rounds in a minute. Their light field-train, from a 12-pounder upwards, are proved with a quantity of powder = 1-3d of the weight of the shot, and fired 150 rounds, at 3 or 4 rounds in a minute. From a 12-pounder downwards, are proved with a quantity of powder = 1-5th of the shot's weight, and fired 300 rounds, at 5 or 6 rounds each minute, properly sprunged and loaded. Their mortars are proved with the chambers full of powder, and the shells loaded. Three rounds are fired as quick as possible. 2d. The Dutch prove all their artillery by firing each piece 5 times; the two first rounds with a quantity of powder = 2-3ds of the weight of the shot; and the three last rounds with a quantity of powder = \( \frac{1}{2} \) the weight of the shot. 3d. The French the same as the Dutch. Proof, in brandy and other spirituous liquors, is a little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> lather which appears on the top of the liquor when poured into a glass. This lather, as it diminishes, forms itself into a circle called by the French the chapelet, and by the English the bead or bubble.

PROPERTIUS

Pages 159-159

a celebrated Latin poet, born at Meyania, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Umbria, now called Bevagna, in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Spoleto. He went to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">Property</a>, Rome after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, who had been put to death by order of Augustus, for having followed Antony's party during the triumvirate. Propertius in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> acquired <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation by his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and abilities, and had a considerable share in the esteem of Maecenas and Cornelius <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALLUS">Gallus</a>. He had also Ovid, Tibullus, Bassus, and the other ingenious men of his time, for his friends. He died at Rome 19 B.C. He is printed with almost all the editions of Tibullus and Catullus: but the best edition of him is that which was given separately of him by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a> Brouckhuis at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> 1702, in 4to. and again in 1714, 4to. cum curis secundis ejusdem. We have four books of his Elegies <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Amours with a lady called Hofia, or Hofilia, to whom he gave the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYNTHIA">Cynthia</a>.

PROPERTY

Pages 159-163

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is described to be the highest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> which a person has <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> can have to any thing. There is nothing which so generally strikes the imagination, and engages the affections of mankind, as the right of property; or that sole and despotic dominion which one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> claims and exercises over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> things of the world, in total <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the right of any other individual in the universe. And yet there are very few that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> give themselves the trouble to consider the original and foundation of this right. Pleaded as we are with the possession, we seem afraid to look back to the means by which it was acquired, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> fearful of some defect in our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a>; or at best we rest satisfied with the decision of the laws in our favour, without examining the reason or authority upon which those laws have been built. We think it enough that our title is derived by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of the former proprietor, by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, or by the last will and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a> of the dying owner: not caring to reflect, that (accurately and strictly speaking) there is no foundation in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> or in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> law, why a set of words upon <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> should convey the dominion of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>; why the son should have a right to exclude his fellow-creatures from a determinate spot of ground, because his father had done so before him; or why the occupier of a particular field or of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JEWEL">jewel</a>, when lying on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> and no longer able to maintain possession, should be entitled to tell the rest of the world which of them should enjoy it after him. These inquiries, it must be owned, would be useless and even troublesome in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. It is well if the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of mankind will obey the laws when made, without scrutinizing too nicely into the reasons of making them. But when law is to be considered not only as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of practice, but also as a rational science, it cannot be improper or useless to examine more deeply the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> and grounds of these positive constitutions of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. In the beginning of the world, we are informed by holy writ, the all-bountiful Creator gave to man "dominion over all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and over the fish of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and over the fowl of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and over every living..." Property: "living thing that moveth upon the earth." This is the only true and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> foundation of man's dominion over external things, whatever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> metaphysical notions may have been started by fanciful writers upon this subject. The earth therefore, and all things therein, are the general property of all mankind, exclusive of other beings, from the immediate gift of the Creator. And, while the earth <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> bare of inhabitants, it is reasonable to suppose, that all was in common among them, and that every one took from the public stock to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> such things as his immediate necessities required. These general notions of property were then sufficient to answer all the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> life; and might perhaps still have answered them, had it been possible for mankind to have remained in a state of primeval simplicity: as may be collected from the manners of many American nations, when first discovered by the Europeans; and from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> method of living among the first Europeans themselves, if we may <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> either the memorials of them preserved in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the poets, or the uniform accounts given by historians of those times wherein erant omnia communia et indivisa omnibus, veluti unum cunctis patrimonium esset. Not that this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of goods seems ever to have been applicable, even in the earliest ages, to ought but the substance of the thing; nor could it be extended to the use of it. For, by the law of nature and reason, he who first began to use it, acquired therein a kind of transient property, that lasted so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he was using it, and no longer: or, to speak with greater precision, the right of possession continued for the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> only that the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of possession lasted. Thus the ground was in common, and no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of it was the permanent property of any man in particular; yet whoever was in the occupation of any determinate spot of it, for rest, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, or the like, acquired for the time a sort of ownership, from which it would have been unjust, and contrary to the law of nature, to have driven him by force; but the instant that he quitted the use or occupation of it, another might <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> it without injustice. Thus also a vine or other tree might be said to be in common, as all were equally entitled to its produce; and yet any private individual might <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the sole property of the fruit, which he had gathered for his own repast. A doctrine well illustrated by Cicero, who compares the world to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, which is common to the public, and yet the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which any man has taken is for the time his own. But when mankind increased in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, craft, and ambition, it became necessary to entertain conceptions of more permanent dominion; and to appropriate to individuals, not the immediate use only, but the very substance of the thing to be used. Otherwise innumerable tumults must have arisen and the good order of the world been continually broken and disturbed, while a variety of persons were striving who should get the first occupation of the same thing, or disputing which of them had actually gained it. As human life also grew more and more refined, abundance of conveniences were devised to render it more easy, commodious, and agreeable; as habitations for shelter and safety, and raiment for warmth and decency. But no man would be at the trouble to provide either, so long as he had only an unfructuary property in them, which was to cease the instant that he quitted possession;—if, as soon as he walked out of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENT">tent</a>, or pulled off his garment, the next stranger who came by would have a right to inhabit the one and to wear the other. In the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of habitations in particular, it was natural to observe, that even the brute <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, to whom every thing else was in common, maintained a permanent property in their dwellings, especially for the protection of their young; that the birds of the air had nests, and the beasts of the field had caverns, the invasion of which they esteemed a very flagrant injustice, and would sacrifice their lives to preserve them. Hence a property was soon established in every man's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and home-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; which seem to have been originally <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> temporary huts or moveable cabins, suited to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> for more speedily peopling the earth, and fitted to the wandering life of their owners, before any extensive property in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> or ground was established. And there can be no doubt, but that moveables of every kind became sooner appropriated than the permanent substantial foil: partly because they were more susceptible of a long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCCUPANCY">occupancy</a>, which might be continued for months together without any sensible interruption, and at length by usage <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> into an established right; but principally because few of them could be fit for use, till improved and meliorated by the bodily labour of the occupant; which bodily labour, bestowed upon any subject which before lay in common to all men, is universally allowed to give the fairest and most reasonable title to an exclusive property therein. The article of food was a more immediate call, and therefore a more early consideration. Such as were not contented with the spontaneous product of the earth, sought for a more solid refreshment in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of beasts, which they obtained by hunting. But the frequent disappointments incident to that method of provision, induced them to gather together such animals as were of a more tame and docile nature; and to establish a permanent property in their flocks and herds, in order to sustain themselves in a less precarious manner, partly by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of their dams, and partly by the flesh of the young. The support of these their cattle made the article of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> also a very important point. And therefore the book of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a> (the most venerable monument of antiquity, considered merely with a view to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>) will furnish us with frequent instances of violent contentions concerning <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>; the exclusive property of which appears to have been established in the first digger or occupant, even in such places where the ground and herbage remained yet in common. Thus we find <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, who was but a sojourner, asserting his right to a well in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABIMELECH">Abimelech</a>, and exacting an oath for his security, "because he had digged that well." And <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, about 90 years afterwards, reclaimed this his father's property; and, after much contention with the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>, was suffered to enjoy it in peace. All this while the soil and pasture of the earth remained still in common as before, and open to every occupant: except perhaps in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of a sole and exclusive property in lands (for the sake of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>) was earlier felt; and therefore more readily complied with. Otherwise Property, therwise, when the multitude of men and cattle had consumed every convenience on one spot of ground, it was deemed a natural right to seize upon and occupy such other lands as would more easily supply their necessities. This practice is still retained among the wild and uncultivated nations that have never been formed into civil states, like the Tartars and others in the east; where the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> itself, and the boundless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of their territory, conspire to retain them still in the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> state of vagrant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, which was universal in the earliest ages, and which Tacitus informs us continued among the Germans till the decline of the Roman empire. We have also a striking example of the same kind in the history of Abraham and his nephew <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>. When their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> substance became so great, that pasture and other conveniences grew scarce, the natural <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, that a strife arose between their servants; so that it was no longer practicable to dwell together. This contention Abraham endeavoured to compose: "Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between thee and me. Is not the whole land before thee? Separate thyself, I pray thee, from me; If thou wilt take the left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, then I will go to the right; or if thou depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left." This plainly implies an acknowledged right, in either, to occupy whatever ground he pleased, that was not pre-occupied by other tribes. "And Lot lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered every where, even as the garden of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>. Then Lot chose him all the plain of Jordan, and journeyed east; and Abraham dwelt in the land of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>." Upon the same principle was founded the right of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a>, or sending colonies to find out new habitations, when the mother-country was overcharged with inhabitants; which was practised as well by the Phoenicians and Greeks, as the Germans, Scythians, and other northern people. And, so long as it was confined to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a> and cultivation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> uninhabited countries, it kept strictly within the limits of the law of nature. But how far the seizing on countries already peopled, and driving out or massacring the innocent and defenceless natives, merely because they differed from their invaders in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, in customs, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, or in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; how far such a conduct was consonant to nature, to reason, or to Christianity, deserves well to be considered by those who have rendered their names immortal by thus civilizing mankind. As the world by degrees grew more populous, it daily became more difficult to find out new spots to inhabit, without encroaching upon former occupants; and, by constantly occupying the same individual spot, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the earth were consumed, and its spontaneous produce destroyed, without any provision for a future supply or succession. It therefore became necessary to pursue some regular method of providing a constant subsistence; and this necessity produced, or at least promoted and encouraged, the art of agriculture. And the art of agriculture, by a regular connection and consequence, introduced and established the idea of a more permanent property in the soil than had hitherto been received and adopted. It was clear that the earth would not produce her fruits in sufficient quantities, without the assistance of tillage: but who would be at the pains of tilling it, if another might watch an opportunity to seize upon and enjoy the product of his industry, art, and labour? Had not therefore a separate property in lands, as well as moveables, been vested in some individuals, the world must have continued a forest, and men have been mere animals of prey; which, according to some philosophers, is the genuine state of nature. Whereas now (so graciously has Providence interwoven our duty and our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> together) the result of this very necessity has been the ennobling of the human <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, by giving it opportunities of improving its rational faculties, as well as of exerting its natural. Necessity begat property: and in order to insure that property, recourse was had to civil society, which brought along with it a long train of inseparable concomitants; states, government, laws, punishments, and the public <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> duties. Thus connected together, it was found that a part only of society was sufficient to provide, by their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> labour, for the necessary subsistence of all; and leisure was given to others to cultivate the human mind, to invent useful arts, and to lay the foundations of science. The only question remaining is, How this property became actually vested; or what it is that gave a man an exclusive right to retain in a permanent manner that specific land, which before belonged generally to everybody, but particularly to nobody? And as we before observed, that occupancy gave the right to the temporary use of the soil; so it is agreed upon all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, that occupancy gave also the original right to the permanent property in the subsistence of the earth itself; which excludes every one else but the owner from the use of it. There is indeed some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> among the writers on natural law, concerning the reason why occupancy should convey this right, and invest one with this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> property: Grotius and Puffendorf insisting, that this right of occupancy is founded upon a tacit and implied assent of all mankind, that the first occupant should become the owner; and Barbeyrac, Titus, Mr. Locke, and others, holding, that there is no such implied assent, neither is it necessary that there should be; for that the very act of occupancy, alone, being a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bodily labour, is from a principle of natural <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, without any consent or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, sufficient of itself to gain a title. A dispute that favours too much of nice and scholastic refinement. However, both sides agree in this, that occupancy is the thing by which the title was in fact originally gained; every man seizing to his own continued use such spots of ground as he found most agreeable to his own convenience, provided he found them unoccupied by any one else. Property, both in lands and moveables, being thus originally acquired by the first taker, which taking amounts to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> that he intends to appropriate the thing to his own use, it remains in him, by the principle of universal law, till such time as he does some other act which shows an intention to abandon it; for then it becomes, naturally speaking, publici juris once more, and is liable to be again appropriated by the next occupant. So if one is possessed of a jewel, and casts it into the sea or a public highway, this is such an express dereliction, that a property will be vested in the first fortunate finder that will seize it. Property to his own use. But if he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> it privately in the earth, or other secret place, and it is discovered, the finder acquires no property therein; for the owner hath not by this act declared any intention to abandon it, but rather the contrary: and if he loses or drops it by accident, it cannot be collected from thence, that he designed to quit the possession; and therefore in such case the property still remains in the loser, who may claim it again of the finder. And this, we may remember, is the doctrine of our law with relation to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TREASURE_TROVE"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">Treasure</a>-Trove. But this method, of one man's abandoning his property, and another seizing the vacant possession, however well founded in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>, could not long subsist in fact. It was calculated merely for the rudiments of civil society, and necessarily ceased among the complicated interests and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> refinements of polite and established governments. In these it was found, that what became inconvenient or useless to one man, was highly convenient and useful to another; who was ready to give in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for it some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> that was equally desirable to the former proprietor. This mutual convenience introduced commercial traffic, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> transfer of property by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, grant, or conveyance: which may be considered either as a continuance of the original possession which the first occupant had; or as an abandoning of the thing by the present owner, and an immediate successive occupancy of the same by the new proprietor. The voluntary delocation of the owner, and delivering the possession to another individual, amount to a transfer of the property; the proprietor declaring his intention no longer to occupy the thing himself, but that his own right of occupancy shall be vested in the new acquirer. Or, taken in the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, if I agree to part with an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> of my land to Titus, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of conveyance is an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of my intending to abandon the property; and Titus, being the only or first man acquainted with such my intention, immediately steps in and seizes the vacant possession: thus the consent expressed by the conveyance, gives Titus a good right against me; and possession, or occupancy, confirms that right against all the world besides. The most universal and effectual way of abandoning property, is by the death of the occupant: when, both the actual possession and intention of keeping possession ceasing, the property, which is founded upon such possession and intention, ought also to cease of course. For, naturally speaking, the instant a man ceases to be, he ceases to have any dominion: else, if he had a right to dispose of his acquisitions one moment beyond his life, he would also have a right to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> their disposal for a million of ages after him; which would be highly absurd and inconvenient. All property must therefore cease upon death, considering men as absolute individuals, and unconnected with civil society: for then, by the principles before established, the next immediate occupant would acquire a right in all that the deceased possessed. But as, under civilized governments, which are calculated for the peace of mankind, such a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> would be productive of endless disturbances, the universal law of almost every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> (which is a kind of secondary law of nature) has either given the dying person a power of continuing his property, by disposing of his possessions by will; or, in case he neglects to dispose of it, or is not permitted to make any disposition at all, the municipal law of the country then steps in, and declares who shall be the successor, representative, or heir of the deceased; that is, who alone shall have a right to enter upon this vacant possession, in order to avoid that confusion which its becoming again common would occasion. And farther, in case no testament be permitted by the laws, or none be made, and no heir can be found so qualified as the law requires, still, to prevent the robust title of occupancy from again taking place, the doctrine of escheats is adopted in almost every country; whereby the sovereign of the state, and those who claim under his authority, are the ultimate heirs, and succeed to those inheritances to which no other title can be formed.
