The right of inheritance, or descent to the children and relations of the deceased, seems to have been allowed much earlier than the right of devising by testament. We are apt to conceive at the first view that it has nature on its side; yet we often mistake for nature what we find established by long and inveterate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. It is certainly a wise and effectual, but clearly a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a>, establishment; since the permanent right of property, vested in the ancestor himself, was no natural, but merely a civil right. It is true, that the transmission of one's possessions to posterity has an evident tendency to make a man a good citizen and a useful member of society: it sets the passions on the side of duty, and prompts a man to deserve well of the public, when he is sure that the reward of his services will not die with himself, but be transmitted to those with whom he is connected by the dearest and most tender affections. Yet, reasonable as this foundation of the right of inheritance may seem, it is probable that its immediate origin arose not from speculations altogether so delicate and refined, and, if not from fortuitous circumstances, at least from a plainer and more simple principle. A man's children or nearest relations are usually about him on his death-bed, and are the earliest witnesses of his decease. They became therefore generally the next immediate occupants, till at length in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time this frequent usage ripened into general law. And therefore also in the earliest ages, on failure of children, a man's servants born under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> were allowed to be his heirs; being immediately on the spot when he died. For we find the old <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> Abraham, expressly declaring, that "since God had given him no seed, his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> Eliezer, one born in his house, was his heir." While property continued only for life, testaments were useless and unknown; and when it became inheritable, the inheritance was long indefeasible, and the children or heirs at law were incapable of exclusion by will. Till at length it was found, that so strict a rule of inheritance made heirs disobedient and headstrong, defrauded creditors of their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> debts, and prevented many provident fathers from dividing or charging their estates as the exigence of their families required. This introduced pretty generally the right of disposing of one's property, or a part of it, by testament; that is, by written or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORAL">oral</a> instructions properly witnessed and authenticated, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of the deceased; which we therefore emphatically style his will. This was established in some countries much later than Property in others. With us in England, till <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, a man could only dispose of one-third of his moveables from his wife and children; and, in general, no will was permitted of lands till the reign of Henry VIII., and then only of a certain portion: for it was not till after the restoration that the power of devising real property became so universal as at present. Wills, therefore, and testaments, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of inheritance, and succeedances, are all of them creatures of the civil or municipal laws, and accordingly are in all respects regulated by them; every distinct country having different ceremonies and requisites to make a testament completely valid; neither does anything vary more than the right of inheritance under different national establishments. In England particularly, this diversity is carried to such a length, as if it had been meant to point out the power of the laws in regulating the succession to property, and how futile every claim must be that has not its foundation in the positive rules of the state. In personal estates, the father may succeed to his children; in landed property, he never can be their immediate heir, by any remote possibility: in general, only the eldest son, in some places only the youngest, in others all the sons together, have a right to succeed to the inheritance: In real estates, males are preferred to females, and the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> will usually exclude the rest; in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of personal estates, the females of equal degree are admitted together with the males, and no right of primogeniture is allowed. This one consideration may help to remove the scruples of many well-meaning persons, who set up a mistaken <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> in opposition to the rules of law. If a man disinherit his son, by a will duly executed, and leaves his estate to a stranger, there are many who consider this proceeding as contrary to natural justice; while others so scrupulously adhere to the supposed intention of the dead, that if a will of lands be attested by only two witnesses instead of three, which the law requires, they are apt to imagine that the heir is bound in conscience to relinquish his title to the devisee. But both of them certainly proceed upon very erroneous principles: as if, on the one hand, the son had by nature a right to succeed to his father's lands; or as if, on the other hand, the owner was by nature entitled to direct the succession of his property after his own decease. Whereas the law of nature suggests, that on the death of the possessor the estate should again become common, and be open to the next occupant, unless otherwise ordered, for the sake of civil peace, by the positive law of society. The positive law of society, which is with us the municipal law of England, directs it to vest in such person as the last proprietor shall by will, attended with certain requisites, appoint; and, in defect of such appointment, to go to some particular person, who, from the result of certain local constitutions, appears to be the heir at law. Hence it follows, that, where the appointment is regularly made, there cannot be a shadow of right in any one but the person appointed: and, where the necessary requisites are omitted, the right of the heir is equally strong and built upon as solid a foundation, as the right of the devisee would have been, supposing such requisites were observed. But, after all, there are some few things, which, notwithstanding the general introduction and continuance of property, must still unavoidably remain in common; being such wherein nothing but an usufructuary property is capable of being had: and therefore they still belong to the first occupant, during the time he holds possession of them, and no longer. Such (among others) are the elements of light, air, and water; which a man may occupy by means of his windows, his gardens, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, and other conveniences: such also are the generality of those animals which are said to be *ferae naturae*, or of a wild and untameable disposition; which any man may seize upon and keep for his own use or pleasure. All these things, so long as they remain in possession, every man has a right to enjoy without disturbance; but if once they escape from his custody, or he voluntarily abandons the use of them, they return to the common stock, and any man else has an equal right to seize and enjoy them afterwards. Again, there are other things in which a permanent property may subsist, not only as to the temporary use, but also the solid substance; and which yet would be frequently found without a proprietor, had not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of the law provided a remedy to obviate this inconvenience. Such are forests and other waste grounds, which were omitted to be appropriated in the general distribution of lands: such also are wrecks, estrays, and that species of wild animals, which the arbitrary constitutions of positive law have distinguished from the rest by the well-known appellation of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a>. With regard to these and some others, as disturbances and quarrels would frequently arise among individuals contending about the acquisition of this species of property by first occupancy, the law has therefore wisely cut up the root of dissension, by vesting the things themselves in the sovereign of the state; or else in his representatives appointed and authorized by him, being usually the lords of manors. And thus our legislature has universally promoted the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> ends of civil society, the peace and security of individuals, by steadily pursuing that wise and orderly maxim, of assigning to every thing capable of ownership a legal and determinate owner.

PROPHET

Pages 163-163

in general, a person who foretells future events; but is particularly applied to such inspired persons among the Jews as were commissioned by God to declare his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> and purposes to that people. Among the canonical books of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, we have the writings of 16 prophets, four of whom are denominated the greater prophets, viz. Isaiah, Jeremiah, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>, and Daniel; so called from the length <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of their writings, which exceed those of the others, viz. Hosea, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOEL">Joel</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMOS">Amos</a>, Obadiah, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JONAH">Jonah</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICAH">Micah</a>, Nahum, Habakkuk, Haggai, Zechariah, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALACHI">Malachi</a>, who are called the lesser prophets, from the shortness of their writings. The Jews do not <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Daniel among the prophets, because, they say, he lived the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of a courtier rather than that of a prophet. An account of the several writings of the prophets may be seen each under its particular head. See the article ISAIAH, &c.

PROPITIATION

Pages 163-163

in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, a sacrifice offered to God to appease his wrath, and render him propitious. Among the Jews there were both ordinary and public sacrifices, as holocausts, &c. offered by way of thanksgiving.

PROPOSITION

Pages 163-164

in logic, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of an argument wherein some <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, either <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> positive, is attributed to a subject. Proposition, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, is either some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> advanced and shown to be such by demonstration, or some operation proposed and its solution shown. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the proposition be deduced from several theoretical definitions compared together, it is called a theorem; if from a praxis, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of operations, it is called a problem. See the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Theorem and Problem. Proposition, in oratory. See Oratory, no 28. Proposition, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, the first part of a poem, wherein the author proposes briefly, and in general, what he is to say in the body of his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. It should comprehend only the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the poem, that is, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> and persons that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>. Horace prescribes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and simplicity in the proposition, and would not have the poet <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> too much, nor raise in the reader too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of what he is going to relate.

PROPREFECT

Pages 164-164

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the prefect's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> an officer whom the prefect of the praetorium commissioned to do <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his duty in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

PROPRETOR

Pages 164-164

a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, who, having discharged the office of pretor at home, was sent into a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> to command there with his former praetorial authority. It was also an appellation given to those who, without having been pretors at Rome, were sent extraordinary into the provinces to administer <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> with the authority of pretors.

PROROGATION

Pages 164-164

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of prolonging, adjourning, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> putting off to another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between a prorogation and an adjournment of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> is, that by prorogation the session is ended, and such bills as passed in either <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, or both houses, and had not the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> assent, must at the next <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> begin again.

PROSCRIPTION

Pages 164-164

a publication made in the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> leader of a party, whereby he promises a reward to any one who shall bring him the head of one of his enemies. Sylla and Marius by turns proscribed each other's adherents.—Under the triumvirate, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the best and bravest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> fell by proscription. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> took its rise from the practice of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the persons names, and posting it in public: from pro, and scribo "I write."

PROSE

Pages 164-164

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of mankind, loose, and unconfined by poetical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, rhymes, &c.—In which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands opposed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. The word comes from the Latin prosa, which some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> poras, which signifies expendit: others deduce it from the Latin prosa, of profus, "going forwards;" by way of opposition to versa, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> "<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> backwards," as is necessary in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>.

PROSECUTION

Pages 164-165

in the criminal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>. The next step towards the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of offenders after <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMITMENT">COMMITMENT</a>, is their prosecution, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the manner of their formal Prosecutor formal <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a>. And this, in the English law, is either upon a previous finding of the fact by an inquest or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURY">jury</a>; or without such previous finding. The former way is either by Presentment or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INDICTMENT">Indictment</a>. See these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. The remaining methods of prosecution are without any previous finding by a jury, to fix the authoritative stamp of verisimilitude upon the accusation. One of these, by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, was when a thief was taken with the mainour, that is, with the thing stolen upon him, in manu. For he might, when so detected, flagrante delicto, be brought into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, arraigned, and tried, without indictment: as by the Danish law he might be taken and hanged upon the spot, without acculation or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. But this proceeding was taken away by several statutes in the reign of Edward III., though in Scotland a similar <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> remains to this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. So that the only <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of proceeding at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, without a previous indictment or presentment by a grand jury, now seems to be that of Information; which see. These are all the methods of prosecution at the suit of the king. There yet remains another, which is merely at the suit of the subject, and is called an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>. See that article. But of all the methods of prosecution, that by indictment is the most general. See Indictment.

PROSECUTOR

Pages 165-165

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he that pursues a cause in another's name.

PROSERPINE

Pages 165-165

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, was carried off by Pluto as she was gathering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> with her companions. Ceres, disconsolate for the loss of her daughter, after having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> sought her, heard where she was, and intreated Jupiter to let her return from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. This request Jupiter granted, on condition she had tasted nothing in Pluto's dominions. Ceres therefore went to fetch her; but when her daughter was preparing to return, Ascalaphus gave information that he had seen Proserpine eat some grains of a pomegranate she had gathered in Pluto's garden, on which she was sentenced to continue in Tartarus in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of Pluto's spouse, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of those gloomy regions: but to mitigate the grief of Ceres for her disappointment, Jupiter granted that her daughter should only spend six months together in hell with her husband, and the other six on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with her mother. Some mythologists imagine that the latter <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> alludes to the corn, which must remain all the winter hid in the earth, in order to sprout forth in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and produce the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>.

PROSEUCHE

Pages 165-165

in antiquity, properly signifies <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>; but it is taken for the places of prayer of the Jews, and was pretty near the same as their synagogues. But the synagogues were originally in the cities, and were covered places: whereas, for the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, the proselytes were out of the cities and on the banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; having no covering, except perhaps the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of some trees <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> covered galleries. The word is Greek, προσευχή, "prayer."

PROSLAMBANOMENE

Pages 165-165

the name of a musical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in the Greek system. As the two tetrachords of the Greeks were conjunctive, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, in other words, as the highest note of the first served likewise for the lowest note of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, it is plain that a complete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> could not be formed. To remedy this deficiency, therefore, one note beneath the lowest tetrachord was added, as an octave to the highest of the last tetrachord. Thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we suppose the first to have begun on B, the last must have ended upon A, to which one note subjoined immediately beneath the lowest B in the diatonic order must have formed an octave. This note was called proslambanomene. But it appears from authors who have scrutinized antiquity with some diligence, and perhaps with as much success as the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATA">data</a> upon which they proceeded could produce, that the names of the notes in the Greek system, which originally signified their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> situation in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of ascending or descending sounds, were afterwards applied to their positions in the lyre. Higher or lower, then, according to this application, did not signify their degrees of acuteness or gravity, but their higher or lower situation upon this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>.

PROSODY

Pages 165-165

that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> which treats of the quantities and accents of syllables, and the manner of making verses. The English prosody turns chiefly on two things, numbers and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHYME">rhyme</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, n° 20. and Part III.

PROSOPOPOEIA

Pages 165-165

a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in oratory, whereby we raise qualities of things inanimate into persons. See Oratory, n° 48.

PROSTATAE

Pages 165-165

in anatomy, a gland, generally supposed to be two separate bodies, though in reality but one, situated <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> before the neck of the bladder, and surrounding the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a>. See Anatomy, n° 371.

PROSTYLE

Pages 165-165

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a range of columns in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of a temple.

PROTAGORAS

Pages 165-165

a famous Greek <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDERA">Abdera</a>, was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEMOCRITUS">Democritus</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> of the Thurians. He was more subtle than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> in his reasonings; however, he taught at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation, but was at length banished from thence for the impiety of his doctrines. He then travelled, and visited the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Mediterranean, where it is said that he was the first philosopher who taught for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. He died in a voyage to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, in a very advanced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> reasoned by dilemmas, and left the mind in suspense with respect to all the questions he propounded. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> against him. He flourished 400 B.C.

PROTASIS

Pages 166-166

in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> drama, the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a comic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> tragic piece, wherein the several persons are shown, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> intimated, and the subject of the piece proposed and entered upon. It might reach as far as our two first acts, and where it ended the epistle commenced. See the article EPISTASIS.

PROTEA

Pages 165-166

the Silver-tree; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the tetrandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>: 1. The conifera, with linear, spear-shaped, entire leaves, grows to the height of 10 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> 12 feet, with a straight regular stem. The branches naturally form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> regular head. The leaves are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and narrow, of a shining silver <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; and as they remain the whole year, make a fine appearance in the greenhouse. 2. The argentea, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called silver-tree, has a strong upright stem covered with purplish bark, dividing into several branches which grow erect, garnished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, shining, filmy leaves, which make a fine appearance when intermixed with other exotics. 3. The nitida, or wagg- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOM">boom</a>, greatly resembles the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sort: the leaves are very silky and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, with erect purple branches. All these plants, being tender exotics, require to be continually kept in the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-GREEN_HOUSE">green-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> during winter. The first may be propagated by <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>, which should be cut off in April, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> before the plants begin to shoot; the second and third sorts may be propagated by seeds.

PROTECTOR

Pages 166-166

a person who undertakes to shelter and defend the weak, helpless, and distressed. Every Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and every <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order, has a protector residing at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome, who is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>, and is called the cardinal protector. Protector is also sometimes used for a regent of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, made choice of to govern it during the minority of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. Cromwell assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> protector of the commonwealth of England, &c.

PROTESILAI TURRIS

Pages 166-166

the sepulchre of Proteuslaus, with a temple, at which Alexander sacrificed, (Arian); situate at the south extremity of the Hellepont, next the Chersonesus Thracia. Proteuslaus was the first Greek who landed on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, and the first Greek slain by the Trojans, (<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Ovid.) His wife Laodamia, to allay her grief, begged the gods for a sight of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>; and obtaining her request, she expired in his embraces, (Hyginus.) Proteuslaus was also called Phylaciades, from Phylace, a town of Thessaly.

PROTEST

Pages 166-166

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a summons written by a notary-public to a merchant, banker, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, to accept or discharge a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> drawn on him, after his having refused either to accept or pay it. See Bill of Exchange.

PROTESTANT

Pages 166-166

a name first given in Germany to those who adhered to the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>; because in 1529, they protested against a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. and the diet of Spires; declaring that they appealed to a general <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. The same name has also been given to those of the sentiments of Calvin; and is now become a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> denomination for all those of the reformed churches.

PROTHONOTARY

Pages 166-166

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> which properly signifies first notary, and which was anciently the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> notaries of the emperors of Constantino- nople. Prothonotary with us is used for an officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-pleas; the former of which courts has one, and the latter three. The prothonotary of the king's bench records all civil actions sued in that court, as the clerk of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-office does all criminal causes. The prothonotaries of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS">common pleas</a> enter and enrol all declarations, pleadings, assizes, judgments, and actions: they also make out all judicial writs, except writs of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABEAS_CORPUS">habeas corpus</a>, and dirigendas jurator, for which there is a particular office, called the habeas corpora office: they likewise enter recognizances acknowledged, and all common recoveries; make exemplifications of records, &c. In the court of Rome there is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of 12 prelates, called apostolical prothonotaries, empowered to receive the last wills of cardinals, to make all informations and proceedings necessary for the canonization of saints, and all such acts as are of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to the Papacy: for which purpose they have the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of admission into all confestories, whether public <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> half public. They also attend on the pope, whenever he performs any extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> out of Rome.

PROTO

Pages 166-166

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, frequently used in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of priority: thus, proto-collum, in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>, signifies the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of a book; proto-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>, the first martyr; proto-plast, the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> formed, &c.

PROTOGENES

Pages 166-166

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> painter, was born at Caunus, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, subject to the Rhodians, and flourished 300 years before the birth of our Saviour. He was at first obliged to paint ships for his livelihood; but afterwards acquired the highest reputation for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>; though <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APELLES">Apelles</a> blamed him for finishing his pieces too highly, and not knowing when to have done. The finest of his pictures was that of Jalilus, which is mentioned by several ancient authors, though none of them give any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it. He worked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years on this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>; during which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he lived entirely upon lupines and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, being of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and simple nourishment left him greater freedom of fancy. Apelles, on seeing this picture, was struck with such admiration, that he was unable to speak, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> to find words sufficient to express his idea of its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. It was this picture that saved the city of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> when besieged by Demetrius <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Macedon; for being able to attack it only on that side where Protagenes worked, which he intended to burn, he chose rather to abandon his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> than to destroy so fine a piece. Pliny says, that Apelles asked him what price he had for his pictures, and Protagenes naming an inconsiderable sum, Apelles, concerned at the injustice done to the beauty of his productions, gave him 50 talents, about 10,000l. for one picture only, declaring publicly that he would sell it for his own. This generosity made the Rhodians sensible of the merit of Protagenes; and they were so eager to purchase the picture Apelles had bought, that they paid him a much greater price for it than he had given.

PROTOTYPE

is the original <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> after which a thing was formed; but chiefly used for the patterns of things to be engraved, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, &c.

PROTRACTOR

the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used for protracting <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> laying <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of a field, or other <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. See Plotting.

PROTUBERANCE

Pages 167-167

in anatomy, is any eminence, whether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> preternatural, that projects or advances out beyond the rest.

PROVEDITOR

Pages 167-167

an officer in several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, particularly at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, who has the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of matters relating to policy.

PROVENCE

Pages 167-167

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of France, bounded by Dauphine on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a> on the east, by the Mediterranean on the south, and by the river <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, which separates it from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, on the west: it is about 100 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and near as many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>.

PROVEND

Pages 167-167
or Provender, originally signified a kind of vessel containing the measure of corn daily given to a horse, or other beast of labour, for his subsistence; but now is generally used to signify the food for cattle, whatever it is.

PROVERB

Pages 167-167

according to Camden, is a concise, witty, and wise speech, grounded upon <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, and for the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> containing some useful instructions. Book of Proverbs, a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, containing a part of the proverbs of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> the son of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Israel. The first 24 chapters are acknowledged to be the genuine <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; the next five chapters are a collection of several of his proverbs made by order of king Hezekiah; and the two last seem to have been added though belonging to different and unknown authors, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGUR">Agur</a> the son of Jakob, and king Lemuel. In this excellent book are contained rules for the conduct of all conditions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; for kings, courtiers, masters, servants, fathers, mothers, children, &c.

PROVIDENCE

Pages 167-167

one of the least of the Bahama <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the American ocean, but the best of those planted and fortified by the English. It is seated on the east side of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 77° 35'. N. Lat. 25° 0'.

PROVIDENCE-PLANTATION

Pages 167-167

a colony of New-England, which, with Rhode-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, formerly constituted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is Newport.

PROVINCE

Pages 167-167

in Roman antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, which, upon being entirely reduced under the Roman dominion, was new-modelled according to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of the conquerors, and subjected to the command of annual governors sent from Rome; being <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> obliged to pay such taxes and contributions as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> thought fit to demand. Of these countries, that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of France next the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> was one, and still retains the name Provence. Nicod derives the word à procul vivendo, "living afar off;" but it is better deduced from pro, and vinco, "I overcome." Province, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> state, comprising several cities, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, &c. all under the same <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and usually distinguished by the extent either of the civil or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> jurisdiction. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> distinguishes its provinces by archbishoprics; in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, England is divided into two provinces, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>. The United Provinces are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> provinces of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, who, revolting from the Spanish dominion, made a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> offensive and defensive, at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, anno 1579. See United Provinces.

PROVINCIAL

Pages 167-167

something relating to a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. It also denotes, in Roman countries, a person who has the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> of a province.

PROVISIONS

Pages 167-167

in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, implies all manner of cattles, food <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> provender, used in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, both for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> and beast. PROVOST of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> or town, is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> municipal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> in several trading cities, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, &c. being much the same with mayor in other places. He presides in city-courts, and, together with the bailies, who are his deputies, determines in all differences that arise among citizens. The provost of Edinburgh, as well as all the other considerable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in Scotland, has the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a>; and the former calls yearly conventions of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> boroughs to Edinburgh by his messives.

PROVOST

Pages 167-168
or Provost Royal, a sort of inferior judge established throughout France, to take cognizance of all civil, personal, real, and mixed causes, among the people only. Grand Provost of France, or of the Household, has jurisdiction in the king's house, and over the officers therein; looks to the policy thereof, the regulation of provisions, &c. Grand Provost of the Constable, a judge who manages processes against the soldiers in the army who have committed any crime. He has four lieutenants distributed throughout the army, called provosts of the army, and particularly provosts in the several regiments. Provost Marshal of an Army, is an officer appointed to seize and secure deserters, and all other criminals. PRU He is to hinder soldiers from pillaging, to indict offenders, and see the sentence passed on them executed. He also regulates the weights and ="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures, and the price of provisions, &c., in the army. For the discharge of his office, he has a lieutenant, a clerk, and a troop of marshal-men on horseback, as also an executioner. There is also a provost-marshal in the navy, who hath charge over prisoners, &c. The French have a provost-general of the marines, who is to prosecute the marines when guilty of any crime, and make report thereof to the council of war; besides a marine provost in every vessel, who is a kind of gaoler, and takes the prisoners into his care, and keeps the vessel clean. Provosts of the Marshals, are a kind of lieutenants of the marshals of France; of these there are 180 seats in France; their chief jurisdiction regards highwaymen, footpads, house-breakers, &c. Provost of the Mint, a particular judge instituted for the apprehending and prosecuting of false coiners. Provost, or Provot, in the king's stables; his office is to attend at court, and hold the king's stirrup when he mounts his horse. There are four provosts of this kind, each of whom attends in his turn, monthly.

PROXIMITY

Pages 168-168

denotes the relation of nearness, either in respect of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, blood, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>.

PRUDENTIUS

Pages 168-168
or Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a famous Christian poet, under the reign of Theodosius the Great, who was born in Spain in the year 348. He first followed the profession of an advocate, was afterwards a judge, then a soldier, and at length had an honourable employment at court. We have a great number of his poems, which, from the choice of his subjects, may be termed Christian poems; but the style is barbarous, and very different from the purity of the Augustan age. The most esteemed editions of Prudentius's works are that of Amsterdam, in 1667, with Heinius's Notes, and that of Paris in 1687, in utrum Delphini.

PRUNES

Pages 168-168

are plumbs dried in the sunshine, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> in an oven.

PRUNING

Pages 168-169

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, is the lopping off the superfluous branches of trees, in order to make them bear better fruit, grow higher, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> appear more regular. Pruning, though an operation of very general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, is nevertheless rightly understood by few. Nor is it to be learned by rote, but requires a strict observation of the different manners of growth of the several sorts of fruit-trees; the proper method of doing which cannot be known without carefully observing how each kind is naturally disposed to produce its fruit: for some do this on the same year's wood, as vines; others, for the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, upon the former year's wood, as peaches, nectarines, &c.; and others upon spurs which are produced upon wood of three, four, &c., to fifteen or twenty years old, as pears, plums, cherries, &c. Therefore, in order to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> management of fruit-trees, provision should always be made to have a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> wood in every part of the trees; and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> there should not be a superfluity of useless branches, which would exhaust the strength of the trees, and cause them to decay in a few years. The reasons for pruning of fruit-trees; are, 1. To preserve them longer in a vigorous bearing-state; 2. To render them more beautiful; and, 3. To cause the fruit to be larger and better tasted. The general instructions for pruning are as follow. The greatest care ought to be taken of fruit-trees in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, when they are in vigorous growth; which is the only proper season for procuring a quantity of good wood in the different parts of the tree, and for disposing all useless branches as soon as they are produced, in order that the vigour of the tree may be entirely distributed to such branches only as are designed to remain. For this reason trees ought not to be neglected in April and May, when their shoots are produced; however, those branches which are intended for bearing the succeeding year should not be shortened during the time of their growth, because this would cause them to produce two lateral shoots, from the eyes below the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where they were stopped, which would draw much of the strength from the buds of the first shoot: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the two lateral shoots are not entirely cut away at the winter-pruning, they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> prove injurious to the tree. This is to be chiefly understood of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-fruit and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>; but pears and apples, being much harder, suffer not so much, tho' it is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disadvantage to those also to be thus managed. It must likewise be remarked, that peaches, nectarines, apricots, cherries, and plums, are always in the greatest vigour when they are least maimed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>; for where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> branches are taken off, they are subject to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a> and decay. It is therefore the most prudent method to rub off all useless buds when they are first produced, and to pinch others, where new shoots are wanted to supply the vacancies of the wall; by which management they may be so ordered as to want but little of the knife in winter-pruning. The management of pears and apples is much the same with these trees in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>; but in winter they must be very differently pruned: for as peaches and nectarines, for the most part, produce their fruit upon the former year's wood, and must therefore have their branches shortened according to their strength, in order to produce new shoots for the succeeding year; so, on the contrary, pears, apples, plumbs, and cherries, producing their fruit upon spurs, which come out of the wood of five, six, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years old, should not be shortened, because thereby those buds which were naturally disposed to form these spurs, would produce wood-branches; by which means the trees would be filled with wood, but would never produce much fruit. The branches of standard-trees should never be shortened unless where they are very luxuriant, and, by growing irregularly on one side of the trees, attract the greatest part of the sap, by which means the other parts are either unfurnished with branches, or are rendered very weak; in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> the branch should be shortened <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as low as is necessary, in order to obtain more branches to fill up the hollow of the tree: but this is only to be understood of pears and apples, which will produce shoots from wood of three, four, or more years old; whereas most sorts of stone-fruit will gum and decay after such amputations: when- whenever this happens to stone-fruit, it should be remedied by stopping or pinching those shoots in the spring, before they have obtained too much vigour, which will cause them to push out side branches; but this must be done with caution. You must also cut out all dead or decaying branches, which cause their heads to look ragged, and also attract noxious particles from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>: in doing of this, you should cut them <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> down to the place where they were produced, otherwise that part of the branch which is left will also decay, and prove equally hurtful to the rest of the tree; for it seldom happens when a branch begins to decay, that it does not die quite down to the place where it was produced, and if permitted to remain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> uncut, often infects some of the other parts of the tree. If the branches cut off are large, it will be very proper, after having smoothed the cut part exactly even with a knife, chisel, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a>, to put on a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a> clay, which will prevent the wet from soaking into the tree at the wounded part. All such branches as run across each other, and occasion a confusion in the head of the tree, should be cut off; and as there are frequently young vigorous shoots on old trees, which rise from the old branches near the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, and grow upright into the head, these should be carefully cut out every year, lest, by being permitted to grow, they fill the tree too full of wood. As to the pruning of forest-trees, if they be large, it is best not to prune them at all; yet, if there be an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, avoid taking off large boughs as much as possible. And, 1. If the bough be small, cut it smooth, close, and sloping. 2. If the branch be large, and the tree old, cut it off at three or four feet from the stem. 3. If the tree grow crooked, cut it off at the crook, sloping upward, and nurse up one of the most promising shoots for a new stem. 4. If the tree grow top-heavy, its head must be lightened, and that by thinning the boughs that grow out of the main branches. But if you would have them spring, rub off the buds, and shroud up the side-shoots. 5. If the side-bough still <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out, and the top be able to sustain itself, give the boughs that put forth in spring a pruning after Midsummer, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> them close.

PRUNUS

Pages 169-169

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the icosandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">Species</a>. 1. The domestica, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> plum-tree, grows 20 or 30 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, garnished with oval, spear-shaped leaves, and with the pedunculi for the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> single, terminated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, succeeded by plums of many different colours, sizes, and shapes in the varieties. 2. The insititia, wild-plum, or bullace-tree, grows 12 or 15 feet high; the branches somewhat spinous; the leaves oval, hairy underneath; and the pedunculi by pairs, terminated by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> flowers succeeded by small, round, plum-like, fruit of different colours in the varieties. 3. The spinosa, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THORN">thorn</a>, or sloe-tree, grows 10 or 12 feet high, very branchy and bushy quite from bottom, armed with strong, sharp spines, small, spear-shaped, smooth leaves, pedunculi growing singly, terminated by flowers, succeeded by small, round, black cherries in autumn. It grows wild everywhere in hedges and woods; and is very proper for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> field hedges, being of very quick growth. 4. The cerasus, or common cherry-tree, grows 20 feet or more in height, garnished with oval clusters of lanceolate, smooth leaves, umbellate flowers, succeeded by clusters of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> roundish fruit of different sizes and properties in the varieties. 5. The avium, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> wild-cherry tree, grows 40 or 50 feet high, having oval, spear-shaped leaves, downy underneath, with umbellate sessile clusters of white flowers, succeeded by small round fruit of different properties in the varieties. 6. The padus, or common <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>-cherry tree, grows 15 or 20 feet high, of a shrub-like growth, with a spreading head, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, rough ferrated leaves, having two glands at the back of the base like the other, and with shorter, more <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> clusters of flowers, succeeded by large red fruit. This grows wild in hedges in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> parts of England. 7. The Virginiana, or Virginian bird-cherry, grows 30 feet high, dividing into a very branchy head, having a dark purple bark, oval, slightly ferrated, shining green leaves, having two glands at the forepart of the base, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> clusters of white flowers, succeeded by small, round, berry-like, black fruit. 8. The Canadensis, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a> bird cherry, grows but four or five feet high, branching horizontally near the ground with smooth branches; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, spear-shaped, rough downy leaves without glands; and long clusters of white flowers, succeeded by small, round, berry-like, black fruit, ripe in autumn. 9. The mahaleb, or perfumed cherry, grows 10 or 15 feet high, with smooth whitish branches, small, oval shining green leaves, and corymbose clusters of white flowers, succeeded by small fruit. 10. The armeniaca, or apricot tree, grows 20 feet high, with a large spreading head, having reddish shoots, large nearly heart-shaped leaves, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>-fitting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>-red flowers rising all along the sides of the young branches; succeeded by large, roundish fruit of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and reddish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> in different varieties. Culture. All the different varieties of plums have at first been raised from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and are afterwards preferred by budding and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a> on any plum-stock. The same method is applicable to cherries; only these are grafted to most advantage upon stocks of the wild black and red cherry raised from the stones of the fruit. The apricot-trees are propagated by budding on any kind of plum-stocks.

PRUSA

Pages 169-169

(anc. geogr.) a town situate at mount Olympus in Mytilene, built by Prusias, who waged <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> with Croesus, (Strabo); with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>, (Stephanus); both <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> princes. Now called Bursa <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Prusa, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Bithynia, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 29° 10'. Lat. 40° 30'.

PRUSIAS

Pages 169-169

the name of several kings of Bithynia. Prusias, a town of Bithynia, anciently called Gios, from a cognominal river, and giving name to the Sinus Cianus of the Propontis; rebuilt by Prusias the son of Zela, after having been destroyed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, the son of Demetrius: it stood on the Sinus Cianus, at the foot of mount Arganthonius. This is the Prusias who harboured Annibal, after the defeat of Antiochus.—Of this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was Asclepiades, farnamed Prusias, the famous physician.

PRUSSIA

Pages 169-184

a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, but deservedly celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, whose monarch, along with Prussia Proper, possesses also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>. Prussia, and some other territories of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. The district properly called Prussia is of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> extent, and divided into the Ducal and Regal Prussia, the latter belonging to the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> till the late partition of the Polish territories. Both together are of great extent; being bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Baltic, on the south by Poland and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Mazovia, on the west by Pomerania, and on the east by Lithuania and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAMOGITIA">Samogitia</a>. The name is by some thought to be derived from the Borussi, a tribe of the Sarmatians, who, migrating from the foot of the Riphzian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, were tempted by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and fertility of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> there. Others think that the name of this country is properly Porussia, Po in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the natives signifying near, and Porussia signifying near Russia. To the latter <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> we find the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Prussia himself afflicting in the treatise intitled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Brandenburg. However, it must be owned, that these <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> any other etymologies of the word are very uncertain, and we find nothing like it mentioned by historians before the tenth century. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> state of Prussia is almost entirely unknown. However, the people are said to have been very <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> and barbarous; living upon raw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and drinking the blood of horses at their feasts, according to Stella, even to intoxication (A). Nay, to extremely savage were this people, that they were even unacquainted with the method of constructing huts, and took up their dwelling in caves and cavities of rocks and trees, where they protected themselves and children from the inclemencies of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Among such a people it is vain to expect that any transactions would be recorded, or indeed that anything worthy of being recorded would be transacted. We shall therefore begin our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Prussia with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEUTONIC">Teutonic</a> knights first got footing in the country. (See Teutonic Knights). On the expulsion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> from the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">Land</a> by Saladin, a settlement was given to the Teutonic knights in Prussia by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONRAD">Conrad</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Mazovia, the competitor of Boleslaus V. for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Poland. Their first residence in this country was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CULM">Culm</a>; to which territory they were confined by the conditions of the donation, excepting what they could conquer from their pagan neighbours, all which the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> granted to them in perpetuity. Encouraged by this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, the knights conquered the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the country which now goes by the name of Prussia; and, not content with this, became very troublesome to Poland, inasmuch that the monarchs of that kingdom were sometimes obliged to carry on dangerous and bloody wars with them; for an account of which, we refer to the article Poland. The Teutonic order <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in Prussia till the year 1531. Their last <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> was Albert marquis of Brandenburg, and nephew to Sigismund I. king of Poland. He was preferred to this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in hopes that his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> to Sigismund might procure a restitution of some of the places which had been taken from the order during the former unsuccessful wars with Poland; but in this the fraternity were disappointed. Albert, however, was so far from endeavouring to obtain any favour from his uncle by fair means, that he refused to do homage to him, and immediately began to make preparations for throwing off his dependence altogether, and recovering the whole of Prussia and Pomerania by force of arms. In this he was so far from succeeding, that, being foiled in every attempt, he was forced to resign the dignity of grand-master; in recompense for which, his uncle bestowed on him that part of Prussia now called Ducal, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> duke. It was now the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of expelled, the house of Brandenburg to assist in the expulsion of the fraternity; and accordingly, being at last driven out of Prussia and Pomerania, they transferred their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> to Mariendal in Franconia; but in that and other provinces of the empire where they settled, little more than the name of the order once so famous now remains. The other most considerable part of his Prussian majesty's dominions is the Electorate of Brandenburg. Like other parts of Germany, it was anciently possessed by Barbarians, of whom no history can be given. These were subdued by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, as is related under the article France; but being on every occasion ready to revolt, in 927 Henry the Fowler established margraves, or governors of the frontiers, to keep the barbarians in awe. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARGRAVE">margrave</a> of Brandenburg was Siegfroy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> to the above-mentioned emperor; under whose administration the bishoprics of Brandenburg and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-HAVELBERG">Havelberg</a> were established by Otho I. From this Siegfroy to the succession of the house of Hohenzollern, from whom the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> is descended, there are reckoned eight different families, who have been margraves of Brandenburg; namely, the family of the Saxons, of Walbeck, Staden, Plenck, Anhalt, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, Luxemburg, and Misnia. The margraves of the four first races had continual wars with the Vandals and other barbarous people; nor could their ravages be stopped till the reign of Albert furred the Bear, the first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the house of Anhalt. He was made margrave by the emperor Conrad III. and afterwards raised to the dignity of elector by Frederic Barbarossa, about the year 1100. Some years afterwards, the king of the Vandals dying without issue, left the middle <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> by his last <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> to the elector, who was besides possessed of the old March, upper <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, the country of Anhalt, and part of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUSATIA">Lusatia</a>. In 1332 this line became extinct, and the electorate devolved to the empire. It was then given by the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> of Bavaria to his son Louis, who was the first of the sixth <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Louis the Roman succeeded his brother; and as he also died without children, he was succeeded by Otho, his third brother, who sold the electorate to the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IV. of the house of Luxemburg for 200,000 florins of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. Charles IV. gave the March to his son Wincelaus, to whom Sigismund succeeded. This elector, being embarrased in his circumstances, sold the new March to the knights of the Teutonic order. Joffe succeeded Sigismund; but, aspiring to the empire, (A) This author does not mention any particular method by which they communicated an inebriating quality to the blood of animals. Possibly, however, the vital fluid may have a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of this kind, though unknown in our days where such barbarous customs are disfused. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">Drunkenness</a> from drinking blood is frequently mentioned in Scripture, but whether literally or metaphorically must be decided by the learned. empire, sold the electorate to William duke of Misnia; who, after he had possessed it for one year, sold it again to the emperor Sigismund. In 1417, Frederic VI, burggrave of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> received the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a> of the country of Brandenburg at the diet of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the emperor Sigismund; who, two years before, had conferred upon him the dignity of elector, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-chamberlain of the Holy Roman empire. This prince, the first of the family of Hohenzollern, found himself possessed of the Old and Middle Marche, but the dukes of Pomerania had usurped the March Ukraine. Against them, therefore, the elector immediately declared <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and soon recovered the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. As the New Marche still continued in the hands of the Teutonic knights, to whom it had been sold as we have already mentioned, the elector, to make up for this, took possession of Saxony, which at that time happened to be vacant by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Albert the last elector of the Anhalt line. But the emperor, not approving of this step, gave the investiture of Saxony to the duke of Misnia; upon which Frederic voluntarily desisted from his acquisitions. This elector made a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of his possessions by will. His eldest son was deprived of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> on account of his having too closely applied himself to search for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER_S_STONE"><a class="xref" hre</a>f="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; so he left him only Voigtsland. The electorate was given to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son Frederic; Albert, farnamed <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>, had the duchies of Franconia; and Frederic, farnamed the Fat, had the old March; but by his death it returned to the electorate of Brandenburg. Frederic I, was succeeded by his son called also Frederic, and farnamed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">Iron</a>-tooth on account of his strength. He might with as great reason have been farnamed the Magnanimous, since he refused two crowns, viz., that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, which was offered him by the pope, and the kingdom of Poland to which he was invited by the people; but Frederic declared he would not accept of it unless Casimir brother to Ladislaus the late king refused it. These instances of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a> had such an effect on the neighbouring people, that the states of Lower Lusatia made a voluntary surrender of their country to him. But as Lusatia was a fief of Bohemia, the king of that country immediately made war on the elector, in order to recover it. However, he was so far from being successful, that, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of peace concluded in 1462, he was obliged to yield the perpetual sovereignty of Corbus, Peits, Sommerfeld, and some other places, to the elector. Frederic then, having redeemed the new March from the Teutonic order for the sum of 100,000 florins, and still further enlarged his dominions, resigned the sovereignty in 1469 to his brother Albert, farnamed the Achilles. Albert was 57 years old when his brother resigned the electorate to him. Most of his exploits for which he had the farname of Achilles had been performed while he was burggrave of Nuremberg. He declared war against <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> duke of Bavaria, defeated and took him prisoner. He gained eight battles against the Nurembergers, who had rebelled and contested his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> to the burgravate. In one of these he fought singly against 16 men, till his people came up to his assistance. He made himself master of the town of Greiffenburg in the same manner that Alexander the Great took the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Oxydrace, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a> from the top of the walls into the town, where he defended himself singly against the inhabitants, till his men forced the gates and rescued him. The confidence which the emperor Frederic III. placed in him, gained him the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of almost the whole empire. He commanded the imperial armies against Lewis the Rich, duke of Bavaria; and against Charles the Bold, duke of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, who had laid siege to Nuis, but concluded a peace at the interposition of Albert. He gained the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> at 17 tournaments, and was never dismounted. All these exploits, however, had been performed before Albert obtained the electorate. From that time Brandenburg met with no very important transactions till the year 1594, when John Sigismund having married <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Albert duke of Prussia, this united that duchy to the electorate, to which it has continued to be united ever since; and obtained pretensions to the countries of Juliers, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERG">Berg</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>, Marck, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAVENSBURG">Ravensburg</a>, and Ravenstein, to the succession of which Anne was heiress. Sigismund died in 1619, and was succeeded by his son George William; during whose <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> the electorate suffered the most miserable calamities. At this time it was that the war commenced between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> and Catholics, which lasted 30 years.
