But if it be precipitated from the water by means of some substance which does not contain fixable air, but which is more strongly disposed than the earth to unite with the water, for instance, spirit of wine, the earth thus precipitated will be in the state of quicklime, that is, caustic, and soluble in water. 2. Quicklime unites with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> without effervescence, which is nothing else than an extrication of the fixable air, of which quicklime has been already deprived. It nevertheless saturates as much acid as it would have done if it had not been calcined. 3. Quicklime is more powerfully disposed to unite with fixable air than fixed or volatile alkalies, or magnesia. Hence, when treated with these substances, it takes from them their fixable air, and is itself rendered mild, and restored to its original weight and properties. Thus two drams of chalk, having been by calcination reduced to one dram and eight grains of quicklime, were thrown into a filtrated solution of an ounce of mild fixed alkali in two ounces of water, and digested during some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; by which the calcareous earth became mild, and weighed one dram and 58 quicklime grains. By means of magnesia, the calcareous earth may be precipitated from lime-water; and this earth is found to be mild, and to have deprived the magnesia of its fixable air. By depriving alkalies of their fixable air, quicklime renders them more caustic and solvent, for the same reason that itself is by this privation of air rendered more caustic and powerfully solvent. This increase of causticity and dissolving power is consistent with a general rule, namely, that the more simple or less compounded any body is, that is, the less its general tendency to union is satisfied, the more disposed it is to unite with or dissolve other substances. 4. Quicklime has a disposition to unite with sulphur, with which it forms a heap of sulphur, similar to that made by sulphur united with an alkali, and, like this, soluble in water. It is also disposed to unite with oils and with animal and vegetable matters, with respect to which it discovers a caustic and corrosive <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. 4. Quicklime mixed with sand forms a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> which hardens, and is used as a cement or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>. All these properties of quicklime have been the objects of consideration to the chemists and philosophers; who have, as usual, been divided in their opinions on the subject. The evident resemblance of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of quicklime to fire, has given occasion for one party to derive all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> properties of this substance from fire; while, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, its want of heat, and incapacity of setting bodies on fire, unless by an accession of water, were objections altogether insurmountable. On the other hand, those who denied the materiality of fire, and affirmed that it consists only in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> mechanically produced among the particles of bodies, were altogether at a loss to show a reason why this motion, or anything resembling it, should continue perhaps for months after the exciting cause is taken away. To remove this difficulty, some have had recourse to the action of a latent acid communicated to the quicklime by the fire; and which one chemist (Mr Meyer) has distinguished by the name of acidum pingue*. But on this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> it may be remarked in the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, that the action of acids is as difficult to be explained as that of fire; and, in the second place, that as all substances, by calcination into quicklime, lose considerably of their weight, it seems very improbable that they should acquire an acid or any other substance which could increase their weight. Besides, from the experiments of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>, it appears, that the diminution of weight in calcareous substances, is owing to their parting with a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fixed air, the weight of which is much more considerable than that of any moisture or fatty <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> they contain. The loss of this fixed air is now also universally allowed to be the reason of the causticity of the quicklime, as its superior <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> for fixed air is looked upon to be the reason why it renders fixed and volatile alkalies caustic like itself. The only question therefore can be, By what means are the calcareous earths deprived of their fixed air? To this question the answer is evident, namely, that the action of the fire expels the fixed air; and if this is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it is evident, that to this action of fire <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, the caustic properties of the lime are owing. We Quicklime. We come now to the discussion of the question, whether quicklime is to be considered as a pure earth, or a combination of it with something else?—Most of the chemists, since the discovery of fixed air, have been inclined to think, that quicklime is a pure earth uncombined with any thing else, and that it approaches more nearly to the state of elementary earth than any other. But this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> seems not to have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> foundation; for there are other earths, such as the basis of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, which, as far as they can be examined by us, are equally pure with quicklime, and yet discover not the smallest causticity, even after the most violent calcination. Besides, from the property which quicklime has of depriving alkaline salts of their fixed air, we may learn, that there exists in it, when kept by itself, a certain principle which prevents it from absorbing again the fixed air, with which it was once so closely united, except in certain circumstances. It is well known, that fixed alkalies, as well as those which are volatile, will absorb fixed air from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> atmosphere; and hence, though they are prepared in the most caustic state, they will in a very short time become mild, by an exposure to the atmosphere; nay, it requires no small <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of care to prevent the atmosphere from having as much access to them as is necessary to change them from a caustic to a mild state. Now, as these substances thus attract the fixed air from the atmosphere, it thence appears that the atmosphere parts very readily with the fixed air which it contains. The quicklime, however, though it has a greater attraction for fixed air than the alkalies, yet does not become near so soon mild from exposure to the air as the alkalies which have less attraction than itself. Hence the necessary inference must be, that quicklime, after being once calcined, instead of attracting, repels fixed air, unless it is placed in certain circumstances, wherein the repelling power is destroyed, and the attractive power again manifests itself. Now it is manifest, that the power which originally repelled the fixed air was the action of fire; and consequently, while the quicklime refuses to attract fixed air, we must conclude that it is the same action which prevents the union. Quicklime, therefore, is not a pure earth, but a combination of a pure earth with fire; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> as chalk, or limestone uncalcined, is not a pure earth, but a combination of a pure earth with fixed air. In all chemical trials, then, where quicklime is used, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a> attraction will manifest itself as much as in a combination of different salts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, and acids. Thus, when water is poured on quicklime, the attraction between that element and earth is stronger than the attraction between earth and fire. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> is, that the water expels the fire, just as vitriolic acid poured upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> expels the marine acid. The fire then, having nothing with which it can form a chemical combination, becomes sensible to the touch, first making the lime very hot, and then gradually dissipating in the atmosphere. However, as the water combines with the earth, but in very small quantity, it can only expel the fire from that quantity with which it does combine; and consequently the lime still retains its caustic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, though in a degree somewhat milder than what it was originally. We must also consider, that water itself has a considerable attraction for fire as well as for earth; and the consequence of this must be, that part of the lime will be dissolved in the water, if more of that element is added than what the earth can absorb without losing the form of a dry powder. Hence the origin of lime-water, which is only a small quantity of lime in its caustic state dissolved in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of water. This <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> is owing to the double attraction of fire to earth and water; for as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the water can admit the calcined earth to that intimate union with itself which is called a chemical combination, the earth must still retain all the causticity which the fire gives it, and dissolve in the water. When the earth is in too large quantity to be thus combined with the water, the latter is only absorbed into the pores of the earth, where by its bulk it splits the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or calcined matter all to pieces, and reduces it to an impalpable powder, expelling a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> quantity of fire from those pores which it now occupies. The water, however, is capable of radically dissolving but a very small portion of calcined earth; and therefore, the same quantity of quicklime will serve for preparing lime-water a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of times over; but at last a large quantity is left, which seems to be quite inert, and has lost the properties of quicklime. Those who have tried the experiment of lixiviating lime with fresh quantities of water till it ceases to be soluble, have fixed the proportion of soluble matter in the lime at about one-third of the whole; but from Dr Black's experiments it appears that quicklime may all be dissolved in water at once, provided the water is in sufficient quantity. Its inactivity, therefore, after repeated affusions of water, must be owing to some change produced by the water; but whether this is owing to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of all the fire it contained by the great quantity of water, or to a supply of fixed air given by the water, has not yet been determined by any experiment. If, instead of pouring <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water upon quicklime, we pour that which is already heated, the absorption is much less complete; because the water, having already a superfluous quantity of heat, is resisted by that which is contained in the quicklime in a latent state; and hence it is a general observation, that hot water is less proper for slaking lime than cold. But if we pour on any acid upon quicklime which contains a great quantity of fire in a latent state, and has likewise a violent attraction for the earth, a much greater degree of heat is produced than with simple water. With the vitriolic acid, indeed, this is not so well perceived, if the common calcareous earths are made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of; because their insolubility in this acid diminishes its effect; but if, instead of these earths, we take magnesia newly calcined, the heat is so great, that the aqueous vapour, not having time to evaporate slowly, is driven off with a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a>. If the common calcareous earths, well calcined, are dissolved in the nitrous acid, a most violent degree of heat is produced; more indeed than in any other case where a liquid is concerned; for the nitrous acid itself contains a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of latent heat; the quicklime does the same; and by the intimate union of the earth with the acid, all this latent heat, at least a great part of it, both in the quicklime and spirit of nitre, is displaced, and attacks the aqueous fluid as being nearest to it; from whence it is dissipated in the air, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a>- Quicklime, absorbed by the neighbouring substances. The same thing happens, only in a less degree, when the marine acid is employed. When quicklime is mixed with a solution of mild alkali, a double decomposition, and two new compositions, take place. The quicklime may be considered as a combination of earth and fire, while the alkali in the present case acts as a combination of salt and air. These two substances, therefore, are no sooner put into such circumstances as enable them to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> on each other, than the quicklime attracts the air from the alkali, and gives its own fire in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, which the alkali takes up, and thus is rendered caustic, while the quicklime becomes mild. Nevertheless, though the alkali here seems to have the greater attraction for fire, and the quicklime for air; yet it appears, that the alkali is by no means capable of keeping the fire which it has imbibed for any length of time; for no sooner is it exposed to the action of the air, than it parts with the fire which it had imbibed, regains its air, and becomes mild. This, however, in all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> is owing to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> solubility in water while in a caustic state; for quicklime itself when dissolved in water very easily regains its fixed air, nay, even more than it contains in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state. See the article SALT. On the whole, then, the properties of quicklime may be explained in a very easy manner on Dr Black's principle of latent heat. That heat consists in a latent state in quicklime, as well as in vapour, we have incontestible proofs; because, in all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where quicklime changes its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and becomes more mild, a degree of heat is produced, and which is always proportionate to the change made on the quicklime. In the making of quicklime, therefore, the air is expelled, and a proportional quantity of fire enters; in dissolving it in an acid, flaking, &c., an acid, air, or water, expels part of the heat, which then becomes sensible. By long exposure to the air, the heat gradually evaporates; the fixed air resumes its place; and the quicklime, being thus increased in bulk, embraces those bodies very closely which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> nearest to it, infomuch, that, when mixed with sand and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, it will harden with them almost into the solidity of a rock. See CEMENT and MORTAR. When mixed with animal or vegetable substances, it destroys or decomposes them both by the action of its internal heat, and by its attraction for a certain acid contained in the animal substances, and an oily matter in the vegetables; and hence its property of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> cloth, though its attraction for the oily matter just mentioned makes it an excellent whitener when properly applied. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLEACHING">BLEACHING</a>.

QUICKSILVER

Pages 277-278
or MERCURY, a metallic substance, fluid, except in extreme degrees of cold, of a shining white appearance, very much resembling silver; its specific gravity the greatest of all metals next to gold and platinum. For the method of extracting this metal from its ore, see METALLURGY, p. 4057. For the various preparations from it, see CHEMISTRY, no 153, 205, 250, 414, and VOL. IX. (a) Pure mercury may also be distinguished from that which is very impure, by this circumstance, viz. that a mixture of lead or tin, at least, very much diminishes its attraction of cohesion. For, when pure mercury is contained in a glass or earthen vessel, there will be a hollow space between the metal and the vessel; whereas, if there be lead or tin in it, the whole surface, even to the place of contact with the vessel, will be perfectly level. Mercury may easily be cleansed from those extraneous matters which adhere only slightly to it, by making it pass through a new, clean, and close cloth, vol. iv. and afterwards by heating it. When mercury has been thus purified, and is free from all metallic alloy, it is considerably fluid. A phosphoric light is produced by shaking in the dark such mercury contained in a barometer. Its integument parts, like those of melted metals, seem mutually to attract each other, and always acquire a convex or spherical form when they touch bodies with which they have no tendency to unite. A new method of purifying quicksilver from lead has been discovered by Dr Priestley; of which he gives the following account. "I take a glass phial with a ground stopper (such being generally pretty strong) containing 10 or 12 ounces of water, and fill about one-fourth of it with the foul quicksilver; then, putting in the stopper, I hold it inverted with both my hands, and shake it violently, generally striking the hand that supports it against my thigh. When I have given it 20 or 30 strokes in this manner, I take out the stopper, and blow into the phial with a pair of bellows; which I do in order to change the air that has become in part phlogisticated, and knowing that the purer the air is the faster the process advances. "After a short time, if the mercury be very foul, the surface will not only become black, but a great quantity of the upper part of it will be, as it were, coagulated, so as to be easily separated from the rest. I therefore invert the phial; and covering the mouth of it with my finger, let out all the mercury that will flow easily, and put the black coagulated part into a cup by itself. This I press repeatedly with the end of my finger, till I make a complete separation of the running mercury from the black powder; and putting the powder by itself, I pour back the mercury to the rest of the mass out of which it was taken, in order to be agitated with it again. "This process I repeat till I find that no more black matter can be separated; and it is not a little remarkable, that the operator will be at no loss to know when the process is completed. For the same quantity of lead seems to come out of it in equal times of agitation, and consequently the whole becomes pure at once. Also, whereas, while the lead was in the mercury, it felt, as I may say, like soft clay, the moment the lead is separated from it, it begins to rattle as it is shaken, so that any person in the room may perceive when it has been agitated enough (a). "That the mercury is made quite pure by this process I ascertained by distillation. For having distilled in a glass vessel a large quantity of quicksilver, in which both lead and tin had been purposely dissolved, and which had only been agitated in this manner afterwards, I found nothing more than a light whitish stain on the bottom of the retort. "When a quantity of the black powder is procured, it Quicksilver: it is very easy, by distillation, to separate the mercury from the calx; and I do not know a readier method of procuring the calx of lead, or tin, and perhaps the calx of other metals also. The quantity of black mercurial powder is very considerable in proportion to the lead or tin mixed with it; though it is not easy to ascertain this with exactness, because, in endeavouring to separate the powder from the running mercury, a good deal of it is, by mere trituration, converted into running mercury; and I do not know but that, in time, the whole might be restored by this means, and the calx of lead, &c. be got quite pure. However, from the following experiments it will be seen what proportion they generally bear to each other, after a tolerably careful separation. It will be seen also, that when all the quicksilver that was converted into black powder is expelled from lead or tin by heat, there will remain more weight of the calx than there was of the metal; as might be expected. But as I applied more heat than was necessary to separate the quicksilver, a good deal of the air, and whatever else contributes to the additional weight of the calx, i.e., no doubt, expelled with it. Having mixed 1 dwt. of lead with about five pounds of quicksilver, I expelled it all by agitation, in the method described above; when, weighing the black powder, it was found to be 1 oz. 10 dwt. 5 gr. Some particles of the running mercury being, however, still visible in it. When the quicksilver was expelled by heat, the calx of the lead appeared in the form of a brownish powder, and weighed 1 dwt. 5 gr. Having mixed 1 dwt. of tin with the abovementioned quantity of quicksilver, and having expelled it again by agitation, the black powder, with some small globules of quicksilver mixed with it, weighed 2 oz. 1 dwt. 5 gr. and the calx, which was a tolerably white powder, weighed 1 dwt. 7 gr. The separation of tin from quicksilver by agitation is not effected near so soon as lead. It requires at least four times the labour. It also requires proportionally more time to separate the black powder from the thick amalgam, in the manner described above. Quicksilver is separated from lead or tin when the mass is agitated in water, as well as in air; but it seems to require more time. In this process it is also easily perceived when all the base metal is expelled; the phenomena of the agitation of this amalgam and of pure mercury in water being very remarkably different. It is even easy to perceive, by this means, in a moment, whether the quicksilver be pure or not. For if it be impure, the water becomes opake the moment the agitation commences; which is by no means the case with pure quicksilver, especially if the water in which it is agitated has not been used for this purpose before. Also, the black matter suspended in the water in which pure quicksilver has been agitated is (except in a case that will be described hereafter) presently deposited; whereas the water in which the amalgam has been agitated does not become clear in several days. It may also be perceived how the quicksilver approaches towards purity, by this deposit being made more or less readily. Also, the phenomena during the agitation in quicksilver these two cases are strikingly different, tho' not easily described in words. More especially, the mixture of quicksilver with lead or tin does not seem to admit the water to mix with it; whereas pure quicksilver, by violent agitation, may be so thoroughly mixed with the water, that it will sometimes be several seconds after the agitation is discontinued, before it have entirely disengaged itself from the water; and in doing this it exhibits a very pleasing spectacle. By this means, as in the process without water, it may be perceived at once when the separation of the base metal and the mercury is completely effected. Having a large quantity of water made very black with the agitation of a mixture of quicksilver and lead, I agitated a quantity of common air in it a long time, and let it stand several days; but the air was not sensibly injured by this means; so that though this water and the calcined amalgam suspended in it do contain phlogiston, it is not by this means imparted to the air. I evaporated a pint of the distilled water in which quicksilver and tin had been agitated, and which had stood till it was quite transparent, when a white sediment remained, but it did not weigh more than a few grains. By long agitation in water, the purest quicksilver will be converted into a black powder. The process succeeds best when as much water is used as is three or four times the bulk of quicksilver. This black matter, however, is not permanent, but becomes running mercury by being merely exposed to the air, without trituration, or any other kind of operation. Spirit of wine answers the purpose as well as water; and the appearance seems to be occasioned by a small quantity of superfluous phlogiston adhering to the metal. Quick-match, among artillery men, a kind of combustible preparation formed of three cotton strands drawn into length, and dipped in a boiling composition of white-wine vinegar, saltpetre, and mealed powder. After this immersion it is taken out hot, and laid in a trough where some mealed powder, moistened with spirits of wine, is thoroughly incorporated into the twits of the cotton, by rolling it about therein. Thus prepared, they are taken out separately, and drawn through mealed powder; then hung upon a line till dried, by which they are fit for immediate service. Quid pro quo, in law, q.d. "what for what," denotes the giving one thing of value for another; or the mutual consideration and performance of both parties to a contract. Quid pro quo, or Qui pro quo, is also used in physic to express a mistake in the physician's bill, where quid is wrote for quo, i.e. one thing for another; or of the apothecary in reading quid for quo, and giving the patient the wrong medicine. Hence the term is in the general extended to all blunders or mistakes committed in medicine, either in the prescription, the preparation, or application of remedies. Quiddity, quidditas, a barbarous term used in the schools for essence. The name is derived hence, that it is by the essence of a thing that it is tale quid, such

QUIETISTS

Pages 278-279

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, famous towards the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the last century. They were so called from a kind <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> rest and inaction, which they supposed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> to be in when arrived at that state of perfection which they called the unitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; in which state, they imagined the soul wholly employed in contemplating its God, to whose influence it was entirely submissive, so that he could turn and drive it where and how he would. In this state, the soul no longer needs prayers, hymns, &c., being laid, as it were, in the bosom and between the arms of its God, in whom it is in a manner swallowed up. The Mahometans seem to be no strangers to quietism. They expound a passage in the seventeenth <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the Koran, viz. "O thou soul, which art at rest, return unto thy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, and be of comfort." A soul, which, having, by pursuing the concatenation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> causes, raised itself to the knowledge of that being which produced them and exists of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, rests fully contented, and acquiesces in the knowledge, &c., of him, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of his perfection.

QUILLET

Pages 279-279

an eminent Latin poet of the 17th century, was born at Chignon, in Touraine, and practised physic there with reputation: but having declared against the pretended possession of the nuns of Loudun, in a manuscript treatise, the original of which is now in the library of the Sorbonne, he was obliged to retire into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he became secretary to the marshal d'Estrees, the French <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> at Rome. In 1655 Quillet having published in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> a Latin poem, entitled Callipedia, under the name of Calvinius Latius, he there inserted some verses against the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> Mazarine and his family; but that cardinal making him some gentle reproaches, he retrenched what related to the cardinal, in another edition, and dedicated it to him, Mazarine having, before it was printed, gave him an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. He died in 1661, aged 59, after having given Menage all his writings, and 500 crowns to pay the expense of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> them; but the abbe took the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and papers, and published none of them. His Callipedia, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the Art of getting beautiful Children, has been translated into English <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>.

QUILLS

Pages 279-279

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> feathers taken out of the end of the wing of a goose, crow, &c. Quills are denominated from the order in which they are fixed in the wing, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third quills being the best for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, as they have the largest and roundest barrels. Crow-quills are chiefly used for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>. In order to harden a quill that is soft, thrust the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> into hot ashes, stirring it till it is soft, and then taking it out, press it almost flat upon your knee with the back of a penknife, and afterwards reduce it to a roundness with your fingers. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> you have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to harden, set <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> over the fire, and while it is <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> put in a handful of quills, the barrels only, for a minute, and then lay them by.

QUIN

Pages 279-279

a celebrated performer on the English stage, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1693. He was intended for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>; but preferring Shakespear to the Statutes at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, he on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, when it was necessary for him to do something with himself, appeared on the stage at Drury-lane. In 1720, he first displayed his comic powers in the character of Falstaff, and soon after appeared to as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage in Sir John Brute; but it was upon Booth's quitting the stage, that Quin appeared to full advantage, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Cato. He <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a favourite performer until the year 1748, when on some dispute between him and Mr Rich the manager, he retired to Bath, and only came up annually to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> for the benefit of his friend Ryan; until the loss of two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> spoilt his utterance for the stage. While Mr Quin continued upon the stage, he constantly kept <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with the greatest geniuses of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was well known to Pope and Swift; and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Chesterfield frequently invited him to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>: but there was none for whom he entertained a higher esteem, than for the ingenious Mr Thomson, to whom he made himself known by an act of generosity, that does the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to his character, and of which we have given a particular account in Mr Thomson's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Mr Quin's judgment in the English <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> recommended him to his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> highness Frederick <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, who appointed him to instruct his children in speaking and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> with a graceful propriety; and Quin being informed of the elegant manner in which his present majesty delivered his first gracious speech from the throne, he cried out in a kind of ecstacy, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AY">Ay</a>—I taught the boy to speak!" Nor did his majesty forget his old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>; for, soon after his accession to the throne, he gave orders, without any application being made to him, that a genteel pension should be paid to Mr Quin during his life. Mr Quin, indeed, was not in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> need of this royal benefaction; for as he was never married, and had none but distant relations, he funk 2000l. which was half his fortune, in an annuity, for which he obtained 200l. a-year; and with about 2000l. more in the funds, lived in a decent manner during the latter part of his life at Bath, from whence he carried on a regular correspondence with Mr Garrick, and generally paid a visit to his friends in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> once a-year, when he constantly passed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> two at Mr Garrick's villa at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPTON">Hampton</a>. He died of a fever in 1766.

QUINARIUS

Pages 279-279

in antiquity, a little Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, equal to half the denarius. It was properly the Roman halfpenny.

QUINAUT

Pages 279-279

a celebrated French poet, born of a good family at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1635. He cultivated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> from his infancy, and 16 dramatic pieces of his were acted between the year 1653 and 1666. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> Quinaut was not so much devoted to poetry, but that he applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and made his fortune by marrying the widow of a rich merchant to whom he had been useful in his profession. Quinaut afterwards turned his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the composing of operas, which were set to music by the famous Lully; and Lully was charmed with a poet whose verses were not too nervous to yield to the capricious <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> of music. He died in 1688, after having enjoyed a handsome pension from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. for many years: and we are told he was extremely penitent in his last illness, for all those of his compositions which tended to inspire <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>.

QUINCUNX

Pages 280-280

in Roman antiquity, denotes anything that consists of five-twelfths of another; but particularly of the ar. Quincunx Order, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>, is a plantation of trees disposed originally in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> consisting of five trees, one at each corner, and a fifth in the middle; which disposition, repeated again and again, forms a regular <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, wood, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> wilderness.

QUINDECAGON

Pages 280-280

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, a plain <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> with 15 sides and 15 <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>.

QUINDECIMVIRI

Pages 280-280

in Roman antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of 15 magistrates, whose business it was to preside over the sacrifices. They were also the interpreters of the Sibyl's books; which, however, they never consulted but by an express order of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>.

QUINQUAGENARIUS

Pages 280-280

in Roman antiquity, an officer who had the command of 50 men. QUINQUAGESIMA <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, Shrove Sunday, so called as being about the 50th <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> before Easter.

QUINQUATRIA

Pages 280-280

in Roman antiquity, festivals celebrated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, with much the same ceremonies as the Panathenæa were at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>.

QUINQUENNALIS

Pages 280-280

in Roman antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> in the colonies and municipal cities of that empire, who had much the same office as the ædile at Rome.

QUINQUEREMIS

Pages 280-280

in the naval <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, a name given to a galley which had five rows of oars. They divided their vessels in general into monocrota and polycrota. The former had only one tier of rowers; the latter had several tiers of them, from two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> three, up to 20, 30, or even 40; for such a vessel we have an account of in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Philopater, which required no less than 4000 men to row it. Meibom has taken off from the imaginary improbability of there ever having been such a vessel, by reducing the enormous height supposed necessary for such a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of rows of oars and men to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> them, by finding a better way of placing the men than others had thought of. The quinqueremes of the ancients had 420 men in each; 300 of which were rowers, and the rest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. The Roman fleet at Melfina consisted of 330 of these ships; and the Carthaginian, at Lilybeum, of 350 of the same size. Each vessel was 150 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. Thus 130,000 men were contained in the one, and 150,000 in the other, with the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> necessary for such expeditions as they were intended for. This gives so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> an idea of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> naval armaments, that some have questioned the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; but we find it related by Polybius, an historian too authentic to be questioned, and who expresses his wonder at it while he relates it.

QUINQUEVIRI

Pages 280-280

in Roman antiquity, an order of five priests, peculiarly appointed for the sacrifices to the dead, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> celebrating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EREBUS">Erebus</a>. QUINQUINA. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CINCHONA">Cinchona</a>.

QUINTESSENCE

Pages 280-280

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> consisting of the essential <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of some vegetable substance, mixed and incorporated with spirit of wine. Quintessence, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCHEMY">alchemy</a>, is a mysterious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, signifying the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> last and highest essence of power in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> body.

QUINTILE

Pages 280-280

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, an aspect of the pla- nets when they are 72 degrees distant from one another, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a fifth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>.

QUINTILIANS

Pages 280-280

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heretics, thus called from their prophetess Quintilia. In this sect the women were admitted to perform the sacerdotal and episcopal functions. They attributed extraordinary gifts to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">Eve</a> for having first eaten of the tree of knowledge; told <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> things of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> the mother of Moles, as having been a prophetess, &c. They added, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> the deacon had four daughters who were all prophetesses and were of their sect. In these assemblies it was usual to see the virgins entering in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> robes, perforating prophetesses.

QUINTILLIANUS

Pages 280-280

a celebrated Latin orator, and the most judicious critic of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was a native of Calagurris, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALAHORRA">Calahorra</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Domitius Afer, who died in the year 59. He taught <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> at Rome for 20 years, with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause; and not only laid <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> rules for speaking, but exhibited his eloquence at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>. Some authors imagine, but with little foundation, that he arrived to the consulship; but it is more certain, that he was preceptor to the grandsons of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Domitian's sister. There is still extant his excellent <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled Institutiones Oratoriae, which is a treatise of rhetoric in 12 books; where his precepts, judgment, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, are justly admired. These institutions were found entire by Poggius, in an old tower of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Gal, and not in a grocer's shop in Germany as some authors have imagined. There is also attributed to Quintilian a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> De causis corruptae eloquentiae; but it is more <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> ascribed to Tacitus. The best editions of Quintilian's works are those of Mr Obreicht, published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a> in 2 vols 4to, in 1668, and of M. Capperonier, in folio. There is an English translation by Mr Guthrie. Quintilian had a son of the same name, on whom he bestows great praises. This son ought not to be confounded with Quintilian, the father, or rather the grandfather, of him who is the subject of this article, and who wrote 145 declamations. Ugolin of Parma published the first 136 in the 15th century; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> others were published in 1563 by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Ayraut, and afterwards by Peter Pithou in 1580. There have also been 19 other declamations, printed under the name of Quintilian the Orator; but, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Voilias, they were written neither by that orator nor his grandfather.

QUINTIN

Pages 280-281

a considerable town of France, in Brittany, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, and a fine castle. It is seated in a valley on the river Goy, near a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> forest of the same name. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 51. N. Lat. 48. 26. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUINTIN_MATSYS">QUINTIN Matsys</a>, also called the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FARRIER">Farrier</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, famous for being transformed, by the force of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, from a blacksmith to a painter. He had followed the trade of a blacksmith and farrier near 20 years; when falling in love with a painter's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, who was very handsome, and disliked nothing but his trade, he quitted it, and betook himself to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, in which he made a very uncommon progress. He was a diligent and careful imitator of ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and succeeded better in representing the defects than the beauties of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Some historical performances of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> deserve commendation, particularly a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">Descent</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">Cross</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> at Antwerp; but his best-known Quintinie known <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> is that of the two Misers in the gallery at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>. He died in 1529.

QUINTINIE

Pages 281-281

a celebrated French gardener, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POITIERS">Poitiers</a> in 1626. He was brought up to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and acquitted himself so well at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, as to acquire the esteem of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. M. Tamboneau, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the chamber of accounts, engaged him to undertake the preceptorship of his only son, which Quintinie executed entirely to his satisfaction; applying his leisure hours to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of writers on <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, to which he had a strong inclination. He gained new lights by attending his pupil to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; for all the gardens about Rome being open to him, he failed not to add practice to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>. On his return to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, M. Tamboneau gave up the management of his garden entirely to him; and Quintinie applied so closely to it, that he became famous all over France. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. erected a new office purposely for him, that of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> fruit and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> gardens; and these gardens, while he lived, were the admiration of the curious. He lived to a good old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, though we learn not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; his Directions for the Management of Fruit and Kitchen Gardens, are esteemed all over <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

QUINTUS CALABER

Pages 281-281

a Greek poet, who wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> Supplement to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s Iliad, in 14 books, in which a relation is given of the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Hector to the destruction of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. It is conjectured, from his style and manner, that he lived in the fifth century. Nothing certain can be collected either concerning his person <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His poem was first made known by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> Bessarion, who discovered it in St Nicholas's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OTRANTO">Otranto</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>; from whence the author was named Quintus Calaber. He was first published at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> by Aldus, but it is not said in what year. QUINTUS CURTIUS. See Curtius.

QUIRINALIA

Pages 281-281

in antiquity, a feast celebrated among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>.

QUIRITES

Pages 281-281

in Roman antiquity. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the agreement entered into by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> and Tatius <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Sabines, Rome was to retain its name, taken from Romulus; and the people were to be called Quirites, from Cures, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town of the Sabines, a name used in all public addresses to the Roman people.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DION">Dion</a>. Hal. says, that each particular citizen was to be called Romanus, and the collective body of them Quirites; yet it appears by this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> form of words used at funerals, Ollus Quiris letho datus est, that each private citizen was also called Quiris. The origin of the word Quirites, which was at first peculiar to the Sabines, and became, in Romulus's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the general name of the inhabitants of Rome, has been much sought for; and the most probable account antiquity gives us of them, is this. The word Quiris, according to Plutarch (p. 36.) and some others, signified in the Sabine <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, both a dart, and a warlike deity armed with a dart. It is uncertain whether the god gave name to the dart, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the dart to the god. But be that as it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, this Quiritis, or Quirinus, was either <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, or some other god of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and the worship of Quiris <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in Rome all Romulus's reign: but after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he was honoured with the name Quirinus, and took the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the god Quiritis.

QUIRK

Pages 281-281

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, a piece of ground taken out of any regular ground-plot, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>: thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the ground-plot were <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, a piece taken out of a corner to make a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> or yard, &c. is called a quirk.

QUIT-RENT

Pages 281-281

(Quietus Redditu, i.e. "quiet rent.") is a certain small rent payable by the tenants of manors, in token of subjection, and by which the tenant goes quiet and free. In <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> records it is called <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> rent, because paid in silver <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, to distinguish it from rent corn, &c.

QUOAD HOC

Pages 281-281

is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in the pleadings and arguments of lawyers; being as much as to say, As to this thing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> is so and so.

QUOIN

Pages 281-281
or Coin, on board a ship, a wedge fastened on the deck close to the breach of the carriage of a gun, to keep it firm up to the ship's side. Cantic quoins are short three-legged quoins put between casks to keep them steady.

QUOINS

Pages 281-281

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, denote the corners of bricks <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> walls. The word is particularly used for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> in the corners of brick buildings. When these stand out beyond the brick-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, their edges being chamfered off, they are called rustic quoins.

QUORUM

Pages 281-281

a word frequently mentioned in our statutes, and in commissions both of justices of the peace and others. It is thus called from the words of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, quorum A. B. unum esse volumus. For an example, where a commission is directed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> persons, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> to any three of them, whereof A. B. and C. D. are to be two; in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, they are said to be of the quorum, because the rest cannot proceed without them: so a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace and quorum is one without whom the rest of the justices in some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> cannot proceed.

QUOTIDIAN

Pages 281-281

anything which happens every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Hence, when the paroxysms of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGUE">ague</a> recur every day, it is called a quotidian ague.

QUOTIENT

Pages 281-282

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> resulting from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of a greater number by a smaller; and which shows how often the smaller is contained in the greater, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> how often the divisor is contained in the dividend. The word is formed from the Latin, quoties; q.d. How often is such a number contained in such another? In division, as the divisor is to the dividend, so is unity to the quotient.—Thus the quotient of 12 divided by 3 is 4; which is thus disposed, 3) 12 (4 quotient. R R, or r, a liquid consonant, being the 17th <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. It's found is formed by a guttural extrusion of the breath vibrated through the mouth, with a fort of quivering <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the tongue drawn from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and cannulated with the tip a little elevated towards the palate. In Greek words it is frequently aspirated with an h after it, as in rhapody, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, &c. otherwise it is always followed by a vowel at the beginning of words and syllables. In the notes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, R or RO signifies Roma; R.C. Romana civitas; R.G.C. rei gerendae causa; R.F.E.D. recte factum & dictum; R.G.F. regis filius; R.P. res publica, or Romani principes; and R.R.R.F.F.F. res Romana ruet ferro, fane, flamma. Used as a numeral, R anciently stood for 80; and with a dash over it, thus R̄, for 80,000; but the Greek ρ, or ρ, signified too. In the prescriptions of physicians, R or R stands for recipe, i.e., "take."

RABBETTING

Pages 282-282

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARPENTRY">carpentry</a>, the planning, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> of channels or grooves in boards, &c. In ship-carpentry, it signifies the letting in of the planks of the ship into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>; which, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> and run of a ship is hollowed away, that the planks may join the clover.

RABBI

Pages 282-282
or RABBINS, a title which the Pharisees and doctors of the law among the Jews assumed, and literally signifies masters or excellents. There were several gradations before they arrived at the dignity of a rabbin; which was not conferred till they had acquired the profoundest knowledge of the law and the traditions. It does not however appear that there was any fixed age or previous examination necessary; but when a man had distinguished himself by his skill in the written and oral law, and passed thro' the subordinate degrees, he was saluted a rabbin by the public voice. Among the modern Jews, for near 700 years past, the learned men retain no other title than that of rabbi, or rabbins; they have great respect paid them, have the first places or seats in their synagogues, determine all matters of controversy, and frequently pronounce upon civil affairs; they have even a power to excommunicate the disobedient.

RABBINISTS

Pages 282-282

among the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Jews, an appellation given to the doctrine of the rabbins concerning traditions, in opposition to the Caraites who reject all traditions. See CARAITE.

RABBIT

Pages 282-283

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEPUS">LEPUS</a>. The buck rabbits, like our boar cats, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> kill the young ones <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they can get at them; and the does in the warrens prevent this, by covering their stocks, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> nests, with gravel or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which they <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to artificially up with the hinder <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their bodies, that it is hard to find them out. They never suckle their young ones at any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> than early in the morning and late at night; and always, for eight or ten days, close up the hole at the mouth of the nest, in this careful manner, when they go out. After this they begin to leave a small opening, which they increase by degrees; till at length, when they are about three weeks old, the mouth of the hole is left wholly open that they may go out; for they are at that time grown big enough to take care of themselves, and to feed on grass. People who keep rabbits tame for profit, breed them in hutches; but these must be kept very neat and clean, else they will be always subject to diseases. Care must be taken also to keep the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUCKS">bucks</a> and does apart till the latter have <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> kindled; then they are to be turned to the bucks again, and to remain with them till they shun and run from them. The general <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> for the choosing of tame rabbits bits is, to pick the largest and fairest; but the breeder should remember that the skins of the silver-haired ones sell better than any other. The food of the tame rabbits may be colewort and cabbage-leaves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARROTS">carrots</a>, parsnips, apple-rinds, green corn, and vetches, in the time of the year; also vine-leaves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, oats, and oatmeal, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>-thistles, sow-thistles, and the like: but with these moist foods they must always have a proportionable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the dry foods, as hay, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, oats, bran, and the like, otherwise they will grow pot-bellied, and die. Bran and grains mixed together have been also found to be very good food. In winter they will eat hay, oats, and chaff, and these may be given them three times a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but when they eat green things, it must be observed that they are not to drink at all, for it would throw them into a droopy. At all other times a very little drink serves their turn, but that must always be fresh. When any green herbs, or grapes, are cut for their food, care must be taken that there be no <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMLOCK">hemlock</a> among it; for though they will eat this greedily among other things when offered to them, yet it is sudden <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a> to them. Rabbits are subject to two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> infirmities. First, the rot, which is caused by giving them too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a quantity of greens, or from giving them fresh gathered with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEW">dew</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> hanging in drops upon them. It is over-moisture that always causes this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. The greens therefore are always to be given dry; and a sufficient quantity of hay, or other dry food, intermixed with them, to take up the abundant moisture of their juices. On this account the very best food that can be given them, is the shortest and sweetest hay that can be got, of which one load will serve two couples a year; and out of this stock of 200, 200 may be eat in the family, 200 sold to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, and a sufficient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> kept in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of accidents. The other general disease of these creatures is a sort of madness: this may be known by their wallowing and tumbling about with their heels upwards, and hopping in an odd manner into their boxes. This distemper is supposed to be owing to the rankness of their feeding; and the general cure is the keeping them low, and giving them the prickly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> called tare-thistle to eat. The general computation of males and females is, that one buck-rabbit will serve for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> does; some allow 10 to one buck; but those who go beyond this, always suffer for it in their breed. The wild rabbits are either to be taken by small cur-dogs, or by spaniels bred up to the sport; and the places of hunting those who struggle from their burrows, is under close hedges or bushes, or among corn-fields and fresh pastures. The owners <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to course them with small greyhounds; and though they are seldom killed this way, yet they are driven back to their burrows, and are prevented from being a prey to others. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> method is by nets called purse-nets, and ferrets. The ferret is sent into the hole to fetch them out; and the purse-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NET">net</a> being spread over the hole, takes them as they come out. The ferrets mouths must be muffled, and then the rabbit gets no harm. For the more certain taking of them, it may not be improper to pitch up a hay-net or two, at a small distance from the burrows that are intended to be hunted: thus very few of the number that are attempted will escape. Some who have not ferrets <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> the rabbits out of their holes with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> brimstone and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORPIMENT">orpiment</a>. This certainly brings them out into the nets: but then it is a very troublesome and offensive method; and is very detrimental to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, as no rabbit will, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time, afterwards come near the burrows which have been fumed with those stinking ingredients. The testicle of a rabbit is a very good object for examining the structure of this part of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> in animals. The whole substance of the testicle in this animal is made up of vessels, which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in round folds in the manner of the smaller intestines: but then both ends of each roll meet at their insertion, which seems to be made into the ductus nervosus; and every one of these little rolls is curiously embroidered with other vessels, which, from their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, appear to be <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> and veins. The several little rolls lie in ranges, disposed with an uniformity which is very agreeable to the eye. Every one of these rolls is not a single and entire tube, but each consists of several tubes, beside the veins and arteries which embroider it. This is best distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> one of the rolls transversely, and then examining the cut end with a glass, which will appear to be made up of the cut and open ends of four, five, or more <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> tubes, which together form the roll, or single tube, as it appears to the eye, being all wrapped up in one common and very thin membrane. These are so tender that they cannot be explicated and viewed distinctly, as De Graeff tells us those of the testicles of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAT">rat</a> and of some other animals may. These however, as well as the others, are only made up of a congeries of vessels, and the liquors, which are their contents, without any intermediate substance, or anything of that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENCHYMA">parenchyma</a> which many authors have talked of. The testicles of a bull have the greatest appearance of a fleshy texture of those of any known animal; yet even these afford no particle of parenchyma, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, when examined by glasses in any sort of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, whether boiled, raw, soaked in spirits, or in whatever other state. The testicles of various animals are very variously composed, but all in this general manner of vessels variously rolled and folded together; and even the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> testicles are of the same sort; being composed solely of rolls of vessels, without any intermediate substance, be it called by whatever name, but only consisting of vessels and their liquors.

RABELLAIS

Pages 282-282

a French writer famous for his facetiousness, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINON">Chinon</a> in Touraine, about the year 1483. He was first a Franciscan friar; but quitting his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, studied physic at Montpelier, where he took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. It is said, that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> du Pratt having abolished the privileges of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of physic at Montpelier by a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, Rabelais had the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to make him revoke what he had done; and that those who were made doctors of that university wear Rabelais's robe, which is there held in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, he came to Rome, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of physician in ordinary to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> John du Bellay bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. Rabelais is said to have used the freedom to jeer pope Paul III. to his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>. He had quitted his religious connections for the sake of leading a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> more agreeable to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; but renewed them on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> journey to Rome, when he obtained, in 1536, a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> to qualify him for holding <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> benefices; and, by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his friend cardinal John du Bellay, he was received as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> canon in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Maur near Paris. His profound knowledge in physic rendered him doubly useful; he being as ready, and at least as well qualified, to prescribe for the body as for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; but as he was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and humour, many ridiculous things are laid to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, of which he was quite innocent. He published several things; but his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> performance is a strange incoherent <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>, called the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Gargantua and Pantagruel; being a satire upon priests, popes, fools, and knaves of all kinds. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> contains a wild <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> profusion of wit, learning, obscenity, low conceits, and arrant nonsense; hence the shrewdness of his satire, in some places where he is to be understood, gains him <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> for as good meanings where no meaning is discoverable. Some allusions may undoubtedly have been so temporary and local as to be now quite lost, but it is too much to conclude thus in favour of every unintelligible rhapsody: for we are not without English writers of great talents, whose sportive geniuses have betrayed them into puerilities, no less incoherent at the times of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, than those of Rabelais appear above two centuries after. He died about 1553.

RACE

Pages 283-285

in general, signifies running with others in order to obtain a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>, either on foot, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> by riding on horseback, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>, &c. The race was one of the exercises among the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Grecian games, which was performed in a course containing 125 paces; and those who contended in these foot-races were frequently clothed in armour. Chariot and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races also made a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of these ancient games. Races were known in England in very early times. Fitz-Stephen, who wrote in the days of Henry II. mentions the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> delight that the citizens of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> took in the diversion. But by his words, it appears not to have been designed for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>, but merely to have sprung from a generous emulation of showing a superior skill in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a>. Races appear to have been in vogue in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, and to have been carried to such excess as to injure the fortunes of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. The famous Racine, famous George <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> is recorded to have wasted more of his estate than any of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>; and chiefly by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to horse-races, tiltings, and other expensive diversions. It is probable that the parsimonious queen did not approve of it; for races are not among the diversions exhibited at Kenelworth by her favourite <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>. In the following reign, were places allotted for the sport: <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROYDON">Croydon</a> in the south, and Garterly in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, were celebrated courses. Camden also says, that in 1607 there were races near <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and the prize was a little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELL">bell</a>. Race, in genealogy, a lineage or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> from father to son. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">DESCENT</a>. RACINE (John) of the French academy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of France in the generality of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOULINS">Moulins</a>, and secretary to his majesty, was born at Ferre-Milon in 1639. He had a fine genius for the Belles Lettres, and became one of the first poets of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He produced his Thébaide when but very young; and afterwards other pieces, which met with great success, though they appeared when Corneille was in his highest reputation. In his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a>, however, he did not fail to meet with all that opposition which envy and cabal are ever ready to set up against a superior genius. It was partly owing to a chagrin from this circumstance that he took a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to quit the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> for ever; although his genius was still in full vigour, being not more than 38 years of age. But he had also imbibed in his infancy a deep <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and this, though it had been smothered for a while by his connections with the theatre, and particularly with the famous actress Champmele, whom he greatly loved, and by whom he had a son, now at length broke out, and bore <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> all before it.
