In the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, he resolved not only to write no more plays, but to do a rigorous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> for those he had written; and he actually formed a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of becoming a Carthusian friar. His <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> however, a good <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> wiser than he, advised him to think more moderately, and to take <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> more suitable to his character. He put him upon marrying, and settling in the world; with which proposal this humble and tractable penitent complied; and immediately took to wife the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a treasurer of France for Amiens, by whom he had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> children. He had been admitted a member of the French academy in 1673, in the room of La Mothe le Vayer deceased; but spoiled the speech he had made upon that occasion, by pronouncing it with too much timidity. In 1677, he was nominated with Boileau, with whom he was ever in strict friendship, to write the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV.; and the public expected great things from two writers of their distinction, but were disappointed. Boileau and Racine, after having for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> laboured at this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, perceived that it was entirely opposite to their genius. He spent the latter years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in composing a history of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Port-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a>, the place of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; which however, though finely drawn up, as many have asserted, has not been published. Too great <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>, say his friends, but more properly an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPOTENCE">impotence</a> of spirit, shortened the days of this poet. Though he had conversed much with the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, he had not learned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, which is usually learned there, of disguising his real sentiments. Having drawn up a well-reasoned and well-written memorial upon the miseries of the people, and the means of relieving them, he one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENT">lent</a> it to Madam de <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAINTENON">Maintenon</a> to read; when the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> coming in, and demanding what and whose it was, commended the zeal of Racine, but disapproved of his meddling with things that did not concern him: and said with an angry tone, "Because he knows how to make good verses, does he think he knows every thing? And would he be a minister of state, because he is a great poet?" These words hurt Racine greatly; he conceived dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the king's displeasure; and his chagrin and fears brought on a fever, of which he died the 22d of April 1699. The king, who was sensible of his great merit, and always loved him, sent often to him in his illness; and finding after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> that he had more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> than <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, settled a handsome pension upon his family. There is nothing in the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> written with more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and elegance than his pieces in prose. Besides his plays several of his letters have been published; he also wrote spiritual songs, epigrams, &c. Racine's works were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1722, in 2 vols 12mo. and the next year a pompous edition was printed in 2 vols quarto. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RACING">Racing</a>, the riding heats for a plate or other premium. The first thing to be considered in this sort of gaming is the choosing a rider; for it is not only necessary that he should be very expert and able, but he must also be very honest. He must have a very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> seat, his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> being turned close to the saddle skirts, and held firmly there, and the toes turned inwards, so that the spurs may be turned outward from the horse's belly; his left-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> governing the horse's mouth, and his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> the whip. During the whole time of the race, he must take care to fit firm in the saddle, without wavering or standing up in the stirrups. Some jockeys fancy this is a becoming seat; but it is certain, that all motions of this kind do really inconvenience the horse. In spurring the horse, it is not to be done by sticking the calves of the legs close to the horse's sides, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were intended to press the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> out of his body; but, on the contrary, the toes are to be turned a little outwards; that the heels being brought in, the spurs may <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> be brought to touch the sides. A sharp touch of this kind <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be of more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> toward the quickening a horse's pace, and will sooner draw blood, than one of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> coarse kicks. The expert jockey will never spur his horse until there is great occasion; and then he will avoid striking him under the fore bowels between the shoulders and girth; this is the tenderest part of a horse, and a touch there is to be reserved for the greatest extremity. As to whipping the horse, it ought always to be done over the shoulder on the near side, except in very hard running and on the point of victory; then the horse is to be struck on the flank with a strong jerk; for the skin is most tender of all there, and most sensible of the lash. When a horse is whipped and spurred, and is at the top of his speed; if he claps his ears in his pole, or whisks his tail, it is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that the jockey heats him him hard, and then he ought to give him as much comfort as he can, by sawing the snaffle backwards and forwards in his mouth; and by that means forcing him to open his mouth, which will give him wind, and be of great service. If there be any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> wind stirring in the time of riding, the artful jockey will let his adversary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, holding hard behind him, till he sees an opportunity of giving a loofe: yet, in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, he must keep so close behind, that the other horse may keep the wind from him: and that he, sitting low, may at once shelter himself under him, and assist the strength of the horse. If the wind happen to be in their back, quite a contrary method is to be taken with it; the expert jockey is to keep directly behind the adversary, that he may have all the advantage of the wind to blow his horse along, as it were, and at the same time intercept it in regard to his adversary. When running on a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> carpet ground, the jockey is to bear his horse as much as the adversary will give him leave, because the horse is naturally more inclined to spend himself on this ground; on the contrary, on deep earths, he may have more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, as he will there spare himself. In riding up-hill the horse is always to be favoured, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> him hard, for fear of running him out of wind; but, in running down-hill, if the horse's feet and shoulders will bear it, and the rider <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> venture his neck, he may have a full loofe. If the horse have the heels of the rest, the jockey must always spare him a little, that he may have a reserve of strength, to make a push at the last <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>. A great deal depends on the jockey's knowing the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the horse that is to run against him; for by managing accordingly, great advantages are to be obtained: thus, if the opposite horse is of a hot and fiery disposition, the jockey is either to run just behind him, or cheek by jowl with him, making a noise with the whip, and by that means forcing him on faster than his rider would have him, and consequently spending him so much the sooner; or else keep just before him, in such a slow gallop, that he may either over-reach, or by treading on the heels of the fore horse endanger tumbling over. Whatever be the ground that the adversary's horse runs worst on, the cunning jockey is to ride the most violently over; that by this means it will often happen, that in following he either stumbles or claps on the back sinews. The several corrections of the hand, the whip, and the spur, are also to be observed in the adversary, and in what manner he makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them; and when it is perceived, by any of the symptoms, of holding down the ears, or whisking the tail, or stretching out the nose like a pig, that the horse is almost blown; the business is to keep him on to this speed, and he will be soon thrown out or distanced. If the horse of the opponent looks dull, it is a sign his strength fails him; and if his flanks <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> much, it is a sign that his wind begins to fail him, and his strength will soon do so too. After every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> for a plate, there must be dry straw, and dry cloths both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and woollen, ready to rub him down all over, after taking off the sweat with what is called a sweat <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>; that is, a piece of an old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> blade, or some such thing. Some advise the sleeping the cloths in urine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a> the day before, and letting them be dried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> for this occasion. After the horse has been well rubbed with these, he should be chafed all over, with cloths wetted in common <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> till the time of starting again. When it is certainly known that the horse is good at the bottom, and will stick at the mark, he should be rid every heat to the best of his performance; and the jockey is, as much as possible, to avoid riding at any particular horse, or staying for any, but to ride out the whole heat with the best speed he can. If, on the contrary, he has a fiery horse to ride, and one that is hard to manage, hard-mouthed, and difficult to be held, he is to be started behind the rest of the horses with all imaginable coolness and gentleness; and when he begins to ride at some command, then the jockey is to put up to the other horses; and if they ride at their ease, and are hard held, they are to be drawn on faster; and if it be perceived that their wind begins to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> hot, and they want a sob, the business is to keep them up to that speed; and when they all are come within three <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> of the post, then is the time to push for it, and use the utmost speed in the creature's power. When the race is over, the horse is to be clothed up and rode home; and immediately on his coming into the stable, the following drink is to be given him. Beat up the yolks of three eggs, and put them into a pint and half of new <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> made warm; let there be added to this three pennyworth of saffron, and three spoonfuls of salad <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and let the whole be given with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>. After this he is to be rubbed well down, and the saddle place rubbed over with warm sack, and the places where the spurs have touched, with a mixture of urine and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and afterwards with a mixture of powder of jet and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> turpentine; after this he should have a feed of rye-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, then a good mash, and at some time after these as much hay and oats as he will eat. His legs after this should be bathed sometimes with a mixture of urine and saltpetre.

RACK

Pages 285-287

an engine of torture, furnished with pulleys, cords, &c. for extorting confession from criminals. Rack, a spirituous liquor made by the Tartars of Tongulla. This kind of rack is made of mare's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, which is left to be four, and afterwards distilled twice <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> thrice between two earthen pots closely stopped; whence the liquor runs through a small wooden pipe. This liquor is more intoxicating than brandy distilled from wine. Rack, or Arack. See ARACK. Various and contradictory accounts have been delivered as to the real subject that gives origin to this fine spirit. The vulgar suppose it to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>; some, the juice of the East <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes; and others, a mixture of the juice of this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANE">cane</a> and of the cocoa tree; finally, some affirm, that it is prepared from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of animals, and other more costly ingredients. The juice of the cocoa-trees and palm-trees is what affords us the finest arracks; but there are many other juices distilled into the same kind of liquors, though though wanting the fine flavour of what is made from these. The manner of making the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRACK">arrack</a> is this. The juice of the trees is not procured in the way of tapping the trees, as we do; but the operator provides himself with a parcel of earthen pots, with bellies and necks, like our ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> bottles; he makes fast a parcel of these to his girdle, and any way else that he commodiously can about him. Thus equipped, he swarms up the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of a cocoa tree; and when he comes to the boughs, he takes out his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off one of the small knots or buttons, he applies the mouth of the bottle to the wound, fastening it to the bough with a bandage; in the same manner he cuts off the other buttons, and fastens on his pots, till the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> is used: this is done in the evenings; and defending from the tree, he leaves things to themselves till the next morning, when climbing up again he takes off the bottles which are mostly filled, and empties the juice into the proper receptacle. This is repeated every night, till there is a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> produced; and the whole being then put together, is left to ferment, which it soon does. When the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> is over, and the liquor, or wash, is grown a little tart, it is put into the still; and a fire being made, the still is suffered to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as what comes over has any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of spirit. The liquor thus procured is the low wine of arrack; and this is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> a liquor, that it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> soon corrupt and spoil, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not distilled again, to separate some of its phlegm: they therefore immediately after pour back this low wine into the still, and rectify it to that very weak kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>-spirit, in which state we find it. The arrack we meet with, notwithstanding its being of a proof test, according to the way of judging by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of bubbles, holds but a fifth, and sometimes but an eighth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a>, or pure spirit; whereas our other spirits, when they show that proof, are generally esteemed to hold one half pure spirit. This shows how very uncertain a way of judging of the strength of spirits, this by the bead or bubble is. And we may from this learn, that it would be much better to have the arrack rectified to the pure alcohol in the East Indies, in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> it would be brought over in one fifth or one eighth part of the room, and might be lowered to its standard with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> here; all that it contains, besides this fifth or eighth part of spirit, being only a poor phlegm, or an acidulated water, valuable only for having been brought from Goa or Batavia. It may appear strange to some, that this spirit should be proof according to the way of judging by the bead or bubble, and yet be so far below the strength which we usually understand to be in proof-spirit. But the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, that this standing crown of bubbles may be owing only to the tenacity of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> that is held in the spirit. Our malt-distillers know very well, that the more oil they work over with the spirit, the stronger proof it will hold, at a somewhat weaker standard of strength than it ought to have; and this case of the arrack shows the fallacy of the other. The finer and more subtle any oil is, the less it refuses to mix with any aqueous menstruum: thus we see that the essential oils of some vegetables, or at least some portion of them, is so fine and fugitive, as to mix without <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> milky, even with water itself, which is the case in many of our simple distilled waters. Hence, it is no wonder, that so fugitive an oil as is contained in that thin and <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a> vegetable juice of which arrack is made, should readily mix with such a mixture as that of one part alcohol and six or eight of water, which, though weak considered as a spirit, is much more likely to retain and embody an oil than simple water alone. The oil of the cocoa is thus suspended imperceptibly in the spirit; and that in such quantity as to give tenacity to the whole, and thereby dispose it to form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROTH">froth</a> or lather at the top when shook, and the bubbles of that froth to hang well together. Sometimes indeed there come over into England, and more frequently into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, arracks that are of the strength of brandy and rum: these chiefly come from the Dutch settlements, and are a piece of frugality of the Dutch to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> freight: it is a wonder the saving spirit had not gone a little farther, and the method of reducing arrack to alcohol been found out on the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>. Besides the common sorts of Goa and Batavia arracks, there are two others less generally known; these are the bitter arrack, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> arrack. The bitter arrack is supposed to have been impregnated with some kind of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEZOAR">bezoar</a>, as that of the porcupine or monkey; which being not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> in the stomachs, as those of other animals, but in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALL">gall</a>-bladder, are of a very strongly bitter taste, and very readily communicate it to other things. Some, on the contrary, are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that there is nothing added to this, but that the taste is owing to the juice of the trees from which the arrack is made; and many think that it is obtained from the juice of that tree which bears the fruit whose insipid juice is what we call terra Japonica. The black arrack is a very coarse spirit; and is usually drawn higher than any of the finer kinds are, being not drank like them, but employed for coarser purposes. The Turkish arrack, or, as it is usually called, rakacee, seems to be of this kind. The finer and better kinds of arrack, tho' ever so good when put on board, are apt to grow foul and black in the carriage; if the leger or cask in which they are brought over be decayed on the inside, or the liquor come to touch any nails or rusty <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> of any kind: for the spirit presently dissolves part of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; and thence, upon account of the tincture of the oak, which it had before obtained from the wood of the cask, it will appear inky. Arrack, that is thus accidentally tinged black, is not to be confounded with such arrack as is originally black, and of the coarse kind named before. This, which has obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> by accident, is not the worse in taste for it; and the tinge may be taken off, and the liquor recovered, by putting into the cask a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of new or skimmed milk; and working it well about, as the vintners do in order to whiten their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> wines. When the bottoms are large, they are to be committed to a conical filter of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a>, through which the arrack runs fine. This art of purifying foul arracks with milk, would be very pardonable, if our dealers only only imposed that upon us; but they have a shameful way of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOWERING">lowering</a> this spirit with water, and that to such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> as is scarce credible. The weakness of some genuine arracks greatly contributes to the countenancing this cheat. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> deceit used in regard to this commodity; for it is not easy to find any other spirit taffelcfs enough to mix with it, without discovering the cheat with us; and in Holland they are not only more deftute of clean spirits than here, but the price of arrack itself is so low there, that it is hardly worth while to do it if they had proper materials. The extravagant price that arrack bears in England, has given <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> occasion to the distillers to endeavour the counterfeiting it. All the attempts which, for cheapness sake, have been made with malt spirit, have naturally proved unsuccessful; but the thing is not impracticable, though these methods have failed. The first requisite must be the making a perfectly tasteless spirit; and the next the treating the juices of vegetables, so as to obtain their flavour, to add to it; or else the obtaining a pulverous dry substance, which would at once mix with the spirit, and prevent the trouble of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. It is possible, also, that the English juices of trees which will bleed freely, such as the birch, maple, fycamore, and the like, may, on proper trials, be found to afford this sort of spirit in some degree of perfection. To Rack Wines, &c. To draw them off from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEES">lees</a>, after having stood long enough to ebb and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>. Hence, rack-vintage is frequently used for the second voyage our wine-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to make into France for racked wines.

RADCLIFF

Pages 287-287

an English physician of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> eminence in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WAKEFIELD">Wakefield</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> in 1650. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and enrolled himself upon the physical line; but it was remarkable that he recommended himself more by his ready <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and vivacity, than by any extraordinary acquisitions in learning. He began to practise at Oxford in 1675; but never paid any regard to established rules, which he censured whenever he thought fit, with great freedom and acrimony; and as this drew all the old practitioners upon him, he lived in a continual state of hostility with them. Nevertheless, his reputation increased with his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; so that before he had been two years in business, his practice was very extensive among persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. In 1684, he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and settled in Bow-street Convent Garden, where in less than a year he got into prime business. In 1687, the princess <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> made him her physician; yet when her husband and she joined the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, Radcliffe, either not choosing to declare himself, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> unwilling to favour the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> then in agitation, excused himself from attending them, on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> of the multitude of his patients. Nevertheless, he was often sent for to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> William and other great personages, though he did not incline to be a courtier. He incurred some censure for his treatment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, who died of the small-pox; and soon after lost his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> about the princess Anne, by his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to his bottle. He also totally lost the favour of king William by his uncourtey freedom; for, in 1699, when the king showed him his swollen ankles, while the rest of his body was emaciated, and asked him what he thought of them? "Why truly I would not have your majesty's two legs for your three kingdoms," replied Radcliffe. He <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> increasing in business and insolence as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he lived, continually at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> with his brethren the physicians; who considered him in no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> than that of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> ingenious empiric, whom constant practice had at length brought to some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of skill in his profession. He died in 1714; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he never attempted to write anything himself, has perpetuated his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> by founding a fine library at Oxford to preserve the writings of other men.

RADIALIS

Pages 287-287

the name of two muscles in the arm. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

RADIANT

Pages 287-287

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, is any point of a visible object from whence rays proceed.

RADIATED FLOWERS

Pages 287-287

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, are such as have several semifloraules set round a disk, in form of a radiant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a>; those which have no such rays are called discous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>.

RADIATION

Pages 287-287

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of a body emitting <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> diffusing rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> all round as from a centre.

RADICAL

Pages 287-287

in general, something that serves as a basis <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> foundation. Hence physicians talk much of a radical moisture. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, we give the appellation radical to primitives, in contradistinction to compounds and derivatives. Algebraists also speak of the radical sign of quantities, which is the character expressing their roots.

RADICLE

Pages 287-287

that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the seeds of all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which upon vegetating becomes their root, and is discoverable by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>. See Plant.

RADIUS

Pages 287-287

in anatomy, the exterior bone of the arm, descending along with the ulna from the elbow to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a>.

RADNOR

Pages 287-287

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>-town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RADNORSHIRE">Radnorshire</a>, in South <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, seated near the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> head of the river Somergil, in a pleasant valley, at the foot of a hill which feeds abundance of sheep and cattle; and on the top of it was seated a castle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> since in ruins. This town is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, consisting of 25 persons and the recorder, out of whom are chosen yearly a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> and two aldermen. It sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>.

RADNORSHIRE

Pages 287-287

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of South <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>; its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very sharp and piercing, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> barren without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cultivation, it being mountainous and rocky, especially in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and west parts, which are only fit for feeding cattle. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from east to west is 24 miles, and from north to south about 22. It has several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>. It is bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a>, on the south and west by Brecknockshire, and on the north by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a>. It has 52 parishes and four market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which is Radnor, the county-town. RADIX. See Root.

RAFT

Pages 287-288

a sort of float, formed by an assemblage of various planks, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, fastened together side by side, so as to be conveyed more commodiously to any short distance in a harbour or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were separate. The timber and plank, with which merchant-ships are laden, in the different parts of the Baltic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, are attached together in this manner, in order to float them off to the shipping.

RAFTERS

Pages 288-288

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, are pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, which standing by pairs on the rafter <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> railing piece, meet in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> at the top, and form the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a building. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>.

RAGMAN'S ROLL

Pages 288-288

Rectius Ragimund's roll, so called from one Ragimund a legate in Scotland, who calling before him all the beneficed clergymen in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, caused them on oath to given in the true value of their benefices; according to which they were afterwards taxed by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome: and this roll, among other records, being taken from the Scots by Edward I. was re-delivered to them in the beginning of the reign of Edward III.

RAGOUT

Pages 288-288
or RACOON, a sauce, or seasoning, intended to rouse the appetite when lost or languishing. This term is also used for any high-seasoned dish prepared of flesh, fish, greens, or the like: by stewing them with bacon, fat, pepper, cloves, and the like ingredients. We have ragouts of celery, of endive, asparagus, cock's-combs, giblets, cray-fish, &c. The ancients had a ragout called garum, made of the putrid guts of a certain fish kept till it dissolved into a mere fancies, which was thought such a dainty, that, according to Pliny, its price equalled that of the richest perfumes.

RAGSTONE

Pages 288-288

a name given by our artificers to a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for setting an edge upon knives, chisels, and other tools. It is a greyish coloured stone, containing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of talcgy particles, and splits easily into thin flakes. It is a soft stone, and used only to finish the setting an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> after the edge has been prepared by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> rubbing the tool upon some other stone of a coarser texture. We have this from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, and many other parts in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England, where there are large rocks of it in the hills.

RAGULED

Pages 288-288
or RAGGED, in heraldry, jagged or knotted. This term is applied to a cross formed of the trunks of two trees without their branches, of which they show only the stumps. Raguled differs from indented, in that the latter is regular, the former not.

RAIN

Pages 290-294

the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> in the form of drops of a considerable size. By this circumstance it is distinguished from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEW">dew</a> and fog: in the former of which the drops are so small that they are quite invisible; and in the latter, though their size is larger, they seem to have very little more specific gravity than the atmosphere itself, and may therefore be reckoned hollow spherules rather than drops. It is universally agreed, that rain is produced by the water previously absorbed by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> otherwise, from the terraqueous globe, into the atmosphere; but very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulties occur when we begin to explain why the water, once so closely united with the atmosphere, begins to separate from it. We cannot ascribe this separation to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, since rain often takes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in very warm <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; and though we should suppose the condensation owing to the superior cold of the higher regions, yet there is a remarkable fact which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not allow us to have recourse to this supposition. It is certain, that the drops of rain increase in size considerably as they descend. On the top of a hill, for instance, they will be small and inconsiderable, forming only a drizzling shower; but at the bottom of the same hill the drops will be excessively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, descending in an impetuous rain; which shows that the atmosphere is disposed to condense the vapours, and actually does so, as well where it is warm as where it is cold. For some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the suppositions concerning the cause of rain were exceedingly insufficient and unsatisfactory. It was imagined, that when various congeries of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> were driven together by the agitation of the winds, they mixed, and run into one body, by which means they were condensed into water. The coldness of the upper parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> also was thought to be a great means of collecting and condensing the clouds into water; which, being heavier than the air, must necessarily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> through it in the form of rain. The reason why it falls in drops, and not in large quantities, was said to be the resistance of the air; whereby being broken, and divided into smaller and smaller parts, it at last arrived to us in small drops. But this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> is entirely contrary to almost all the phenomena: for the weather, when coldest, that is, in the time of severe frosts, is generally the most serene; the most violent rains also happen where there is little or no rain to condense the clouds; and the drops of rain, instead of being divided into smaller and smaller ones as they approach the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, are plainly increased in size as they descend. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a> accounted for the precipitation of the drops of rain from the vesicule being full of air, and meeting with an air colder than they contained, the air they contained was of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> contracted into a smaller space; and consequently the watery shell rendered thicker, and thus specifically heavier, than the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> atmosphere. But, under the article <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVAPORATION">Evaporation</a> it has been shown, that the vesicule, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> such they are, of vapour, are not filled with air, but with fire, or heat; and consequently, till they <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> with this latent heat, the vapour cannot be condensed. Now, cold is not always sufficient to effect this, since in the most severe frosts the air is very often serene, and parts with little or none of its vapour for a very considerable time. Neither can we admit the winds to have any considerable agency in this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, since we find that blowing upon vapour is so far from condensing it, that it unites it more closely with the air, and <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is found to be a great promoter of evaporation. According to Rohault, the great cause of rain is the heat of the air, which, after continuing for some time near the earth, is raised on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> by a wind, and there thawing the snowy villi or flocks of half-frozen vesicule, reduces them to drops; which, coalescing, descend. Here, however, we ought to be informed by what means these vesicules are suspended in their half-frozen state; since the thawing of them can make but little <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in their specific gravity, and it is certain that they ascended through the air not in a frozen but in an aqueous state. Dr Clarke and others ascribe this descent of the rain rather to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of the atmosphere than of the vesicules; and suppose it to arise from a diminution of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> force of the air. This elasticity, which, they say, depends chiefly or wholly upon terrane exhalations, being weakened, the atmosphere sinks under its burden, and the clouds fall. Now, the little vesicles being once upon the descent will continue therein, notwithstanding the increase of resistance they every moment meet with. For, as they all tend to the centre of the earth, the farther they fall, the more coalitions they will make; and the more coalitions, the more matter will there be under the same surface; the surface increasing only as the squares, but the solidity as the cubes; and the more matter under the same surface, the less resistance will there be to the same matter. Thus if the cold, wind, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> early enough to precipitate the ascending vehicles before they are arrived at any considerable height, the coalsitions being but few, the drops will be proportionally small; and thus is formed a dew. If the vapours be more copious, and rise a little higher, we have a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MIST">mist</a> or fog. A little higher still, and they produce a small rain; if they neither meet with cold nor wind, they form a heavy thick dark sky. This hypothesis is equally unsatisfactory with the others; for, granting that the descent and condensation of the vapours are owing to a diminution of the atmosphere's elasticity, by what is this diminution occasioned? To say that it is owing to terrestrial exhalations, is only solving one difficulty by another; since we are totally unacquainted both with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and operation of these exhalations. Besides, let us suppose the cause to be what it will, if it acts equally and at once upon all the vapour in the air, then all that vapour must be precipitated at once; and thus, instead of gentle showers continuing for a considerable length of time, we would have the most violent waterspouts, continuing only for a few minutes, or perhaps seconds, which, instead of refreshing the earth, would drown and lay waste everything before them. Since philosophers have admitted the electric fluid to such a large share in the operations of nature, almost all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> phenomena have been accounted for by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of that fluid; and rain, among others, has been reckoned an effect of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>. But this word, unless it is explained, makes us no wiser than we were before; the phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> electricity having been explained on principles which could scarcely apply in any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to the electricity of nature; and therefore all the solution we can obtain of the natural appearances of which we speak comes to this, that rain is occasioned by a moderate electrification, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a> and snow by one more violent, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> by the most violent of all; but in what manner this electrification is occasioned, hath not yet been explained.—Throughout the various parts of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> where electricity hath been occasionally mentioned, the principles of artificial electricity, laid down in the treatise appropriated to that subject, have been applied to the solution of the phenomena of nature; those which are necessary to be attended to here, are the following. 1. The electric fluid and solar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> are the same substance in two different modifications. 2. Electricity is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the fluid when running, or attempting to run, in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> stream from one place to another: heat is when the fluid has no tendency but to vibrate outwards and inwards to and from a centre; or at least when its streams converge to a point or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a>. 3. The fluid acting as electricity, like water, or any other fluid, always tends to the place where there is least resistance. On these three principles may the phenomena of atmospherical electricity, and the descent of rain by its means, be explained as follows. 1. The light or heat of the sun, acting in that peculiar manner which we call heat, unites itself with the moisture of the earth, and forms it into vapour, which thus becomes specifically <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than air, and of consequence ascends in the atmosphere to a certain height. 2. Besides the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of light which is thus united to the water, and forms it into vapour, a very considerable quantity enters the earth, where it assumes the nature of electric fluid. 3. As the earth is always full of that fluid, every quantity which enters must displace an equal quantity which is already there. 4. This quantity which is displaced must escape either at a distance from the place where the other enters, or very near it. 5. At whatever place a quantity of electric matter escapes, it must electrify the air above that place where it has escaped; and as a considerable quantity of light must always be reflected from the earth into the atmosphere, where it does not combine with the aqueous vapour, we have thence another source of electricity to the air; as this quantity must undoubtedly assume the action of electric fluid, especially after the action of the sun has ceased. Hence the reason why in serene weather the atmospherical electricity is always strongest, and rather more so in the night than in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. 6. From these considerations, we see an evident reason why there must <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> be a difference between the electricity of the earth, and that of the atmosphere, excepting when an earthquake is about to ensue. The consequence of this must be, that as the action of the solar light continues to bring down the electric matter, and the earth continues to discharge an equal quantity of it into the atmosphere, some part of the atmosphere must at last become overloaded with it, and attempt to throw it back into the earth. This attempt will be vain, until a vent is found for the electricity at some other place; and as soon as this happens, the electrified atmosphere begins to throw off its superfluous electricity, and the earth to receive it. As the atmosphere itself is a bad conductor, and the more so the drier it is, the electric matter attacks the small aqueous particles which are detained in it by means of the latent heat. These, being unable to bear the impetus of the fluid, throw out their latent heat, which easily escapes, and thus makes a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a> in the electrified part of the atmosphere. The consequences of this are, that the aqueous particles being driven together in large quantity, at last become visible, and the sky is covered with clouds; at the same time a wind blows against these clouds, and, if there is no resistance in the atmosphere, will drive them away. 7. But if the atmosphere all round the cloud is exceedingly electrified, and the earth is in no condition to receive the superfluous fluid excepting in that place which is directly under the cloud; then the whole electricity of the atmosphere for a vast way round will tend to that part only, and the cloud will be electrified to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> degree. A wind will now blow against the cloud from all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, more and more of the vapour will be extricated from the air by the electric matter, and the cloud will become darker and thicker, at the same time that it is in a manner <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a>, as being acted upon by opposite winds; winds; though its size is enlarged with great rapidity by the continual supplies of vapour brought by the winds. 8. The vapours which were formerly suspended invisibly by means of the latent heat, are now suspended visibly by the electric fluid which will not let them fall to the earth, until it is in a condition to receive the electric matter descending with the rain. It is easy to see, however, that thus every thing is prepared for a violent storm of thunder and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> as well as rain. The surface of the earth becomes electrified from the atmosphere; but when this has continued for some time, a zone of earth considerably below the surface acquires an electricity opposite to that of the clouds and atmosphere; of consequence the electricity in the cloud being violently pressed on all sides will at last burst out towards that zone where the resistance is least, as explained under the article Lightning.—The vapours now having lost that which supported them, will fall down in rain, if there is not a sufficient quantity of electric matter to keep them in the same state in which they were before: but if this happens to be the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the cloud will instantly be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> again, while little or no rain will fall; and hence very violent thunder sometimes takes place without any rain at all, or such as is quite inconsiderable in quantity. 9. When the electricity is less violent, the rain will descend in vast quantity, especially after every flash of lightning; and great quantities of electric matter will thus be conveyed to the earth, inasmuch that sometimes the drops have been observed to shine as if they were on fire, which has given occasion to the reports of fiery rain have fallen on certain occasions. If the quantity of electric matter is smaller, so that the rain can convey it all gradually to the ground, there will be rain without any thunder; and the greater the quantity of electricity, the more violent will be the rain. From this account of the causes of rain, we may see the reason why in warm climates the rains are excessive, and for the most part accompanied with thunder; for there the electricity of the atmosphere is immensely greater than it is with us. We may also see why in certain places, according to the situation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, seas, &c. the rains will be greater than in others, and likewise why some parts of the world are exempted from rain altogether; but as a particular discussion of these would necessarily include an explanation of the causes and phenomena of Thunder, we shall for this reason refer the whole to be treated of under that article. Preternatural Rains. We have numerous accounts, in the historians of our own as well as other countries, of preternatural rains; such as the raining of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, of dust, of blood, nay, and of living animals, as young frogs, and the like. We are not to doubt the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of what those who are authors of veracity and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> relates to us of this kind, so far as to suppose that the falling of stones and dust never happened; the whole mistake is, the supposing them to have fallen from the clouds: but as to the blood and frogs, it is very certain that they never fell at all, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> has been a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> deception of the eyes. Men are extremely fond of the marvellous in their relations; but the judicious reader is to examine strictly whatever is reported of this kind, and is not to suffer himself to be deceived. There are two natural methods by which quantities of stones and dust may fall in certain places, without their having been <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> in the clouds or fallen as rain. The one is by means of hurricanes; the wind which we frequently see tearing off the tiles of houses, and carrying them to considerable distances, being equally able to take up a quantity of stones, and drop them again at some other place. But the other, which is much the most powerful, and probably the most usual way, is for the eruptions of volcanoes and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> mountains to toss up, as they frequently do, a vast quantity of stones, ashes, and cinders, to an immense height in the air: and these, being hurried away by the hurricanes and impetuous winds which usually accompany these eruptions, and being in themselves much lighter than common stones as being half calcined, may easily be thus carried to vast distances; and there falling in places where the inhabitants know nothing of the occasion, they cannot but be supposed by the vulgar to fall on them from the clouds. It is well known, that, in the great eruptions of Etna and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>, showers of ashes, dust, and small cinders, have been seen to obscure the air, and overspread the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> for a great way, and cover the decks of ships; and this at such a distance, as it should appear scarce conceivable that they should have been carried to: and probably, if the accounts, of all the showers of these substances mentioned by authors be collected, they will all be found to have fallen within such distances of volcanoes; and, if compared as to the time of their falling, will be found to correspond in that also with the eruptions of those mountains. We have known instances of the ashes from Vesuvius having been carried thirty, nay, forty leagues, and peculiar accidents may have carried them yet farther. It is not to be supposed that these showers of stones and dust fall for a continuance in the manner of showers of rain, or that the fragments or pieces are as frequent as drops of water; it is sufficient that a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of stones, or a quantity of dust, fall at once on a place, where the inhabitants can have no knowledge of the part from whence they came, and the vulgar will not doubt their dropping from the clouds. Nay, in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, the inhabitants accounted it a miracle that it rained earth and sulphur upon them, at a time that a small volcano terrified them; and even while the wind was so boisterous, and hurricanes so frequent, that they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> almost every moment the dust, sand, and little stones torn up from the surface of the earth in whirlwinds, and carried to a considerable height in the air, they never considered, that both the sulphur thrown up by the volcano, and the dust, &c. carried from their feet must fall soon after somewheres. It is very certain that in some of the terrible storms of large hail, where the hail-stones have been of many inches round, that on breaking them there have been found what people have called stones in their middle; but these observers needed only to have waited the dissolving of one of these hail stones, to have seen the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in its centre disunite also, it being only formed of the particles of loose earthy matter, which the water, exhaled by the sun's heat, had taken up in extremely small molecule with with it; and this only having served to give an opake hue to the inner part of the congelation, to which the freezing of the water alone gave the apparent hardnes of stone. The raining of blood has been ever accounted a more terrible sight and a more fatal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OMEN">omen</a> than the other preternatural rains already mentioned. It is very certain that nature forms blood no where but in the vessels of animals, and therefore showers of it from the clouds are by no means to be credited. Those who suppose that what has been taken for blood has been actually seen falling through the air, have had recourse to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> insects for its origin, and suppose it the eggs or dungs of certain butterflies discharged from them as they were high up in the air. But it seems a very wild conjecture, as we know of no butterfly whose excrements, or eggs, are of such a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, or whose abode is so high, or their flocks so numerous, as to be the occasion of this. It is most probable that these bloody waters were never seen falling; but that people seeing the standing waters blood-coloured, were assured, from their not knowing how it should else happen, that it had rained blood into them. A very memorable instance of this there was at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> in the year 1670. Swammerdam, who relates it, tells us, that one morning the whole town was in an uproar on finding their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and ditches full of blood, as they thought; and having been certainly full of water the night before, they agreed it must have rained blood in the night; but a certain physician went down to one of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, and taking home a quantity of this blood-coloured water, he examined it by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, and found that the water was water still, and had not at all changed its colour; but that it was full of prodigious swarms of small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> animals, all alive, and very nimble in their motions, whose colour and prodigious number gave a red tinge to the whole body of the water they lived in, on a less accurate inspection. The certainty that this was the case, did not however persuade the Hollanders to part with the miracle; they prudently concluded, that the sudden appearance of such a number of animals was as great a prodigy as the raining of blood would have been; and are assured to this day, that this portent foretold the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> and destruction which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. afterwards brought into that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which had before enjoyed 40 years uninterrupted peace. The animals which thus colour the water of lakes and ponds, are the pulices arborecentes of Swammerdam, or the water-fleas with branched horns. These creatures are of a reddish-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> colour: they live about the sides of ditches, under weeds, and among the mud; and are therefore the least visible, except at a certain time, which is in the end or beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>: it is at this time that these little animals leave their recesses to float loose about the water, to meet for the propagation of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, and by that means become visible in the colour they give the water. This is visible, more or less, in one part or other of almost all standing waters at this season; and it is always at this season that the bloody waters have alarmed the ignorant. The raining of frogs is a thing not less wonderful in the accounts of authors who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> the marvellous, than those of blood or stones; and this is supposed to happen so often, that there are multitudes who pretend to have been eye-witnesses of it. These rains of frogs always happens after very dry seasons, and are much more frequent in the hotter countries than in the cold ones. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> they are very frequent; and it is not uncommon to see the streets of Rome swarming both with young frogs and toads in an instant, in a shower of rain; they hopping everywhere between the people's legs as they walk, though there was not the least appearance of them before. Nay, they have been seen to fall through the air down upon the pavements. This seems a strong circumstance in favour of their being rained down from the clouds; but, when strictly examined, it comes to nothing; for these frogs that are seen to fall, are always found dead, lamed, or bruised by the fall, and never hop about as the rest; and they are never seen to fall, except <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> under the walls of houses, from the roofs and gutters of which they have accidentally slipped down. People, who love to add to strange things yet stranger, affirm that people have had the young frogs fall into their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a> in the midst of an open field; but this is idle, and wholly false. People, who cannot agree to their falling from the clouds, have tried to solve the difficulty of their sudden appearance, by supposing them hatched out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, or spawn, by these rains. Nay, some have supposed them made immediately out of the dust; but there are unanswerable arguments against all these suppositions. Equivocal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, or the spontaneous production of animals out of dust, is now wholly exploded. The fall from the clouds must destroy and kill these tender and soft-bodied animals; and they cannot be at this time hatched immediately out of eggs; because the young frog does not make its appearance from the egg in this form, but has its hinder legs enveloped in a skin, and is what we call a tadpole; and the young frogs are at least 100 times larger at the time of their appearance, than the egg from which they should be hatched. It is a certainty, that the frogs, which make their appearance at this time, were hatched and in being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before; but that the dry seasons had injured them, and kept them sluggish in holes, or coverts; and that all the rain does, is the enlivening them, giving new spirits, and calling them forth to seek new habitations, and enjoy the element they were destined in great part to live in. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>, the greatest of all the naturalists of antiquity, has affirmed the same thing. We find that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of supposing these creatures to fall from the clouds was as early as that author's time; and also that the truth, in regard to their appearance, was as early known; though, in the ages since, authors have taken care to conceal the truth, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> down to us the error. We find this venerable sage, in a fragment of his on the generation of animals which appear on a sudden, bantering the opinion, and asserting that they were hatched and living long before. The world owes, however, to the accurate Signor Redi the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of this truth, which Theophrastus only has affirmed: for this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, dissecting some of these new-appearing frogs, found in their stomachs herbs and other half-digested food, and openly showing this to his credulous countrymen, asked them whether they thought that nature, which engendered, according to their opinion, these animals in the clouds, had also been so provident as to engender grass there also for their food and nourishment. To the raining of frogs we ought to add the raining of grasshoppers and locusts, which have sometimes appeared in prodigious numbers, and devoured the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the earth. There has not been the least pretence for the supposing that these animals descended from the clouds, but that they appeared on a sudden in prodigious numbers. The naturalist, who knows the many accidents attending the eggs of these and other like animals, cannot but know that some seasons will prove particularly favourable to the hatching them, and the prodigious number of eggs that many insects lay could not but every year bring us such abundance of the young, were they not liable to many accidents, and had not provident nature taken care, as in many <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, to continue the species by a very numerous stock of seeds, of which perhaps not one in 500 need take root in order to continue an equal number of plants. As it is thus also in regard to insects, it cannot but happen, that if a favourable season encourage the hatching of all those eggs, a very small number of which alone were necessary to continue the species, we must, in such seasons, have a proportionate abundance of them. There appeared about 40 years ago, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, such a prodigious swarm of the little beetle we call the lady-bug, that the very posts in the streets were everywhere covered with them. But thanks to the progress of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> among us, we had no body to assert that it rained cow-ladies, but contented ourselves with saying that it had been a favourable season for their eggs. The prodigious number of a sort of grub which did vast mischief about the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> among the corn and grass by eating off their roots, might also have been supposed to proceed from its having rained grubs by people fond of making everything a prodigy; but our knowledge in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> assured us, that these were only the hexapode <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> of the common hedge-beetle called the cockchafer. The raining of fishes has been a prodigy also much talked of in France, where the streets of a town at some distance from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, after a terrible hurricane in the night, which tore up trees, blew down houses, &c., were found in a manner covered with fishes of various sizes. Nobody here made any doubt of these having fallen from the clouds; nor did the absurdity of fish, of five or six inches long, being generated in the air, at all startle the people, or shake their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> in the miracle, till they found, upon inquiry, that a very well-stocked fish-pond, which stood on an eminence in the neighbourhood, had been blown dry by the hurricane, and only the great fish left at the bottom of it, all the smaller fry having been tossed into their streets. Upon the whole, all the supposed marvellous rains have been owing to substances naturally produced on the earth, and either never having been in the air at all, or only carried thither by accident. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, after a great dearth of wheat in that country, there happened a violent storm of wind and rain, and the earth was afterwards covered, in many places, with small round seeds. The vulgar cried out that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> had sent them food, and that it had rained millet; but these were, in reality, only the seeds of a species of veronica, or speed-well, very common in that country; and whose seeds being <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> ripe at that time, the wind had dislodged them from their capsules, and scattered them about. In our own country, we have histories of rains of this marvellous kind, but all fabulous. It was once said to rain wheat in Wiltshire, and the people were all alarmed at it as a miracle; till Mr Cole showed them, that what they took for wheat was only the seeds or kernels of the berries of ivy, which being then fully ripe, the wind had dislodged from the sides of housetops, and trunks of trees, on which the ivy which produced them crept. And we even once had a raining of fishes near the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> in a terrible hurricane, with thunder and lightening. The people who saw small sprats flew about afterwards, would have it that they had fallen from the clouds; but those who considered how far the high winds have been known to carry the seawater, did not wonder that they should be able to carry small fish with it so small a part of the way. RAINBOW. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, Part III. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> 1. § 1. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUNAR">Lunar</a> Rainbow. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> sometimes also exhibits the phenomenon of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, by the refraction of her rays in drops of rain in the night-time. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> says, he was the first that ever observed it; and adds, that it is never visible but at the time of full moon. The lunar iris has all the colours of the solar, only fainter. Marine Rainbow, the Sea-bow, is a phenomenon sometimes observed in a much agitated sea, when the wind, sweeping part of the tops of the waves, carries them aloft; so that the rays of the sun are refracted, &c., as in a common shower.

RAISINS

Pages 294-295
grapes prepared by suffering them to remain on the vine till they are perfectly ripe, and then drying them in the sun, or by the heat of an oven. The difference between raisins dried in the sun, and those dried in ovens, is very obvious: the former are sweet and pleasant; but the latter have a latent acidity with the sweetness, that renders them much less agreeable. The common way of drying grapes for raisins, is to tie two or three bunches of them together while yet on the vine, and dip them into a hot lixivium of woodashes, with a little of the oil of olives in it. This dopes them to shrink and wrinkle, and after this they are left on the vine three or four days separated on sticks in an horizontal situation, and then dried in the sun at leisure, after being cut from the tree. The finest and best raisins are those called in some places Damascene and Judean raisins; which are distinguished from the others by their size and figures: they are flat and wrinkled on the surface, soft and juicy within, and near an inch long; and, when fresh and growing on the bunch, are of the size and shape of a large olive. The raisins of the sun, and jar-raisins, are all dried by the heat of the sun; and these are the sorts used in medicine. However, all the kinds have much the same virtues: they are all nutritive and balsamic; they are allowed to be attenuant, are said to be good in nephritic complaints, and are an ingredient in pectoral decoctions; in which cases, as also in all others where where asstringency is not required of them, they should have the stones carefully taken out. RAISIN-WINE. See WINE.

RAJA

Pages 288-290

the Ray-Fish, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>; a genus belonging to the order of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMPHIBIA">amphibia</a> nantes. There are five spiracula below towards the peak; the body compressed; and the mouth is situated under the head. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The batis, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> skate: this species is the thinnest in proportion to its bulk of any of the genus, and also the largest, some weighing near 200 pounds. The nose, though not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, is sharp pointed; above the eyes is a set of short spines: the upper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, sometimes streaked with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>: the lower part is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, marked with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of minute black spots. The jaws are covered with small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANULATED">granulated</a> but sharp-pointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>. The tail is of moderate length: near the end are two fins: along the top of it is one row of spines, and on the edges are irregularly dispersed a few others, which makes us imagine with Mr Ray, that in this respect these fish vary, some having one, others more orders of spines on the tail. It is remarked, that in the males of this species the fins are full of spines. Skates <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> and April; at which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> they swim near the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, several of the males pursuing one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>. They adhere so fast together in coition, that the fishermen frequently draw up both together, though only one has taken the bait. The females begin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> their purfs, as the fishermen call them (the bags in which the young are included) in May, and continue doing it till September. In October they are exceedingly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and thin; but in November they begin to improve, and grow gradually better till May, when they are in the highest perfection. The males go sooner out of season than the females. 2. The oxyrinchus, or sharp-nosed ray, in length near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet, and breadth five feet two inches; when <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> brought on shore, it makes a remarkable snorting noise. The nose is very long, narrow, and sharp-pointed, not unlike the end of a pontoon. The body is smooth, and very thin in proportion to the size; the upper part ash-coloured, spotted with numerous white spots, and a few black ones. The tail is thick; towards the end are two small fins; on each side is a row of small spines, with another row in the middle, which run some way up the back. The lower part of the fish is quite white. The mouth very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and furnished with numbers of small sharp teeth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> inwards. This fish has been supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOS">bos</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; which was certainly some enormous species of ray, though we cannot pretend to determine the particular kind.
