Oppian styles it, the broadest among fishes: he adds an account of its fondness of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and the method it takes of destroying men, by over-laying and keeping them <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by its vast <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> till they are drowned. Phile (De propriet. anim. p. 85.) gives much the same relation. We are inclined to give them <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, since a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writer, of undoubted authority †, gives the very same account of a fish found in the South Seas, the terror of those employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>-fishery. It is a species of ray, called there mania, or the quilt, from its surrounding and wrapping up the unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a>, till they are suffocated; therefore the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> never go down, without a sharp <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> to defend themselves against the assaults of this terrible enemy. 3. The aspera, or rough ray, is found in Loch-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BROOM">Broom</a> in Scotland. The length from the nose to the tip of the tail is two feet <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. The tail is almost of the same length with the body. Nose very short. Before each eye is a large hooked spine; and behind each another, befit with lesser. The upper part of the body is of a cinereous brown mixed with white, and spotted with black; and entirely covered with small spines. On the tail are three rows of great spines: all the... the rest of the tail is irregularly beset with lesser. The fins and under side of the body are equally rough with the upper. The teeth are flat, and rhomboidal. 4. The fullonica, or fuller, derives its Latin name from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> fullers make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in smoothing cloth, the back being rough and spiny. The nose is short and sharp. At the corner of each eye are a few spines. The membrane of nictitation is fringed. Teeth small, and sharp. On the upper part of the pectoral fins are three rows of spines pointing towards the back, crooked like those on a fuller's instrument. On the tail are three rows of strong spines; the middle row reaches up part of the back. The tail is slender, and rather longer than the body. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the upper part of the body is cinereous, marked usually with numerous black spots; the lower part is white. This, as well as most other species of rays, vary a little in colour, according to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. This grows to a size equal to the skate. It is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SCARBOROUGH">Scarborough</a>, where it is called the white bans, or gullet. 5. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHAGREEN">shagreen</a> ray increases to the size of the skate; is fond of launces or sand-eels, which it takes generally as a bait. The form is narrower than that of the common kinds; the nose long and very sharp; pupil of the eye sapphire-like; on the nose are two short rows of spines; on the corner of the eyes another of a semicircular form; on the tail are two rows, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a little up the back, small, slender, and very sharp: along the sides of the tail is a row of minute spines, intermixed with innumerable little spiculae. The upper part of the body is of a cinereous brown, covered closely with shagreen-like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a>, resembling the skin of the dog-fish: the under side of the body is white; from the nose to the beginning of the pectoral fins is a tuberculated space. The teeth slender, and sharp as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>. 6. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TORPEDO">torpedo</a>, or cramp-fish, or electric ray, is frequently taken in Torbay; has been once caught off <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>, and sometimes near <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATERFORD">Waterford</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. It is generally taken, like other flat fish, with the trawl; but there is an instance of its taking the bait. It <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> lies in water of about 40 fathoms depth; and in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with the congenerous rays. The torpedo brings forth its young at the autumnal equinox, as affirmed by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>. A <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of La <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>, on dissecting certain females of this species, the 10th of September, found in the matrices several of the fetuses quite formed, and nine eggs in no state of forwardness; superfoetation seems therefore to be a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of this fish. The food of the torpedo is fish; a surmullet and a plaice have been found in the stomach of two of them. The surmullet is a fish of that swiftness, that it was impossible for the torpedo to take it by pursuit. It is probable, that by their electric stroke they stupefy their prey; yet the crab and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-leech <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> venture to annoy them. They will live 24 hours out of the sea; and but very little longer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> placed in fresh water. They inhabit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> places; and will <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURY">bury</a> themselves superficially in it, by flinging the sand over, by a quick flapping of all the extremities. It is in this situation that the torpedo gives his most forcible shock, which throws down the astonished passenger who inadvertently treads upon him. In our seas it grows to a great size, and above 80 pounds weight. The tail is thick and round; the caudal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIN">fin</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and abrupt. The head and body, which are indistinct, are nearly round; attenuating to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> thinness on the edges; below the body, the ventral fins form on each side a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a circle. The two dorsal fins are placed on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of the tail. The eyes are small, placed near each other: behind each is a round spiracle, with six small cutaneous rags on their inner circumference. Mouth small; teeth minute, spicular. Five openings to the gills, as in others of this genus. The skin everywhere smooth; cinereous brown above, white beneath. See further the article Torpedo. 7. The clavata, or thornback, is easily distinguished from the others by the rows of strong sharp spines disposed along the back and tail. In a large one seen by Mr Pennant, were three rows on the back, and five on the tail, all inclining towards its end. On the nose, and on the inner side of the forehead, near the eyes, were a few spines, and others were scattered without any order on the upper part of the pectoral fins. The mouth was small, and filled with granulated teeth. The upper part of the body was of a pale ash colour, marked with short streaks of black, and the skin rough, with small tubercles like shagreen. The belly white, crossed with a strong semilunar cartilage beneath the skin; in general, the lower part was smooth, having only a few spines on each side. The young fish have very few spines on them; and their backs are often spotted with white, and each spot is encircled with black. This species frequents our sandy shores; are very voracious, and feed on all sorts of flat fish; are particularly fond of herrings and sand-eels; and sometimes eat crustaceous animals, such as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>. These sometimes weigh 14 or 15 pounds, but with us seldom exceed that weight. They begin to generate in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and bring forth their young in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and August, which (as well as those of the skate) before they are old enough to breed, are called maids. The thornback begins to be in season in November, and continues so later than the skate, but the young of both are good at all times of the year. 8. The patinaca, or sting ray, does not grow to the bulk of the others: The body is quite smooth, of shape almost round, and is of a much greater thickness and more elevated form in the middle than any other rays, but grows thin towards the edges. The nose is very sharp pointed, but short; the mouth small, and filled with granulated teeth. The irides are of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> colour: behind each eye the orifice is very large. The tail is very thick at the beginning: the spine is placed about a third the length of the former from the body; is about five inches long, flat on the top and bottom, very hard, sharp pointed, and the two sides thin, and closely and sharply bearded the whole way. The tail extends four inches beyond the end of this spine, and grows very slender at the extremity. These fish are observed to shed their spine, and renew them annually; sometimes the new spine appears before the old one drops off; and the Cornish call this species <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> tri-loft, or three-tailed, when so circumstanced. The colour of the upper part of the body is a dirty <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, the middle part of an obscure blue: the lower side white, the tail and spine dusky. The weapon with which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has armed this fish, hath supplied the ancients. cients with many tremendous fables relating to it. Pliny, Aelian, and Oppian, have given it a venom that affects even the inanimate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>: trees that are struck by it instantly lose their verdure and perish, and rocks themselves are incapable of resisting the potent <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a>. The enchantress Circe armed her son with a spear headed with the spine of the trygon, as the most irresistible weapon she could furnish him with; and with which he afterwards committed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARRICIDE">parricide</a>, unintentionally, on his father Ulysses. That spears and darts might, in very early times, have been headed with this bone instead of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, we have no kind of doubt; that of another species of this fish being still used to point the arrows of some of the South American Indians, and is, from its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>, sharpness, and beards, a most dreadful weapon. But in respect to its venomous qualities, there is not the least credit to be given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, though it was believed (as far as it affected the animal world) by Rondelletius, Aldrovand, and others, and even to this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> by the fishermen in several parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It is in fact the weapon of offence belonging to the fish, capable of giving a very bad wound, and which is attended with dangerous symptoms when it falls on a tendinous part or on a person in a bad <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of body. As to any fish having a spine <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with actual poison, it seems very dubious, though the report is sanctified by the name of Linnaeus. He instances the *pistinaca*, the *torpedo*, and the *tetradon lineatus*. The first is incapable of conveying a greater injury than what results from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> wound; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, from its electric effluvia; and the third, by imparting a pungent pain like the sting of nettles, occasioned by the minute spines on its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>.

RAKKATH

Pages 295-295

(anc. geog.) a town of Upper Galilee, thought to be Tiberias, (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALMUD">Talmud</a>;) but this is denied by Reland, who says that Rakkath was a town of the tribe of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPHTHALI">Naphthali</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">RAKE</a> of a SHIP, is all that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">hull</a> which hangs over both ends of her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>. That which is before is called the fore-rake, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> rake forward; and that part which is at the setting on of the stern-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a> is called the rake aft, or afterward.

RALEIGH

Pages 295-296

of Fardei in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Cornwood in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, was born in 1552, at Hayes, in the parish of Budley, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FARM">farm</a> belonging to his father. About the year 1568, he was sent to Oriel <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> but a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; for in the following year he embarked for France, being one of the hundred voluntiers, commanded by Henry Champernon, who, with other English troops, were sent by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Elisabeth to assist the queen of Navarre in defending the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he continued for five <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> six years; after which he returned to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and probably resided in the Middle Temple. But his enterprising genius would not suffer him to remain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in a state of inactivity. In 1577 or 1578, he embarked for the Low Countries with the troops sent by the queen to assist the Dutch against the Spaniards, and probably shared the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the decisive victory over <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> John of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> in 1578. On his return to England, a new enterprise engaged his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. His half-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, Sir Humphrey Gilbert, having obtained a patent to plant and inhabit some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, Mr Raleigh embarked in this adventure; but, meeting with a Spanish fleet, after a smart engagement they returned, without success, in 1579. The following year, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in conjunction with the pope, having projected a total conquest of the English dominions, sent troops to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> to assist the Demonds in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> rebellion. Raleigh obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Grey of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WILTON">Wilton</a>, then <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> of Ireland, and embarked for that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; where, by his conduct and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, he was principally instrumental in putting an end to the rebellious attempt. He returned to England; and attracted the notice of queen Elisabeth, on the following occasion, as we are told in Naunton's Fragmenta Regalia. It seems, as the queen was one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> taking a walk, being stopped by a slippery <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, our gallant young soldier took off his new plush mantle, and spread it on the ground. Her majesty trod gently over the fair foot-cloth, surprised and pleased with the adventure. The queen employed him first as an attendant on the French <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> Simier on his return home, and afterward to escort the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Anjou to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>. During this excursion he became personally known to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>; from whom, at his return, he brought special acknowledgments to the queen, who now frequently conversed with him. But the inactive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of a courtier did not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the enterprising spirit of Mr Raleigh. In the year 1583, he embarked with his brother, Sir Humphrey Gilbert, on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> expedition to Newfoundland, in a ship called the Raleigh, which he built at his own expense; but was obliged to return, on account of an infectious distemper on board. He was, however, so little affected by this disappointment, that he now laid before the queen and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> a proposal for exploring the continent of North America, and in 1584 obtained a patent empowering him to possess such countries as he should discover in that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the globe. Accordingly Mr Raleigh fitted out two ships at his own expense, which sailed in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April, and returned to England about the middle of September, reporting that they had discovered and taken possession of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> called Windangooco, to which the queen gave the name of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>. About this time he was elected <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the shire for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Devon, and soon after received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>; and to enable him to carry on his designs abroad, the queen granted him a patent for licensing the vendors of wine throughout the kingdom. In 1605 he sent a fleet of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> ships to Virginia, commanded by his relation Sir Richard Greenville, who left a colony at Roanah of 107 persons, under the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Mr Lane. In the same year Sir Walter Raleigh obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of 12,000 acres of the forfeited lands in the county of Corke in Ireland. About the same time he was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Cornwall, and warden of the stannaries; and grew into such favour with the queen, that even Leicesters was jealous of his influence. In 1587, he sent another colony of 150 men to Virginia, with a governor, Mr John <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a>, and 12 assistants. About this time we find our knight distinguished by the titles of Captain of the queen's guards, and Lieutenant-general of Cornwall. From this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to the year 1594, he was continually engaged in projecting new expeditions, sending succours to colonies abroad, defending the kingdom from the insults of the Spaniards, and transacting parliamentary business, with equal ability and resolution. Whilst thus employed, he was publicly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIBEL">libel</a> written by the infamous Jesuit Parsons, with being an Atheist; a groundless and ridiculous imputation. In 1594, he obtained from the queen a grant of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHERBORNE">Sherborne</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, where he built a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; but Sir Walter fell under the queen's displeasure on account of an intrigue with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir Nicholas Throgmorton, one of the maids of honour; however, he married the lady, and lived with her in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> conjugal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>. During his disgrace at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, he projected the conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUIANA">Guiana</a> in South America, and in 1595 sailed for that country; of which having taken possession, after defeating the Spaniards who were settled there, he returned to England the same year, and soon after published an account of his expedition. In the following year he was one of the admirals in the successful expedition against <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>, under the command of Howard and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>; and in 1597 he sailed with the same commanders against the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AZORES">Azores</a>. Soon after these expeditions, we find him assiduously engaged in parliamentary business, and a distinguished personage in jousts and tournaments. In 1600 he was sent on a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> embassy with Lord Cobham to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, and at his return made governor-of-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>. Queen Elisabeth died in the beginning of the year 1603; and with her Raleigh's glory and felicity sunk, never to rise again. Her successor James was an enemy to every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of virtue and heroism. He was Raleigh, scarce seated on the throne, before this valuable subject was stripped of his preferments, tried, and condemned for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>; but after a month's imprisonment, in daily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of his execution, he was reprieved, and sent to the Tower; and his estates were given to Car, earl of Somerset, the king's favourite. During this confinement he wrote many of his most valuable pieces, particularly his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the World. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1615, after 16 years imprisonment, he obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and immediately began to prepare for another voyage to Guiana. In August 1616, the king granted him a very ample commission for that purpose; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, the year following, he sailed from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>; but, strange as it may appear, it is most certain, that the whole scheme was revealed to the Spaniards by the king himself, and thus necessarily rendered abortive. He returned to England in 1618; where he was soon after seized, imprisoned, and beheaded, not for any pretended misdemeanor on the late expedition, but in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his former attainder. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is, he was sacrificed by the pusillanimous monarch to appease the Spaniards; who, whilst Raleigh lived, thought every part of their dominions in danger. He was executed in Old <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">Palace</a> Yard, and buried in St Margaret's adjoining, in the 66th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of admirable parts, extensive knowledge, undaunted resolution, and strict honour and honesty. He was the author of a great many works, some of which have not been printed.

RALLUS

Pages 296-296

the Rail, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>; a genus belonging to the order of grallae. The beak is thickest at the base, compressed, equal, acute, and somewhat sharp on the back near the point; the nostrils are oval; the feet have four toes, without any web; and the body is compressed. There are 10 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, principally distinguished by their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The most remarkable are, 1. **The aquaticus**, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-rail, is a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> slender body, with short concave wings. It delights less in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> than running; which it does very swiftly along the edges of brooks covered with bushes; as it runs, it every now and then flirts up its tail, and in flying hangs <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> its legs; actions it has in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with the water-hen. Its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> is four ounces and a half. The length to the end of the tail is 12 inches; the breadth 16. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is slender, slightly incurved, one inch three <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> long: the upper mandible <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, edged with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>; the lower, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-coloured: the head, hind <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the neck, the back, and coverts of the wings and tail, are black, edged with an olive <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; the throat, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and upper part of the belly, are ash-coloured: the sides under the wings as far as the rump, finely varied with black and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> bars. The tail is very short, consists of 12 black feathers; the ends of the two middle tipped with rust colour; the feathers immediately beneath the tail white. The legs are placed far behind, and are of a dusky <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-colour. The toes very long, and divided to their very origin; though the feet are not webbed, it takes the water; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> swim on it with much ease, but is often observed to run along the surface. 2. **The porzana**, or gallinule, is not very frequent in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and is said to be migratory. Inhabits the sides of small streams, concealing itself among the bushes. Its length is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches; its breadth, 15; its weight, four ounces five drachms. The head is brown, spotted with black; the neck a deep olive, spotted with white: the feathers of the back are black next their shafts, then olive-coloured, and edged with white: the scapulars are olive, finely marked with two small white spots on each web: the legs of a yellowish green. 3. **The crex, crake, or corn-crek**, has been supposed by some to be the same with the water-rail, and that it differs only by a change of colour at a certain season of the year: this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> is owing to inattention to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, both which differ entirely. The bill of this species is short, strong, and thick; formed exactly like that of the water-hen, and makes a generical distinction. It never frequents watery places; but is always found among corn, grass, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>, or furze. It quits the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> before winter; but the water-rail endures our sharpest seasons. They agree in their aversion to flight; and the legs, which are remarkably long for the size of the bird, hang down whilst they are on the wing; they trust their safety to their swift nets on foot, and seldom are sprung a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> but with great difficulty. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> rail lays from 12 to 20 eggs, of a dull white colour, marked with a few <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> spots; notwithstanding this, they are very numerous in this kingdom. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> is singular, resembling the word crex often repeated. They are in greatest plenty in Anglesea, where they appear about the 20th of April, supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, where they abound: at their first arrival it is common to shoot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight in a morning. They are found in most of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>, and the Orkneys. On their arrival they are very lean, weighing only six ounces; but before they leave this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, grow so fat as to weigh above eight. The feathers on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of the head and hind-part of the neck, are black, edged with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> colour: the coverts of the wings of the same colour, but not spotted; the tail is short, and of a deep bay: the belly white; the legs ash-coloured.

RALPH

Pages 296-296

a late ingenious historical and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> writer, was born, we know not when nor where, being first known as a school-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. He came to England about the beginning of the reign of George I. and wrote some things in the dramatic way, which were not received with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause: but though he did not succeed as a poet, he was a very ingenious prose-writer. He wrote A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of England, commencing with the Stuarts, which is much esteemed; as were his political essays and pamphlets, some of which were looked upon as master-pieces. His last publication, The Cave of Authors by profession, is an excellent and entertaining performance. He died in 1762.

RAMADAN

Pages 296-296

a solemn season of fasting among the Mahometans. See MAHOMETANISM.

RAMAH

Pages 296-297

a town of Benjamin, near Gibea, (Judges); called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAMA">Rama</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a> (1 Sam. xxii.), six miles from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; memorable for the story of the Levite and his concubine: Taken and fortified by Baasa <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Israel, in order to annoy the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Judah. This Rama is mentioned Isa. x. Jer. xxxi. and Matth. ii. and is to be distinguished from Rama of Samuel, 1 Sam. xix. called also Ramatha, 1 Sam. i. 19. and Ramathaim Zophim, ibid. i. i., which lay a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> way to the west, towards Joppa, near Lydda, 1 Maccab. ii. the birth-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Samuel; adjoining to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Ephraim, and the place of his residence, 1 Sam. xv. &c. (Josephus.) Called Ramula in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, (Gul. Tyrius.)

RAMATH-MIZPEH

Pages 297-297

(Joshua xiii.); Ramoth-Maspha, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>, Vulgate); Ramoth in Gilead, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Remmath Galaad, (Seventy); a town in that tract of Gilead called Maspha, or Mizpe, one of the cities of refuge.

RAMAZZINI

Pages 297-297

an Italian physician, born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARPI">Carpi</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a> in 1633. He was professor of physic in the university of Modena for 18 years; and in 1700 accepted an invitation from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, where he was made rector of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>; and died in 1714. His works were collected and published in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1716; of which, his treatise De Morbis Artificum, "Of the peculiar maladies of artificers," <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> always be esteemed useful and curious.

RAMESES

Pages 297-297
king of the Lower Egypt when Jacob went thither with his family, in the 1706th year before the Christian era. Ancient authors mention several other kings of Egypt of the same name; and it is thought that one of those princes erected in the temple of the sun at Thebes, the magnificent obelisk which the emperor Constantine caused to be removed to Alexandria in the year 334, and that prince dying, his son Constantius had the obelisk transported from Alexandria to Rome in 352, where it was erected in the grand Circus. Its height was 132 feet. When the Goths sacked the city of Rome in 409, they overthrew this obelisk, which continued buried in the sand till the time of Sixtus V. in 1587, when it was found broken in three pieces, which being joined together, set up in the square of St John de Lateran. On the four sides of this wonderful obelisk are a number of figures and hieroglyphical characters, which, according to the explication of Ammianus Marcellinus, contain the praises of Ramees.

RAMIFICATION

Pages 297-297

the production of boughs <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> branches, or of figures resembling branches.

RAMMER

Pages 297-297

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used for driving <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> piles into the ground; or for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in order to render it more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> for a foundation. RAMMER of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">Gun</a>, the Gun-slick; a rod used in charging of a gun, to drive home the powder, as also the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, and the wad, which keeps the shot from rolling out.

RAMPANT

Pages 297-297

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to a lion, leopard, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other beast that stands on its hind legs, and rears up his fore-feet in the posture of climbing, showing only half his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>, as one eye, &c. It is different from falciant, in which the beast seems springing forward as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> making a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>.

RAMPART

Pages 297-297

in fortification, is an elevation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> round a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> capable of resisting the cannon of an enemy; and formed into battions, curtins, &c.

RAMPHASTOS

Pages 297-308

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of picae. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, convex, and ferrated outwardly; the nostrils are situated behind the base of the beak; the feet in most <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are toed. There are eight species; of which the most remarkable is the toucan, whose bill is almost as large fig. 8. as the rest of its body. There are four <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> five varieties, but we shall only describe that which has a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> beak. This is about the size of a jack-daw, and shaped like that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, with a large head to support its monstrous bill: this bill, from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of the mouth to its point, is six inches and an half; and its breadth, in the thickest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, is a little more than two. Its thickness near the head, is one inch and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; and it is a little rounded along the top of the upper chap, the under side being round also; the whole of the bill extremely slight, and a little thicker than <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>. The upper chap is of a bright <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, except on each side, which is of a fine scarlet <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; as is also the lower chap, except at the base, which is purple. Between the head and the bill there is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> line of separation all round the base of the bill; in the upper part of which the nostrils are placed, and are almost covered with feathers; which has occasioned some writers to say, that the toucan has no nostrils. Round the eyes, on each side of the head, is a space of bluish skin, void of feathers; above which the head is black, except a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> spot on each side joining to the base of the upper chap. The hinder part of the neck, the back, wings, tail, belly, and thighs, are black. The under side of the head, throat, and the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, are white. Between the white on the breast, and the black on the belly, is a space of red feathers, in the form of a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, with its horns upwards. The legs, feet, and claws, are of an ash-colour; and the toes stand like those of parrots, two before, and two behind. It is reported by travellers, that this bird, though furnished with so formidable a beak, is harmless and gentle, being so easily made tame, as to fit and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HATCH">hatch</a> its young in houses. It feeds chiefly upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, which it devours very greedily, gorging itself in such a manner, that it voids it crude and uncooked. This, however, is no objection to the natives from using it again: they even prefer it before that pepper which is fresh gathered from the tree; and seem persuaded that the strength and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the pepper is qualified by the bird, and that all its noxious qualities are thus exhausted. Whatever be the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this report, nothing is more certain than that the toucan lives only upon a vegetable diet; and, in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> state, to which it is frequently brought in the warm countries where it is bred, it is seen to prefer such food to all others. Pozzo, who bred one tame, affirms, that it leaped up and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, wagged the tail, and cried with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> resembling that of a magpie. It fed upon the same things. things that parrots do; but was most greedy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, which, being plucked off one by one, and thrown in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, it would most dexterously catch before they fell to the ground. Its bill, like ours, was hollow, and upon that account very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, so that it had but little strength in so apparently formidable a weapon; nor could it peck or strike smartly therewith. But its tongue seemed to assist the efforts of this unwieldy machine: it was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, thin, and flat, not unlike one of the feathers on the neck of a dunghill cock; this it moved up and down, and often extended five or six inches from the bill. It was of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> colour, and remarkably fringed on each side with very small filaments, exactly resembling a feather. It is probable that this long tongue has greater strength than the thin hollow beak that contains it. It is likely that the beak is only a kind of sheath for this peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, used by the toucan, not only in making itself a nest, but also in obtaining its provision. Nothing is more certain, than that this bird builds its nest in holes of trees, which have been previously scooped out for this purpose; and it is not very likely that so feeble a bill could be very serviceable in working upon such hard materials. Be this as it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, there is no bird secures its young better from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> injury than the toucan. It has not only birds, men, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against; but a numerous tribe of monkeys, still more prying, mischievous, and hungry, than all the rest. The toucan, however, scoops out its nest into the hollow of some tree, leaving only a hole large enough to go in and out at. There it sits, with its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> beak, guarding the entrance; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the monkey ventures to offer a visit of curiosity, the toucan gives him such a welcome, that he presently thinks proper to pack off, and is glad to escape with safety. This bird is only found in the warm climates of South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, where it is in great request, both for the delicacy of its flesh, which is tender and nourishing, and for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of its plumage, particularly the feathers of the breast. The skin of this part the Indians pluck off, and, when dry, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GLUE">glue</a> to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>; and this they consider as an irresistible addition to their beauty. RAMSDEN'S ENGINE for Dividing Mathematical Instruments, is a late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> by which these divisions can be performed with exceeding great accuracy, such as would formerly have been deemed incredible. On a discovery of the method of constructing this machine, its inventor, Mr. Ramsden of Piccadilly, received £615l. from the commissioners of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>; engaging himself to instruct a certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons, not exceeding ten, in the method of making and using this machine from the 28th October 1775, to 28th October 1777: also binding himself to divide all octants and sextants by the same engine, at the rate of three shillings for each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OCTANT">octant</a>, and six shillings for each <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> sextant, with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NONIUS">Nonius</a>'s divisions to half minutes, for as long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> as the commissioners should think proper to let the engine remain in his possession. Of this sum of £615l. paid to Mr. Ramsden, £300l. was given him as a reward for the improvement made by him in discovering the engine, and the remaining £315l. for his giving up the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of it to the commissioners. The following <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the engine, is that given upon oath by Mr. Ramsden himself. "This engine consists of a large wheel of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-metal, supported on a mahogany stand, having three legs, which are strongly connected together by braces, so as to make it perfectly steady. On each leg of the stand is placed a conical friction-pully, whereon the dividing-wheel rests: to prevent the wheel from sliding off the friction-pulleys, the bell-metal centre under it turns in a socket on the top of the stand. "The circumference of the wheel is ratched or cut (by a method which will be described hereafter) into 2160 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, in which an endless screw acts. Six revolutions of the screw will move the wheel a space equal to one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. "Now a circle of brass being fixed on the screw arbor, having its circumference divided into 60 parts, each <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> will consequently answer to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the wheel of 10 seconds, six of them will be equal to a minute, &c. "Several different arbors of tempered <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> are truly ground into the socket in the centre of the wheel. The upper parts of the arbors that stand above the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> are turned of various sizes, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the centres of different pieces of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> to be divided. "When any instrument is to be divided, the centre of it is very exactly fitted on one of these arbors; and the instrument is fixed down to the plane of the dividing wheel by means of screws, which fit into holes made in the radii of the wheel for that purpose. "The instrument being thus fitted on the plane of the wheel, the frame which carries the dividing-point is connected at one end by finger-screws with the frame which carries the endless screw; while the other end embraces that part of the steel arbor, which stands above the instrument to be divided, by an angular notch in a piece of hardened steel: by this means both ends of the frame are kept perfectly steady and free from any shake. "The frame carrying the dividing-point or tracer, is made to slide on the frame which carries the endless screw to any distance from the centre of the wheel as the radius of the instrument to be divided may require, and may be there fastened by tightening two clamps; and the dividing-point or tracer being connected with the clamps by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> jointed frame, admits a free and easy motion towards or from the centre for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the divisions, without any lateral shake. "From what has been said, it appears, that an instrument thus fitted on the dividing-wheel may be moved to any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> by the screw and divided circle on its arbor, and that this angle may be marked on the limb of the instrument with the greatest exactness by the dividing-point or tracer, which can only move in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line tending to the centre, and is altogether freed from those inconveniences that attend cutting by means of a straight edge. This method of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> will also prevent any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> that might arise from an expansion or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the metal during the time of dividing. "The screw-frame is fixed on the top of a conical pillar, which turns freely round its axis, and also moves freely towards or from the centre of the wheel, so that the screw-frame may be entirely guided by the frame which connects it with the centre: by this means any eccentricity of the wheel and the arbor would not pro- produce any error in the dividing; and, by a particular contrivance, (which will be described hereafter,) the screw when pressed against the teeth of the wheel always moves <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to itself; so that a line joining the centre of the arbor and the tracer <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, will always make equal angles with the screw. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">Figure</a> 1 represents a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> view of the engine. Fig. 2 is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, of which fig. 3 represents a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECTION">section</a> on the line II A. The large wheel A is 45 inches in diameter, and has ten radii, each being supported by edge-bars, as represented in fig. 3. These bars and radii are connected by the circular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> B, 24 inches in diameter, and 3 deep; and, for greater strength, the whole is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in one piece in bell-metal. As the whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the wheel A rests on its ring B, the edge-bars are deepest where they join it; and from thence their depth diminishes, both towards the centre and the circumference, as represented in fig. 3. The surface of the wheel A was worked very even and flat, and its circumference turned true. The ring C, of fine brass, was fitted very exactly on the circumference of the wheel; and was fastened thereon with screws, which, after being screwed as tight as possible, were well riveted. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of a large chuck being turned very true and flat in the lathe, the flattened surface A of the wheel was fastened against it with hold-fasts; and the two surfaces and circumference of the ring C, a hole through the centre and the plane part round (b) it, and the lower edge of the ring B, were turned at the same time. D is a piece of hard bell-metal, having the hole, which receives the steel-arbor (d), made very straight and true. This bell-metal was turned very true on an arbor; and the face, which rests on the wheel at (b), was turned very flat, so that the steel arbor (d) might stand perpendicular to the plane of the wheel: this bell-metal was fastened to the wheel by six steel screws (l). A brass socket Z is fastened on the centre of the mahogany stand, and receives the lower part of the bell-metal piece D, being made to touch the bell-metal in a narrow part near the mouth, to prevent any obliquity of the wheel from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> the arbor; good fitting is by no means necessary here; since any shake in this socket will produce no bad effect, as will appear hereafter when we describe the cutting frame. The wheel was then put on its stand, the lower edge of the ring B resting on the circumference of three conical friction pulleys W, to facilitate its motion round its centre. The axis of one of these pulleys is in a line joining the centre of the wheel and the middle of the endless screw, and the other two placed so as to be at equal distances from each other. F is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of wood strongly fastened to one of the legs of the stand; the piece (g) is screwed to the upper side of the block, and has half holes, in which the transverse axis (h) turns: the half holes are kept together by the screws (i). The lower extremity of the conical pillar P terminates in a cylindric steel <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIN">pin</a> (k), which passes through and turns in the transverse axis (h), and is confined by a cheek and screw. To the upper end of the conical pillar is fastened the frame G, in which the endless screw turns: the pivots of the forewheels are formed in the manner of two frustrums of cones joined by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, as represented at X. These pivots are confined between half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, which press only on the conical parts, and do not touch the cylindric parts: the half holes are kept together by screws (a), which may be tightened at any time, to prevent the screw from shaking in the frame. On the screw arbor is a small wheel of brass K, Fig. 1, 2, having its outside edge divided into 60 parts, and 45 numbered at every 6th division with 1, 2, &c. to 10. The motion of this wheel is shown by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> (y) on Fig. 4 and 5, the screw frame G. H represents a part of the stand, having a parallel slit in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> towards the centre of the wheel, large enough to receive the upper part of the conical brass pillar P, which carries the screw and its frame: and as the resistance, when the wheel is moved by the endless screw, is against that side of the slit H which is towards the left-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, that side of the slit is faced with brass, and the pillar is pressed against it by a steel <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> on the opposite side: by this means the pillar is strongly supported laterally, and yet the screw may be easily pressed from or against the circumference of the wheel, and the pillar will turn freely on its axis to take any direction given it by the frame L. At each corner of the piece I are screws (n) of tempered steel, having polished conical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>: two of them turn in conical holes in the screw-frame near (o), and the points of the other two screws turn in holes in the piece Q; the screws (p) are of steel, which being tightened prevent the conical pointed screws from unturning when the frame is moved. L is a brass frame, which serves to connect the endless screw, its frame, &c. with the centre of the wheel: each arm of this frame is terminated by a steel screw, that may be passed through any of the holes (q) in the piece Q, as the thickness of work to be divided on Fig. 4, the wheel may require, and are fastened by the finger-nuts (r). At the other end of this frame is a flat piece of tempered steel (b), wherein is an angular notch: when Fig. 6, the endless screw is pressed against the teeth on the circumference of the wheel, which may be done by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the finger-screw S, to press against the spring (t), this notch embraces and presses against the steel arbor (d). This end of the frame may be raised or depressed by moving the prismatic slide (u), which may be fixed at any height by the four steel screws (v). The bottom of this slide has a notch (k), whose Fig. 1, 2, 6, plane is parallel to the endless-screw; and by the point of the arbor (d) resting in this notch, this end of the Fig. 3, frame is prevented from tilting. The screw S is prevented from unturning by tightening the finger-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> (w). The teeth on the circumference of the wheel were cut by the following method. Having considered what number of teeth on the circumference would be most convenient, which in this engine is 2160, or 360 multiplied by 6, I made two screws of the same dimensions, of tempered steel, in the manner hereafter described, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the threads being such as I knew by calculation would come within the limits of what might be turned off the circumference of the wheel: one of these screws, Ramsden's which was intended for ratching or cutting the teeth, Engine. Plate CCLVI. &c. cut in the manner of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a>. Then having a segment of a circle a little greater than 60 degrees, of about the same radius with the wheel, and the circumference made true, from a very fine centre, I described an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> near the edge, and set off the chord of 60 degrees on this arch. This segment was put in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the wheel, the edge of it was ratched, and the number of revolutions and parts of the screw contained between the interval of the 60 degrees were counted. The radius was corrected in the proportion of 360 revolutions, which ought to have been in 60 degrees, to the number actually found; and the radius, so corrected, was taken in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of beam-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a>: while the wheel was on the lath, one foot of the compasses was put in the centre, and with the other a circle was described on the ring; then half the depth of the threads of the screw being taken in dividers was set from this circle outwards, and another circle was described cutting this point; a hollow was then turned on the edge of the wheel of the same curvature as that of the screw at the bottom of the threads: the bottom of this hollow was turned to the same radius or distance from the centre of the wheel, as the outward of the two circles before-mentioned. The wheel was now taken off the lath; and the bell-metal piece D was screwed on as before directed, which after this ought not to be removed. From a very exact centre a circle was described Fig. 1, 2, 3 on the ring C, about \( \frac{4}{5} \) of an inch within where the bottom of the teeth would come. This circle was divided with the greatest exactness I was capable of, first into 5 parts, and each of these into 3. These parts were then bisected 4 times: (that is to say) supposing the whole circumference of the wheel to contain 2160 teeth, this being divided into 5 parts, each would contain 432 teeth; which being divided into 3 parts, each of them would contain 144; and this space bisected 4 times would give 72, 36, 18, and 9: therefore each of the last divisions would contain 9 teeth. But, as I was apprehensive some error might arise from quintuple division and trisection, in order to examine the accuracy of the divisions, I described another circle on the ring C, \( \frac{4}{5} \) inch within the former, and divided it by continual bisections, as 2160, 1080, 540, 270, 135, 67\(\frac{1}{2}\), and 33\(\frac{1}{2}\); and, as the fixed wire (to be described presently) crossed both the circles, I could examine their agreement at every 135 revolutions; (after ratching, could examine it at every 33\(\frac{1}{2}\)): but, not finding any sensible <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the two sets of divisions, I, for ratching, made choice of the former; and, as the coincidence of the fixed wire with an intersection could be more exactly determined than with a dot or division, I therefore made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of intersections in both circles before described. The arms of the frame L were connected by a thin piece of brass of \( \frac{1}{4} \) of an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, having a hole in the middle of \( \frac{7}{10} \) of an inch in diameter; across this hole a silver wire was fixed exactly in a line to the center of the wheel; the coincidence of this wire with the intersections was examined by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENS">lens</a> \( \frac{7}{10} \) inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a>, fixed in a tube which was attached to one of the arms Ramsden's L (a). Now a handle or winch being fixed on the end of the screw, the division marked 10 on the circle K was set to its index, and, by means of a clamp and adjusting screw for that purpose, the intersection marked 1 on the circle C was set exactly to coincide with the fixed wire; the screw was then carefully pressed against the circumference of the wheel, by turning the finger-screw S; then, removing the clamp, I turned the screw by its handle 9 revolutions, till the intersection marked 240 came nearly to the wire; then, unturning the finger-screw S, I released the screw from the wheel, and turned the wheel back till the intersection marked 2 exactly coincided with the wire, and, by means of the clamp before-mentioned, the division 10 on the circle being set to its index, the screw was pressed against the edge of the wheel by the finger-screw S; the clamps were removed, and the screw turned 9 revolutions till the intersection marked 1 nearly coincided with the fixed wire; the screw was released from the wheel by unturning the finger-screw S as before, the wheel was turned back till the intersection 3 coincided with the fixed wire; the division 10 on the circle being set to its index, the screw was pressed against the wheel as before, and the screw was turned 9 revolutions, till the intersection 2 nearly coincided with the fixed wire, and the screw was released; and I proceeded in this manner till the teeth were marked round the whole circumference of the wheel. This was repeated three times round, to make the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of the screw deeper. I then ratched the wheel round continually in the same direction without ever disengaging the screw; and, in ratching the wheel about 300 times round, the teeth were finished. Now it is evident, if the circumference of the wheel was even one tooth or ten minutes greater than the screw would require, this error would in the first instance be reduced to \( \frac{1}{34} \) part of a revolution or two seconds and a half; and these errors or inequalities of the teeth were equally distributed round the wheel at the distance of 9 teeth from each other. Now, as the screw in ratching had continually hold of several teeth at the same time, and, these constantly changing, the abovementioned inequalities soon corrected themselves, and the teeth were reduced to a perfect equality. The piece of brass which carries the wire was now taken away, and the cutting screw was also removed, and a plain one (hereafter described) put in its place: on one end of the screw is a small brass circle, having its edge divided into 60 equal parts, and numbered at every fifth division, as beforementioned. On the other end of the screw is a ratchet-wheel C, having 60 teeth, covered by the hollowed circle (d), which carries two clicks that catch upon the opposite sides of the ratchet when the screw is to be moved forwards. The cylinder S turns on a strong steel arbor F, which passes through and is firmly screwed to the piece Y: this piece, for greater firmness, is attached to the screw-frame G by the braces (v): a spiral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> or thread is cut on the outside of the cylinder S, which serves both for holding the string, and also giving motion to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> J on its centre by means of a steel tooth (u), that works (b) The intersections are marked for the sake of illustration, though properly invisible, they lying under the brass plate. Ramden's works between the threads of the spiral. To the lever is attached a strong steel pin (m), on which a brass socket (r) turns; this socket passes through a slit in the piece (p), and may be tightened in any part of the slit by the finger-nut (f); this piece serves to regulate the number of revolutions of the screw for each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> of the treadle R. "T," is a brass box containing a spiral spring; a strong gut is fastened and turned 3 or 4 times round the circumference of this box; the gut then passes several times round the cylinder S, and from thence down to the treadle R. Now, when the treadle is pressed down, the string pulls the cylinder S round its axis, and the clicks catching hold of the teeth on the ratchet carry the screw round with it, till, by the tooth (n) working in the spiral groove, the lever J is brought near the wheel (d), and the cylinder stopped by the screw-head (x) striking on the top of the lever J; at the same time the spring is wound up by the other end of the gut passing round the box T. Now, when the foot is taken off the treadle, the spring unbending itself pulls back the cylinder, the clicks leaving the ratchet and screw at rest till the piece (t) strikes on the end of the piece (p); the number of revolutions of the screw at each tread is limited by the number of revolutions the cylinder is allowed to turn back before the stop strikes on the piece (p). When the endless screw was moved round it axis with a considerable velocity, it would continue that motion a little after the cylinder S was stopped; to prevent this the angular lever n was made; that when the lever J comes near to stop the screw (x), it, by a small chamfer, presses down the piece x of the angular lever; this brings the other end n of the same lever forwards, and stops the endless screw by the steel pin striking upon the top of it; the foot of the lever is raised again by a small spring pressing on the brace (v). "D," two clamps, connected by the piece a, slide one on each arm of the frame L, and may be fixed at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> by the four finger-screws t, which press against steel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> to avoid spoiling the arms; the piece (q) is made to turn without shake between the two conical pointed screws (f), which are preventing from unturning by tightening the finger-nuts N. The piece M is made to turn on the piece (q), by the conical pointed screws (f) resting in the hollow centers (e). As there is frequent occasion to cut divisions on inclined planes, for that purpose the piece y, in which the tracer is fixed, has a conical axis at each end, which turn in half holes; when the tracer is set to any inclination, it may be fixed there by tightening the steel screws s. Description of the Engine by which the endless screw of the Dividing Engine was cut. Fig. 9 represents this engine of its full dimensions seen from one side. Fig. 8. The upper side of the same as seen from above. A represents a triangular <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of steel, to which the triangular holes in the pieces B and C are accurately fitted, and may be fixed on any part of the bar by the screws D. E is a piece of steel wherein the screw is intended to be cut; which, after being hardened and tempered, has its pivots turned in the form of two frustums of cones, as represented in the drawings of the dividing engine (fig. 5). These pivots were exactly fitted to the half holes F and T, which were kept together by the screws Z. H represents a screw of untempered steel, having a pivot I, which turns in the hole K. At the other end of the screw is a hollow centre, which receives the hardened conical point of the steel pin M. When this point is sufficiently pressed against the screw, to prevent its shaking, the steel pin may be fixed by tightening the screws Y. N is a cylindric nut, moveable on the screw H; which, to prevent any shake, may be tightened by the screws O. This nut is connected with the saddle-piece P by means of the intermediate universal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> W, thro' which the arbor of the screw H passes. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> view of this piece, with a section across the screw-arbor, is represented at X. This joint is connected with the nut by means of two steel slips S, which turn on pins between the cheeks T on the nut N. The other ends of these slips S turn in like manner on pins (a). One axis of this joint turns in a hole in the cock (b), which is fixed to the saddle-piece; and the other turns in a hole (d), made for that purpose in the same piece on which the cock (b) is fixed. By this means, when the screw is turned round, the saddle-piece will slide uniformly along the triangular bar A. K is a small triangular bar of well-tempered steel, which slides in a groove of the same form on the saddle-piece P. The point of this bar or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTER">cutter</a> is formed to the shape of the thread intended to be cut on the endless screw. When the cutter is set to take proper hold of the intended screw, it may be fixed by tightening the screw (e), which press the two pieces of brass G upon it. Having measured the circumference of the dividing-wheel, I found it would require a screw about one thread in a hundred coarser than the guide-screw H. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> on the guide-screw arbor H, and that on the steel E, on which the screw was to be cut, were proportioned to each other to produce that effect, by giving the wheel L 198 teeth, and the wheel Q 200. These wheels communicated with each other by means of the intermediate wheel R, which also served to give the threads on the two screws the same direction. The saddle-piece P is confined on the bar A by means of the pieces (g), and may be made to slide with a proper degree of tightness by the screws (n). Ramsden's Portable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BAROMETER">Barometer</a>. See Barometer in the Appendix. Ramsay (Allan), the Scots pastoral poet, was a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARBER">barber</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in the early part of the present century. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, however, has justly raised him to a degree of fame that may in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> be considered as a recompense for the frowns of fortune. His songs are in universal esteem; as is also the only dramatic performance attributed to him, viz., Patie and Roger, or The Gentle Shepherd, a Scots pastoral. He died in 1743; and was father to the ingenious Mr Ramsay, a celebrated painter of the present <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and who has likewise distinguished himself by some well-written tracts on various branches RAN Ramsay (Andrew Michael), generally known by the name of the Chevalier Ramsay, was a polite Scots writer, born of a good family at Ayre, in 1686. His good parts and learning recommended him to be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the son of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Weems; after which, conceiving a disgust at the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> in which he had been educated, he in the same ill-humour reviewed other Christian churches; and, finding none to his liking, retired for a while in Deifim. While he was in this uncertain state of mind, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; where, falling into the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of one Poiret a mystic divine, he received the infection of mysticism: which prompted him to consult M. Fenelon, the famed archbishop of Cambrai, who had imbibed principles of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; and who gained him over to the Catholic religion in 1709. The subsequent course of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> received its direction from his friendship and connections with this prelate; and, being appointed governor to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de Chateau Thierry, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> de Turenne, he was made a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the order of St Lazarus. He was sent for to Rome by the chevalier de St George, to undertake the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of his children; but he found so many intrigues and diffusions on his arrival there in 1724, that he obtained the Chevalier's leave to return to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He died in 1743, in the office of intendant to the duke of Bouillon, prince de Turenne. The most <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> work of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> is the Travels of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>, which has been several times printed in English.

RAMUS

Pages 308-308

in general, denotes a branch of anything, as of a tree, an artery, &c. Ramus (<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>), was one of the most famous professors of the 16th century. He was born in Picardy in 1515. A thirst for learning prompted him to go to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> when very young, and he was admitted a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Navarre. Spending the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> in waiting on his masters, and the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the night in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, he made such surprising progress, that, when he took his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, he offered to maintain a quite opposite doctrine to that of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>. This raised him many enemies; and the two first books he published, Institutiones Dialecticae, and Arisotelicae Animadversiones, occasioned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disturbances in the university of Paris: and the opposition against him was not a little heightened by his deserting the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and professing that of the Reformed. Being thus forced to retire from Paris, he visited the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Germany, and received great honours wherever he came. He returned to France in 1571, and lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> miserably in the massacre of St Bartholomew's day. He was a great orator, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of universal learning, and endowed with very fine moral qualities. He published many books, which Teissier enumerates.

RANA

Pages 308-311

the frog, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMPHIBIA">amphibia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REPTILIA">reptilia</a>. The body is naked, furnished with four feet, and without any tail. There are 17 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. The most remarkable are, 1. The temporaria, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> frog. This is an animal so well known, that it needs no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>; but some of its properties are very singular. Its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, or power of taking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> leaps, is remarkably <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and it is the best swimmer of all four-footed animals. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> hath finely adapted its parts for those ends, the fore members of the body being very lightly made, the hind legs and thighs very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and furnished with very strong muscles.
