While in a tadpole state, it is entirely a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> animal; the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> is performed in that element, as may be seen in every pond during spring, when the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> remains oppressed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of days. The work of propagation is extremely singular, it being certain that the frog has not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENIS">penis</a> intrans. There appears a strong <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> between a certain class of the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> and those animals; for it is well known, that when the female frog deposits its spawn, the male instantaneously impregnates it with what we may call a farina secundans, in the same manner as the palm tree conveys fructification to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of the female, which would otherwise be barren. As soon as the frogs are released from their tadpole state, they immediately take to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> has been hot, and there <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> any refreshing showers, you may see the ground for a considerable space perfectly blackened by myriads of these animalcules, seeking for some secure lurking places. Some philosophers, not giving themselves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to examine into this phenomenon, imagined them to have been <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, and showered on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; but had they, like our <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a>, but traced them to the next pool, they would have found a better solution of the difficulty. As frogs adhere closely to the backs of their own species, so we know they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> do the same by fish. Walton mentions a strange story of their destroying British pike; but that they will injure, if not entirely kill carp, is a fact indubitable, from the following relation. A very few years ago, on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> a pond belonging to Mr Pit, of Encomb, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, great numbers of the carp were found each with a frog mounted on it, the hind legs clinging to the back, and the fore legs fixed in the corner of each eye of the fish, which were thin and greatly wasted, seized by carrying so disagreeable a load. These frogs Mr Pennant supposes to have been males disappointed of a mate. The croaking of frogs is well known; and from that in fenny countries they are distinguished by ludicrous titles: thus they are styled Dutch nightingales, and Boflon wailers. Yet there is a time of the year when they become <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a>, neither croaking nor opening their mouths for a whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>: this happens in the hot season, and that is in many places known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people by the name of the paddock <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. It is said, that during that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> their mouths are so closed, that no force (without killing the animal) will be capable of opening them. These, as well as other reptiles, feed but a small space of the year. The food of this genus is flies, insects, and snails. Toads are said to feed also on bees, and to do great injury to those useful insects. During winter, frogs and toads remain in a torpid state: the last of which will dig into the earth, and cover themselves with almost the same agility as the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOLE">mole</a>. 2. The eculenta, or edible frog, differs from the former, in having a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> protuberance in the middle of of the back, forming a very sharp <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>. Its colours are also more vivid, and its marks more distinct; the ground <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> or yellowish green, marked with rows of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> spots from the head to the rump. This, and (Mr Pennant thinks) the former, are eaten. He has seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> whole hampers full, which the vendors were preparing for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, by skinning and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the fore-parts, the loins and legs only being kept; but his strong dislike to these reptiles prevented a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> into the species. 3. In the country of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>, and some other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, there is a very large species of frogs called the bull-frog. These make a monstrous roaring noise like a bull, only somewhat more hoarse. Their size is superior to that of any other of the genus, and they can spring forward three yards at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>. By this means they will equal in speed a very good <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> in its swiftest course. Their places of abode are ponds, or bogs with stagnant water; but they never frequent streams. When many of them are together, they make such a horrid noise, that two people cannot understand each other's speech. They croak all together, and then stop for a little and begin again. It seems as if they had a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> among them: for when he begins to croak, all the others follow; and when he stops, they also become silent. When this captain gives the signal for stopping, you hear a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> like pooh coming from him. In the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>-time they seldom make any great noise unless the sky is covered; but in the night-time they may be heard at the distance of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and an half. When they croak, they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> near the surface of the water, under the bushes, and have their heads out of the water. By going slowly, therefore, one may get up almost quite close to them before they go away. As soon as they are quite under water, they think themselves safe, though it be ever so shallow. These creatures kill and eat young ducklings and goslings, and sometimes carry off chickens that come too near the water; when beaten, they cry out almost like little children. As soon as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> begins to grow a little cool in autumn, they hide themselves under the mud in the bottom of stagnant waters, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> there torpid during the winter. As soon as the weather grows mild towards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, they begin to get out of their holes and croak. 4. The buf, or toad, is the most deformed and hideous of all animals. The body is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; the back flat, and covered with a pimply dusky hide; the belly large, faggoting, and swelling out; the legs short, and its pace laboured and crawling; its retreat gloomy and filthy: in short, its general appearance is such as to strike one with disgust and horror. Yet it is said by those who have <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to view it with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, that its eyes are fine: to this it seems that Shakespeare alludes, when he makes his Juliet remark, Some say the lark and loathed toad change eyes: As if they would have been better bestowed on so charming a frogster than on this raucous reptile. But the hideous appearance of the toad is such as to make this one advantageous feature overlooked, and to have rendered it in all ages an object of horror, and the origin of most tremendous inventions. Aelian makes its venom so potent, that basilisk-like, it conveyed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by its very look and breath; but Juvenal is content with making the Roman ladies who were weary of their husbands, form a potion from its entrails, in order to get rid of the good <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> begat others of a more dreadful nature; for in after-times <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> gave it preternatural powers, and made it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ingredient in the incantations of nocturnal hags. This animal was believed by some old writers to have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in its head, fraught with great virtues medical and magical: it was distinguished by the name of the reptile, and called the toad-stone, bufoniter, crapaudine, krottenstein; but all its fancied powers vanished on the discovery of its being nothing but the fossil tooth of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>*, or of some other flat-toothed fish, not unfrequent in our <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> as well as several other countries. But these fables have been long exploded. And as to the notion of its being a poisonous animal, it is probable, that its excessive <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a>, joined to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> it has of emitting a juice from its pimples, and a dusky liquid from its hind parts, is the foundation of the report. That it has any noxious qualities there seem to have been no proofs in the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> satisfactory, tho' we have heard many strange relations on that point. On the contrary, there have been many who have taken them in their naked <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and held them long without receiving the least injury: it is also well known that quacks have eaten them, and have besides squeezed their juices into a glass and drank them with impunity. We may say also, that these reptiles are a common food to many animals; to buzzards, owls, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> plovers, ducks, and snakes, who would not touch them were they in any degree noxious. So far from having venomous qualities, they have of late been considered as if they had beneficent ones; particularly in the cure of the most terrible of diseases, the cancer, by suction: (See British Zoology, vol. iii. Append. p. 389. et seq.) But, from all circumstances, they seem only, as Mr Pennant observes, to have rendered a horrible complaint more loathsome. The most full information concerning the nature and qualities of this animal is contained in the following letters from Mr Arscott and Mr Pittfield to Dr Milles. "It would give me great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> (says Mr Arscott) to be able to inform you of any particulars worthy Mr Pennant's notice, concerning the toad who lived so many years with us, and was so great a favourite. The greatest curiosity in it was its becoming so remarkably tame. It had frequented some steps before the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a>-door some years before my acquaintance commenced with it, and had been admired by my father for its size (which was of the largest I ever met with), who constantly paid it a visit every evening. I knew it myself above 30 years; and by constantly feeding it, brought it to be so tame, that it always came to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, and looked up as if expecting to be taken up and brought upon the table, where I always fed it with insects of all sorts: it was fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> maggots, which I kept in bran; it would follow them, and, when within a proper distance, would fix its eye, and remain motionless for near a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a minute, as if preparing for the stroke, which was an instantaneous throwing its tongue at a great distance upon the insect, which stuck to the tip by a glutinous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> is quicker than the eye can follow (a). "I always imagined that the root of its tongue was placed in the forepart of its under jaw, and the tip towards its throat, by which the motion must be a half circle; by which, when its tongue recovered its situation, the insect at the tip would be brought to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of deglutition. I was confirmed in this by never observing any internal motion in its mouth, excepting one swallow the instant its tongue returned. Possibly I might be mistaken; for I never dissected one, but contented myself with opening its mouth, and slightly inspecting it. "You may imagine, that a toad, generally detested, (although one of the most inoffensive of all animals) so much taken notice of and befriended, excited the curiosity of all comers to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, who all desired to see it fed; so that even ladies so far conquered the horrors infilled into them by nurses, as to desire to see it. This produced innumerable and improbable reports, making it as large as the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of a hat, &c. &c." The following are answers from the same <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> to some queries proposed by Mr Pennant. "Firstly, I cannot say how long my father had been acquainted with the toad before I knew it; but when I first was acquainted with it, he used to mention it as the old toad I've known so many years; I can answer for 36 years. "Secondly, No toads that I ever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> appeared in the winter season. The old toad made its appearance as soon as the warm weather came, and I always concluded it retired to some dry <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a> to repose till the spring. When we new-lay'd the steps, I had two holes made in the third step on each, with a hollow of more than a yard long for it, in which I imagine it slept, as it came from thence at its first appearance. "Thirdly, It was seldom provoked: neither that toad (nor the multitudes I have seen tormented with great cruelty) ever showed the least desire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> by spitting or emitting any juice from their pimples. Sometimes, upon taking it up, it would let out a great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of clear water, which, as I have often seen it do the same upon the steps when quite quiet, was certainly its urine, and no more than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> evacuation. "Fourthly, A toad has no particular enmity for the spider; he used to eat five or six with his millipedes (which I take to be its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> food) that I generally provided for it before I found out that flesh maggots, by their continual motion, was the most tempting bait; but, when offered, it eat blowing flies and humble bees that come from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAT">rat</a>-tailed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGGOT">maggot</a> in gutters, or in short any insect that moved. I imagine, if a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEE">bee</a> was to be put before a toad, it would certainly eat it to its cost; but as bees are seldom stirring at the same time that toads are, they can seldom come in their way, as they seldom appear after <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>-rising or before sun-set. In the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the day they will come to the mouth of their hole, I believe, for air. I once from my parlour window observed a large toad I had in the bank of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOWLING">bowling</a>-green, about 12 at noon, a very hot day, very busy and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> upon the grass; so uncommon an appearance made me go out to see what it was, when I found an innumerable swarm of winged ants had dropped round his hole, which temptation was as irresistible as a turtle would be to a luxurious <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>. "Fifthly, Whether our toad ever propagated its species, I know not; rather think not, as it always appeared well, and not lessened in bulk, which it must have done, I should think, if it had discharged so large a quantity of spawn as toads generally do. The females that are to propagate in the spring, I imagine, instead of retiring to dry holes, go into the bottom of ponds, and lie torpid among the weeds: for to my great surprize, in the middle of the winter, having for amusement put a long pole into my pond, and twisted it till it had gathered a large volume of weed, on taking it off I found many toads; and having cut some asunder with my <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, by accident, to get off the weed, found them full of spawn not thoroughly formed. I am not positive, but think there were a few males in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>; I know there are 30 males (b) to one female, 12 or 14 of whom I have seen clinging round a female: I have often disengaged her, and put her to a solitary male, to see with what eagerness he would <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> her. They impregnate the spawn as it is drawn (c) out in long strings, like a necklace, many yards (a) This rapid capture of its prey might give occasion to the report of its fascinating powers, Linnæus says, In- fecta in faucis fascino revocat. (b) Mr John Hunter has assured me, that during his residence at Belleisle, he dissected some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of toads, yet never met with a single female among them. (c) I was incredulous as to the obstetrical offices of the male toad; but since the end is so well accounted for, and the fact established by such good authority, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> must take place. Mr Demours, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the French Academy, as translated by Dr Templeman, vol. i. p. 371, has been very particular in respect to the male toad as acting the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of an accoucheur; his account is curious, and claims a place here. "In the evening of one of the long days in summer, Mr Demours, being in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s garden, perceived two toads coupled together at the edge of an hole, which was formed in part by a great stone at the top. "Curiosity drew him to see what was the occasion of the motions he observed, when two facts equally new surprized him. The first was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> difficulty the female had in laying her eggs, inasmuch that she did not seem capable of being delivered of them without some assistance. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> was, that the male was mounted on the back of the female, and exerted all his strength with his hinder feet in pulling out the eggs, whilst his fore-feet embraced her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. "In order to apprehend the manner of his working in the delivery of the female, the reader must observe, that the paws of these animals, as well those of the fore-feet as of the hinder, are divided into several toes, which can perform the office of fingers. "It must be remarked likewise, that the eggs of this species of toads are included each in a membranous coat that is very firm, in which is contained the embryo; and that these eggs, which are <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> and about two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in length, being fastened one to another by a short but very strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, form a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPLET">chaplet</a>, the beads of which are distant from each other about the half of their length. It is by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> this cord with his paw that the male performs the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> of a midwife, and acquires himself in it with a dexterity that one would not expect from so lumpish an animal." yards long, not in a large quantity of jelly, like frogs spawn. "Sixthly, Insects being their food, I never saw any toad show any liking or dislike to any plant (p). "Seventhly, I hardly remember any persons taking it up except my father and myself; I do not know whether it had any particular <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to us. "Eighthly, In respect to its end, I answer this last query. Had it not been for a tame raven, I make no doubt but it would have been now living; who one day seeing it at the mouth of its hole, pulled it out, and although I rescued it, pulled out one eye, and hurt it so, that notwithstanding its living a twelve-month it never enjoyed itself, and had a difficulty of taking its food, missing the mark for want of its eye: before that accident, it had all the appearance of perfect <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>." 5. The rubeta, or natter-jack, frequents dry and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> places: it is found on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PUTNEY">Putney</a> common, and also near Revelsby <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>. It never leaps, neither does it crawl with the slow pace of a toad, but its motion is liker to running. Several are found commonly together, and, like others of the genus, they appear in the evenings. The upper part of the body is of a dirty <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, clouded with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, and covered with porous pimples of unequal sizes: on the back is a yellow line. The upper side of the body is of a paler hue, marked with black spots, which are rather rough. On the fore-feet are four divided toes; on the hind five, a little webbed. The length of the body is two inches and a quarter; the breadth, one and a quarter; the length of the fore-legs, one inch one-sixth; of the hind-legs, two inches. We are indebted to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks, Esq; for this account. 7. The pipal, or Surinam toad, is more ugly than even the common one. The body is flat and broad; the head small; the jaws, like those of a mole, are extended, and evidently formed for rooting in the ground: the skin of the neck forms a sort of wrinkled collar: the colour of the head is of a dark chestnut, and the eyes are small: the back, which is very broad, is of a lightish grey, and seems covered over with a number of small eyes, which are round, and placed at nearly equal distances. These eyes are very different from what they seem; they are the animal's eggs, covered with their shells, and placed there for hatching. These eggs are buried deep in the skin, and in the beginning of incubation but <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> appear; and are very visible when the young animal is about to burst from its confinement. They are of a reddish, shining yellow colour; and the spaces between them are full of small warts, resembling pearls. This is their situation previous to their coming forth; but nothing so much demands our admiration as the manner of their production. The eggs, when formed in the ovary, are sent, by some internal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, which anatomists have not hitherto described, to lie and come to maturity under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONY">bony</a> substance of the back: in this state they are impregnated by the male, whose seed finds its way by pores very singularly contrived, and pierces not only the skin but the periosteum: the skin, however, is still apparently entire, and forms a very thick covering over the whole brood; but as they advance to maturity, at different intervals, one after another, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a> seems to start forward, and burgeons from the back, becomes more yellow, and at last breaks; when the young one puts forth its head: it still, however, keeps its situation until it has acquired a proper degree of strength, and then it leaves the shell, but still continues to keep upon the back of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. In this manner the pipal is seen travelling with her wonderful family on her back, in all the different stages of maturity. Some of the strange progeny, not yet come to sufficient perfection, appear quite torpid, and as yet without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the egg: others seem just beginning to rise through the skin; here peeping forth from the shell; and there, having entirely forlorn their prison: some are sporting at large upon the parent's back, and others descending to the ground to try their own fortune below. The male pipal is every way larger than the female, and has the skin left tightly drawn round the body. The whole body is covered with pustules, resembling pearls; and the belly, which is of a bright yellow, seems as if it were sewed up from the throat to the vent, a beam being seen to run in that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. This animal, like the rest of the frog kind, is most probably harmless.

RANCID

Pages 311-311

denotes a fatty substance that is become <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> musty, or that has contracted an ill smell by being kept <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>.

RANDOLPH

Pages 311-311

an eminent English poet in the 17th century, born in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a> 1605. He was educated at Westminster and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and very early distinguished for his excellent genius; for at about <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> ten years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> he wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Incarnation of our Saviour, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. His subsequent writings established his character, and gained him the esteem and friendship of some of the greatest men of that age; particularly of Ben Jonson, who adopted him one of his sons in the mules. He died in 1644, and was honourably interred. He wrote, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a> Looking-glass, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>. 2. Amyntas, or the Impossible Dowry, a pastoral, acted before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>. 3. Arlituppus, or the Jovial <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">Philosopher</a>. 4. The Conceited Pedlar. 5. The Jealous Lovers, a comedy. 6. Hey for Honesty, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with Knavery, a comedy; and several poems.

RANDOM SHOT

Pages 311-312

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUNNERY">gunnery</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> made when the muzzle of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a> is raised above the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> line, and is not designed to shoot directly <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> point-blank. The presence of the observer did not a little discompose the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a>: for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he stopped short, and threw on the curious impertinence a fixed look that marked his disquietness and fear; but he soon returned to his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> with more precipitation than before, and a moment after he appeared undetermined whether he should continue it or not. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> likewise discovered her uneasiness at the sight of the stranger, by motions that interrupted sometimes the male in his operation. At length, whether the silence and steady posture of the spectator had diffused their fear, or that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> was urgent, the male resumed his work with the same vigour, and successfully performed his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>. (b) This question arose from an assertion of Linnæus, that the toad delighted in filthy herbs. Delectatur cotulae, aliae, flachyde fetidi. The unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> of the animal seems to be the only ground of this as well as another misrepresentation, of its conveying a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a> with its pimples, its touch, and even its breath. Verruca lacteifcentes venenata infuse talia, anhebita. The utmost random of any piece is about ten times as far as the bullet <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> go point-blank. The bullet will go farther when the piece is mounted to about 45° above the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> range. See Gunnery.

RANGE

Pages 312-312

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUNNERY">gunnery</a>, the path of a bullet, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the line it describes from the mouth of the piece to the point where it lodges. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the piece <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in a line <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon, it is called the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> range; if it be mounted to 45°, it is said to have the utmost range, all others between 90 and 45° are called the intermediate ranges.

RANGER

Pages 312-312

a sworn officer of a forest, appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s letters-patent; whose business is to walk through his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, to drive back the deer out of the purlieus, &c. and to present all trespasses within his jurisdiction at the next forest-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>.

RANK

Pages 312-313

the order <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> assigned a person suitable to his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> or merit. **Rank**, is a straight line made by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of a battalion, or squadron, drawn up side by side: this order was established for the marches, and for regulating the different bodies of troops and officers which compose an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. **Rank and Precedence**, in the army and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, as follow: *Engineers Rank.* <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">Chief</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-colonel; sub-director, as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>; engineer in ordinary, as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>; engineer extraordinary, as captain-lieutenant; sub-engineer, as lieutenant; practitioner-engineer, as ensign. *Navy Rank.* <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a>, or commander in chief of his majesty's fleet, has the rank of a field-marshal; admirals, with their flags on the main-topmast head, rank with generals of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and foot; vice-admirals, with lieutenant-generals; rear-admirals, as major-generals; commodores, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> pendants, as brigadier-generals; captains of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>-ships, after three years from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a> of their first <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, as colonels; other captains, as commanding post-ships, as lieutenant-colonels; captains, not taking post, as majors; lieutenants, as captains. ### Rank between the Army, Navy, and Governors. | Army | Navy | Governors | |-----------------------|-------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------| | General in chief | Admiral in chief | Commander in chief of the forces in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> | | Generals of horse | Admiral with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> at the main-top-mast. | Captain-general of provinces | | Lieutenant-generals | Vice-admirals | Lieutenant-generals of provinces | | Major-generals | Rear-admirals | Lieutenant-governors and presidents | | Colonels | Post-captains of 3 years | Lieutenant-governors not commanding | | Lieutenant-colonels | Post-captains | Governors of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> colonies | | Majors | Captains | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">Deputy</a> governors | | Captains | Lieutenants | Established by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, 1760 | **Doubling of the Ranks,** is the placing two ranks in one, frequently used in the manoeuvres of a regiment. **Rank and Files,** are the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> and vertical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of soldiers when drawn up for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">RANSOM</a>,** a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> paid for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a> of a slave, or the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of a prisoner of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>. In our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>-books, ransom is also used for a sum paid for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> of some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> offence, and to obtain the offender's liberty. **RANULA,** a tumour under a child's tongue, which, like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGATURE">ligature</a>, hinders it from speaking or sucking. **RANUNCULUS,** crowfoot; a genus of the polygamia order, belonging to the polyandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. **<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">Species</a>.** There are near 40 different species of this genus, six or eight of which claim general esteem as flowery plants for ornamenting the gardens, and a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> weeds in the fields, waters, and pasture ground, not having merit for garden culture. Of the garden kinds, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sort is the Asiatic or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> and Persian ranunculus, which comprises many hundred varieties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, most beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of various colours: but several other species having varieties with fine double flowers, make a good appearance in a collection, though as those of each species consist only of one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, others <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, they are inferior to the Asiatic ranunculus, which is large, and diversified a thousand ways in rich colours, in different varieties. However, all the garden kinds in general, effect a very agreeable diversity in appearance in the flower compartments, &c. and they being all very hardy, succeed in any open beds and borders, &c. **Culture.** The Asiatic species in all its varieties <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> succeed in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, rich, garden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; but the florists often prepare a particular compost for the fine varieties, consisting of good garden-mould or pasture-earth, sward and all, a fourth-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of rotted cow-dung, and the like portion of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-fland; and with this they prepare beds four feet wide and two deep: however, in default of such compost, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> beds of any good light earth of your garden; or, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> necessary, it may be made light and rich with a portion of drift-sand and and rotten dung, cow-dung is most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> recommended; but they will also thrive in beds of well-wrought <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-garden earth, and they often prosper well in the common flower-borders. The season for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> the roots is both in autumn and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; the autumn plantings generally flower stronger and sooner by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> at least, and are succeeded by the spring planting in May and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. Perform the autumnal planting in October, and early part of November, but some plant towards the latter end of September in order to have a very early bloom; but those planted in that month and beginning of October often come up with rank leaves soon after, in winter, so as to require protection in hard frosts; those however planted about the middle or latter end of October, and beginning of November, rarely shoot up strong till towards spring, and will not require so much care of covering during winter; and the spring planting may be performed the end of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> or beginning of February, or as soon as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> is settled; they will not require any trouble of covering, and will succeed the autumnal plants regularly in bloom, and will flower in good perfection. Thus by two or three different plantings you may obtain a succession of these beautiful flowers in constant bloom from April till the middle of June; but the autumnal plants, for the general part, not only flower stronger, but the roots increase more in size, and furnish the best offsets for propagation; it is, however, proper to plant both in spring and autumn. Prepare for the choicest sorts, four-feet beds of light earth, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> the surface smooth; then plant the roots in rows lengthwise the beds, either by drilling them in two inches deep, and six inches distance in the row, and the rows six or eight asunder; or may plant them by bedding-in, or by dibble-planting, the same depth and distance. Those designed for the borders should be planted generally towards the spring, in little clumps or patches, three, four, or five roots in each, putting them in either with a dibble or trowel, two or three inches deep, and three or four asunder in each patch, and the patches from about three to five or ten feet distance, placing them rather forward in the border. Propagation. All the varieties of the Asiatic ranunculus propagate abundantly by offsets from the root, and new varieties are gained by seed.—1. By offsets. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> for separating the offsets is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> when the flower is past, and the leaves and stalks are withered; then taking up all the roots in dry weather, separate the offsets from each main root, and after drying the whole gradually in some shady <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> room, put them up in bags till the autumn and spring seasons of planting; then plant them as before, placing all the offsets in separate beds: many of them will blow the first year, but in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> they will all flower in good perfection.—2. By seed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">Save</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of seed from the finest semi-double flowers, and sow it either in August, or in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> or April, though, to save trouble of winter-covering, some prefer the spring; it should be sowed in light rich mould, either in pots or in an east border, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> very shallow flat drills five or six inches asunder, in which sow the seeds thinly, and cover them lightly with earth, giving frequent refreshments of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> in dry weather, and in a month or six weeks the plants will rise with Rapacious, small leaves; observing to continue the light waterings in dry weather, to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> moist during their summer's growth to increase the size of the roots; and in June when the leaves decay, take up the roots and preserve them till the season for planting, then plant them in common beds, as before directed, and they will flower the spring following, when all the doubles of good properties should be marked, and the singles thrown away. The juice of many species of ranunculus is so acrid as to raise blisters on the skin, and yet the roots may be eaten with safety when boiled.

RAPE

Pages 313-315

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the carnal knowledge of a woman forcibly and against her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>. This, by the Jewish law, was punished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> the damsel was betrothed to another <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>: and, in case she was not betrothed, then a heavy fine of fifty shekels was to be paid to the damsel's father, and she was to be the wife of the ravisher all the days of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; without that power of divorce, which was in general permitted by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOSAIC_LAW">Mosaic law</a>. The civil law punishes the crime of ravishment with death and confiscation of goods; under which it includes both the offence of forcible <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDUCTION">abduction</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> taking away a woman from her friends; and also the present offence of forcibly dishonouring her; either of which, without the other, is in that law sufficient to constitute a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> crime. Also the stealing away a woman from her parents or guardians, and debauching her, is equally penal by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s edict, whether the consent or is forced. And this, in order to take away from women every opportunity of offending in this way; whom the Roman laws suppose never to go astray, without the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEDUCTION">seduction</a> and arts of the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; and therefore, by restraining and making so highly penal the solicitations of the men, they meant to secure effectually the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the women. But our English law does not entertain quite such sublime <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the honour of either sex, as to lay the blame of a mutual fault upon one of the transgressors only; and therefore makes it a necessary ingredient in the crime of rape, that it must be against the woman's will. Rape was punished by the Saxon laws, particularly those of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Athelstan, with death: which was also agreeable to the old Gothic or Scandinavian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. But this was afterwards thought too hard: and in its stead another severe, but not capital, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> was inflicted by William the Conqueror, viz. caltiration and loss of eyes; which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till after Bracton wrote, in the reign of Henry the Third. But in order to prevent malicious accusations, it was then the law, (and, it seems, still continues to be so in appeals of rape), that the woman should, immediately after, go to the next town, and there make discovery to some credible persons of the injury she has suffered; and afterwards should acquaint the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> of the hundred, the coroners, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, with the outrage. This seems to correspond in some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> with the laws of Scotland and Arragon, which require that complaint must be made within 24 hours: though afterwards by statute Westm. i. c. 13. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of limitation in England. England was extended to 40 days. At present there is no time of limitation fixed; for, as it is usually now punished by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of the king, the maxim of law takes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, that "nullum tempus occurrit regi;" but the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURY">jury</a> will rarely give <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STALE">stale</a> complaint. During the former <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> also it was held for law, that the woman (by consent of the judge and her parents) might redeem the offender from the execution of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, by accepting him for her husband; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he also was willing to agree to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, but not otherwise. In the 3 Edw. I. by the statute Westm. 1. c. 13., the punishment of rape was much mitigated; the offence itself, of ravishing a damsel within <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, (that is, twelve years old) either with her consent or without, or of any other woman against her will, being reduced to a trespass, if not prosecuted by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> within 40 days, and subjecting the offender only to two years imprisonment, and a fine at the king's will. But, this lenity being productive of the most terrible consequences, it was, in ten years afterwards, 13 Edw. I. found necessary to make the offence of forcible rape felony by statute Westm. 2. c. 34. And by statute 18 Eliz. c. 7, it is made felony without benefit of clergy: as is also the abominable wickedness of carnally knowing or abusing any woman child under the age of ten years; in which case the consent or non-consent is immaterial, as by reason of her tender years she is incapable of judgment and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. Sir Matthew Hale is indeed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that such profligate actions committed on an infant under the age of twelve years, the age of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> discretion by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, either with or without consent, amount to rape and felony; as well since as before the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>: but that law has in general been held only to extend to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> under ten; tho' it should seem that damels between ten and twelve are still under the protection of the statute Westm. 1. the law with respect to their seduction not having been altered by either of the subsequent statutes. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> infant, under the age of fourteen years, is presumed by law incapable to commit a rape, and therefore it seems cannot be found guilty of it. For though in other felonies "malitia supplet etatem;" yet, as to this particular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of felony, the law supposes an imbecillity of body as well as mind. The civil law seems to suppose a prostitute or common <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARLOT">harlot</a> incapable of any injuries of this kind: not allowing any punishment for violating the chastity of her, who hath indeed no chastity at all, or at least hath no regard to it. But the law of England does not judge so hardly of offenders, as to cut off all opportunity of retreat even from common strumpets, and to treat them as never capable of amendment. It therefore holds it to be felony to force even a concubine or harlot; because the woman may have forsaken that unlawful course of life: for, as Bracton well observes, "licet meretrice fuerit antea, certe tunc temporis non fuit, cum reclamando nequitiae ejus consentire noluit." As to the material facts requisite to be given in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> and proved upon an indictment of rape, they are of such a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that, though necessary to be known and settled, for the conviction of the guilty and preservation of the innocent, and therefore are to be found in such criminal treatises as discourse of these matters in detail, yet they are highly improper to be publicly discussed, except only in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. We shall therefore merely add upon this head a few remarks from Sir Matthew Hale, with regard to the competency and credibility of witnesses; which may, salvo pudore, be considered. And, first, the party ravished may give evidence upon oath, and is in law a competent witness; but the credibility of her testimony, and how far forth she is to be believed, must be left to the jury upon the circumstances of fact that concur in that testimony. For instance: if the witness be of good fame; if she presently discovered the offence, and made search for the offender; if the party accused fled for it; these and the like are concurring circumstances, which give greater <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> to her evidence. But, on the other side, if she be of evil fame, and stand unsupported by others; if she concealed the injury for any considerable time after she had opportunity to complain; if the place, where the fact was alleged to be committed, was where it was possible the might have been heard, and she made no outcry; these and the like circumstances carry a strong, but not conclusive, presumption that her testimony is false or feigned. Moreover, if the rape be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> to be committed on an infant under 12 years of age, she may still be a competent witness, if she hath <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and understanding to know the nature and obligations of an oath: and, even if she hath not, it is thought by Sir Matthew Hale that she ought to be heard without oath, to give the court information; though that alone will not be sufficient to convict the offender. And he is of this opinion, first, Because the nature of the offence being secret, there may be no other possible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the actual fact; though afterwards there may be concurrent circumstances to corroborate it, proved by other witnesses; and, secondly, Because the law allows what the child told her mother, or other relations, to be given in evidence, since the nature of the case admits frequently of no better proof; and there is much more reason for the court to hear the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> of the child herself, than to receive it at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> from those who swear they heard her say so. And indeed, it seems now to be settled, that in these <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> infants of any age are to be heard; and, if they have any idea of an oath, to be also sworn: it being found by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that infants of very tender years often give the clearest and truest testimony. But in any of these cases, whether the child be sworn or not, it is to be wished, in order to render her evidence credible, that there should be some concurrent testimony, of time, place, and circumstances, in order to make out the fact; and that the conviction should not be grounded singly on the unsupported <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of an infant under years of discretion. There may be therefore, in many cases of this nature, witnesses who are competent, that is, who may be admitted to be heard; and yet, after being heard, may prove not to be credible, or such as the jury is bound to believe. For one excellence of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> by jury is, that the jury are triors of the credit of the witnesses, as well as of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the fact. "It is true, (says this learned judge), that rape is RAPHAEL "a most detestable crime, and therefore ought severely and impartially to be punished with death; but it must be remembered, that it is an accusation easy to be made, hard to be proved, but harder to be defended by the party accused, though innocent." He then relates two very extraordinary cases of malicious prosecution for this crime, that had happened within his own observation; and concludes thus: "I mention these instances, that we may be the more cautious upon trials of offences of this nature, wherever in the court and jury may with so much ease be imposed upon, without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care and vigilance; the heinousness of the offence many times transporting the judge and jury with so much indignation, that they are overhastily carried to the conviction of the person accused thereof, by the confident testimony of sometimes false and malicious witnesses."

RAPHAEL D'URBINO

Pages 315-315

the greatest, most sublime, and most excellent painter that has appeared since the revival of the fine arts, was the son of an indifferent painter named Sanzio, and was born at Urbino on Good Friday 1482. The popes Julius II. and Leo X. who employed him, loaded him with wealth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>; and it is said that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> de St Bibiana had such a value for him, that he offered him his niece in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. He had <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Perugino for his first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; but he immediately surpassed him, and endeavoured to improve by copying the works of Leonardo da Vinci and Michael Angelo. His genius is admired in all his pictures; his contours are free, his ordonnances magnificent, his designs correct, his figures elegant, his expressions lively, his attitudes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, his heads graceful; in fine, every thing is beautiful, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>, sublime, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a>, and adorned with graces. These various perfections he derived not only from his excellent abilities, but from his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of antiquity and anatomy; and from the friendship he contracted with Ariosto, who contributed not a little to the improvement of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. His pictures are principally to be found in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. That of the Transfiguration, preserved at Rome in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Peter Monterio, passes for his master-piece. He had a handsome person, was well proportioned, and had <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sweetness of temper; was polite, affable, and modest. He, however, lived in the utmost splendour; most of the eminent masters of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> were ambitious of working under him; and he never went out without a crowd of artists and others, who followed him purely through respect. He was not only the best painter in the world, but perhaps the best <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> too; on which account Leo X. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> him with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> St Peter's church at Rome: but he was too much addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, which occasioned his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> at 37 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He left a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of disciples; among whom were Julio Romano, and John Francis Penni, who were his heirs. Many able engravers, as Raimondi, George Mantuan, and Bloemart, engraved after Raphael.

RAPHAIM

Pages 315-315
or REPHAIM, (Moses), a name signifying Giants, as they really were, and an actual people too, situated in Bafan or Batanea, beyond Jordan, separated from the Zauzumim by the river Jabbok. Also a valley near Jerusalem, Joshua x.

RAPHANUS

Pages 315-315

RADISH; a genus of the siliquosa order, belonging to the tetradynamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is only one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. the sativus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> garden radish; of which there are several varieties. They are annual plants, which being sowed in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, attain perfection in two or three months, and shoot up soon after into stalk for flower and seed, which, ripening in autumn, the whole plant, root and top, perishes; so that a fresh supply must be raised annually from seed in the spring, performing the sowings at several different times, from about Christmas until May, in order to continue a regular succession of young tender radishes throughout the season: allowing only a fortnight or three weeks <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the sowings; for one crop <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not continue good longer than that space of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, before they will either run to seed, or become tough, sticky, and too hot to eat.

RAPIER

Pages 315-315

formerly signified a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> old-fashioned <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, such as those worn by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>; but it now denotes a small sword, as contradistinguished from a back-sword.

RAPIN

Pages 315-316

a Jesuit and eminent French writer, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a> in 1621. He taught polite literature in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of the Jesuits with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause, and was justly esteemed one of the best Latin poets and greatest wits of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1687. He wrote, 1. A great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Latin poems, which have rendered him famous throughout all <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; among which are his Hortorum libri quatuor, which is reckoned his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-piece. 2. Reflections on Eloquence, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>. 3. Comparisons between <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a> and Cicero, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> and Titus Livius. 4. The History of Janseanism. 5. Several works on <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> subjects. The best edition of his Latin poems, is that of Paris in 1723, in 3 vols 12mo. RAPIN de THOYRAS (Paul de), a celebrated historian, was the son of James de Rapin <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Thoyras, and was born at Castres in 1661. He was educated at first under a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> in his father's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and afterwards sent to Puylaurens, and thence to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAUMUR">Saumur</a>. In 1667 he returned to his father, with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to apply himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and was admitted an advocate: but some time after, reflecting that his being a Protestant would prevent his advancement at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, he resolved to quit the profession of the law, and apply himself to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; but his father would not consent to it. The revocation of the edict of Nantes in 1685, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, which happened two months after, made him resolve to come to England; but as he had no hopes of any settlement here, his stay was but short. He therefore soon after went to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and fitted himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of French volunteers at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, commanded by M. Rapin his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>-german. He attended the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> into England in 1688; and the following year the lord <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a> made him an ensign in his regiment, with which he went into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, where he gained the esteem of his officers at the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARRICKFERGUS">Carrickfergus</a>, and had soon a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>. He was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOYNE">Boyne</a>, and was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> through the shoulder at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIMERICK">Limerick</a>. He was soon after <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the company in which he had been ensign; but, in 1693, resigned his company to one of his brothers, in order to be tutor to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Portland's son. son. In 1699, he married Marianne Testard; but this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> neither abated his care of his pupil, nor prevented his accomplishing him in his travels. Having finished this employment, he returned to his family, which he had settled at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>; and here he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> some years. But as he found his family increase, he resolved to retire to some cheap <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and accordingly removed, in 1707, to Wezel, where he wrote his History of England, and some other pieces. Though he was of a strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, yet seventeen years application (for so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> was he in composing the history <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned) entirely ruined his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. He died in 1725. He wrote in French, 1. A Dissertation on the Whigs and Tories. 2. His History of England, printed at the Hague in 1727 and 1726, in 9 vols 4to, and reprinted at Trevoux in 1728, in 10 vols 4to. This last edition is more complete than that of the Hague. It has been translated into English, and improved with Notes, by the Rev. Mr Tindal, in 2 vols folio. This performance, though the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of a foreigner, is deservedly esteemed as the fullest and most impartial collection of English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> transactions extant. The readers of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and vivacity may be apt to complain of him for being sometimes rather tedious and dull.

RAPINE

Pages 316-316

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the taking away another's goods, &c. by violence.

RAPPERSWIL

Pages 316-316

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, on the confines of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>, and of the territory of Gaster, with an old castle. It is strong by situation, being seated on a neck of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> which advances into the lake of Zurich, and over which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> 850 paces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. It is subject to the cantons of Zurich and Bern. E. long. 8° 57'. N. lat. 47° 20'.

RAPPOLSTEIN

Pages 316-316

a town of France in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARONY">barony</a>. All the musicians of Alsace depend upon this baron, and are obliged to pay him a certain tribute, without which they cannot play upon their instruments. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 7° 28'. N. lat. 48° 15'.

RAREFACTION

Pages 316-316

in physics, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> whereby a body is rendered rare; that is, brought to possess more room, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> appear under a larger bulk, without accession of any new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>.—This is very frequently the effect of fire, as has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been universally allowed. In many <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, however, philosophers have attributed it to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of a repulsive principle. However, from the many discoveries concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and properties of the electric fluid and fire, there is the greatest reason to believe that this repulsive principle is no other than elementary fire. See Repulsion. RASOR-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">BILL</a>. See Alca. RASOR-FISH. See Solen.

RASTALL

Pages 316-316

a printer and miscellaneous writer, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, probably about the end of the 15th century, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. Returning from the university, he settled in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, and commenced printer, "then esteemed (says Wood) a profession fit for any scholar <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>." He married the sister of Sir Thomas More, with whom, we are told, he was very intimate, and whose writings he strenuously defended. From the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a>-page of one of his books, he appears to have lived in Cheapside, at the sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERMAID">mermaid</a>. He died in the year 1536; and left two sons, William and John: the first of whom became a judge in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s reign, and the latter a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of peace. This John Rastall, the subject of the present article, was a zealous Papist; but <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALE">Bale</a> says, that he changed his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He wrote, 1. Natura naturata. Pits calls it a copious (prolifica) and ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, describing <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; with cuts. What sort of a comedy this was, is not easy to conceive. Probably it is a cosmographical <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, written in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a>, and therefore styled a comedy. 2. The pastyme of the people; the chronicles of diverse realmys, and most especially of the realm of England, brevily compiled and emprinted in Cheapefyde, at the sign of the mermaid, next Pollygate, cum privilegio, fol. 3. Ecclesia Johannis Rastalli, 1542. Was one of the prohibited books in the reign of Henry VIII. 4. Legum Anglicanarum vocabula explicata. French and Latin. Lond. 1567, 8vo. And some other works.

RASTAT

Pages 316-316

a town of Germany, in the circle of Suabia and marquisate of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BADEN">Baden</a>, with a handsome castle. It is remarkable for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> concluded here between the French and Imperialists in 1714; and is seated on the river Merg, near the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 9° 14'. N. lat. 48° 52'.

RAT

Pages 316-317

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>. See Mus. The following receipt is said to have been found effectual for the destruction of rats. Take of the seeds of starflower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> lousewort, powdered, more or less as the occasion requires, one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>; of oat-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, three parts; mix them well, and make them up into a paste with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. Lay pieces of it in the holes, and on the places where mice and rats frequent; and it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> effectually kill or rid the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of those kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> by their eating thereof. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> ago, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> for encouraging arts proposed a premium of 50l. for a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> capable of alluring or fascinating rats so that they might be taken alive. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of new traps, &c. were invented; and the following methods of alluring the rats to a certain place were published. One of those most easily and efficaciously practised is the trailing some pieces of their most favorite food, which should be of the kind that has the strongest scent, such as toasted cheese or broiled <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> herrings, from the holes or entrances of the closet to their recesses in every part of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> or contiguous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. At the extremities, and in different parts of the course of this trailed track, small quantities of meal, or any other kind of their food, should be laid, to bring the greater number into the tracks, and to encourage them to pursue it to the place where they are intended to be taken: at that place, when time admits of it, a more plentiful repast is laid for them, and the trailing repeated for two or three nights. Besides this trailing and way-baiting, some of the most expert of the rat-catchers have a shorter, and perhaps perhaps more effectual method of bringing them together; which is, the calling them, by making such a kind of whistling noise as resembles their own call; and by this means, with the assistance of the way-baits, they call them out of their holes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them to the repast prepared for them at the place designed for taking them. But this is much more difficult to be practised than the art of trailing; for the learning the exact notes or cries of any kind of beasts or birds, so as to deceive them, is a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> which is seldom attained: though some persons have been known who could call together a great number of cats; and there was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> who could bring nightingales, when they were within hearing, about him, and even allure them to perch on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, so as to be taken. In practising either of those methods, of trailing or calling, great caution must be used by the operator to suppress and prevent the scent of his feet and body from being perceived; which is done by overpowering that scent by others of a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>.
