In order to this, the feet are to be covered with cloths rubbed over with alfaeida, or other strong-smelling substances; and even <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of rhodium is sometimes used for this purpose, but sparingly, on account of its dearth, though it has a very alluring as well as disguising effect. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this caution of avoiding the scent of the operator's feet, near the track, and in the place where the rats are proposed to be collected, be not properly observed, it will very much obstruct the success of the attempt to take them; for they are very shy of coming where the scent of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> feet lies very fresh, as it intimates to their sagacious <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> the presence of human creatures, whom they naturally dread. To the abovementioned means of alluring by trailing, way-baiting, and calling, is added another of a very material efficacy, which is, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of oil of rhodium, which, like the marum Syriacum in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of cats, has a very extraordinary fascinating power on these animals. This oil is extremely dear, and therefore sparingly used. It is exalted in a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in the place, and at the entrance of it, where the rats are intended to be taken; particularly at the time when they are to be last brought together, in order to their destruction; and it is used also by smearing it on the surface of some of the implements used in taking by the method below described; and the effect it has in taking off their caution and dread, by the delight they appear to have in it, is very extraordinary. It is usual, likewise, for the operator to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> as well as scent, which is done by putting on a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> or cloak, of one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> form, and makes him appear like a poet or some such inanimate thing; which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> must likewise be scented as above, to overpower the smell of his person; and besides this, he is to avoid all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> till he has secured his point of having all the rats in his power. When the rats are thus enticed and collected, where time is afforded, and the whole in any house and out-buildings are intended to be cleared away, they are suffered to regale on what they most like, which is ready prepared for them, and then to go away quietly for two or three nights; by which means those that are not allured the first night are brought afterwards, either by their fellows, or the effects of the trailing, &c., and will not fail to come duly again, if they are not disturbed or molested. But many of the rat-catchers make shorter <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and content themselves with what can be brought together in one night or two; but this is never effectual, unless where the building is small and entire, and the rats but few in number. The means of taking them, when they are brought together, are various. Some entice them into a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bag, the mouth of which is sufficiently capacious to cover nearly the whole <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of the place where they are collected; which is done by smearing some vessel, placed in the middle of the bag, with oil of rhodium, and laying in the bag baits of food. This bag, which before lay flat on the ground with the mouth spread open, is to be suddenly closed when the rats are all in. Others drive or fright them, by slight noises or motions, into a bag of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> form, the mouth of which, after all the rats are come in, is drawn up to the opening of the place by which they entered, all other ways of retreat being secured. Others, again, intoxicate or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a> them, by mixing with the repast prepared for them the cocculus Indicus or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUX_VOMICA">nux vomica</a>. They <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> four ounces of the cocculus Indicus, with twelve ounces of oat-meal, and two ounces of treacle or honey, made into a moist paste with strong-beer; but if the nux vomica be used, a much less proportion will serve than is here given of the cocculus. Any similar <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of these drugs, with that kind of food the rats are most fond of, and which has a strong flavour, to hide that of the drugs, will equally well answer the end. If indeed the cocculus Indicus be well powdered, and infused in the strong-beer for some time, at least half the quantity here directed will serve as well as the quantity before-mentioned. When the rats appear to be thoroughly intoxicated with the cocculus, or sick with the nux vomica, they may be taken with the hand, and put into a bag or cage, the door of the place being first drawn to, lest those who have strength and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> remaining escape. Rat-Tails, or Arrefts. See Farriery, § xxxvi. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RATAFIA">Ratafia</a>, a fine spirituous liquor, prepared from the kernels, &c. of several kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, particularly of cherries and apricots. Ratafia of cherries is prepared by bruising the cherries, and putting them into a vessel wherein brandy has been long kept; then adding to them the kernels of cherries, with strawberries, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUTMEG">nutmeg</a>, cloves; and to 30 <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of cherries, 10 quarts of brandy. The vessel is left open ten or twelve days, and then stopped <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> for two months before it be tapped. Ratafia of apricots is prepared two ways, viz. either by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> the apricots in white-wine, adding to the liquor an equal quantity of brandy, with sugar, cinnamon, mace, and the kernels of apricots; infusing the whole for eight or ten days; then straining the liquor, and putting it up for use; or else by infusing the apricots, cut in pieces, in brandy, for a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two, passing it through a straining bag, and then putting in the usual ingredients. Ratchet, or Rask, in clock-work, a sort of wheel having twelve fangs, which serve to lift up the detents every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, and make the clock strike. See Clock. Ratchets, in a watch, are the small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> at the bottom of the fusey, or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>, which stops it in winding up.

RATEEN

Pages 319-319
or RATTEN, in commerce, a thick woollen stuff, quilled, woven on a loom with four tredles, like sarges and other stuffs that have the whale or quilling. There are some rateens dressed and prepared like cloths; others left simply in the hair, and others where the hair or knap is frizzed. Rateens are chiefly manufactured in France, Holland, and Italy, and are mostly used in linings. The frize is a sort of coarse rateen, and the drugget is a rateen half linen half woollen.

RATES

Pages 318-319

in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, the orders <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> classes into which the ships of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> are divided, according to their force and magnitude. The regulation, which limits the rates of men of war to the smallest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> possible, seems to have been dictated by considerations of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> economy, or of that of the simplicity of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> dockyards. The British fleet is accordingly distributed into five rates, exclusive of the inferior vessels that usually attend on naval armaments; as sloops of war, armed ships, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a>-ketches, fire-ships and cutters, or schooners commanded by lieutenants. Ships of the first rate mount 100 cannon, having 42-pounders on the lower deck, 24-pounders on the middle deck, 12-pounders on the upper deck, and 6-pounders on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-deck and fore-castle. They are manned with 850 men, including their officers, fakemen, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARINES">marines</a>, and servants. In general, the ships of every rate, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, have the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, the boatwain, the gunner, the chaplain, the purser, the surgeon, and the carpenter; all of whom, except the chaplain, have their mates or assistants, in which are comprehended the sail-maker, the master at arms, the armourer, the captain's clerk, the gunsmith, &c. The number of other officers are always in proportion to the rate of the ship. Thus a first rate has six lieutenants, six master's mates, twenty-four midshipmen, and five surgeon's mates, who are considered as gentlemen: besides the following petty officers; quarter-masters and their mates, fourteen; boatwain's mates and yeomen, eight; gunner's mates and assistants, six; quarter-gunners, twenty-five; carpenter's mates, two, besides fourteen assistants, with one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, and steward's mate to the purser. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the dimensions of all ships of the same rate were equal, it would be the simplest and most perspicuous method to collect them into one point of view in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>: but as there is no invariable rule for the general dimensions, it must suffice to remark those of some particular ships in each rate; for which purpose we have selected some of the latest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>. The Victory, which is among the last built of our first rates, is 222 feet 6 inches in length, from the head to the stern; the length of her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, 151 feet 3 inches; that of her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-deck, or lower deck, 186 feet; her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> breadth is 51 feet 10 inches; her depth in the hold, 21 feet 6 inches; her burden, 2162 tons; and her poop reaches 6 feet before the mizen-mast. Ships of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> rate carry 90 guns upon three decks, of which those on the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> are 32-pounders; those on the middle, 18-pounders; on the upper deck, 12-pounders; and those on the quarter-deck, 6-pounders, which usually amount to four or six. Their complement of men is 750, in which there are six lieutenants, four master's mates, 24 midshipmen, and four surgeon's mates, 14 quarter-masters and their mates, eight boatwain's mates and yeomen, six gunner's mates and yeomen, with 22 quarter-gunners, two carpenter's mates, with 10 assistants, and one steward and steward's mate. Ships of the third rate carry from 64 to 80 cannon, which are 31, 18, and 9 pounders. The 80-gun ships however begin to grow out of repute, and to give way to those of 74, 70, &c. which have only two whole batteries; whereas the former have three, with 28 guns planted on each, the cannon of their upper deck being the same as those on the quarter-deck and fore-castle of the latter, which are 9-pounders. The compliment in a 74 is 650, and in a 64, 500 men; having, in peace, four lieutenants, but in war, five; and when an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> is aboard, six. They have three master's mates, 16 midshipmen, three surgeon's mates, 10 quarter-masters and their mates, six boatwain's mates and yeomen, four gunner's mates and yeomen, with 18 quarter-gunners, one carpenter's mate, with eight assistants, and one steward and steward's mate under the purser. Ships of the fourth rate mount from 60 to 50 guns, upon two decks, and the quarter-deck. The lower tier is composed of 24-pounders, the upper tier of 12-pounders, and the cannon on the quarter-deck and fore-castle are six-pounders. The complement of a 50 gun ship is 350 men, in which there are three lieutenants, two master's mates, 10 midshipmen, two surgeon's mates, eight quarter-masters and their mates, four boatwain's mates and yeomen, one gunner's mate and one yeoman, with 12 quarter-gunners, one carpenter's mate and six assistants, and a steward and steward's mate. All vessels of war, under the fourth rate, are usually comprehended under the general name of frigates, and never appear in the line of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. They are divided into the 5th and 6th rates; the former mounting from 40 to 32 guns, and the latter from 28 to 20. The largest of the fifth rate have two decks of cannon, the lower battery being of 18-pounders, and that of the upper deck of 9-pounders; but those of 36 and 32 guns have one complete deck of guns, mounting 12-pounders, besides the quarter-deck and fore-castle, which carry 6-pounders. The complement of a ship of 44 guns, is 280 men; and that of a frigate of 36-guns, 240 men. The first has three, and the second two, lieutenants; and both have two master's mates, six midshipmen, two surgeon's mates, six quarter-masters and their mates, two boatwain's mates and one yeoman, one gunner's mate and one yeoman, with 10 or 11 quarter-gunners, and one purser's steward. Frigates of the 6th rate carry <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a>-pounders, those of 28 guns having three-pounders on their quarter-deck, with 200 men for their complement; and those of 24, 160 men: the former has two lieutenants, the latter, one; and both have two master's mates four midshipmen, one surgeon's mate, four quarter-masters and their mates, one boatwain's mate and one yeoman, one gunner's mate and one yeoman, with six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> quarter-gunners, and one purser's steward. The sloops of war carry from 18 to 8 cannon, the largest of which have six-pounders; and the smallest, viz. those of 8 or 10 guns, four-pounders. Their officers are generally the same as in the 6th rates, with little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>; and their complements of men are from 120 to 60, in proportion to their force or magnitude. N.B. Bomb-vessels are on the same establishment as sloops; but fire-ships and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>-ships are on that of fifth rates. Nothing more evidently manifests the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> improvement of the marine art, and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection, to which it has arrived in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, than the facility of managing our first rates; which were formerly esteemed incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, unless in the most favourable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. Ships of the second rate, and those of the third, which have three decks, carry their sails remarkably well, and labour very little at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. They are excellent in a general <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, or in cannonading a fortress. Those of the third rate, which have two tiers, are fit for the line of battle, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> the convoys and squadrons of ships of war in action, and in general to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the different exigencies of the naval service. The fourth-rates may be employed on the same occasions as the third-rates, and may be also destined amongst the foreign colonies, or on expeditions of great distance; since these vessels are usually excellent for keeping and sustaining the sea. Vessels of the fifth rate are too weak to suffer the shock of a line of battle; but they may be destined to lead the convoys of merchant ships, to protect the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> in the colonies, to cruise in different stations, to accompany squadrons, or be sent express with necessary intelligence and orders. The same may be observed of the sixth rates. The frigates, which mount from 28 to 38 guns upon one deck, with the quarter-deck, are extremely proper for cruising against <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a>, or for short expeditions, being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and usually excellent sailors.

RATIBOR

Pages 319-319

a town of Germany, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name, with a castle. It has been twice taken by the Swedes, and is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> fertile in corn and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, 15 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROPPAU">Troppau</a>, and 142 east of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 22. 24. N. Lat. 50. 14.

RATIFICATION

Pages 319-319

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> approving of and confirming something done by another in our name.

RATIO

Pages 319-319

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, is that relation of homogeneous things which determines the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of one from the quantity of another, without the intervention of a third. Two numbers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> quantities, A and B, being proposed, their relation one to another may be considered under one of these two heads: 1. How much A exceeds B, or B exceeds A; and this is found by taking A from B, or B from A, and is called arithmetic reason, or ratio. 2. Or how many times, and parts of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, A contains B, or B contains A; and this is called geometric reason or ratio; (or, as Euclid defines it, it is the mutual habitude, or respect, of two magnitudes of the same kind, according to quantity; that is, as to how often the one contains, or is contained in, the other;) and is found by dividing A by B, or B by A; and here <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, that that quantity which is referred to another quantity, is called the antecedent of the ratio; and that to which the other is referred, is called the consequent of the ratio; as, in the ratio of A to B, A is the antecedent, and B the consequent. Therefore any quantity, as antecedent, divided by any quantity as a consequent, gives the ratio of that antecedent to the consequent. Thus the ratio of A to B is $\frac{A}{B}$, but the ratio of B to A is $\frac{B}{A}$; and, in numbers, the ratio of 12 to 4 is $\frac{12}{4} = 3$, or triple; but the ratio of 4 to 12 is $\frac{4}{12} = \frac{1}{3}$, or subtriple. And here note, that the quantities thus compared must be of the same kind; that is, such as by multiplication may be made to exceed one the other, or as these quantities are said to have a ratio between them, which, being multiplied, may be made to exceed one another. Thus a line, how short forever, may be multiplied, that is, produced so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as to exceed any given <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line; and consequently these may be compared together, and the ratio expressed: but as a line can never, by any multiplication whatever, be made to have breadth, that is, to be made equal to a superficies, how small forever; these can therefore never be compared together, and consequently have no ratio or respect one to another, according to quantity; that is, as to how often the one contains, or is contained in, the other.

RATION

Pages 319-319
or RATIAN, in the army, a portion of ammunition, bread, drink, and forage, distributed to each soldier in the army, for his daily subsistence, &c. The horse have ratios of hay and oats when they cannot go out to forage. The rations of bread are regulated by weight. The ordinary ration of a foot soldier is a pound and a half of bread per day. The officers have several rations according to their quality and the number of attendants they are obliged to keep. When the ration is augmented on occasions of rejoicings, it is called a double ration. The ship's crews have also their rations or allowances of biscuit, pulse, and water, proportioned according to their stock.

RATIONALE

Pages 319-319

a solution, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> account of the principles of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, phenomenon, or the like.

RATISBON

Pages 319-320

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, rich, handsome, and strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, free and imperial, with a bishop's see, whose bishop is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the empire. It is full of gentry; and there are very handsome structures, particularly three monasteries and three abbeys. The town-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is very magnificent, and in its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> the general diets of the empire meet; only in 1740, there being a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> in Germany, the meeting of the diet was transferred to Frankfort on the Main, till after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VII. It is seated on the Danube, and is pretty well fortified, over which river there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of 15 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, so that in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of war it is a passage of very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. The inhabitants are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, and all their magistrates must be of that persuasion; however, the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> have the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of saying <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> there once a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>, and... RAV and the two abbesses have the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of prelates of the empire. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">Provisions</a> are very plentiful here, and they have a good trade in time of peace, the river on which it stands being navigable, and by which it communicates with a great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Germany. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. II. N. Lat. 48. 56.

RATLINES

Pages 320-320
or, as the sailors call them ratlines, those lines which make the ladder steps to go up the shrouds' and puttocks, hence called the ratlines of the shrouds. RATTLESNAKE. See Crotalus. RATTLESNAKE Root. See Polygala.

RATOLFZEL

Pages 320-320

a strong town of Germany, in Swabia, near the west end of the lake <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>. It is seated on that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of it called Bodensee; and belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, who took it from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Württemberg, after the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Nordlingen. It is 12 miles west of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Constance.

RATZEBURG

Pages 320-320
or RATZENBURG, an ancient town of Germany, in the circle of Lower Saxony, and in the duchy of Lawenburg, with a bishop's see and a castle. The town depends on the duchy of Lawenburg, and the cathedral church on that of Ratzeburg. It is seated on an eminence, and almost surrounded with a lake 25 miles in length and three in breadth. This place is noted for its excellent beer. E. Long. 10. 58. N. Lat. 53. 47.

RAURICUM

Pages 320-320

(anc. geog.) a town of the Raurici, situate over against Abnoba, a mountain from which the Danube takes its rise. A Roman colony led by L. Manius Plancus the scholar and friend of Cicero: called Colonia Rauriaca (Pliny), Raurica (Inscription), Augusta Rauricorum. The town was destroyed in Julian's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. It is now <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Augs, a village greatly decayed from what it formerly was. It is situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, distant about two hours to the east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is now the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Basil.

RAVA

Pages 320-320

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of the same name, with a fortified castle, where they keep state prisoners. The houses are built of wood, and there is a Jesuits <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. It is seated in a morass covered with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which proceeds from the river Rava, with which it is surrounded. It is 45 miles south of Błonie, and 50 south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARSAW">Warsaw</a>. The palatinate is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by that of Błonie, on the east by that of Mazovia, on the south by that of Sandomierz, and on the west by that of Leczyca.

RAVELIN

Pages 320-320

in fortification, was anciently a flat bastion placed in the middle of a curtain; but now a detached <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> composed only of two faces, which make a salient <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> without any flanks, and raised before the counterfacing of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. See Fortification.

RAVENGLAS

Pages 320-320

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> in England, situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Irt and Esk, which, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a> three parts of it; it is a well-built <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and has a good <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> for shipping, which brings its some trade. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 5. N. Lat. 54. 20.

RAVENNA

Pages 320-320

(anc. geog.), a noble <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Galia Cispadana; a colony of Thessalians, on the Adriatic, in washes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a boggy situation, which proved Ravenna a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> security to it. The houses all of wood, Ray. the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> by bridges and boats, and the town kept sweet and clean by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> carrying away the mud and foil, (Strabo). Anciently it had a port at the mouth of the Bedesfs; Augustus added a new port, spacious to hold a fleet, for the security of the Adriatic, between which and the city lay the Via Caesaria. In the lower <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> it was the seat of the Ostrogoths for 72 years; but being recovered by Nariss, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>'s general, it became the residence of the exarchs, magistrates sent by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> from Constantinople, for 175 years, when it was taken by the Longobards. It is still called Ravenna, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Romania, in the pope's territory. It had a very flourishing trade till the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> withdrew two miles from it, which has been a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> detriment. The fortifications are of little importance, and the citadel is gone to ruin. It is now most remarkable for the excellent wine produced in its neighbourhood. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> of Theodoric is still to be seen, remarkable for being covered by a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> 28 feet in diameter and 15 thick. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 15. N. Lat. 44. 22.

RAVENSBURG

Pages 320-320

a free and imperial town of Germany in Algow in the circle of Swabia. It is well built, and the public structures are handsome. The inhabitants are partly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> and partly Papists. It is seated on the river Chems, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 46. N. Lat. 47. 44.

RAY

Pages 320-321

a celebrated botanist, was the son of Mr Roger Ray, a blacksmith, and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Notley in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> in 1628. He received the first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of learning at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRAINTREE">Braintree</a>; and in 1644 was admitted into Catharine <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, from whence he afterwards removed to Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in that university. He was at length made one of the senior fellows of that college, and took the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts; but his intense application to his studies having injured his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, he was obliged at his leisure hours to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> himself by riding <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> walking in the fields, which led him to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. He noted from Johnston, Parkinson, and the Phytologia Britannica, the places where curious plants grew; and in 1658 rode from Cambridge to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, from whence he went into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, visiting many places, and among others the famous hill of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SNOWDON">Snowdon</a>; returning by Shrewsbury and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>. In 1660 he published his Catalogus Plantarum circa Cantabrigiam nascentium, and the same year was ordained deacon and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. In 1661 he accompanied Francis Willoughby, Esq; and others in search of plants and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> curiosities, in the north of England and Scotland; and the next year made a western tour from Chester, and through Wales, to Cornwall, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, Wilshire, and other countries. He afterwards travelled with Mr Willoughby and other gentlemen through <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, France, &c. took several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">tours</a> in England, and was admitted fellow fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. In 1672, his intimate and beloved friend Mr Willoughby died in the 37th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, at Middleton Hall, his seat in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>; "to the infinite and unpealkable loss and grief (says Mr Ray,) of myself, his friends, and all good men." There having been the closest and sincerest friendship between Mr Willoughby and Mr Ray, who were men of similar natures and tastes, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their being fellow collegians, Mr Willoughby not only confided in Mr Ray, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>-time, but also at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>: for he made him one of the executors of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> him with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of his sons Francis and Thomas, leaving him also for life £60. per annum. The eldest of these young gentlemen not being four years of age, Mr Ray, as a faithful trustee, betook himself to the instruction of them; and for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> composed his *Nomenclator Clavifex*, which was published this very year 1672. Francis the eldest dying before he was of age, the younger became <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Middleton. Not many months after the death of Mr Willoughby, Mr Ray lost another of his best friends, bishop Wilkins; whom he visited in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> the 18th of November 1672, and found near expiring by a total suppression of urine for eight days. As it is natural for the mind, when it is hurt in one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, to seek relief from another; so Mr Ray, having lost some of his best friends, and being in a manner left destitute, conceived thoughts of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>; and accordingly, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1673, did actually marry a gentlewoman of about 20 years of age, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Mr Oakely of Launton in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>. Towards the end of this year, came forth his "Observations Topographical, Moral, &c." made in foreign countries; to which was added his *Catalogus Stirpium in exterris regionibus observatarum*: and about the same time, his *Collection of unusual or local English words*, which he had gathered up in his travels through the counties of England. After having published many books on subjects foreign to his profession, he at length resolved to publish in the character of a divine, as well as in that of a natural <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>: in which view he published his excellent demonstration of the being and attributes of God, entitled *The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of God manifested in the works of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">Creation</a>*, 8vo. 1697. The rudiments of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> were laid in some college lectures; and another collection of the same kind he enlarged and published under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of *Three Physico-theological Discourses, concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAOS">Chaos</a>, Deluge, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLUTION">Dissolution</a> of the World*, 8vo. 1692. He died in 1705. He was modest, affable, and communicative; and was distinguished by his probity, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, sobriety, and piety. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of works, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which, besides those already mentioned, are, 1. *Catalogus Plantarum Angliae*. 2. *Dicionarium Trilingue secundum locos communis*. 3. *Historia Plantarum, Speciei, hactenus editae, aliisque infuere multas noviter inventas et descriptas complectens*, 3 vols. 4. *Methodus Plantarum nova, cum Tabulis*, 8vo. and several other works on plants. 6. *Synopsis Methodica Animalium quadrupedum et serpintini generis*, 8vo. 6. *Synopsis Methodica Avium et Piscium*. 7. *Historia Infectorum, opus posthumum*. 7. *Methodus Infectorum*. 9. Philosophical letters, &c. Ray, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, a beam of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> emitted from a radiant or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> body. See Light. Inflected Rays, those rays of light which, on their near approach to the edges of bodies, in passing by them, are bent out of their course, being turned either from the body or towards it. This <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the rays of light is generally termed diffraction by foreigners, and Dr Hooke sometimes called it deflection. Reflected Rays, those rays of light, which, after falling upon the body, do not go beyond the surface of it, but are thrown back again. Refracted Rays, those rays of light which, after falling upon any medium, enter its surface, being bent either towards or from a perpendicular to the point on which they fell. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">Pencil</a> of Rays, a number of rays issuing from a point of an object, and diverging in the form of a cone.

RAZOR

Pages 321-321

a well-known <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, used by surgeons, barbers, &c., for shaving off the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> from various parts of the body.

RE ACTION

Pages 321-321

in physiology, the resistance made by all bodies to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> impulse of others that endeavour to change its state whether of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> or rest.

RE-EXCHANGE

Pages 335-335

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> payment of the price of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> rather the price of a new exchange due upon a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of exchange that comes to be protested and to be refunded the bearer by the drawer or indorser.

READING

Pages 328-329

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a> in England, pleasantly seated on the river Kennet, near the confluence with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>. It had once a fine rich <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, of which there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ruins remaining. It had also a castle built by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Henry I. but it was afterwards levelled with the ground. It is a corporation, enjoys several privileges, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The two navigable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> render it a fit <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for trade. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, i. o. N. Lat. 51° 25'.

READINGS

Pages 329-329
or Various Readings, in criticism, are the different manner of reading the texts of authors in ancient manuscripts, where a diversity has arisen from the corruption of time, or the ignorance of copyists. A great part of the business of critics lies in settling the readings by confronting the various readings of the several manuscripts, and considering the agreement of the words and sense. Readings are also used for a sort of commentary or glofs on a law, text, passage, or the like, to show the sense an author takes it in, and the application he conceives to be made of it.

REAL

Pages 329-329

a polite French writer, son of a counsellor to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of Chambery in Savoy. He came young to France, distinguished himself at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> by several ingenious productions, and resided there a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, intent upon literary pursuits. He died at Chambery in 1692, advanced in years, though not in circumstances. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> parts and penetration, a lover of the sciences, and particularly fond of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. A complete edition of his works was printed at Paris, in 3 vols 4to. 1745; and another in 6 vols 12mo.

REALISTS

Pages 329-329

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of school-philosophers formed in opposition to the nominalists. Under the Realists are included the Scotists, Thomists, and all excepting the followers of Ocham. Their distinguishing tenet is, that universals are realities, and have an actual existence out of an idea <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> imagination; or, as they express it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, a parte rei; whereas the nominalists contend, that they exist only in the mind, and are only <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, or manners of conceiving things.

REALITY

Pages 329-329

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of res, "thing," first used by the Scotists, to denote a thing which may exist of itself; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> which has a full and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> being of itself, and is not considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of any other.

REALM

Pages 329-329

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which gives its head <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> governor the denomination of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>.

REAR

Pages 329-329

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> frequently used in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, to denote something behind, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> backwards, in respect of another; in opposition to van. REAR of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">Army</a>, signifies, in general, the hindermost <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of an army, battalion, regiment, or squadron; also the ground behind either. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REAR_GUARD">REAR-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">Guard</a>, is that body of an army which marches after the main-body: for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a> of an army is always composed of an advance-guard, a main-body, and a rear-guard; the first and last commanded by a general. The old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-guards of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, always form the rear-guard of the army, and are to see that everything come safe to the new camp. REAR Half-filts, are the three hindmost ranks of the battalion, when it is drawn up fix deep. REAR-Line, of an army encamped, is always 1200 feet at least from the centre line; both of which run <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> line, as also to the reserve. REAR-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">Rank</a>, is the last rank of a battalion, when drawn up, and generally 16 or 18 feet from the centre-line, when drawn in open order.

REASON

Pages 329-329

a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> power of the mind, whereby it distinguishes good from evil, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> from falsehood. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, n° 266—282.

REASONING

Pages 329-329

ratiocination, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of the mind called reason; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> it is an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> or operation of the mind, deducing some unknown proposition from other previous ones that are evident and known. See Logic, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> III.

REAUUMUR

Pages 329-329

a celebrated French <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born of a good family at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a> in 1683. He early discovered a genius for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and physics, which he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> to improve; he was admitted a member of the academy of sciences in 1708, and justified their choice by his many observations in various branches of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> was his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Insects, 6 vols 4to. He died in 1757, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>; and left a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of papers and natural curiosities to the academy of sciences. He is represented as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of most amiable qualities.

REBATE

Pages 329-329
or Rebatement, in commerce, a term much used at Amsterdam for an abatement in the price of several commodities, when the buyer, instead of taking time, advances ready money. Rebatement, in heraldry, a diminution or abatement of the bearings in a coat of arms. See Abatement.

REBELLION

Pages 329-329

Rebellio, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was where those who had been formerly overcome in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and yielded to their subjection, made a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> resistance: But with us it is generally used for the taking up of arms traiterously against the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, whether by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> subjects, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> others when once subdued; and the word rebel is sometimes applied to him who wilfully <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>; also to a villain disobeying his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a>. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between enemies and rebels. Enemies are those who are out of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>; therefore subjects of the king, either in open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, or rebellion, are not the king's enemies, but traitors. And <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, who levied war against Edward I. because he was within the allegiance of the king, had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> pronounced against him as a traitor and rebel. Private persons may arm themselves to suppress rebels, enemies, &c.

REBELLIOUS ASSEMBLY

Pages 329-329

is a gathering together of twelve persons <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> more, intending or going about to practise or put in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> unlawfully, of their own authority, any thing to change the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> or statutes of the realm; or to destroy the inclosures of any ground, or banks of any fish-pond, pool, or conduit, to the intent the same shall <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> waste and void; or to destroy the deer in any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARK">park</a>, or any warren of conies, dove-houses, or fish in ponds; or any <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, barns, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, or bays; or to burn stacks of corn; or abate rents, or prices of victuals, &c.

REBUS

Pages 330-330

an enigmatical representation of some name, &c., by using figures <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> pictures instead of words, or parts of words. Camden mentions an instance of this absurd kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> in a gallant who expressed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to a woman named Rose Hill, by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in the border of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> a rose, a hill, an eye, a loaf, and a well; which, in the style of the rebus, reads, "Rose Hill I love well." This kind of wit was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> practised by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, who took the pains to find devices for their names. It was, however, happily ridiculed by Ben Jonson, in the humorous <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABEL">Abel</a> Drugger's device in the Alchemist; by the Spectator, in the device of Jack of Newbery; at which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> this rebus, being raised to sign posts, was grown out of fashion at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>.

REBUTTER

Pages 329-330

(from the Fr. boutier, i.e. repeller, to put back <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>) is the answer of defendant to plaintiff's surrejoinder; and plaintiff's answer to the rebutter is called a surrebuter: but it is very rare the parties go so far in pleading. Rebutter is also where a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> or fine grants to warranty any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> or hereditament to another; and the person making the warranty, or his heir, sue him to whom the warranty is made, or his heir or affiancee, for the same thing; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he who is so sued, plead the deed or fine with warranty, and pray judgment, if the plaintiff shall be received to demand the thing which he ought to warrant to the party, against the warranty in the deed, &c., this is called a rebutter. And if I <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to a tenant to hold without impeachment of waste, and afterwards implead him for waste done, he may debar me of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> by shewing my grant; which is a rebutter.

RECAPITULATION

Pages 330-330

is a summary, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a concise and transient enumeration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> things inflicted on in the preceding discourse, whereby the force of the whole is collected into one view. See Oratory, n° 35; 127.

RECEIPT

Pages 330-330
or Receipt, in commerce, an acquittance, or discharge, in writing, intimating that the party has received a certain sum of money, either in full for the whole debt, or in part, or on account.

RECEIVER

Pages 330-330

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PNEUMATICS">pneumatics</a>, a glass vessel for containing the thing on which an experiment in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> is to be made. Receiver, receptor <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> receptator, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> understood in a bad <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and used for such as knowingly receive stolen goods from thieves, and conceal them. This crime is felony, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> is transportation for 14 years.

RECEPTACULUM

Pages 330-330

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> parts of fructification defined by Linnaeus to be the base which connects <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> supports the other parts. RECEPTACULUM chyli, or Pecquet's reservoir, the reservoir or receptacle for the chyle, situated in the left side of the upper vertebra of the loins, under the aorta and the vessels of the left kidney.

RECHABITES

Pages 330-330

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order among the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Jews, instituted by Jonadab the son of Rechab, comprehending only his own family and posterity. Their founder prescribed them three things: first, not to drink any wine; secondly, not to build any houses, but to dwell in tents; and thirdly, not to sow any corn, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> plant vines. These rules the Rechabites observed with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strictness.

RECHEAT

Pages 330-330

in hunting, a lesson which the huntsman plays on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, when the hounds have lost their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a>, to call them back from pursuing a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a> scent.

RECIPE

Pages 330-330

in medicine, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> remedy, to be taken by a patient; so called because always beginning with the word recipe, i.e., takes; which is generally denoted by the abbreviation R.

RECIPROCAL

Pages 330-330

in general, something that is mutual, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> which is returned equally on both sides, or that affects both parties alike. Reciprocal Terms, among logicians, are those which have the same signification; and consequently are convertible, or may be used for each other. Reciprocal Figures, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, those which have the antecedents and consequents of the same ratio in both figures.

RECITATIVO

Pages 330-330
or Recitative, in music, a kind of singing, that differs but little from ordinary pronunciation; such as that in which the several parts of the liturgy are rehearsed in cathedrals; or that wherein the actors commonly deliver themselves on the theatre at the opera, when they are to express some action or passion; to relate some event; or reveal some design.

RECKONING

Pages 330-330
or a Ship's Reckoning, in navigation, is that account whereby at any time it may be known where the ship is, and on what course or courses she is to steer, in order to gain her port; and that account taken from the log-board is called the dead reckoning. See Navigation.

RECLAIMING

Pages 330-330
or Reclaiming, in our ancient customs, a lord's pursuing, prosecuting, and recalling, his vassal, who had gone to live in another place without his permission. Reclaiming is also used for the demanding of a person, or thing, to be delivered up to the prince or state to which it properly belongs; when, by any irregular means, it is come into another's possession. Reclaiming, in falconry, is taming a hawk, &c., and making her gentle and familiar. A partridge is said to reclaim, when she calls her young ones together, upon their scattering too much from her.

RECLUSE

Pages 330-331

among the Papists, a person shut up in a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CELL">cell</a> of an hermitage, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, and cut off, not only from all conversation with the world, but even with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. This is a kind of voluntary imprisonment, from a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> either of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>. The word is also applied to incontinent wives, whom their husbands procure to be thus kept in perpetual imprisonment in some <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> house. Recluses were anciently very numerous. They took an oath never to stir out of their retreat: and having entered it, the bishop set his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> upon the door; and the recluse was to have everything necessary for the support of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, conveyed to him through a window. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he was a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, he was allowed a small oratory, with a window, which looked into the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, thro' which he might make his offerings at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, hear the ringing, and answer those who spoke to him; but this window had curtains before it, so that he could not be seen. He was allowed a little garden, adjoining to his cell, in which he might plant a few herbs, and breathe a little fresh <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. If he had disciples, their cells cells were contiguous to his, with only a window of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>, through which they conveyed necessaries to him, and received his instructions. If a recluse fell sick, his door might be opened for persons to come in and assist him, but he himself was not to stir out.

RECOGNITION

Pages 331-331

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, an acknowledgment; a word particularly used in our law-books for the first <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the statute 1 Jac. I. by which the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> acknowledged, that, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> had rightfully descended to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> James.

RECOGNIZANCE

Pages 331-331

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is an obligation of record, which a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> enters into before some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of record <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> duly authorized, with condition to do some particular <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>; as to appear at the assizes, to keep the peace, to pay a debt, or the like. It is in most respects like another bond: the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> being chiefly this, that the bond is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of a fresh debt or obligation de novo, the recognizance is an acknowledgment of a former debt upon record; the form whereof is, "that A. doth acknowledge to owe to our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, to the plaintiff, to C. D. or the like, the sum of ten pounds," with condition to be void on performance of the thing stipulated: in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> the king, the plaintiff, C. D. &c. is called the cognizor, is cui cognoscitur; as he that enters into the recognizance is called the cognizor, is qui cognoscit. This being certified to, or taken by the officer of some court, is witnessed only by the record of that court, and not by the party's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>: so that it is not in strict propriety a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, though the effects of it are greater than a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> obligation; being allowed a priority in point of payment, and binding the lands of the cognizor from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of enrolment on record.

RECOIL

Pages 331-331
or REBOUND, the starting backward of a fire-arm after an explosion. Merfennus tells us, that a cannon 12 feet in length, weighing 6400 lb., gives a ball of 24 lb. an uniform velocity of 640 feet per second. Putting, therefore, $W = 6400$, $w = 14$, $V = 640$, and $v =$ the velocity with which the cannon recoils; we shall have (because the momentums of the cannon and ball are equal) $Wv = wV$; and so $v = \frac{wV}{W} = \frac{24 \times 64}{6400} = 2$, 4; that is, it would recoil at the rate of 24 feet per second, if free to move.

RECOLLECTION

Pages 331-331

a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of thinking, by which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> sought after by the mind are found and brought to view.

RECONNOITRE

Pages 331-331

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, implies to view and examine the state of things, in order to make a report thereof. Parties ordered to reconnoitre are to observe the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and the enemy; to remark the routes, conveniences, and inconveniences of the first; the position, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> forces of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. In either <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, they should have an expert geographer, capable of taking plans readily: he should be the best mounted of the whole, in case the enemy happen to scatter the escort, that he may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> his works and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">WAR</a>.

RECORD

Pages 331-331

an authentic testimony in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, contained in rolls of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, and preserved in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of record. See COURT. Vol. IX. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">Trial</a> by RECORD, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of trial which is used only in one particular instance: and that is where a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of record is pleaded in any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, as a fine, a judgment, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the like; and the opposite party pleads, nul tiel record, that there is no such matter of record existing. Upon this, issue is tendered and joined in the following form, "and this he prays may be inquired of by the record, and the other doth the like;" and hereupon the party pleading the record has a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> given him to bring it in, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> is made in court for him to "bring forth the record by him in pleading alleged, or else he shall be condemned;" and, on his failure, his antagonist shall have judgment to recover. The trial, therefore, of this issue, is merely by the record: for, as Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> observes, a record or enrolment is a monument of so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and importeth in itself such <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> verity, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be pleaded that there is no such record, it shall not receive any trial by witnese, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, or otherwise, but only by itself. Thus titles of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, as whether <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> or no earl, baron or no baron, shall be tried by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s writ or patent only, which is matter of record. Also in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of an alien, whether alien friend or enemy, shall be tried by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> between his sovereign and ours; for every league or treaty is of record. And also, whether a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> be held in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> demesne or not, shall be tried by the record of domeday in the king's exchequer.

RECORDER

Pages 331-331

a person whom the mayor and other magistrates of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> corporation associate to them, for their better <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and proceedings in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>; on which account this person is generally a counsellor, or other person well skilled in the law. The recorder of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> is chosen by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mayor and aldermen; and as he is held to be the mouth of the city, delivers the judgment of the courts therein, and records and certifies the city-customs.

RECOVERY

Pages 331-333
or Common Recovery, in English law, a species of assurance by matter of record; concerning the original of which it was observed under the article TAIL, that common recoveries were invented by the ecclesiastics to elude the statutes of mortmain; and afterwards encouraged by the finesse of the courts of law in 12 Ed. IV. in order to put an end to all fettered inheritances, and bar not only estates-tail, but also all remainders and reverions expectant thereon. We have here, therefore, only to consider, first, the nature of a common recovery; and, secondly, its force and effect. 1. A common recovery is a suit or action, either Blackft. actual or fictitious: and in it the lands are recovered Comment. against the tenant of the freehold; which recovery, being a supposed adjudication of the right, binds all persons, and vests a free and absolute fee-simple in the recoveror. To explain this as clearly and concisely as possible, let us, in the first place, suppose David Edwards to be tenant of the freehold, and desirous to suffer a common recovery, in order to bar all entails, remainders, and reverions, and to convey the same in fee-simple to Francis Golding. To effect this, Golding is to bring an action against him for the lands; and he accordingly files out a writ called a praecipe quod reddat, because these were its initial or most operative words when the law-proceedings were in Latin. In this writ the demandant Golding alleges, that the defend- Recovery. ant Edwards (here called the tenant) has no legal title to the land; but that he came into possession of it after one Hugh Hunt had turned the defendant out of it. The subsequent proceedings are made up into a record or recovery roll, in which the writ and complaint of the defendant are first recited: whereupon the tenant appears, and calls upon one Jacob Morland, who is supposed, at the original purchase, to have warranted the title to the tenant; and thereupon he prays, that the said Jacob Morland may be called in to defend the title which he so warranted. This is called the voucher, "vocatio," or calling of Jacob Morland to warranty; and Morland is called the vouchee. Upon this Jacob Morland, the vouchee, appears, is implored, and defends the title. Whereupon Golding the defendant desires leave of the court to imparl, or confer with the vouchee in private; which is (as usual) allowed him. And soon afterwards the defendant Golding returns to court; but Morland the vouchee disappears, or makes default. Whereupon judgment is given for the defendant Golding, now called the recoveror, to recover the lands in question against the tenant Edwards, who is now the recoveree: and Edwards has judgment to recover of Jacob Morland lands of equal value, in recompense for the lands so warranted by him, and now lost by his default; which is agreeable to the doctrine of warranty mentioned in the preceding chapter. This is called the recompense, or recovery in value. But Jacob Morland having no lands of his own, being usually the crier of the court, (who, from being frequently thus vouched, is called the common vouchee), it is plain that Edwards has only a nominal recompense for the lands so recovered against him by Golding; which lands are now absolutely vested in the said recoveror by judgment of law, and seisin thereof is delivered by the sheriff of the county. So that this collusive recovery operates merely in the nature of a conveyance in fee-simple, from Edwards the tenant in tail to Golding the purchaser. The recovery here described, is with a single voucher only; but sometimes it is with a double, treble, or farther voucher, as the exigency of the case may require. And indeed it is now usual always to have a recovery with double voucher at the least: by first conveying an estate of freehold to any indifferent person, against whom the praecipe is brought; and then he vouches the tenant in tail, who vouches over the common vouchee. For, if a recovery be had immediately against tenant in tail, it bars only such estate in the premises of which he is then actually seised; whereas if the recovery be had against another person, and the tenant in tail be vouched, it bars every latent right and interest which he may have in the lands recovered. If Edwards therefore be tenant of the freehold in possession, and John Barker be tenant in tail in remainder, here Edwards doth first vouch Barker, and then Barker vouches Jacob Morland the common vouchee; who is always the last person vouched, and always makes default; whereby the defendant Golding recovers the land against the tenant Edwards, and Edwards recovers a recompense of equal value against Barker the first vouchee; who recovers the like against Morland the common vouchee, against whom such ideal recovery in value is always ultimately awarded. This supposed recompense in value is the reason why the issue in tail is held to be barred by a common recovery. For, if the recoveror should obtain a recompence in lands from the common vouchee (which there is a possibility in contemplation of law, though a very improbable one, of his doing) these lands would supply the place of those so recovered from him by collusion, and would descend to the issue in tail. The reason will also hold with equal force as to most remainders and reverions, to whom the possibility will remain and revert, as a full recompense for the reality which they were otherwise entitled to: but it will not always hold; and therefore, as Pigott says, the judges have been even astute, in inventing other reasons to maintain the authority of recoveries. And, in particular, it hath been said, that though the estate-tail is gone from the recoveror; yet it is not destroyed, but only transferred, and still subsists; and will ever continue to subsist (by construction of law) in the recoveror, his heirs and assigns; and as the estate-tail so continues to subsist for ever, the remainders or reverions expectant on the determination of such estate-tail can never take place. To such awkward shifts, such subtle refinements, and such strange reasoning, were our ancestors obliged to have recourse, in order to get the better of that stubborn statute de donis. The design for which these contrivances were set on foot, was certainly laudable; the unvetting the fetters of estate-tail, which were attended with a legion of mischiefs to the commonwealth: but, while we applaud the end, we cannot but admire the means. Our modern courts of justice have indeed adopted a more manly way of treating the subject: by considering common recoveries in no other light than as the formal mode of conveyance by which tenant in tail is enabled to alien his lands. But, since the ill consequences of fettered inheritances are now generally seen and allowed, and of course the utility and expediency of setting them at liberty are apparent, it hath often been wished, that the process of this conveyance was shortened, and rendered less subject to niceties, by either totally repealing the statute de donis, which perhaps, by reviving the old doctrine of conditional fees, might give birth to many litigations: or by vesting in every tenant in tail, of full age, the same absolute fee-simple at once, which now he may obtain whenever he pleases, by the collusive fiction of a common recovery; though this might possibly bear hard upon those in remainder or reverion, by abridging the chances they would otherwise frequently have, as no recovery can be suffered in the intervals between term and term, which sometimes continue for near five months together: or, lastly, by empowering the tenant in tail to bar the estate-tail by a solemn deed, to be made in term-time, and enrolled in some court of record; which is liable to neither of the other objections, and is warranted not only by the usage of our American colonies, but by the precedent of the statute 21 Jac. I. c. 19, which, in the case of a bankrupt tenant in tail, empowers his commissioners to sell the estate at any time, by deed indented and enrolled. And if, in so national a concern, the emoluments of the officers concerned in passing recoveries are thought to be worthy attention, those might be provided for in the fees to be paid upon each enrollment. 2. The force and effect of common recoveries may appear, from what has been said, to be an absolute bar not only of all estates tail, but of remainders and reversions expectant on the determination of such estates. So that a tenant in tail may, by this method of alluvance, convey the lands held in tail to the recoveror, his heirs and assigns, absolutely free and discharged of all conditions and limitations in tail, and of all remainders and reversions.
