But, by statute 34 & 35 H. VIII. c. 20, no recovery had against tenant in tail of the king's gift, whereof the remainder or reversion is in the king, shall bar such estate-tail, or the remainder or reversion of the crown. And by the statute 11 H. VII. c. 20, no woman, after her husband's death, shall suffer a recovery of lands settled on her by her husband, or settled on her husband and her by any of his ancestors. And by statute 14 Eliz. c. 8, no tenant for life, of any sort, can suffer a recovery so as to bind them in remainder or reversion. For which reason, if there be tenant for life, with remainder in tail, and other remainders over, and the tenant for life is desirous to suffer a valid recovery, either he, or the tenant to the praepice by him made, must vouch the remainder-man in tail, otherwise the recovery is void; but if he does vouch such remainder-man, and he appears and vouches the common vouchee, it is then good; for if a man be vouched and appears, and suffers the recovery to be had, it is as effectual to bar the estate-tail as if he himself were the recoveror. In all recoveries, it is necessary that the recoveree, or tenant to the praepice, as he is usually called, be actually seised of the freehold, else the recovery is void. For all actions to recover the seisin of lands must be brought against the actual tenant of the freehold, else the suit will lose its effect; since the freehold cannot be recovered of him who has it not. And, though these recoveries are in themselves fabulous and fictitious, yet it is necessary that there be actores fabulae, properly qualified. But the nicety thought by some modern practitioners to be requisite in conveying the legal freehold, in order to make a good tenant to the praepice, is removed by the provisions of the statute 14 Geo. II. c. 20, which enacts, with a retrospect and conformity to the ancient rule of law, that, though the legal freehold be vested in lessees, yet those who are entitled to the next freehold estate in remainder, or reversion, may make a good tenant to the praepice; and that, though the deed or fine which creates such tenant be subsequent to the judgment of recovery, yet if it be in the same term, the recovery shall be valid in law; and that though the recovery itself do not appear to be entered, or be not regularly entered on record, yet the deed to make a tenant to the praepice, and declare the uses of the recovery, shall after a possession of 20 years be sufficient evidence on behalf of a purchaser for valuable consideration, that such recovery was duly suffered.

RECREMENT

Pages 333-333

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, some superfluous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> separated from some other that is useful; in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is the same with scoria, scaces, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a>.

RECRIMINATION

Pages 333-333

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> brought by the accused against the accuser upon the same fact.

RECRUITS

Pages 333-333

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, new-raised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> designed to supply the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of those who have lost their lives in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> who are disabled by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> or wounds.

RECTANGLE

Pages 333-333

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, the same with a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-angled parallelogram. See Geometry.

RECTIFICATION

Pages 333-333

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, is nothing but the repetition of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> sublimation several times, in order to render the substance purer, finer, and freer from aqueous and earthy parts. RECTIFICATION of Spirits. See Distillation.

RECTIFIER

Pages 333-333

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> consisting of two parts, which are two circles, either laid one upon, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> let into the other, and so fastened together in their centres, that they represent two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a>, one fixed, the other moveable; each of them divided into the 32 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass, and 360°, and numbered both ways, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and the south, ending at the east and west, in 90°. The fixed compass represents the horizon, in which the north and all the other points of the compass are fixed and immovable. The moveable compass represents the mariners compass; in which the north and all other points are liable to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>. In the centre of the moveable compass is fastened a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a> thread, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough to reach the outside of the fixed compass. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the instrument be made of wood, there is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> instead of the thread. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is to find the variation of the compass, to rectify the course at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; having the amplitude or azimuth given. RECTIFYING the Globe. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, n° 33—35.

RECTILINEAR

Pages 333-333

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-lined; thus figures whose perimeter consists of right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, are said to be rectilinear.

RECTITUDE

Pages 333-333

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, refers either to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of judging <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> of willing; and therefore whatever comes under the denomination of rectitude is either what is true or what is good, these being the only objects about which the mind exercises its two faculties of judging and willing. Moral rectitude, or uprightness, is the choosing and pursuing those things which the mind, upon due inquiry and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, clearly perceives to be good; and avoiding those that are evil.

RECTOR

Pages 333-333

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to several persons whose offices are very different: as, 1. The rector of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> is a clergyman that has the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> and cure of a parish, and possesses all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>, &c. 2. The same name is also given to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a> officer in several foreign <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, particularly in that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. 3. Rector is also used in several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> for the superior officer who governs the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>: and the Jesuits give this name to the superiors of such of their houses as are either seminaries <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> colleges.

RECTORY

Pages 333-333

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, parsonage, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> spiritual living, with all its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, tythes and glebes. Rectory is also sometimes used for the rector's mansion or parsonage-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>.

RECTUM

Pages 333-333

in anatomy, the third and last of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> intestines <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> guts. See Anatomy, n° 354.

RECTUS

Pages 333-333

in anatomy, a name <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of muscles, so called on account of the straightness of their fibres.

RECURVIROSTRA

Pages 333-334

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of gallinae. The beak is subulated, bent back, sharp and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> at the point; the feet are webbed, and furnished with three toes. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. the avocetta, a native of the southern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. See CCLIV, fig. 9.

RECUSANTS

Pages 334-334

such persons as acknowledge the pope to be the supreme head of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and refuse to acknowledge the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s supremacy; who are hence called Popish recusants. These are, in England, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> taxes; not merely as Romanists, but as recusants.

RED

Pages 334-334

one of the colours called simple <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> primary; being one of the shades into which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> naturally divides itself when refracted through a prism. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHROMATICS">CHROMATICS</a>. Red, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, see that article.—Some reckon six kinds or casts of red, viz. scarlet-red, crimson-red, madder-red, half-grain red, lively <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-red, and scarlet of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a>: but it is easy to see that there can be but one proper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of red; namely, the reflection of the light exactly in such a manner as it is refracted by the prism; all other shades being adulterations of that pure <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, &c. Red, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GULES">GULES</a>. Red-Breasts, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTACILLA">Motacilla</a>. Red-Book of the exchequer, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> record or manuscript volume, in the keeping of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s remembrancer, containing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> miscellaneous treatises relating to the times before the conquest. Red Ruffia, or Little Ruffia, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, bounded on the west by Upper Poland; on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Lithuania, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Little Tartars, and on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a>, Transilvania, and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. It comprehends Ruffia properly so called, Volhnia, and Podolia. It is about 650 miles in length, and from 150 to 250 in breadth. It consists chiefly of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fields, but little cultivated on account of the frequent inroads of the Tartars, and because there is no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-carriage. It had the name of Red Ruffia, from the colour of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of its inhabitants. Ruffia, properly so called, comprehends the three palatinates of Leopol, or Lemburg, Belsko, and Chelm. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA">Red <a </a>class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, or Arabic Gulph, a sea which separates <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in proportion to its breadth; and its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> is extremely difficult on account of the many rocks and shoals with which it abounds. It extends from the Capes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADEN">Aden</a> and Socotra, which form the Straits of Babelmandel to the town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a>, situated on the isthmus between Asia and Africa. Red-Shank, in ornithology. See Scolopax. Red Start, a species of Motacilla. Red-Wing. See Turdus.

REDANS

Pages 334-334

in field fortification, are a kind of indented works, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> faces, forming saluting and re-entering <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, flanking one another; generally used on the sides of a river which runs through a garrison town. They were used before battalions were invented, and are by some thought preferable to them.

REDDENDUM

Pages 334-334

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is used substantively for the clause in a lease wherein the rent is referred to the lessor. The proper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for it is next after the limitation of estate.

REDEMPTION

Pages 334-334

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of re-entering upon lands, &c. that have been sold and assigned, upon reimbursing the purchase-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> with legal costs.

REDI

Pages 334-334

an Italian physician and polite scholar, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AREZZO">Arezzo</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> in 1626. His ingenuity and learning recommended him to the office of first physician to Ferdinand II, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Tuscany; and he contributed not a little toward the compiling of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> of La Crusca. He wrote upon vipers, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of insects, and composed a good <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. All his writings are in Italian; and his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is so fine and pure, that the authors of the dictionary of La Crusca have often cited them as standards of perfection. He died in 1697.

REDLE

Pages 334-334

a soft, heavy, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> marle, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in colouring; and being washed and freed from sand is often sold by our druggists under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALE">bale</a> armenic.

REDOUBT

Pages 334-334

in fortification, a small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> fort, without any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> but in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>; used in trenches, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of circumvallation, contravallation, and approach; as also for the lodgings of corps-de-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GARD">gard</a>, and to defend pas sagés.

REDUCTION

Pages 335-335

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, denotes an operation whereby a dislocated, luxated, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> fractured bone, is restored to its former state or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

REDUNDANCY

Pages 335-335

a fault in discourse, consisting in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a superfluity of words. Words perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> are redundant, and ought to be retrenched.

REDUNDANT

Pages 335-335

in music. What the French call une <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> superflue, which we have translated a redundant chord in the article Music (from D'Alembert), has by others been rendered a chord extremely sharp, as in the translation of Rameau's Principles of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">Composition</a>. Their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be best understood by a few examples, and an account of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of tones, semitones, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> lesser intervals, contained in each. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> redundant is composed of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> tone, and a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> semitone; as from \( fa \) to \( sol \) sharp. Its proportion is as 64 to 75. The third redundant consists of two tones, and a semitone, as \( fa \), \( la \), sharp. Its proportion is as 96 to 125. The fourth redundant is the same with the tritone. From these examples compared with the same intervals in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state, the reader may form a general idea of what is meant by redundant.

REED

Pages 335-335

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. See ARUNDO, and BAMBOO. There are two sorts of reed, says Hasselquist, growing near the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. One of them has scarcely any branches; but is furnished with numerous leaves, which are narrow, smooth, channeled on the upper surface; and the plant is about 11 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The Egyptians make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> of the leaves. They lay them in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> like <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and then make them into good strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>. These, with the bark of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a>-tree, form almost the only cable used in the Nile. The other sort is of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. It is a small reed, about two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> three feet high, full branched, with short, sharp, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>-shaped leaves. The roots, which are as thick as the stem, creep and mat themselves together to a considerable distance. This plant seems useless in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>: but to it, continues the learned author, is the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> owing: for the matted roots have stopped the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> which floated in the waters, and thus formed, out of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> that is habitable.

REEF

Pages 335-335

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. When there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALE">gale</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> roll up <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sail below, that by this means it may become the narrower, and not draw so much wind; which contracting <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> taking up the sail they call a reef, or reefing the sail: so also when a topmast is sprung, as they call it, that is, when it is cracked, or almost broken in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, they cut off the lower piece that was near broken off, and setting the other part, now much shorter, in the step again, they call it a reefed topmast.

REELING

Pages 335-335

in the manufactories, the winding of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, into a skein, or upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUTTON">button</a>, to prevent its entangling. It is also used for the charging or discharging of bobbins, or quills, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> them in the manufacture of different stuffs, as thread, silk, cotton, &c. Reeling is performed in different ways, and on different engines.

REEVING

Pages 335-335

in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, the putting a rope through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>: hence to pull a rope out of a block is called unreveving.

REFECTION

Pages 335-335

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, a spare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> repast, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> sufficing for the support of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>: hence the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, and other communities, where the monks, nuns, &c., take their refectory or meals in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, is called the refectory.

REFERENCE

Pages 335-335

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, &c. a mark relative to another similar one in the margin, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> at the bottom of the page, where something omitted in the text is added, and which is to be inserted either in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> or copying.

REFINING

Pages 335-336

in general, is the art of purifying a thing; including not only the effaying <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> refining of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, but likewise the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DEPURATION">depuration</a> or clarification of liquors. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METALLURGY">METALLURGY</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. CLARIFICATION, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">PHARMACY</a>, n° 185.—192. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> and silver may be refined by several methods, which are all founded on the essential properties of these metals, and acquire different names according to their kinds. Thus, for instance, gold, having the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> which no other metal, not even silver, has, of resisting the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of sulphur, of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, of nitrous acid, of marine acid, may be purified by these agents from all other metallic substances, and consequently may be refined. These operations are distinguished by proper names, as purification of gold by antimony, parting, concentrated parting, dry parting. In a similar manner, as silver has the property, which the imperfect metals have not, of resisting the action of nitre, it may be refined by this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>: but the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> refining is chiefly applied to the purification of gold and silver by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> in the cupel. This is performed by the destruction, vitrification, and scoriification, of all the extraneous and destructible. Refining. Structible metallic substances with which they are all allayed. As none but the perfect metals can resist the combined action of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> and fire, without losing their inflammable principle, and being changed into earthy or vitreous matters, incapable of remaining any longer united with substances in a metallic state, there is then a possibility of purifying gold and silver from all alloy of imperfect metals merely by the action of fire and air; only by keeping them fused till all the alloy be destroyed: but this purification would be very expensive, from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> consumption of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and would be exceedingly tedious. Silver alloyed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, has been exposed longer than 60 hours to a glass-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> fire without being perfectly refined: the reason of which is, that when a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> only of imperfect metal remains united with gold or silver, it is covered and protected from the action of the air, which is necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBUSTION">combustion</a> of the imperfect metals, as of all combustible matters. This refining of gold and silver merely by the action of fire, which was the only method anciently known, was very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, difficult, expensive, and imperfect: but a much shorter and more advantageous method has been discovered. This method consists in adding to the alloyed gold and silver a certain quantity of lead, and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> afterwards this mixture to the action of the fire. Lead is one of the metals which loses most quickly and easily a sufficient quantity of its inflammable principle to cease to be in a metallic state; but, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, this metal has the remarkable property of retaining, notwithstanding the action of the fire, enough of this same inflammable principle to be very easily melted into a vitrified and powerfully vitrifying <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, called <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LITHARGE">litharge</a>. The lead then which is to be added to the gold and silver to be refined, or which happens naturally to be mixed with these metals, produces in their refining the following advantages: 1. By increasing the proportion of imperfect metals, it prevents them from being so well covered and protected by the perfect metals. 2. By uniting with these imperfect metals, it communicates to them a property it has of losing very easily a great part of its inflammable principle. 3. By its vitrifying and fusing property which it exercises with all its force upon the calcined and naturally refractory parts of the other metals, it facilitates and accelerates the fusion, the scorification, and the separation of these metals. These are the advantages procured by lead in the refining of gold and silver. The lead, which in this operation is scorified, and scorifies along with it the imperfect metals, separates from the metallic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, with which it is then incapable of remaining united. It floats upon the surface of the melted mass; because, by losing part of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a>, it loses also part of its specific gravity, and lastly it vitrifies. These vitrified and melted matters accumulating more and more upon the surface of the metal while the operation advances, would protect this surface from the contact of air which is so absolutely necessary for the scorification of the rest, and would thus stop the progress of the operation, which could never be finished, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a method had not been contrived for their removal. This removal of the vitrified matter is procured either by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the vessel in which the melted matter is contained; and which being porous, absorbs and imbibes the scorified matter as fast as it is formed, or by a channel cut in the edge of the vessel through which the matter flows out. The vessel in which the refining is performed is flat and shallow, that the matter which it contains may present to the air the greatest surface possible. This form resembles that of a cup, and hence it has been called cupel. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> ought to be vaulted, that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> may be applied upon the surface of the metal during the whole time of the operation. Upon this surface a crust of dark-colored pellicle is continually forming. In the instant when all the imperfect metal is destroyed, and consequently the scorification ceases, the surface of the perfect metals is seen, and appears clean and brilliant. This forms a kind of fulguration or coruscation. By this mark the metal is known to be refined. If the operation be so conducted that the metal sustains only the precise <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat necessary to keep it fused before it be perfectly refined, we may observe that it fixes or becomes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> all at once in the very instant of the coruscation; because a greater heat is required to keep silver or gold in fusion, when they are pure, than when alloyed with lead. The operation of refining may be performed in small or in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities, upon the same principles, but only with some differences in the management. As the refining of small quantities of perfect metals is performed in the same manner as these metals are assayed, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> being only a very accurate refining, we refer to the article Essay of the Value of Silver. Large quantities of silver are thus purified, after the operations by which that metal is obtained from its ores. This silver, being always much alloyed, is to be mixed with a sufficient quantity of lead to complete its purification, unless lead has been added in its first fusion from the ore, or unless it has been extracted from an ore which also contains lead; in which latter <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it is alloyed naturally with a sufficient quantity, or more than sufficient, for the refining of it.

REFLECTION

Pages 336-336

the return <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> progressive <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of a moving body, occasioned by some obstacle which hindered it from pursuing its former <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. Reflection of the Rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CATOPTRICS">catoptrics</a>, is their return, after approaching too near the surface of bodies as to be thereby repelled or driven backwards. For the causes of reflection, see <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, p. 554. Reflection is also used, figuratively, for an operation of the mind, whereby it turns its view backwards as it were upon itself, and makes itself and its own operation the object of its disquisition; and by contemplating the manner, order, and laws, which it observes in perceiving <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, comparing them together, reasoning, &c., it frames new ideas of the relations discovered therein. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, no 21. 22.

REFORMATION

Pages 336-348

in general, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of reforming <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> correcting an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> or abuse in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, or the like. By way of eminence the word is used for that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> and reformation in the corrupted system of Christianity, begun by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> in the year 1517. Under the article <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. ii.) the various corruptions in religion, the oppressions and usurpations of the clergy, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> influence of of the popes, have been so fully treated of, that any further detail here is unnecessary. It is sufficient to observe, that, before the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the Reformation, the Pope had in the most audacious manner declared himself the sovereign of the whole world. All the parts of it which were inhabited by those who were not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, he accounted to be inhabited by nobody; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Christians took it into their heads to possess any of those countries, he gave them full <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to make <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> upon the inhabitants without any provocation, and to treat them with no more <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> than they would have treated wild beasts. The countries, if conquered, were to be parcelled out according to the pope's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; and dreadful was the situation of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> who refused to obey the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the holy pontiff, of which many instances will occur to the reader in the various historical <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this extraordinary authority which the pope had assumed, he at last granted to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> all the countries to the eastward of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Non in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> all the countries to the westward of it. In this, according to the opinions of some, was completed in his person the character of Antichrist sitting in the temple of God, and assuming himself as God. He had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before, say they, assumed the supremacy belonging to the Deity himself in spiritual matters; and now he assumed the same supremacy in worldly matters also, giving the extreme regions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to whom he pleased. The Reformation, therefore, they consider as the immediate effect of divine power taking vengeance on this and all other deviations from the system of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; while others consider it merely as an effect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> causes, and which might have been foreseen and prevented, without abridging the papal power in any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. Be this as it will, however, the abovementioned partition was the last piece of insolence which the pope ever had, or in all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> ever will have, in his power to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, in the way of parceling out the globe to his adherents. Every thing was quiet, every heretic exterminated, and the whole Christian world supinely acquiesced in the enormous absurdities which were incanted upon them, when, in 1517, the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> began to decline, and has <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to do ever since. The person who made the first attack on the extravagant superstitions then prevailing was Martin Luther; the occasion of which is fully related under the article Luther. By some it is pretended, that the only <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> which Luther had in beginning the Reformation was his enmity to the Dominican friars, who had excluded his order (the Augustins) from all share in the gainful traffic of indulgences. But this does not seem at all probable, if we consider that such a motive would not naturally have led him to deny the virtue of indulgences, as such conduct could not but exclude him for ever from any chance of a share in the traffic, which otherwise perhaps he might have obtained. Besides, the extreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRARIETY">contrariety</a> of this traffic to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> principles of reason and honesty was so great, that we cannot wonder at finding one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> in the world who had <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> enough to discern it, and virtue enough to oppose such an infamous practice. In all probability, however, the insignificance of the first reformer was the reason why he was not persecuted and exterminated at his first beginning, as others had been before him. Another reason probably might be, that he did not at once attack the whole errors of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>, but brought about his reformation gradually, probably as it occurred to himself, and as we have related in the account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The Reformation began in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Wittemberg in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, but was not long confined either to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> by that city or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. In 1520 the Franciscan friars, who had the care of promulgating indulgences in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, were opposed by Zwinglius, a man not inferior in understanding and knowledge to Luther himself. He proceeded with the greatest vigour, even at the very beginning, to overturn the whole fabric of Popery; but his opinions were declared erroneous by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>. Notwithstanding this, the magistrates of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a> approved of his proceedings; and that whole <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTON">canton</a>, together with those of Bern, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCHAFFHAUSEN">Schaffhausen</a>, embraced his opinions. In Germany, Luther continued to make great advances, without being in the least intimidated by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> censures which were thundered against him from all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, he being continually protected by the German princes either from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> motives, so that his adversaries could not accomplish his destruction as they had done that of others. Melanchthon, Carladius, and other men of eminence, also greatly forwarded the work of Luther; and in all probability the Popish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a> would have soon come to an end, in the northern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> at least, had not the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. given a severe check to Opposed in the progress of reformation in Germany. In order Germany to follow out the schemes dictated by his ambition, he Charles V. thought it necessary to ingratiate himself with the pope; and the most effectual method of doing this was by destroying Luther. The pope's legates insisted that Luther ought to be condemned by the diet of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a> without either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> or hearing; as being a most notorious, avowed, and incorrigible heretic. However, this appeared unjust to the members of the diet, and he was summoned to appear; which he accordingly did without hesitation. There is not the least doubt that his appearance there had been his last in this world, had not the astonishing respect that was paid him, and the crowds who came daily to see him, deterred his judges from delivering the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> from the author of such a pestilent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>; which they were strongly solicited by the pope's party to do. He was therefore permitted to depart with a safe conduct for a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; after which he was in the state of a profligate criminal, to whom it was unlawful to perform any of the offices of humanity. During the confinement of Luther in a castle near Warburg, the Reformation advanced rapidly; almost every city in Saxony embracing the Lutheran opinions. At this time an alteration in the established forms of worship was first ventured upon at Wittemberg, by abolishing the celebration of private masses, and by altering in giving the cup as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>. In a short time, however, the new opinions were condemned by the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and a refutation of them was attempted by Henry VIII. of England. But Luther was not to be thus intimidated. Reformation dated. He published his animadversions on both with as much acrimony as if he had been refuting the meanest adversary; and a controversy managed by such illustrious antagonists drew a general <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and the Reformers daily gained new converts both in France and England. But while the efforts of Luther were thus everywhere crowned with success, the divisions began to prevail which have since so much agitated the reformed churches. The first dispute was between Luther and Zwinglius concerning the manner in which the body and blood of Christ were present in the eucharist. Luther and his followers, though they had rejected the notion of transubstantiation, were nevertheless of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the body and blood of Christ were really present in the Lord's supper, in a way which they could not pretend to explain. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARLSTADT">Carlstadt</a>, who was Luther's colleague, first suggested another view of the subject, which was afterwards confirmed and illustrated by Zwinglius, namely, that the body and blood of Christ were not really present in the eucharist; and that the bread and wine were no more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> symbols to excite the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of Christ's sufferings in the minds of those who received it. Both parties maintained their tenets with the utmost obstinacy; and, by their divisions, first gave their adversaries an argument against them, which to this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> the Catholics urge with great force; namely, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> are so divided, that it is impossible to know who is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or wrong; and that there cannot be a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> than these divisions, that the whole doctrine is false. To these intestine divisions were added the horrors of a civil war, occasioned by oppression on the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and enthusiasm on the other. In 1525, a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of seditious fanatics arose on a sudden in different parts of Germany, took arms, united their forces, and made war against the empire, laying waste the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> with fire and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and committing everywhere the greatest cruelties. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of this furious mob was composed of peasants and vassals, who groaned under heavy burdens, and declared that they were no longer able to bear the despotic <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of their chiefs; and hence this sedition had the name of the rustic war, or the war of the peasants. At first this rabble declared, that they had no other motives than the redress of their grievances; but no sooner had the enthusiastic Munzer, or Münster, the anabaptist, put himself at their head, than the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of thing was entirely changed, and the civil commotions in Saxony and Thuringia exceedingly increased, of which an account is given under the article <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time Frederic summoned the Württemberg <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Saxony, and Luther's great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, departed this life, and was succeeded by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> John. Frederic, though he had protected and encouraged Luther, yet was at no pains to introduce the reformed religion into his dominions. But with his successor it was otherwise; for he, convinced that Luther's doctrine must soon be totally destroyed and suppressed unless it received a speedy and effectual support, ordered Luther and Melanchthon to draw up a body of laws relating to the form of ecclesiastical government, the method of public worship, &c., which was to be proclaimed by heralds throughout his dominions. This example was followed by all the princes and states of Germany who renounced the papal supremacy; and a like form of worship, discipline, and government, was thus introduced into all the churches which dissented from that of Rome. This open renunciation of the Romish jurisdiction soon changed the face of affairs; and the patrons of Popery soon intimated, in a manner not at all ambiguous, that they intended to make war on the Lutheran party; which would certainly have been put in execution, had not the troubles that took <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in Europe disconcerted their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. On the other hand, the Lutherans, apprized of these hostile intentions, began also to deliberate on a proper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against that sanguinary violence with which they were in danger of being assailed. The diet of the empire assembled at Spire, in the year 1526; where the emperor's ambaassadors were desired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> their utmost endeavours of Spire favourable to suppress all disputes about religion, and to insist upon the rigorous execution of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> which had been pronounced against Luther and his followers at Worms. The greatest part of the German princes opposed this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> with the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, declaring that they could not execute that sentence, nor come to any determination with regard to the doctrines by which it had been occasioned, before the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> was submitted to the decision of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> lawfully assembled; alleging farther, that the decision of controversies of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> belonged properly to it, and to it alone. This opinion, after long and very warm debates, was adopted by a great majority, and at length consented to by the whole <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>; for it was unanimously agreed to present a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to the emperor, intreating him to assemble, without delay, a free and general council; while in the mean time it was also agreed, that the princes of the empire should, in their respective dominions, be at liberty to manage ecclesiastical affairs in the manner they should think most proper; yet so as to be able to give to God and the emperor a proper account of their administration when it should be required of them. These resolutions proved extremely favourable to the cause of reformation; neither had the emperor any leisure for some time to give disturbance to the reformed. The war which at this time ensued between him and the pope, gave the greatest advantage to the friends of the reformed, and considerably augmented their number. Several princes, whom the fear of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> had hitherto prevented from lending their assistance, publicly renounced the Romish superstition, and introduced among their subjects the same forms of religious worship, and the same system of doctrine, that had been received in Saxony. Others, though placed in such circumstances as discouraged them from acting in an open manner against the interests of the Roman pontiff, were, however, far from discovering the smallest opposition to those who withdrew the people from his despotic yoke; nor did they molest the private assemblies of those who had separated themselves from the church of Rome. And in general, all the Germans, who, before these resolutions of the diet of Spire, had rejected the papal discipline and doctrine, were now, in consequence of the liberty they enjoyed, wholly employed in bringing their their schemes and plans to a certain degree of consistence, and in adding vigour and firmness to the cause in which they were engaged. But this tranquillity and liberty was of no long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. In 1529, a new diet was assembled at the same place by the emperor, after he had quieted the troubles in various parts of his dominions, and concluded a peace with the pope. The power which had been granted to princes of managing ecclesiastical affairs till the meeting of a general council, was now revoked by a majority of votes; and every change declared unlawful that should be introduced into the doctrine, discipline, or worship of the established religion, before the determination of the approaching council was known. This <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> was considered as injurious and intolerable by the elector of Saxony, the landgrave of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>, and other members of the diet, who were persuaded of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of a reformation. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of speedily assembling a general council, they looked upon to be an artifice of the church of Rome; well knowing, that a free and lawful council would be the last thing to which the pope would consent. When, therefore, they found that all their arguments and remonstrances made no <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon Ferdinand the emperor's brother, who presided in the diet, Charles himself being then at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>, they entered a solemn protest against this decree on the 19th of April, and appealed to the emperor and a future council. Hence arose the denomination of Protestants, which from this period has been given to those who separate from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the church of Rome. The princes of the empire who entered this protest, were John, elector of Saxony; George, elector of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>; Ernest and Francis dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNENBURG">Lunenburg</a>; the landgrave of Hesse; and the prince of Anhalt. These were seconded by 13 imperial <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ULM">Ulm</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>, Rottingen, Windstein, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMMINGEN">Memmingen</a>, Nortlingen, Lindau, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEMPTEN">Kempten</a>, Heilbronn, Wilsenburg, and St <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALL">Gall</a>. The dissenting princes, who were the protectors and heads of the reformed churches, had no sooner entered their protest, than they sent proper persons to the emperor, who was then upon his passage from Spain to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, to acquaint him with their proceedings in this matter. The ministers employed in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> executed it with the greatest intrepidity and presence of mind; but the emperor, exasperated at the audacity of those who presumed to differ from him, caused the ambassadors to be arrested. The news of this violent step made the Protestant princes conclude, that their personal safety, and the success of their cause, depended entirely upon their courage and union. They determined, therefore, to enter into a solemn confederacy: for which purpose they held several meetings at Rot, Nuremberg, Smalcald, and other places; but so different were their opinions and views, that they could determine upon nothing. One great obstacle to the intended confederacy was the dispute which had arisen between Luther and Zwinglius concerning the real presence of Christ in Lord's Supper. To terminate this dispute, if possible, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, landgrave of Hesse, invited, in the year 1529, to a conference at Marpurg, Luther and Zwinglius, together with several other of the more eminent doctors who adhered to the respective parties of these contending chiefs: but this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> was not attended with the salutary effects which were expected from it. The divines disputed for four days in presence of the landgrave. Luther attacked Occolampadius, and Zwinglius was attacked by Melanchthon. Zwinglius was accused of heresy, not only on account of his explanation of the nature and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the Lord's Supper, but also in consequence of the false notions he supposed to have adopted concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of Christ, the efficacy of the divine word, original sin, and some other parts of the Christian doctrine. This illustrious reformer, however, cleared himself from the greatest part of these charges with the most triumphant <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, and in such a manner as appeared satisfactory even to Luther himself: but their dissension concerning the manner of Christ's presence in the eucharist still remained; nor could either of the contending parties be persuaded to abandon, or even to modify, their opinions on that matter. The only advantage, therefore, which resulted from the meeting was, that the jarring doctors formed a kind of truce, by agreeing to a mutual toleration of their sentiments, and leaving to the disposal of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> the cure of their divisions. In the mean time news were received that the emperor designed to come into Germany, with a view to terminate all religious differences at the approaching diet of Augsburg. Having foreseen some of the consequences of those disputes, and, besides, taken the advice of men of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, sagacity, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, he became at certain times more cool in his proceedings, and more impartial in his opinions both of the contending parties and the merits of the cause. He, therefore, in an interview with the pope at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, insisted, in the most serious and urgent manner, on the necessity of a general council. His remonstrances and expostulations, however, could not move the pontiff; who maintained with zeal the papal prerogatives, reproached the emperor with an ill-judged <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>, and alleged that it was the duty of that prince to support the church, and to execute speedy vengeance upon that obstinate heretical <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> who dared to call in question the authority of Rome and its pontiff. To this discourse the emperor paid no regard; looking upon it as a most iniquitous thing, and a measure directly opposite to the laws of the empire, to condemn unheard a set of men who had always approved themselves good citizens, and deserved well of their country in several respects. Hitherto indeed it was not easy for the emperor to form a clear idea of the matters in debate, since there was no regular system as yet Augsburg-composed, by which it might be known with certainty what were the true causes of Luther's opposition to the pope. The elector of Saxony, therefore, ordered Luther, and other eminent divines, to commit to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> articles of their religious system, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> in which they differed from the church of Rome. Luther, in compliance with this order, delivered to the elector at Torgau, 17 articles which had been agreed upon in a conference at Sultzbach in 1529; from whence these received the name of the articles of Torgau. But though these were deemed by Luther a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of the sentiments of the reformers, yet it was judged proper to enlarge them, in order to give perspicuity to their arguments, and strength to their cause. In this work Melancthon was employed, in which he showed a proper deference to the counsels of Luther, and expressed his sentiments and doctrine with the greatest elegance and perspicuity; and thus came forth to view the famous Confession of Augsburg. On the 15th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1530, Charles arrived at Augsburg, and the diet was opened five days after. The Protestants received a formal permission to present an account of their tenets to the diet on the 25th of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; in consequence of which, at the time appointed, Christian Bayer, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of Saxony, read, in the German <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, before the emperor and the princes assembled, the confession of Augsburg above-mentioned. It contained 28 chapters, of which 21 were employed in representing the religious opinions of the Protestants, and the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> in pointing out the errors and superstitions of the church of Rome. The princes heard it with the deepest attention and recollection of mind: it confirmed some in the principles they had embraced; surprized others; and many, who before this time had little or no idea of the religious sentiments of Luther, were now not only convinced of their innocence, but delighted with their purity and simplicity. The copies of this Confession, which after being read were delivered to the emperor, were signed by John elector of Saxony, George marquis of Brandenburg, Ernest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Lunenburg Philip landgrave of Hesse, Wolfgang prince of Anhalt, and by the imperial cities of Nuremberg and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REUTLINGEN">Reutlingen</a>. The creatures of the church of Rome who were present at this diet employed John Faber, afterwards bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, together with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECKIUS">Eckius</a>, and another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> named Cockleus, to draw up a refutation of the Protestant confession; which refutation having been publicly read, the emperor required the Protestant members to acquiesce in it, and put an end to the religious disputes by an unlimited submission to the opinions and doctrines contained in this answer. But this demand was far from being complied with. The Protestants declared on the contrary, that they were by no means satisfied with the reply of their adversaries; and earnestly desired a copy of it, that they might more fully demonstrate its extreme insufficiency and weakness. But this reasonable request was refused by the emperor; who interposed his supreme authority to prevent any farther proceedings in this matter, and solemnly prohibited the publication of any new writings or declarations that might contribute to lengthen out these religious debates. This, however, did not reduce the Protestants to silence. The divines of that communion, who had been present at the diet, endeavored to recollect the arguments and objections employed by Faber, and had again recourse to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of Melancthon, who refuted them in an ample and satisfactory manner in a piece which was presented to the emperor on the 22nd of September, but which Charles refused to receive. This answer was afterwards enlarged by Melancthon when he had obtained a copy of Faber's reply; and was published in the year 1531, with the other pieces that related to the doctrine and discipline of the Lutheran church, under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of A Defence of the Confession of Augsburg. Matters now began to draw towards a crisis. There were only three ways of bringing to a conclusion these religious differences. 1. To <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> the Protestants a toleration, and privilege of serving God as they thought proper; 2. To compel them to return to the church of Rome by the violent methods of persecution; or, 3. That a reconciliation should be made, upon fair, candid, and equitable terms, by engaging each of the parties to temper their zeal with moderation, to abate reciprocally the rigour of their pretensions, and remit something of their respective claims. The third expedient was most generally approved of, being peculiarly agreeable to all who had at heart the welfare of the empire; nor did the pope seem to look upon it either with aversion or contempt. Various conferences therefore were held between persons eminent for piety and learning on both sides; and nothing was omitted that might have the least tendency to calm the animosities and heal the divisions which reigned between the contending parties. But the differences were too great to admit of a reconciliation; and therefore the votaries of Rome had recourse to the powerful arguments of imperial edicts, and the force of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> arm. On the 19th of November, a severe decree was issued out by the express order of the emperor (during the absence of the Hessian and Saxon princes, who were the chief supporters of the Protestant cause) in which everything was manifestly adapted to defeat the friends of religious liberty, excepting only a faint and dubious promise of engaging the pope to assemble a general council about six months after the separation of the diet. In this decree the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and excellence of the Popish religion were extolled beyond measure, a new degree of severity and force added to that which had been published at Worms against Luther and his adherents, the changes which had been introduced into the doctrine and discipline of the Protestant churches severely censured, and a solemn order addressed to the princes, cities, and states, who had thrown off the Papal yoke, to return to their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to Rome, on pain of incurring the indignation and vengeance of the emperor as the patron and protector of the church. Of this formidable decree the elector of Saxony and confederated princes were no sooner informed, than they assembled in order to deliberate on the measures proper to be taken in such a crisis. In the years 1530 and 1531 they met, first at Smalcald, and afterwards at Frankfort, where they formed a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> and confederacy, with the intention of defending vigorously their religion and liberties against the dangers and encroachments with which they were threatened by the edict of Augsburg, without attempting, however, anything offensive against the votaries of Rome; and into this confederacy they invited the kings of England, France, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, &c. Leaving no means unemployed that might corroborate and cement this important alliance. This confederacy was at first opposed by Luther, from an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of the calamities and troubles which it might produce: but, at last, perceiving the necessity of it, he consented; though he uncharitably, as well as imprudently, refused to comprehend in it the followers of Zwinglius among the Swits, together with the German states and cities who had adopted the sentiments and confession of Bucer. In the invitation addressed to Henry VIII. of England, whom the confederate princes were willing to declare the head and pro- protector of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, the following things, among others, were expressly stipulated: That the king should encourage, promote, and maintain the true doctrine of Christ, as it was contained in the confession of Augsburg, and defend the same at the next general council; that he should not agree to any council summoned by the bishop of Rome, but protest against it; and neither submit to its decrees, nor suffer them to be respected in his dominions; that he should never allow the Roman pontiff to have any pre-eminence or jurisdiction in his dominions; that he should advance 100,000 crowns for the use of the confederacy, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> that sum if it became necessary: all which articles the confederate princes were equally obliged to observe on their part. To these demands the king replied, That he would maintain and promote the true doctrine of Christ; but, at the same time, as the true ground of that doctrine lay only in the Holy Scriptures, he would not accept at any one's hand what should be his own <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, or that of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and therefore desired that they would send over two learned men to confer with him, in order to promote a religious union between him and the confederates. However, he declared himself of their opinion with regard to the meeting of a free general council, and promised to join with them in all such councils for the defense of the true doctrine; but thought the regulation of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a> part of religion, being a matter of indifference, ought to be left to the choice of each sovereign for his own dominions. After this the king gave them a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> answer more full and satisfactory; but after the execution of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, this negociation came to nothing. On the one hand, the king grew <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> when he perceived that the confederates were no longer of use to him in supporting the validity of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>; and, on the other hand, the German princes became sensible that they could never succeed with Henry unless they allowed him an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> dictatorship in matters of religion. While everything thus tended to an open war between the two opposite parties, the elector Palatine, and the elector of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, offered their mediation, and endeavored to procure a reconciliation. The emperor himself, for various reasons, was at this time inclined to peace: for, on the one hand, he stood in need of succours against the Turks, which the Protestant princes refused to grant as long as the edicts of Worms and Augsburg remained in force; and, on the other, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of his brother Ferdinand to the dignity of king of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, which had been carried by a majority of votes at the diet of Cologne in 1531, was by the same princes contested, as being contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> laws of the empire. In consequence of all this, after many negotiations and projects of reconciliation, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of peace was concluded at Nuremberg in 1532, between the emperor and the Protestant princes, on the following conditions; viz. That the latter should furnish a subsidy for carrying on the war against the Turks, and acknowledge Ferdinand lawful king of the Romans; and that the emperor on his part should abrogate and annul the edicts of Worms and Augsburg, and allow the Lutherans the free and undisturbed exercise of their religious doctrine and discipline, until a rule of faith was fixed either in the free general council that was to be assembled in the space of six months, or in a diet of the empire. Soon after conclusion of the peace at Nuremberg, died John, elector of Saxony, who was succeeded by his son John Frederic, a prince of invincible fortitude and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>, but whose reign was little better than one continued train of disappointments and calamities. The religious truce, however, gave new vigour to the reformation. Those who had hitherto been only secret enemies to the Roman pontiff, now publicly threw off his yoke; and various cities and provinces of Germany enlisted themselves under the religious standards of Luther. On the other hand, as the emperor had now no other hope of terminating the religious disputes but by the meeting of a general council, he repeated his requests to the pope for that purpose. The pontiff (Clement VII.) whom the history of past councils filled with the greatest uneasiness, endeavoured to retard what he could not with decency refuse. At last, in 1533, he made a proposal by his legate to assemble a council at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a>, or Bologna; but the Protestants refused their consent to the nomination of an Italian council, and insisted that a controversy which had its rise in the heart of Germany should be determined within the limits of the empire. The pope, by his usual artifices, eluded the performance of his own promise; and, in 1534, was cut off by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in the midst of his intrigues. His successor Paul III. seemed to show less reluctance to the assembling a general council, and in the year 1535 expressed his inclination to convolve one at Mantua; and, the year following, actually sent circular letters for that purpose through all the states and kingdoms under his jurisdiction. This council was summoned, by a bull issued out on the 2d of June 1536, to meet at Mantua the following year; but several obstacles prevented its meeting, one of the most material of which was, that Frederic, duke of Mantua, had no inclination to receive at once so many guests, some of them very turbulent, into the place of his residence. On the other hand the Protestants were firmly persuaded, that, as the council was assembled in Italy, and by the authority of the pope alone, the latter must have had an undue influence in that assembly; of consequence, that all things must have been carried by the votaries of Rome. For this reason they assembled at Smalcald in the year 1537, where they solemnly protested against this partial and corrupt council, and, at the same time, had a new summary of their doctrine drawn up by Luther, in order to present it to the assembled <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> if it should be required of them. This summary, which had the title of The Articles of Smalcald, is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> joined with the creeds and confessions of the Lutheran church. After the meeting of the general council in Mantua was thus prevented, many schemes of accommodation were proposed both by the emperor and the accommodated Protestants; but, by the artifices of the church of Rome, all of them came to nothing. In 1541, the emperor appointed a conference at Worms on the subject of religion between persons of piety and learning chosen from the contending parties. This conference, however, was, for certain reasons, removed to the diet which was to be held at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RATISBON">Ratisbon</a> that same year, and in which the principal subject of deliberation was a memorial presented by a person unknown, containing a project of peace. But the conference produced no other effect. effect than a mutual agreement of the contending parties to refer their matters to a general council, or, if the meeting of such a council should be prevented, to the next German diet. This resolution was rendered ineffectual by a variety of incidents, which widened the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREACH">breach</a>, and put off to a farther day the deliberations which were designed to heal it. The pope ordered his legate to declare to the diet of Spire, assembled in 1542, that he would, according to the promise he had already made, assemble a general council, and that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a> should be the place of its meeting, if the diet had no objection to that city. Ferdinand, and the princes who adhered to the cause of the pope, gave their consent to this proposal; but it was vehemently objected to by the Protestants, both because the council was summoned by the authority of the pope only, and also because the place was within the jurisdiction of the Pope; whereas they desired a free council, which should not be biased by the dictates, nor awed by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a>, of the pontiff. But this protestation produced no effect. Paul III. persisted in his purpose, and issued out his circular letters for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> of the council, with the approbation of the emperor. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to this pontiff, however, it must be observed, that he shewed himself not to be adverse to every reformation. He appointed four cardinals, and three other persons eminent for their learning, to draw up a plan for the reformation of the church in general, and of the church of Rome in particular.
