Not only sympathetic ink, but also regulus of cobalt, may be made from the zaffre <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> sold, which is nothing else than the calx of regulus of cobalt mixed with more or less pulverised flints. For this purpose we must separate as well as we can the powder of flints from it, by washing, as Mr Beaumé does, and then reduce it with black flux and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. Regulus of cobalt seems incapable of uniting with sulphur; but it easily unites with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> of sulphur; and the union it forms is so intimate, that Mr Beaumé could not separate these two substances, otherwise than by precipitation with an acid. Many curious and interesting remarks are still to be discovered concerning this singular semi-metal, and we may hope to receive further information from the endeavours of chemists who have undertaken the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of it. Mr Beaumé particularly has made considerable experiments on this subject, part of which he communicates to the public in his Course of Chemistry. All the new remarks in this article are from him. See Chemistry, no 159, 212, 213, 259.

REHEARSAL

Pages 352-352

in music and the drama, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> experiment of some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, generally made in private, previous to its representation or performance in public, in order to render the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> and performers more perfect in their parts.

REIGNIER

Pages 350-350

the first French poet who succeeded in satire, was born at Chartres in 1573. He was brought up to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for which his debaucheries rendered him very unsuitable; and these by his own confession were so excessive, that at 30 he had all the infirmities of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Yet he obtained a canonry in the church of Chartres, with other benefices; and died in 1613. There is a neat Elzevir edition of his works, 12mo, 1652, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; but the most elegant is that with notes by M. Brofette, 4to, 1729, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>.

REIGNIER DES MARETS

Pages 350-350

a French poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1632. He distinguished himself early by his poetical talents, and in 1684 was made perpetual secretary to the French academy on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Mezeray: it was he who drew up all those papers in the name of the academy against Furetiere: the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> gave him the priory of Grammont, and he had also an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. He died in 1713, and his works are, French, Italian, Spanish, and Latin poems, 2 vols; a French <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>; and an Italian translation of Anacreon's odes, with some other translations.

REINS

Pages 352-352

in anatomy, the same with Kidneys. Reins of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDLE">Bridle</a>, are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> slips of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, fastened on each side of a curb <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> snaffle, which the rider holds in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, to keep the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> in subjection. There is also what is called false reins which is a lath of leather, passed sometimes through the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of the banquet, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> the horse's neck.

REJOINER

Pages 352-352

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is the defendant's answer to the plaintiff's replication <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> reply. Thus, in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, the defendant puts in an answer to the plaintiff's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, which is sometimes also called an exception; the plaintiff's answer to that is called a replication, and the defendant's answer to that a rejoinder.

RELAND

Pages 352-352

an eminent Orientalist, born at Ryp, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, in 1676. During three years <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> under Surenhusius, he made an uncommon progress in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Syriac, Chaldee, and Arabic languages; and these languages were always his favourite study. In 1701, he was, by the recommendation of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> William, appointed professor of Oriental languages and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> antiquities in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>; and died of the small-pox in 1718. He was distinguished by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, and learning; and carried on a correspondence with the most eminent scholars of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. An excellent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>. 2. Five dissertations on the Medals of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Hebrews, and several other dissertations on different subjects. 3. An Introduction to the Hebrew <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>. 4. The Antiquities of the ancient Hebrews. 5. On the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>. These works are all written in Latin.

RELATION

Pages 352-352

the mutual respect of two things, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> what each is with regard to the other. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, no 50, 54, 94, 98, 121, &c.

RELATIVE

Pages 352-352

in music. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">Mode</a>. RELATIVE Terms, in logic, are words which imply a relation: such are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, husband and wife, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, relative words are those which answer to some other word foregoing, called the antecedent; such are the relative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRONOUNS">pronouns</a> qui, quæ, quod, &c., and in English, who, whom, which, &c. The word answering to these relatives is often understood, as, "I know whom you <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>;" for "I know the person whom you mean."

RELAXATION

Pages 352-352

in medicine, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of loosening <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> slackening; or the looseness or slackness of the fibres, nerves, muscles, &c.

RELAY

Pages 352-352

a supply of horses, placed on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and appointed to be ready for a traveller to change, in order to make the greater expedition.

RELEASE

Pages 352-353

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is a discharge <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> conveyance of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> in lands or tenements, to another that hath some former estate in possession. The words generally used therein are "remitted, released, and for ever quit-claimed." And these releases may ensue, either, 1. By way of enlarging an estate, or enlarger l' estate: as, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be tenant for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> or years, remainder to another in fee, and he in remainder releases all his right to the particular tenant and his heirs, this gives him the estate in fee. But in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> the releasor must be in possession of some estate, for the release to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> upon; for if there be lette for years, and, before he enters and is in possession, the lessor releases to him all his right in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a>, such release is void for want of possession in the releasor. 2. By way of passing an estate, or passer l' estate: as, when one of two coparceners releaseth all her right to the other, this passeth the fee-simple of the whole. And in both these <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> there must be a privity of estate between the releasor and releasee; that is, one of their estates must be so related to the other, as to make but one and the same estate in law. 3. By way of passing a right, or passer le droit: as if a man be disseised, and releaseth to his disseisor all his right; hereby the disseisor acquires a new right, which changes the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of his estate, and renders that lawful which before was tortious. 4. By way of extinguishment: as if my tenant for life makes a lease to A for life, remainder to B and his heirs, and I release to A; this Relevancy extinguishes my right to the reversion, and shall ensue to the advantage of B's remainder as well as of A's particular estate. 5. By way of entry and feoffment; as if there be two <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> disseisors, and the disseisor releases to one of them, he shall be sole seised, and shall keep out his former <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>; which is the same in effect as if the disseisor had entered, and thereby put an end to the disseisin, and afterwards had enfeoffed one of the disseisors in fee. And hereupon we may observe, that when a man has in himself the possession of lands, he must at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law convey the freehold by feoffment and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a>; which makes a notoriety in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but if a man has only a right or a future <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, he may convey that right or interest by a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> release to him that is in possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>: for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCCUPANCY">occupancy</a> of the releasor is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of sufficient notoriety already.

RELICS

Pages 353-353

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the remains of the bodies <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> cloaths of saints or martyrs, and the instruments by which they were put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, devoutly preserved, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>; kissed, revered, and carried in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>.

RELIEF

Pages 353-353

(Relevamen; but, in Domesday, Relativatio, Relivium), signifies a certain sum of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, which the tenant, holding by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> serjeanty, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>, (for which homage or legal service is due), and being at full <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his ancestor, paid unto his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> at his entrance. Though reliefs had their original while fees were only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>-fees, yet they <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> after fees became <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>; and were therefore looked upon, very justly, as one of the greatest grievances of tenure; especially when, at the first, they were merely arbitrary and at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the lord; so that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he pleased to demand an exorbitant relief, it was in effect to disinherit the heir. The English ill brooked this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their new-adopted policy; and therefore William the conqueror by his laws ascertained the relief, by directing (in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Danish hezots), that a certain <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of arms, and habitments of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, should be paid by the earls, barons, and vassals respectively; and, if the latter had no arms, they should pay 100s. William Rufus broke thro' this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, and again demanded arbitrary uncertain reliefs, as due by the feudal laws; thereby in effect obliging every heir to new-purchase or redeem his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>; but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Henry I. by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> beforementioned, restored his father's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and ordained, that the relief to be paid should be according to the law so established, and not an arbitrary <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>. But afterwards, when, by an ordinance in 27 Hen. II. called the affise of arms, it was prov'd, that every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s armour should descend to his heir, for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the realm, and it thereby became impracticable to pay these acknowledgments in arms according to the laws of the conqueror, the composition was universally accepted of 100s. for every knight's fee, as we find it ever after established. But it must be remembered, that this relief was only then payable, if the heir at the death of his ancestor had attained his full age of 21 years. To RELIEVE the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">Guard</a>, is to put fresh men upon guard, which is generally every 24 hours. To RELIEVE the Trencher, is to relieve the guard of the trenches, by appointing those for that duty who have been there before. To RELIEVE the Sentry, is to put fresh men upon that duty from the guard, which is generally done every two hours, by a corporal who attends the relieving to see the proper orders are delivered to the soldier who relieves.

RELIEVO

Pages 353-353
or Relief, in painting, is the degree of boldness with which the figures seem, at a due distance, to stand out from the ground of the painting. The relievo depends much upon the depth of the shadow, and the strength of the light; or on the height of the different colours, bordering on one another; and particularly on the difference of the colour of the figure from that of the ground: thus, when the light is so disposed as to make the nearest parts of the figure advance, and is well diffused on the masses, yet infinitely diminishing, and terminating in a large spacious shadow, brought off insensibly, the relievo is said to be bold, and the chiaroscuro well understood.

RELIGION

Pages 353-354

that worship and homage which is due to God, considered as our Creator, Preserver, and most bountiful Benefactor. As our affections depend on our opinions of their objects, it seems to be among the first duties we owe to the Author of our being, to form the least imperfect, since we cannot form perfect conceptions of his character and administration: for such conceptions <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> render our religion rational, and our dispositions refined. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> our opinions are <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> and distorted, our religion will be superstitious, and our temper abject. Thus, if we ascribe to the Deity that false majesty which consists in the unbenevolent and fulsome <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> will <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> power, or suppose him to delight in the prostrations of servile fear, or as fervent praise, he will be worshipped with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> adulation, and a profusion of compliments. If he be looked upon as a stern and implacable Being, delighting in vengeance, he will be adored with pompous offerings, or whatever else may be thought proper to soothe and mollify him. But if we believe perfect goodness to be the character Religion, ter of the Supreme Being, and that he loves those who resemble him most in this the most amiable of his attributes, the worship paid him will be rational and sublime, and his worshippers will seek to please him by imitating that goodness which they adore. Indeed, wherever <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> conceptions of the Deity, and his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, prevail, when he is considered as the inexhausted source of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, and joy, as acting in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> character of a father and governor, what veneration and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> must such conceptions, thoroughly believed, excite in the mind? how <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and delightful must it be, to one whose heart is open to the perception of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and of every thing fair, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and wonderful in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, to engage in the exercises of religion, and to contemplate and adore him, who is the first fair, first great, and first wonderful; in whom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, power, and goodness dwell vitally, essentially, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a>? what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> is here, to fill the most enlarged capacity, what <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> to engage the most ardent love, what a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of wonders, in such exuberance of perfection, to astonish and delight the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind, through an unfailing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>! When we consider the unalloyed purity and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> perfection of the divine nature, and reflect on the imperfection and various blemishes of our own, and the ungrateful returns we have made to his goodness, we must sink, or be convinced we ought to sink, into the deepest humility and prostration of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> before him, and be conscious that it is our duty to repent of a temper and conduct so unworthy of our nature, and so unbecoming our obligations to its author; and to resolve to act a wiser and better <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> for the future. And if the Deity is considered as the father of mercies, who loves his creatures with infinite tenderness, and, in a particular manner, all good men; nay, who delights in goodness even in its most imperfect degrees; what resignation, what dependence, what generous confidence, what hope in God, and in his all-wise providence, must arise in the soul that is possessed of such amiable views of him! We must further observe, that all those affections which regard the Deity as their immediate and primary object, are vital energies of the soul, and consequently exert themselves into acts, and, like all other energies, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> strength or greater <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> by that exertion: it is therefore our duty, as well as highest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, often, at stated times, and by decent and solemn acts, to adore the great original of our existence, to express our veneration and love by a devout recognition of his perfections, and to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> our gratitude by celebrating his goodness, and thankfully acknowledging all his benefits; by proper exercises of sorrow and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a> to confess our ingratitude and folly, to signify our dependence on God, our confidence in his goodness, and our resignation to the dispersions of his Providence; and this not only in private, but in public worship, where the presence of our fellow-creatures and the powerful contagion of the social affections, conspire to kindle and spread the devout <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> with greater warmth and energy. Religion is divided into natural and revealed. By natural religion is meant that knowledge, veneration, and love of God, and the practice of those duties to him, our fellow-creatures, and ourselves, which are discoverable by the right exercise of our rational faculties, from considering the nature and perfections of God, and our relation to him and to one another. (See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">Moral <a class="</a>xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>.) And by revealed religion is meant, natural religion explained, enforced, and enlarged, from the express declarations of God himself from the mouths or pens of his prophets, &c. Religion, in a more contracted <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is used for that system of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and worship, which obtains in several countries of the world; (see Christianity, Mahometanism, Jews, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>;) And even for the various sects into which religion is divided; (see Roman-Catholics, Lutherans, Calvinists, &c.)

RELIGIOUS

Pages 354-354

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, something that relates to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>.—We say, a religious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, religious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, &c.—Churches and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-yards are religious places.—A religious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> is also called a croisade. See Croisade. Religious, is also used substantially for a person engaged by solemn vows to the monastic life; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a person shut up in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a life of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> and austerity, under some rule or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> religious we popularly call monks and friars; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, nuns and canonesses.

REMBRANDT

Pages 354-355

a Flemish painter and engraver of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> eminence, was born in 1606, in a mill upon the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, from whence he derived his name of Van Rhin. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> was born with a creative genius, which never attained perfection. It was said of him, that he would have invented <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had not found it already discovered. Without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, without the assistance of any master, but by his own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a>, he formed rules, and a certain practical method for colouring, and the mixture produced the designed effect. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> is not set off to the greatest advantage in his pictures; but there is such a striking <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and simplicity in them, that his heads, particularly his portraits, seem animated, and rising from the canvas. He was fond of strong contrasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. The light entered in his working-room only by a hole, in the manner of a camera obscura, by which he judged with greater certainty of his productions. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> considered painting like the stage, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> do not strike unless they are exaggerated. He did not pursue the method of the Flemish painters of finishing his pieces. He sometimes gave his light such thick touches, that it seemed more like modelling than painting. A head of his has been shown, the nose of which was so thick of paint, as that which he copied from nature. He was told one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, that by his peculiar method of employing colours, his pieces appeared rugged and uneven—he replied, he was a painter, and not a dyer. He took a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in dressing his figures in an extraordinary manner: with this view he had collected a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of eastern caps, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> armour, and drapery <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> since out of fashion. When he was advised to consult antiquity to attain a better <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, as his was usually heavy and uneven, he took his counsellor to the closet where these old vestments were deposited, saying, by way of derision, those were his antiques. Rembrandt, like most men of genius, had many caprices. Being one day at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, painting a whole family in a single <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, word being brought him that his monkey was dead, he was so affected at the loss of this this animal, that, without paying any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the persons who were fitting for their pictures, he painted the monkey upon the same canvas. This whim could not fail of displeasing those the piece was designed for; but he would not efface it, choosing rather to lose the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of his picture. This freak <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear still more extraordinary in Rembrandt, when it is considered that he was extremely avaricious; which vice daily grew upon him. He practised various stratagems to sell his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price. The public were very desirous of purchasing them, and not without reason. In his prints the same taste prevails as in his pictures; they are rough and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, but picturesque. In order to heighten the value of his prints, and increase their price, he made his son sell them as if he had purchased them from his father; others he exposed at public sales, and went thither himself in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> to bid for them; sometimes he gave out that he was going to leave <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. These stratagems were successful, and he got his own price for his prints. At other times he would print his plates half finished, and expose them to sale; he afterwards finished them, and they became fresh plates. When they wanted retouching, he made some alterations in them, which promoted the sale of his prints a third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, though they differed but little from the first impressions. His pupils, who were not ignorant of his avarice, one day painted some pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> upon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>; and Rembrandt no sooner <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> them, than he was going to take them up. He was not angry at the pleasantry, but his avarice still prevailed. He died in 1674.

REMEMBRANCE

Pages 355-355

is when the idea of something formerly known recurs again to the mind, without the operation of a like object on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> senses. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">MEMORY</a> and REMINISCENCE.

REMEMBRANCERS

Pages 355-355

anciently called chirks of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a>, certain officers in the exchequer, whereof three are distinguished by the names of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s remembrancer, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>'s remembrancer, and the remembrancer of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. The king's remembrancer enters in his office all recognizances taken before the barons for any of the king's debts, for appearances <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> observing of orders; he also takes all bonds for the king's debts, &c. and makes out processes thereon. He likewise issues processes against the collectors of the customs, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>, and others, for their accounts; and informations upon penal statutes are entered and sued in his office, where all proceedings in matters upon English bills in the exchequer-chamber remain. His duty further is to make out the bills of compositions upon penal laws, to take the statement of debts; and into his office are delivered all kinds of indentures and other evidences which concern the assuring any lands to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. He, every year in crassino animarum, reads in open <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> the statute for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of sheriffs; and likewise openly reads in court the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of all the officers, when they are admitted. The lord treasurer's remembrancer is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> to make out processes against all sheriffs, etcheaters, receivers, and bailiffs, for their accounts. He also makes out writs of fieri facias, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> for debts due to the king, either in the pipe or with the auditors; and processes for all such revenue as is due to the king on account of his tenures. He takes the account of sheriffs; and also keeps a record, by which it appears whether the sheriffs or other accountants pay their proffers due at Easter and Michaelmas; and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he makes a record, whereby the sheriffs or other accountants keep their prefixed days: there are likewise brought into his office all the accounts of customers, comptrollers, and accountants, in order to make entry thereof on record; also all attrears and arrearsments are certified here, &c. The remembrancer of the first-fruits takes all compositions and bonds for the payment of first-fruits and tenths; and makes out processes against such as do not pay the same.

REMINISCENCE

Pages 355-355

that power of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind, whereby it recollects itself, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> calls again into its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> or notions as it had really forgot; in which it differs from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, which is a treasuring up of things in the mind, and keeping them there, without forgetting them.

REMISSION

Pages 355-355

in physics, the abatement of the power <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> efficacy of any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; in opposition to the increase of the same, which is called intensification. Remission, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, &c. denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> of a crime, or the giving up the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> due thereto. Remission, in medicine, is when a distemper abates for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, but does not quite off.

REMITTANCE

Pages 355-355

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, the traffick <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> return of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> from one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another, by bills of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, orders, or the like.

REMONSTRANCE

Pages 355-355

an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPOSTULATION">expostulation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> humble supplication, addressed to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, or other superior, beseeching him to reflect on the inconveniences or ill consequences of some order, edict, or the like. This word is also used for an expostulatory counsel, or advice; or a gentle and handsome reproof, made either in general, or particular, to apprize of or correct some fault, &c.

REMORA

Pages 355-355
or Sucking-fish, a species of Echeneis. Many incredible things are related of this animal by the ancients; as that it had the power of stopping the largest and swiftest vessel in its course; and even to this day it is affected by the fishermen in the Mediterranean, that it has a power of retarding the motion of their boats by attaching itself to them; for which reason they kill it whenever they perceive this retardation. But in what manner the remora performs this, we have no account. Action of REMOVING in Scots law. See LAW, No clxvii. 18.

RENCOUNTER

Pages 355-355

in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, the encounter of two little bodies <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> parties of forces. In which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> rencounter is used in opposition to a pitched <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. Rencontre, in single combats, is used by way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUEL">DUEL</a>.—When two persons <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> out, and fight on the spot, without having premeditated the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, it is called a rencontre.

RENDEZVOUS

Pages 355-355
or Rendezvous, a place appointed to meet in, at a certain day and hour.

REPELLENTS

Pages 355-356

in medicine, remedies which drive back a morbid humour into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of blood, from whence it was, unduly secreted.

REPETITION

Pages 356-356

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> which gracefully and emphatically repeats either the same word, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> in different words. See Oratory, n° 66—79. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of this figure is to make deep impressions on those we <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>. It expresses <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> and indignation, full assurance of what we affirm, and a vehement concern for what we have espoused.

REPHIDIM

Pages 356-356

(anc. geog.) a station of the Israelites near mount Horeb, where they murmured for want of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>; when Moses was ordered to smite the rock Horeb, upon which it yielded water. Here Joshua discomfited the Amalekites. This rock, out of which Moses brought water, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of a prodigious height and thickness, rising out of the ground; on two sides of which are several holes, by which the water ran. (Thevenot.)

REPLEGIARE

Pages 356-356

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies to redeem a thing taken <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> detained by another, by putting in legal suerices. DE HOMINE REPLEGIANDO. See Homine.

REPLEVIN

Pages 356-356

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a remedy granted on a distress, by which the first possessor has his goods restored to him again, on his giving security to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> that he <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> pursue his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> against the party distraining, and return the goods <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> cattle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the taking them shall be adjudged lawful. In a replevin the person distrained becomes plaintiff; and the person distraining is called the defendant or avowant, and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a> an avowry. At the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-law replevins are by writ, either out of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> or common-places; but by statute, they are by plaint in the sheriff's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and court-baron, for a person's more speedily obtaining the goods distrained. If a plaint in replevin be removed into the court of king's-bench, &c. and the plaintiff makes default and becomes non-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, or judgment is given against him, the defendant in replevin shall have the writ of retorno habendo of the goods taken in distress. See the article Replevy.

REPLEVY

Pages 356-357

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is a tenant's bringing a writ of replevin, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> replegiari facias, where his goods are taken by distress for rent; which must be done within five days after the distress, otherwise at the five days end they are to be appraised and sold. This word is also used for bailing a person, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a homine replegiando.

REPORT

Pages 357-357

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is a public relation of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> judicially argued, debated, resolved, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> adjudged in any of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s courts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, with the causes and reasons of the same, as delivered by the judges. Also when the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, or any other court, refers the stating of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, or the comparing of an account, to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of chancery, or other referee, his certificate thereon is called a report.

REPOSE

Pages 357-357

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, certain masses <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> assemblages of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, which being well conducted, prevent the confusion of objects and figures, by engaging and fixing the eye so as it cannot attend to the other parts of the painting for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and thus leading it to consider the several groups gradually, proceeding, as it were, from stage to stage.

REPRESENTATION

Pages 357-357

in the drama, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of a theatrical piece, together with the scenes, machinery, &c.

REPRESENTATIVE

Pages 357-357

one who personates <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> supplies the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of another, and is invested with his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and authority. Thus the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons are the representatives of the people in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. See COMMONS and PARLIAMENT.

REPRIEVE

Pages 357-357

in criminal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, (from reprendre, "to take back,") is the withdrawing of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> for an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; whereby the execution is suspended. See JUDGEMENT. This may be, first, ex arbitrio judicis, either before <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> after judgment; as, where the judge is not satisfied with the verdict, or the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> is insufficient, or the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> is insufficient, or he is doubtful whether the offence be within clergy; or sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be a small felony, or any favourable circumstances appear in the criminal's character, in order to give room to apply to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> for either an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> or conditional <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>. These arbitrary reprieves may be granted or taken off by the justices of goal-delivery, although their session be finished, and their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> expired; but this rather by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> usage than of strict <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. Reprieves may also be ex necessitate legis: as where a woman is capitally convicted, and pleads her pregnancy. Though this is no cause to stay judgment, yet it is to relpite the execution till she be delivered. This is a mercy dictated by the law of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, in favorem prolis; and therefore no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bloody proceedings in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> hath been more justly detested, than the cruelty that was exercised in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUERNSEY">Guernsey</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> a woman big with child; and, when through the violence of the flames the infant sprang forth at the stake, and was preferred by the bystanders, after some deliberations of the priests who assisted at the sacrifice, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> it into the fire as a young heretic. A barbarity which they never learned from the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Rome; which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, with the same <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> as our own, quod praegnantis mulieris damnae pana differatur, quoad pariat: which doctrine has also prevailed in England, as early as the first memo- rials of our law <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> reach. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> be made in stay of execution, the judge must direct a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURY">jury</a> of 12 matrons or discreet women to inquire into the fact; and if they bring in their verdict quick with child (for barely with child, unless it be alive in the womb, is not sufficient) execution shall be stayed generally till the next session; and so from session to session, till either she is delivered, or proves by the course of nature not to have been with child at all. But if she once hath had the benefit of this reprieve, and been delivered, and afterwards becomes pregnant again, she shall not be entitled to the benefit of a farther respite for that cause. For she may now be executed before the child is quick in the womb; and shall not, by her own incontinence, evade the sentence of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Another cause of regular reprieve is, if the offender become non compos between the judgment and the award of execution: for regularly, though a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> be compos when he commits a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> crime, yet if he becomes non compos after, he shall not be indicted; if after indictment, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> shall not be convicted; if after conviction, he shall not receive judgement; if after judgment, he shall not be ordered for execution: for furiusus solo furore punitur, and the law knows not but he might have offered some reason, if in his senses, to have stayed these respective proceedings. It is therefore an invariable rule, when any time intervenes between the attainder and the award of execution, to demand of the prisoner what he hath to allege why execution should not be awarded against him; and, if he appears to be insane, the judge in his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> may and ought to reprieve him. Or, the party may plead in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of execution; which plea may be either pregnancy, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s pardon, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, or diversity of person, viz. that he is not the same that was attainted, and the like. In this last case a jury shall be impannelled to try this collateral issue, namely, the identity of his person; and not whether guilty or innocent, for that has been decided before. And in these collateral issues the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> shall be infanter; and no time allowed the prisoner to make his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> or produce his witnesses, unless he will make oath that he is not the person attainted: neither shall any peremptory challenges of the jury be allowed. The prisoner, though formerly such challenges were held to be allowable whenever a man's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was in question. If neither pregnancy, insanity, non-identity, nor other plea, will avail to avoid the judgment, and lay the execution consequent thereupon, the last and surest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> is in the king's most gracious pardon; the granting of which is the most amiable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of the crown. See the article PARDON.

REPRISALS

Pages 357-357

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> which princes claim of taking from their enemies anything <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to what they unjustly detain from them.

REPROBATION

Pages 357-357

in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> by which God is supposed, either from all eternity, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of the world, to consign over to eternal misery the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of mankind, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> none of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a>, except those whom he made the heirs of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>.

REPTILES

Pages 358-358

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a kind of animals denominated from their creeping <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> advancing on the belly. Or reptiles are a genus of animals and insects, which, instead of feet, rest on one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body, while they advance forward with the rest. Such are earthworms, snakes, caterpillars, &c. Indeed, most of the class of reptiles have feet; only those very small, and the legs remarkably short in proportion to the bulk of the body. Naturalists observe a world of artful contrivance for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of reptiles. Thus, particularly in the earthworm, Dr Willis tells us, the whole body is only a chain of annular muscles; or, as Mr <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a> says, it is only one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> spiral muscle, the orbicular fibres whereof being contracted, render each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> narrower and longer than before; by which means it is enabled, like the worm of an auger, to bore its passage into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Its reptile motion might also be explained by a wire wound on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, which when slipped off, and one end extended and held fast, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> bring the other near to it. So the earth-worm having <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> out or extended his body (which is with a wreathing), it takes hold by these small feet it has, and to contracts the hinder part of its body. Dr Tyson adds, that when the forepart of the body is stretched out, and applied to a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> at a distance, the hinder part relaxing and shortening is easily drawn towards it as a centre. Its feet are disposed in a quadruple row the whole length of the worm, with which, as with so many hooks, it fastens <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> sometimes this and sometimes that part of the body to the plane, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> stretches out or drags after it another. The creeping of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> is effected after a somewhat different manner; there being a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in their structure, in that these last have a compages of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> articulated together. The body here is not drawn together, but as it were complicated; part of it being applied on the rough ground, and the rest ejaculated and shot from it, which being let on the ground in its turn, brings the other after it. The spine of the back variously wreathed has the same effect in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a>, as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> in the feet of other animals; they make their leaps by means of muscles, and extend the pliace or folds.

REPUBLIC

Pages 358-358
or commonwealth, a popular state or government; or a nation where the people have the government in their own hands. See Government. Republic of Letters, a phrase used collectively of the whole body of the studious and learned people.

REPUDIATION

Pages 358-358

in the civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of divorcing. See Divorce.

REPULSION

Pages 358-358

in physics, that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of bodies whereby they recede from each other, and, on certain occasions, mutually avoid coming into contact. Repulsion, as well as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a>, has of late been considered as one of the primary qualities of all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and has been much used in explaining the phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: thus the particles of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, fire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>, electric fluid, &c., are all said to have a repulsive power with respect to one another.—That this is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> with the air, and vapour of all kinds, is certain; because when they are compressed into a small space, they expand with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force: but as to fire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>, our experiments fail; nay, the supposition of a repulsive power among the particles of the electric fluid is inconsistent with the phenomena, as has been demonstrated under the article Electricity, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. V. and VI. Even in those <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, air and steam, where a repulsive power most manifestly exists, it is demonstrable that the repulsion cannot be a primary <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, since it can be increased to a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and diminished by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>: but it is impossible that a primary quality of matter can be increased <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> diminished by any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> circumstances whatever; for whatever property depends upon external circumstances, is not a primary but a secondary one.—The repulsion of electrified bodies is explained under the article Electricity: that of others is less subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>; and the most that can be said concerning it is, that in many <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> it seems to be the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a modification of fire, and in others of electricity.

REQUEST

Pages 358-359

In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a supplication <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> petition preferred to a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, or to a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; beg- Court of Request (<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CURIA">curia</a> requisitionum) was a court of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with the court of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, but inferior to it; principally instituted for the relief of such petitioners as in conscionable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> addressed themselves by supplication to his majesty. Of this court the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> privy-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> judge, assisted by the masters of requests; and it had beginning about the 9 H. 7. according to Sir Julius Cæsar's tractate upon this subject; though Mr Gwyn, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to his Readings, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> it began from a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> first granted by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Henry VIII. This court, having assumed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> power to itself, so that it became burdensome, Mich. anno 40 and 41 Eliz. in the court of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-pleas it was adjudged upon solemn argument, that the court of requests was no court of judicature, &c. and by Stat. 16 & 17 Car. I. c. 10. it was taken away.

REQUIEM

Pages 359-359

in the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> sung for the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of a person deceased.

RESCISSION

Pages 359-359

in the civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> intended for the annulling <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> setting aside any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, &c.

RESEDA

Pages 359-360

dyers weed, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>-weed, weld, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> wild-woad; a genus of the order of triggynia, belonging to the dodecanidia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are 11 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable is the lutola or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> dyers weed, growing naturally in waste places in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The young leaves are often undulated; the stalk is a yard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, or more, terminated with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> naked spike of yellowish-green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; the plant is cultivated and much used for dying <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> of a yellow <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> recommendation of the plant is, that it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> grow with very little trouble, without dung, and on the very worst soils. For this reason it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> sown with, or immediately after, barley or oats, without any additional care, except <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> a bush over it to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARROW">harrow</a> it in. The reaping of the corn does it little or no hurt, as it grows but little the first year; and the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> it is pulled and dried like <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>. Much care and nicety, however, is requisite, so as not to injure either the seed or stalk; or, which sometimes happens, damaging both, by letting it stand too long, or pulling it too green. To avoid these inconveniences, a better method of culture has been devised. This new method is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> and harrow the ground very fine, without dung, as equally as possible, and then sowing about a gallon of seed, which is very small, upon an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August. In about two months it will be high enough to hoe, which must be carefully done, and the plants left about six inches asunder. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> it is to be hoed again, and this labour is to be repeated a third time in May. About the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, when the flower is in full vigour, and the stalk is become of a greenish-yellow, it should be pulled; a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of stems being left growing for seed till September. By this means the flower and stalk, both of them being carefully dried, will sell at a good price to the dyers, who employ it constantly, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities; add to this, that the seed being ripe and in perfect order, will yield a very considerable profit. In a tolerable year, when the seasons have not been unfavourable, the advantages derived from this vegetable will answer very well; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the summer should be remarkably fine, and proper care is taken in getting it in, there will be a very large produce upon an acre. The crop being, as has been shown, so early removed, the ground may be conveniently prepared for growing wheat the next year. Upon the whole, weld is in its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> a very valuable commodity in many respects, as it serves equally for woollen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, or silk; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> not only a rich and lasting yellow, but also, properly managed, all the different shades of yellow with brightness and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; and if these be previously dipped blue, they are by the weld changed into a very pleasing green, which our artists can also diversify into a great variety of shades. RESEMBLANCE and Dissimilitude, the relations of likeness and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> among objects. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">Comparison</a>. The connection that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> hath with the beings around him, requires some acquaintance with their nature, their powers, and their qualities, for regulating his conduct. For acquiring a branch of knowledge so essential to our well-being, motives alone of reason and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> are not sufficient: nature hath providentially superadded curiosity, a vigorous propensity, which never is at rest. This propensity alone attaches us to every new object*; and incites us to compare objects, in order to discover their differences and resemblances. Resemblance among objects of the same kind, and dissimilitude among objects of different kinds, are too obvious and familiar to gratify our curiosity in any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; its gratification lies in discovering differences among things where resemblance prevails, and resemblances where difference prevails. Thus a difference in individuals of the same kind of plants or animals, is deemed a discovery, while the many particulars in which they agree are neglected; and in different kinds, any resemblance is greedily remarked, without attending to the many particulars in which they differ. A comparison of the former neither tends to gratify our curiosity, nor to set the objects compared in a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>: two apartments in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, similar in shape, size, and furniture, make separately as good a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> as when compared; and the same observation is applicable to two similar compartments in a garden: on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, oppose a regular <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or a good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> to a towering hill, or even a little dog to a large <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> will produce no effect. But a resemblance between objects of different kinds, and a difference between objects of the same kind, have remarkably an enlivening effect. The poets, such of them as have a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, draw all their similes from things that in the main differ widely from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> subject; and they never attempt a contrast, but where the things have a common genus, and a resemblance in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> circumstances: <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> together a large and a small-sized animal of the same species, the one will appear greater, the other less, than when viewed separately: when we oppose beauty to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a>, each makes a greater figure by the comparison. We compare the dress of different nations with curiosity, but without surprise; because they they have no such resemblance in the capital parts as to please us by contrasting the smaller parts. But a new cut of a sleeve, or of a pocket, enchants by its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>; and, in opposition to the former fashion, raises some degree of surprize. That resemblance and dissimilitude have an enlivening effect upon objects of sight, is made sufficiently evident; and that they have the same effect upon objects of the other senses, is also certain. Nor is that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> confined to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> senses; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> contrasted make a greater figure by the opposition: Iago, in the tragedy of Othello, says, He hath a daily beauty in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, That makes me ugly. The character of a fop, and of a rough <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>, are nowhere more successfully contrasted than in Shakespeare: Hotspur. My <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEGE">liege</a>, I did deny no prisoners: But I remember, when the fight was done, When I was dry with rage, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> toil, Breathless and faint, leaning upon my <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; Came there a certain <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, neat, trimly dress'd, Fresh as a bridegroom; and his chin, new-reap'd, Show'd like a stubble-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>-home. He was perfumed like a milliner; And 'twixt his finger and his thumb he held A pouncet-box, which ever and anon He gave his nose—and fill he smil'd and talk'd; And as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> bare dead bodies by, He call'd them untaught knaves, unmannerly, To bring a slovenly, unhandsome corse Betwixt the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. With many holiday and lady terms He question'd me: among the rest, demanded My pris'ners, in your majesty's behalf. I then, all smarting with my wounds; being <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALL">gall</a>'d To be so better'd with a popinjay, Out of my grief, and my impatience, Answer'd, neglectingly, I know not what: He should, or should not; for he made me mad, To see him shine so brisk, and smell so sweet, And talk so like a waiting gentlewoman, Of guns, and drums, and wounds, (God <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the mark!) And telling me, the sovereign't thing on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> Was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, for an inward bruise; And that it was great pity, so it was, This villanous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-petre should be digg'd Out of the bowels of the harmless earth, Which many a good, tall fellow had destroy'd So cowardly: and but for these vile guns, He would himself have been a soldier. First <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, Henry IV. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> 1. sc. 4. Passions and emotions are also enflamed by comparison. A man of high <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> humbles the bye-standers even to annihilate them in their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>: Cæsar, beholding the statue of Alexander, was greatly mortified, that now at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 32, when Alexander died, he had not performed one memorable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. Our opinions also are much influenced by comparison. A man whose opulence exceeds the ordinary standard, is reputed richer than he is in reality; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> or weakness, if at all remarkable in an individual, is generally carried beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. The opinion a man forms of his present distress is heightened by contrasting it with his former <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>: Could I forget What I have been, I might the better bear What I'm destin'd to. I'm not the first That have been wretched: but to think how much I have been happier. Southern's Innocent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">Adultery</a>, act 2. The distress of a long journey makes even an indifferent inn agreeable; and, in travelling, when the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> is good and the horseman well covered, a bad <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> may be agreeable, by making him sensible how snug he is. The same effect is equally remarkable, when a man opposes his condition to that of others. A ship tossed about in a storm, makes the spectator reflect upon his own ease and security, and puts these in the strongest light. A man in grief cannot bear mirth; it gives him a more lively notion of his unhappiness, and of course makes him more unhappy. Satan, contemplating the beauties of the terrestrial paradise, has the following exclamation. With what delight could I have walk'd thee round, If I could joy in ought, sweet interchange Of hill and valley, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, woods, and plains, Now land, now <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and shores with forest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>'d, Rocks, dens, and caves! but I in none of these Find place or refuge; and the more I see Pleasures about me, so much more I feel Torment within me, as from the hateful siege Of contraries: all good to me becomes bane, and in heav'n much worse would be my state. Paradise lost, book 9. l. 114. The appearance of danger gives sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, sometimes pain. A timorous person upon the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a> of a high tower, is seized with fear, which even the consciousness of security cannot dissipate. But upon one of a firm head, this situation has a contrary effect: the appearance of danger heightens, by opposition, the consciousness of security, and consequently the satisfaction that arises from security: here the feeling resembles that abovementioned, occasioned by a ship labouring in a storm.

RESEN

Pages 363-363

(Moses); a town on the Tigris, built by Nimrod; thought to be the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LARISSA">Larissa</a> of Xenophon; which see. But as Larissa is a name in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>; and as there were no Greek cities, consequently no Larissa in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, before Alexander the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>; it is probable that the Greeks asking of what city those were the ruins they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, the Assyrians might answer, Laresen, "Of Resen;" which word Xenophon expressed by Larissa, a more familiar <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> to a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>).

RESERVATION

Pages 363-363

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> clause whereby something is reserved, or secured to one's self. Mental Reservation, a proposition, which strictly taken, and according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> import of the terms, is false; but, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> qualified by something concealed in the mind, becomes true. Mental reservations are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> refuge of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> hypocrites, who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> them to accommodate their consciences with their interests: the Jesuits are zealous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for mental reservations; yet are they real lies, as including an intention to deceive.

RESERVE

Pages 363-363

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the same with reservation. See the article RESERVATION. Body of Reserve, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Corps de Reserve, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, the third or last line of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, drawn up for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; so called because they are reserved to sustain the rest as occasion requires, and not to engage but in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>.

RESERVOIR

Pages 363-363

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> is collected and reserved, in order to be conveyed to distant places through <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> supply a fountain or jet d'eau.

RESET

Pages 363-363

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the receiving <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> harbouring an outlawed person. See OUTLAWRY.

RESOLUTION

Pages 364-364

in medicine, the disappearing of any tumour without coming to suppuration <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> forming an abscess.

RESOLVENTS

Pages 364-364

in medicine, such as are proper for dissipating tumours, without allowing them to come to suppuration.

RESONANCE

Pages 364-364

RESOUNDING, in music, &c. a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> returned by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> inclosed in the bodies of stringed instruments, such as lutes, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> even in the bodies of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>-instruments, as flutes, &c.

RESPIRATION

Pages 364-365
