the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of respiring <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> breathing the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Respiration constitutes one of those functions which are properly termed vital, as being essential to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; for to live and to breathe are in fact <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> terms. It consists in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> of the thorax, by first inspiring air into the lungs, and then expelling it from them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a>. It <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> perhaps be easy to distinguish and point out the several phenomena of respiration; but to explain their physical cause will be attended with difficulty: for it will naturally be inquired, how the lungs, when emptied of their air, and contracted by expiration, become again inflated, they themselves being perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>?—How the ribs are elevated in opposition to their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> situation? and why the diaphragm is contracted downwards towards the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>? Were we to assert, that the air, by forcing its way into the cavity of the lungs, dilated them, and consequently elevated the ribs and pressed <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the diaphragm, we should speak erroneously. What induces the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a> it is not easy to ascertain; but after an animal has once respired, it would seem likely that the blood, after expiration, finding its passage through the lungs obstructed, becomes a stimulus, which induces the intercostal muscles and the diaphragm to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, and enlarge the cavity of the thorax, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> perhaps of a certain nervous influence, which we will not here attempt to explain. The air then rushes into the lungs; every branch of the bronchial tubes, and all the cellular spaces into which they open, become fully dilated; and the pulmonary vessels being equally distended, the blood flows thro' them with ease. But as the stimulus which first occasioned this dilatation ceases to operate, the muscles gradually contract, the diaphragm rises upwards again and diminishes the cavity of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, the ribs return to their former state, and as the air passes out in expiration, the lungs gradually collapse, and a resistance to the passage of the blood again takes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. But the heart continuing to receive and expel the blood, the pulmonary artery begins again to be distended, the stimulus is renewed, and the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is repeated, and continues to be repeated, in a regular succession during life: for though the muscles of respiration, having a mixed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, are Respiration (unlike the heart) in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> dependent on the will, yet no <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> being, after having once respired, can live many moments without it.—In an attempt to hold one's breath, the blood soon begins to distend the veins, which are unable to empty their contents into the heart, and we are able only during a very little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to resist the stimulus to inspiration. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DROWNING">drowning</a>, the circulation seems to be stopped upon this principle; and in hanging, the pressure made on the jugular veins may co-operate with the stoppage of respiration in bringing on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Boerhaave takes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> uses of respiration to be the further <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of the chyle, its more accurate mixture with the blood, and its conversion into a nutritious juice proper to repair the decays of the body. Other authors take a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of respiration to be, by the neighbourhood of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> nitrous air, to cool the blood coming reeking hot out of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> ventricle of the heart through the lungs, and to act as a refrigeratory; others assert one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> use of respiration to be the throwing off the fuliginous vapours of the blood, along with the expelled air; and for inspiration they assert, that it conveys a nitro-aerial ferment to the blood, to which the animal-spirits and all muscular motion are owing. But Dr Thurston rejects all these as being the principal uses of respiration; and from the experiments of Dr Croon, Dr Hooke, and others, made before the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, he shows the principal use of respiration to be that of moving or passing the blood from the right to the left ventricle of the heart, and so to effect circulation; whence it is that persons hanged, drowned, or strangled, so suddenly die, viz., because the circulation of the blood is stopped; and for the same reason it is that animals die so speedily in the air-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>. This use of respiration Dr Drake not only confirms, but carries farther, making it the true cause of the diaffole of the heart, which neither Borelli, Dr Lower, nor Mr Cowper, had well accounted for. From experiments made on dogs and other animals, Dr Hales shows, that without respiration the blood would soon turn putrid and pestilential; and indeed the only animal exempted from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of respiration is a fetus. With regard to the force of respiration, the last mentioned author observes, that though a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, by a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of his mouth and tongue, may suck <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> 22 inches, and some men 27 or 28 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; yet he found from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that by the bare inspiring action of the diaphragm and dilating thorax, he himself could scarcely raise the mercury two inches, at which time the diaphragm must act with a force equal to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> of mercury, whose base is commensurate to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of the diaphragm, and its height two inches, whereby the diaphragm must at the same time sustain a weight equal to many pounds; neither are its counteracting muscles, those the abdomen, able to exert a greater force. With regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of moisture carried off by respiration, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>, from an experiment on wood-ashes, estimates that quantity to be equal to 17 grains in 50 respirations; whence there will proportionably be 408 grains evaporated or breathed off in 1200 respirations, being the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> in an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, and thence in 24 hours 9792 grains, or 1.39 pounds; which supposing the surface of the lungs to be 41,635 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> inches, then the quantity evaporated from that inward surface will be \( \frac{1}{3574} \) <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of an inch deep. From the violent and fatal effects of very noxious vapours on the respiration and life of animals, the Doctor shows how the respiration is proportionably incommoded when the air is loaded with lesser degrees of vapours, which vapours do in some measure clog and lower the air's elasticity, which it best regains by having these vapours dispelled by the ventilating motion of the free open air, that is best rendered wholesome by the agitation of winds; thus what we call a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> warm air, such as has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> confined in a room, without having the vapours in it carried off by communicating with the open air, is apt to give us more or less uneasiness in proportion to the quantity of vapours which are floating in it. And thus many of those who have weak lungs, but can breathe very well in the fresh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> air, are greatly incommoded in their breathing when they come into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cities, where the air is full of fuliginous vapours; and even the most robust and healthy, in changing from a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> to a country air, find an exhilarating <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> arising from a more free and kindly inspiration, whereby the lungs being less loaded with condensing air and vapours, and thereby the vehicles more dilated with a clearer and more <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> air, a freer course is thereby given to the blood, and probably a purer air mixed with it. Dr Priestley has shown, that one of the great uses of respiration is to carry off the phlogistic or putrid particles from animal-bodies, by which they are prevented from putrefying while alive, to which, without respiration, they would be as liable as though they were dead. See Air, n° 46; Blood, n° 29, et seq., and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUTREFACTION">Putrefaction</a>, passim. Respiration of Fishes. See Fish, n° 5 & 6.

RESPITE

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies a delay, forbearance, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> prolongation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, granted to any one for the payment of a debt or the like.

RESPONDENT

Pages 365-365

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, one who maintains a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THESIS">thesis</a> in any art <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> science; who is thus called from his being to answer all the objections proposed by the opponent. RESPONDENTIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOTTOMRY">BOTTOMRY</a>.

RESPONSE

Pages 365-365

an answer <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> reply. A word chiefly used in speaking of the answers made by the people to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, in the litany, the psalms, &c.

RESSORT

Pages 365-365

a French word, sometimes used by English authors to signify the jurisdiction of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and particularly one from which there is no <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>.—Thus it is said, that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords judge en dernier ressort, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> in the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>.

RESTAURATION

Pages 365-365

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of re-establishing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> setting a thing or person in its former good state.

RESTITUTION

Pages 365-366

in a moral and legal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is restoring a person to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> returning something <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESURRECTION">Resurrection</a> unjustly taken or detained from him. Restitution of Medals, or Restituted Medals, is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by antiquaries, for such medals as were struck by the emperors, to retrieve the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their predecessor. Hence, in several medals, we find the letters REST. This practice was first begun by Claudius, by his striking afresh several medals of Augustus. Nero did the same; and Titus, after his father's example, struck restitutions of most of his predecessors. Gallienus struck a general restitution of all the preceding emperors, on two medals, the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> an altar, the other an eagle, without the REST.

RESTIVE

Pages 366-366
or RESTY, in the manege, a stubborn, unruly, ill-broken horse, that stops, or runs back, instead of advancing forward.

RESTORATION

Pages 366-366

the same with restoration. See RESTAURATION. In England, the return of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. in 1660, is, by way of eminence, called the Restoration; and the 29th of May is kept as an anniversary festival, in commemoration of that event, by which the regal and episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was restored.

RESTORATIVE

Pages 366-366

in medicine, a remedy proper for restoring and retrieving the strength and vigour both of the body and animal-spirits. All under this class, says Quincy, are rather nutrimental than medicinal; and are more administered to repair the wastes of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, than to alter and rectify its disorders.

RESTRICTION

Pages 366-366

among logicians, is limiting a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, so as to make it signify less than it usually does.

RESULT

Pages 366-366

what is gathered from a conference, inquiry, meditation, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the like; or the conclusion and effect thereof.

RESURRECTION

Pages 366-366

in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, rising again from the dead; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a person's returning to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, with new bodily organs adapted to the state of its new existence. One of the greatest arguments for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of Christianity is drawn from the resurrection of our Saviour; the circumstances of which are handed <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to us in so plain and distinct a manner by the Evangelists, as make the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of this important truth amount to a demonstration. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> generally believe, that at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of judgment the very identical body they have now, with the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, blood, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be raised from the dead. But, in opposition to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, many texts of Scripture have been urged, particularly the account given of this important event by St Paul; besides several philosophical objections, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are these. That the same substance may happen to be a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of two or more bodies: thus a fish feeding on a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and another man afterwards feeding on the fish, part of the body of the first man becomes incorporated with the fish, and afterwards with the body of the last man. Again, instances have been known of one man's immediately feeding on the body of another; and among the cannibals in the West Indies, who devour their enemies, the practice is frequent. Now it is alleged, where the substance of one is thus converted into the substance of another, each cannot arise with his whole body; to which then shall the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> part be allotted? To this objection some answer, That as all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is not capable of being assimilated to the body, and incorporated with it, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> flesh may very probably be of this kind; and therefore what is thus eaten, may be again excreted and carried off. But Mr Leibnitz observes, that all that is essential to the body, is the original stamen, which existed in the semen of the father: that this may be conceived as the most minute point imaginable, and therefore not to be separated, nor any part of it united to the stamen of any other man: that all this bulk we see in the body, is only an accretion to this original stamen; and therefore there is no reciprocation of the proper matter of the human body. Another objection is, that we know, by the late discoveries in the animal economy, that the human body is continually changing, and that a man has not entirely the same body to-day as he had yesterday; and it is even computed, that in less than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the whole body undergoes a change. Which of those many bodies, then, which the same person has in the course of his life, is it that shall rise? or does all the matter that has ever belonged to him rise again? or does only some particular system thereof? the body, for example, he had at 20, at 40, or at 60 years old? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> only this or that body arise, how shall it be rewarded or punished for what was done by the other? and with what <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> does one person suffer for another? To this it has been answered, on the principles of Leibnitz, that notwithstanding these successive changes, this stamen, which is the only essential part of the body, has always remained the same; and that, on Mr Locke's principles, personal identity, or the sameness of a rational being, consists in self-consciousness, in the power of considering itself the same thing in different times and places. By this, every one is to himself what he calls self; without considering whether that self be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the same, or in several substances. It is the same self now it was then; and it was by the same self which now reflects on an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, that that action was performed. Now it is this personal identity that is the object of rewards and punishments, which it is observed may exist in different successions of matter; so that to render the rewards and punishments <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> and pertinent, we need only to rise again with such a body, as that we retain the consciousness of our past actions.

RESUSCITATION

Pages 366-366

the same with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVIVIFICATION">revivification</a>. See the preceding article. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> resuscitation, however, is more particularly used by chemists, for the reproducing a mixed body from its ashes; an art to which many have pretended, as to reproduce <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, &c. from their ashes.

RETAIL

Pages 366-366

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, is the selling of goods in small parcels, in opposition to wholesale. See COMMERCE.

RETAINER

Pages 366-366

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> who does not continually dwell in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, but only attends upon special occasions.

RETAINING FEE

Pages 366-366

the first fee given to a serjeant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> counsellor at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, in order to make him sure, and

RETARDATION

Pages 367-367

in physics, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of diminishing the velocity of a moving body. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>. RETE mirabile, in anatomy, a small plexus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NET">net</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of vessels in the brain, surrounding the pituitary gland.

RETENTION

Pages 367-367

is defined by Mr Locke to be a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of the mind, whereby it keeps, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> retains, those simple <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> it has once received, by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> or reflection. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, n° 40.—43. Retention, is also used, in medicine, &c. for the state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> in the solids or vascular parts of the body, which makes them hold fast their proper contents. In this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, retention is opposed to evacuation and excretion.

RETICULAR BODY

Pages 367-367

corpus reticulare, in anatomy, a very fine membrane, perforated, in the manner of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NET">net</a>, with a multitude of foramina. It is placed immediately under the cuticle; and when that is separated from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTIS">cutis</a>, whether by art <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> accident, this adheres firmly to it, and is scarce possible to be parted from it, seeming rather to be its inner superficies than a distinct substance. In regard to this, we are to observe, first, the places in which it is found, being all those in which the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of feeling is most acute, as in the palms of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, the extremities of the fingers, and on the soles of the feet. The tongue, however, is the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> where it is most accurately to be observed: it is more easily distinguishable there than anywhere else, and its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and structure are most evidently seen there. Its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> in the Europeans is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; but in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> nations, it is black; in the tawny, it is yellowish: the skin itself in both is white; and the blackness and yellowness depend altogether on the colour of this membrane. The uses of the corpus reticulare are to preserve the structure of the other parts of the integuments and keep them in their determinate form and situation. Its apertures give passage to the hairs, and set through the papillae and excretory ducts of the skin: it retains these in a certain and determinate order, that they cannot be removed out of their places, and has some share in preserving the softness of the papillae, which renders them fit for the sense of feeling. See Anatomy, n° 82.

RETINA

Pages 367-367

in anatomy, the expansion of the optic nerves over the bottom of the eye, where the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of vision is first received. See Anatomy, n° 406, o. and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, n° 115 &c.

RETINUE

Pages 367-367

the attendants <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> followers of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or person of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, chiefly in a journey.

RETIRADE

Pages 367-367

in fortification, a kind of retrenchment made in the body of a bastion, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which is to be disputed, inch by inch, after the defences are dismantled. It usually consists of two faces, which make a re-entering <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>. When a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> is made in a bastion, the enemy may also make a retirade or new fortification behind it.

RETORT

Pages 367-367

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> globular vessel with its neck bent, proper for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. See Chemistry, n° 77.

RETRACTS

Pages 367-367

among horsemen, pricks in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s feet, arising from the fault of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FARRIER">farrier</a> in driving nails that are weak, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> in driving them ill-pointed, or otherwise amiss.

RETREAT

Pages 367-367

in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. An <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> body of men are said to retreat when they turn their backs upon the enemy, or are retiring from the ground they occupied: hence, every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a> in withdrawing from the enemy is called a retreat. That which is done in flight of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> enemy, who pursues with a superior force, makes our present subject; and is, with reason, looked upon as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the profession. It is a manoeuvre the most delicate, and the properest to display the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, genius, courage, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, of an officer who commands: the historians of all ages testify it; and historians have never been so lavish of eulogiums as on the subject of the brilliant retreats of our heroes. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it is important, it is no less difficult to regulate, on account of the variety of circumstances, each of which demands different principles, and an almost endless detail. Hence a good retreat is esteemed, by experienced officers, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-piece of a general. He should therefore be well acquainted with the situation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> through which he intends to make it, and careful that nothing is omitted to make it safe and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>. Retreat, is also a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> of the drum, at the firing of the evening-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a>; at which the drum-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, with all the drums of the battalion, except such as are upon duty, beats from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>-colours on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to those on the left, on the parade of encampment: the drums of all the guards beat also; the trumpets at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> sounding at the head of their respective troops. This is to warn the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to forbear firing, and the sentinels to challenge, till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>: that the reveille is beat. The retreat is likewise called setting the watch.

RETRENCHMENT LITERALLY

Pages 367-367

T literally signifies something cut off <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> taken from a thing; in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is the same with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUBTRACTION">subtraction</a>, diminution, &c. Retrenchment, in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, any kind of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> raised to cover a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>, and fortify it against the enemy, such as fascines loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, gabions, barrels of earth, sand-bags, and generally all things that can cover the men and stop the enemy. See Fortification and War.

RETRIBUTION

Pages 367-367

a handsome present, gratuity, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> acknowledgment, given instead of a formal salary or hire, to persons employed in affairs that do not so immediately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> under estimation, nor within the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>.

RETROMINGENTS

Pages 367-367

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a class <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of animals, whose characteristic is, that they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STALE">stale</a> or make <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> backwards, both <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>.

RETURN

Pages 367-368

(returna, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> retorno), in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> senses. 1. Return of writs by sheriffs and bailiffs is a certificate made by them to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, of what they have done in relation to the execution of the writ directed to them. This is wrote on the back of the writ by the officer, who thus sends the writ back to the court from whence it issued, in order that it may be filed. 2. Return of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, is a certificate or answer sent to the court from whence the com- commission issues, concerning what has been done by the commissioners. 3. Returns, or days in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, are certain days in each <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, appointed for the return of writs, &c. Thus Hillary term has four returns, viz. in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> next after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a>, or eighth day after Hillary; on the day next after the fifteenth day from St Hilary, on the day after purification; and on the next after the octave of the purification. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas, in eight days of St Hillary: from the day of St Hillary, in fifteen days: on the day after the purification: in eight days of the purification. Easter term has five returns, viz. in the king's bench, on the day next after the fifteenth day from Easter: on the day next after the three weeks from Easter: on the day next after one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> from Easter: on the day next after three weeks from Easter: and on the day next after the day following ascension-day. In the common pleas, in fifteen days from the feast of Easter: in three weeks from the feast of Easter: in one month from Easter day: in five weeks from Easter day: on the day after the ascension-day. Trinity term has four returns, viz. on the day following the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day after Trinity: on the day following the eighth day after Trinity: on the day next after the fifteenth day from Trinity: on the day next after three weeks from Trinity. In the common pleas, on the day after Trinity: in eight days of Trinity: in fifteen days from Trinity: in three weeks from Trinity. Michaelmas term has six returns, viz. on the day next after three weeks from St Michael: on the day next after one month of St Michael: on the day following the second day after All-souls: on the day next after the second day after St Martin: on the day following the octave of St Martin: on the day next after fifteen days of St Martin. In the common pleas, in three weeks from St Michael: in one month from St Michael: on the day after All-souls: on the day after St Martin: on the octave of St Martin: in fifteen days from St Martin. It is to be observed, that, as in the king's-bench, all returns are to be made on some particular day of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> in each term, care must be taken not to make the writs out of that court returnable on a non-judicial day; such as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALL_SAINTS">All-saints</a>, in Michaelmas term, the purification in Hillary, the ascension in Easter, and Midsummer-day, except it should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the first day of Trinity term. Returns, in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, are of various sorts, but all tending to explain the state of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, regiment, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; namely, how many capable of doing duty, on duty, sick in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, infirmary, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>; prisoners, absent with or without leave; total effective; wanting to complete the establishment, &c. RETZ (<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> de). See Gondi.

REUTLINGEN

Pages 368-368

a handsome, free, and imperial town of Germany, in the circle of Swabia and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Wirtemberg; seated in a plain on the river Elzach near the Neckar, adorned with handsome public buildings, and has a well frequented <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9°. N. Lat. 48°. 31'.

REVEILLE

Pages 368-368

a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> of drum about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to give notice that it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to arise, and that the centries are to forbear challenging.

REVEL

Pages 368-368

a port-town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, situated at the south entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>: E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 24°. N. Lat. 59°.

REVELATION

Pages 368-368

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of revealing, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> making a thing public that was before unknown; it is also used for the discoveries made by God to his prophets, and by them to the world; and more particularly for the books of the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">BIBLE</a>, CHRISTIANITY, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">THEOLOGY</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> tests of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of any revelation are, its being worthy of God, and consistent with his known attributes, its being agreeable to the clear dictates of unprejudiced reason, and its having a tendency to refine, purify, and exalt the mind of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> to an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Deity in his moral perfections. Mr Locke, in laying <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the distinct provinces of reason and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, observes, 1. That the same truths may be discovered by revelation which are discoverable to us by reason. 2. That no revelation can be admitted against the clear <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of reason. 3. That there are many things of which we have but imperfect notions, or none at all; and others, of whose past, present, or future existence, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of our faculties we cannot have the least knowledge; and these, being beyond the discovery of our faculties, and above reason, when revealed, become the proper object of our faith. He then adds, that our reason is not injured or disturbed, but assisted and improved, by new discoveries of truth coming from the fountain of knowledge. Whatever God has revealed is certainly true; but whether it be a divine revelation or no, reason must judge, which can never permit the mind to reject a greater evidence to embrace what is less evident. There can be no evidence that any traditional revelation is of divine original, in the words we receive it, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we understand it, so clear and so certain as that of the principles of reason; and, therefore, nothing that is contrary to the clear and self-evident dictates of reason, has a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to be urged or assented to as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of faith, wherein reason has nothing to do. REVELATION of ST JOHN. See APOCALYPSE.

REVELS

Pages 368-368

entertainments of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, maiming, acting comedies, farces, &c. anciently very frequent in the inns of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> and in noblemen's houses, but now much disused. The officer who has the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the revels at court is called the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of the Revels.

REVENUE

Pages 368-373

the annual income a person receives from the rent of his lands, houses, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in the stocks, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Revenue, that which the British <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> hath vested in the royal person, in order to support his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and maintain his power; being a portion which each subject contributes of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, in order to secure the remainder. This revenue is either ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> extraordinary. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s ordinary revenue is such as has either subsisted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> out of mind in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; or else has been granted by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, by way of purchase or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for such of the king's inherent <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> In saying that it has subsisted time out of mind in the crown, we do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> that the king is at present in the actual possession of the whole of his revenue. Much (nay the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>) of it is at this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of subjects; to whom it has been granted out from time to time by the kings of England: which has rendered the crown in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> dependant on the people for its ordinary support and subsistence. So that we must be obliged to recount, as part of the royal revenue, what lords of manors and other subjects frequently look upon to be their own <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>; because they are and have been vested in them and their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> for ages, though in reality originally derived from the grants of our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> princes. 1. The first of the king's ordinary revenues, which may be taken notice of, is of an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> kind, (as are also the three succeeding ones), viz. the custody of the temporalities of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. See TEMPORALITIES. 2. The king is entitled to a corody, as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> calls it, out of every bishopric; that is, to send one of his chaplains to be maintained by the bishop, or to have a pension allowed him till the bishop promotes him to a benefice. This is also in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of an acknowledgment to the king, as founder of the see, since he had formerly the same corody or pension from every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> or priory of royal foundation. It is supposed to be now fallen into total disuse; tho' Sir Matthew Hale says, that it is due of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and that no preception <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> discharge it. 3. The king also is entitled to all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a> arising in extraparochial places: though perhaps it may be doubted how far this article, as well as the last, can be properly reckoned a part of the king's own royal revenue; since a corody supports only his chaplains, and these extraparochial tithes are held under an implied trust that the king will distribute them for the good of the clergy in general. 4. The next branch consists in the first-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and tenths of all spiritual preferments in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. See TENTHS. 5. The next branch of the king's ordinary revenue (which, as well as the subsequent branches, is of a lay or temporal nature) consists in the rents and profits of the demesne lands of the crown. These demesne lands, terrae dominicales regis, being either the share referred to the crown at the original distribution of landed property, or such as came to it afterwards by forfeitures or other means, were anciently very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and extensive; comprising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> manors, honours, and lordships; the tenants of which had very peculiar privileges, when we speak of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> in ancient demesne. At present they are contracted within a very narrow compass, having been almost entirely granted away to private subjects. This has occasioned the parliament frequently to interpose; and particularly after king William III. had greatly impoverished the crown, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> passed, whereby all future grants or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a> from the crown for any longer <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> than 31 years or three lives, are declared to be void; except with regard to houses, which may be granted for 50 years. And no reverification lease can be made, so as to exceed, together with the estate in being, the same term of three lives or 31 years; that is, when there is a subsisting lease, of which there are 20 years still to come, the king cannot <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> a future interest, to commence after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of the former, for any longer term than 11 years. The tenant must also be made liable to be punished for committing waste; and the usual rent must be reserved, or, where there has usually been no rent, one-third of the clear yearly value. The misfortune is, that this act was made too late, after almost every valuable possession of the crown had been granted away for ever, or else upon very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> leases; but may be of benefit to posterity, when those leases come to expire. 6. Hither might have been referred the advantages which were used to arise to the king from the profits of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> tenures, to which most lands in the kingdom were subject, till the statute 12 Car. II. c. 24. which in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> measure abolished them all. Hither also might have been referred the profitable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of conveyance and pre-emption: which was a right enjoyed by the crown of buying up <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and other necessaries, by the intervention of the king's purveyors, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his royal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, at an appraised valuation, in preference to all others, and even without content of the owner: and also of forcibly impressing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> and horses of the subject, to do the king's business on the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, in the conveyance of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, baggage, and the like, however inconvenient to the proprietors, upon paying him a settled price. A prerogative which prevailed pretty generally throughout <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> during the scarcity of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> valuation of money consequential thereupon. In those early times the king's household (as well as those of inferior lords) were supported by specific renders of corn, and other victuals, from the tenants of the respective demesnes; and there was also a continual market kept at the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>-gate to furnish viands for the royal use. And this answered all purposes, in those ages of simplicity, so long as the king's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in any certain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. But when it removed from one part of the kingdom to another, (as was formerly very frequently done), it was found necessary to fend purveyors beforehand, to get together a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of provisions and other necessaries for the household: and, lest the unusual demand should raise them to an exorbitant price, the powers beforementioned were vested in these purveyors; who in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time very greatly abused their authority, and became a great oppression to the subject, though of little advantage to the crown; ready money in open market (when the royal residence was more permanent, and specie began to be plenty) being found upon <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> to be the best provender of any. Therefore, by degrees, the powers of purvance have declined, in foreign countries as well as our own: and particularly were abolished in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> by Gustavus Adolphus, towards the beginning of the last century. And, with us in England, having fallen into disuse during the suspension of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, king <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> at his restoration, consented, by the same statute, to resign entirely those branches of his revenue and power: and the parliament, in part of recon- pense, settled on him, his heirs, and successors, for ever, the hereditary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a> of 15 d. per <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> on all beer and ale sold in the kingdom, and a proportionable sum for certain other liquors. So that this hereditary Revenue. Hereditary excise, now forms the sixth branch of his majesty's ordinary revenue. 7. A seventh branch might also be computed to have arisen from wine-licences; or the rents payable to the crown by such persons as are licensed to sell wine by retail throughout <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, except in a few privileged places. These were first settled on the crown by the statute 12 Car. II. c. 25, and, together with the hereditary excise, made up the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> in value for the loss sustained by the prerogative in the abolition of the military tenures, and the right of pre-emption and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PURVEYANCE">purveyance</a>: but this revenue was abolished by the statute 30 Geo. II. c. 19, and an annual sum of upwards of 7000 l. per annum, issuing out of the new stamp-duties imposed on wine-licences, was settled on the crown in its stead. 8. An eighth branch of the king's ordinary revenue is usually reckoned to consist in the profits arising from his forests. See Forests. These consist principally in the amercements or fines levied for offences against the forest-laws. But as few, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any, courts of this kind for levying amercements have been held since 1632, 8 Car. I. and as, from the accounts given of the proceedings in that court by our histories and law-books, nobody would wish to see them again revived, it is needless to pursue this inquiry any farther. 9. The profits arising from the king's ordinary courts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> make a ninth branch of his revenue. And these consist not only in fines imposed upon offenders, forfeitures of recognizances, and amercements levied upon defaulters; but also in certain fees due to the crown in a variety of legal matters, as, for setting the great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> to charters, original writs, and other forensic proceedings, and for permitting fines to be levied of lands in order to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> entails, or otherwise to infuse their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. As none of these can be done without the immediate intervention of the king, by himself or his officers, the law allows him certain perquisites and profits, as a recompense for the trouble he undertakes for the public. These, in process of time, have been almost all granted out to private persons, or else appropriated to certain particular uses; so that, though our law-proceedings are still loaded with their payment, very little of them is now returned into the king's exchequer; for a part of whole royal maintenance they were originally intended. All future grants of them, however, by the statute 1 Ann. st. 2, c. 7, are to endure for no longer time than the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> who grants them. 10. A tenth branch of the king's ordinary revenue, said to be grounded on the consideration of his guarding and protecting the seas from pirates and robbers, is the right to royal fish, which are whale and sturgeon: and these, when either thrown ashore, or caught near the coasts, are the property of the king, on account of their superior excellence. Indeed, our ancestors seem to have entertained a very high notion of the importance of this right; it being the prerogative of the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> and the dukes of Normandy; and from one of these it was probably derived to our princes. 11. Another <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> revenue, and founded partly upon the same reason, is that of shipwrecks. See Wrecks. 12. A twelfth branch of the royal revenue, the right to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, has its original from the king's prerogative of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COINAGE">coinage</a>, in order to supply him with materials; and therefore those mines which are properly royal, and to which the king is entitled when found, are only those of silver and gold. See Mine. 13. To the same original may in part be referred the revenue of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TREASURE_TROVE"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>-trove. See Treasure-Trove. 14. Waifs. See Waifs. 15. Estrays. See Estray. Besides the particular reasons, given in the different <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, why the king should have the several revenues of royal fish, shipwrecks, treasure-trove, waifs, and estrays, there is also one general reason which holds for them all; and that is, because they are <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BONA">bona</a> vacantia, or goods in which no one else can claim a property. And, therefore, by the law of nature, they belonged to the first occupant or finder; and so continued under the imperial law. But, in settling the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> constitutions of most of the governments in Europe, it was thought proper (to prevent that strife and contention, which the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> title of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCCUPANCY">occupancy</a> is apt to create and continue, and to provide for the support of public authority in a manner the least burdensome to individuals) that these rights should be annexed to the supreme power by the positive laws of the state. And so it came to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, that, as Bracton expresses it, "haec, quae nullius in bonis sunt, et olim fuerunt inventoris de jure naturali, jam efficiantur principis de jure gentium." 16. The next branch of the king's ordinary revenue consists in forfeitures of lands and goods for offences; bona confiscata, as they are called by the civilians, because they belonged to the fiscus or imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>; or, as our lawyers term them, forisfacta, that is, such whereof the property is gone away or departed from the owner. The true reason and only substantial ground of any forfeiture for crimes, consist in this; that all property is derived from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, being one of those civil rights which are conferred upon individuals, in exchange for that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> freedom which every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> must sacrifice when he enters into social communities. If, therefore, a member of any national <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> violates the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>, by transgressing the municipal law, he forfeits his right to such privileges as he claims by that contract; and the state may very justly resume that portion of property, or any part of it, which the laws have before affigned him. Hence, in every offence of an atrocious kind, the laws of England have exacted a total confiscation of the moveables or personal estate; and, in many <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> a perpetual, in others only a temporary, loss of the offender's immoveables or landed property; and have vested them both in the king, who is the person supposed to be offended, being the one visible <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> in whom the majesty of the public resides. See Forfeiture and Deodand. 17. Another branch of the king's ordinary revenue arises from escheats of lands, which happen upon the defect of heirs to succeed to the inheritance; whereupon they in general revert to and vest in the king, who is esteemed, in the eye of the law, the original proprietor of all lands in the kingdom. The last branch of the king's ordinary revenue, consists in the custody of idiots, from whence we shall be naturally led to consider also the custody of lunatics. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IDIOT">IDIOT</a> and LUNATIC. This may suffice for a short view of the king's ordinary revenue, or the proper patrimony of the crown; which was very large formerly, and capable of being increased to a magnitude truly formidable: for there are very few estates in the kingdom that have not, at some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> or other since the Norman conquest, been vested in the hands of the king, by forfeiture, ejectment, or otherwise. But, fortunately, for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the subject, this hereditary landed revenue, by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of improvident management, is sunk almost to nothing; and the casual profits, arising from the other branches of the census regalis, are likewise almost all of them alienated from the crown. In order to supply the deficiencies of which, we are now obliged to have recourse to new methods of raising money, unknown to our early ancestors; which methods constitute, II. The king's extraordinary revenue. For, the public patrimony being got into the hands of private subjects, it is but reasonable that private contributions should supply the public <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Which, though it may perhaps <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> harder upon some individuals, whose ancestors have had no share in the general plunder, than upon others, yet, taking the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> throughout, it amounts to nearly the same; provided the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> by the extraordinary should appear to be no greater than the loss by the ordinary revenue. And perhaps, if every <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in the kingdom was to be stripped of such of his lands as were formerly the property of the crown, was to be again subject to the inconveniences of purveyance and pre-emption, the oppression of forest-laws, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> of feudal-tenures; and was to resign into the king's hands all his royal franchises of waifs, wrecks, eltries, treasure-trove, mines, deodands, forfeitures, and the like; he would find himself a greater loser than by paying his quota to such taxes as are necessary to the support of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. The thing, therefore, to be wished and aimed at in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> of liberty, is by no means the total abolition of taxes, which would draw after it very pernicious consequences, and the very supposition of which is the height of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> absurdity. For as the true idea of government and magistracy will be found to consist in this, that some few men are deputies by many others to preside over public affairs, so that individuals may the better be enabled to attend their private concerns; it is necessary that those individuals should be bound to contribute a portion of their private gains, in order to support that government, and reward that magistracy, which protects them in the enjoyment of their respective properties. But the things to be aimed at are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and moderation, not only in granting, but also in the method of raising, the necessary supplies; by contriving to do both in such a manner as may be most conducive to the national welfare, and at the same time most consistent with economy and the liberty of the subject; who, when properly taxed, contributes only, as was before observed, some part of his property in order to enjoy the rest. These extraordinary grants are usually called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> names of aids, subsidies, and supplies; and are granted by the commons of Great Britain, in parliament assembled. See PARLIAMENT and TAX. The clear neat produce of the several branches of the revenue, after all charges of collecting and management paid, amounts at present annually to about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> millions and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>; besides more than two millions and a quarter raised by the land and malt-tax. How these immense sums are appropriated, is next to be considered. And this is, first and principally, to the payment of the interest of the national debt. See NATIONAL DEBT, and FUNDS. The respective produces of the several taxes were originally separate and distinct funds; being securities for the sums advanced on each several tax, and for them only. But at last it became necessary, in order to avoid confusion, as they multiplied yearly, to reduce the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these separate funds, by uniting and blending them together; superadding the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of parliament for the general security of the whole. So that there are now only three <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> funds of any account, the aggregate <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUND">fund</a>, and the general fund, so called from such union and addition; and the South-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> fund, being the produce of the taxes appropriated to pay the interest of such part of the national debt as was advanced by that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> and its annuitants. Whereby the separate funds, which were thus united, are become mutual securities for each other; and the whole produce of them, thus aggregated, liable to pay such interest or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a> as were formerly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> upon each distinct fund; the faith of the legislature being moreover engaged to supply any casual deficiencies. The customs, excises, and other taxes, which are to support these funds, depending on contingencies, upon exports, imports, and consumptions, must necessarily be of a very uncertain amount; but they have always been considerably more than was sufficient to answer the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> upon them. The surpluses, therefore, of the three great national funds, the aggregate, general, and South-Sea funds, over and above the interest and annuities charged upon them, are directed by statute 3 Geo. I. c. 7. to be carried together, and to attend the disposition of parliament; and are usually denominated the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SINKING_FUND">sinking fund</a>, because originally destined to sink and lower the national debt. To this have been since added many other entire duties, granted in subsequent years; and the annual interest of the sums borrowed on their respective credits is charged on, and payable out of, the produce of the sinking fund. However, the neat surpluses and savings, after all deductions paid, amount annually to a very considerable sum. For as the interest on the national debt has been at several times reduced, (by the consent of the proprietors, who had their option either to lower their interest or be paid their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>), the savings from the appropriated revenues must needs be extremely large. This sinking fund is the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of the nation; its only <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> resource, on which must chiefly depend all the hopes we can entertain of ever discharging or moderating our incumbrances. And therefore the prudent and steady application of the large sums, now arising from this fund, is a point of the utmost importance, and well worthy the serious <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of parliament; which was thereby enabled, in the year 1765, to reduce above two millions sterling. But, before any part of the aggregate fund (the surpluses whereof are one of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ingredients that form the sinking fund) can be applied to diminish the principal of the public debt, it stands mortgaged by Parliament to raise an annual sum for the maintenance of the king's household and the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a>. For this purpose, in the late reigns, the produce of certain branches of the excise and customs, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST_OFFICE"><a class="x</a>ref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>-office, the duty on wine-licences, the revenues of the remaining crown-lands, the profits arising from courts of justice, (which articles include all the hereditary revenues of the crown), and also a clear annuity of £120,000l. in money, were settled on the king for life, for the support of his majesty's household, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and dignity of the crown. And, as the amount of these several branches was uncertain, (though in the last reign they were computed to have sometimes raised almost a million), if they did not arise annually to £800,000l. the parliament engaged to make up the deficiency. But his present majesty having, soon after his accession, spontaneously signified his consent that his own hereditary revenues might be so disposed of as might best conduce to the utility and satisfaction of the public, and having graciously accepted a limited sum, the said hereditary and other revenues are now carried into, and made a part of, the aggregate fund; and the aggregate fund is charged with the payment of the whole annuity to the crown. The limited annuity accepted by his present majesty was at first £800,000l. but it has been since augmented to £900,000l. The expenses themselves, being put under the same care and management as the other branches of the public patrimony, produce more, and are better collected than heretofore; and the public is a gainer of upwards of £100,000l. per annum by this disinterested bounty of his majesty. The civil list, thus liquidated, together with the four millions and an half interest of the national debt, and the two millions produced from the sinking fund, make up the seven millions and a quarter per annum, neat money, which were before stated to be the annual produce of our perpetual taxes; besides the immense, though uncertain, sums arising from the annual taxes on land and malt, but which, at an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>, may be calculated at more than two millions and a quarter; and, added to the preceding sum, make the clear produce of the taxes, exclusive of the charge of collecting, which are raised yearly on the people of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, amount to near ten millions sterling. See Civil List. Revenue, in hunting, a fleshy lump formed chiefly by a cluster of whitish <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> on the head of the deer, supposed to occasion the casting of their horns by gnawing them at the root. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVERBERATION">Reverberation</a>, in physics, the act of a body repelling or reflecting another after its impinging thereon. Reverberation, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, denotes a kind of circulation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> by means of a reverberatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>. See Chemistry, No. 98, et seq., and Furnace. Reverend, a title of respect given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>.—The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> abroad are called reverend fathers; and abbesses, prioresses, &c. reverend mothers. With us, bishops are right reverend; and archbishops most reverend. In France, their bishops, archbishops, and abbots, are all alike most reverend. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVERIE">Reverie</a>, the same with delirium, raving, or distraction. It is used also for any ridiculous, extravagant imagination, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, or proposition, a chimera, or vision. But the most ordinary use of the word among English writers, is for a deep disorderly musing or meditation. Reversal of Judgment, in law. A judgment may be falsified, reversed, or voided, in the first place, without a writ of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, for matters foreign to or debors the record, that is, not apparent upon the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of it; so that they cannot be assigned for error in the superior court, which can only judge from what appears in the record itself; and therefore, if the whole record be not certified, or not truly certified, by the inferior court, the party injured thereby (in both civil and criminal cases) may allege a diminution of the record, and cause it to be rectified. Thus, if any judgment whatever be given by persons who had no good <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to proceed against the person condemned, it is void; and may be falsified by shewing the special <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, without writ of error. As, where a commission issues to A and B, and twelve others, or any two of them, of which A or B shall be one, to take and try indictments; and any of the other twelve proceed without the interposition or presence of either A or B: in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> all proceedings, trials, convictions, and judgments, are void for want of a proper authority in the commissioners, and may be falsified upon bare inspection, without the trouble of a writ of error; it being a high misdemeanor in the judges so proceeding, and little (if any thing) short of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> in them all, in case the person so attainted be executed and suffer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. So likewise if a man purchases land of another; and afterwards the vendor is, either by outlawry, or his own confession, convicted and attainted of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> or felony previous to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a> or alienation; whereby such land becomes liable to forfeiture or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ESCHEAT">escheat</a>: now, upon any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, the purchaser is at liberty, without bringing any writ of error, to falsify not only the time of the felony or treason supposed, but the very point of the felony or treason itself; and is not concluded by the confession or the outlawry of the vendor; though the vendor himself is concluded, and not suffered now to deny the fact, which he has by confession or flight acknowledged. But if such attainder of the vendor was by verdict, on the oath of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>, the alienee cannot be received to falsify or contradict the fact of the crime committed; though he is at liberty to prove a mistake in time, or that the offence was committed after the alienation, and not before. Secondly, a judgment may be reversed, by writ of error; which lies from all inferior criminal jurisdictions to the court of king's-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, and from the king's-bench to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of peers; and may be brought for notorious mistakes in the judgment or other parts of the record: as where a man is found guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>, and receives the judgment of felony, or for other less palpable errors; such as any irregularity, omission, or want of form in the process of outlawry, or proclamations; the want of a proper addition to the defen- REVERSAL Reversal of a medal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, &c., denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> or back side, in opposition to the head or principal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>.

REVERSION

Pages 373-375

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>. See LAW, No clxix. 1—3. Reversion, in the law of England, has two significations; the one of which is an estate left, which continues during a particular estate in being; and the other is the returning of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, &c., after the particular estate is ended; and it is further said, to be an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in lands, when the possession of it fails, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> where the estate which was for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> parted with, Reversion returns to the grantors, or their heirs. But, according to the usual <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of a reversion, it is the residue of an estate left in the grantor, after a particular estate granted away ceases, continuing in the grantor of such an estate. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between a remainder and a reversion consists in this, that the remainder may belong to any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> except the grantor; whereas the reversion returns to him who conveyed the lands, &c. In order to render the doctrine of reversions easy, we shall give the following <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; which shows the present value of one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, to be received at the end of any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years not exceeding 40; discounting at the rate of 5, 4, and 3 per cent. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> interest. | Year | Value at 5 per cent. | Value at 4 per cent. | Value at 3 per cent. | |------|---------------------|---------------------|---------------------| | 1 | .9524 | .9615 | .9709 | | 2 | .9070 | .9245 | .9426 | | 3 | .8638 | .8898 | .9151 | | 4 | .8227 | .8548 | .8885 | | 5 | .7835 | .8219 | .8626 | | 6 | .7462 | .7903 | .8375 | | 7 | .7107 | .7599 | .8131 | | 8 | .6768 | .7307 | .7894 | | 9 | .6446 | .7026 | .7664 | | 10 | .6139 | .6756 | .7441 | | 11 | .5847 | .6496 | .7224 | | 12 | .5568 | .6246 | .7014 | | 13 | .5303 | .6006 | .6809 | | 14 | .5051 | .5775 | .6611 | | 15 | .4810 | .5553 | .6419 | | 16 | .4581 | .5339 | .6232 | | 17 | .4363 | .5134 | .6050 | | 18 | .4155 | .4936 | .5874 | | 19 | .3957 | .4746 | .5703 | | 20 | .3769 | .4564 | .5537 | | 21 | .3589 | .4388 | .5375 | | 22 | .3418 | .4219 | .5219 | | 23 | .3255 | .4057 | .5067 | | 24 | .3100 | .3901 | .4919 | | 25 | .2953 | .3757 | .4776 | | 26 | .2812 | .3607 | .4637 | | 27 | .2678 | .3468 | .4502 | | 28 | .2551 | .3335 | .4371 | | 29 | .2429 | .3206 | .4243 | | 30 | .2314 | .3083 | .4120 | | 31 | .2204 | .2965 | .4000 | | 32 | .2099 | .2851 | .3883 | | 33 | .1999 | .2741 | .3770 | | 34 | .1903 | .2636 | .3660 | | 35 | .1813 | .2534 | .3554 | | 36 | .1726 | .2437 | .3450 | | 37 | .1644 | .2343 | .3350 | | 38 | .1566 | .2253 | .3252 | | 39 | .1491 | .2166 | .3158 | | 40 | .1420 | .2083 | .3066 | The The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the preceding table.—To find the present value of any sum to be received at the end of a given <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> of years, discounting at the rate of 3, 4, or 5 per cent. compound interest.
