Find by the above table the present value of £1. to be received at the end of the given term; which multiply by the number of pounds proposed, (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off four figures from the product on account of the decimals) then the result <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the value sought: For example, the present value of £10,000l. to be received in ten years hence, and the rate of interest 5 per cent. is equal to .6139 × 10,000 = 6139.0000l. or 6139l. Again, the present value of £10,000l. due in ten years, the rate of interest being 3 per cent. is .7441 × 10,000 = 7441l. Revolution of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">Series</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, a kind of reversed operation of an infinite series. See Series. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVIVIFICATION">Revivification</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, a term generally applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> of quicksilver from cinnabar. Review (<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of), is a commission sometimes granted, in extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, to revise the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of delegates, when it is apprehended they have been led into a material <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>. This commission the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> may <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, although the statutes 24 and 25 Hen. VIII., declare the sentence of the delegates definitive: because the pope as supreme head by the canon law used to grant such commission of review; and such authority as the pope heretofore exerted is now annexed to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> by statutes 26 Hen. VIII. c. 1. and 1 Eliz. c. 1. But it is not <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, which the subject may demand ex debito justitia; but merely a matter of favour, and which therefore is often denied. Review, is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> out all or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in line of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, to be viewed by the king, or a general, that they may know the condition of the troops. At all reviews, the officers should be properly armed, ready in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, salute well, in good time, and with a good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>; their uniform genteel, &c. The men should be clean and well dressed; their accoutrements well put on; very well fixed in their ranks; the sergeants expert in their duty, drummers perfect in their beatings, and the fifers play correct. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> exercise must be performed in good time, and with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and the men carry their arms well; <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, wheel, and form with exactness. All manoeuvres must be performed with the utmost regularity, both in quick and slow time. The firings are generally 36 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a>; viz. by companies; by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> divisions; by sub-divisions; obliquely, advancing, retreating; by files; in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; street firings, advancing and retreating; and lastly, a volley. The intention of a review is, to know the condition of the troops, to see that they are complete and perform their exercise and evolutions well. Revolution, in politics, signifies a grand change or turn in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the revolution is used by way of eminence for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> turn of affairs in England in 1688, when king James II. abdicating the throne, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and princess of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> were declared king and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of England, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, the revolution of any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> quite round a fixed line as an axis. The revolution of a planet or comet is nothing but its course from one point of its orbit till it returns to the same point again. Revulsion, in medicine, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> of humours from one part to another by bleeding, cupping, friction, finapins, blisters, fomentations, bathings, influes, setons, strong purging of the bowels, &c. Reyn (Jan de), an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> painter, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a> in 1610. He had the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to be a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Vandyck, was the best performer in his school, and was so attached to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> that he followed him to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where it is thought he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he lived. In these kingdoms he is mostly known by the name of Lang Jan. He died in 1678; and it is imagined that the scarcity of his works is occasioned by so many of them being imputed to Vandyck; a circumstance which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> true, is beyond any thing that could be said in his praise. Rezan, or Rezanskoï, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of Russia, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name, with an archbishop's see. It was formerly considerable for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>; but it was almost ruined by the Tartars in 1568. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is populous, and was formerly governed by its own princes. E. Long. 42° 37'. N. Lat. 54° 54'. Rhadamantus, a severe judge, and king of Lydia; the poets make him one of the three judges of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. Rhagades, in medicine, denotes chaps or clefts in any part of the body. If seated in the anus, and recent, the patient must sit still, and sit over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> of warm <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The epulotic cerate may also be applied. If the lips of these fissures are callous, they must be cut or otherwise treated as to become new ulcerations. Rhamnus, the buckthorn; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the pentandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are 20 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable are, 1. The catharticus, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> purging buckthorn, growing naturally in some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. This grows to the height of 12 or 14 feet, with many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> branches at the extremities. The leaves are oval-lanceolate, finely <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a> on the edges, their nerves converging together. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> grow in clusters, one on each footstalk, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and, in this species, divided into four segments: the fruit is a round <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> berry, containing four seeds. The juice of the berries is a strong purgative, and is made use of for making the common syrup of buckthorn kept in the shops. The bark is emetic; the juice of the unripe berries with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> dyes <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, of the ripe ones green; the bark also dyes yellow. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOTUS">lotus</a>, famous in the Odyssey of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> for its enchanting <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, by which those who eat of it forget their country and relations. Dr Shaw, in his travels into Barbary, had frequent opportunities of examining this shrub. He says, "This shrub, which is very common in the Jereede, and other parts of Barbary, has the leaves, prickles, flowers, and fruit of the zizyphus or jube; only with this difference, that the fruit is here round, smaller, and more lucious, and at the same time the branches, like those of the palmyrus, are neither so much jointed nor crooked." The fruit is in great repute, tastes something like gingerbread, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and is sold in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> all over the southern districts of these kingdoms. The Arabs call it *anabentaelfeedra*, or the *jubebe of the feedra*; which Olavus Celsius had so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of, that he has described it as the *dudum of the scriptures*." It is proper, however, to distinguish between this shrub and an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> often mentioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> under the name of *lotus*, which Homer mentions as being fed upon by the horses of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> as proper to increase the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of sheep.

RHAPOSODI

Pages 375-375

Rhapsodists, in antiquity, persons who made a business of singing pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s poems. Cuper informs us, that the Rhapsoi were clothed in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> when they sung the Iliad, and in blue when they sung the Odyssey. They performed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, and sometimes strove for prizes in contests of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, singing, &c. After the two antagonists had finished their parts, the two pieces <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> papers they were written in were joined together again: whence the name, viz., from *παρα*, *συν*, and *εἰς*, *canticum*; but there seem to have been other Rhapsoi of more antiquity than these people, who composed heroic poems or songs in praise of heroes and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men, and sung their own compositions from town to town for a livelihood; of which profession Homer himself is said to be. See Bard.

RHAPSODOMANCY

Pages 375-375

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kind of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a> performed by pitching on a passage of a poet at hazard, and reckoning on it as a prediction of what was to come to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. There were various ways of practising this rhapsodomancy. Sometimes they wrote several papers <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> sentences of a poet on so many pieces of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, or the like, shook them together in an urn, and drew out one which was accounted the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>: sometimes they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> dice on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a> whereon verses were written, and that wherein the die lodged contained the prediction. A third manner was by opening a book, and pitching on some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> at first sight. This method they particularly called the *fortes praefestinae*; and afterwards, according to the poet made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, *fortes Homericae, fortis Virgilianae*, &c. See Sortes.

RHAPSODY

Pages 375-375

in antiquity, a discourse in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> sung <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> rehearsed by a rhapsodist. Others <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have rhapsody to signify a collection of verses, especially those of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, which having been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> dispersed in pieces and fragments, were at length, by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PISISTRATUS">Pisistratus</a>'s order, digested into books called *rhapsodies*, from *παρα*, *συν*, and *εἰς*, *canticum*. Hence, among moderns, rhapsody is also used for an assemblage of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, thoughts, and authorities raked together from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> authors, to compose some new piece.

RHEGIUM

Pages 375-375

(anc. geog.) so very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, as to be supposed to take its name from the violent bursting of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; thought to have been formerly conjoined, (Mela, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>). A city of the Bruttii, a colony of Chalcidians from Euboea: a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> opposed to Sicily, (Strabo); mentioned by Luke; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> *Julium*, (<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>), from a fresh supply of inhabitants sent thither by Augustus, after driving Sextus Pompeius out of Sicily, (Strabo); and thus was in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> a colony, retaining still the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of a municipium, Inscription. The city is now called <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REGGIO">Reggio</a>, in the Farther <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>.

RHEIMS

Pages 375-375

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France in Champagne, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Rheimois. It is one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, celebrated, and largest places in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, with an archbishop's see, whose archbishop is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> and peer of France. It is about four miles in circumference, and contains several fine squares, well-built houses, and magnificent churches. It has a mint, an university, and five abbeys, the most famous of which is that of St. Remy. There are also several triumphal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> and other monuments of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It is seated on the river Vesle, on a plain surrounded by hills, which produce excellent wine. E. Lon. 4° 8'. N. Lat. 49° 14'.

RHENISH WINE

Pages 375-375

that produced on the hills about <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>. This wine is much used in medicine as a solvent of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, for which it is well calculated on account of its acidity. Dr Percival observes, that it is the best solvent of the Peruvian barks; in which, however, he thinks its acidity has no share, because an addition of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> does not augment its solvent power.

RHETORIANS

Pages 375-375

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, so denominated from Rhetorius their leader. The distinguishing tenets of this heresarch, as represented by Philastrius, was, that he approved of all the heresies before him, and taught that they were all in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>.

RHETORIC

Pages 375-375

the art of speaking copiously on any subject, with all the advantages of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and force. See Oratory.

RHEUM

Pages 375-376
Rhubarb**; a genus of the monogyne order, belonging to the enneandra class of plants. There are five species, viz. 1. The rhaponticum, or common rhubarb, hath a large, thick, fleshy, branching, deeply-striking root, yellowish within; crowned by very large, roundish, heart-shaped smooth leaves, on thick, slightly-furrowed foot-stalks; and an upright strong stem, two or three feet high, adorned with leaves singly, and terminated by thick close spikes of white flowers. It grows in Thrace and Scythia, but has been long in the English gardens. Its root affords a gentle purge. It is however of inferior quality to some of the following sorts; but the plant being astringent, its young stalks in spring, being cut and peeled, are used for tarts. 2. The palmatum, palmated-leaved true, Chinese rhubarb; hath a thick fleshy root, yellow within; crowned with a very large palmated leaves, being deeply divided into acuminate segments, expanded like an open hand; upright stems, five or six feet high or more, terminated by large spikes of flowers. This is now proved to be the true foreign rhubarb, the purgative quality of which is well known. 3. The compactum, or Tartarian rhubarb, hath a large, fleshy, branched root, yellow within; crowned by very large heart-shaped somewhat lobated, sharply indented, smooth leaves; and an upright large stem, five or six feet high, garnished with leaves singly, and branching above; having all the branches terminated by nodding panicles of white flowers. This has been supposed to be the true rhubarb; which, however, though of su- RHEUM Rheum. perior quality to some sorts, is accounted inferior to the rheum palmatum. 4. The undulatum, undulated or waved-leaved Chinese rhubarb, hath a thick, branchy, deep-striking root, yellow within; crowned with large oblong, undulate, somewhat hairy leaves, having equal foot-stalks, and an upright firm stem, four feet high; garnished with leaves singly, and terminated by long loose spikes of white flowers. 5. The Arabian ribes, or currant rhubarb of Mount Libanus, hath a thick fleshy root, very broad leaves, full of granulated protuberances, and with equal foot-stalks; and upright firm stems, three or four feet high, terminated by spikes of flowers, succeded by berry-like seeds, being surrounded by a purple pulp. All these plants are perennial in root, and the leaves and stalks are annual. The roots being thick, fleshy, generally divided, strike deep into the ground; of a brownish colour without, and yellow within: the leaves rise in the spring, generally come up in a large head folded together, gradually expanding themselves, having thick foot-stalks; and grow from one to two feet high, or more, in length and breadth, spreading all round; amidst them rise the flower-stems, which are garnished at each joint by one leaf, and are of strong and expeditious growth, attaining their full height in June, when they flower; and are succeeded by large triangular seeds, ripening in August. Some plants of each sort merit culture in gardens for variety; they will effect a singularity with their luxuriant foliage, spikes, and flowers. And as medical plants, they demand culture both for private and public use. They are propagated by seeds sowed in autumn soon after they are ripe, or early in the spring, in any open bed of light deep earth; remarking, those intended for medical use should generally be sowed where they are to remain, that the roots, being not disturbed by removal, may grow large. Scatter the seeds thinly, either by broad-cast all over the surface, and raked well in; or in shallow drills a foot and half distance, covering them near an inch deep. The plants will rise in the spring, but not flower till the second or third year: when they, however, are come up two or three inches high, thin them to eight or ten inches, and clear out all weeds; though those designed always to stand should afterwards be hoed out to a foot and a half or two feet distance: observing, if any are required for the pleasure ground, &c. for variety, they should be transplanted where they are to remain in autumn, when their leaves decay, or early in spring before they shoot: the others remaining where sowed, must have the ground kept clean between them; and in autumn when the leaves and stalks decay, cut them down, and slightly dig the ground between the rows of plants, repeating the same work every year. The roots remaining, they increase in size annually; and in the second or third year many of them will shoot up stalks, flower, and perfect seeds; and in three or four years the roots will be arrived to a large size; though older roots are generally preferable for medical use. Two sorts of rhubarb are met with in the shops. The first is imported from Turkey and Russia, in roundish pieces freed from the bark, with a hole thro' the middle of each: they are externally of a yellowish colour, and on cutting appear variegated with lively reddish streaks. The other, which is less esteemed, comes immediately from the East-Indies, in longish pieces, harder, heavier, and more compact than the foregoing. The first sort, unless kept very dry, is apt to grow mouldy and worm-eaten; the second is less subject to these inconveniences. Some of the more industrious artists are said to fill up the worm-holes with certain mixtures, and to colour the outside of the damaged pieces with powder of the finer sorts of rhubarb, and sometimes with cheaper materials: this is often so nicely done, as effectually to impose upon the buyer, unless he very carefully examines each piece. The marks of good rhubarb are, that it be firm and solid, but not flinty; that it be easily pulverable, and appear, when powdered, of a fine bright yellow colour; that, upon being chewed, it impart to the spittle a tartish tinge, without proving slimy or mucilaginous in the mouth. Its taste is subacid, bitterish, and somewhat astringent; the smell lightly aromatic. Rhubarb is a mild cathartic, which operates without violence or irritation, and may be given with safety even to pregnant women and children. Besides its purgative quality, it is celebrated for an astringent one, by which it strengthens the tone of the stomach and intestines, and proves useful in diarrhoeas and disorders proceeding from a laxity of the fibres. Rhubarb in substance operates more powerfully as a cathartic than any of the preparations of it. Watery tinctures purge more than the spirituous ones; whilst the latter contain in greater perfection the aromatic, astringent, and corroborating virtues of the rhubarb. The dose, when intended as a purgative, is from a scruple to a dram or more. The Turkey rhubarb is, among us, universally preferred to the East-India sort, though this last is for some purposes at least equal to the other; it is manifestly more astringent, but has somewhat less of an aromatic flavour. Tinctures drawn from both with rectified spirit, have nearly the same taste; on distilling off the menstruum, the extract left from the tincture of the East-India rhubarb proved considerably the strongest. Of late, rhubarb has been cultivated in this country with tolerable success, and is found not to be inferior for medical purposes to the foreign.

RHI

Pages 377-378

Rhizophora RHIZOPHORA, the mangrove, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Mangle; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the decandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. These plants are natives of the East and West Indies, and often grow 40 or 50 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. They grow only in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> and on the banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, where the tide flows up twice a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. They preserve the verdure of their leaves throughout the year. From the lowest branches issue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> roots, which hang <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the water, and penetrate into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. In this position they resemble to many arcades, from five to ten feet high, which serve to support the body of the tree, and even to advance it daily into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the water. These arcades are so closely intertwined one with another, that they form a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and transparent terrace, raised with such solidity over the water, that one might walk upon them, were it not that the branches are too much encumbered with leaves. The most natural way of propagating these trees, is to suffer the several slender small filaments which issue from the main branches, to take root in the earth. The most <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> method, however, is that of laying the small lower branches in baskets of mould or earth, till they have taken root. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> given, pertains chiefly to a particular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of mangrove, termed by the West Indians <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mangroves, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> dusky <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the wood. The bark is very brown, smooth, pliant when green, and generally used in the West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. Below this bark lies a cuticle, or skin, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>, thinner, and more tender. The wood is nearly of the same colour as the bark; hard, pliant, and very heavy. It is frequently used for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, for which purpose it is said to be remarkably proper; the fires which are made of this wood, being both clearer, more ardent and durable than those made of any other materials whatever.—The wood is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>; almost incorruptible; never splinters; is easily worked; and were it not for its enormous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, would be commodiously employed in almost all kinds of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, as it possesses every <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. To the roots and branches of mangroves that are immersed in the water, oysters frequently attach themselves; so that wherever this curious plant is found growing on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore, oyster-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> is very easy; as in such <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, these shell-fish may be literally said to be gathered upon trees. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> mangroves, or mangrove, grows on the seashore, and at the mouth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rivers; but does not advance, like the former, into the water. It generally rises to the height of 20 or 30 feet, with crooked, knotty branches, which proceed from all parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>. The bark is slender, of a brown colour, and, when young, is smooth, and adheres very closely to the wood; but when old, appears quite cracked, and is easily detached from it. Under this bark is a skin as thick as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, red, and adhering closely to the wood, from which it cannot be detached till the tree is felled and dry. The wood is hard, compact, heavy, of a deep red, with a very fine grain. The pith or heart of the wood being cut into small pieces, and boiled in water, imparts a very beautiful red to the liquid, which communicates the same colour to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> weight and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of the wood prevents it from being generally used. From the fruit of this tree, which, when ripe, is of a violet colour, and resembles some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, is prepared an agreeable liquor, much esteemed by the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee islands</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a> mangle, so termed from the colour of its wood, grows like the two former, upon the banks of rivers, but is seldom found near the sea. The bark is grey; the wood, as we have said, white, and when green, supple; but dries as soon as cut down, and becomes very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and brittle. This species is generally called rope-mangrove, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to which the bark is applied by the inhabitants of the West Indies. This bark, which, by reason of the great abundance of sap, is easily detached, when green, from the wood, is beaten or bruised between two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, until the hard and woody <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> is totally separated from that which is soft and tender. This last, which is the true cortical substance, is twisted into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> of all sizes, which are exceedingly strong, and not apt to rot in the water.

RHINE

Pages 376-377

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river of Germany, famous both in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. It rises among the Alpes Leontiae, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRISONS">Grisons</a>; and first traversing the Lacus Aconius, divides the Rhaeti and Vindelici from the Helveti; and then the Germans from the Gauls and Belgae; and running from south to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> for the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of its way, and at length <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> its course west, it empties itself at several mouths, (Caesar); at three mouths into the German ocean, (Pliny); viz. the western, or Helius; the northern, or Fleuvus; and the middle between both these, which retains the original name, Rhenus: and in this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> agrees. Mela and Tacitus mention two channels and as many mouths, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left; the former running by Germany, and the latter by Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>: and thus also Afinius Pollio, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>; the cut or trench of Drusus not being made in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, whereby the middle channel was much drained and reduced, and therefore overlooked by Tacitus and Mela; and which Pliny calls the Scanty. To account for Caesar's several RHI ral mouths, is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of no small difficulty with the commentators; and they do it no otherwise, than by admitting that the Rhine naturally formed small <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> or rivulets from itself; the cut of Drusus being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> to him; in whose time Afinius Pollio, quoted by Strabo, who agrees with him therein, affirmed that there were but two mouths, finding fault with those who made them more: and he must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> the larger mouths, which emitted larger streams. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, especially the poets, used the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> Rhenus for Germany, (Martial).—At present, the river, after entering the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a> at Schenkinkhaus, is divided into several channels, the two largest of which obtain the names of the Lech and the Wael, which running through the United Provinces, falls into the German ocean below <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>. Rhine, Lower Circle of, consists of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of the Rhine, and the three <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> electorates, viz. those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIER">Trier</a>. Rhine, Upper Circle of, consisted of the landgraviates of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>, comprehending the Wetterau: but now only Hesse can be accounted a part of Germany, Alsace being long ago united to France. Rhineberg, a town of Germany, in the circle of the Lower Rhine, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Cologne. It was in the possession of the French, but restored to the archbishop of Cologne by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>. It is seated on the Rhine, in E. Long. 6° 39'. N. Lat. 51° 30'. Rhineck, a town of Germany, in the archbishopric of Cologne, seated on the Rhine, E. Long. 7° 53'. N. Lat. 50° 27'—There is another town of the same name in Swifterland, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Rhinthal, seated on the Rhine, near the lake of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>, with a good castle. E. Long. 9° 53'. N. Lat. 47° 38'. Rhinfeld, a small but strong town of Germany, in the circle of Swabia, and the best of the four forest-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. It has been often taken and retaken in the German wars; and is seated on the Rhine, over which there is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. E. Long. 7° 53'. N. Lat. 47° 40'. Rhinfels, a castle of Germany, in the circle of the Lower Rhine, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name. It is looked upon as one of the most important places seated on the Rhine, as well in regard to its strength as situation. It is near St Goar, and built on a craggy rock. This fortress commands the whole breadth of the Rhine, and those who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> are always obliged to pay a considerable toll. In the time of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> it is of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance to be masters of this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. E. Long. 7° 43'. N. Lat. 50° 3'. Rhineland, a name given to a part of South <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, which lies on both sides the Rhine, and of which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> is the capital town. Rhinoceros, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> belonging to the order of bovines. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. the unicornis, with a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, placed near the end of the nose, sometimes three feet and a half long, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and smooth; the upper lip long, hangs over the lower, ends in a point, is very pliable, and serves to collect its food, and deliver it into the mouth: the nostrils are placed transversely; the ears large, erect, pointed; eyes small and dull: the skin is naked, rough, or tuberculated, lying about the neck in folds; there is another fold from the shoulders to the rhinoceros' fore-legs; another from the hind-part of the back to the thighs: the skin is so thick and so strong, as to turn the edge of a scymetar, and resist a musket-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a>: the belly hangs low: the legs are short, strong, and thick: the hoofs divided into three parts, each pointing forward. Those which have been brought to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> have been young and small: Bonius says, that in respect to bulk of body, they equal the elephant; but are lower on account of the shortness of their legs. Inhabits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, Cochin-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, Quangsi in China, the isles of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAVA">Java</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a>, Ethiopia, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> as low as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>: loves shady forests, the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and marshy places: fond of wallowing in mire like the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>; is said by that means to give shelter in the folds of its skin to scorpions, centipedes, and other insects. Is a solitary animal; brings one young at a time, and is very solicitous about it. It is quiet and inoffensive; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> provoked, furious, very swift, and very dangerous: Mr Pennant knew a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who had his belly ripped up by one, but survived the wound. Is dull of sight; but has a most exquisite scent: feeds on vegetables, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>, and thistles: grunts like a hog: is said to comfort with the tiger; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> founded on their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the sides of rivers, and on that account are sometimes found near each other. Is said, when it has flung <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, to lick the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> quite from the bone with its rough tongue; this very doubtful; that which wounded the gentleman retired instantly after the stroke. Its flesh is eaten; Kolben says it is very good: the skin, the flesh, hoofs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and very dung, are used in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> medicinally. The horn is in great repute as an antidote against <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, especially that of a virgin rhinoceros: but it is not every horn that has this virtue; some are held very cheap, while others take a vast price. Cups are made of them.—Found sometimes with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> horns: <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, in his voyage to the East Indies, L. 8. says, that he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> brought from <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-NATAL">Natal</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, three horns growing from one root; the longest 18, the next 12, and the third 8 inches long. Martial alludes to a variety of this kind by his urufus cornu genuino. It is the unicorn of Holy Writ, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; the oryx and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> asa of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, who says it has but one horn: his informers might well compare the clumsy shape of the rhinoceros to that of an asa; so that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> might easily be induced to pronounce it a whole-footed animal. This was also the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOS">bos</a> unicorns and fera monoceros of Pliny; both were of India, the same country with this animal; and in his account of the monoceros, he exactly describes the great black horn and the hog-like tail. The unicorn of Holy Writ has all the properties of the rhinoceros, rage, untameableness, great swiftness, and great strength. It was known to the Romans in very early times; its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is among the animals of the Prenestine pavement. Augustus introduced one into the shows, on his triumph over Cleopatra; and there is extant a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> of Domitian, with a double-horned rhinoceros on it. The combats between the elephant and rhinoceros, a fable derived from Pliny. Rhinoceros-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">Bird</a>. See Buceros.

RHODES

Pages 378-389

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> in very ancient times known by the names of Ophiusa, names and Asteria, Ethrea, Trinacria, Corymbia, Poecia, Ata-clymoglyra, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARCIA">Marcia</a>, Oloeffa, Stadia, Telchinia, Pelagia, and Rhodus. In later ages, the name of Rhodus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Rhodes, prevailed, from the Greek word rhodon, as is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> supposed, signifying a "rose;" the island abounding very much with these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. Others, however, give different etymologies, among which it is difficult to find one preferable to another. It is about 20 miles distant from the coasts of Lycia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>; and about 120 miles in compass. The first inhabitants of Rhodes, according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIONYSUS">Dionysus</a> Siculus, were called the Telchines, who came originally from the island of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. These, by their skill in astrology, perceiving that the island was soon to be drowned with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, left their habitations, and made room for the Heliades, or grandsons of Phoebus, who took possession of the island after that god had cleared it from the water and mud with which it was overwhelmed. These Heliades, it seems, excelled all other men in learning, and especially in astrology; invented <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, &c. In after ages, however, being infested with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> which bred in the island, they had recourse to an oracle in Delos, which advised them to admit Phorbas, a Thessalian, with his followers, into Rhodes. This was accordingly done; and Phorbas having destroyed the serpents, was, after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, honoured as a demigod. Afterwards a colony of Cretans settled in some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island, and a little before the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, Tlepolemus the son of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, who was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of the whole island, and governed with great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and moderation. After the Trojan war, all the ancient inhabitants were driven out by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORIANS">Dorians</a>, who <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be the masters of the island for many ages. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was at first monarchical; but a little before the expedition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, a republican form of government was introduced; during which the Rhodians applied themselves to navigation, and became very powerful by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> several colonies in distant countries. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Peloponnesian war, the republic of Rhodes was rent into two factions, one of which favoured the Athenians, and another the Spartans; but at length the latter prevailing, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEMOCRACY">democracy</a> was abolished, and an aristocracy introduced. About 351 B.C. we find the Rhodians oppressed by Mausolus. Rhodes, king of Caria, and at last reduced by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTEMISIA">Artemisia</a> his widow. In this emergency, they applied to the Athenians; by whose affiance, probably, they regained their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. From this time to that of Alexander the Great, the Rhodians enjoyed an uninterrupted tranquillity. To him they voluntarily submitted, and were on that account highly favoured by him; but no sooner did they hear of his death, than they drove out the Macedonian garrisons, and once more became a free people. About this time happened a dreadful inundation at Rhodes; which, being accompanied with violent storms of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and hailstones of an extraordinary hight, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> many houses, and killed great numbers of the inhabitants. As the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> was built in the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, and no care had been taken to clear the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> and conduits which conveyed the water into the sea, the lower parts of the city were in an instant laid under water, several houses quite covered, and the inhabitants drowned before they could get to the higher places. As the deluge increased, and the violent showers continued, some of the inhabitants made to their ships, and abandoned the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, while others miserably perished in the waters. But while the city was thus threatened with utter destruction, the wall on a sudden burst asunder, and the water discharging itself by a violent current into the sea, unexpectedly delivered the inhabitants from all danger. The Rhodians suffered greatly by this unexpected accident, but soon retrieved their losses by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> application to trade. During the wars which took place among the successors of Alexander, the Rhodians observed a strict neutrality; by which means they enriched themselves so much, that Rhodes became one of the most opulent states of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; insomuch that, for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> good of Greece, they undertook the piratical war, and, at their own <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, cleared the seas of the pirates who had for many years infested the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. However, notwithstanding the neutrality they professed, as the most advantageous branches of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> were derived from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, they were more attached to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, king of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, than to any of the neighbouring princes. When therefore Antigonus, having engaged in a war with Ptolemy about the island of Cyprus, demanded succours of them, they earnestly intreated him not to compel them to declare war against their ancient friend and ally. But this answer, prudent as it was, drew upon them the displeasure of Antigonus, who immediately ordered one of his admirals to sail with his fleet to Rhodes, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> all the ships that came out of the harbour for Egypt. The Rhodians, finding their harbour blocked up by the fleet of Antigonus, equipped a good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of galleys, fell upon the enemy, and obliged him, with the loss of many ships, to quit his station. Hereupon Antigonus, charging them as aggressors, and beginners of an unjust war, threatened to besiege their city with the strength of his whole <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. The Rhodians endeavoured by frequent embassies to appease his wrath. But all their remonstrances served rather to provoke than allay his resentment; and the only terms upon which he would hearken to any accommodation were, that the Rhodians should declare war against Ptolemy, that they should admit his fleet into their harbour, and that an hundred of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> citizens should be delivered up to him as hostages for the performance of these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. The Rhodians sent embassadors to all their allies, and to Ptolemy in particular, imploring their affiance, and representing to the latter, that their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> had drawn upon them the danger to which they were exposed. The preparations on both sides were immense. As Antigonus was near four score years of age at that time, he committed the whole management of the war to his son Demetrius, who appeared before the city of Rhodes with 200 ships of war, 170 transports having on board 40,000 men, and 1000 other vessels laden with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and all sorts of warlike engines. As Rhodes had enjoyed for many years a profound tranquillity, and been free from all devastations, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of booty, in the plunder of so wealthy a city, allured multitudes of pirates and mercenaries to join Demetrius in this expedition; insomuch that the whole sea between the continent and the island was covered with ships; which struck the Rhodians, who had a prospect of this mighty armada from the walls, with great terror and consternation. Demetrius, having landed his troops without the reach of the enemy's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, detached several small bodies to lay waste the country round the city, and cut down the trees and groves, employing the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, and materials of the houses without the walls, to fortify his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> with strong ramparts and a treble palisade; which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, as many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> were employed, was finished in a few days. The Rhodians, on their part, prepared for a vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. Many great commanders, who had signalized themselves on other occasions, threw themselves into the city, being desirous to try their skill in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs against Demetrius, who was reputed one of the most experienced captains in the conduct of sieges, that antiquity had produced. The besieged began with dismissing from the city all such persons as were useless; and then taking an account of those who were capable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> arms, they found that the citizens amounted to 6000, and the foreigners to 1000. Liberty was promised to all the slaves who should distinguish themselves by any glorious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and the public engaged to pay the masters their full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> was likewise made, declaring, that whoever died in defence of their country should be buried at the expense of the public; that his parents and children should be maintained out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>; that fortunes should be given to his daughters; and his sons, when they were grown up, should be crowned and presented with a complete <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of armour at the great solemnity of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>; which <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> kindled an incredible ardour in all ranks of men. Demetrius, having planted all his engines, began Engines of to batter with incredible fury the walls on the side Demetrius of the harbour; but was for eight days successively repulsed by the besieged, who set fire to most of his warlike engines, and thereby obliged him to allow them some respite, which they made good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in repairing the breaches, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> new walls where the old ones were either weak or low. When Demetrius had repaired his engines, he ordered a general assault to be made, and caused his troops to advance with loud shouts, thinking by this means to strike ter- Rhodes. ror into the enemy. But the besieged were so far from being intimidated, that they repulsed the aggressors with great slaughter, and performed the most astonishing feats of bravery. Demetrius returned to the assault next <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but was in the same manner forced to retire, after having lost a great number of men, and some officers of distinction. He had seized, at his first landing, an eminence at a small distance from the city; and, having fortified this advantageous <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>, he caused several batteries to be erected there, with engines, which incessantly discharged against the walls <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of 150 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. The towers, being thus furiously battered night and day, began to totter, and several breaches were opened in the walls: but the Rhodians, unexpectedly falling out, drove the enemy from their post, overturned their machines, and made a most dreadful havoc; insomuch that some of them retired on board their vessels, and were with much ado prevailed upon to come ashore again. Demetrius now ordered a scalade by sea and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> at the same time; and so employed the besieged, that they were at a loss what place they should chiefly defend. The attack was carried on with the utmost fury on all sides, and the besieged defended themselves with the greatest intrepidity. Such of the enemy as advanced first were thrown down from the ladders, and miserably bruised. Several of the chief officers, having mounted the walls to encourage the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> by their example, were there either killed, or taken prisoners. After the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> had lasted many hours, with great slaughter on both sides, Demetrius, notwithstanding all his valour, thought it necessary to retire, in order to repair his engines and give his men some days rest. Demetrius being sensible that he could not reduce the city till he was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the port, after having refreshed his men, he returned with new vigour against the fortifications which defended the entry into the harbour. When he came within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of a dart, he caused a vast <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> torches and firebrands to be thrown into the Rhodian ships, which were riding there; and at the same time galled, with dreadful showers of darts, arrows, and stones, such as offered to extinguish the flames. However, in spite of their utmost efforts, the Rhodians put a stop to the fire; and, having with great expedition manned three of their strongest ships, drove with such violence against the vessels on which the enemy's machines were planted, that they were shattered in pieces, and the engines dismounted and thrown into the sea. Exceptus the Rhodian <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, being encouraged by this success, attacked the enemy's fleet with his three ships, and sunk a great many vessels; but was himself at last taken prisoner: the other two vessels made their escape, and regained the port. As unfortunate as this last attack had proved to Demetrius, he determined to undertake another; and, in order to succeed in his attempt, he ordered a machine of a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> to be built, which was thrice the height and breadth of those he had lately lost. When the work was finished, he caused the engine to be placed near the port, which he was resolved, at all adventures, to force. But, as it was upon the point of entering the harbour, a dreadful storm arising, drove it against the shore, with the vessels on which it had been reared. The besieged, who were attentive to improve all favourable conjunctures, while the tempest was still raging made a fallacy against those who defended the eminence mentioned above; and, though repulsed several times, carried it at last, obliging the Demetrians, to the number of 400, to throw down their arms and submit. After this victory gained by the Rhodians, there arrived to their aid 150 Gnosticians, and 500 men sent by Ptolemy from Egypt, most of them being natives of Rhodes, who had served among the king's troops. Demetrius being extremely mortified to see all his batteries against the harbour rendered ineffectual, resolved to employ them by land, in hopes of carrying the city by assault, or at least reducing it to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of capitulating. With this view, having got Demetrius together a vast quantity of timber and other materials, he framed the famous engine called helepolis, which was by many degrees larger than any that had ever been invented before. Its basis was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, each side being in length near 50 cubits, and made up of square pieces of timber, bound together with plates of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. In the middle part he placed thick planks, about a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a> distance from each other; and on these the men were to stand who forced the engine forward. The whole was moved upon eight strong and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, whose fellows were strengthened with strong iron plates. In order to facilitate and vary the movements of the helepolis, casters were placed under it, whereby it was turned in an instant to what side the workmen and engineers pleased. From each of the four <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> a large pillar of wood was carried to about the height of 100 cubits, and inclining to each other; the whole machine consisting of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> stories, whose dimensions gradually lessened in the ascent. The first story was supported by 43 beams, and the last by no more than nine. Three sides of the machine were plated over with iron, to prevent its being damaged by the fire that might be thrown from the city. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of each story were windows of the same size and shape as the engines that were to be discharged from thence. To each window were shutters, to draw up for the defence of those who managed the machines, and to deaden the force of the stones thrown by the enemy, the shutters being covered with skins stuffed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. Every story was furnished with two large staircases, that whatever was necessary might be brought up by one, while others were going down by the other, and to every thing may be dispatched without tumult or confusion. This huge machine was moved forwards by 3000 of the strongest men of the whole army; but the art with which it was built, greatly facilitated the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. Demetrius caused likewise to be made several testudoes or pent-houses, to cover his men while they advanced to fill up the trenches and ditches; and invented a new sort of galleries, through which those who were employed at the siege might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> and repass at their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, without the least danger. He employed all his men in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVELLING">levelling</a> the ground over which the machines were to be brought up, to the space of four furlongs. The number of workmen who were employed on this occasion amounted to 30,000. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time the Rhodians, observing these formidable preparations, were busy in raising a new wall wall within that which the enemy intended to batter with the helepolis. In order to accomplish this work, they pulled down the wall which surrounded the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>; some neighbouring houses, and even some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, after having solemnly promised to build more magnificent structures in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the gods, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the city were preserved. At the same time they sent out nine of their best ships to seize such of the enemy's vessels as they could meet with, and thereby distress them for want of provisions. As these ships were commanded by their bravest sea-officers, they soon returned with an immense booty, and a great many prisoners. Among other vessels, they took a galley richly laden, on board of which they found great variety of valuable furniture, and a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> robe, which Phila herself had wrought and sent as a present to her husband Demetrius, accompanied with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> written with her own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The Rhodians sent the furniture, the royal robe, and even the letter, to Ptolemy; which exasperated Demetrius to a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. While Demetrius was preparing to attack the city, the Rhodians having assembled the people and magistrates to consult about the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> they should take, some proposed in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> the pulling down of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of Antigonus and his son Demetrius, which till then had been held in the utmost veneration. But this proposal was generally rejected with indignation, and their prudent conduct greatly allayed the wrath both of Antigonus and Demetrius. However, the latter continued to carry on the siege with the utmost vigour, thinking it would reflect no small dishonour on him were he obliged to quit the place without making himself master of it. He caused the walls to be secretly undermined: but, when they were ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, a deserter very opportunely gave notice of the whole to the townsmen; who, having with all expedition drawn a deep trench all along the wall, began to counteract, and, meeting the enemy under ground, obliged them to abandon the work. While both parties guarded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, one Athenagoras a Miletian, who had been sent to the assistance of the Rhodians by Ptolemy with a body of mercenaries, promised to betray the city to the Demetrians, and let them in through the mines in the night-time. But this was only in order to ensnare them; for Alexander, a noble Macedonian, whom Demetrius had sent with a choice body of troops to take possession of a post agreed on, no sooner appeared but he was taken prisoner by the Rhodians, who were waiting for him under arms. Athenagoras was crowned by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and presented with five talents of silver. Demetrius now gave over all thoughts of undermining the walls, and placed all his hopes of reducing the city in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTERING">battering</a>-engines which he had contrived. Having therefore levelled the ground under the walls, he brought up his helepolis, with four tetraedoes on each side of it. Two other tetraedoes of an extraordinary size, bearing battering-rams, were likewise moved forwards by 1000 men. Each story of the helepolis was filled with all sorts of engines for discharging of stones, arrows, and darts. When all things were ready, Demetrius ordered the signal to be given; when his men, setting up a shout, assaulted the city on all sides, both by sea and land. But, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the attack, when the walls were ready to fall by the repeated strokes of the battering-rams, ambassadors arrived from Cnidus, earnestly soliciting Demetrius to suspend all further hostilities, and at the same time giving him hopes that they should prevail upon the Rhodians to submit to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>. A suspension of arms was accordingly agreed on, and ambassadors sent from both sides. But, the Rhodians refusing to capitulate on the conditions offered them, the attack was renewed with so much fury, and the machines played off in so brisk a manner, that a large tower built with square stones, and the wall that flanked it, were battered down. The besieged nevertheless fought in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> with so much courage and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, that the enemy, after various unsuccessful attempts, were forced to abandon the enterprise, and retire. In this conjuncture, a fleet which Ptolemy had freighted with 300,000 measures of corn, and different kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> for the use of the Rhodians, arrived very seasonably in the port, notwithstanding the provisions, vigilance of the enemy's ships, which cruised on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the island to surprise them. A few days after came in safe two other fleets, one sent by Cander with 100,000 bushels of barley; the other by Lysimachus, with 400,000 bushels of corn, and as many of barley. This seasonable and plentiful supply arriving when the city began to suffer for want of provisions, inspired the besieged with new courage, and raised their drooping spirits. Being thus animated, they formed a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of setting the enemy's engines on fire; and with this view ordered a body of men to fall out the night ensuing, about the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> watch, with torches and firebrands, having first placed on the walls an incredible number of engines, to discharge stones, arrows, darts, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIRE_BALLS">fire-balls</a>, against those who should attempt to oppose their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a>. The Rhodian troops, pursuant to their orders, all on a sudden fell into line, and advancing, in spite of all opposition, to the batteries, set them on fire, while the engines from the walls played incessantly on those who endeavoured to extinguish the flames. The Demetrians on this occasion fell in great numbers, being incapable, in the darkness of the night, either to see the engines that continually discharged showers of stones and arrows upon them, or to join in one body and repulse the enemy. The conflagration was so great, that, several plates of iron falling from the helepolis, that vast engine would have been entirely consumed, had not the troops that were stationed in it, with all possible speed quenched the fire with water, before prepared, and ready in the apartments of the engine against such accidents. Demetrius, fearing lest all his machines should be consumed, called together, by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, those whose <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> it was to move them; and, by their help, brought them off before they were entirely destroyed. When it was day, he commanded all the darts and arrows that had been <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> by the Rhodians, to be carefully gathered, that he might from their number form some judgment of the number of machines in the city. Above 800 firebrands were found on the spot, and no fewer than 1500 darts, all discharged in a very small portion of the night. This struck the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> himself with no small terror; for he never imagined that they would have been able to bear the charges of such formidable preparations. However, after having caused the slain to be buried, and given directions for the curing of the wounded, he applied himself to the repairing of his machines which had been dismounted and rendered quite unserviceable. In the meantime the besieged, improving the respite allowed them by the removal of the machines, built a third wall in the form of a crelent, which took in all that part that was most exposed to the enemy's batteries; and besides, drew a deep trench behind the breach, to prevent the enemy from entering the city that way. At the same time they detached a squadron of their best ships, under the command of Amyntas, who made over to the continent of Asia; and there meeting with some <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a> who were commissioned by Demetrius, took both the ships and the men, among whom were Timoecles the chief of the pirates, and several other officers of distinction belonging to the fleet of Demetrius. On their return they fell in with several vessels laden with corn for the enemy's camp, which they likewise took, and brought into the port. These were soon followed by a numerous fleet of small vessels loaded with corn and provisions sent them by Ptolemy, together with 1500 men, commanded by Antigonus a Macedonian of great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> in military affairs. Demetrius in the mean time having repaired his machines, brought them up anew to the walls; which he incessantly battered, till he opened a great breach, and threw down several towers. But when he came to the assault, the Rhodians, under the command of Aminias, defended themselves with such resolution and intrepidity, that he was in three successive attacks repulsed with great slaughter, and at last forced to retire. The Rhodians likewise, on this occasion, lost several officers; and amongst others, the brave Aminias their commander. While the Rhodians were thus signalizing themselves in the defence of their country, a second embassy arrived at the camp of Demetrius from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and the other cities of Greece, soliciting Demetrius to compose matters and strike up a peace with the Rhodians. At the request of the ambassadors, who were in all above 50, a cessation of arms was agreed upon; but the terms offered by Demetrius being anew rejected by the Rhodians, the ambassadors returned home without being able to bring the contending parties to an agreement. Hostilities were therefore renewed; and Demetrius, whose imagination was fertile in expedients for succeeding in his projects, formed a detachment of 1500 of his best troops, under the conduct of Alcinus and Mancius, two officers of great resolution and experience, ordering them to enter the breach at midnight, and, forcing the entrenchment behind it, to possess themselves of the posts about the theatre, where it would be no difficult <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to maintain themselves against any efforts of the townsmen. In order to facilitate the execution of so important and dangerous an undertaking, and amuse the enemy with false attacks, he at the same time, upon a signal given, ordered the rest of the army to set up a shout, and attack the city on all sides both by sea and land. By this means he hoped, that, the besieged being alarmed in all parts, his detachment might find an opportunity of forcing the entrenchments which covered the breach, and afterwards of seizing the advantageous post about the theatre. This feint had all the success the prince could expect; for the troops having set up a shout from all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, as if they were advancing to a general assault, the detachment commanded by Alcinus and Mancius entered the breach, and fell upon those who defended the ditch and the wall that covered it, with such vigour, that, having slain the most part of them and put the rest in confusion, they advanced to the theatre, and seized on the post adjoining to it. This occasioned a general uproar in the city, as if it had been already taken: but the commanding officers dispatched orders to the soldiers on the ramparts not to quit their posts, nor stir from their respective stations. Having thus secured the walls, they put themselves at the head of a chosen body of their own troops, and of those who were lately come from Egypt, and with these <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> the enemy's detachment. But the darkness of the night prevented them from dillooding the enemy and regaining the advantageous posts they had seized. Day, however, no sooner appeared than they renewed their attack with wonderful bravery. The Demetrians without the walls, with loud shouts endeavoured to animate those who had entered the place, and inspire them with resolution to maintain their ground till they were relieved with fresh troops. The Rhodians being sensible that their fortunes, liberties, and all that was dear to them in the world, lay at stake, fought like men in the utmost despair, the enemy defending their posts for several hours without giving ground in the least. At length the Rhodians, encouraging each other to exert themselves in defence of their country, and animated by the example of their leaders, made a last effort, and, breaking into the very heart of the enemy's battalions, killed both their commanders. After their death killed or the rest were easily put in disorder, and all to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> taken, either killed or taken prisoners. The Rhodians likewise on this occasion lost many of their best commanders; and among the rest Damotetis, their chief <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, a man of extraordinary valour, who had signalized himself during the whole time of the siege.
