It is proper at all times to lay upon the banks what is dug from the bed, by which they are continually strengthened against the force of the current. 4thly, It is often necessary to diminish the windings and sinuosities in the channel as much as possible, by making new cuts whereby its course may approach towards a right line. This is a great resource in flat countries subject to inundations; because thereby all the declivity of a great extent of the river, through its turns and windings, may be thrown into a small space by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> a new channel in a straight line; as may generally be done without obstacle in such countries as we are speaking of, and hereby the velocity of the current will be very greatly augmented, and the backwaters carried off to a surprising degree. 5thly, Wherever there is a confluence of rivers or canals, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of their junction must be made as acute as possible, or else the worst of consequences will arise from the corrosion of their respective streams; what they carry of from the sides will be thrown into irregular banks in the bottom of the bed. This acute angle of the junction may always be procured by taking the direction at some distance from the point of confluence. 6thly, Wherever the sides or banks of a river are liable to a more particular corrosion, either from the confluence of streams, or from irremediable windings and turns in the channel, they must be secured against it as much as possible by weirs; for this corrosion not only destroys the banks, and alters by degrees the course of the river, but also fills up the bed, and thereby produces all the bad effects we have spoken of above. 7thly, But the principal and greatest attention in digging the beds of rivers and canals must be had to the quantity and form of their declivity. This must be done uniformly throughout their whole extent, or so much of it as is necessary for the purposes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, according to the principles laid down. Conformable thereto, the depths of their beds, and of the floors of their sluices, at the mouths whereby they discharge their waters, being fixed, the depth of the rest of the beds, and the quantity of declivity therein, must be regulated in consequence thereof, so as to increase regularly the quantity of the declivity in equal spaces the farther we recede from their mouths, and proceed towards their sources or to the part where the regular current is to take place. If the depth and volume of water in a river or canal is considerable, it will suffice, in the part next the mouth, mouth, to allow one foot perpendicular of declivity through six, eight, or even, according to Deschales, ten thousand feet in horizontal extent; at most it must not be above one in six or seven thousand. From hence the quantity of declivity in equal spaces must slowly and gradually increase as far as the current is to be made fit for navigation; but in such a manner, as that at this upper end there may not be above one foot of perpendicular declivity in four thousand feet of horizontal extent. If it be made greater than that in a regular-bed containing a considerable volume of water, the current will be so strong as to be found very unfit for the purposes of navigation. I dare boldly affirm, says Mr Mann, from the certain principles of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">hydrodynamics</a> laid down in this essay, that if the abovementioned things were carried into execution in a proper manner, the velocity of currents, and the acceleration of motion of the waters in rivers, and in canals when their sluices are open, might be increased to any degree that can be required for opening their beds, and for preventing inundations during great rains or sudden floods; by carrying off more swiftly the great accretion of water which then takes place. It would not be difficult, by these means, to increase the velocity of the current to double and triple what it is in rivers and canals, whose beds for a long space of time have been left to themselves. There is not, perhaps, a country on earth but what might be freed from inundations by these means. But it may be objected, that if all I have advised were put in execution, even in the flattest countries, the currents of rivers (for canals shut up with sluices are here out of the question) would become inconvenient, if not unfit for navigation, especially against their streams. This objection would be of weight, if it were not evident that the various means which I have pointed out may be executed in whole or in part, to a certain degree, and no farther than necessary for the purposes required. But, as it is certain that a strong and regular current in a river is the best of all means for keeping it open and deep, and for preventing the formation of banks in the bed, by the subsidence of mud, &c. which it does not allow time to precipitate; I leave it to be considered, whether it is better to have a free and open navigation something incommodeed by the strength of the current, or soon to have no navigation at all, without repeatedly digging the bed anew. Rivers flowing along plains, as well as through valleys, have naturally their beds in the lowest part of the ground comprised between the opposite hills and mountains: nevertheless, the surface of the water of a river in the midst of a plain is often higher than the surface of the grounds adjacent to the banks of the river. This proceeds from the continual subsiding of the mud, &c. brought down by the stream during floods; the waters in that case usually overflowing the banks spread themselves over the plain, where they lose a great part of the swiftness of their current, which contributes greatly to the subsiding of the mud they contain; so that the farther they flow upon the plain, the clearer they grow, and the less remains to subside. From hence the greatest precipitation of mud must be in the parts of the plain nearest the sides of the river, which in length of time will raise these grounds above the rest of the plain. Again, the waters in the bed itself de- posing incessantly a part of the mud, &c. brought down by the stream, must continually, though insensibly (for a long space of time), raise the channel and banks of the river above the rest of the plain. These causes may at last contribute to the forming of an entire new bed for the river: for as all rivers carry down in their streams more or less mud and other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> matters, which do not subside regularly in all parts alike, but must precipitate fastest where the current is slowest; there must accumulate by little and little in these parts, such banks of sand and mud as will in time hinder the current of the waters, make them reflow, and at last totally change their direction. Canals are still more subject than rivers to have their beds raised and their currents stopped by the subsiding of mud and heterogeneous matter in different places, and especially just above their sluices; because of the sudden stagnation of the water which first begins there as often as the sluices are shut; and as there is a necessity for keeping them for the most part shut, the stagnating waters in their beds must precipitate their mud, &c. in a much greater proportion than can be done in the currents of rivers which are in a continual motion towards the sea. Mr Mann calls centre of the current, or, more properly, line of greatest current, that line which passes through all the sections of a river, in the point where the velocity of the current is the greatest of all. If the current of a river is regular, and in a right line, its centre or line of greatest velocity will be precisely in the centre of the sections: but, on the contrary, if the bed is irregular and full of turns and windings, the centre, or line of greatest current, will likewise be irregular, and often change its distance and direction with regard to the centres of the sections through which the waters flow, approaching successively, and more or less, to all parts of the bed, but always in proportion and conformably to the irregularities in the bed itself. This deviation of the line of greatest current from the centres of the sections through which it passes, is a cause of many and great changes in the beds of rivers, such as the following: 1stly, In a straight and regular bed, the greatest corrosion of the current will be in the middle of the bottom of the bed; because it is that part which is nearest to the line of greatest current, and at the same time which is most acted upon by the perpendicular compression of the water. In this case, whatever matters are carried off from the bottom will be thrown, by the force of the current, equally towards the two sides, where the velocity of the stream is the least in the whole section. 2ndly, If the bed is irregular and winding, the line of greatest current will be thrown towards one side of the river, where its greatest force will be exerted in proportion to the local causes which turn it aside; in short turns of a river there will be a gyration, or turning round of the stream, by reason of its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> against the outer side of the angle; this part will be corroded away, and the bottom near it excavated to a great depth. The matters so carried off will be thrown against the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river where the current is the least, and produce a new ground, called an alluvion. 3rdly, Inequalities at the bottom of a river retain and di- diminish the velocity of the water, and sometimes may be so great as to make them reflow: all these effects contribute to the subsiding of sand, earth, and other matters thereon, which cease not to augment the volume of the obstacles themselves, and produce shallows and banks in the channel. These in time, and by a continuance of the causes, may become islands, and so produce great and permanent changes and irregularities in the beds of rivers. 4thly, The percussions of the centre of the current against the sides of the bed are so much the greater as they are made under a greater angle of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INCIDENCE">incidence</a>; from whence it follows, that the force of percussion, and the quantity of corrosion and of detriment done to the banks and weirs of rivers, and to the walls of buildings made therein, and which are exposed to that percussion, are always in a direct <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> proportion of the angle of incidence, of the greatness and depth of the section together, and of the quantity of velocity of the current. 5thly, It may happen in time, that the excavation of the bottom, and the corrosion of the sides, will have so changed the form of the bed as to bring the force of percussion into equilibrium with the velocity and direction of the current; in that case, all farther corrosion and excavation of the bed ceases. 6thly, This gives the reason why when one river falls into another almost in a perpendicular direction, and makes with it too great an angle of incidence, this direction is changed in time, by corrosions and alluvions, into an angle much more acute, till the whole comes into equilibrium. 7thly, So great and such <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> irregularities, from local causes, may happen in the motion of a river as will entirely change its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> bed, corrode thro' the banks where they are exposed to the greatest violence of percussion of the stream, and open new beds in grounds lower than what the old one is become. 8thly, Hereupon the state of the old bed will entirely depend on the quantity of water, and on the velocity and direction of the current in the new one; for immediately after this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the waters into two beds is made, the velocity of the current in the old one will be diminished in proportion to its less depth. In consequence thereof, the waters therein will precipitate more of their mud, &c. in equal spaces than they did before; which will more and more raise up the bottom, sometimes even till it becomes equal with the surface of the stream. In this case, all the water of the river will pass into the new bed, and the old one will remain entirely dry. It is well known, that this has happened to the Rhine near <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, and to many other rivers. 9thly, Hence the cause of the formation of the new branches and mouth, whereby many great rivers discharge their waters into the sea. But in proportion as a river that has none of these obstacles in its bed, approaches towards its mouth, we see the velocity of its current augment, at the same time that the declivity of the bed diminishes, the causes of which have been explained above. It is for this reason that inundations are more frequent and considerable, and do more damage in the interior parts of a country, than towards the mouths of most rivers. In the Po, for example, the height of the banks made to keep in the waters, diminishes as the river approaches to the sea. At <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, they are 20 feet high; whereas, nearer the sea, they do not exceed 10 or 12 feet, although the channel of the river is not larger in one place than in the other. The mouths of rivers, by which they discharge their waters into the sea, are liable to great variations, which produce many changes in them. 1st, The velocity and direction of the current at these mouths are in a continual <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>, caused by the tides, which alternately retard and accelerate the stream. 2ndly, During the flowing of the tide, the current of the river is first stopped, then turned into a direction entirely contrary throughout a considerable extent: if we may believe Mr. de Buffon, there are rivers in which the effect of the tides is sensible at 150 or 200 leagues from the sea. 3rdly, This state of things is a cause of a great quantity of sand, mud, &c. being precipitated and accumulated in the channel near the mouth. This continually raises and widens the bed, and at last changes it entirely into a new place, or at least opens new mouths to discharge the waters at. The Rhine, the Danube, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>, the Indus, the Ganges, the Nile, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>, and many other rivers, are instances of this. 4thly, All these effects are less sensible at the mouths of little rivers, as their currents oppose no sensible obstacle to the flowing of the tides; so that the ebb carries off again what the flow had brought in. Whenever the course of a river throughout a considerable extent of country, approaches towards a right line, its current will have a very great rapidity; and the velocity wherewith it runs diminishing the effect of its natural gravitation, the middle of the current will rise up, and the surface of the river will form a convex curve of sufficient elevation to be perceived by the eye; the highest point of this curve is always directly above the line of greatest current in the stream. On the contrary, when rivers approach near enough to their mouths for a sensible effect to be produced in them by the flowing of the tides; and also, when in other parts of their course they meet with obstacles at the sides of their channel; in both these <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the surface of the water at the sides of the current is higher than in the middle, even though the stream be rapid. In this situation of things, the surface of the river forms a concave curve, the lowest point of which, or that of inflection, is directly over the line of greatest current. The reason thereof is, that there are in this case two different and opposite currents in the river; that whereby the waters flow towards the sea, and preserve their motion therein even to a considerable distance; and that of the waters which re-mount, either by the flowing of the tide, or by their meeting with local obstacles, which form a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a> current, so much the more sensible as the flowing of the tide is stronger, or as the percussion of the water is made against greater obstacles, and in a direction nearer to a perpendicular to them. From both these causes, the greater of which by far is that of the tides, the water near the sides of the channel, where the velocity of the descending stream is naturally the least, takes a contrary direction, and runs back in the river, while that that in the middle continues to flow towards the sea. This counter current is what the French call a remous. An <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the middle of a river produces the same effect as obstacles at the sides, regard being had to the difference of situation of each. Eddies and whirlpools in rivers, in the centre of which there appears a conical or spiral cavity, and about which the water turns with great rapidity and sucks in whatever approaches it, proceed in general from the mutual percussion of these two counter currents; and the vacuity in the middle is produced by the action of the centrifugal force, whereby the water endeavours to recede, in a direct ratio of its velocity, from the centre about which it moves. If rivers persevered always nearly in the same state, the best means of diminishing the velocity of the current, when it is found too great for the purposes of navigation, would be by widening the canal; but as all rivers are subject to frequent increase and diminution, and consequently to very different degrees of velocity and force in the current, this method is liable to produce very detrimental effects; for, when the waters are low, if the channel is very large in proportion, the stream will excavate a particular bed, which, according to the irregularities of the bottom, will form various turnings and windings with regard to the principal bed; and, when the waters come to increase, they will follow, to a certain degree, the directions which the bottom waters take in this particular bed, and thereby will strike against the sides of the channel, so as to destroy the banks and cause great damages. It would be possible to prevent in part the bad effects proceeding from the current striking against the banks, by opening, at those places where it strikes, little gulps into the land, dug in such a form and direction as that the striking current should enter and circulate therein, so as to destroy, or at least greatly diminish, its velocity. This effect would be felt for a considerable way down the river. This same method might probably be used with success against the destruction of bridges, weirs, &c. by the violence of the stream during floods. Such gulps being dug into the outer-side of those turnings in the river which are immediately above the place to be secured from the violence of the stream, would successively diminish its velocity, its force and dangerous effects, a considerable way down the river. It is true, this method might contribute to produce an overflowing of the river upon the grounds adjacent to those artificial gulps, this being a natural consequence of the decrease of the velocity of the current in those places; and it would remain to be considered whether those local inundations, or the danger of destruction of the bridges or edifices in the river, were the lesser evil. The nature of inundations, and the manner of their formation, merit a particular attention in this place. While the volume of water in the bed of a river increases, the velocity of the current increases in proportion; but from the moment that part of this water overflows the bed, the velocity thereof begins to diminish, and does so more and more, the farther it flows and spreads on the plain. So that the overflowing being once begun, it is a natural consequence, that the inundation should continue for several days; for though the volume of water brought down by the flood during that time should decrease, yet, as the quantity of what runs off decreases likewise, from the great decrease of velocity in what overflows the plains, it will continue to produce the same effect as if the volume of water coming down had not diminished, until the whole of the stream be everywhere contained again within the bed of the river. When that is become the case, the waters that have overflowed the plain will decrease theron, by gradually and slowly running off, and also by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>, till they wholly disappear. If this was not so, we should see rivers overflow for an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> or two, and then return again within their beds, a thing contrary to general observation; for we constantly see inundations, once begun in flat countries, last for several days together, although in the mean while the rain ceases, and the quantity of water coming down diminishes. This must be so, because as the overflowing diminishes the velocity, and consequently the quantity of water carried off, it has the same effect as if a greater quantity still continued to come down. It may not be useless to remark here, that if the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows directly contrary to the current of the river, the overflowing will be greater than it would have been otherwise, because this accident diminishes the velocity of the stream; but, on the contrary, if the winds blow in the same direction with the current of the river, the inundation will be less than otherwise, and sooner at an end; because this accidental cause augments the velocity of the stream. River-Water. This is generally much softer and better accommodated to economical purposes than spring-water. For though rivers proceed originally from springs, yet, by their rapid motion, and by being exposed during a long course to the influence of the sun and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, the earthy and metallic salts which they contain are decomposed, the acid flies off, and the terrestrial parts precipitate to the bottom. Rivers are also rendered softer by the vast quantity of rain-water, which, passing along the surface of the earth, is conveyed into their channels. But all rivers carry with them a great deal of mud and other impurities; and, when they flow near large and populous <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, they become impregnated with a number of heterogeneous substances, in which state the water is certainly unfit for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; yet, by remaining for some time at rest, all the feculencies subside, and the water becomes sufficiently pure and potable.

ROAD

Pages 419-421

an open way, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> public passage, forming a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and another. Of all the people in the world the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> took the most pains in forming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>; and the labour and expenses they were at in rendering them spacious, firm, straight, and smooth, are incredible. They usually strengthened the ground by ramming it, laying it with flints, pebbles, or sands, and sometimes with a lining of masonry, rubbish, bricks, &c. bound together with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>. In some places in the Lionois, F. Menefrier observes, that he has found huge clutters of flints cemented with lime, reaching 10 or 12 feet deep, and making a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> as hard and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> as marble; and which, which, after resisting the injuries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> for 1600 years, is still scarce penetrable by all the force of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a>, mattocks, &c. and yet the flints it consists of are not bigger than eggs. The most noble of the Roman roads was the Via Appia, which was carried to such a vast length, that Procopius reckons it five days journey to the end of it, and Leipfius computes it at 350 miles: it is 12 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and made of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> free-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> generally a foot and a half on each side; and though this has lasted for above 1800 years, yet in many places it is for several miles together as entire as when it was first made. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> roads are distinguished into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> roads, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> roads, subterraneous roads, &c. The military roads were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> roads, formed by the Romans for marching their armies into the provinces of the empire; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of these Roman roads in England are, Watling-street, Ikenild-street, Fols-way, and Erminage-street. Double roads among the Romans, were roads for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, with two pavements, the one for those going one way, and the other for those returning the other: these were separated from each other by a causeway raised in the middle, paved with bricks, for the conveniency of foot passengers; with borders and mounting-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> from space to space, and military columns to mark the distance. Subterraneous roads are those dug through a rock, and left vaulted; as that of Puzzoli near <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, which is near half a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and is 15 feet broad and as many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. Road, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, or place of anchorage; at some distance from the shore, on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, whither ships or vessels occasionally repair to receive intelligence, orders, or necessary supplies; or to wait for a fair <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, &c. The excellence of a road consists chiefly in its being protected from the reigning winds and the swell of the sea; in having a good anchoring-ground, and being at a competent distance from the shore. Those which are not sufficiently enclosed are termed open roads. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAN">Roan</a>, in the manege. A roan <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> is one of a bay, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with grey or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> spots interspersed very thick. When this party-coloured coat is accompanied with a black head and black extremities, he is called a roan-horse with a black-a-moor's head: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the same mixture is predominant upon a deep sorrel, he is called claret-roan. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROANOAK">Roanoak</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, near the coast of North Carolina. Here the English first attempted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in 1585, but were obliged to leave it for want of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. E. Long. 75°. O. N. Lat. 35°. 40'. Roanoke, a river of North America, which rises in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, runs through Carolina, and at length falls into the sea, where it forms a long narrow bay called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. Roasting, in metallurgic operations, signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> of the volatile parts of an ore by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, passim. Rob, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, the juices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> purified and infusified till it is of the consistence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. Robbery, the rapina of the civilians, is the felonious and forcible taking, from the person of another, of goods or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to any value, by violence or putting him in fear. 1. There must be a taking, otherwise it is no robbery. A <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> attempt to rob was indeed held to be felony, so late as Henry the Fourth's time; but afterwards it was taken to be only a misdemeanor, and punishable with fine and imprisonment; till the statute 7 Geo. II. c. 21, which makes it a felony (transportable for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years) unlawfully and maliciously to assault another, with any offensive weapon or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>;—or by menaces, or by other forcible or violent manner, to demand any money or goods;—with a felonious intent to rob. If the thief, having once taken a purse, returns it, still it is a robbery; and so it is whether the taking be strictly from the person of another, or in his presence only; as where a robber by menaces and violence puts a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> in fear, and drives away his sheep or his cattle before his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>. 2. It is immaterial of what value the thing taken is: a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>, as well as a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, thus forcibly extorted, makes a robbery. 3. Lastly, the taking must be by force, or a previous putting in fear; which makes the violation of the person more atrocious than privately stealing. For, according to the maxim of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, "qui vi rapuit, fur improbiter effe videtur." This previous violence, or putting in fear, is the criterion that distinguishes robbery from other larcenies. For if one privately steals a piece from the person of another, and afterwards keeps it by putting him in fear, this is no robbery, for the fear is subsequent: neither is it <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> as privately stealing, being under the value of twopence. Not that it is indeed necessary, though usual, to lay in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> that the robbery was committed by putting in fear: it is sufficient, if laid to be done by violence. And when it is laid to be done by putting in fear, this does not imply any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of terror or affright in the party robbed: it is enough that too much force or threatening, by word or gesture, be used, as might create an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of danger, or induce a man to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> with his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> without or against his consent. Thus, if a man be knocked <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> without previous warning, and stripped of his property while senseless, though strictly he cannot be said to be put in fear, yet this is undoubtedly a robbery. Or, if a person with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> drawn begs an alms, and I give him through mistrust and apprehension of violence, this is a felonious robbery. So if, under a pretence of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, a man forcibly extorts money from another, neither shall this subterfuge avail him. But it is doubted, whether the forcing a higler, or other chapman, to sell his wares, and giving him the full value of them, amounts to so heinous a crime as robbery. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of larceny is debarred of the benefit of clergy by statute 23 Hen. VIII. c. 1. and other subsequent statutes; not indeed in general, but only when committed in a dwelling-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, or in or near the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s highway. A robbery therefore in a distant field, or footpath, was not punished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; but was open to the benefit of clergy, till the statute 3 & 4 W. and M. c. 9. which takes away clergy from both principals and accessories before the fact, in robbery, wherever committed. See Law, No. clxxxvi: 30. Robert Bruce, king of Scotland, in 1306; a renowned general, and the deliverer of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from a state of vassalage to the English. See Scotland. Robert (of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>), <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> palatine of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>; the son of Frederic, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> Palatine, by Elisabeth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of James I. king of England. Distinguished himself by his valour as a general and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>; first in the Dutch, and then in the English <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. He was unsuccessful in the cause of his uncle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. against the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> forces; but under Charles II. he defeated the Dutch fleet, and was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> high admiral of England in 1673. This prince was a lover of the sciences, and particularly skilful in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>. Died in 1682. ROBIN HOOD. See MAY-GAMES. Robin <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">Red</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">Breast</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTACILLA">Motacilla</a>.

ROBINIA

Pages 421-421

FALSE-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACACIA">ACACIA</a>; a genus of the decandra order, belonging to the diadelphia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, but the most remarkable is the caragana. The leaves of this species are conjugated, and composed of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small folioles, of an oval <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and ranged by pairs on one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> stock. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEGUMINOUS">leguminous</a>, and are clustered on a filament. Every flower consists of a small <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-shaped petal, cut into four segments at the edge, the upper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> being rather the widest. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> is small, open, and rounded. The wings are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, oval, and a little raised. Within are 10 stamens united at the base, curved towards the top, and rounded at the summit. In the midst of a sheath, formed by the filaments of the stamens, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PISTIL">pistil</a> is perceivable, consisting of an oval germen, terminated by a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUTTON">button</a>. This germen becomes afterwards an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> flatish curved pod, containing four <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> five seeds, of a size and shape <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> and unequal; yet in both respects somewhat resembling a lentil. This tree grows naturally in the severe climates of Northern <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. It is particularly found on the banks of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBY">Oby</a>, Jenissei, &c. It is very rarely met with in the inhabited parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, because cattle are very fond of its leaves, and hogs of its roots; and it is so hardy, that the severest winters do not affect it. Gmelin found it in the neighbourhood of Tobolsk, buried under 15 feet of snow and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, yet had it not suffered the least damage. Its culture consists in being planted or sowed in a lightish sandy soil, which must on no account have been lately manured. It thrives best near a river, or on the edge of a brook or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; but presently dies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> planted in a marshy spot, where the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> stagnates. If it is planted on a rich soil, well tilled, it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> grow to the height of 20 feet, and in a very few years will be as big as a common birch tree. In a very bad soil this tree degenerates, and becomes a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> shrub: the leaves grow hard, and their fine bright green <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is changed to a dull deep green. The Tungusian Tartars, and the inhabitants of the northern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, are very fond of the fruit of this tree, it being almost the only sort of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> they eat. M. Strahlemberg, author of a well-esteemed <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of Siberia, affirms us that this fruit is tolerably pleasant food, and very nourishing. These peas are first infused in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water, to take off a certain acid <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> they have; and are afterwards dressed like common peas or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> beans; and being ground into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, pretty good cakes are made of them. The leaves and tender shoots of this tree make excellent fodder for several sorts of cattle. The roots, being sweet and succulent, are very well adapted to fattening hogs; and the fruit is greedily eaten by all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>. After several experiments somewhat similar to the methods used with anil and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, a fine blue colour was procured from its leaves. The smaller kind of this tree seems still better adapted to answer this purpose. The striking elegance of its foliage, joined to the pleasing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour of its beautiful flowers, should, one would imagine, bring it into request for forming nosegays, or for speedily making an elegant hedge. Besides the qualities above recited, it possesses the uncommon advantage of growing exceedingly quick, and of being easily transplanted. There are large plantations of it now in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>. Linnaeus affirms us, that, after the Pinus sylvestris, erroneously called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a> tree of Siberia, this tree, of all that are to be found in Siberia, is most worthy of cultivation.

ROBINS

Pages 421-422

a most ingenious English mathematician, born at Bath in 1707. His parents were <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a> and of low condition, consequently neither able nor willing to have him much instructed in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> learning. Nevertheless his own propensity to science procured him a recommendation to Dr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEMBERTON">Pemberton</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; by whose assistance, while he attained the sublimer parts of mathematical knowledge, he commenced teacher of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. But the business of teaching, which required confinement, not suiting his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> disposition, he gradually declined it, and engaged in business that required more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. Hence he tried many laborious experiments in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUNNERY">gunnery</a>, from the persuasion that the resistance of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> has a much greater influence on swift <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROJECTILES">projectiles</a> than is generally imagined. Hence also he was led to consider the mechanic arts that depend on mathematical principles; as the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of bridges, the draining of fens, the rendering of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> navigable, and the making of harbours. Among other arts, fortification much engaged his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; and he met with opportunities of perfecting himself by viewing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> strong places of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, in some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">tours</a> he made abroad with persons of distinction. Upon his return from one of these excursions, he found the learned amused with Dr Berkley's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, intitled The Analyst, in which an attempt was made to explode the method of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLUXIONS">fluxions</a>. Mr Robins was therefore advised to clear up this affair by giving a distinct account of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton's doctrines, in such a manner as to obviate all the objections that had been made without naming them. Accordingly he published, in 1735, A Discourse concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> and Certainty of Sir Isaac Newton's Method of Fluxions; and some exceptions being made to his manner of defending Sir Isaac Newton, he afterwards wrote two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> three additional discourses. In 1738 he defended the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> against an objection contained in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> at the end of a Latin piece, called Mathe, seu Cosmographia puerilis; and the following year printed Remarks on M. Euler's Treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">Motion</a>, on Dr Smith's System of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, and on Dr Jurin's Discourse of distinct and indistinct Vision. annexed to Dr Smith's work. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> while Mr Robins did not solely confine himself to mathematical subjects; for in 1739 he published three pamphlets on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> affairs, without his name; when two of them, relating to the convention and negotiations with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, were so universally esteemed, as to occasion his being employed in a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>; for on a committee being appointed to examine into the past conduct of Sir Robert Walpole, he was chosen their secretary. In 1742, Mr Robins published a small treatise, intitled New Principles of Gunnery, containing the result of many experiments; when a Discourse being published in the Philosophical Transactions, in order to invalidate some of his opinions, he thought proper, in an account he gave of his book in the same Transactions, to take notice of those experiments: in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which several of his Dissertations on the Resistance of the Air were read, and the experiments exhibited before the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, for which he was presented by that honourable body with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> medal. In 1748 appeared <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Anson's Voyage round the World, which, though Mr Walter's name is in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, was in reality written by Mr Robins. Mr Walter, chaplain on board the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CENTURION">Centurion</a>, had indeed brought it <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to his departure from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MACAO">Macao</a> for England, when he proposed to print the work by subscription. It was however thought proper that an able judge should review and correct it, and Mr Robins was appointed; when, upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, it was resolved that the whole should be written by Mr Robins, and that what Mr Walter had done should only serve as materials. Hence the introduction entire, and many dissertations in the body of the work, were composed by him, without receiving the least assistance from Mr Walter's manuscript, which chiefly related to the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, the currents, courses, bearings, distances, the qualities of the ground on which they anchored, and such particulars as generally fill up a sailor's account. No production of this kind ever met with a more favourable reception; four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> impressions were sold within a twelvemonth; and it has been translated into most of the languages of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The fifth edition printed at London in 1749, was revised and corrected by Mr Robins himself. Having thus rendered himself famous for his ability in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, he was desired to compose an apology for the unfortunate affair at Preston-Pans in Scotland, which was prefixed as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to The Report of the Proceedings of the Board of general Officers, on their examination into the conduct of Lieu. Gen. Sir John Cope; and this preface was esteemed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-piece in its kind. He afterwards, through the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of lord Anson, contributed to the improvements made in the royal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>. Having thus established his reputation, he was offered the choice of two considerable employments; either to go to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> as one of the commissaries for adjusting the limits of Acadia, or to be engineer general to the East <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. He chose the latter, and arrived in the East Indies in 1750; but the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> not agreeing with his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, he died there the year following.

ROBORANTS

Pages 422-422

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, medicines which strengthen the parts, and give new vigour to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>.

ROCHEFORT

Pages 422-422

a handsome and considerable seaport town of France, in the territory of Aunis, with a very commodious harbour, and one of the most famous in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It is a department of the marine, and has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> magazines of naval stores. There is also one of the finest halls of arms in the kingdom, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many workmen employed in making them; there are also forges for anchors, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>-houses for ship carpenters, who are employed in every thing that relates to the fitting out of ships, that comes within the compass of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. They likewise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> great guns here; and have artists, whose employment is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. There are also stocks for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> men of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, rope-walks, magazines of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and powder, a manufactory of sail-cloth, an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for sailors, and proper places to clean the ships. Add to these, the houses of the intendant, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of the capuchins, and the superb structure which contains lodgings for 300 marine guards, where they are taught the business and exercises belonging to seamen and officers who go on board the men of war. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>, four miles from its mouth; and the entrance of the river is defended by several forts. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 54. N. Lat. 46. 3. ROCHEFOUCAULT (Francis, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de la) <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Marsillac, governor of Poitou, was the son of Francis, the first duke of Rochefoucault, and distinguished himself on several occasions by his courage and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>. He wrote two excellent works; the one a book of Maxims, which M. de Voltaire says has contributed more than any thing else to form the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the French <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and the other, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Regency of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. It was partly at the instigation of the beautiful duchess de Longueville, that the duke de Rochefoucault engaged in the civil wars, in which he signalized himself particularly at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTOINE">Antoine</a>. Beholding one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of this lady, he wrote underneath it those two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> from the tragedy of Alcyoneus. "Pour meriter son coeur, pour plaire a ses beaux yeux, J'ai fait la guerre aux rois, je l'aurais fait aux deux." Which may be thus rendered in English: "To <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> her heart, and please her sparkling eyes, I've war'd with kings, and would have brav'd the skies." The author of the maxims was not a member of the French academy. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of making a public speech the day of his reception, was the only cause that he did not claim admittance. This nobleman, with all the courage he had displayed upon various critical occasions, and with his superiority of birth and understanding over the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> run of men, did not think himself capable of facing an audience, to utter only four lines in public, without being out of countenance. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1680, aged 68.

ROCHELLE

Pages 422-423

a handsome, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, strong, rich, and celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the territory of Aunis, with a very commodious and safe harbour, a bishop's see, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> for humanities, an academy, a school for medicine, anatomy, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, and a mint. The houses are fine, and supported with piazzas, under which persons may walk in all weathers; and the streets in general as straight as a line: there are several handsome churches, and other structures, besides a remark- markable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of Dauphiny, which throws out the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> through several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>. There are no remains of the old fortifications, except on the side of the harbour, where there are bulwarks and strong towers to defend the entrance. The new fortifications are in the manner of Vauban. The inhabitants carry on a considerable trade, especially in wines, brandy, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>-cloth, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERGE">serge</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIII. took this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a> in 1628, after 13 months siege. It is seated on the ocean, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 11. N. Lat. 46. 10.

ROCHESTER

Pages 423-423

an episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> in England, seated on the river Medway in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 34. N. Lat. 51. 22. It was formerly much more considerable than at present; and had a castle, now in ruins.

ROCK

Pages 423-423

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Vultur. Rock-Crystal, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, otherwise called sprig-crystal, a name given to the third order of crystals, from their being affixed to a rock <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body. This kind of crystal is the most <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> of all others, and is what the generality of authors describe under the name of crystal of the shops. The clearest, purest, and most transparent that can be had is to be chosen; and to prove its genuineness, it may be tried with aquafortis; true crystal making no effervescence with that medium. Rock-Fish. See GOBIUS.

ROCKET

Pages 423-423

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> fire-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, consisting of a cylindrical <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, filled with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of certain combustible ingredients; which, being tied to a stick, mounts into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and then bursts. See PROTECHNY. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">Theory</a> of the Flight of Sky-Rockets. Mariotte takes the rise of rockets to be owing to the impulse <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> resistance of the air against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>. Dr Desaguliers accounts for it otherwise. Conceive the rocket to have no vent at the choak, and to be set on fire in the conical bore; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be, either that the rocket would burst in the weakest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, or, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> all its parts were equally strong, and able to sustain the impulse of the flame, the rocket would burn out immoveable. Now, as the force of the flame is equable, suppose its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> downwards, or that upwards, sufficient to lift 40 pounds. As these forces are equal, but their directions contrary, they will destroy each other's action. Imagine then, the rocket opened at the choak; by this means the action of the flame downwards is taken away, and there remains a force equal to 40 pounds acting upwards, to carry up the rocket, and the stick it is tied to. Accordingly, we find that if the composition of the rocket be very weak, so as not to give an impulse greater than the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the rocket and stick, it does not rise at all; or if the composition be slow, so that a small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of it only kindles at first, the rocket will not rise. The stick serves to keep it perpendicular; for if the rocket should begin to stumble, moving round a point in the choak, as being the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> centre of gravity of rocket and stick, there would be so much friction against the air by the stick between the centre and the point, and the point would <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> against the air with so much velocity, that the friction of the medium would restore it to its perpendicularity. When the composition is burnt out, and the impulse upwards is ceased, the common centre of gravity is brought lower towards the middle of the stick; by which means the velocity of the point of the stick is decreased, and that of the point of the rocket increased; so that the whole will tumble <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, with the rocket-end foremost. All the while the rocket burns, the common centre of gravity is shifting and getting downwards, and still the faster and the lower as the stick is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>, so that it sometimes begins to tumble before it be burnt out; but when the stick is a little too heavy, the weight of the rocket <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> a less proportion to that of the stick, the common centre of gravity will not get so low but that the rocket will rise straight, though not so fast.

ROGA

Pages 423-423

in antiquity, a present which the emperors made to the senators, magistrates, and even to the people; and the popes and patriarchs to their clergy. These rogæ were distributed by the emperors on the first <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the year, on their birth-day, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> on the natalis dies of the cities; and by the popes and patriarchs in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. Roga is also used for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pay of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>.

ROGATION

Pages 423-423

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>, a demand made by the consuls <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> tribunes of the Roman people, when a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> was proposed to be passed. Rogatio is also used for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> itself made in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the people's giving their assent to this demand; to distinguish it from a senatus consultum, or decree of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. Rogation-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">Week</a>, the week immediately succeeding Whitunday; so called from the three fasts therein, viz. on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday.

ROGER DE HOVEDEN

Pages 423-424

a learned <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the 13th century, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, most probably at the town of that name, now called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOWDEN">Howden</a>, some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the reign of Henry I. After he had received the first parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he studied the civil and canon <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, which were then become the most fashionable and lucrative branches of learning. He became <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> chaplain to Henry II. who employed him to transact several <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> affairs; in which he acquitted himself with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. But his most meritorious <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> was, his Annals of England, from A.D. 731, when Bede's ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> ends, to A.D. 1202. This work, which is one of the most voluminous of our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> histories, is more valuable for the sincerity with which it is written, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of facts which it contains, than for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of its style, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the regularity of its arrangement.

ROGUE

Pages 424-424

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, an idle sturdy beggar; who by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> statutes is for the first offence called a rogue of the first <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and punished by whipping, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BORING">boring</a> through the gristle of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a> with a hot <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; and for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> offence, is termed a rogue of the second degree, and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> above 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, ordered to be executed as a felon.

ROHAULT

Pages 424-424

a celebrated Cartesian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was the son of a merchant of Amiens, where he was born in 1620. He became well skilled in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and taught them at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he became acquainted with M. Clerfelier, an advocate, who gave him his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. Rohault also taught <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> in the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, with uncommon applause. He there improved the arts, and gave excellent lectures to the artists and workmen. He died at Paris in 1675. He wrote, in French, 1. A Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Philosophy. 2. The Elements of the Mathematics. 3. A Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, which is very curious. 4. Philosophical Conversations; and other works. His Physica have been translated into Latin, by Dr Samuel Clarke, with notes, in which the Cartelian errors are corrected upon the Newtonian system.

ROLL

Pages 424-424

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCHEDULE">schedule</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> which may be rolled up by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> into the form of a pipe. In these schedules of parchment all the pleadings, memorials, and acts of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, are entered and filed by the proper officer; which being done, they become records of the court. Of these there are in the exchequer several kinds, as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> wardrobe roll, the cofferer's roll, the subsidy-roll, &c. Roll is also used for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the names of persons of the same condition, or of those who have entered into the same engagement. Thus a court-roll of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>, is that in which the names, rents, and services, of each tenant are copied and enrolled. Calves-head Roll, a roll in the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, in which every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> is taxed yearly at 2s. every barrister at 1s. 6d. and every <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> at 1s. to the cook and other officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, in consideration of a dinner of calves' heads provided in Easter-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">Master</a>-Roll, that in which are entered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of every troop, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, regiment, &c. As soon as a soldier's name is written <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the roll, it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> for him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. Rolls-Office, is an officer in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">Chancery</a>-lane, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, appointed for the custody of the rolls and records in chancery. Rider-Roll, a schedule of parchment frequently sewed or added to some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a roll or record. Rolls of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a>, are the manuscript registers or rolls of the proceedings of our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> parliaments, which before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> were all engrossed on parchment, and proclaimed openly in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. In these rolls are also contained a great many decisions of difficult <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of law, which were frequently in former times referred to the decision of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> court. Roll, or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROLLER">Roller</a>, is also a piece of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, &c. of a cylindrical form, used in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, and in several works and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. Thus in the glass manufacture they have a running-roll, which is a thick <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> brass, which serves to conduct the melted glass to the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a> on which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> looking-glasses, &c. are cast. Founders also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a roll to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> the sand which they use in making their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>. The presses called calendars, as serving to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> stuffs withal, consist, among other essential parts, of two rollers. It is also between the two rollers that the waves are given to silks, mohairs, and other stuffs proper to be tabbied. Impressions from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>-plates are also taken by passing the plate and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> between two rollers. See Rolling-press Printing. Rolls, in fluting-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, &c. are two iron instruments of a cylindrical form, which serve to draw or stretch out plates of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. Rolls, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-works, are two large iron barrels which serve to bruise the canes, and to express the juice. These are cast hollow, and their cavities are filled up with wood, the cylinders of which are properly the rollers.

ROLLER

Pages 424-424

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> bandage, usually of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>-cloth, rolled round any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body, to keep it in, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> dispose it to a state of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>.

ROLLIN

Pages 424-425

a justly celebrated French writer, was the son of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTER">cutter</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and was born there on the 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1661. He studied at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> du Pleissis; and acquired the regard of M. Gobinet, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of that college, who had a particular esteem for him. He afterwards became professor of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> in the same college; and, in 1688, succeeded Horfan, his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, as professor of eloquence, in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> college. No <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> ever exercised the functions of it with greater eclat: he often made Latin orations, to celebrate the memorable events of the times; and frequently accompanied them with poems, which were read and esteemed by every body. In 1694, he was chosen rector of the university; and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in that office two years, which was then a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mark of distinction. By virtue of his office, he spoke the annual <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAN">pan</a>- <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> upon <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. He made many very useful regulations in the university; and particularly reanimated the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, which was then growing into great neglect. He was a man of indefatigable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; and trained innumerable persons, who did <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the state, and the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> Portail was pleased one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> to reproach Rollin in a jocular strain, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he exceeded even himself in doing business: to whom Rollin replied, with that plainness and sincerity which was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to him, "It becomes you well, Sir, to reproach me with this; it is this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of labour in me which has distinguished you in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of advocate-general, which has raised you to that of first president: you owe the greatness of your fortune to me." Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of the rectorship, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> Noailles engaged him to superintend the studies of his nephews, who were in the college of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAON">Laon</a>; and in this office he was agreeably employed, when, in 1699, he was with great reluctance made coadjutor to the principal of the college of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUVAIS">Beauvais</a>. This college was then a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, inhabited by very few students; and without any manner of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>: but Rollin's great reputation and industry soon re-peopled it, and made it that flourishing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> it has ever since continued. In this situation he continued till 1712; when the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> between the Jesuits and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANSENISTS">Jansenists</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> towards a crisis, he fell a sacrifice to the prevalence of the former. Father le Tellier, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s confessor, and furious <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> of the Jesuits, infused into his master prejudices against Rollin, whose connections with cardinal de Noailles would alone have sufficed to have made him a Jansenist; and on this account he lost his share in the principality of Beauvais. No man, however, could have lost less in this than Rollin, who had everything left him that was necessary to make him happy: retirement, books, and enough to live on. He now began to employ himself upon Quintilian; an author he justly valued, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> neglected not without uneasiness. He retrenched in him whatever he thought rather curious, than useful for the instruction of youth; he placed summaries <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> contents at the head of each <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>; and he accompanied the text with short select notes. His edition appeared in 1715, in 2 vols 12mo. with an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> setting forth his method and views.
