In 1710, the university of Paris willing to have a head suitable to the importance of their interests in the then critical conjuncture of affairs, chose Rollin again rector; but he was displaced in about two months by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> de cachet. The university had presented to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> a petition, in which it protested against taking any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> in the adjustment of the late disputes; and their being congratulated in a public <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> by Rollin on this step, occasioned the letter which ordered them to choose a rector of more moderation. Whatever the university might suffer by the removal of Rollin, the public was probably a gainer; for he now applied himself to compose his excellent treatise upon the Manner of Studying and Teaching the Belles Lettres. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> was published, two volumes in 1726, and two more in 1728, 8vo. Encouraged by the great success of this work, he undertook another of equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and entertainment: his Histoire Ancienne, &c. or "<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Egyptians, Carthaginians, Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes and Persians, Macedonians, and Greeks," which he finished in 13 vols 8vo. and published between 1730 and 1738. M. Voltaire, after having observed that Rollin was "the first member of the university of Paris who wrote French with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and correctness," says of this work, that "though the last volumes, which were written in too great a hurry, are not equal to the first, it is nevertheless the best compilation that has yet appeared in any language; because it is seldom that compilers are eloquent, and Rollin was remarkably so." While the last volumes of his ancient history were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, he published the first of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman History</a>; which he lived to carry on, through the eighth and into part of the ninth, to the war against the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CIMBRI">Cimbri</a>, about 70 years before the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIUM">Actium</a>. Mr Crevier, the worthy <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Rollin, continued the history to the battle of Actium, which closes the tenth volume; and has since completed the original <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of Rollin, in 16 vols 12mo, which was to bring it <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the foundation of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, to the reign of Constantine the Great. All these works of Rollin have met with universal approbation, and been translated into several languages. This excellent person died in 1741. He had been named by the king a member of the academy of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> and belles lettres in 1701: but as he had not then brought the college of Beauvais into repute, and found he had more business upon his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> than was consistent with a decent attendance upon the functions of an academician, he begged the privileges of a veteran, which were honourably granted him. Nevertheless, he maintained his connections with the academy, attended their assemblies as often as he could, laid the plan of his ancient history before them, and demanded an academician for his censor. Rollin was a man of an admirable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>: very ingenious, consummate in polite learning, of rigid morals, and eminently pious. He was rather too <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> carrying him into the territories <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; and he wanted nothing but a mixture of the philosophic in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, to make him a very complete person. When he was discharged from the rectorship in 1720, the words of the lettre de cachet were, That the university should choose a rector of more moderation. But this was hardly possible: for nothing could be more benign, more pacific, more sweet, more moderate, than Rollin's temper. He showed, it must be owned, some zeal for the cause of Jansenism. In all other respects he was a most respectable person. We find in his works generous and exalted sentiments, a zeal for the good of society, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of virtue, a veneration for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, and in short every thing, though on profane subjects, sanctified with a spirit truly religious; so that it is impossible to read him without feeling ourselves more virtuous. How noble his reflections! <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> reason, religion, honour, probity, inspired them; and we can never enough admire the art which has made them appear so natural. This is Mr Voltaire's eulogy on Rollin: to which we may add the testimony of the celebrated poet Rousseau, who conceived such a veneration for him, that he came out of banishment incognito to Paris, on purpose to visit and pay his respects to him. He looked upon his histories, not only as the best models of the historic kind, but as a complete system of politics and morals, and a most

ROLLING

Pages 425-426

the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> by which a ship rocks from side to side like a cradle, occasioned by the agitation of the waves. Rolling, therefore, is a sort of revolution about an imaginary axis passing through the centre of gravity of a ship; so that the nearer the centre of gravity is to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, the more violent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the rolling-motion; because the centre about which the vibrations are made, is placed so low in the bottom, that the resistance made by the keel to the volume of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> which it displaces in rolling, bears very little proportion to the force of the vibration above the centre of gravity, the radius of which extends as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as the mast-heads. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the centre of gravity is placed higher above the keel, the radius of vibration will not only be diminished, but an additional force to oppose the motion of rolling will be communicated to that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship's bottom which is below the centre of gravity. So far as relates to the effect of rolling, when produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> flowage of the ballast, and to the manner by which it may be prevented, viz. a change of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> or disposition of the ballast, we shall endeavour to explain under the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIM">Trim</a>. It may, however, be necessary to remark, that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the ship's bottom may also contribute to diminish this movement considerably. Many fatal disasters have happened to ships, arising from a violent rolling; as the loss of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, loosening of the cannon, and straining violently on the decks and sides, so as to weaken the ship to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. See Pitching. ROLLING-Tackle, a pulley or purchase fastened to that part of a sail-yard which is to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> of the mast, in order to confine the yard <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the leeward when the sail is furled. It is used to prevent the yard from having a great friction against the mast in a high <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which would be equally pernicious to both.

ROLLO

Pages 426-426

the conqueror of Normandy, was a Norwegian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, banished from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> by Harold Harfagre, who conquered <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> in 870, on account of the piracies he exercised. He first retired with his fleet among the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Scotland, whither the flower of the Norwegian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> had fled for refuge ever since Harold had become <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. He was there received with open arms by those warriors, who, eager for conquest and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, waited only for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> to undertake some glorious enterprise. Rollo setting himself at their head, and seeing his power formidable, sailed towards England, which had been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as it were a field open on all sides to the violences of the northern nations. But the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Alfred had some years before established such order in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, that Rollo, after several fruitless attempts, despaired of forming there such a settlement as should make him amends for the loss of his own country. He pretended, therefore, to have had a supernatural dream, which promised him a glorious fortune in France, and which served at least to support the ardour of his followers. The weakness of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> in that kingdom, and the confusion in which it was involved, were still more persuasive reasons to insure them of success. Having therefore sailed up the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>, he immediately took that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, then called Neustria, and making it his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of arms, he advanced up to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, to which he laid siege in form. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> at length ended in the entire cession of Neustria, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the Simple was obliged to give up to Rollo and his Normans in order to purchase a peace. Rollo received it in perpetuity to himself and his posterity, as a feudal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> dependant on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of France. A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the interview between Charles and this new duke, gives us a curious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the manners of these Normans, (as they were called by foreigners); for the latter would not take the oath of fealty to his sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, any other way than by placing his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> within those of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>; and absolutely refused to kiss his feet, as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> then required. It was with great difficulty he was prevailed on to let one of his warriors perform this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> in his stead; but the officer to whom Rollo deputed this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, suddenly raised the king's foot so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, that he overturned him on his back; a piece of rudeness which was only laughed at; to such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> were the Normans feared and Charles despised. Soon after, Rollo was persuaded to embrace Christianity, and he was baptized with much ceremony by the archbishop of Rouen in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>. As soon as he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> himself in full possession of Normandy, he exhibited such virtues as rendered the province happy, and deserved to make his former outrages forgotten. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">Religious</a>, wise, and liberal, this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of pirates became, after Alfred, the greatest and most humane <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

ROMAGNA

Pages 427-427

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the pope's territories, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Ferrarese, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Urbino, on the east by the gulph of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, and on the west by the Bolognese and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Tuscany. It is fertile in corn, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and pastures. It has also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, mineral waters, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-works, which make its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> revenue. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

ROMAN

Pages 426-426

in general, something belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Rome. See Rome. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> elected to be successor to the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Germany.

ROMANCE

Pages 426-427

in matters of literature, a fabulous relation of certain adventures designed for the entertainment and instruction of the readers. The true <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and genuine characteristics of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, are excellently explained by the ingenious author of the Rambler; who observes, that the works of fiction, with which the present <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> seems more particularly delighted, are such as exhibit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in its true state, diversified only by the accidents that daily happen in the world, and influenced by those passions and qualities which are really to be found in conversing with mankind. This kind of writing may be termed not improperly the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> of romance, and is to be connected nearly by the rules of comic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> is to bring about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> events by easy means, and to keep up curiosity without the help of wonder: it is therefore precluded from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> and expedients of the heroic romance, and can neither employ giants to snatch away a lady from the nuptial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, nor knights to bring her back from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>; it can neither bewilder its personages in defarts, nor lodge them in imaginary castles. Scaliger, upon Pontanus, remarks, that all his writings are filled with images; and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you take from him his lilies and his roses, his fayrs and his dryads, he <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have nothing left that can be called poetry. In like Romance, like manner, almost all the fictions of the last <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> will vanish, if you deprive them of a hermit and a wood, a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> and a shipwreck. Why this wild strain of imagination found reception so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, in polite and learned ages, it is not easy to conceive; but we cannot wonder, that, while readers could be procured, the authors were willing to continue it; for when a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> had, by practice, gained some fluency of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, he had no farther care than to retire to his closet, to let loose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> his mind with incredibilities; and a book was produced without fear of criticism, without the toil of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, without knowledge of nature, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> acquaintance with life. The task of our present writers is very different; it requires, together with that learning which is to be gained from books, that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> which can never be attained by solitary diligence, but must arise from general <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a>, and accurate observation of the living world. Their performances have, as Horace expresses it, plus oneris quantum veniae minus, little <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>, and therefore more difficulty. They are engaged in portraits of which every one knows the original, and can therefore detect any deviation from exactness of resemblance. Other writings are safe, except from the malice of learning; but these are in danger from every <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> reader; as the slipper was censured by a shoemaker, who happened to stop in his way at the Venus of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APELLES">Apelles</a>. But the danger of not being approved as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> copiers of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> manners, is not the most important <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> that an author of this sort ought to have before him. These books are written chiefly to the young, the ignorant, and the idle, to whom they serve as lectures of conduct, and introductions into life. They are the entertainment of minds unfurnished with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, and therefore easily susceptible of impressions; not fixed by principles, and therefore easily following the current of fancy; not informed by experience, and consequently open to every false suggestion and partial account. That the highest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of reverence should be paid to youth, and that nothing indecent or unseemly should be suffered to approach their eyes or ears, are precepts extorted by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and virtue from an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writer, by no means eminent for chastity of thought. The same kind, though not the same degree of caution, is required in every thing which is laid before them, to secure them from unjust prejudices, perverse opinions, and improper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of images. In the romances formerly written, every transaction and sentiment was so remote from all that passes among men, that the reader was in very little danger of making any applications to himself; the virtues and crimes were equally beyond his sphere of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>; and he amused himself with heroes and with traitors, deliverers and prosecutors, as with beings of another species, whose actions were regulated upon motives of their own, and who had neither faults nor excellencies in common with himself. But, when an adventurer is levelled with the rest of the world, and acts in such scenes of the universal drama as may be the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of any other man, young spectators fix their eyes upon him with closer <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and hope, by observing his behaviour and success, to regulate their own practices when they shall be engaged in the like <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>. For this reason, these familiar histories may perhaps be made of greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> than the solemnities of professed morality, and convey the knowledge of vice and virtue with more accuracy than axioms and definitions. But, if the power of example is so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> as to take possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> by a kind of violence, and produce effects almost without the intervention of the will, care ought to be taken, that, when the choice is unrestrained, the best examples only should be exhibited; and that which is likely to operate so strongly, should not be mischievous or uncertain in its effects. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> advantages which these fictions have over real life, is, that their authors are at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, though not to invent, yet to select objects, and to cull from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of mankind those individuals upon which the attention ought most to be employed; as a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a>, though it cannot be made, may be polished by art, and placed in such a situation as to display that lustre which before was buried among common <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>.

ROMANIA

Pages 427-427

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Bulgaria, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, on the south by the Archipelago and the sea of Marmora, and on the west by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> and Bulgaria; being 200 miles in length, and 150 in breadth. It was formerly called Thrace, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and largest of all the provinces the Turks possess in Europe. It is a fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in corn and pastures, and there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>. It is divided into three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> governments <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANGA">sanga</a>-cates; namely, Kırkeli, of which Philippoli is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALIPOLI">Galipoli</a>, whose capital is of the same name; and Byzantium, or Byzia, or Viza, of which Constantinople is the capital. The Turks bestow the name of Romelia on all the territories they possess in Europe.

ROMANO

Pages 427-428

a famous painter, was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Raphael, who had such an affection for him, that he appointed him, with John Francis Penni, his heir. His conceptions were more extraordinary and more elevated than even those of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, but not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. He was wonderful in the choice of attitudes; but did not perfectly understand the lights and shades, and is frequently harsh and ungraceful. The folds of his draperies, says Du Fresnoy, are neither beautiful nor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, ugly nor natural, but all extravagant, like the fantastic habits of comedians. He was, however, superior to most painters, by his profound knowledge of antiquity; and, by conversing with the works of the most excellent poets, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, he made himself master of the qualifications necessarily required in a great designer. Julio Romano was also well skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. He was employed by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> de Medicis, who was afterwards pope under the name of Clement VII.; and afterwards went to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>. Mantua, whither he was invited by Frederic Gonzaga, marquis of that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, in order to avoid his being justly punished for his having drawn at Rome the designs of 20 obscene plates, engraved by Mark Antony, to which Aretine added the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of sonnets. Julio Romano embellished the city of Mantua with many of his performances both in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and architecture; and died in that city in 1545, at 54 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, much regretted by the marquis, who had an extraordinary friendship for him.

ROME

Pages 428-434

a very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated on the river Tiber, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13°. N. Lat. 41°. 45'. once the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the greatest empire in the world; and famous in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> for being the centre of an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> tyranny, by which for many ages the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world was held in subjection. The ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> derived their original from Æneas the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERO">hero</a>: and though some historians pretend to treat his voyage into Italy as a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, yet no sufficient reasons for rejecting this account have been offered, nor has any more probable history of the origin of the Roman name been given; so that, without entering into the dispute, we shall proceed to the history of Æneas and his successors as they are recorded by the generality of Latin writers. When the Greeks, by the treachery of the sons of Antenor, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> by whatever other means it happened, were become masters of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, Æneas with the forces under his command retired into the fortresses of the city, and defended it bravely for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but yielding at length to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, he conveyed away his gods, his father, wife, and children, with everything he had that was valuable, and, followed by a numerous crowd of Trojans, fled to the strong places of mount Ida. Hither all those of his countrymen, who were more anxious than the rest to preserve their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, flocked to him from the several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Troas. His <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> thus augmented and advantageously posted, he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> quiet, waiting for the departure of the Greeks, who, it was imagined, would return home as soon as they had pillaged the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. But these, after they had enriched themselves with the spoils of Troy and of the neighbouring towns, turned their arms against the fugitives, resolving to attack them in their strong-holds upon the mountain. Æneas, to avoid the hazard of being forced in his last refuge, had recourse to negotiation; and, by his heralds, intreated the enemy not to constrain him to a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. Peace was granted him, on condition that he with his followers quitted the Trojan territories; and the Greeks, on their part, promised not to molest him in his retreat, but to let him safely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through any country within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of their domination. Upon this assurance Æneas equipped a fleet, in order to seek a settlement in some foreign <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>. We are told, that at his departure he left his eldest son <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASCANIUS">Ascanius</a> with the Dardanites, a people of Bithynia, who desired to have him for their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>; but that the young <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> did not remain long with them: for when Scamandrius (Altynax), with the rest of the Hebridae whom Neoptolemus permitted to return home from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, repaired to him, he put himself at their head, and led them back to their native country. The Trojan having crossed the Hellespont, arrived in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Pallene, where he built a city, called from him Æneia, and left in it a part of that multitude which had followed him. From thence he failed to Delos; and thence to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-CYTHERA">Cythera</a>, where he erected a temple to Venus. He built another to the same goddefs in Zacynthus, in which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> he likewise instituted games, called the races of Æneas and Venus: the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of both, says Dionysius, are standing to this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. In Leucas, where the Trojans landed, was to be seen in the same author's time, a temple erected to Venus the mother of Æneas. Nor were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIUM">Actium</a> and Ambracia without monuments that testified his arrival in those places. At <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a> were found brazen vases, upon which the name of the Trojan hero, who had made an offering of them to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, was engraven in old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. Not far from Buthrotos, in Epirus, a Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> which had escaped the injuries of time, retained the name of Troya. All these antiquities, still subsisting in the reign of Augustus, were then looked upon as indisputable proofs of Æneas's voyage to Epirus: "and that he came into Italy, (adds the same Dionysius) we have the concurrent testimony of all the Romans; the ceremonies they observe in their sacrifices and festivals bear witness to it, as also the Sibylline books, the Pythian <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a>, and many other things which nobody can reasonably reject as invented merely for ornament." The first land of Italy which Æneas made, after crossing the Ionian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, in Iapygia; and here he went on shore. Sailing afterwards from hence, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COASTING">coasting</a> along the south-east of Italy and the east and south sides of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, he arrived with his fleet either by choice or stress of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> at the port of Drepanum in that island. Elymus and Ægeletus who had escaped from Troy a little before him, had brought a Trojan colony to this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Æneas augmented it by a good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his followers, whom, pleased to have found a safe resting place after many dangers and fatiguing voyages, he willingly left behind him at their request; though certain authors pretend that he was constrained to it by the difficulty of transporting them, because some Trojan women, weary of the sea, had burnt a considerable part of his ships. Æneas, leaving Drepanum, steered his course for Italy across the Tyrrhenian sea. To the cape where he first landed, he gave the name Palinurus, from one of his pilots who died there. The little island of Leucasia, not far distant, whither he sailed next, got its name in like manner from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Æneas's sister, who there ended her days. The port of Mitenum, the island of Prochyta, and the promontory of Cajeta, where he successively arrived, were so called from being the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-places, the first of a noble Trojan his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of his kinswoman, and the third of his nurse. At length the Trojan prince and his chosen band finished their tedious and painful voyages on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the since famous Latium. This was a small land in territory on the east side of the river Tiber, containing a part of the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> di Roma: <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LATINUS">Latinus</a> was the king of it; his capital town, Laurentum; his subjects, a people who, till his time called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABORIGINES">Aborigines</a>, had from him taken the name of Latins. Here, far removed from their implacable enemies the Greeks, Æneas and his followers undertook to raise a second Troy: they fortified a camp near the mouth of the Tyber, While Æneas was thus employed, the Rutuli, ancient enemies of the Latin name, entering into an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with Mezentius king of the Tyrrhenians, took the field with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to drive out those new-comers, of whose power they began to conceive no small jealousy. Æneas marched out against them at the head of his Trojans and Latins. Hereupon a battle ensued, which lasted till night; when Æneas being pushed to the banks of the Numicus, which ran <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAVINIUM">Lavinium</a>, and forced into that river, was there drowned. The Trojans concealed his body; and pretending that he had vanished away on a sudden, made him pass for a deity among his credulous subjects, who accordingly erected a temple to him under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Jupiter Indiges. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Æneas, his son Euryleon, called Succeeding also Afcanius and Iulus, ascended the throne; but as by his son the young king did not think it advisable to venture a battle in the very beginning of his reign, with a formidable enemy, who promised himself <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success from the death of Æneas, he had the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> to confine himself within the walls of Lavinium, and to try whether he could, by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, put an end to so dangerous a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>. But the haughty Mezentius demanding of the Latins, as one of the conditions of a peace, that they should pay him yearly, by way of tribute, all the wine produced in the territory of Latium, Afcanius rejected the proposal with the utmost indignation; and having caused all the vines throughout his dominions to be consecrated to Jupiter, and by that means put it out of his power to comply with the enemy's request, he resolved to make a vigorous sally, and try whether he could, by force of arms, bring the insulting Tyrrhenian to more reasonable terms. The main body of the enemy's army was encamped at some distance from Lavinium; but Laufus, the son of Mezentius, with the flower of their youth under his command, lay entrenched at the very gates of the city. The Trojans, who had been long accustomed to make vigorous sallies, marching out in the night, attacked the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a> where Laufus commanded, forced his intrenchments, and obliged the troops he had with him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> themselves by flight to the main body of the army encamped on the plain; but the unexpected arrival and overthrow of their advance-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> struck them with such feats the terror, that, instead of stopping the flight of their companions, they fled with them, in great disorder, to the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The Latins pursued them, and in the pursuit Laufus was killed: whose death so discouraged Mezentius, that he immediately sued for peace; which was granted him, upon condition, that for the future the Tiber should be the boundary between the Latin and Hetrurian territories. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time Lavinia, who had been left with His kind-child by Æneas, entertaining a strong jealousy of the ambition of her son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, retired to the woods, and her son, was there peaceably delivered of a son, who, from his father, was named Æneas, and, from the place of his birth, had the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Sylius: but as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s flight, who had disappeared on a sudden, raised suspicions at Lavinium prejudicial to the reputation of Afcanius, he used all possible means to remove them, caused diligent search to be made after Lavinia, calmed her fears, and prevailed upon her to return to the town with her son, whom he ever after treated as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>. Lavinium grew every day more populous; but as it was in reality the patrimony of Lavinia, and the inheritance of her son Sylvius, Ascanius resolved to resign it to them, and build elsewhere another city for himself. This he made the place of his residence, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a> capital of his new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, calling it Alba Longa; Alba, from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> sow, which we are told Æneas had found in the place where it was built; and Longa, to distinguish it from another town of the same name in the country of the Marsi; or rather, because it extended, without having much breadth, the whole length of a lake near which it was built. It was 30 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of Lavinium, that Ascanius fixed his abode at Alba; and there he died, after a reign of about 38 years, 12 of which he had resided at his new settlement. He left a son called Iulus; so that between him and Sylvius lay the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of succession to the Latin throne; the latter being the son, and the former the grandchild, of Æneas. The Latins not thinking it their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to continue divided, as it were, into two states, resolved to unite Alba and Lavinium into one sovereignty; and as Sylvius was born of Lavinia the daughter of Latinus, and had thereby an undoubted title to the kingdom of his grandfather, whereas the other was but the son of a stranger, the Latins bestowed the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on Sylvius; and, to make Iulus some amends, decreed to him the sovereign power in affairs of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; a power which thenceforth continued in his family. Sylvius was succeeded by 13 kings of the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a>, who for near 400 years reigned at Alba; but we scarce know anything of them besides their names, and the years of their respective reigns. Æneas Sylvius died, after a reign of 29 years. His son, called also Æneas Sylvius, governed Latium 31 years. Latinus Sylvius, who succeeded him, swayed the sceptre for the space of 51 years. Alba reigned 39; Capetus, by Livy named Atys, 26; Capis, 28; and Capetus, 13. Tiberinus, who succeeded him, engaged in a war which proved fatal to him; for in a battle which was fought on the banks of the Albula, he was forced into that river and drowned. From him the river took the name of Tiber, which it has borne ever since. Agrippa succeeded Tiberinus, after a reign of eight years; and left the throne, which he had held 41 years, to Alladius; who reigned 19, and was succeeded by Aventinus, who left his name to the hill Aventinus, where he was interred. Procas, who succeeded him, and reigned 23 years, was the father of Numitor and Amulius; and at his death, bequeathed the throne to his elder son Numitor. But Amulius, who surpassed his brother in courage and understanding, drove him from the throne; and to secure it to himself, murdered Ægeus, Numitor's only son, and consecrated his daughter Rhea Sylvia to the worship of Vesta, by which she was obliged to perpetual virginity. But this precaution proved insufficient; for as the Veletai was going to a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> to fetch <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> for the performance of a sacrifice to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, she was met and ravished by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, like that in which the god Mars is represented. Some authors think that this counterfeit Mars was a lover come thither by her appointment; others <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> Amulius himself with using this violence to his niece, not so much to gratify his lust, as to have a pretence to destroy her. For ever after he caused her to be carefully watched, till she was delivered of two sons; and then exaggerating her crime in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the people, he prevailed upon them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> her to death, and to condemn the fruit of her criminal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a> to be thrown into the Tiber. The sentence against Rhea was, according to some authors, changed by Amulius, at the request of his daughter Antro, into perpetual confinement, but executed against the twins; who being laid in a wooden trough, and carried to the foot of mount Palatine, were there turned adrift on the Tiber, which at that time overflowed its banks. But the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and stream proved both so favourable, that at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the water the two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> were left safe on the strand, and there happily found by Faustulus, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the king's shepherds, and suckled by his wife Acca Laurentia, who for her disorderly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was called Lupa; and this probably gave rise to the fabulous miracle of their being nursed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>. As Faustulus was probably well acquainted with the birth of the twins, he took more than ordinary care of their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and sent them to Gabii to be instructed there in Greek literature. As they grew up, they appeared to have something great in their mien and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> which commanded respect; and the ascendant which they assumed over the other shepherds, made them dreaded in the forests, where they exercised a sort of empire. A quarrel happening between the herdsmen of Amulius and those of Numitor, the two brothers took the part of the former against the latter; and some blood being shed in the fray, the adverse party to be revenged on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> and Remus (for so the twins were called), on the festival of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUPERCALIA">Lupercalia</a>, surprized Remus, and carried him before Numitor, to be punished according to his deserts. But Numitor feeling himself touched in the prisoner's favour, asked him where he was born, and who were his parents. His answer immediately struck Numitor with a lively <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of his two grandsons; their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, which was about 18 years, agreed with the time when the two infants were exposed upon the Tiber; and there needed no more to change his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> into tenderness. In the mean time Romulus, eager to rescue his brother, and pursue those who had carried him off, was preparing to be revenged on them; but Faustulus dissuaded him from it, and, on that occasion, disclosing to him his birth, awakened in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> sentiments worthy of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. He resolved, at all adventures, to attempt the delivering of his mother and grandfather from oppression. With this view, he assembled the country people, over whom he had assumed a kind of sovereignty, and engaged them to come to the city on an appointed day, and enter it by different gates, provided with arms, which they were to conceal. While Romulus was thus disposing everything for the execution of his design, Numitor made the same discovery to Remus concerning his parents, and the oppressions they groaned under; which so fired him, that he was ready to embark in any enterprise. But Numitor took care to moderate the transports of his grandson, and only desired him to acquaint his brother with what he had heard from him, and to send him to his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Romulus soon came, and was followed by Faustulus, who took with him the trough or skiff in which the twins had been exposed, to show it to Numitor; but, as the shepherd betrayed an air of concern and earnestness in his looks, he was stopped at the gate of the city, led before Amilius, and examined concerning his burden. It was easily known by its make and inscription, which was still legible; and therefore Faustus owned what it was, and confessed that the twins were living; but, in order to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> time, pretended that they were feeding flocks in a remote defart. In the mean time, the usurper's death being resolved on, Remus undertook to raise the city, and Romulus to invest the king's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. The country people came at the time appointed, and formed themselves into companies each consisting of 100 men. They had no other ensigns but bundles of hay hanging upon long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, which the Latins at that time called manipuli; and hence came the name of manipulares, originally given to troops raised in the country. With this tumultuous army Romulus beset the avenues of the palace, forced the guard, and having killed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, after he had reigned 42 years, restored his grandfather Numitor to the throne. Affairs being thus settled at Alba, the two brothers, by the advice of Numitor, undertook the founding of a new colony. The king bestowed on them those lands near the Tiber where they had been brought up, supplied them with all manner of instruments for breaking up ground, with slaves, and beasts of burden, and granted full liberty to his subjects to join them. Hereupon most of the Trojans, of whom there still remained 50 families in Augustus's time, chose to follow the fortune of Romulus and Remus, as did also the inhabitants of Pallantium and Suturnia, two small towns. For the more speedy carrying on of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, it was thought proper to divide those who were to be employed in the building of the city into two companies, one under the command of Romulus, the other of Remus; but this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, which was designed purely with a view to the public welfare, and that the two parties might work by way of emulation, gave birth to two factions, and produced a jealousy between the two brothers, which broke out when they came to choose a place for the building of their new city; for Remus was for the Aventine, and Romulus for the Palatine mount. Upon which, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> being referred to their grandfather, he advised the contending parties to have recourse to the gods, and to put an end to the dispute by augury, to which he was himself greatly addicted. The day appointed for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> being come, the brothers posted themselves each upon his hill; and it was agreed, that whoever should see the first flight, or the greatest number, of vultures, should gain his cause. After the two rivals had waited some time for the appearance of a favourable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>, Romulus, before any had appeared, sent to acquaint his brother, that he had seen some vultures; but Remus, having actually seen six, while his brother's messengers were yet on their way, hastened, on their arrival, to mount Palatine, to examine the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of what they had told him. He had no sooner got thither, than by an unexpected <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> twelve vultures appeared to Romulus. These he immediately showed to his brother; and, transported with joy, desired him to judge himself of the truth of what his messengers had told him. However, Remus discovered the deceit; and, being told that Romulus had not seen the twelve vultures still after he had seen six, he insisted on the time of his seeing them, and the other on the number of birds he had seen. This widened the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> between the two brothers; and, their parties being divided, while each man espoused the cause of his leader, the dispute grew so warm, that, from words they came at length to blows. The shepherd Faustulus, who was equally dear to both the brothers, endeavouring to part the combatants, was, by an unknown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, laid dead on the spot. Some writers tell us, that Remus likewise lost his life in the fray; but the greater number place his death later, and say that he was killed by one Fabius, for having, in derision, leaped over the wall of the new city: but Livy says, the more <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> report was, that Remus fell by the hand of his brother. Romulus, being now head of the colony, by having got the better of his brother's party in the late engagement, applied his thoughts wholly to the building of Rome, the city, which he proposed to call after his own name. He chose mount Palatine for its situation, and performed all those ceremonies which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ETRUSCANS">Etruscans</a> had introduced. He first offered sacrifices to the gods, and ordered all the people to do the same: and, from that time decreed, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a> should be the auspices of his new colony. After this, great fires were kindled before their tents, and all the people leaped through the flames to purify themselves. When this ceremony was over, they dug a trench round the spot where the assemblies of the people were afterwards held, and threw into it the first-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of whatever they were allowed to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for food: every man of the colony was ordered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into the same trench a handful of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, brought either from his own, or some neighbouring country. The trench they called Mundus, that is, the world, and made it the centre round which the city was to be built. Then Romulus, yoking an ox and a cow to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, the coulter whereof was brafs, marked out, by a deep furrow, the whole compass of the city. These two animals, the symbols of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, by which cities are peopled, were afterwards slain upon the altar. All the people followed the plough, throwing inwards the clods of earth which the plough-share sometimes turned outwards. Wherever a gate was to be made, the plough was lifted up, and carried; and hence came the Latin word porta, "a gate," derived from the verb portare, "to carry." As mount Palatine stood by itself, the whole was inclosed within the line made by the plough, which formed almost the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; whence by Dionysius Halicarnassensis, it is called Roma Quadrata. As to the exact year of the foundation of Rome, there is a great disagreement among historians and chronologers. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FABIUS_PICTOR">Fabius Pictor</a>, the most ancient of all the Roman writers, places it in the end of the seventh Olympiad; that is, according to the computation of Usher, in the year of the world 3256, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> 1600, and 748 before the Christian era. The Romans, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may so call them, began to build, as Plutarch and others inform us, on the 21st of April; which day was then consecrated to Pales, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of the shepherds; whence the festival of Pales, and that of the foundation of the city, were afterwards jointly celebrated at Rome. At first but when Rome had received the utmost perfection a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> village which its poor and rude founder could give it, it con- fitted of about 1000 houses, or rather huts; and was, properly speaking, a beggarly village, whereof the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants followed the plough, being obliged to cultivate with their own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> the ungrateful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of a barren country which they had shared among themselves. Even the walls of Romulus's palace were made of rushes, and covered with thatch. As every one had chosen his ground to build upon, without any regard to the regularity and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the whole, the streets, if we may so call them, were both crooked and narrow. In short, Rome, till it was rebuilt after the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of it by the Gauls, was rather a disordered heap of huts, than a city built with any regularity or order. As soon as the building of the city was finished, Romulus assembled the people, and desired them to choose what kind of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> they would obey. At that electing time <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> was the unanimous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of the Romans, and Romulus was elected king. Before he ascended the throne, however, he consulted the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the gods by augury; and having received a favourable answer, it thence became an established <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to have recourse to augury before raising any one to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of king, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, or any public employment. After this he applied himself to the establishment of good order and subordination among his subjects. He put on a habit of distinction for himself, appointed 12 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LICTORS">lictors</a> to attend him as guards, divided his subjects, who at this time consisted only of 33,000 men, into curiae, decuriae, patricians, plebeians, patrons, clients, &c. for an account of which, see these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> as they occur in the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. After this he formed a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> consisting of 100 persons, chosen from among the patricians; and a guard of 300 young men called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CELEBES">celebes</a>, who attended the king, and fought either on foot or on horseback as occasion required. The king's office at home was to take care of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> affairs, to be the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of laws and customs; to decide the weightier causes between man and man, referring those of smaller moment to the senate; to call together the senators, and assemble the people, first delivering his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> concerning the affair he proposed, and then ratifying by his consent what was agreed on by the majority. Abroad, and in the time of war, he was to command the army with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> authority, and to take care of the public <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. The senate were not only to be judges in matters of small importance, but to debate and resolve upon such public affairs as the king proposed, and to determine them by a plurality of voices. The people were allowed to create magistrates, enact laws, and resolve upon any war which the king proposed; but in all these things the consent of the senate was necessary. Romulus next proceeded to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the religious affairs of his people. Many of the Trojan and Phrygian deities were added to those whom the Aborigines or Italian natives already worshipped. He chose priests, instituted festivals, and laid the foundation of a regular system of religion; after which, as his colony was still thinly peopled, he opened an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> for fugitive slaves, homicides, outlaws, and debtors. These, however, he did not at first receive within the walls, but appointed for their habitation the hill Saturnius called afterwards Capitolinus, on which he erected a temple to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, whom he named the Aylean god, under whose protection all criminals were to live securely. But afterwards, when the city was enlarged, the asylum was inclosed within the walls, and those who dwelt in it included among the citizens of Rome. When Romulus had thus settled everything relating to his new colony, it was found that a supply of women were wanting to perpetuate its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. This occasioned some difficulty; for the neighbouring nations refused to give their daughters in marriage to such a crew of vagabonds as had settled in Rome; wherefore Romulus at last resolved on the following expedient. By the advice of his grandfather Numitor, and with the consent of the senate, he proclaimed a solemn feast and public games in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Equestrian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> called Consus. This occasioned a great concourse of people, who flocked from the adjacent parts to behold these pompous shows together with the new city. But, in the midst of the solemnity, the Romans, rushing in with their swords drawn, seized all the young women, to the number of 683, for whom Romulus chose husbands. Among all those who were thus seized, only one married woman, named Herfilia, was found; and Romulus is said to have kept her for himself. This violence soon brought on a war with the neighbouring nations. Acron king of Caenina, a city on the confines of Latium, having entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> with the inhabitants of Crutuminiun and Antemnes, invaded the Roman territories. Romulus marched against them without delay, defeated the confederate army, killed their king in single <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, decreed himself a triumph, and consecrated the spoils of Acron to Jupiter Feretrius, under the name of Opima Spolia. The city of Caenina was razed to the ground, and the inhabitants transplanted to Rome, where they were admitted to the privileges of citizens. The king then marched with one legion (consisting at this time of 3000 foot and 300 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>) against the Crutuminiun and Antemnates, both of whom he defeated in battle, and transplanted the inhabitants to Rome; which being incapable of holding such a number, Romulus took in the hill Saturnius abovementioned, on the largest top of which he built a citadel, committing the care of it to a noble Roman named Tarpeius. The citadel was surrounded on all sides with ramparts and towers, which equally commanded the city and country. From the foot of the hill Saturnius a wall was carried quite to the Tiber, and a gate opened in it named Carmentalis, from Carmenta the mother of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVANDER">Evander</a>, who either lived there, or had some chapel or altar erected to her. Romulus had now become so formidable to his neighbours, and had so well established his reputation for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>, that several cities of Etruria voluntarily submitted to him. Caelius, an Etrurian general, led the troops under his command to Rome, and settled on a hill near the city, which from him took the name of Mount Caelius. The Sabines, however, not in the least dismayed at this increase of the Roman forces, sent a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a> to Romulus, demanding restitution of the young women who had been carried off; and, upon his refusal, marched to Rome with an army of 25,000 foot and 1000 horse, under the command of Invasion of their king Titus Tatius. Romulus, having received the Sabines' supplies supplies from Numitor and from Hetruria, likewise took the field with 20,000 foot and 800 horse, with whom he seized an advantageous post, and fortified himself so strongly that he could not be attacked. The Sabine monarch, perceiving the military skill of Romulus, began to be apprehensive of the event; but was extricated out of his difficulties by the treachery of Tarpeia daughter to the governor of the citadel, who agreed to betray that important fortress to the enemy, on condition of being rewarded with the bracelets which the Sabines wore on their left arms. But when once they became masters of this important place, they are said to have crushed Tarpeia under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of their bucklers, pretending that thus they discharged their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, as they wore their bucklers also on their left arms. The possession of the citadel enabled the Sabines to carry on the war with more success; but, at last, in a general engagement, they had the misfortune to be driven back into the citadel, whither they were pursued by the Romans, who expected to have retaken that important post; but the enemy, rolling <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> from the top of the hill, wounded Romulus on the head, so that he was carried insensible out of the field of battle, while in the meantime his troops were repulsed, and pursued to the very gates of Rome. However, the king soon recovering himself, encouraged his routed troops, and drove the enemy back into the citadel. But while the two nations were thus fiercely contending, the women, for whose cause the war had been commenced, undertook the office of mediators; and having obtained leave from the senate, marched in a body to the camp of the Sabines, where they pleaded the cause of their husbands so effectually, that a treaty of union between the two nations was set on foot, and a peace was at last concluded on the following terms. 1. That the two kings should reside and reign jointly at Rome. 2. That the city should still, from Romulus, be called Rome; but the inhabitants Quirites, a name till then peculiar to the Sabines. 3. That the two nations should become one; and that the Sabines should be made free in Rome, and enjoy all the privileges of Roman citizens. As Rome was chiefly indebted for this increase of her power and splendor to the Sabine women, honourable privileges and marks of distinction were allowed them. Every one was commanded to give way to them; in capital causes they were exempted from the jurisdiction of the ordinary judges; and their children were allowed to wear a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a> hanging from their necks, and a particular kind of robe called praetexta, to distinguish them from the vulgar. The two kings reigned with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> for the space of five years; during which time the only military exploit they accomplished was the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the city of Cameria, at a small distance from Rome. Four thousand of the Camerini were transplanted to Rome, and a Roman colony sent to repopulate Cameria; soon after which the Sabine king was murdered by the Lavinians, on account of his granting protection to some of his friends who had ravaged their territories. The Lavinians, fearing the resentment of Romulus, delivered up the assassins into his hands; but he sent them back unpunished, which gave occasion to suspect that he was not displeased with the death of his colleague. Soon after the death of Tatius, Rome was afflicted with famine and pestilence, which encouraged the Camerini to revolt; but Romulus marching against them suddenly, defeated them with the loss of 600 men. After which he attacked the Fidenates, whose city stood about five miles from Rome, took their capital, and made it a Roman colony. This drew upon him the resentment of the Veientes, a powerful <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> in the neighbourhood, who claimed Fidene as within their jurisdiction; but their forces being defeated in two engagements, and a great number of them taken prisoners, they were obliged to sue for peace. Romulus granted them a truce for 100 years, on condition that they delivered to him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> small towns on the Tiber, together with some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-pits near the mouth of that river, and send 50 of their chief citizens as hostages to Rome. The prisoners taken in this war were all sold for slaves. The remaining part of the life of Romulus was spent in making laws for the good of his people; but towards the latter end of his reign, being elated with success, he began to enlarge the bounds formerly set to his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, and to behave in an arbitrary manner. He paid no longer any regard to the voice of the senate, but assembled them only for form's sake to ratify his commands. The senate therefore conspired to destroy him, and accomplished their purpose while he was reviewing his troops. A violent storm of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> dispersed the army; and the senators taking this opportunity, when they were left alone with the king, instantly killed him, and conveyed his body out of sight. Some writers tell us, that, the better to conceal the fact, they cut his body in pieces, each of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> carrying away a part under his robe; after which they told the multitude that their king was on a sudden surrounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, and snatched up into heaven. This stratagem, however, did not satisfy the soldiery, and violent disturbances were about to ensue, when Julius Proculus, a senator of great distinction, having assembled the Curiae, told them that Romulus had appeared to him, and enjoined him to acquaint the people, that their king was returned to the gods from whom he originally came, but that he would continue to be propitious to them under the name of Quirinus; and to the truth of this story Julius swore. Romulus reigned, according to the common computation, 37 years; but some historians reduce the length of his reign to little more than 17; it being very unlikely, as they observe, that a prince of such an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> disposition should perform nothing worthy of record during a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of 20 years. Be this as it will, his death however, the death of Romulus was followed by an interregnum, during which the senators, to prevent anarchy and confusion, took the government into their own hands. Tatius added another hundred to that body; and these 200 senators divided themselves into decuries or tens. These decuries drew lots which should govern first; and the decury to whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> fell, enjoyed the supreme authority for five days; yet in such a manner, that one person only of the governing decury had the ensigns of sovereignty at a time. To these another decury succeeded, each of them fitting on the throne in his turn, &c. But the people soon growing weary of such frequent change of masters, obliged the senate to resolve on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of a king. The senate referred the election to the people, and the people to the senate, who at last undertook the task. Some difficulties, however, occurred; the Romans did not choose to be subject to a Sabine; and the Sabines, as they had been subject to Romulus after the death of Tatus, insisted that the king should be chosen out of their nation. At last it was agreed, that the king should be a Sabine, but that the Romans should make the choice. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this determination, the Romans elected Numa Pompilius, an austere <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, who had married Tatia, the daughter of Tatus the late king. After the death of his wife, he gave himself entirely up to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and superstition, wandering from solitude to solitude, in search of sacred woods and fountains, which gave the people a great opinion of his sanctity. The philosopher at first rejected the offer of the kingdom; but being at last prevailed upon, he set out for Rome, where he was received with loud acclamations, and had his election unanimously confirmed by the senate.

ROME

Pages 515-534

Rome, was Naples. The crowds there were so great, and the curiosity of the people so carried in hearing him, that they did not perceive an earthquake that happened while he was singing. His desire of gaining the superiority over the other actors was truly ridiculous: he made intercess with his judges, reviled his competitors, formed private factions to support him, all in imitation of those who got their livelihood upon the stage. While he continued to perform, no man was permitted to depart from the theatre, upon any pretence whatsoever. Some were so fatigued with hearing him, that they leaped privately from the walls, or pretended to fall into fainting fits, in order to be carried out. Nay, it is said, that several women were delivered in the theatre. Soldiers were placed in several parts to observe the looks and gestures of the spectators, either to direct them where to point their applause, or restrain their displeasure. An old senator, named Vespasian, afterwards emperor, happening to fall asleep upon one of these occasions, very narrowly escaped with his life. After being fatigued with the praises of his countrymen, Nero resolved upon going over into Greece, to receive new theatrical honours. The occasion was this. The cities of Greece had made a law to send him the crowns from all the games; and deputies were accordingly dispatched with this (to him) important embassy. As he one day entertained them at his table in the most sumptuous manner, and conversed with them with the utmost familiarity, they treated to hear him sing. Upon his complying, the artful Greeks testified all the marks of ecstasy and rapture. Applauses so warm, were peculiarly pleasing to Nero: he could not refrain from crying out, That the Greeks alone were worthy to hear him; and accordingly prepared without delay to go into Greece, where he spent the whole year ensuing. In this journey, his retinue resembled an army in number; but it was only composed of singers, dancers, tailors, and other attendants upon the theatre. He passed over all Greece, and exhibited at all their games, which he ordered to be celebrated in one year. At the Olympic games he resolved to show the people something extraordinary; wherefore, he drove a chariot with ten horses: but being unable to sustain the violence of the motion, he was driven from his seat. The spectators, however, gave their unanimous applause, and he was crowned as conqueror. In this manner he obtained the prize at the Isthmian, Pythian, and Nemean games. The Greeks were not sparing of their crowns; he obtained 1800 of them. An unfortunate finger happened to oppose him on one of these occasions, and exerted all the powers of his art, which, it appears, were prodigious. But he seems to have been a better finger than a politician; for Nero ordered him to be killed on the spot. Upon his return from Greece, he entered Naples, through a breach in the walls of the city, as was customary with those who were conquerors in the Olympic games. But all the splendor of his return was reserved for his entry into

ROME

Pages 533-552

Rome, where the most magnificent preparations were made for his arrival. However, he had not got farther than the province of Cilicia, when he found himself too weak to proceed in his usual manner. He therefore caused himself to be carried on ship-board to the city of Seleucia, where he died of the apoplexy, having been attacked by that disorder once before. During the time of his indisposition, his wife Plotina constantly attended near him; and, knowing the emperor's dislike to Adrian, it is thought forged the will, by which he was adopted to succeed. Trajan died in the 63rd year of his age, after a reign of nineteen years six months and fifteen days.
