in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> chiefly applied to the circumvolution of any surface round a fixed and immoveable line, which is called the axis of its rotation: and by such rotations it is that solids are conceived to be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a>.

ROTHERAM

Pages 569-569

a town in the West Riding of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a>, near which there is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. It is a well-built <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the market is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 10. N. Lat. 53. 25.

ROTHSAY

Pages 569-569

a town in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Bute, of which it is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. It is a well-built town of small houses, and about 200 families; and is within these few years much improved. It has a good pier, and is seated at the bottom of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, whose mouth lies exactly opposite to Loch Steven in Cowal. Here is a fine depth of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, a secure retreat, and a ready <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the Frith for an export trade. Magazines.

ROUEN

Pages 569-570

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Normandy, with an archbishop's see, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, a mint, a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, an academy, two abbeys, and an old castle. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles in circumference, and surrounded with six suburbs; and contains 35 parishes, and 24 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> for men and women. The metropolitan <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> has a very handsome <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, on which are two lofty steeples, whence there is a fine view of the town and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELL">bell</a> is 13 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and 11 in diameter. The church of the Benedictine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> is much admired by travellers. The parliament-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is adorned with beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a> and fine pictures. There are a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fountains, though the houses are ordinary; but the walk upon the quay is very pleasant, and there are 13 gates from thence into the city. The number of the inhabitants are about 60,000, and they have several woollen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>; and the tide rises so high, that vessels of 200 tons may come up to the quay: but one of the greatest curiosities is the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of 270 paces in length, supported by boats, and consequently is higher <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> lower according to the tide. It is paved, and there are ways for foot-passengers on each side, with benches to sit upon; and coaches may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over it at any <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> or night. It is often called Rouen by English historians; and is 50 miles south-west of Amiens, and 70 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 10. N. Lat. 49. 26.

ROUERGUE

Pages 570-570

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Guienne; bounded on the east by the Cévennes and Gévaudan, on the west by Quercy, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the same and Auvergne, and on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>. It is 75 miles in length, and 50 in breadth; not very fertile, but feeds a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cattle, and has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, vitriol, and sulphur. It is divided into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, and the upper and lower marche. Rhodez is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

ROUNDELAY

Pages 571-571

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poem, thus termed, according to Menage, from its form; because it turns back again to the first <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, and thus goes round. This poem is little known among us; but is very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among the French, who call it rondeau. It consists <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of 13 verses, eight whereof are in one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHYME">rhyme</a>, and five in another. It is divided into couplets; at the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third whereof, the beginning of the roundelay is repeated, and that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible, in an equivocal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> pausing tenne.

ROUSSILLON

Pages 571-571

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, in the Pyrenees, bounded on the east by the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, on the west by Cerdagne, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, and on the south by Catalonia, from which it is separated by the Pyrenees. It is a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, about 50 miles in length and 25 in breadth, and remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of olive-trees. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERPIGNAN">Perpignan</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

ROUTE

Pages 572-572

a public <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-way, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> course, especially that which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> forces take. This word is also used for the defeat and flight of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>.

ROVERE

Pages 570-570
or Roveredo, a strong town of the Tyrol, on the confines of the republic of Venice; seated on the river Adige, at the foot of a mountain, and on the side of a stream, over which there is a bridge, defended by two large towers and a strong castle, 10 miles south of Trent. E. Long. 11. 1. N. Lat. 46. 12.

ROVIGNO

Pages 570-571

a populous town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in Istria, with two good harbours, and quarries of fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. It is seated in a territory which produces excellent wine, in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on the western <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 53. N. Lat. 45. 14. ROUND <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, a kind of prison for the nightly watch in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> to secure disorderly persons till they can be carried before a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUND_HOUSE">Round-House</a>, in a ship, the uppermost room, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> cabin on the stern of a ship where the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> lies. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUNDS">Rounds</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> matters, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> from the main-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, of an officer or a non-commissioned officer and six men, who go round the rampart of a garrison, to listen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any thing be stirring without the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and to see that the sentinels be diligent upon their duty, and all in order. In strict garrisons the rounds go every half-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. The sentinels are to challenge at a distance, and to rest their arms as the round passes. All guards turn out, challenge, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> the parole, and rest their arms, &c. Rounds are ordinary and extraordinary. The ordinary rounds are three; the town-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>'s round, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-round, and the visiting round. Manner of going the Rounds. When the town-major goes his round, he comes to the main-guard, and demands a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a> and four or six men to escort him to the next guard; and when it is dark, one of the men is to carry a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. As soon as the sentry at the guard perceives the round coming, he shall give notice to the guard, that they may be ready to turn out when ordered; and when the round is advanced within about 20 or 30 paces of the guard, he is to challenge briskly; and when he is answered by the sergeant who attends the round, Town-major's round, he is to say, Stand round! and rest his arms; after which he is to call out immediately, Sergeant, turn out the guard, town-major's round. Upon the sentry calling, the sergeant is to turn out the guard immediately, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up the men in good order with shouldered arms, the officer placing himself at the head of it, with his arms in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. He then orders the sergeant and four or six men to advance toward the round, and challenge; the sergeant of the round is to answer, Town-major's round; upon which the sergeant of the guard replies, Advance, sergeant, with the parole! at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> ordering his men to rest their arms. The sergeant of the round advances alone, and gives the sergeant of the guard the parole in his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, that none else may hear it; during which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the sergeant of the guard holds the spear of his halbert at the other's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. The sergeant of the round then returns to his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>, whilst the sergeant of the guard leaving his men to keep the round from advancing, gives the parole to his officer. This being found <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, the officer orders his sergeant to return to his men; says, Advance, town-major's round! and orders the guard to rest their arms; upon which the sergeant of the guard orders his men to wheel back from the centre, and form a lane, through which the town-major is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> (the escort remaining where they were), and go up to the officer and give him the parole, laying his mouth to his ear. The officer holds the spear of his espontoon at the town-major's breast while he gives him the parole. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of rounds is not only to visit the guards, and keep the sentinels alert; but likewise to discover what passes in the outworks, and beyond them.

ROWE

Pages 572-572

an English lady, eminent for her excellent writings both in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ILCHESTER">Ilchester</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a> in 1647, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of worthy parents, Mr Walter Singer and Mrs Elisabeth Portneil. She received the first serious impressions of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> as soon as she was capable of it. There being a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, this lady, who had a vein for the one, naturally had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for the other. She was also very fond of music; chiefly of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and solemn kind, as best suited to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of her sentiments, and the sublimity of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. But poetry was her favourite employment, her distinguishing excellence. So prevalent was her genius this way, that her prose is all poetical. In 1696, a collection of her poems was published at the desire of two friends. Her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> on the xxxviith <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOB">Job</a>, was written at the request of bishop Ken. She had no other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> for the French and Italian languages, than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Mr Thynne, who willingly took the task upon himself. Her shining merit, with the charms of person and conversation, had procured her a great many admirers. Among others, it is said, the famous Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a> made his addresses to her. But Mr Thomas Rowe was to be the happy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> was honourably descended; and his superior genius, and insatiable thirst after knowledge, were conspicuous in his earliest years. He had formed a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to compile the lives of all the illustrious persons in antiquity omitted by Plutarch; which indeed he partly executed. Eight lives were published since his decease. They were translated into French by the abbe Bellenger in 1734. He spoke with ease and fluency; had a frank and benevolent temper, an inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and a communicative disposition. Such was the man, who, charmed with the person, character, and writings, of our authoress, married her in 1710; and made it his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> to repay the felicity with which she crowned his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Too intense an application to study, beyond what the delicacy of his frame would bear, broke his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and threw him into a consumption; which put a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to his valuable life in 1715, when he was but <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> past the 28th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Mrs Rowe wrote a beautiful elegy on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to the last moments of her life to express the highest veneration and affection for his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. As soon after his decease as her affairs would permit, she indulged her inclination to solitude, by retiring to Frome in Somersetshire, in the neighbourhood of which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of her estate lay. In this recess it was that she composed the most celebrated of her works, Friendship in Death, and the Letters Moral and Entertaining. She had been favoured with an uncommon strength of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; owing much, no doubt, to her exact <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> and calmness of mind, till about half a year before her decease, when she was attacked by a dangerous distemper. Yet she got the better of it, and recovered her usual health for some months; till one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> she was seized with an apoplexy, and expired in 1737.

ROWEL

Pages 572-572

among farriers, a kind of issue answering to what in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a> is called a feton. See FARRIERY, § xxii.

ROWLEY

Pages 572-572

who stands in the third class of dramatic writers, lived in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Char. I. and received his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the university of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>: but whether he took any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> there, is not evident; there being but few particulars preserved in regard to him, more than his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> intimacy and connection with all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> wits and poetical geniuses of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, by whom he was well beloved, and with some of whom he joined in their writings.—Wood styles him, "the ornament, for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and ingenuity, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in Cambridge."—In a word, he was a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> benefactor to the English stage, having, exclusive of his aid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENT">lent</a> to Middleton, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">Day</a>, Heywood, Webster, &c. left us five plays of his own composing, and one in which even the immortal Shakspere afforded him some assistance.

ROXBURGH-SHIRE

Pages 572-573
or TEVIOTDALE, a county of Scotland, deriving its name from the town of Roxburgh, which is now destroyed, and the river Teviot, that runs through the shire into the Tweed, is divided into the three districts of Teviotdale, Liddisdale, and Eskdale or Ewesdale, so called from their respective rivers, Teviot, Liddel, and Esk. It is bounded on the east and south-east by Northumberland and Cumberland, on the south and south-west by Annandale, on the west by Tweeddale; on the north by the Merse and Lauderdale; extending about 30 miles from east to west, and about 15 in breadth from the border of England to the blue Cairn in Lauder-moor. The shire exhibits a rough irregular appearance of hills, moors, and Roxburgh and mountains, interspersed however with narrow valleys, and watered with delightful streams. Though the face of the country is bare of woods, the valleys yield plenty of corn, and the hills abound with pasture for sheep and black cattle. The principal mountains of this country are known by the name of Cocklaw; from whence a range of very high hills runs westward, dividing Scotland from England. On the confines of this shire are the debateable lands; the property of which was formerly disputed by the Scots and English borderers, but adjudged to the Scots at the union of the crowns. Roxburghshire yields plenty of lime and freestone, which in former times was freely used by the inhabitants in building castles to defend them from the invasions of their English neighbours. The most distinguished families in this county are the Scots and Kers, who raised themselves to wealth and honours by their bravery and success in a sort of predatory war with their enemies of South Britain. The shire is very populous; and the people are stout and valiant. They were formerly inured to military discipline and all the dangers of war, by living on dry marches contiguous to those of England; being so numerous and alert, that this, and the neighbouring shire of Berwick, could in 24 hours produce 10,000 men on horseback, well armed and accoutred. In the shire of Roxburgh, we still meet with a great number of old castles and seats belonging to private gentlemen, whose ancestors signalized themselves in this manner; and we find the remains of old encampments, and a Roman military way, vulgarly called the causeway, running from Hauum to the Tweed. The principal town called Roxburgh, giving the title of duke to the chief of the Kers, was anciently a royal borough, containing divers parishes, large and flourishing, defended by a strong citadel, which was often alternately reduced by the English and Scots adventurers. It was in besieging this castle that James II. of Scotland lost his life by the bursting of a cannon. In consequence of the almost continual wars between the two nations, this fortress was razed, the town ruined, and its royalty translated to Jedburgh, which is now a royal borough, situated between the Teyf and Jed.

ROXENT-CAPE

Pages 573-573
or Rock of Lisbon, a mountain and remarkable promontory in Portugal, situated in the Atlantic ocean, at the north entrance of the Tagus, 22 miles north of Lisbon.

ROYAL

Pages 573-575

something belonging to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>: thus we say, royal family, royal assent, royal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, &c. Royal Family. The first and most considerable branch of the king's royal family, regarded by the laws of England, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>. 1. The queen of England is either queen regent, queen consort, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> queen dowager. The queen regent, regnant, or sovereign, is she who holds the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> in her own <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; as the first (and perhaps the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>) queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, queen <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, and queen <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>; and such a one has the same powers, prerogatives, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, dignities, and duties, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she had been a king. This is expressly declared by statute 1 Mar. I. st. 3. c. 1. But the queen consort is the wife of the reigning king; and she by virtue of her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> is participant of diverse prerogatives above other women. And, first, she is a public person, exempt and distinct from the king; and not, like other married women, so closely connected as to have lost all legal or separate existence so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the marriage continues. For the queen is of ability to purchase lands and to convey them, to make <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> copyholds, and do other acts of ownership, without the concurrence of her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a>; which no other married woman can do: a privilege as old as the Saxon era. She is also capable of taking a grant from the king, which no other wife is from her husband; and in this particular she agrees with the Augusta, or piissima <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-REGINA">regina</a> conjux divi imperatoris of the Roman laws; who, according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>, was equally capable of making a grant to, and receiving one from, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. The queen of England hath separate courts and officers distinct from the king's, not only in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, but even of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and her attorney and solicitor general are intitled to a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> within the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of his majesty's courts, together with the king's counsel. She may likewise sue and be sued alone, without joining her husband. She may also have a separate <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in goods as well as lands, and has a right to dispose of them by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>. In short, she is in all legal proceedings looked upon as a feme sole, and not as a feme <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COVERT">covert</a>; as a single, not as a married woman. For which the reason given by Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> is this: because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law would not have the king (whose continual care and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> is for the public, and circa ardua regni), to be troubled and disquieted on account of his wife's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> affairs; and therefore it vests in the queen a power of tranfacting her own concerns, without the intervention of the king, as if she was an unmarried woman. The queen hath also many exemptions, and minute prerogatives. For instance: she pays no toll; nor is she liable to any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERCEMENT">amercement</a> in any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>. But in general, unless where the law has expressly declared her exempted, she is upon the same footing with other subjects; being to all intents and purposes the king's subject, and not his equal: in like manner as in the imperial law, Augustus legibus soluta non est. The queen hath also some pecuniary advantages, which form her a distinct revenue: as, in the first place, she is intitled to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> perquisite called queen-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, or aurum reginae; which is a royal revenue belonging to every queen-consort during her marriage with the king, and due from every person who hath made a voluntary offering or fine to the king, amounting to ten merks or upwards, for and in consideration of any privileges, grants, licences, pardons, or other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of royal favour conferred upon him by the king: and it is due in the proportion to one tenth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> more, over and above the entire offering or fine made to the king, and becomes an actual debt of record to the queen's majesty by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> recording of the fine. As, if 100 merks of silver be given to the king for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to take in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORTMAIN">mortmain</a>, or to have a fair, market, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARK">park</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, or free-warren: there the queen is intitled to 10 merks in silver, or (what was formerly an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> denomination) to one merk in gold, by the name of queen-gold, or aurum reginae. But no such payment is due for any aids or subsidies granted to the king in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>; or for fines imposed by courts on offenders against their will; nor for voluntary presents to the king, without any consideration moving from him. him to the subject; nor for any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> whereby the present revenues or possessions of the crown are granted away or diminished. The original revenue of our ancient queens, before and soon after the conquest, seems to have consisted in certain reservations or rents out of the demesne lands of the crown, which were expressly appropriated to her majesty, distinct from the king. It is frequent in domeday book, after specifying the rent due to the crown, to add likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of gold or other renders referred to the queen. These were frequently appropriated to particular purposes; to buy wood for her majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, to purchase <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> for lamps, or to furnish her attire from head to foot, which was frequently very costly, as one single robe in the fifth year of Henry II. stood the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in upwards of 80 pounds: A practice somewhat similar to that of the eastern countries, where whole cities and provinces were specifically assigned to purchase particular parts of the queen's apparel. And for a farther addition to her income, this duty of queen-gold is supposed to have been originally granted; those matters of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> and favour, out of which it arose, being frequently obtained from the crown by the powerful intercession of the queen. There are traces of its payment, though obscure ones, in the book of domeday, and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pipe-roll of Henry I. In the reign of Henry II. the manner of collecting it appears to have been well understood; and it forms a distinct head in the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> of the exchequer written in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and usually attributed to Gervase of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TILBURY">Tilbury</a>. From that time downwards, it was regularly claimed and enjoyed by all the queen-consorts of England till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Henry VIII.; though after the accession of the Tudor family, the collecting of it seems to have been much neglected; and there being no queen consort afterwards till the accession of James I. a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of near 60 years, its very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and quantity then became a matter of doubt; and being referred by the king to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> justices and chief baron, their report of it was so very unfavourable, that his consort queen Anne (though she claimed it) yet never thought proper to exact it. In 1635, 11 Car. I. a time fertile of expedients for raising <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> upon dormant precedents in our old records (of which ship-money was a fatal instance), the king, at the petition of his queen Henrietta <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a>, issued out his writ for levying it; but afterwards purchased it of his consort at the price of 10,000 pounds; finding it, perhaps, too trifling and troublesome to levy. And when afterwards, at the restoration, by the abolition of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> tenures, and the fines that were consequent upon them, the little that legally remained of this revenue was reduced to almost nothing at all; in vain did Mr Prynne, by a treatise that does <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to his abilities as a painful and judicious antiquarian, endeavour to excite queen Catherine to revive this antiquated claim. Another ancient perquisite belonging to the queen consort, mentioned by all our old writers, and, therefore only, worthy notice, is this: that on the taking a whale on the coasts, which is a royal fish, it shall be divided between the king and queen; the head only being the king's property, and the tail of it the queen's. De flurgione obfervetur, quod rex illum habeat integrum: de <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol2.html#article-BALENA">balena</a> vero fufficit, si rex habeat caput, et regina caudam. The reason of this whimsical <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, as assigned by our ancient records, was, to furnish the queen's wardrobe with whale-bone. But farther: though the queen is in all respects a subject, yet, in point of the security of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and person, she is put upon the same footing with the king. It is equally <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> (by the statute 25 Edward III.) to imagine or compass the death of our lady the king's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, as of the king himself; and to violate or defile the queen consort, amounts to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> crime; as well in the person committing the fact, as in the queen herself if consenting. A law of Henry VIII. made it treason also for any woman who was not a virgin, to marry the king without informing him thereof: but this law was soon after repealed; it trespassing too strongly, as well on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>. If however the queen be accused of any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of treason, she shall (whether consort or dowager) be tried by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> of parliament, as queen Ann Boleyn was in 28 Hen. VIII. The husband of a queen regnant, as prince George of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> was to queen Anne, is her subject; and may be guilty of high treason against her: but, in the instance of conjugal fidelity, he is not subjected to the same penal restrictions. For which the reason seems to be, that if a queen consort is unfaithful to the royal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>, this may debauch or bastardize the heirs to the crown; but no such danger can be consequent on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> of the husband to a queen regnant. 2. A queen dowager is the widow of the king, and as such enjoys most of the privileges belonging to her as queen consort. But it is not high treason to conspire her death, or to violate her chastity; for the same reason as was before alleged, because the succession to the crown is not thereby endangered. Yet still, pro dignitate regali, no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> can marry a queen-dowager without special licence from the king, on pain of forfeiting his lands and goods. This Sir Edward Coke tells us was enacted in parliament in 6 Henry VI., though the statute be not in print. But she, though an alien born, shall still be intitled to dower after the king's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a>, which no other alien is. A queen dowager when married again to a subject, doth not lose her regal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, as peeresses-dowager do when they marry commoners. For Katherine, queen dowager of Henry V. though she married a private <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, Owen ap Meredith ap Theodore, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Owen Tudor; yet, by the name of Katherine queen of England, maintained an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> against the bishop of Carlisle. And so the dowager of Navarre marrying with Edmond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of king Edward I. maintained an action of dower by the name of queen of Navarre. 3. The prince of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, or heir apparent to the crown, and also his royal consort, and the princess royal, or eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the king, are likewise peculiarly regarded by the laws. For, by statute 25 Edw. III. to compass or conspire the death of the former, or to violate the chastity of either of the latter, are as much high treason as to conspire the death of the king, or violate the chastity of the queen. And this upon the same reason as was before given; because the prince of Wales is next in succession to the crown, and to violate his wife might taint the blood-royal with bastardy: and the eldest daughter of the king is also alone inheritable to the crown on failure of of issue <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a>, and therefore more respected by the laws than any of her younger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>; insomuch that upon this, united with other (feudal) principles, while our military tenures were in force, the king might levy an aid for marrying his eldest daughter, and her only. The heir apparent to the crown is usually made prince of Wales and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, by special <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a>; but being the king's eldest son, he is by inheritance <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Cornwall, without any new creation. 4. The rest of the royal family may be considered in two different lights, according to the different senses in which the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> royal family is used. The larger <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> includes all those who are by any possibility inheritable to the crown. Such, before the revolution, were all the descendants of William the Conqueror; who had branched into an amazing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, by intermarriages with the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. Since the revolution and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of settlement, it means the Protestant issue of the princess Sophia; now comparatively few in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, but which in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time may possibly be as largely diffused. The more confined sense includes only those who are in a certain <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of propinquity to the reigning prince, and to whom therefore the law pays an extraordinary regard and respect; but, after that degree is past, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of ordinary subjects, and are seldom considered any farther, unless called to the succession upon failure of the nearer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. For though collateral <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSANGUINITY">consanguinity</a> is regarded indefinitely with respect to inheritance or succession, yet it is and can only be regarded within some certain limits in any other respect, by the natural <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of things and the dictates of positive law. The younger sons and daughters of the king, and other branches of the royal family, who are not in the immediate line of succession, were therefore little farther regarded by the ancient law, than to give them a certain degree of precedence before all peers and public officers as well <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> as temporal. This is done by the statute 31 Henry VIII. c. 10, which ensues, that no person except the king's children shall presume to fix or have place at the side of the cloth of estate in the parliament chamber; and that certain great officers therein named, shall have precedence above all dukes, except only such as shall happen to be the king's son, brother, uncle, nephew (which Sir Edward Coke explains to signify grandson or nepos) or brother's or sister's son. But under the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the king's children, his grandsons are held to be included, without having recourse to Sir Edward Coke's interpretation of nephew; and therefore when his late majesty king George II. created his grandson Edward, the second son of Frederick prince of Wales deceased, duke of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and referred it to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> his place and precedence, they certified that he ought to have precedence next to the late duke of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, the then king's youngest son; and that he might have a seat on the left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the cloth of estate. But when, on the accession of his present majesty, these royal personages ceased to take place as the children, and ranked only as the brother and uncle of the king, they also left their seats on the side of the cloth of estate; so that when the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, his majesty's second brother, took his seat in the house of peers, he was placed on the upper end of the earls <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> (on which the dukes usually sit) next to his royal highness the duke of York. And in 1717, upon a question referred to all the judges by king George I. it was resolved, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of ten against the other two, that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and care of all the king's grandchildren while minors, did belong of right to his majesty as king of this realm, even during their father's life. But they all agreed, that the care and approbation of their marriages, when grown up, belonged to the king their grandfather. And the judges have more recently concurred in opinion, that this care and approbation extend also to the presumptive heir of the crown; though to what other branches of the royal family the same did extend, they did not find precisely determined. The most frequent instances of the crown's interposition go no farther than nephews and nieces; but examples are not wanting of its reaching to more distant collaterals. And the statute 6 Henry VI. before-mentioned, which prohibits the marriage of a queen-dowager without the consent of the king, affords this reason for it: "because the disparagement of the queen shall give greater comfort and example to other ladies of estate, who are of the blood royal, more lightly to disparage themselves." Therefore by the statute 28 Hen. VIII. c. 18. (repealed, among other statutes of treasons, by 1 Edw. VI. c. 12.) it was made high treason for any man to contract marriage with the king's children or reputed children, his sisters or aunts ex parte paterna, or the children of his brethren or sisters; being exactly the same degrees to which precedence is allowed by the statute 31 Hen. VIII. before-mentioned. And now, by statute 12 Geo. III. c. 11. no descendant of the body of king George II. (other than the issue of princesses married into foreign families) is capable of contracting matrimony, without the previous consent of the king signified under the great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>; and any marriage contracted without such a consent is void. Provided, that such of the said descendants as are not above of 25, may after a twelvemonth's notice given to the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, contract and solemnize marriage without the consent of the crown; unless both houses of parliament shall, before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of the said year, expressly declare their disapprobation of such intended marriage. And all persons solemnizing, afflicting, or being present at any such prohibited marriages, shall incur the penalties of the statute of praemunire. Royal Oak, a fair spreading tree at Boscobel, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DONNINGTON">Donnington</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, the boughs whereof were once covered with ivy; in the thick of which king <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. sat in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>-time with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> Careels, and in the night lodged in Boscobel house: so that they are mistaken who speak of it as an old hollow oak; it being then a gay flourishing tree, surrounded with many more. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> remains thereof are now fenced in with a handsome wall, with this inscription in gold letters: Felicissimae arborum quam in alium potentissimi regis Caroli II. Deus op. max. per quem reges regnant, hic crevere voluit, &c. Royal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. See Society.

ROYALTIES

Pages 575-575

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, otherwise called the king's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, and the regalia. See Prerogative and Regalia.

ROYSTON

Pages 575-576

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a> in England, seated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. i. N. Lat. 52. 3. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, place, seated in a fertile vale full of inns, and the market is very considerable for corn. There was lately discovered, almost under the market-place, a subterranean chapel of one Rosa, a Saxon Lady: it has several altars and images cut out of the chalky sides, and is in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-loaf, having no entrance but at the top.

RUBENS

Pages 576-576

a famous painter, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> in 1577. He was the most accomplished of all the Flemish masters, and would have come up to the most celebrated Italians, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, instead of being educated under <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Van Noort and Octavio Venius, he had been bred in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Lombard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. Notwithstanding, perhaps, none of his predecessors can boast a more beautiful colouring, a nobler <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, or a more luxuriant fancy in their compositions. Besides his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, and his admirable skill in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, he was universally learned, spoke <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> languages perfectly, was well read in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and withal so excellent a statesman, that he was employed in several public negotiations of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance. His usual abode was at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, where he built a spacious apartment in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Rotunda at Rome, for a noble collection of pictures which he had purchased in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; some of which, together with his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, medals, and other antiquities, he sold to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a> for 10,000l. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> performances in painting are in the banqueting-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Whitehall, the Escorial in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and the Luxembourg galleries at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He died in 1640, leaving vast <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> to his children, the eldest of whom succeeded him in the office of secretary of state in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>.

RUBIA

Pages 576-576

madder; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the tetrandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, of which the most remarkable is the tinctorum, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> dyer's madder, so much used by the dyers and calico-printers. This hath a perennial root and annual stalk: the root is composed of many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, thick, succulent fibres, almost as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s little finger; these are joined at the top in a head like asparagus, and run very deep into the ground. From the upper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, or head of the root, come out many side-roots, which extend <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> under the surface of the ground to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance, whereby it propagates very fast; for these send up a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of shoots, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> carefully taken off in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> soon after they are above ground, become so many plants. These roots are of a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, somewhat transparent; and have a yellowish pith in the middle, which is tough and of a bitterish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. From this root arise many large four-cornered jointed stalks, which, in good <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> grow five or six feet long; and, if supported, sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight: they are armed with short herbaceous prickles; and at each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> are placed five or six spear-shaped leaves: their upper surfaces are smooth; but their midrib on the under side is armed with rough herbaceous spines, and the leaves fit <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the branches in whorls. From the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the stalk come out the branches, which sustain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>: they are placed by pairs opposite; each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> crossing the other: these have a few small leaves toward the bottom, which are by threes, and upwards by pairs opposite: the branches are terminated by loose branching spikes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> flowers, which are cut into four parts resembling stars. These appear in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and are sometimes succeeded by seeds, which seldom <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> in England. For the manner of its cultivation and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of dyers, see the article Madder. Madder-root is used in medicine. The virtues attributed to it, are those of a detergent and aperient; whence it has been usually ranked among the opening roots, and recommended in obstructions of the viscera, particularly of the kidneys, in coagulations of the blood from falls or bruises, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JAUNDICE">jaundice</a> and beginning dropsies. It is an ingredient in the icteric decoction of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> pharmacopoeia. It is observable, that this root taken internally, tinged the urine of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> colour; and in the Philosophical Transactions we have an account of its producing a like effect upon the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of animals who had it mixed with their food: all the bones, particularly the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> ones, were said to be changed, both externally and internally, to a deep red; but neither the fleshy nor cartilaginous parts suffered any alterations: some of these bones macerated in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> for many weeks together, and afterwards steeped and boiled in spirit of wine, lost none of their colour, nor communicated any tinge to the liquors. This root, therefore, was concluded to be possessed of great subtilty of parts, and its medical virtues hence to deserve inquiry. The same trials, however, made by others, have not been found to produce the same effects as those above mentioned.—Of late the root has come into great reputation as an emenagogue.

RUBININSKA

Pages 576-576

one of the northern provinces of Russia, bounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Dwina on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by Syrians on the east, by Belozera on the south, and by the lake <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ONEGA">Onega</a> on the west.

RUBRIC

Pages 576-576

in the canon <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> article in certain <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> law-books; thus called because written, as the titles of the chapters in our ancient bibles are, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> letters.

RUBUS

Pages 576-576

the Bramble, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Raspberry bush; a genus of the polygynia order, belonging to the icelandica class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> raspberry, which, with its varieties, demands culture in every garden for their fruit; particularly the common <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> kind, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> sort, and twice-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> raspberry; all of which are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> bearers; but for the general plantations, choose principally the common red and the white kind, as being generally the greatest bearers of all; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> also a share of the twice-bearing sort, both as a curiosity, and for the sake of its autumnal crops of fruit, which in favourable seasons <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> in tolerable perfection; observing to allow all the sorts some open exposure in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> garden, tho' they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> prosper in almost any situation. The other species are considered as plants of variety, for hardy plantations in the shrubbery. Some of them are also very ornamental flowering plants; particularly the Virginian flowering raspberry, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>-blossomed bramble, which have great merit as furniture for ornamental compartments; and the white-berried bramble, which is a great curiosity. All the other species and varieties serve to diversify <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> collections.

RUBY

Pages 576-579

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of gems, being a beautiful gem of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> with an admixture of purple. This, in its most perfect and best coloured state, is a gem of prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> value; it is often found perfectly pure and free from blemishes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> foul- foulness, but much more frequently debased greatly in its value by them, especially in the larger specimens. It is of very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>, equal to that of the sapphire, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> only to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a>. It is various in size, but less subject to variations in its shape than most of the other gems. It is usually found very small, its most <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> size being equal to that of the head of the largest sort of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIN">pin</a>; but it is found of four, eight, or ten carats, and sometimes, tho' very rarely, up to 30, 30, or 40. It is never found of an angular or crystalliform shape; but always of a pebble-like <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, often roundish, sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, and much larger at one end than the other, and in some form resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, and is usually flattened on one side. It <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> is naturally so bright and pure on the surface, as to need no polishing; and when its figure <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit of being set without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>, it is often worn in its rough state, and with no other than its native polish. We have the true ruby only from the East Indies; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of it are in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ceylon.

RUCTATION

Pages 579-579

a ventosity arising from indigestion, and discharging itself at the mouth with a very disagreeable noise.

RUDBECK

Pages 579-579

a learned Swedish physician, born of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family in 1630. He became professor of medicine at Upsal, where he acquired <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause by his extensive knowledge; and died in 1702. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. Exercitatio anatomica exhibens ductus novos hepaticos aquosi, &c., &c., glandularum forsa, in 4to. He there affirms his claim to the discovery of the lymphatic vessels, against the pretensions of Thomas Bartholin. 2. Atlantica, five Manheim, vera Japhethi posterorum sedes ac patria, 4 vols folio, is full of strange paradoxes supported with profound learning: he there endeavours to prove, that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> whence all the ancient Pagan divinities and our first parents were derived; and that the Germans, English, French, Danes, Greeks, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, with all other nations, originally came from thence.

RUDBECKIA

Pages 579-579

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of the syn-geneia polygamia fructuane clas. The receptacle is conical and paleaceous; the pappus has four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> on its edge; and the calyx consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> row of scales. There are six <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, none of them natives of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>.

RUDDER

Pages 579-579

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> on hinges in the stern of the ship, and which, opposing sometimes one side in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> and sometimes another, turns <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> directs the vessel this way or that. See Helm.

RUDIMENTS

Pages 579-579

the first principles <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> grounds of any art or science, called also the elements thereof.

RUFFHEAD

Pages 579-579

was the son of his Majesty's baker, in Piccadilly; who buying a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOTTERY">lottery</a> ticket for him in his infancy, which happened to be drawn a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of 500l, this sum was applied to educate him for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>. He accordingly entered in the Middle Temple; and seconded so well the views of his father, that he became a good scholar and an acute barrister. While he was waiting for opportunities to distinguish himself in his profession, he wrote a variety of pamphlets on temporary politics; and was afterwards distinguished by his accurate edition of The Institutes at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in 4to. He now obtained good business, though more as a chamber-counsellor in framing bills for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> than as a pleader; but his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> application to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, with the variety of works he engaged in as an author, so impaired his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, that after the last exertion of his abilities to defend the conduct of administration toward Mr Wilkes, by a pamphlet intitled, "The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">Case</a> of the late <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a> considered," he was prevented from receiving the reward of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">Treasury</a>, by dying in 1769, at about 46 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, bishop Warburton engaged him to write his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> promised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Alexander Pope; which, however, when executed, was very far from giving general satisfaction: the author attributed his ill success to the deficiency of his materials; while the public seemed rather to be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that, as a lawyer he ventured beyond his proper line, when he assumed the task of a critic in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>.

RUFFLING

Pages 579-579
or RUFFING, a beat on the drum. Lieutenant-generals have three ruffles, major-generals two, brigadiers one, and governors one, as they pass by the regiment, guard, &c.

RUGEN

Pages 579-579

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Baltic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Pomerania, over against <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STRALSUND">Stralsund</a>, about 23 miles in length and 15 in breadth, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality. It is strong both by art and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, abounds in corn and cattle, and belongs to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 30. N. Lat. 54. 32.

RUINS

Pages 579-579

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> particularly used for magnificent buildings fallen into decay by length of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and whereof there only remains a confused heap of materials.—The most remarkable ruins, now existing, of whole cities, are those of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALMYRA">Palmyra</a> and Persepolis; of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of which, some idea may be formed from the views given in Plate CCLIX.—The magnificent ruins still remaining in Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, &c. of particular edifices, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, palaces, amphitheatres, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, &c. it were endless to enumerate, and beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> to represent.

RULE

Pages 579-580

in matters of literature, a maxim, canon, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> precept, to be observed in any art or science. Rule, in a monastic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, a system of laws or regulations, whereby <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses are governed, and which the religious make a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOW">vow</a>, at their entrance, to observe. Such are the rules of the Augustins, Benedictins, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARTHUSIANS">Carthusians</a>, Franciscans, &c. See Augustins, &c. Rules of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, are certain orders made from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time in the courts of law, which attorneys are bound to observe, in order to avoid confusion; and both the plaintiff and defendant are at their peril also bound to pay obedience to rules made in court relating to the cause depending between them. It is to be observed, that no court <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> make a rule for any thing that may be done in the ordinary course; and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a rule be made, grounded upon an affidavit, the other side may move the court against it, in order to vacate the same, and thereupon shall bring into court a copy of the affidavit and rule. On the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> and contempt of a rule of court an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> lies; but it is not granted for disobedience to a rule, when the party has not been personally served; nor for disobeying a rule made by a judge in his chamber, which is not of force to ground a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> upon, unless the same be entered. A rule of court is granted every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> the courts at Westminster sit, to prisoners of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> or Fleet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a>, to go at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> about their private affairs. Rule of Threes. See Proportion. Rule, or Ruler, an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of wood or metal, with several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> delineated on it; of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in practical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MENSURATION">mensuration</a>. When a ruler has the lines of chords, tangents, sines, &c. it is called a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>.

RUM

Pages 580-580

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of brandy <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> vinous spirits, distilled from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes. Rum, according to Dr Shaw, differs from simple sugar-spirit, in that it contains more of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> flavour or essential <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of the sugar-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANE">cane</a>; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of raw juice and parts of the cane itself being often fermented in the liquor or solution of which the rum is prepared. The unctuous or oily flavour of rum is often supposed to proceed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fat used in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> the sugar; which fat, indeed, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> coarse, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> usually give a flanking flavour to the spirit, in our distillations of the sugar liquor, or wash, from our refining sugar-houses; but this is nothing of kin to the flavour of the rum, which is really the effect of the natural flavour of the cane. The method of making rum is this: When a sufficient stock of the materials are got together, they add <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> to them, and ferment them in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> method, though the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> is always carried on very slowly at first; because at the beginning of the season for making rum in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, they want yeast, or some other ferment to make it <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>; but by degrees, after this, they procure a sufficient quantity of the ferment, which rises up as a head to the liquor in the operation; and thus they are able afterwards to ferment and make their rum with a great deal of expedition, and in large quantities. When the wash is fully fermented, or to a due <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of acidity, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> is carried on in the common way, and the spirit is made up <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>; though sometimes it is reduced to a much greater strength, nearly approaching to that of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a> or spirit of wine; and it is then called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>-distilled rum. It might be easy to rectify the spirit, and bring it to much greater purity than we usually find it to be of; for it brings over in the distillation a very large quantity of the oil; and this is often so disagreeable, that the rum must be suffered to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to mellow before it can be used; whereas, if well rectified, it would grow mellow much sooner, and would have a much less potent flavour. The best state to keep rum in, both for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> and other uses, is doubtless that of alcohol, or rectified spirit. In this manner it would be transported in one half the bulk it usually is, and might be let <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the common proof-strength with water when necessary; for the common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of making <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNCH">punch</a>, it would likewise serve much better in the state of alcohol; as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> would be cleaner, and the strength might always be regulated to a much greater exactness than in the ordinary way. The only use to which it would not so well serve in this state, would be the common practice of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERATION">adulteration</a> among our distillers; for when they want to mix a large portion of cheaper spirit with the rum, their business is to have it of the proof-strength, and as full of the flavouring oil as they can, that it may drown the flavour of the spirits they mix with it, and extend its own. If the business of rectifying rum was more nicely managed, it seems a very practicable scheme to throw out so much of the oil, as to have it in the fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> state of a clear spirit, but lightly impregnated with it; in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> it would very nearly resemble arac, as is proved by the mixing a very small quantity of it with a tafteless spirit, in which case the whole bears a very near resemblance to arac in flavour. Rum is usually very much adulterated in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; some are so bare-faced as to do it with malt-spirit; but when it is done with molasses spirit, the tastes of both are so nearly allied, that it is not easily discovered. The best method of judging of it is by setting fire to a little of it; and, when it has burnt away all the inflammable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, examining the phlegm both by the taste and smell.

RUMELIA

Pages 580-580

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, the same with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; now a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

RUMEN

Pages 580-580

the paunch, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> first stomach of such animals as chew the cud; thence called ruminant animals. See <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPARATIVE_ANATOMY">Comparative Anatomy</a>, no. 92.

RUMEX

Pages 580-580
dock; a genus of the trigynia order, belonging to the hexandria class of plants. There are 27 species, of which the most remarkable are, 1. The patientia, commonly called patience rhubarb. This was formerly much more cultivated in the British gardens than at present: the roots of this have been generally used for the monk's rhubarb, and has even been thought to be the true kind; but others suppose the second sort should be used as such. The root is large, and divides into many thick fibres; their outer cover is brown, but they are yellow within, with some reddish veins; the leaves are broad, long, and acute-pointed; their footstalks are of a reddish colour; the stalks rise six or seven feet high, and divide towards the top into several erect branches garnished with a few narrow leaves terminating with loose spikes of large staminous flowers.
