He looked upon the Germans and Hollanders as the most civilized nations; because the former had already erected some of those arts and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> in Moscow, which he was desirous of spreading throughout his empire; and the latter excelled in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, which he considered as more necessary than any other. During the administration of the princess Sophia, he had formed a design of establishing a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> power in Russia; and for this purpose he took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> from an old English sloop, which with much difficulty he got repaired by a Dutch ship-builder residing at Moscow, which he first used as a pleasure-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> on a river, and afterwards caused to be removed to a large lake, on which he also caused two frigates and three yachts to be built, which he piloted himself. In 1694 he took a journey to Archangel, where he caused the Dutchman build him a small vessel, in which he embarked on the White Sea; which had never been visited by any Russian sovereign before. On this occasion he was escorted by a Dutch man of war, and attended by all the merchant-ships in the harbour of Archangel. He had already learned the method of working a ship; but, notwithstanding the eagerness with which courtiers generally imitate the example of their sovereigns, Peter himself was the only man in the court by whom this art was understood. Having reformed his army and introduced new discipline among them, he led his troops against the Turks, from whom, in 1696, he took the fortress of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AZOPH">Azoph</a>, and had the satisfaction to see his fleet defeat that of the enemy. On his return to Moscow were struck the first medals which had ever appeared in Vol IX. celebrated Ruysch on anatomy. He also attended the lectures of burgomaster Witzen on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. From this place he went for a few days to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, in order to pay a visit to king William III. of England; and on his return sent to Archangel a 60 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a> ship, in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of which he had assisted with his own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. In 1768 he went over to England, where he employed himself in the same manner as he had done in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. Here he perfected himself in the art of ship building; and having engaged a great number of artificers, he returned with them to Holland: from whence he set out for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, where he paid a visit to the emperor; and was on the point of setting out for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> to finish his improvements, when he was informed of a rebellion having broken out in his dominions.—This was occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> and obstinacy of the Russians, who having an almost invincible <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to their old ignorance and barbarism, had resolved to dethrone the czar on account of his innovations. But Peter arriving unexpectedly at Moscow, quickly put an end to their machinations, and took a most severe revenge of those who had been guilty. Having then made great reformation in every part of his empire, in 1700 he entered into a league with the kings of Denmark and Poland against Charles XII. of Sweden. The particulars of this famous war are related under the article Sweden. Here we shall only observe, that from the conclusion of this war Sweden ceased not only to be a formidable enemy to Russia, but even lost its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> consequence in a great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> altogether. In 1725 this great monarch died; and was succeeded by his wife Catherine, who governed the empire with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> till her death, which happened in the year 1727. She was succeeded by Peter II., a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>, and who died in 1730. After his death the regular succession was broken through, and the princess Anne Ivanovna, the second daughter of John the brother of Peter the Great, was declared empress. She maintained the credit of the empire in as high a degree as any of her predecessors, settled Augustus III. on the throne of Poland, carried on a successful war against the Turks, and totally broke the power of the Crimean Tartars. The only <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in her government was her confiding almost wholly in strangers, and particularly Germans, with whom she filled her councils and armies; which raised such a spirit of jealousy among the Russians, that in 1741 a revolution took place in favour of Elizabeth Petrovna, the daughter of Peter the Great and the empress Catherine, who was crowned at Moscow in 1742. The most remarkable transaction in her reign was her war with the king of Prussia, of which an account has already been given under the article Prussia. When by her means this monarch had been reduced almost to the brink of destruction, he was suddenly freed by her death from such a formidable enemy, and in her successor Peter III. found as warm a friend. This weak prince, however, pushing his plans of reformation to too great a length, was deposed by his wife Catherine II. the present empress; under whose reign a most successful war has been carried on against the Turks, (see <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>;) so that now the empire of Russia may be looked upon as superior in power to any in Europe, though as yet far behind with regard to arts and civilization. Moscow is in general a flat <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> country, except towards the north, where it is rough and mountainous. Forests abound everywhere throughout this empire. The plains are marshy, or flooded with a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, some of which extend above 40 leagues in length. The Ladoga and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ONEGA">Onega</a>, on the borders of Finland, are the largest in Europe. The other noted lakes are Brela-ozera, from whence a province derives its name; Iwanofo-cargopol, which lends its name to another province; and Honent, in the neighbourhood of the Great Novgorod. Moscow likewise boasts a considerable number of large and famous rivers. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBY">Oby</a>, formed by the junction of the Tobal and the Irtis, in the 65th degree of northern latitude, runs northward into the Frozen Ocean, opposite to <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol16.html#article-NOVA_ZEMBLA">Nova Zembla</a>, and is the boundary between Europe and Asia. The Dwina takes its origin in Wologda, runs a northerly course, and falls into the White Sea below Archangel. The Wolga, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>, formerly known by the name of Rha, owes its origin to the lake Uranow, near the frontiers of Lithuania; directs its course south-easterly thro' European Russia, receiving in its route the rivers Mologo, Mocho, Kioma, Ocka, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAMAR">Samar</a>, and above 30 more; then enters Asiatic Russia, and by several channels discharges itself into the Caspian sea, below Afrakan: this is the largest and deepest river in Russia. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a>, formerly called the Tanais, takes its rise in the middle of Russia, is swelled by the Weronetz, runs in a south-east <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> to Kamishka; then winding to the south-west, receives the Donets, and falls into the Palus Maeotis, or sea of Azoph. The Nieper, formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BORISTHENES">Boristhenes</a>, rises in the province of Moscow, runs through Poland, re-enters Moscow, passes Kiof, waters the Ukrain, and, after a southerly course through Tartary, falls into the Euxine sea at Ocakow. The Lower Dwina, rising also in the province of Moscow, runs through Poland, which it divides from Livonia, and discharges itself into the Baltic, below Riga. Some of these rivers run a surprising length of course; that of the Wolga exceeds 2000 miles; it washes the walls of near four score towns, and supplies the country with prodigious quantities of sturgeon, salmon, pikes, and other fishes of stupendous size and exquisite delicacy. Along its banks are found trouts, and wild asparagus, of a most delicious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and flavour: here likewise grow the only oaks that are produced in Moscow. Tho' the length of the Don, or Tanais, which arises in the province of Rezan, does not exceed 400 miles in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line from its source to the Palus Maeotis, in which it is lost, it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found to run above 1000, if traced in all its windings; in the course of which it is swelled by many rivers, waters many cities, and forms a great number of beautiful <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, in one of which is situated Tckercalke, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of Circassia. In such a vast extent of country, stretching from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">Climate</a>, Temperate so far into the Frigid Zone, the climate must vary considerably in different places. In the southern parts of Moscow the longest day does not exceed fifteen hours and a half; whereas in the most northern, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> is seen two months above the horizon. The country in general, though lying under different climates, is excessively cold in the winter. Towards the north, the country is covered near three <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the year with snow and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICE">ice</a>; and by the severity of the cold, many unfortunate persons are maimed, or perish. This sort of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> commonly sets in about the latter end of August, and continues till the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May; in which interval the rivers are frozen to the depth of four or five feet. Water thrown up into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, will fall down in icicles; birds are frozen in their flight, and travellers in their sledges. In some provinces the heats of summer are as scorching as the winter colds are rigorous. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of Muscovy varies still more than the climate, according to the influence of the sun and the situation of the country. The warmer provinces produce wheat, oats, barley, peas, and rye, together with a variety of herbs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; and the vegetation is so quick, that corn is commonly reaped in two months after it begins to appear above the surface of the ground. The natives use no other manure than the snow; which is supposed to enrich the ground, and to cherish and shelter the grain that is sown immediately after <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. The great variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSHROOMS">mushrooms</a> produced spontaneously in Russia, may be considered as a comfortable relief to the poor, while they appear as delicacies at the tables of the rich. Above 1000 waggon-loads of them used to be sold annually in Moscow. Perhaps it is on account of the scarcity of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, that such a number of fasts are instituted in the Muscovite religion. Besides the abovementioned productions, Muscovy yields <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">rhubarb</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, pasture for cattle, wax, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. Among other vegetables, we find in Russia a particular kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> called pflaum, plenty of excellent melons, and in the neighbourhood of Astrakhan, the famous zoophyton, or animal-plant, which the Muscovites call bonnaret, or lambkin, from its resemblance to a lamb. [See the article Scythian Lamb.] <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> in general was but little understood, and less prosecuted in this country, until it was improved under the encouragement and influence of that great patriot the czar Peter, who was indefatigable in executing his plans of reformation. The natural ignorance, sloth, and obstinacy of the people, together with the tyranny of the nobles, by whom they are miserably enslaved, were such obstructions to the improvement of husbandry, as nothing but his genius could have surmounted. The most considerable articles in the economy of a Russian <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FARM">farm</a> are wax and honey, by which the peasant is often enriched. He cuts down a great number of trees in the forest, and sawing the trunks into a number of parts, bores each of these, and stops up the hollow at both ends, leaving only a little hole for the admittance of the bees; thus the honey is secured from all the attempts of the bear, who is extremely fond of it, and tries many different experiments for making himself master of the luscious treasure. Of this honey the Russians make a great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of strong <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEAD">mead</a>, for their ordinary drink. They likewise extract from rye a spirit, which they prefer to brandy. Muscovy is very rich in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and iron, which are worked in different parts of the country, and yield a very considerable revenue to the sovereign. The wild beasts in the northern part of Russia are the same with those we have mentioned in the articles of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> and Lapland: such as rein-deer, bears, foxes, ermines, martens, sables, hares, and squirrels. In the more southern provinces the Muscovites breed black cattle, small but hardy horses, sheep, goats, and camels. The breed of cattle and horses has been enlarged by the care and under the protection of Peter. The whole empire abounds with wild-fowl and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a> of all sorts, and a variety of birds of prey; besides the different kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, which are raised in this as well as in other countries. The external parts and provinces of Muscovy are well supplied with sea-fish from the Northern Ocean, the Baltic, or gulph of Finland, the White Sea, the Black Sea, and the Caspian: but the whole empire is plentifully provided with fresh-water fish from the numerous lakes and rivers, yielding immense quantities of salmon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, pike, sturgeon, and beluga; the last being a large fish, of whose roe the best caviare is made. Innumerable insects, like those of Lapland, are hatched by the summer's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in the sand, morasses, and forests, with which this empire abounds; and are so troublesome, as to render great part of the country altogether uninhabitable. This vast empire is but thinly inhabited, in proportion to its extent; great part of it consisting of dreary wastes of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, forests, and morasses. Many parts of it are possessed by people who are in all respects different from the native Muscovites. The kingdom of Siberia, including the province of Dauria, was originally peopled with Tartars, who lived in little hordes or tribes, under distinct governments, and shifted their habitations occasionally; but since the establishment of Russian colonies in these countries, they have learned to dwell in houses, to till the ground, and pay an annual tribute of furs to the czar or emperor. There are other Tartars, however, who still live in tents, leading a vagrant life, without acknowledging the czar's sovereignty. A large tract of land, between Nife Novogrod and Cazan, on both sides of the river Volga, is occupied by the Zemelisses and Morduans, who live peaceably, employing themselves in agriculture, and pay taxes like the other subjects of Russia; but they never furnish recruits for the army. From Cazan to the frontiers of Siberia, the country is inhabited by the Bashkirs, a powerful nation, who have some villages, and enjoy certain privileges, of which they are very tenacious. The rest of this tract, as far as Astrakhan and the frontiers of the Ufbeckes, is frequented by the wandering Khalmucks, who remove with their tents, according to the season, for the convenience of subsistence. They receive annually from the czar presents of cloth, money, and arms; in return for which they are obliged to serve in his army without pay. This, however, is ill-served: for they plunder friend and foe, without distinction; and are, on the whole, barbarous, brutal, and savagely cruel. The Cossacks are distinguished into three tribes, known by the places where they make their first settlements; though they are all of the same nation, speak the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, profess the same religion, and live under the same form of government.† The Samoiedes and Laplanders are described in their proper places. The empire of Russia, including all these different nations, is not supposed to contain above seven millions of souls, the bulk of which number is composed of people by the native Russians. These are stigmatized by their neighbours as ignorant brutal people, totally... Rus Rusia resigned to sloth, and addicted to drunkenness, even in the most beastly excesses; nay, they are accused of being arbitrary, perfidious, inhuman, and destitute of every social virtue. The severity of the country they inhabit, their want of letters, polity, and commercial intercourse, joined to the depopulation of their government, and the tyranny of the grandees, may doubtless have an unhappy effect on the dispositions and morals of the people, which, however, have been meliorated and improved by the care, affability, and example of some of their late sovereigns. Certain it is, the vice of drunkenness was so universally prevalent among them, that Peter I. was obliged to restrain it by very severe edicts, which, however, have not produced much effect. They numbered in the city of Moscow no fewer than 4000 brandy-shops, in which the inhabitants used to set away their time in drinking strong liquors and smoking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>. This last practice became so dangerous, among persons in the most beastly state of intoxication, that a very severe law was found necessary to prevent the pernicious consequences, otherwise the whole city might have been consumed by conflagrations. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> were heretofore very powerful, each commanding a great number of vassals, whom they ruled with the most despotic and barbarous authority; but their possessions have been gradually circumscribed, and their power transferred in a great measure to the czar, on whom they are now wholly dependant. At present there is no other degree of the nobility; but that of the boyars: these are admitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and from among them the vaivodes, governors, and other great officers, are nominated. A Russian boyar is very proud of being corpulent, believing that nothing gives such a dignified air as does a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> or portly belly. Their surnames are no other than patronymics; for example, the son of Alexis calls himself Alexiowitz. They formerly wore long beards, and long robes with strait sleeves hanging down to their ankles; their collars and shirts were generally wrought with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a> of different colours: in lieu of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, they covered their heads with furred caps; and, instead of shoes, wore <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> boots. The dress of the women rarely resembled that of the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; with this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that their garments were more loose, their caps fantastic, and their shift-sleeves three or four ells in length, gathered up in folds from the shoulder to the fore-arm. By this time, however, the French fashions prevail among the better sort throughout all Muscovy. The common people are generally tall, healthy, and robust, patient of cold and hunger, inured to hardships, and remarkably capable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the most sudden transition from the extremes of hot or cold weather. Nothing is more customary than to see a Russian, who is over-heated and sweating at every pore, strip himself naked, and plunge into a river; nay, when their pores are all opened in the hot bath, to which they have daily recourse, they either practise this immersion, or subject themselves to a discharge of some pailfuls of cold water. This is the custom of both men and women, who enter the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> promiscuously, and appear naked to each other, without scruple or hesitation. A Russian will subsist for many days upon a little oatmeal and water, and even raw roots: an onion is a regale; but the food they generally use in their journeys is a kind of rye-bread, cut into small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> pieces, and dried again in the oven: these, when they are hungry, they soak in water, and eat as a very comfortable repast. Both sexes are remarkably healthy and robust, and accustom themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> every day after dinner. The Russian women are remarkably fair, comely, strong, and well-shaped, obedient to their lordly husbands, and patient under discipline: they are even said to be fond of correction, which they consider as an infallible mark of their husband's conjugal affection; and they pout and pine if it be withheld, as if they thought themselves treated with contempt and disregard. Of this neglect, however, they have very little cause to complain; the Russian husband being very well disposed, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and inclination, to exert his arbitrary power. Some writers observe, that, on the wedding-day, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> presents the bridegroom with a whip of her own making, in token of submission; and marriages, this he fails not to employ as the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of his authority. Very little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> is here used in match-making, which is the work of the parents. Perhaps the bridegroom never sees the woman until he is joined to her for life. The marriage being proposed and agreed to, the lady is examined, stark-naked, by a certain number of her <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> relations; and if they find any bodily defect, they endeavour to cure it by their own skill and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. The bride, on her wedding-day, is crowned with a garland of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMWOOD">wormwood</a>, implying the bitterness that often attends the married state; when the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> has tied the nuptial knot at the altar, his clerk or sexton throws upon her head a handful of hops, wishing that she may prove as fruitful as the plant thus scattered. She is muffled up, and led home by a certain number of old women, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-priest carrying the crofs before; while one of his subalterns, in a rough goat-skin, prays all the way that she may bear as many children as there are hairs on his garment. The new-married couple, being seated at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, are presented with bread and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; and a chorus of boys and girls sing the epithalamium, which is always grossly obscene. This ceremony being performed, the bride and bridegroom are conducted to their own chamber by an old woman, who exhorts the wife to obey her husband, and retires. Then the bridegroom defiles the lady to pull off one of his boots, giving her to understand, that in one of them is contained a whip, and in the other a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JEWEL">jewel</a> or a purse of money. She takes her choice; and if she finds the purse, interprets it into a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>; whereas should the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on the whip, she contemplates it into an unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRESAGE">presage</a>, and instantly receives a lash, as a specimen of what she has to expect. After they have remained two hours together, they are interrupted by a deputation of old women, who come to search for the signs of her virginity: if these are apparent, the young lady ties up her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, which before consummation hung loose over her shoulders, and visits her mother, of whom she demands the marriage-portion. It is generally agreed, that the Muscovite husbands are barbarous even to a proverb; they not only administer frequent and severe correction to their wives, but sometimes even torture them to death, without being subject to any punishment for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. The canon law of Muscovy forbids the conjugal commerce on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays; and whoever transgresses this law, must bathe himself before he enters the church-porch. He that marries a second wife, the first being alive, is not admitted farther than the church-door; and if any man espouses a third, he is excommunicated: so that though bigamy is tolerated, they nevertheless <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> it infamous. If a woman is barren, the husband generally persuades her to retire into a convent; if fair means will not succeed, he is at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to whip her into conciliation. When the czar, or emperor, has an inclination for a wife, the most beautiful maidens of the empire are presented to him for his choice. The education of the czarowitz, or prince <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, is intrusted to the care of a few persons, by whom he is strictly kept from the eyes of the vulgar, until he hath attained the 15th year of his age: then he is publicly exposed in the market-place, that the people, by viewing him attentively, may remember his person, in order to ascertain his identity; for they have more than once been deceived by impostors. Such is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> in which the Muscovites of both sexes are kept by their parents, their patrons, and the emperor, that they are not allowed to dispute any match that may be provided for them by these directors, however disagreeable or odious it may be. Officers of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the army, both natives and foreigners, have been saddled with wives by the sovereign in this arbitrary manner. A great general some time ago deceased, who was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, having been pressed by the late czarina to wed one of her ladies, saved himself from a very disagreeable marriage, by pretending his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was so unfound, that the lady would be irreparably injured by his compliance. The Muscovites are fond of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAGPIPE">bagpipe</a>, and have a kind of violin, with a large belly like that of a lute: but their music is very barbarous and defective. Nevertheless, there are public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, in which the children are regularly taught to sing. The very beggars ask alms in a whining cadence and ridiculous sort of recitative. A Russian ambassador at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, having been regaled with the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> of vocal and instrumental music that could be procured, was asked how he liked the entertainment; and replied, "Perfectly well: the beggars in my country sing <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> in the same manner." The warlike music of the Russians consists in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KETTLE_DRUMS">kettle-drums</a> and trumpets: they likewise use hunting horns; but they are not at all expert in the performance. The Muscovites think it beneath them to dance; but they call in their Polish or Tartarian slaves to divert them with this exercise, in their hours of dissipation. The Muscovites speak a dialect of the old Slavonic, mixed with barbarisms from the Polish and other languages: but the pure Slavonic is still retained in their bibles and homilies, and even spoken by those who affect to be thought men of letters. The Russians have adopted the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, which, however, they have corrupted and altered in the shape, and increased the letters to the number of 38. The whole empire was overwhelmed with the grossest ignorance: indeed, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> learning was in so little request, that the nobility themselves were wholly illiterate; and even the clergy could hardly read their prayers. They had neither university nor school for the instruction of youth, until Peter, their great reformer, in some measure dispelled those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of ignorance, by inviting foreigners into his dominions, encouraging the liberal arts and sciences, obliging his nobles to send their sons to more civilized countries for their improvement, and instituting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> and seminaries in Moscow and Petersburg. These steps were so contrary to the natural disposition of the Muscovites, that no other prince could have taken them with any prospect of success. Nay, since the death of this great man, they seem returning to their old bigotry. Foreigners are discouraged at the court of Petersburg; a gaudy tinsel fop is substituted in the room of real grandeur and magnificence; little or no progress has been made in prosecuting the wise plans projected by the czar Peter; and perhaps the whole nation would relapse into its primitive barbarity, were it not for the great commerce with different nations which must necessarily be carried on at Petersburg, and other Russian ports in the Baltic. The Russians were converted to the Christian religion towards the latter end of the tenth century, as has been already related. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> they have confessed the articles of the Greek church, mingled with certain superstitious ceremonies of their own. They do not believe in transubstantiation, purgatory, or the pope's infallibility or supremacy: they use auricular confession, communicate in both kinds, adopt the Athanasian creed, and adhere to the established liturgy of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>. They worship the Virgin Mary, and other saints; and pay their adorations to crosses and relics. They observe four great fasts in the year, during which they neither taste fish, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, nor any animal production: they will not drink after a man who has eaten flesh, nor use a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> that has cut meat in less than 24 hours after it has been used; nor will they, even though their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> is at stake, touch any thing in which hartshorn or any animal substance has been infused. While this kind of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENT">Lent</a> continues, they fast upon cabbages, cucumbers, and rye-bread, drinking nothing stronger than a sort of small-beer called quaffi. They likewise fast every Wednesday and Friday. Their common <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> is to abstain from every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of food and drink, but bread, salt, cucumbers, and water. They are ordered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> their bodies, and continue in that painful posture, and between whiles to strike their head against an image. The Muscovites at all times reject as impure, horse-flesh, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELK">elk</a>, veal, hare, rabbit, ass's milk, mare's milk, and Venice-treacle because the flesh of vipers is an ingredient; also every thing that contains even the smallest quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>, civet, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASTOR">castor</a>: yet they have no aversion to swine's flesh; on the contrary, the country produces excellent <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACON">bacon</a>. They celebrate 15 grand festivals in the year. On Palm-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> there is a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, at which the czar assists in person and on foot. He is apparelled in cloth of gold: his train is borne up by the prime of the nobility, and he is attended by his whole court. He is immediately preceded by the officers of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, one of whom carries his handkerchief on his arm, lying upon another of the richest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>. He halts at a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of free-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, where, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> to the east, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> bending his body almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, he pronounces a short prayer: then he proceeds to the church of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, where he renews his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. This exercise being performed, he returns to his palace, the bride of the patriarch's horse resting upon his arm. The horse's head being covered with white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, is held by some nobleman; while the patriarch, sitting side-wise, and holding a crofs in his hand, distributes benedictions as he moves along; on his head he wears a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> edged with ermin, adorned with loops and buttons of gold and precious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>: before him are displayed banners of consecrated stuff, in a variety of colours. Above 500 priests walk in the procession; those who are near the patriarch bearing pictures of the Virgin Mary, richly ornamented with gold, jewels, and pearls, together with crofes, relics, and religious books, including a copy of the Gospels, which they reckon to be of inestimable value. In the midst of this procession is borne a triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>; and on the top an apple-tree covered with fruit, which several little boys inclosed in the machine endeavour to gather. The lawyers and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> carry branches of willow; the guards and the spectators prostrate themselves on the ground while the procession halts; and after the ceremony, the patriarch presents a purse of 100 rubles to the czar, who perhaps invites him to dine at his table. During the season of Easter the whole empire is filled with mirth and rejoicing: which, however, never fails to degenerate into heat and debauchery; even the ladies may indulge themselves with strong liquors to intoxication, without scandal. When a lady sends to inquire concerning the health of her guests whom she entertained over-night, the usual reply is, "I thank your mistress for her good cheer: by my troth, I was so merry that I don't remember how I got home." During these carnivals a great number of people, in reeling <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> drunk, fall down and perish among the snow. It is even dangerous to relieve a person thus overtaken; for, should he die, the person who endeavoured to assist him is called before the judge, and generally pays dear for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. The Mucovote priests use exorcisms at the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>. They plunge the child three times over head and ears in water, and give it the sacrament of the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a> in one species, until it hath attained the age of seven; after which the child is indulged with it in both kinds. They likewise administer the sacrament to dying persons, together with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> unction; and if this be neglected, the body is denied Christian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>. Soon as the person expires, the body is deposited in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, with a luncheon of bread, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of shoes, some few pieces of money, and a certificate signed by the parish-priest, and directed to St Nicholas, who is one of their great patrons. They likewise hold St Andrew in great veneration, and ridiculously pretend they were converted by him to Christianity. But next to St Nicholas, they adore St Anthony of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, who is supposed to have sailed upon a mill-stone through the Mediterranean and Atlantic, and over the lakes Ladoga and Onega, as far as Novgorod. Every house is furnished with an image of St Nicholas, carved in the most rude and fantastic manner; and when it becomes old and worm-eaten, the owner either throws it into the river with a few pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, saying, "Adieu, brother;" or returns it to the maker, who accommodates him with a new image for a proper consideration. The good women are very careful in adorning their private St Nicholas with rich cloaths and jewels; but on any emergency, these are resumed, and the saint left as naked as he came from the hand of the carpenter. There are monasteries in Russia; but neither the monks nor the nuns are subject to severe restrictions. The friars are either horse-jockeys, or trade in hops, wheat, and other commodities; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> are at liberty to go abroad when they please, and indulge themselves in all manner of freedoms. Heretofore liberty of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> was denied, and every convicted heretic was committed to the flames; but since the reign of Peter, all religions and sects are tolerated throughout the empire. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, Lutherans, Calvinists, Armenians, Jews, and Mahometans, enjoy the free exercise of their respective forms of worship; though it was not without great difficulty, and by dint of extraordinary solicitation from different powers, that the Romish religion was allowed. Peter knowing the dangerous tenets of a religion that might fet the spiritual power of the pope at variance with the temporal power of the emperor, and being well acquainted with the meddling genius of its professors, held out for some time against the intercession of Germany, France, and Poland; and though at length he yielded to their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> interposition, he would by no means suffer any Jesuit to enter his dominions. The government of Russia is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> despotism. The government of the whole empire is ruled by the arbitrary will and pleasure of the sovereign, who is styled the czar, a title which is probably a corruption of Caesar. Heretofore he was styled grand duke of Muscovy; but since the reign of Peter, he is dignified with the appellation of emperor of Russia. He is absolute lord, not only of all the estates in the empire, but also of the lives of his subjects: the greatest noblemen call themselves his slaves, and execute his commands with the most implicit obedience. The common people revere him as something supernatural: they never mention his name, or anything immediately belonging to him, without marks of the most profound respect and awful veneration. A man asking a carpenter at work upon one of the czar's warehouses, what the place was intended for, answered, "None but God and the czar knows." The nobility of Russia were formerly rich and powerful, and ruled despotic over their inferiors: but their wealth and influence are now swallowed up by the importance and authority of the crown, and they are become venal dependants on the government. The czar appoints voivodes, or governors of provinces; and bestows all offices of consequence, whether <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a>, civil, or military. In a word, he is vested with the whole legislative and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a>, and all his subjects are slaves existing at his will. The people of Russia are distinguished into three degrees; namely, the nobility, called knex, or knexi; the gentry, known by the name of duormini; and the peasants. The knex, or dukes, were anciently the princes of Russia, who exercised supreme power, each in his own territory, as an independent prince; but all of them either submitted, or were subdued by the princes of Voldomir, who translated their residence to Moscow, and assumed the title of veliki knexi, or "great dukes." The descendants of these noblemen still retain their appellation, though many of them are reduced to the most abject poverty and contempt. In the beginning of this century above 300 knex served as common troopers in the regiment of dragoons commanded by prince Menzikoff. The czar Peter introduced the titles of count and prince of the empire, and instituted an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> in honour of St Andrew, distinguished by a blue ribbon and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>. The dourmins are country gentlemen, who generally hold their lands by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; and in time of war are obliged to appear in arms on horseback. Those are the most happy who live at the greatest distance from court; because they may enjoy their estates unknown and unmolested. In general, they are extremely insolent and oppressive to the peasants, and meanly submissive to the nobility. All the peasants in the empire are considered as immediate slaves belonging to the czar, to the boyars, or to the monasteries. The value of estates is computed, not by the extent or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the land, but from the number of those peasants, who may be sold, alienated, or given away, at the pleasure of their masters. The number of these husbandmen, whether living in villages or in the open country, being known, the czar, by requiring a certain proportion of each lord or proprietor, can raise 300,000 men in less than 40 days. The administration is managed by a grand council, called dumnoy boyaren, or "council of the boyars," who are the grandees of the empire, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> as privy-counsellors. To this are subfervient five inferior chambers and courts of judicature, provided each with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>. The first regulates every thing relating to ambassadors and foreign negociations; the second takes cognizance of military affairs; the third manages the public revenues of the empire; the business of the fourth is to encourage, protect, and improve trade and commerce. The two last hear and determine in all causes, whether civil or criminal. Peter divided the empire into the eight governments of Mosco, Archangel, Asoph, Cafan, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASTRACAN">Astracan</a>, Chioff and the Ukraine, Siberia, Livonia, comprehending Ingria, Plefsow, and Novogrod, Smolensko, and Veronizz. The governors or waiwodes were vested with power to dispose of all employments civil and military, and receive the revenues. They were directed to defray all expenses in their respective governments, and send a certain yearly sum to the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>. In a word, they enjoyed absolute power in every thing but what related to the regular troops, which, though quartered in their jurisdiction, were neither paid nor directed by them, but received their orders immediately from the czar or his generals. The decision of causes heretofore depended upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> of the judge; but about the middle of the last century, a code of laws was compiled in one volume, intitled, fabrona ulofcinia, signifying universal law; and according to this the sentences are now regulated. Besides these tribunals, there is an inferior court of judicature or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> established in every province, having a president, chancellor, and secretary or diack. The law-suits are neither tedious nor expensive, as all the proceedings are summary; but the judge is very seldom incorruptible; and unless he is tampered with beforehand, the plaintiff generally obtains the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> in his favour. Few crimes are capital in Russia: murder may be atoned by paying a sum of money; nay, the civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> takes no cognizance of murder, without having previously received information at the suit of some individuals. Criminals were punished with torture and the most cruel deaths, till the reign of the illustrious Catherine I., when a more merciful system took place, and which the present empress has since confirmed by law. See the articles Catherine I. of Russia, and Elizabeth Petrovna. The Russians drive a considerable traffic with different nations, both of Asia and Europe. One of the commerce most considerable articles is the iron manufacture, in its different branches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> cannon, mortars, bombs, anchors, and small arms. They have likewise at Petersburg large magazines of naval stores, leather, tallow, and pot-ashes. The southern parts furnish great quantities of caviar; the north-eastern provinces supply plenty of spermaceti, sea-horses <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, ifinglas, and train-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; and Russia produces an infinite number of the best furs in the world, together with abundance of honey, castor, rhubarb, and some other drugs. At the port of Petersburg 1000 ships are loaded yearly by foreigners, with the commodities produced in the northern part of this great empire. But the Mulcovites likewise carry on a considerable commerce by land with China and the East Indies, for gold, silk, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>. The court monopolizes this trade, and imports these commodities by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> of camels. With respect to the revenue of Russia, it continually fluctuates, according to the increase of commerce or the pleasure of the czar, who has all the wealth of the empire at his disposal. He monopolizes all the best furs, the mines, minerals, and trade by land to the East Indies; he farms out all the tobacco, wine, brandy, beer, mead, and other liquors; the inns, taverns, public houses, bath, and sweating-houses. The customs upon merchandize, the imposts upon corn, and toll exacted from cities, towns, and villages, are very considerable. He possesses demesnes to a very great value; inherits the effects of all those that die intestate, or under <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of capital crimes; derives a duty from all lawsuits; and to sum up the whole, can command the fortunes of all his subjects. All these articles added together, are said to produce about 3,000,000 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>; but then the intrinsic value of money is at least three times greater in Mulcovy than in Britain. The czar Peter seized the lands of the church, and annexed them to his own demesnes; but the greater part was restored in the sequel. As for the lands belonging to the dignity and office of patriarch, they were distributed among the monasteries and nobility. The standing army of Russia is computed at 250,000 men; besides these, the Russians can assemble a body force, &c. of 40,000 irregulars, Calmucks, Cossacks, and other Tartars, who live under their dominion. But the number may be doubled on any emergency. The czarina has likewise a considerable fleet in the Baltic, and a great number of formidable gallows, frigates, fire-ships, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a> ketches.

RUST

Pages 597-598

the flower, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> of any metal, procured by corroding and dissolving its superficial parts RUSTIC by some menstruum. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">Water</a> is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in producing rust; and hence oils, and other fatty bodies, secure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> from rust; water being no menstruum for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and therefore not able to make its way through it. All metals except <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> are liable to rust; and even this also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> exposed to the fumes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>.

RUSTIC

Pages 598-598

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, implies a manner of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, rather than according to the rules of art. See Architecture. Rustic <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">Work</a>, is where the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>, &c. of a building, instead of being smooth, are hatched, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> picked with the point of a hammer. Rustic Order, that decorated with rustic quoins, rustic work, &c.

RUSTRE

Pages 598-598

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a>-shape, pierced through in the middle with a round hole. See Heraldry.

RUTA

Pages 598-598

RUE; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the decandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable is the hortensis, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>-leaved garden rue, which has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> cultivated for medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. This rises with a shrubby stalk to the height of five or six feet, sending out branches on every side, garnished with decomposed leaves, whose small lobes are wedge-shaped, of a grey <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and have a strong odour. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are produced at the end of the branches, in bunches almost in the form of umbels; they are composed of four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> concave petals which are cut on their edges, and eight yellow stamens which are longer than the petals, terminated by roundish summits. The germs become a roundish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a>, with four lobes punched full of holes containing rough <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> seeds. Rue has a strong ungrateful smell, and a bitterish penetrating <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; the leaves, when full of vigour, are extremely acid, insomuch as to inflame and blister the skin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> much handled. With regard to their medicinal virtues, they are powerfully stimulating, attenuating, and detergent; and hence, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> phlegmatic habits, they quicken the circulation, dissolve tenacious juices, open obstructions of the excretory glands, and promote the fluid secretions. The writers on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a> in general, have entertained a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the virtues of this plant. Boerhaave is full of its praises; particularly of the essential <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and the distilled <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> cohabated or re-distilled several times from fresh parcels of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a>: after extravagantly commending other waters prepared in this manner, he adds, with regard to that of rue, that the greatest commendations he can bestow upon it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> short of its merit: "What medicine (says he) can be more efficacious for promoting sweat and perspiration, for the cure of the hysterical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, and of epilepsies, and for expelling <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a>?" Whatever <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> rue may be of in the two last <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, it undoubtedly has its use in the others: the cohabated water, however, is not the most efficacious <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of it. An extract made by rectified spirit, contains in a small compass the whole virtues of the rue; this menstruum taking up by infusion all the pungency and flavour of the plant, and elevating nothing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. With water, its peculiar flavour and warmth arise; the bitters, and a considerable share of the pungency, remaining behind.

RUTLANDSHIRE

Pages 598-598

is the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in England, it being but 40 miles in circumference; in which are 2 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 48 parishes, and 3263 houses. However, for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> it may be compared with any other county; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> being good, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> fertile both for tillage and pastures; and it not only affords plenty of corn, but feeds a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of horned cattle and sheep. It is well watered with brooks and rivulets, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Weland and the Wash. It is bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>; on the south by the river Weland, which parts its from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>; and on the west and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>. It has only two market-towns; namely, Okeham, where the assizes and sessions are held, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UPPINGHAM">Uppingham</a>.

RUYSCHE

Pages 598-598

son of Henry Ruysech <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the States-general, was born in 1638, and proved one of the greatest anatomists that ever appeared in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. He studied at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> and at Franeker, where he took his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic, and settled at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>. A piece which he published in 1665, De vesis lymphaticis & lacteis, procured him an invitation to be professor of anatomy at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>; which he gladly accepted, and where he was continually employed in dissections, to examine every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body with the most scrupulous exactness. He died in 1731, after having writ several books, in which he published many discoveries, yet not so many as he himself from his confined <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> imagined.

RYE

Pages 598-599

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, with two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, on Wednesdays and Saturdays, but no fair. It is one of the cinque-ports; is a handsome well-built <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, governed by a mayor and jurats; and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> built with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and a town-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; and consists of three streets, paved with stone. One side of the town has been walled in, and the other is guarded by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It has two gates, and is a place of considerable trade in the shipping way. From thence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of corn are exported, and many of the inhabitants are fishermen. It is 34 miles south-east by south of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUNBRIDGE">Tunbridge</a>, and 64 on the same point from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The mouth of the harbour is of late choked up with sand; but, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> well opened, it would be a good station for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a> that cruise against the French. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 50'. N. Lat. 51°.

RYMER

Pages 599-599

Esq.; was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England, and educated at the university of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. On his settling in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, he became a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Gray's-Inn; and, in 1692, succeeded Mr Shadwell as historiographer to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> William III. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning, and a lover of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; but, when he sets up for a critic, seems to prove that he has very few of the requisites for that character; and was indeed almost totally disqualified for it, by his want of candour. The severity which he has exerted, in his View of the Tragedies of the last <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">Age</a>, against the inimitable Shakespeare, are scarcely to be forgiven. Mr Rymer was, however, a very excellent antiquarian and historian. Some of his pieces relating to our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> are extremely good; and his well-known, valuable, and most useful <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, intitled the Fœdera, printed in 17 vols folio, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> stand an everlasting monument of his worth, his indefatigable assiduity, and clearness of judgment as an historical compiler. He died in 1713.

RYNCHOPS

Pages 599-599

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of anseres. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> is flat; and the superior mandible much shorter than the inferior, which is truncated at the point. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are two, viz. the nigra and fulva, both natives of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>.

RYSWICK

Pages 599-599

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> village in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, seated between the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> and Delft, where the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> has a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; and is remarkable for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> concluded here in 1667, between England, Germany, Holland, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 20'. N. Lat. 52°. S. S, f, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> s, the 18th <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> and 14th consonant of our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of which is formed by driving the breath through a narrow passage between the palate and the tongue elevated near it, together with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the lower jaw and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> towards the upper, the lips being a little way open; with such a configuration of every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the mouth and larynx, as renders the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> somewhat sibilous and hissing. Its sound however varies; being strong in some words, as this, thus, &c., and soft in words which have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> e, as wife, wife, &c. It is generally doubled at the end of words, whereby they become hard and harsh, as in kia, loa, &c. In some words it is silent, as <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, viscount, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, the long character f, is used at the beginning and middle of words, but the short s, at the end. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBREVIATIONS">abbreviations</a>, S stands for societas or facsim; as, R. S. S. for regiae societatis facsim, i.e. fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. In medicinal prescriptions, S.A. signifies secundum artem, i.e. according to the rules of art: And in the notes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, S stands for Sextus; S.P. for Spurius; S.C. for senatus consultum; S. P. Q. R. for senatus populique Romanus; S. S. S. for stratum super stratum, i.e. one layer above another alternately; S. V. B. E. E. Q. V. for si valeas bene et, ego quoque valeo, a form used in Cicero's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, in the beginning of letters. Used as a numeral, S anciently denoted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>; in the Italian music, S signifies solo: And in books of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, S stands for south; S.E. for south-east; S.W. for south-west; S.S.E. for south south-east; S.S.W. for south south-west, &c.

RYTER

Pages 598-598
lieutenant-admiral of the United Provinces, was born at Flushing in 1607, and was the son of a burgler of that city. He frequented the sea from his being 11 years of age; and was successively a sailor, mate, captain of a vessel, commodore, rear-admiral, vice-admiral, and at length lieutenant-admiral-general, which is the highest dignity to which he could be raised, since that of admiral belongs only to the governor of Holland. He succoured the Portuguese against the Spaniards; acquired great glory before Salé; engaged several times with the English; took many Turkish vessels, with the famous renegade Amand de Dias, whom he caused to be hanged in 1655. In 1659, he sailed to the assistance of the king of Denmark against the Swedes, and gave proofs of uncommon bravery in the island of Funen. In 1661, he humbled the Algerine corsairs; took a great number of vessels in 1665; and obtained a remarkable victory over the English in 1666. These brave exploits occasioned his being the same year chosen lieutenant-admiral-general; and he continued to distinguish himself till the year 1676, when he was mortally wounded by a cannon-ball, in an engagement with the French, before the town of Augusta in Sicily, and died of his wounds a few days after. His body was carried to Amsterdam, where the States General erected a magnificent monument to his memory.

SAAVEDRA

Pages 599-600

a celebrated Spanish writer, and the inimitable author of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> Quixote, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> in the year 1549. From his infancy he was fond of books; but he applied himself wholly to books of entertainment, such as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOVELS">novels</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> of all kinds, especially Spanish and Italian authors. From <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> he went to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, either to serve <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> Aquaviva, to whom he was chamberlain at Rome; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> else to follow the profession of a soldier, as he did some years under the victorious banners of Marco Antonio Colonna. He was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEPANTO">Lepanto</a>, fought in the year 1571; in which he either lost his left-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> of an harquebus, or had it so maimed that he lost the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it. After this he was taken by the Moors, and carried to Algiers, where he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a captive five years and a half. Then he returned to Spain, and applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of comedies and tragedies; and he composed several, all of which were well received by the public, and acted with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. In the year 1584, he published his Galatea, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> in six books; which he presented to Ascanio Colonna, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, as the first-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a>. But the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> which has done him the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> immortalize his name, is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Don Quixote; the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of which was printed at Madrid in the year 1605. This is a satire upon books of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>-errantry; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the sole, end of it was to destroy the reputation of these books, which had so infatuated the greater part of mankind, especially those of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. This work was universally read; and the most eminent painters, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>-workers, engravers, and sculptors, have been employed in representing the history of Don Quixote. Cervantes, even in his lifetime, obtained the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of having his work receive a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> approbation. As <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> the Third was standing in a balcony of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Madrid, and viewing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he observed a student on the banks SAB Snavedra, banks of the river Manzanares <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> in a book, and Sabaeans from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time breaking off and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> his forehead with extraordinary tokens of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and delight; upon which the king said to those about him, "That scholar is either mad, or reading Don Quixote;" the latter of which proved to be the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>. But virtus landatur et alget: notwithstanding the vast applause his book everywhere met with, he had not <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> enough to procure a small pension, but had much ado to keep himself from starving. In the year 1615, he published a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part; to which he was partly moved by the presumption of some scribbler, who had published a continuation of this work the year before. He wrote also several novels; and among the rest, "The Troubles of Perfiles and Sigismunda." He had employed many years in writing this novel, and finished it but <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; for he did not live to see it published. His sickness was of such a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that he himself was able to be, and actually was, his own historian. At the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the Troubles of Perfiles and Sigismunda, he represents himself on horseback upon the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a>; and a student overtaking him, entered into conversation with him: "And happening to talk of my illness, (says he,) the student soon let me know my doom, by saying it was a drop of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> I had got, the thirst attending which, all the water of the ocean, though it were not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, would not suffice to quench. Therefore Senor Cervantes, says he, you must drink nothing at all, but do not forget to eat; for this alone will recover you without any other physic. I have been told the same by others, answered I; but I can no more forbear tippling, than if I were born to do nothing else. My <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> to an end; and from the daily journal of my <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, I shall have finished my course by next <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> at the farthest.—But adieu, my merry friends all, for I am going to die; and I hope to see you ere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the other world, as happy as heart can wish." His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a> increased, and at last proved fatal to him; yet he continued to say and to write bons mots. He received the last sacrament on the 18th of April 1616; yet the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> after wrote a Dedication of the Troubles of Perfiles and Sigismunda, to the Condé de Lemos. The particular day of his death is not known. SABÆANS, in church-history, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of idolaters much more <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> than the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>. In the early ages of the world, idolatry was divided between two sects; the worshippers of images, called Sabaeans or Sabians; and the worshippers of fire, called <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a>. See MAGI. The Sabaeans began with worshipping the heavenly bodies, which they fancied were animated by inferior deities. In the consecration of their images, they used many incantations to draw <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into them from the stars those intelligences for whom they erected them, whose power and influence they held afterwards dwelt in them. This <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, it is said, first began among the Chaldeans, with their knowledge in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>; and from this it was that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> separated himself, when he came out of Chaldea. From the Chaldeans it spread all over the east; and from thence to the Grecians, who propagated it to all the nations of the world. The remainder of this sect still subsists in the east, and pretend to derive their name from Sabius a son of Seth; and among the books in which the doctrines of this sect are contained, they have one which they call the book of Seth, and which they pretend was written by that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>.

SABBATH

Pages 600-601
or the day of rest, a solemn festival of the Jews, on the seventh day of the week, or Saturday, beginning from sun-set on Friday to sun-set on Saturday. The observation of the Sabbath began with the world: for God having employed six days in its creation, appointed the seventh as a day of rest to be observed by man, in commemoration of that great event. On this day the Jews were commanded to abstain from all labour, and to give rest to their cattle. They were not allowed to go out of the city farther than two thousand cubits, or a mile; a custom which was founded on the distance of the ark from the tents of the Israelites, in the wilderness, after their leaving Egypt; for being permitted to go, even on the Sabbath-day, to the tabernacle to pray, they from thence inferred, that the taking a journey of no greater length, though on a different account, could not be a breach of the sabbatical rest. As the seventh day was a day of rest to the people, so was the seventh year to the land: it being unlawful in this year to plough or sow, and whatever the earth produced belonged to the poor; this was called the sabbatical year. The Jews, therefore, were obliged, during the six years, and more especially the last, to lay up a sufficient store for the sabbatical year.
