The modern as well as the ancient Jews are very superstitious in the observance of the Sabbath: they carry neither arms, nor gold, nor silver, about them, and are permitted neither to touch these, nor a candle, nor anything belonging to the fire; on which account they light up lamps on Friday, which burn till the end of the Sabbath. Christian Sabbath. See SUNDAY. SABBATH-Breaking, or profanation of the Lord's day, is punished by the municipal laws of England. For, besides the notorious indecency and scandal of permitting any secular business to be publicly transacted on that day in a country professing Christianity, and the corruption of morals which usually follows its profanation, the keeping one day in seven holy, as a time of relaxation and refreshment, as well as for public worship, is of admirable service to a state, considered merely as a civil institution. It humanizes, by the help of conversation and society, the manners of the lower classes; which would otherwise degenerate into a forid ferocity and savage selfishness of spirit: it enables the industrious workman to pursue his occupation in the ensuing week with health and cheerfulness: it imprints on the minds of the people that sense of their duty to God, so necessary to make them good citizens; but which yet would be worn out and defaced by an unremitting continuance of labour, without any stated times of recalling them to the worship of their Maker. And therefore the laws of king Athelstan forbid all merchandizing on the Lord's day, under very severe penalties. And by the statute 27 Hen. VI. c. 5. no fair or market shall be held on the principal festivals, Good-friday, or any Sunday, (except the four Sundays in harvest), on pain of forfeiting the goods exposed to sale. And, since, by the statute 1 Car. I. c. 1. no persons shall assemble, out of their own parishes, for any sport whatsoever upon this day; Sabellians nor, in their parishes, shall use any bull or bear baiting, interludes, plays, or other unlawful exercises or pastimes; on pain that every offender shall pay 3s. 4d. to the poor. This statute does not prohibit, but rather impliedly allows, any innocent recreation or amusement, within their respective parishes, even on the Lord's day, after divine service is over. But by Statute 29 Car. II. c. 7., no person allowed to work on the Lord's day, or use any boat or barge, or expose any goods to sale, except meat in public houses, milk at certain hours, and works of necessity or charity, on forfeiture of 5s. Nor shall any drover, carrier, or the like, travel upon that day, under pain of 20s.

SABELLIANS

Pages 601-601

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the 3d century, that embraced the opinions of Sabellius, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, who openly taught that there is but one person in the Godhead. The Sabellians maintained, that the Word and the Holy Spirit are only virtues, emanations, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> functions of the Deity; and held, that he who is in heaven is the Father of all things, descended into the virgin, became a child, and was born of her as a son; and that having accomplished the mystery of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>, he diffused himself on the apostles in tongues of fire, and was then denominated the Holy Ghost. This they explained by resembling God to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, the illuminative virtue or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of which was the Word, and its warming virtue the Holy Spirit. The Word, they taught, was darted, like a divine ray, to accomplish the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>; and that, being re-ascended to heaven, the influences of the Father were communicated after a like manner to the apostles.

SABINA

Pages 601-601

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territories of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Umbria, on the east by Farther Abruzzo, on the south by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> of Rome, and on the west by the patrimony of St <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>. It is 22 miles in length, and almost as much in breadth; watered by several small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and abounding in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and wine. There is no walled town in it, and Magliano is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

SABINUS

Pages 601-601

a celebrated Latin poet, born in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> in 1508. His poem Res gestae Caesarum Germanorum, spread his reputation all over Germany, and procured him the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of all the princes who had any regard for polite literature: he was made professor of the belles lettres at Frankfort on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>, rector of the new academy at Konigburg, and counsellor to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Brandenburg. He married two wives, the first of which was the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the famous reformer Melanchthon; and died in 1560. His poems are well known, and have been often printed.

SABLE

Pages 601-602
or Sable Animal, in zoology, a creature of the weasel-kind, called by authors mustela zibellina. See Mustela. Sable Trade, the trade carried on in the skins or furs of sables: of which the following commercial history was translated by Mr J. R. Forster, from a Russian performance on that subject by Mr Muller. "Sable, soble, in Russian; zobel in German. Their price varies, from 1l. to 10l. sterling, and above; fine and middling sable-skins are without bellies, and the coarse ones are with them. Forty skins make a collection called zimmer. The finest sables are sold in pairs perfectly similar, and are dearer than single ones of the same goodness; for the Russians want those in pairs for facing caps, cloaks, tippets, &c. the blackest are reputed the best. Sables are in season from November to February; for those caught at any other time of the year are short-haired, and then called nadofiski. The hair of sables differs in length and quality: the long hairs, which reach far beyond the inferior ones, are called os; the more a skin has of such long hairs, the blacker they are, and the more valuable is the fur; the very best have no other but those long and black hairs. Motchka is a technical term used in the Russian fur-trade, expressing the lower part of the long hairs; and sometimes it comprehends likewise the lower and shorter hairs: the abovementioned best sable furs are said to have a black motchka. Below the long hairs are, in the greater part of the sable-furs, some shorter hairs, called podofie, i.e. under-os; the more podofie a fur has, the less valuable: in the better kind of sables the podofie has black tips, and a grey or rufly motchka. The first kind of motchka makes the middling kind of sable furs; the red one the worst, especially if it has but few os. Between the os and podofie is a low woolly kind of hair, called podfada. The more podfada a fur has, the less valuable: for the long hair will, in such case, take no other direction than the natural one; for the characters of sable is, that notwithstanding the hair naturally lies from the head towards the tail, yet it will lie equally in any direction as you strike your hand over it. The various combinations of these characters, in regard to os, motchka, podofie, and podfada, make many special divisions in the goodness of furs: besides this, the furriers attend to the size, preferring always, exeteris paribus, the biggest, and those that have the greatest glofs. The size depends upon the animal being a male or a female, the latter being always smaller. The glofs vanishes in old furs: the fresh ones have a kind of bloomy appearance, as they express it; the old ones are said to have done blooming: the dyed sables always lose their glofs; become less uniform, whether the lower hairs have taken the dye or not; and commonly the hairs are somewhat twisted or crisped, and not so straight as in the natural ones. Some fumigate the skins, to make them look blacker; but the smell, and the crisped condition of the long hair, betrays the cheat; and both ways are detected by rubbing the fur with a moist linen-cloth, which grows black in such cases. "The Chinese have a way of dyeing the sables, so that the colour not only lasts, (which the Russian cheats cannot do), but the fur keeps its glofs, and the crisped hairs only discover it. This is the reason that all the fables, which are of the best kind, either in pairs or separate, are carried to Russia; the rest go to China. The very best sables come from the environs of Nertchinsk and Yakutsk; and in this latter district, the country about the river Ud affords sometimes sables, of whom one single fur is often sold at the rate of 60 or 70 rubles, 12l. or 14l. The bellies of sables, which are sold in pairs, are about two fingers breadth, and are tied together by 40 pieces, which are sold from 1l. to 2l. sterling. Tails are sold by the hundred. The very best sable-furs must have their tails; but ordinary sables are often cropped, and 100 sold from 4l. to 8l. sterling. The legs or feet of sables are seldom sold separately: white sables are rare, and no common merchandise, but bought only as curiosities: some are yellowish, and Sable, in heraldry, signifies "black;" and is borrowed from the French, as are most terms in this science; in engraving it is expressed by both horizontal and perpendicular lines crossing each other. Sable itself signifies constancy, learning, and grief; and ancient heralds will have it, that it is compounded with Or [Honour] Arg. [Fame] Gui. [Respect] Azur. [Application] Ver. [Comfort] Pur. [Austerity] The occasion that introduced this colour into heraldry is thus related by Alexander Nissett, p. 8. The duke of Anjou, king of Sicily, after the loss of that kingdom, appeared at a tournament in Germany all in black, with his shield of that tincture, somé de larmes, i.e. besprinkled with drops of water, to represent tears, indicating by that both his grief and loss.

SABLESTAN

Pages 602-602
or SABUSTAN, a province of Asia, in Persia, on the frontiers of Indostan; bounded on the north by Khorasan; on the east, by the mountains of Balk and Candahar; on the south, by Sagistan, or Segestan; and on the west, by Heri. It is a mountainous country, very little known to Europeans; nor is it certain which is the capital town.

SABRE

Pages 602-602

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> scimitar, with a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and heavy blade, thick at the back, and a little falced or crooked towards the point. It is the ordinary weapon worn by the Turks, who are said to be very expert in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it.

SABURRA

Pages 602-602

in medicine, usually denotes any collection of half putrid indigested <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in the stomach and intestines, by which the operation of digestion is impeded.

SABURRAE

Pages 602-602

gritts, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; a genus of fossils, found in minute masses, forming together a kind of powder, the several particles of which are of no determinate shape, nor have any tendency to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of crystal, but seem rudely broken fragments of larger masses; not to be dissolved <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> disunited by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, but retaining their figure in it, and not cohering by means of it into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>; considerably opake, and in many <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> fermenting with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>; often fouled with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> matters, and not unfrequently taken in the coarser stony and mineral or metalline particles. Gritts are of various colours, as, 1. The stony and sparry gritts, of a bright or greyish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> stony gritts. 3. The green stony gritts, composed of homogene sparry particles. 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> gritt, of which there is only one species. 5. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and blackish gritts, composed of stony or talky particles.

SACCADE

Pages 602-602

in the manege, is a jerk more <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> less violent, given by the horseman to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, in pulling or twitching the reins of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a> all on a sudden and with one pull, and that when a horse lies heavy upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, or obstinately arms himself. This is a correction used to make a horse carry well; but it ought to be used discreetly, and but seldom.

SACCHARUM

Pages 602-602
Sugar, or the Sugar-Cane; in botany, a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the triandria clas of plants. There is but one species of this genus, viz. the officinarum; a genus of both the Indies, where it grows naturally, and is cultivated for its juice, which when boiled affords the sweet salt called sugar. See that article.

SACCHI

Pages 602-602

a celebrated painter, born at Rome in 1594. He was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Francisco <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANO">Albano</a>, whom he afterwards surpassed in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and correctness. He distinguished himself in a very eminent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> by his paintings in fresco; and a strong emulation subsisting between him and Pietro de Cortona, they each arrived at a degree of perfection that neither of them might have known, without such a competition. The works of Sacchi have such intrinsic merit, and are finished with such uncommon care and skill, as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> always secure the applause of the judicious, and preserve their true value. He died in 1668.

SACCULUS

Pages 602-602

in anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of saccus, signifies a little bag, and is applied to many parts of the body.

SACHEVEREL

Pages 602-602

a famous clergyman of the Tory <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>; who distinguished himself by indecent and scurrilous sermons and writings against the dissenters and revolution principles. He owed his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, however, to being indiscreetly prosecuted by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords, for his affiz-sermon at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, and his 5th of November sermon at St Paul's in 1709; in which he asserted the doctrine of non resistance to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> in its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; and reflected severely on the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of toleration. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and low <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> parties were very violent at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of Sacheverel inflamed the high-church party to dangerous riots and excesses: he was, however, furlonged for three years, and his sermons burned by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> hangman. The Tories being in administration when Sacheverel's suspension expired, he was freed with every circumstance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and public rejoicing; was ordered to preach before the commons on the 29th of May, had the thanks of the house for his discourse, and obtained the valuable rectory of St Andrew's, Holborn. SACK of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">Wool</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of wool containing <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> 22 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and every stone 14 pounds. In Scotland, a sack is 24 stone, each stone containing 16 pounds. Sack of Cotton Wool, a quantity from one hundred and a half to four hundred <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. Sacks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>, in fortification, are canvas bags filled with earth. They are used in making retrenchments in haste, to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on parapets, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the head of the breaches, &c., to repair them, when beaten <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>.

SACKBUT

Pages 602-602

a musical <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> kind, being a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, though different from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> trumpet both in form and size; it is fit to play a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>, and is contrived to be drawn out <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> shortened, according to the tone required, whether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> or acute. The Italians call it trombone, and the Latins tuba ductilis.

SACKVILLE

Pages 602-603

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and poet, descended from the foregoing, was born in 1637. He was, like Villiers, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, Sedley, &c. one of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIBERTINES">libertines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and sometimes indulged himself in inexcusable excesses. He openly discountenanced the violent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of James II. and engaged early for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>. Sackville. Orange, by whom he was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chamberlain of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, and taken into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. He died in 1706, and left several poetical pieces, which, though not considerable enough to make a volume by themselves, may be found among the works of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> poets, published in 1749. Sackville (Thomas, Lord Buckhurst, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Dorset), a statesman and poet, the son of Richard Sackville, Esq; of Buckhurst, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Witham in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, was born in the year 1536. He was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HART">Hart</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in the latter end of the reign of Edward VI. whence he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he took a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and thence to the Inner Temple. He now applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and was called to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>. We are told that he commenced poet whilst at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and that these his juvenile productions were much admired, none of which however have been preserved. In the fourth and fifth year of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, we find him a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons; about which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, in 1557, he wrote a poetical piece, intitled The Induction, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> The Mirror of Magistrates. This last was meant to comprehend all the unfortunate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> from the beginning of our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> being dropped, it was inserted in the body of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The Mirror of Magistrates is formed on a dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; in which the persons is introduced speaking. The Induction is written much in the style of Spencer, who, with some <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, is supposed to have imitated this author. In 1561, his tragedy of Gorboduc was acted before queen <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> by the gentlemen of the Inner Temple. This was the first tolerable tragedy in our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">Companion</a> to the Play-house tells us, that the three first acts were written by Mr Tho. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol13.html#article-NORTON">Norton</a>. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Sidney, in his Apology for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, says, "it is full of stately speeches and well-founded phrases, climbing to the height of Seneca in his style, &c." Rymer speaks highly in its commendation. Mr Spence, at the instigation of Mr Pope, republished it in 1736, with a pompous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>. It is said to be our first dramatic piece written in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. In the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of this reign, Mr Sackville was member for Sussex, and for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, he made the tour of France and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and in 1566 was imprisoned at Rome, when he was informed of his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, by which he became possessed of a very considerable fortune. Having now obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, he returned to England; and being first knighted, was created Lord Buckhurst. In 1570 he was sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to France. In 1586 he was one of the commissioners appointed to try the unfortunate Mary queen of Scots; and was the messenger employed to report the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, and to see it executed. The year following he went ambassador to the States-General, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their complaint against the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>; who, disliking his impartiality, prevailed on the queen to recall him, and confine him to his house. In this state of confinement he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> about 10 months, when Leicester dying, he was restored to favour, and in 1580 was installed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>: but the most incontrovertible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the queen's partiality for lord Buckhurst appeared in the year 1591, when she caused him to be elected <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> in the university of Oxford, in opposition to her favourite <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>. In 1598, on the death of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Burleigh, lord Buckhurst succeeded him, and by virtue of his office became in effect prime minister; and when, in 1601, the earls of Essex and Southampton were brought to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, he sat as lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> on that awful occasion. On the accession of James I. he was graciously received, had the office of lord high treasurer confirmed to him for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and was created earl of Dorset. He continued in high favour with the king till the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of his death; which happened suddenly, on the 19th of April 1608, in the council-chamber at Whitehall. He was interred with great solemnity in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. He was a good poet, an able minister, and an honest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>. From him is descended the present noble family of the Dorsets. "It were needless (says Mr Walpole) to add, that he was the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a> of genius and wit."

SACRAMENT

Pages 603-607

t signifies, in general, a sign of a thing sacred and holy; and is defined to be an outward and visible sign of a spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>. Thus there are two objects in a sacrament; the one the object of the senses, and the other the object of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> admit only of two sacraments, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, and the eucharist <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, viz. baptism, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>, the eucharist, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> unction, ordination, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. The Romanists, however, by way of eminence, call the eucharist the holy sacrament. Thus to expose the holy sacrament, is to lay the consecrated <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOST">host</a> on the altar to be adored. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> of the holy sacrament, is that in which this host is carried about the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, or about a town. Sacramentary, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman church-book, which contains all the prayers and ceremonies practised at the celebration of the sacraments. It was wrote by pope Gelasius, and afterwards revised, corrected, and abridged by St Gregory. Sacred, something holy, or that is solemnly offered and consecrated to God, with benedictions, uncions, &c. Sacrifice, a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship, which consisted in dedicating or offering up something animate or inanimate on an altar, by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, either as an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to the Deity for some signal mercy, or to acknowledge their dependence on him, or to conciliate his favour. The origin of sacrifices is by some ascribed to the Phoenicians; but Porphyry ascribes it to the Egyptians, who first offered the first-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their grounds to the gods, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> them upon an altar of turf: thus in the most ancient sacrifices there were neither living creatures, nor any thing costly or magnificent, and no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a> or frankincense. At length they began to burn perfumes: and afterwards men, leaving their ancient diet of herbs and roots, and beginning to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> living creatures for food, began also to change their sacrifices. The scriptures, however, furnish us with a different account: for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>, it is said, sacrificed animals at his coming out of the ark; and even <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABEL">Abel</a> himself sacrificed the best and fattest of his flock; but Grotius thinks it more probable that he contented himself with making a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> oblation of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a>, &c. without slaying them. The Jews had two sorts of sacrifices, taking the word in its largest signification: The first were offerings of tythes, first-fruits, cakes, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and the like; and the last, offerings of slaughtered animals. When an Israelite offered a loaf or a cake, the priest broke it in two parts; and setting aside that half which he reserved for himself, broke the other into crumbs, poured oil, wine, incense, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> upon it, and spread the whole upon the fire of the altar. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> these offerings were accompanied with the sacrifice of an animal, they were thrown upon the victim to be consumed along with it. If the offerings were of the ears of new corn, they were parched at the fire, rubbed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and then offered to the priest in a vessel, over which he poured oil, incense, wine, and salt, and then burnt it upon the altar, having first taken as much of it as of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> belonged to himself. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sacrifices among the Hebrews consisted of bullocks, sheep, and goats; but doves and turtles were accepted from those who were not able to bring the other; these beasts were to be perfect, and without blemish. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of sacrificing were various; all of which are very minutely described in the books of Moses. The manner of sacrificing among the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> was as follows. In the choice of the victim, they took care that it was without blemish or imperfection; its tail was not to be too small at the end; the tongue not <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, nor the ears cleft; and that the bull was one that had never been yoked. The victim being pitched upon, they girt his forehead and horns, especially if a bull, heifer, or cow. The head they also adorned with a garland of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, a woollen insula or holy <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FILLET">fillet</a>, whence hung two rows of chaplets with twisted ribands; and on the middle of the body a kind of stole, pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, hung <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on each side; the lesser victims were only adorned with garlands and bundles of flowers, together with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> tufts or wreaths. The victims thus prepared were brought before the altar; the lesser being driven to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the greater led by an halter; when, if they made any struggle, or refused to go, the resistance was taken for an ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>, and the sacrifice frequently set aside. The victim thus brought was carefully examined, to see that there was no defect in it; then the priest, clad in his sacrificial <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and accompanied with the sacrificers and other attendants, and being washed and purified according to the ceremonies prescribed, turned to the right-hand, and went round the altar, sprinkling it with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> and holy-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and also betaking those who were present. Then the crier proclaimed with a loud <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, Who is here? To which the people replied, Many and good. The priest then having exhorted the people to join with him by saying, Let us pray, confessed his own unworthiness, acknowledging that he had been guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> sins; for which he begged <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> of the gods, hoping that they would be pleased to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> his requests, accept the oblations offered them, and send them all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>; and to this general form added petitions for such particular favours as were then desired. Prayers being ended, the priest took a cup of wine; and having tasted it himself, caused his assistants to do the like; and then poured forth the remainder between the horns of the victim. Then the priest or the crier, or sometimes the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> person in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, killed the beast, by knocking it down or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> its throat. If the sacrifice was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the celestial gods, the throat was turned up towards heaven; but if they sacrificed to the heroes or infernal gods, the victim was killed with its throat towards the ground. If by accident the beast escaped the stroke, leaped up after it, or expired with pain and difficulty, it was thought to be unacceptable to the gods. The beast being killed, the priest inspected its entrails, and made predictions from them. They then poured wine, together with frankincense, into the fire, to increase the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, and then laid the sacrifice on the altar; which in the primitive times was burnt whole to the gods, and thence called an holocaust; but in after-times, only <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the victim was consumed in the fire, and the remainder reserved for the sacrificers; the thighs, and sometimes the entrails, being burnt to their honour, the company feasted upon the rest. While the priest was sacrificing, the priest, and the person who gave the sacrifice, jointly prayed, laying their hands upon the altar. Sometimes they played upon musical instruments in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the sacrifice, and on some occasions they danced round the altar, singing sacred hymns in honour of the god. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> Sacrifices. One would think it scarce possible, that so unnatural a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> as that of human sacrifices should have existed in the world: but it is very certain, that it did not only exist, but almost universally prevail. The Egyptians of old brought no victims to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, nor shed any blood at their altars: But human victims and the blood of men must be here excepted; which at one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> they most certainly offered to their gods. The Cretans had the same custom; and adhered to it a much longer time. The nations of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> did the same. The people of Duma, in particular, sacrificed every year a child; and buried it underneath an altar, which they made use of instead of an idol: for they did not admit of images. The Persians buried people alive. Amestris, the wife of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>, entombed 12 persons quick under ground for the good of her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. It would be endless to enumerate every <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, or every <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, where these dire practices obtained. The Cyprians, the Rhodians, the Phoceans, the Ionians, those of Chios, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENEDOS">Tenedos</a>, all had human sacrifices. The natives of the Tauric Chersonesus offered up to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> every stranger whom chance threw upon their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. Hence arose that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> expofulation in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>, upon the insufficiency of the proceeding; wherein much good reasoning is implied. Iphigenia wonders, as the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> delighted in the blood of men, that every villain and murderer should be privileged to escape, nay, be driven from the threshold of the temple; whereas, if an honest and virtuous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> chanced to stray thither, he only was seized upon, and put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The Pelasgi, in a time of scarcity, vowed the tenth of all that should be born to them, for a sacrifice, in order to procure plenty. Arisotomenes the Messenian slew 300 noble Lacedemonians, among whom was Theopompus the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, at the altar of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> at Ithome. Without doubt the Lacedemonians did not fail to make ample returns: for they were a severe and revengeful people, and offered the like victims to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>. Their festival of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAMASTIGOSIS">Diamastigosis</a> is well known; when the Spartan boys were whipped in the sight of their parents with such Such severity before the altar of Diana Ortilia, that they often expired under the torture. Phylarchus affirms, as he is quoted by Porphyry, that of old every Grecian state made it a rule, before they marched towards an enemy, to solicit a blessing on their undertakings by human victims. The Romans were accustomed to the like sacrifices. They both devoted themselves to the infernal gods, and constrained others to submit to the same horrid doom. Hence we read in Titus Livius, that, in the consulship of Emilius Paulus and Terentius Varro, two Gauls, a man and a woman, and two in like manner of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, were buried alive at Rome in the Ox-Market; where was a place under ground, walled round to receive them; which had before been made use of for such cruel purposes. He says it was a sacrifice not properly Roman, that is, not originally of Roman <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>; yet it was frequently practised there, and that too by public authority. Plutarch makes mention of a like instance a few years before, in the consulship of Flaminius and Furius. There is reason to think, that all the principal captives who graced the triumphs of the Romans, were at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of that cruel pageantry put to death at the altar of Jupiter Capitolinus. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Marius offered up his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> for a victim to the Dii Averrunci, to procure success in a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CIMBRI">Cimbri</a>; as we are informed by Dorotheus, quoted by Clemens. It is likewise attested by Plutarch, who says that her name was Calpurnia. Marius was a man of a sour and bloody disposition; and had probably heard of such sacrifices being offered in the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, among whom they were very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>: or he might have beheld them exhibited at a distance; and therefore murdered what was nearest, and should have been dearest, to him, to counteract their fearful spells, and outdo them in their wicked machinery. Cicero making mention of this custom being common in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, adds, that it prevailed among that people even at the time he was speaking: from whence we may be led to infer, that it was then discontinued among the Romans. And we are told by Pliny, that it had then, and not very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, been discouraged. For there was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> enacted, when Lentulus and Crassus were consuls, so late as the 657th year of Rome, that there should be no more human sacrifices: for till that time those horrid rites had been celebrated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> without any mask or contrivance; which, had we not the best <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> for the fact, would appear scarce credible. And however they may have been discontinued for a time, we find that they were again renewed; tho' they became not so public, nor so general. For not very long after this, it is reported of Augustus Caesar, when <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERUGIA">Perugia</a> surrendered in the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> triumvirate, that besides multitudes executed in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> manner, he offered up, upon the Ides of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, 300 chosen persons, both of the equestrian and senatorial order, at an altar dedicated to the manes of his uncle Julius. Even at Rome itself this custom was revived: and Porphyry affirms us, that, in his time a man was every year sacrificed at the shrine of Jupiter Latarius. Heliogabalus offered the like victims to the Syrian deity, which he introduced among the Romans. The same is said of Aurelian. The Gauls and the Germans were so devoted to this shocking custom, that no business of any moment was transacted among them without being prefaced with the blood of men. They were offered up to various gods; but particularly to Helus, Taranis, and Thautates. These deities are mentioned by Lucan, where he enumerates the various nations who followed the fortunes of Caesar. The altars of these gods were far removed from the common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of men; being generally situated in the depth of woods, that the gloom might add to the horror of the operation, and give a reverence to the place and proceeding. The persons devoted were led thither by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRUIDS">Druids</a>, who presided at the solemnity; and performed the cruel offices of the sacrifice. Tacitus takes notice of the cruelty of the Hermunduri, in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Catti, wherein they had greatly the advantage; at the close of which they made one general sacrifice of all that was taken in battle. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> remains of the legions under Varus suffered in some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> the same fate. There were many places destined for this purpose all over Gaul and Germany; but especially in the mighty woods of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARDENNES">Ardennes</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Hercinian forest; a wild that extended above 30 days journey in length. The places set apart for this solemnity were held in the utmost reverence, and only approached at particular seasons. Lucan mentions a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> of this sort near Massilia, which even the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were afraid to violate, the commandant by Caesar. It was one of those set apart for the sacrifices of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Claudian compliments Stilicho, that, among other advantages accruing to the Roman armies through his conduct, they could now venture into the awful forest of Hercinia, and follow the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> in those so much dreaded woods, and otherwise make use of them. These practices prevailed among all the people of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, of whatever denomination. The Massagetae, the Scythians, the Getes, the Sarmatians, all the various nations upon the Baltic, particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUEVI">Suevi</a> and Scandinavians, held it as a fixed principle, that their happiness and security could not be obtained but at the expense of the lives of others. Their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> gods were Thor and Woden, whom they thought they could never sufficiently glut with blood. They had many very celebrated places of worship; especially in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Rugen, near the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>; and in Zeeland; some, too, very famous among the Semones and Naharvali. But the most reverenced of all, and the most frequented, was at Upsal; where there was every year a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> celebrity, which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> days. During this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> they sacrificed animals of all sorts: but the most acceptable victims, and the most numerous, were men. Of these sacrifices none were esteemed so auspicious and salutary, as a sacrifice of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the country. When the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> fell for the king to die, it was received with universal acclamations and every expression of joy; as it once happened in the time of a famine, when they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> lots, and it fell to king Domaldor to be the people's victim: and he was accordingly put to death. Olaus Tretelger, another prince, was burnt alive to Woden. They did not spare their own children. Harald the son of Gunild, the first of that name, slew two of his children to obtain a storm of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. "He did not let (says Verstegan) to sacrifice two of his sons unto his idols, to the end he might obtain of them such a tempest." tempest at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, as should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> and disperse the shipping of Harald king of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>." Saxo Grammaticus mentions a like fact. He calls the king Haquin; and speaks of the persons put to death as two very hopeful young princes. Another king slew nine sons, in order to prolong his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; in hopes, perhaps, that what they were abridged of would in great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> be added to himself. Such instances, however, occur not often: but the common victims were without end. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Bremensis, speaking of the awful grove at Upsal, where these horrid rites were celebrated, says, that there was not a single tree but what was reverenced, as if it were gifted with some portion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and all this because they were stained with gore, and foul with human <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. The same is observed by Scheffer in his account of this place. The manner in which the victims were slaughtered, was diverse in different places. Some of the Gaulish nations chined them with a stroke of an ax. The Celts placed the man who was to be offered for a sacrifice upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, or an altar, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> upwards, and with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> struck him forcibly across the sternum; then tumbling him to the ground, from his agonies and convulsions, as well as from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of blood, they formed a judgment of future events. The Cimbri ripped open the bowels; and from them they pretended to divine. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> they <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> men's brains out with an ox-yoke. The same operation was performed in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>, by dashing them against an altar of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. In many places they transfixed them with arrows. After they were dead they suspended them upon the trees, and left them to putrefy. One of the writers above quoted, mentions that in his time 70 carcases of this sort were found in a wood of the Scavi. Dithmar of Merlburgh, an author of nearly the same <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, speaks of a place called Ledur in Zeeland, where there were every year 99 persons sacrificed to the god Swantowite. During these bloody festivals a general joy prevailed; and banquets were most royally served. They fed, caroused, and gave a loafe to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>, which at other times was not permitted. They imagined that there was something mysterious in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> nine: for which reason these feasts were in some places celebrated every ninth year, in others every ninth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; and continued for nine days. When all was ended, they washed the image of the deity in a pool; and then dismissed the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. Their servants were numerous, who attended during the term of their feasting, and partook of the banquet. At the close of all, they were smothered in the same pool, or otherwise made away with. On which Tacitus remarks, how great an awe this circumstance must necessarily infuse into those who were not admitted to these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>. These accounts are handed down from a variety of authors in different ages; many of whom were natives of the countries which they describe, and to which they seem strongly attached. They would not therefore have brought so foul an imputation on the part of the world in favour of which they were each <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, nor could there be that concurrence of testimony, were not the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in general true. The like custom prevailed to a great degree at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, and even under the mild <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Peruvians; and in most parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> it is still kept up; where, in the inland parts, they sacrifice some of the captives taken in war to their fetishes, in order to secure their favour. Snellgrave was in the king of Dahomee's camp, after his inroad into the countries of Ardra and Whidaw; and says, that he was a witness to the cruelty of this prince, whom he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> sacrifice multitudes to the deity of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. The sacrifices of which we have been treating, if we except some few instances, consisted of persons doomed by the chance of war, or assigned by lot, to be offered. But among the nations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, the victims were peculiarly chosen. Their own children, and whatever was nearest and dearest to them, were deemed the most worthy offering to their god. The Carthaginians, who were a colony from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>, carried with them the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of their mother-country, and instituted the same worship in the parts where they settled. It consisted in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of several deities, but particularly of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KRONUS">Kronus</a>; to whom they offered human sacrifices, and especially the blood of children. If the parents were not at hand to make an immediate offer, the magistrates did not fail to make choice of what was most fair and promising; that the god might not be defrauded of his dues. Upon a check being received in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and some other alarming circumstances happening, Himilcar without any hesitation laid hold of a boy, and offered him on the spot to Kronus; and at the same time drowned a number of priests, to appease the deity of the sea. The Carthaginians another time, upon a great defeat of their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> by Agathocles, imputed their miscarriages to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> of this god, whose services had been neglected. Touched with this, and seeing the enemy at their gates, they seized at once 300 children of the prime <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and offered them in public for a sacrifice. Three hundred more, being persons who were somehow obnoxious, yielded themselves voluntarily, and were put to death with the others. The neglect of which they accused themselves, consisted in sacrificing children purchased of parents among the poorer sort, who reared them for that purpose; and not selecting the most promising, and the most honourable, as had been the custom of old. In short, there were particular children brought up for the altar, as sheep are fattened for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHAMBLES">shambles</a>; and they were bought and butchered in the same manner. But this indiscriminate way of proceeding was thought to have given offence. It is remarkable, that the Egyptians looked out for the most specious and handsome person to be sacrificed. The Albanians pitched upon the best man of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, and made him pay for the wickedness of the rest. The Carthaginians chose what they thought the most excellent, and at the same time the most dear to them; which made the lot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> heavy upon their children. This is taken notice of by Silius Italicus in his fourth book. Kronus, to whom these sacrifices were exhibited, was an oriental deity, the god of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and fire; and therefore always worshipped with some reference to that element. See PHOENICIA. The Greeks, we find, called the deity to whom these offerings were made Agraulos; and feigned that she was a woman, and the daughter of Cecrops. But how came Cecrops to have any connection with Cyprus? Agraulos is a corruption and transposition of the ori- original name, which should have been rendered Uk El Aur, or Uk El Aurus; but has, like many other oriental titles and names, been strangely sophicated; and is here changed to Agraulos. It was in reality the god of light, who was always worshipped with fire. This deity was the Moloch of the Tyrians and Canaanites, and the Molech of the east; that is, the great and principal god, the god of light, of whom fire was esteemed a symbol; and at whose shrine, instead of other victims, they offered the blood of men. Such was the Kronos of the Greeks, and the Moloch of the Phoenicians: and nothing can appear more shocking than the sacrifices of the Tyrians and Carthaginians, which they performed to this idol. In all emergencies of state, and times of general calamity, they devoted what was most necessary and valuable to them, for an offering to the gods, and particularly to Moloch. But besides these undetermined times of bloodshed, they had particular and prescribed seasons every year, when children were chosen out of the most noble and reputable families, as before mentioned. If a person had an only child, it was the more liable to be put to death, as being esteemed more acceptable to the deity, and more efficacious of the general good. Those who were sacrificed to Kronos were thrown into the arms of a molten idol, which stood in the midst of a large fire, and was <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. The arms of it were stretched out, with the hands turned upwards, as it were to receive them; yet flopping downwards, so that they dropt from thence into a glowing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> below. To other gods they were otherwise slaughtered, and, as it is implied, by the very hands of their parents. What can be more horrid to the imagination, than to suppose a father leading the dearest of all his sons to such an infernal shrine? or a mother the most engaging and affectionate of her daughters, just rising to maturity, to be slaughtered at the altar of Ashteroth or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAAL">Baal</a>? Justin describes this unnatural custom very pathetically: Quippe homines, ut vires, immolabant; et impubes (quae etas sofitur misericordiam provocat) aris adnuehant; pucem sanguine eorum expolcentes, pro quorum vitâ Dii regari maxime solent. Such was their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> zeal, that this was continually practised; and to much of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> affection still left unextinguished, as to render the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> ten times more shocking from the tenderness which they seemed to express. They embraced their children with great fondness, and encouraged them in the gentlest terms, that they might not be appalled at the sight of the hellish <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>; begging of them to submit with cheerfulness to this fearful operation. If there was any appearance of a tear rising, or a cry unawares escaping, the mother smothered it with her kisses, that there might not be any show of backwardness or constraint, but the whole be a free-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> offering. These cruel endearments over, they stabbed them to the heart, or otherwise opened the sluices of life; and with the blood warm, as it ran, besmeared the altar and the grim visage of the idol. These were the customs which the Israelites learned of the people of Canaan, and for which they are upbraided by the Psalmist: "They did not destroy the nations, concerning whom the Lord commanded them; but were mingled among the heathen, and learned their works: yea, they sacrificed their sons and their daughters unto devils, and shed innocent blood, even the blood of their sons and of their daughters, whom they sacrificed unto the idols of Canaan; and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> was polluted with blood. Thus were they defiled with their own works, and went a-whoring with their own inventions." These cruel rites, practised in so many nations, made Plutarch debate with himself, "Whether it would not have been better for the Galates, or for the Scythians, to have had no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of any superior beings, than to have formed to themselves notions of gods who delighted in the blood of men; of gods, who esteemed human victims the most acceptable and perfect sacrifice? Would it not," says he, "have been more eligible for the Carthaginians to have had the atheistical Critias, or Diagorus, their lawgiver at the commencement of their polity, and to have been taught, that there was neither god nor daemon, than to have sacrificed, in the manner they were wont, to the god which they adored? Wherein they acted, not as the person did whom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEDOCLES">Empedocles</a> describes in some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, where he exposes this unnatural custom. The fire there with many idle vows offers up unwittingly his son for a sacrifice; but the youth was so changed in feature and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, that his father did not know him. These people used, knowingly and wilfully, to go through this bloody <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and slaughter their own offspring. Even they who were childless would not be exempted from this cursed tribute; but purchased children, at a price, of the poorer sort, and put them to death with as little remorse as one would kill a lamb or a chicken. The mother, who sacrificed her child, stood by, without any seeming <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of what she was losing, and without uttering a groan. If a sigh did by chance escape, she lost all the honour which she professed to herself in the offering; and the child was notwithstanding slain. All the time of this celebrity, while the children were murdering, there was a noise of clarions and tabors sounding before the idol, that the cries and shrieks of the victims might not be heard. Tell me now," says Plutarch, "if the monsters of old, the Typhons, and the giants, were to expel the gods, and to rule the world in their stead; could they require a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> more horrid than these infernal rites and sacrifices?"

SACRILEGE

Pages 607-607

the crime of profaning sacred things, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> those devoted to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of God.

SACRISTY

Pages 607-607

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an apartment in a church where the sacred utensils were kept, being the same with our Vestry.

SADDLE

Pages 607-607

is a seat upon a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s back, contrived for the conveniency of the rider. A hunting-saddle is composed of two bows, two bands, fore-bolsters, pannels, and saddle-straps; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> saddle has, besides these parts, corks, hind-bolsters, and a trouslequin. The pommel is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to both.

SADDUCEES

Pages 607-608

in Jewish antiquity, a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Jews, so called from their founder Sadoc Antigonus of Socho, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the sanhedrim at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, and teacher of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>-school of that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Having often, in his lectures, asserted to his scholars, that they ought not to serve God in a servile manner, with respect to reward, but only out of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and fear, two of his scholars, Sadoc and Baithus, inferred from thence, that there were no rewards <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> punishments after this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and, therefore, separating from the school of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, they taught, that there was no <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> nor future state. Many embracing this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, gave rise to the sect of the Sadducees, who were a kind of epicureans; but differing from them in this, that tho' they denied a future state, yet they allowed the world was created by the power of God, and governed by his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>; whereas the followers of Epicurus denied both. The Sadducees denied all manner of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREDESTINATION">predestination</a> whatever; and not only rejected all unwritten traditions, but also all the books of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, excepting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>.

SADLER

Pages 608-608

was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>; born in 1615; and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he became eminent for his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> knowledge in the oriental languages. He removed to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s-Inn, where he made no small progress in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and in 1644 was admitted one of the masters in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">Chancery</a>, as also one of the two masters of Requests. In 1649, he was chosen town-clerk of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and the same year published his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">Rights</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">Kingdom</a>. He was greatly esteemed by Oliver Cromwell, by whose special warrant he was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in Chancery, when their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> was reduced to six. By his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> it was that the Jews obtained the privilege of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> for themselves a synagogue in London. In 1658, he was made member of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a>; and next year was appointed first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> under the great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> with Mr Taylor, Mr Whitelocke, and others, for the probate of wills. In 1660, he published his Obia. Soon after the Restoration, he lost all his employments. In the fire of London in 1666, he was a great sufferer; which obliged him to retire to his seat of Warmwell in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, where he lived in a private manner till 1674, when he died.

SADOC

Pages 608-608

a famous Jewish rabbi, and founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Sadducees. He was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Antigonus, who taught, that virtue was to be practised for its excellency alone, without regard to any recompence whatever; from whence Sadoc drew this erroneous inference, That no rewards were to be hoped for, nor punishments to be dreaded, in another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The sect still subsists in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. Sadoc flourished about 220 B.C.

SADOLET

Pages 608-608

a polite and learned <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> of the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a> in 1477. Leo X. made him and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Bembus his secretaries, an office for which they were both well qualified; and Sadolet was soon after made bishop of Carpentras, near <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>: he was made a cardinal in 1536 by Paul III. and employed in several negotiations and embassies. He died in 1547, not without the suspicion of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, for corresponding too familiarly with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, and for testifying too much regard for some of their doctors. His works, which are all in Latin, were collected in 1607 at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, in one vol. 8vo. All his contemporaries spoke of him in the highest terms.

SAFE-CONDUCT

Pages 608-608

is a security given by a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, to a stranger for his safe-coming into and passing out of the realm; the form whereof is in Reg. Orig. 25. There are letters of safe-conduct which must be enrolled in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>; and the persons to whom granted must have them ready to show; and touching which there are several statutes. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREROGATIVE">PREROGATIVE</a>.

SAFE-GUARD

Pages 608-608

a protection formerly granted to a stranger who feared violence from some of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s subjects for seeking his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> by course of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>.

SAFFRON

Pages 608-610

in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>, is formed of the stigmata of the crocus officinalis *, dried on a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KILN">kiln</a>, and pressed together into cakes. Of this there are two kinds, the English and Spanish; of which the latter is by far the most esteemed. Saffron is principally cultivated in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>, in a circle of about ten miles diameter. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of this tract is an open <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with few inclosures; and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> there is, as in most other places, to crop two years, and let the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> be fallow the third. Saffron is generally planted upon fallow ground, and, all other things being alike, they prefer that which has borne barley the year before. The saffron ground is seldom above three acres, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> less than one; and, in choosing, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> thing they have regard to is, that they be well exposed, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, nor a very stiff clay, but a temperate dry mould, such as <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> lies upon chalk, and is of an hazel-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; though, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> every thing else answers, the colour of the mould is pretty much neglected. The ground being made choice of, about Lady-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, or the beginning of April, it must be carefully ploughed, the furrows being drawn much closer together, and deeper, if the soil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> allow it, than is done for any kind of corn; and accordingly the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> is greater. About five weeks after, during any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May, they lay between 20 and 30 loads of dung upon each <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, and having spread it with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> it in as before. The shortest rotten dung is the best; and the farmers, who have the convenience of making it, spare no pains to make it good, being sure of a proportionable price for it. About Midsummer they plough a third time, and between every 16 feet and an half they leave a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> furrow or trench, which serves both as a boundary to the several parcels, and for throwing the weeds into at the proper season. The time of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> is commonly in the month of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. The only <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used at this time is a small narrow spade, commonly called a spit-shovel. The method is this: One <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> with his shovel rakes about three or four inches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and throws it before him about six or more inches. Two persons, generally women, follow with roots, which they <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the farther edge of the trench made by the digger, at about three inches from each other. As soon as the digger has gone once the breadth of the ridge, he begins again at the other side; and, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> as before, covers the roots last set, which makes room for another row of roots at the same distance from the first that they are from one another. The only dexterity necessary in digging is, to leave some part of the first stratum of earth untouched, to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> under the roots; and, in setting, to place the roots directly upon their bottom. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of roots planted on an acre is generally Generally about 16 <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, or 128 bushels. From the time of planting till the beginning of September, or sometimes later, there is no more labour required; but at that time they begin to vegetate, and are ready to shew themselves above ground, which may be known by digging up a few of the roots. The ground is then to be pared with a sharp hoe, and the weeds raked into the furrows, otherwise they would hinder the growth of the saffron. In some time after, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> appear. They are gathered before they are full-blown, as well as after, and the proper time for it is early in the morning. The owners of the saffron-fields get together a sufficient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, who pull off the whole flowers, and throw them by handfuls into a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>, and so continue till about 11 o'clock.
