Having then carried home the flowers, they immediately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to picking out the stigmata or chives, and together with them a pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> proportion of the stylos itself, or string to which they are attached: the rest of the flower they throw away as useless. Next morning they return to the field, without regarding whether the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> be wet or dry; and so on daily, even on Sundays, till the whole crop is gathered.—The next labour is to dry the chives on the kiln. The kiln is built upon a thick plank, that it may be moved from place to place. It is supported by four short legs; the outside consists of eight pieces of wood of three inches thick, in form of a quadrangular frame about twelve inches <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> at the bottom on the inside, and 22 on the upper part; which last is likewise the perpendicular height of it. On the fore-side is left a hole of about eight inches square, and four inches above the plank, through which the fire is put in; over all the rafters are laid pretty thick, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to one another, and nailed to the frame already mentioned. They are then plastered over on both sides, as are also the planks at bottom, very thick, to serve for an hearth. Over the mouth is laid a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>-cloth, fixed to the edges of the kiln, and likewise to two rollers, or moveable pieces of wood, which are turned by wedges or screws, in order to stretch the cloth. Instead of the hair-cloth, some people <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NET">net</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-wire, by which the saffron is sooner dried, and with less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>; but the difficulty of preserving it from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> makes the hair-cloth preferred by the best judges. The kiln is placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> part of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and they begin with putting five or six sheets of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on the hair-cloth, and upon these they lay out the wet saffron two or three inches thick. It is then covered with some other sheets of paper, and over these they lay a coarse <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLANKET">blanket</a> five or six times doubled, or instead of this, a canvas pillow filled with straw; and after the fire has been lighted for some time, the whole is covered with a board having a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> upon it. At first they apply a pretty strong <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, to make the chives sweat, as they call it; and at this time a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of care is necessary to prevent burning. When it has thus been dried about an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, they turn the cakes of saffron upside <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, putting on the coverings and weight as before. If no sinister accident happens during these first two hours, the danger is thought to be over; and nothing more is requisite than to keep up a very gentle fire for 24 hours, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the cake every half hour. That fuel is best which yields the least <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>; and for this reason <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> is preferable to all others. The quantity of saffron produced at a crop is uncertain. Sometimes five or six pounds of wet chives are got from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOD">rood</a>, sometimes not above one or two; and sometimes not so much as is sufficient to defray the expense of gathering and drying. But it is always observed, that about five pounds of wet saffron go to make one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of dry for the first three weeks of the crop, and six pounds during the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. When the heads are planted very thick, two pounds of dry saffron may, at a medium be allowed to an acre for the first crop, and 24 pounds for the two remaining ones, the third being considerably larger than the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. To obtain the second and third crops, the labour of hoeing, gathering, picking, &c. already mentioned, must be repeated; and about midsummer, after the third crop is gathered, the roots must all be taken up and transplanted. For taking up the roots, sometimes the plough is made use of, and sometimes a forked hoe; and then the ground is harrowed once or twice over. During all the time of ploughing, harrowing, &c.; 15 or more people will find work enough to follow and gather the heads as they are turned up. The roots are next to be carried to the house in sacks, where they are cleaned and raked. This labour consists in cleaning the roots thoroughly from earth, decayed old pieces, involucra, or excrements; after which they become fit to be planted in new ground immediately, or they may be kept for some time, without danger of spoiling. The quantity of roots taken up in proportion to those planted, is uncertain; but, at a medium, 24 quarters of clean roots, fit to be planted, may be had from each acre.—There sometimes happens a remarkable change in the roots of saffron and some other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. As soon as they begin to shoot upwards, there are commonly two or three large tap-roots sent forth from the side of the old one, which will run two or three inches deep into the ground. At the place where these bulbs first come out from, the old one will be formed sometimes, though not always, and the tap-root then decays. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> increases in bigness, and at last falls quite off; which commonly happens in April. But many times these tap-roots never produce any bulbs, and remain barren for ever after. All such roots therefore should be thrown away in the making a new plantation. This degeneracy of the roots is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> for which no cure is as yet known. When saffron is offered to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, that kind ought to be chosen which has the broadest blades; this being the mark by which English saffron is distinguished from the foreign. It ought to be of an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, or fiery-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> colour, and to yield a dark <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> tincture. It should be chosen fresh, not above a year old, in close cakes, neither dry nor yet very moist, tough and firm in tearing, of the same colour within as without, and of a strong, acid, diffusive smell. This drug has been reckoned a very elegant and useful aromatic. Besides the virtues it has in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with other substances of that class, it has been accounted one of the highest cordials, and is said to exhilarate the spirits to such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> as, when taken in large doses, to occasion immoderate mirth, involuntary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>, Saffron and the ill effects which follow from the abuse of spurious liquors. This medicine is particularly serviceable in hysteric depressions proceeding from a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> cause or obstruction of the uterine secretions, where other aromatics, even those of the more generous kind, have little effect. Saffron imparts the whole of its virtue and colour to rectified spirit, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> spirit, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>: A tincture drawn with vinegar, loses greatly of its colour in keeping; the watery and vinous tinctures are apt to grow four, and then lose their colour also: that made in pure spirit keeps in perfection for many years. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEADOW">Meadow</a>-Saffron. See Colchicum.

SAGAPENUM

Pages 610-610

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, &c. a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-resin, brought to us in two forms; the finer and purer is in loose granules, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> single drops; the coarser kind is in masses composed of these drops of various sizes, cemented together by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the same kind. In either <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it is of a firm and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> substance, considerably heavy, and of a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> on the outside, brownish within, and spotted in many places with small yellowish or whitish specks. Its smell is strong and disagreeable; its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> acrid and unpleasant. It is brought to us from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and the East-Indies. The plant which produces it has never been described; but is supposed to be, as Dioscorides says, of the fennel kind, from the seeds and fragments of the stalks sometimes met with in the body of it. Sagapenum is a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> attenuant, aperient, and discutent. It is good in all disorders of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> that owe their origin to a tough phlegm. It has also been found to dissolve tumours in the nervous parts, in a remarkable manner; and to give relief in habitual headaches, where almost all things else have failed. Its dose is from ten grains to two scruples; but it is now seldom given alone. It has been found, however, to do great things in asthmas; in obstructions of the viscera, particularly the spleen; in nervous complaints; and even in epilepsies. It also promotes the meninges, and expels the secundines; and is an ingredient in the theriac, mitridate, and many other of the shop compositions.

SAGE

Pages 610-610

an ingenious French <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>-writer, was born at Ruy in Brittany in the year 1667. He had a fine flow of imagination, was a complete <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the French and Spanish languages, and wrote several admired romances in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Spanish authors. These were, The Bachelor of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a>, 2 vols 12mo; New Adventures of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> Quixote, 2 vols 12mo. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEVIL">Devil</a> on Sticks, 2 vols 12mo; and Gil Blas, 4 vols 12mo. He produced also some comedies, and other pieces of pleasantry; and died in 1747, in a little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he supported himself by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>.

SAGENE

Pages 610-610

a Russian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, 500 of which make a werft; the sagene is equal to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> English feet.

SAGITTARIA

Pages 610-610
arrow-head; a genus of the polyandria order, belonging to the monoecea clas of plants. There are four species, of which the most remarkable is the sagittifolia, growing naturally in many parts of England. The root is composed of many strong fibres, which strike into the mud; the footstalks of the leaves are in length proportionate to the depth of the water in which they grow; so they are sometimes almost a yard long; they are thick and fungous; the leaves, which float upon the water, are shaped like Sagittarius the point of an arrow, the two ears at their base spreading wide asunder, and are very sharp-pointed. The flowers are produced upon long stalks which rise above the leaves, standing in whorls round them at the joints. They consist of three broad white petals, with a cluster of stamens in the middle, which have purple filaments. There is always a bulb at the lower part of the root, growing in the solid earth beneath the mud. This bulb constitutes a considerable part of the food of the Chinese; and upon that account they cultivate it. Horses, goats, and swine, eat it; cows are not fond of it.

SAGITTARIUS

Pages 610-610

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, the name of one of the 12 signs of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>.

SAGO

Pages 610-610

a simple brought from the East Indies, of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in diet as a restorative. It is produced from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of palm tree growing spontaneously in the East Indies without any culture. It rises to the height of about 20 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> 30 feet; its circumference being sometimes from five to six. Its ligneous bark is about an inch in thickness, and covers a multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> fibres; which, being interwoven one with another, envelop a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of a gummy kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>. As soon as this tree is ripe, a whitish dust, which transpires through the pores of the leaves, and adheres to their extremities, proclaim its maturity. The Malays then cut them <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> near the root, divide them into several sections, which they split into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>; they then scoop out the mass of mealy substance, which is enveloped by and adheres to the fibres; they <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a> it in pure <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> it through a straining bag of fine cloth, in order to separate it from the fibres. When this paste has lost <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of its moisture by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>, the Malays throw it into a kind of earthen vessels, of different shapes, where they allow it to dry and harden. This paste is wholesome nourishing food, and preserves for many years.

SAGUM

Pages 610-610

in Roman antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, open from top to bottom, and usually fastened on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> shoulder with a buckle <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> clasp. It was not different in shape from the chlamys of the Greeks, and the paludamentum of the generals. The only <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them was, that the paludamentum was made of a richer stuff, was generally of a purple-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and both longer and fuller than the sagum.

SAICK

Pages 610-610
or Saique, a Turkish vessel, very common in the Levant for carrying merchandise.

SAIL

Pages 610-614

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, an assemblage of several breadths of canvas sewed together by the laths, and edged round with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, fastened to the yards of a ship, to make it drive before the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. See Ship. The edges of the cloths, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> pieces, of which a sail is composed, are generally sewed together with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> seam; and the whole is skirted round at the edges with a cord, called the bolt-rope. Although the form of sails is extremely different, they are all nevertheless triangular or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRILATERAL">quadrilateral</a> figures; or, in other words, their surfaces are contained either between three or four sides. The former of these are sometimes spread by a yard, as lateen-falls; and otherwise by a stay, as stay-falls; or by a mast, as shoulder-of-mutton sails; in all which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the foremost leech or edge is attached to the said yard, mast, or stay, throughout its whole length. The latter latter, or those which are four-sided, are either extended by yards, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sails of a ship; or by yards and booms, as the studding-sails, drivers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>-tails, and all those sails which are set occasionally; or by gaffs and booms, as the main-sails of sloops and brigantines. The principal sails of a ship (Plate CCLX, fig. 2.) are the courses or lower sails a; the top-sails b, which are next in order above the courses; and the top-gallant sails c, which are expanded above the top-sails. The courses are the main-fail, fore-fail, and mizen, main stay-fail, fore-stay fail, and mizen-stay fail; but more particularly the three first. The main-stay fail is rarely used except in small vessels. In all quadrangular sails the upper edge is called the head; the sides or skirts are called leeches; and the bottom or lower edge is termed the foot. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the head is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the foot, the two lower corners are denominated clues, and the upper corners earings. In all triangular sails, and in those four-sided sails wherein the head is not parallel to the foot, the foremost corner at the foot is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TACK">tack</a>, and the after lower corner the clue; the foremost perpendicular or sloping edge is called the fore-leech, and the hindmost the after-leech. The heads of all four-sided sails, and the fore-leeches of lateen-sails, are attached to their respective yard or gaff by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small cords called ro-bands; and the extremities are tied to the yard arms, or to the peak of the gaff, by earings. The stay-sails are extended upon stays between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, whereon they are drawn up or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> occasionally, as a curtain slides upon its rod, and their lower parts are stretched out by a tack and sheet. The clues of a top-fail are drawn out to the extremities of the lower yard, by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> called the top-fail sheets; and the clues of the top-gallant sails are in like manner extended upon the top-fail yard-arms, as exhibited by fig. 2. The studding-sails are set beyond the leeches or skirts of the main-fail and fore-fail, or of the top-sails or top-gallant sails of a ship. Their upper and lower edges are accordingly extended by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> run out beyond the extremities of the yards for this purpose. Those sails, however, are only set in favourable winds and moderate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. All sails derive their name from the mast, yard, or stay, upon which they are extended. Thus the principal sail extended upon the main-mast is called the main sail, d; the next above, which stands upon the main-top mast is termed the main-top sail, e; and the highest, which is spread across the main-top-gallant-mast, is named the main top gallant sail, f. In the same manner there is the fore-fail, g; the fore-top-fail, h; and the fore-top-gallant-fail, i; the mizen, k; the mizen top-fail, l; and mizen top-gallant-fail, m. Thus also there is the main-stay-fail, o; main-top-mast stay-fail, p; and main-top-gallant stay-fail, q; with a middle stay-fail which stands between the two last. N.B. All these stay-sails are between the main and fore masts. The stay-sails between the main-mast and mizen-mast are the mizen stay-fail, r; and the mizen top-mast stay-fail, s; and sometimes a mizen top-gallant stay-fail above the latter. The stay-sails between the fore-mast and the bowsprit are the fore stay-fail, t; the fore top-mast stay-fail, u; and the jib, x. There is besides two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> sails extended by yards under the bowsprit, one of which is called the sprit-sail, y; and the other the sprit-sail top-fail, z. The studding-sails being extended upon the different yarps of the main-mast and fore-mast, are likewise named according to their stations, the lower, top-mast, or top gallant studding sails. The ropes by which the lower yards of a ship are hoisted up to their proper height on the masts, are called the jears. In all other sails the ropes employed for this purpose are called haliards. The principal sails are then expanded by haliards, sheets, and bowlines; except the courses, which are always stretched out below by a tack and sheet. They are drawn up together, or trussed up, by bunt-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, clue-lines, dds; leech-lines, eee; reef tackles, fff; slab-line, ggg; and spiling-lines. As the bunt-lines and leech-lines <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> on the other side of the sail, they are expressed by the dotted lines in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The courses, top-sails, and top-gallant sails, are wheeled about the mast, so as to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the various directions of the wind by braces. The higher studding-sails, and in general all the stay-sails, are drawn down, so as to be furled, or taken in, by down-hauls. Sail is also a name applied to any vessel beheld at a distance under sail. To Set Sail, is to unfurl and expand the sails upon their respective yards and stays, in order to begin the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of sailing. To Make Sail, is to spread an additional <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sail, so as to increase the ship’s velocity. To Shorten Sail, is to reduce or take in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sails, with an intention to diminish the ship’s velocity. To Strike Sail, is to lower it suddenly. This is particularly used in saluting or doing homage to a superior force, or to one whom the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW_OF_NATIONS"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nations acknowledges as superior in certain regions. Thus all foreign vessels strike to a British <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> in the British seas. Sailing, the movement by which a vessel is wafted along the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, by the action of the wind upon her sails. When a ship changes her state of rest into that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, as in advancing out of a harbour, or from her station at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, she acquires her motion very gradually, as a body which arrives not at a certain velocity till after an infinite repetition of the action of its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. The first <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of the wind greatly affects the velocity, because the resistance of the water might destroy it; since the velocity being but small at first, the resistance of the water which depends on it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be very feeble: but as the ship increases her motion, the force of the wind on the sails will be diminished; whereas, on the contrary, the resistance of the water on the bow will accumulate in proportion to the velocity with which the vessel advances. Thus the repetition of the degrees of force, which the action of the sails adds to the motion of the ship, is perpetually decreasing; whilst, on the contrary, the new degrees added to the effort of resistance on the bow are always augmenting. The velocity Sailing. Velocity is then accelerated in proportion as the quantity added is greater than that which is subtracted; but when the two powers become equal; when the impulsion of the wind on the sails has lost so much of its force, as only to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in proportion to the opposite impulse of resistance on the bow, the ship will then acquire no additional velocity, but continue to sail with a constant uniform motion. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> weight of the ship may indeed prevent her from acquiring her greatest velocity; but when she has attained it, she will advance by her own intrinsic motion, without gaining any new <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of velocity, or lessening what she has acquired. She moves then by her own proper force in vacuo, without being afterwards subject either to the effort of the wind on the sails, or to the resistance of the water on the bow. If at any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the impulsion of the water on the bow should destroy any part of the velocity, the effort of the wind on the sails will revive it, so that the motion will continue the same. It must, however, be observed, that this state will only subsist when these two powers act upon each other in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> opposition; otherwise they will mutually destroy one another. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of working ships depends on this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>-action, and the perfect equality which should subsist between the effort of the wind and the impulsion of the water. The effect of sailing is produced by a judicious arrangement of the sails to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the wind. Accordingly the various modes of sailing are derived from the different degrees and situations of the wind with regard to the course of the vessel. To illustrate this observation by examples, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of a number of ships proceeding on various courses are represented by fig. 3, which exhibits the 32 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass, of which C is the centre; the direction of the wind, which is northerly, being expressed by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>. It has been observed in the article <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a>-Hauled, that a ship in that situation will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> nearly within six points of the wind. Thus the ships B and y are close-hauled; the former being on the larboard tack, steering E.N.E. and the latter on the starboard tack, sailing W.N.W. with their yards a b braced obliquely, as suitable to that manner of sailing. The line of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> on the larboard tack would accordingly be expressed by CB, and on the starboard by Cy. When a ship is neither close-hauled, nor steering afore the wind, she is in general said to be sailing large. The relation of the wind to her course is precisely determined by the number of points between the latter and the course close-hauled. Thus the ships c and x have the wind one point large, the former steering E. b N. and the latter W. b N. The yards remain almost in the same position as in B and y; the bowlines and sheets of the sails being only a little slackened. The ships d and a have the wind two points large, the one steering east and the other west. In this manner of sailing, however, the wind is more particularly said to be upon the beam, as being at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, and coinciding with the position of the ship's beams. The yards are now more across the ship, the bowlines are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> off, and the sheets more relaxed; so that the effort of the wind being applied nearer to the line of the ship's course, her velocity is greatly augmented. In e and f the ships have the wind three points large, or one point abaft the beam, the course of the former being E. b S. and that of the latter W. b S. The sheets are still more flowing, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> which the yards make with the keel further diminished, and the course accelerated in proportion. The ships f and j, the first of which steers E. S. E. and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> W. S. W. have the wind four points large, or two points abaft the beam. In g and r the wind is five points large, or three points abaft the beam, the former sailing S.E. b E. and the latter S.W. b W. In both these situations the sheets are still farther slackened, and the yards laid yet more athwart the ship's length, in proportion as the wind approaches the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. The ships h and q, steering S. E. and S. W. have the wind six points large, or more properly on the quarter; which is considered as the most favourable manner of sailing, because all the sails cooperate to increase the ship's velocity; whereas, when the wind is right aft, as in the ship m, it is evident, that the wind in its passage to the foremost sails, will be intercepted by those which are farther aft. When the wind is on the quarter, the fore-tack is brought to the cat-head; and the main-tack being cast off, the weather-clue of the main-sail is hoisted up to the yard, in order to let the wind pass freely to the fore-fall; and the yards are disposed so as to make an angle of about two points, or nearly 22°, with the keel. The ships i and p, of which the former sails S.E.b S. and the latter S.W. b S. are said to have the wind three points on the larboard or starboard quarter; and those expressed by k and o, two points; as steering S.S.E. and S.S.W. in both which positions the yards make nearly an angle of 169°, or about a point and a half, with the ship's length. When the wind is one point on the quarter, as in the ships l and n, whose courses are S. b E. and S. b W. the situation of the yards and sails is very little different from the last mentioned; the angle which they make with the keel being somewhat less than a point, and the stay-falls being rendered of very little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The ship m sails right afore the wind, or with the wind right aft. In this position the yards are laid at right angles with the ship's lengths; the stay-falls being entirely useless, are hauled down; and the main-fall is drawn up in the brails, that the fore-fall may operate; a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> which considerably facilitates the steerage, or effort of the helm. As the wind is then intercepted by the main-top-sail and main-top-gallant-sail, in its passage to the fore-top-sail and fore-top-gallant-sail, these latter are by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> entirely becalmed; and might therefore be furled, to prevent their being fretted by flapping against the mizzen; but that their effort contributes greatly to prevent the ship from broaching-to, when she deviates from her course to the right or left thereof. Thus all the different methods of sailing may be divided into four, viz. close-hauled, large, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERING">quartering</a>, and afore the wind; all which relate to the direction of the wind with regard to the ship's course, and the arrangement of the sails.

SAILING ALSO

Pages 614-614

g also implies a particular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, formed on the principles, and regulated by the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a>. Hence we say, Plain Sailing.

SAINT

Pages 615-615

in the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a holy person deceased, and since his decease canonized by the pope, after several informations and ceremonies. See the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> CANONIZATION, &c. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> wherein the Roman-Catholics and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> differ is, that the former <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, invoke, and supplicate saints, &c. to intercede for them; whereas the latter hold it sufficient to propose their good examples for our <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of saints, allowed as such in the Romish church, is prodigious. Father Papebroche reckons 17 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> 18 to have died on the first of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> only. Father Mabillon, in an express dissertation on the worship of unknown saints, observes, that honours are given to saints who perhaps were not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and whose very names were never known: hence, being under a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of giving them names, they are therefore called baptized saints. He adds, that they every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> beseech saints to intercede for them with God, when it is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of doubt whether they themselves be in heaven. SAINT-Foin, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the hedyarum. See HEDYSARUM; and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a>, no 136. SAINT Januarius's Blood. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a>, no 237. SAL. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">SALT</a>. SAL Alembroth. See CHEMISTRY, no 337. SAL Ammoniac, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. See CHEMISTRY, no 253. SAL Fixed. See CHEMISTRY, no 234. SAL Glauber's secret. See CHEMISTRY, no 125. SAL Nitrous. See CHEMISTRY, no 189. SAL Vegetable. See CHEMISTRY, no 276. SAL Volatile. See CHEMISTRY, no 331. SAL Digestivus, Sylvii. See CHEMISTRY, no 231. SAL Diureticus. See CHEMISTRY, no 274. SAL Microcosmicus. See CHEMISTRY, no 308. SAL Prunellae. See CHEMISTRY, no 188. SAL Sedativus. See CHEMISTRY, no 265. SAL Volatile Oleofum. See CHEMISTRY, no 332.

SALADIN

Pages 615-615

famous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, equally renowned as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. He supported himself by his valour, and the influence of his amiable character, against the united efforts of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> Christian potentates of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, who carried on the most unjust wars against him, under the false appellation of Holy Wars. See the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> EGYPT, and CROISADE.

SALAMANCA

Pages 615-615

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, rich, and populous <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Leon, situated on the river Tormes, about 75 miles west from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. It is said to have been founded by Teucer the son of Telamon, who called it <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Salamanica, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the ancient Salamis. Here is an university, the greatest in Spain, and perhaps inferior to none in the whole world, in respect at least to its revenues, buildings, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of scholars, and masters. Here are also many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and magnificent palaces, squares, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, churches, colleges, chapels, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>. The bishop of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is suffragan to the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOSTELLA">Compostella</a>, and has a yearly revenue of 1000 ducats. A Roman way leads from hence to Merida and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>, and there is an old Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river. Of the colleges in the university, four are appropriated to young men of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and near it is an infirmary for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> sick scholars. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 10. N. Lat. 41. 0.

SALAMIS

Pages 615-616

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 34. N. Lat. 37. 32.—It was famous in antiquity for a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> between the Greek and Persian fleets. In the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> held among the Persians on this occasion, all the commanders were for engaging, because they knew this advice to be most agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s inclinations. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTEMISIA">Artemisia</a> was the only person who opposed this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. She was queen of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>; and followed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> in this war with five ships, the best equipped of any in the fleet, except those of the Sidonians. This princess distinguished herself on all occasions by her singular courage, and still more by her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and conduct. She represented, in the council of war we are speaking of, the dangerous consequences of engaging a people that were far more expert in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs than the Persians; alleging, that the loss of a battle at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> would be attended with the ruin of their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; whereas, by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> out the war, and advancing into the heart of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, they would create jealousies and divisions among their enemies, who would separate from one another, in order to defend each of them their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and that the king might, almost without striking a blow, make himself <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Greece. This advice, though very prudent, was not followed, but an engagement unanimously resolved upon. Xerxes, in order to encourage his men by his presence, caused a throne to be erected on the top of an eminence, whence he might safely behold whatever happened; having several scribes about him, to write <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the names of such as should signalize themselves against the enemy. The approach of the Persian fleet, with the news that a strong <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> from the army was marching against Cleombrotus, who defended the isthmus, struck such a terror into the Peloponnesians, that they could not by any intrigues be prevailed upon to stay any longer at Salamis. Being therefore determined to put to sea, and fail to the isthmus, Themistocles privately dispatched a trusty friend to the Persian commanders, informing them of the intended flight; and exhorting them to fend <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their fleet round the island, in order to prevent their escape. The same messenger assured Xerxes, that Themistocles, who had sent him that advice, designed to join the Persians, as soon as the battle began, with all the Athenian ships. The king giving <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to all he said, immediately caused a strong squadron to fail round the island in the night, in order to cut off the enemy's flight. Early next morning, as the Peloponnesians were preparing to set sail, they found themselves encompassed on all sides by the Persian fleet; and were against their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> obliged to remain in the straits of Salamis, and expose themselves to the same dangers with their allies. The Grecian fleet consisted of 380 sail, that of the Persians of 2000 and upwards. Themistocles avoided the engagement till a certain <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, which rose regularly every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and was entirely contrary to the enemy, began to blow. As soon as he found himself favoured by this wind, he gave the signal for battle. The Persians, knowing that they fought under their king's eye, advanced with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> resolution; but the wind blowing directly in their faces, and the largeness and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of their ships embarrassing them in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> so strait and narrow, narrow, their courage soon abated; which the Greeks observing, used such efforts, that in a short time breaking into the Persian fleet, they entirely disordered them; some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> towards Phalarus, where their army lay encamped, others saving themselves in the harbours of the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. The Ionians were the first that betook themselves to flight. But queen Artemisia distinguished herself above all the rest, her ships being the last that fled: which Xerxes observing, cried out, that the men behaved like women, and the women with the courage and intrepidity of men. The Athenians were so incensed against her, that they offered a reward of 10,000 drachmas to any one that should take her alive; but she, in spite of all their efforts, got clear of the ships that pursued her, and arrived safe on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. In this engagement, which was one of the most memorable actions we find recorded in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the Grecians lost 40 ships; and the Persians 200, besides a great many more that were taken, with all the men and ammunition they carried.

SALARY

Pages 616-616

a recompense <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> consideration made to a person for his pains and industry in another <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s business. The word is used in the statute 23 Ed. III. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 1. Salarium at first signified the rents or profits of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; (and in Gascoigne they now call the seats of the gentry salars, as we do bales;) but afterwards is was taken for any <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, stipend, or annual allowance.

SALE

Pages 616-616

is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> of a commodity for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARTER">barter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> permutation, is the exchange of one commodity for another. When the bargain is concluded, an obligation is contracted by the buyer to pay the value, and by the seller to deliver the commodity at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> agreed on, or immediately, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> no time be specified. In this, as well as other mercantile contracts, the safety of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> requires the utmost good <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and veracity. Therefore, although, by the laws of England, a sale, above the value of £10, be not binding, unless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> be paid, or the bargain confirmed by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, a merchant would lose all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> who refused from his agreement, although these legal requisites were omitted. When a specific thing is sold, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, even before delivery, is in some respect vested in the buyer; and if the thing perishes, the buyer must bear the loss. For example, if a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> dies before delivery, he must pay the value; but if the bargain only determines the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the goods, without specifying the identical <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, and the seller's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, with all his goods, be burned, he is entitled to no payment. He must also bear the loss if the thing perish through his fault; or when a particular time and place of delivery is agreed on, if it perish before it be tendered, in terms of the bargain. If a person purchase goods at a shop without agreeing for the price, he is liable for the ordinary market-price at the time of purchase. If the buyer proves insolvent before delivery, the seller is not bound to deliver the goods without payment or security. If the importation, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the commodities sold, be prohibited by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, or if the buyer knows that they were smuggled, no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> lies for delivery. The property of goods is generally presumed, in favour of commerce, to belong to the possessor, and cannot be challenged in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of an onerous purchaser. But to this there are some exceptions. By the Scots law, stolen good may in all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> be reclaimed by the proprietor, and also by the English law, unless they were bought <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BONA">bona</a> fide in open market; that is, in the accustomed public places, on stated days in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, or in a shop in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and horses may be reclaimed, unless the sale be regularly entered by the book-keeper of the market. In all cases, if the goods be evicted by the lawful proprietor, the seller is liable to the purchaser for the value. Actions for payment of shop-accounts, as well as other debts not constituted by writing, are limited in England to six years. The testimony of one witness is admitted; and the seller's books, although the person that kept them be dead, are good <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> for one year. In Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> books may be proved within three years of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the last article, by one witness, and the creditor's books and oath in supplement. After three years, they can only be proved by the oath or writ of the debtor. A merchant's books are, in all cases, good evidence against him.

SALEP

Pages 616-617

in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>, the dried root of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of orchis. See ORCHIS. Several methods of preparing salep have been proposed and practiced. Geoffroy has delivered a very judicious <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> for this purpose, in the Histoire de l'Academie Royale des Sciences, 1740; and Retmus, in the Swedish Transactions 1764, has improved Geoffroy's method. But Mr Moult of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROCHDALE">Rochdale</a> has lately favoured the public with a new manner of curing the orchis root; by which salep is prepared, at least equal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not superior, to any brought from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>. The new root is to be washed in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and the fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> skin which covers it is to be separated by means of a small <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the root in hot water, and rubbing it with a coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth. When a sufficient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of roots have been thus cleaned, they are to be spread on a tin plate, and placed in an oven heated to the usual <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, where they are to remain six or ten minutes, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have lost their milky whiteness, and acquired a transparency like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, without any diminution of bulk. Being arrived at this state, they are to be removed, in order to dry and harden in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which will require several days to effect; or by using a very gentle <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, they may be finished in a few hours. Salep thus prepared, may be afforded in this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of England, where labour bears a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> value, at about eight-pence or ten-pence per <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a>: And it might be sold still cheaper, if the orchis were to be cured, without separating from it the brown skin which covers it; a troublesome part of the process, and which does not contribute to render the root either more palatable or salutary. Whereas the foreign salep is now sold at five or six shillings per pound. Salep is said to contain the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of vegetable nourishment in the smallest bulk. Hence a very judicious writer, to prevent the dreadful calamity of famine at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, has lately proposed that the powder of it should constitute part of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of every ship's This powder and portable soup, dissolved in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water, form a rich thick jelly, capable of supporting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for a considerable length of time. An ounce of each of these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, with two quarts of boiling water, will be sufficient subsistence for a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and as being a mixture of animal and vegetable food, must prove more nourishing than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>-cake, made by boiling rice in water: which last, however, sailors are often obliged solely to subsist upon for several months; especially in voyages to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, when the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and flour are exhausted, and the beef and pork, having been salted in hot countries, become unfit for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. "But as a wholesome nourishment," says Dr Percival, "rice is much inferior to salep. I digested several alimentary mixtures prepared of mutton and water, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> up with bread, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEA">tea</a>-biscuit, salep, rice-flour, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-powder, potatoes, old cheese, &c., in a heat equal to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. In 48 hours they had all acquired a vinous smell, and were in brisk <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, except the mixture with rice, which did not emit many air-bubbles, and was but little changed. The third day several of the mixtures were sweet, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to ferment; others had lost their intestine <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and were sour; but the one which contained the rice was become putrid. From this experiment it appears, that rice as an aliment, is slow of fermentation, and a very weak corrector of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. It is therefore an improper diet for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>-patients; but more particularly for sailors in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> voyages; because it is incapable of preventing, and will not contribute much to check the progress of that fatal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, the sea-scurvy. Under certain circumstances, rice seems disposed of itself, without mixture, to become putrid; for by long keeping it sometimes acquires an offensive flavor. Nor can it be considered as a very nutritious kind of food, on account of its difficult solubility in the stomach. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a> confirms the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this conclusion; for it is observed by the planters in the West-Indies, that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> grow thin, and are less able to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, whilst they subsist upon rice. "Salep has the singular <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of concealing the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> water; a circumstance of the highest importance at sea, when there is a scarcity of fresh water. I dissolved a dram and a half of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> salt in a pint of the mucilage of salep, so liquid as to be potable, and the same quantity in a pint of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>-water. The salep was by no means disagreeable to the taste, but the water was rendered extremely unpalatable. "This experiment suggested to me the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of the orchis root as a corrector of acidity, a property which would render it a very useful diet for children. But the solution of it, when mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, seemed only to <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a> like an equal proportion of water, and not to cover its sharpness. "Salep, however, appears by my experiments, to retard the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACETOUS">acetous</a> fermentation of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; and consequently would be a good lithing for milk-pottage, especially in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, where the cattle being fed upon four draft, must yield acidulent milk. "Salep in a certain proportion, which I have not yet been able to ascertain, would be a very useful and profitable addition to bread. I directed one ounce of the powder to be dissolved in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of water, and the mucilage to be mixed with a sufficient quantity of flour, salt, and yeast. The flour amounted to two pounds, the yeast to two ounces, and the salt to 80 grains. The loaf when baked was remarkably well fermented, and weighed three pounds two ounces. Another loaf, made with the same quantity of flour, &c., weighed two pounds and twelve ounces; from which it appears, that the salep, though used in so small a proportion, increased the gravity of the loaf six ounces, by absorbing and retaining more water than the flour alone was capable of. Half a pound of flour and an ounce of salep were mixed together, and the water added according to the usual method of preparing bread. The loaf when baked weighed thirteen ounces and a half; and would probably have been heavier, if the salep had been previously dissolved in about a pint of water. But it should be remarked, that the quantity of flour used in this trial was not sufficient to conceal the peculiar taste of the salep. "The restorative, mucilaginous, and demulcent qualities of the orchis root, render it of considerable use in various diseases. In the sea-scurvy it powerfully obtunds the acrimony of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, and at the same time is easily assimilated into a mild and nutritious chyle. In diarrhoeas and the dysentery it is highly serviceable, by sheathing the internal coat of the intestines, by abating irritation, and gently correcting putrefaction. In the symptomatic fever, which arises from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of pus from ulcers in the lungs, from wounds, or from amputation, salep used plentifully is an admirable demulcent, and well adapted to resist the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the crisis of the blood, which is so evident in these <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. And by the same mucilaginous <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, it is equally efficacious in the strangury and dysury; especially in the latter, when arising from a venereal cause, because the discharge of urine is then attended with the most exquisite pain, from the ulceration about the neck of the bladder and through the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a>. I have found it also a useful aliment for patients who labour under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or gravel."

SALERNO

Pages 617-617

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Hither Principato, with an archbishop's see, a castle, harbour, and an university chiefly for medicine. It is seated at the bottom of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 43'. N. Lat. 40° 45'.

SALET

Pages 617-617

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> covering <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> armour for the head, anciently worn by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LIGHT_HORSE">light-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, only different from the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-CASQUE">casque</a> in that it had no crest and was little more than a bare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>.

SALIANT

Pages 617-617

SAILENT, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> SAILLANT, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, is applied to a lion, or other beast, when its fore-legs are raised in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a> posture.

SALIC

Pages 617-618
or SALIQUE, LAW, (Lex Salica,) an ancient and fundamental law of the kingdom of France, usually supposed to have been made by Pharamond, or at least by Clovis; in virtue whereof males only are to inherit. Some, as Postellus, would have it to have been called Salic, q. d. Gallic, because peculiar to the Gauls. Fer Montanus insists, it was because Pharamond Salicornia ramond was at first called Salicur. Others will have it to be so named, as having been made for the Salisbury falc lands. These were noble fiefs which their first kings used to bestow on the fallians, that is, the great lords of their falle or court, without any other tenure than military service; and for this reason, such fiefs were not to descend to women, as being by nature unfit for such a tenure. Some, again, derive the origin of this word from the Salians, a tribe of Franks that settled in Gaul in the reign of Julian, who is said to have given them lands on condition of their personal service in war. He even passed the conditions into a law, which the new conquerors acquiesced in, and called it falc, from the name of their former countrymen.

SALICORNIA

Pages 618-618

jointed glass-wort, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Saltwort, a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONANDRIA">monandria</a> clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, of which the most remarkable are, 1. The fruticola, with obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, grows plentifully in most of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> marshes which are overflowed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> in many parts of England. It is an annual plant, with thick, succulent, jointed stalks, which trail upon the ground. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are produced at the ends of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> toward the extremity of the branches, which are small, and scarce discernible by the naked eye. 2. The perennis, with a shrubby branching stalk, grows naturally in Sheppey <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. This hath a shrubby branching stalk about six inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; the points of the articulations are acute; the stalks branch from the bottom, and form a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>. They are perennial, and produce their flowers in the same manner as the former. The inhabitants near the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coasts where these plants grow, cut them up toward the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, when they are fully grown; and, after having dried them in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, they burn them for their ashes, which are used in making of glaas and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>. These herbs are by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people called kelp, and promiscuously gathered for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. See the article Salsola; also <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DYEING">Dyeing</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">Leather</a>, p. 4161, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> A.

SALII

Pages 618-618

in Roman antiquity, priests of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, whereof there were twelve, instituted by Numa, wearing painted, parti-colored garments, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> bonnets; with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> cuirass on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. They were called salii, from saltare "to dance;" because, after assiting at sacrifices, they went <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> about the streets, with bucklers in their left-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a rod in their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, striking musically with their rods on one another's bucklers, and singing hymns in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the gods.

SALISBURY

Pages 618-618

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Wiltshire in England, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 55. N. Lat. 51. 3. This <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> owed its first rise to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, which was begun in 1219, and finished in 1258. According to an estimate delivered in to Henry III, it cost forty thousand merks. It is a Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and is certainly the most elegant and regular in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. The doors and chapels are equal in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to the months, the windows to the days, and the pillars and pilasters to the hours in a year. It is built in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a>, with a spire in the middle, and nothing but buttresses and glaas windows on the outside. The spire is the highest in the kingdom, being 410 feet, which is twice the height of the monument in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The pillars and pilasters in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> are of fusile marble; the art of making which is now either entirely lost, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> little known. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which is 50 feet in diameter and 150 in circumference, bears all upon one slender pillar, which is such a curiosity as can hardly be matched in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> of the western <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> through the city in the reign of Edward III, was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage to it. The chancellorship of the most noble order of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>, which is annexed to this see, was first conferred on bishop Richard Beauchamp. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> of St Michael's near this city, was founded by one of its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. Dr Seth <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARD">Ward</a>, bishop of this see in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, contributed greatly to the making the river Avon navigable to Christ-church in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>. The same prelate, in 1683, built an hospital for the entertainment of the widows of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> ministers of the gospel. There are three other churches besides the cathedral, which is without the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the city, and a greater number of boarding-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, especially for young ladies, than in any other town in England. Here is a manufacture of druggets, flannels, bonelace, and those cloaths called Salisbury-whites; in consideration of which, and its <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, affizes, boarding-schools, and clergy, the city may be justly said to be in a flourishing condition. It was incorporated by Henry III, and is governed by a mayor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, recorder, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>-recorder, 24 aldermen, and 30 assistants or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> men. The number of souls is about 10,000. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, where the canons and prebendaries live, is like a fine city of itself. Here is an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> for the ladies every Tuesday, and coaches set out from hence to London every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. In this town are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>-schools; the expense of one of them is entirely defrayed by the bishop. The city gives <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the noble family of Cecil.

SALIVA

Pages 618-618

is that fluid by which the mouth and tongue are continually moistened in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state; and is supplied by glands which form it, that are called salivary glands. This humour is thin and pellucid, incapable of being concreted by the fire, almost without <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and smell. By chewing, it is expressed from the glands which separate it from the blood, and is intimately mixed with our food, the digestion of which it greatly promotes. In hungry persons it is acrid, and copiously discharged; and in those who have fasted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> it is highly acrid, penetrating, and refulgent. A too copious evacuation of it produces thirst, loss of appetite, bad digestion, and an atrophy.

SALIVATION

Pages 618-618

in medicine, a promoting of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> of saliva, by means of medicines, mostly by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of salivation is in diseases belonging to the glands and membrana adiposa, and principally in the cure of the venereal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>; though it is sometimes also used in epidemic diseases, cutaneous diseases, &c. whose crises tend that way.

SALIX

Pages 618-619

the willow, a genus of the diandria order, belonging to the dioecia clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are 31 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable are, 1. The caprea, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fallow-tree, grows to but a moderate height, having smooth, dark-green, brittle branches; oval, waved, rough leaves, indented at top, and woolly underneath. It grows abundantly in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but more frequently in dry than moist situations; it is of a brittle <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, so is unfit for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>-makers; but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, stakes, and to lop for fire-wood; and its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> is good for many purposes. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, or silver-leaved willow, grows to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height and considerable bulk, having smooth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>-green shoots; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, spear-shaped, acuminate, sawed, silvery-white leaves, being downy on both sides, with glands below the ferratures. This is the common white willow, which grows abundantly about <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, and by the sides of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and brooks, &c. 3. The vitellina, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> willow, grows but to a moderate height; having yellow, very pliant, shoots; oval, acute, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>, very smooth leaves, with the ferratures cartilaginous, and with callous punctures on the foot-stalks. 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PURPUREA">purpurea</a>, purple, or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> willow, grows to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> height, having long, reddish, very pliable shoots, and long spear-shaped, serrated, smooth leaves, the lower ones being opposite. 5. The viminalis, or osier-willow, grows but a moderate height, having slender rod-like branches, very long, pliant, greenish shoots; and very long, narrow, spear-shaped, acute, almost entire leaves, hairy, and silky underneath. 6. The pentandra, pentandrous, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>-leaved, sweet-scented willow, grows to some considerable stature, having brownish-green branches; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, broad, serrated, smooth, sweet-scented leaves, shining above; and pentandrous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. 7. The triandra, or triandrous willow, grows to a large stature, having numerous, erect, greyish-green branches, and pliant shoots; oblong, acute-pointed, serrated smooth, shining-green leaves, eared at the base; and triandrous flowers. 8. The fragilis, fragile or crack-willow, rises to a middling stature, with brownish, very fragile, or brittle branches, long, oval-lanceolate, sawed, smooth leaves of a shining-green on both sides, having dentated-glandular foot-stalks. This sort in particular being exceedingly fragile, so that it easily cracks and breaks, is unfit for culture in osier-grounds. 9. The Babylonica, Babylonian pendulous salix, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called weeping willow, grows to a largish size, having numerous, long, slender, pendulous branches, hanging <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> loosely all round in a curious manner, and long, narrow, spear-shaped, serrated, smooth leaves. This curious willow is a native of the east, and is retained in our hardy plantations for ornament, and exhibits a most agreeable variety; particularly when disposed singly by the verges of any piece of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or in spacious openings of graft-ground. All the species of salix are of the tree kind, very hardy, remarkably fast growers, and several of them attaining a considerable stature when permitted to run up to standards. They are mostly of the aquatic tribe, being generally the most abundant and most prosperous growth in watery situations; they however will grow freely almost anywhere, in any common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and exposure; but grown considerably the fastest and strongest in low moist <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, particularly in marshy situations, by the verges of rivers, brooks, and other waters; likewise along the sides of watery ditches, &c. which places often lying waste, may be employed to good advantage, in plantations of willows, for different purposes.

SALLEE

Pages 619-619
