an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, with a harbour and several ports. The harbour of Sallee is one of the best in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and yet, on account of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> that lies across it, ships of the smallest draught are forced to unload and take out their guns before they can get into it. There are docks to build ships; but they are hardly ever used, for want of skill and materials. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, divided into the Old and New <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">Towns</a>, by the river Guero. It has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been famous for its rovers <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> pirates, which make prizes of all Christian ships that come in their way, except there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> to the contrary. W. Long. 6. 30. N. Lat. 34. 0.

SALLO

Pages 619-619

a French writer, famous for being the projector of literary journals, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1626. He studied the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and was admitted a counsellor in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Paris in 1652. It was in 1664 he schemed the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the Journal des Scavans; and the year following began to publish it under the name of Sieur de Heronville, which was that of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VALET">valet</a> de chambre. But he played the critic so severely, that authors, surprized at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of such attacks, retorted to powerfully, that M. de Sallo, unable to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> the storm, after he had published his third Journal, declined the undertaking, and turned it over to the abbe Gallois; who, without presuming to criticise, contented himself merely with giving titles, and making extracts. Such was the origin of literary journals, which afterwards sprang up in other countries under different titles; and the success of them, under judicious management, is a clear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of their utility. M. de Sallo died in 1669.

SALLUSTIUS

Pages 619-620

a celebrated Roman historian, was born at Amiternum, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the year of Rome 669, and before Christ 85. His <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> was liberal, and he made the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it; of which we need no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, than those valuable historical monuments of his, that are happily transmitted to us among the few remains of antiquity. No <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> has inveighed more sharply against the vices of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> than this historian; yet no man had less pretensions to virtue than he. His youth was spent in a most lewd and profligate manner; and his patrimony almost squandered away, when he had scarcely taken possession of it. Marcus Varro, a writer of undoubted <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, relates, in a fragment preserved by Aulus Gellius, that Sallust was actually caught in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> with Fausta the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sylla, by Milo her husband; who scourged him very severely, and did not suffer him to depart till he had redeemed his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> with a considerable sum. A.U.C. 694, he was made quæstor, and in 702 tribune of the people; in neither of which places is he allowed to have acquitted himself at all to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. By virtue of his quæstorship, he obtained an admission into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>; but was expelled thence by the censors in 704, on account of his immoral and debauched way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In the year 705 Cæsar restored him to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a senator; and to introduce him into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> with a better <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, made him quæstor a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. In the administration of this office he behaved himself very scandalously; exposed every thing to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a> that he could find a purchaser for; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may believe the author of the invective, thought nothing wrong which he had a mind to do: Nihil non venale habuerit, cujus aliqua emptor fuit, nihil non In the year 707, when the African <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> was at an end, he was made praetor for his services to Caesar, and sent to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>. Here he acted the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> as Verres had done in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; outrageously plundered the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>; and returned with such immense <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> to Rome, that he purchased a most magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> upon mount Quirinal, with those gardens which to this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> retain the name of Sallustian gardens, besides his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> house at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TIVOLI">Tivoli</a>. How he spent the remaining part of his life, we have no account from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers. Eusebius tells us, that he married Terentia, the divorced wife of Cicero; and that he died at the age of 50, in the year 710, which was about four years before the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIUM">Actium</a>. Of the many things which he wrote, we have nothing remaining but his Histories of the Catilinarian and Jugurthine wars; together with some orations <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> speeches, printed with his fragments.

SALLY-PORTS

Pages 620-620

in fortification, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Postern-Gates, as they are sometimes called, are those under-ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> from the inner works to the outward ones; such as from the higher flank to the lower, or to the tenailles, or the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> from the middle of the curtain to the ravelin. When they are made for men to go through only, they are made with steps at the entrance and going out. They are about 6 feet wide, and 8½ feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. There is also a gutter or shore made under the sally-ports, which are in the middle of the curtains, for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> which runs <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the streets to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into the ditch; but this can only be done when there are wet ditches. When sally-ports serve to carry guns through them for the out-works, instead of making them with steps, they must have a gradual slope, and be 8 feet wide.

SALMASIUS

Pages 620-620

a French writer of uncommon abilities and immense erudition, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> near Semur in 1596. His mother, who was a Protestant, infused her notions of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> into him, and he at length converted his father: he settled at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; and in 1630 paid a visit to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, who is reported to have shown him extraordinary marks of regard. Upon the violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. of England, he was prevailed on by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family, then in exile, to write a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>; which was answered by our famous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> in 1651, in a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled Defensio pro Populo Anglicano contra Claudii Salmasii Defensionem Regiam. This book was read over all <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and conveyed such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the writer's abilities, that he was respected even by those who hated his principles. Salmasius died in 1653; and some did not scruple to say, that Milton killed him by the acuteness of his reply. His works are numerous and of various kinds; but the greatest monuments of his learning are, his Notae in Historiae Augustae Scriptores, and his Exercitationes Pliniiane in Solinum.

SALMO

Pages 620-623

the Salmon; a genus of the order of abdominales. The head is smooth, and furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> and a tongue; the rays of the gills are from four to ten; the back-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIN">fin</a> is fat behind; and the belly-fins have many rays. There are 29 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, of which the most remarkable are, 1. The falar, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> salmon, is a northern fish, being unknown in the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and other warm climates; it is found in France in some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that empty themselves into the ocean, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> as far as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>; they are also very common in Newfoundland, and the northern parts of North <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. Salmon are taken in the rivers of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KAMTSCHATKA">Kamtschatka</a>; but whether they are of the same species with the European kind, is not very certain. They are in several countries a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> article of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, being cured different ways, by salting, pickling, and drying: there are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and the Baltic; but we believe nowhere greater than those at Colraine in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; and in Great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, at Berwick and in some of the rivers of Scotland. The salmon was known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, but not to the Greeks. Pliny speaks of it as a fish found in the rivers of Aquitaine; Ausonius enumerates it among those of the Mosel. The salmon is a fish that lives both in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and fresh waters; quitting the sea at certain seasons for the sake of depositing its spawn in security, in the gravelly beds of rivers remote from their mouths. There are scarce any difficulties but what they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> overcome, in order to arrive at places fit for their purpose; they will ascend rivers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of miles, force themselves against the most rapid streams, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> with amazing agility over cataracts of several feet in height. Salmon are frequently taken in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> up as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>; they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the sources of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a> rivers in spite of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>-like currents, and surpasse the perpendicular falls of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol9.html#article-LEIXLIP">Leixlip</a>, Kennerth, and Pont Aberglastyn. It may here be proper to contradict the vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of their taking their tail in their mouth when they attempt to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>; such as Mr Pennant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, sprung up quite straight, and with a strong tremulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. The salmon is a fish so generally known, that a very <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> will serve. The largest we ever heard of weighed 74 pounds. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the back and sides are grey, sometimes spotted with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, sometimes plain: the covers of the gills are subject to the same variety; the belly silvery; the nose sharp-pointed; the end of the under jaw in the males often turns up in the form of a hook; sometimes this curvature is very considerable: it is said that they lose this hook when they return to the sea. The teeth are lodged in the jaws and on the tongue, and are slender, but very sharp; the tail is a little forked. 2. The trutta, or sea-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, migrates like the true salmon up several of our rivers; spawns, and returns to the sea. That described by Mr Pennant was taken in the Tweed below Berwick, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1769. The shape was more thick than the common trout; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> three pounds two ounces. The irides silver; they head thick, smooth, and dusky, with a glost of blue and green; the back of the same colour, which grows fainter towards the side-line. The back is plain, but the sides as far as the lateral line are marked with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> distinct irregularly-shaped spots of black: the lateral line straight; the sides beneath the line, and the belly, are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. Tail <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and even at the end. The dorsal fin had 12 rays; the pectoral 14; the ventral 9; the anal 10. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> when boiled is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, but well-flavoured. 3. The fario, or trout; the colours of which vary greatly in different waters, and in different seasons. Trout differ also in size. One taken in Llynallet, Denbighshire, which is famous for an excellent kind, measured 17 inches, its depth three and three <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, its weight one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> ten ounces; the head thick; the nose rather sharp; the upper jaw a little longer than the lower; both jaws, as well as the head, were of a pale <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, blotched with black; the teeth sharp and strong, disposed in the jaws, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the mouth, and tongue. The back was dusky; the sides tinged with a purplish bloom, marked with deep purple spots, mixed with black above and below the side-line which was straight; the belly white. The first dorsal fin was spotted; the spurious fin brown, tipped with red; the pectoral, ventral, and anal fins, of a pale brown; the edges of the anal fin white; the tail very little forked when extended.—The stomachs of the common trouts are uncommonly thick and muscular. They feed on the shell-fish of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and rivers, as well as on small fish. They likewise take into their stomachs gravel or small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, to assist in comminuting the teafacous parts of their food. The trouts of certain lakes in Ireland, such as those of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALWAY">Galway</a> and some others, are remarkable for the great thickness of their stomachs, which, from some slight resemblance to the organs of digestion in birds, have been called gizzards; the Irish name the species that has them, gillaroo trouts. These stomachs are sometimes served up to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a> under the former appellation. Trouts are most voracious fish, and afford excellent diversion to the angler. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for the sport of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLING">angling</a> is so great in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> in some of the streams in the adjacent counties is purchased at the rate of 10l. per annum. These fish shift their quarters to spawn; and like salmon, make up towards the heads of rivers to deposit their roes. The under jaw of the trout is subject, at certain times, to the same curvature as that of the salmon. 4. The species, called from its colour the white, migrates out of the sea into the river Esk in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> to September. When dressed, their flesh is red, and most delicious eating. They have, on their first appearance from the salt <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the lernaea salmonea, or salmon louse, adhering to them. They have both <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> and spawn; but no fry has as yet been observed. This is the fish called by the Scots phineer. They never exceed a foot in length. The upper jaw is a little longer than the lower; in the first are two rows of teeth, in the last one; on the tongue are six teeth. The back is straight; the whole body of an elegant form; the lateral line is straight; colour, between that and the top of the back, dusky and silvery intermixed; beneath the line, of an exquisite whiteness; first dorsal fin spotted with black; tail black, and much forked. 5. The smelt is the least of the trout kind; is frequent in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>, in the upper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, and the rivers that run into it, in the north of England, and in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. It is by several imagined to be the fry of the salmon; but Mr Pennant differs from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. See his Brit. Zool. III. 303. This species has a general resemblance to the trout, therefore must be described comparatively. 1stly, The head is proportionably narrower, and the mouth less than that of the trout. 2ndly, Their body is deeper. 3rdly, They seldom exceed six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> inches in length; at most, eight and a half. 4thly, The pectoral fins have generally but one large black spot, though sometimes a single small one attends it; whereas the pectoral fins of the trout are more numerously marked. 5thly, The spurious or fat fin on the back is never tipped with red; nor is the edge of the anal fin white. 6thly, The spots on the body are fewer, and not so bright; it is also marked from the back to the sides with six or seven large bluish bars; but this is not a certain character, as the same is sometimes found in young trouts. 7thly, The tail of the smelt is much more forked than that of the trout. These fish are very frequent in the rivers of Scotland, where they are called pars. They are also common in the Wye, where they are known by the name of skirlings, or laffings. 6. The alpinus, or charr, is an inhabitant of the lakes of the north, and of those of the mountainous parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It affects clear and pure waters, and is very rarely known to wander into running streams, except into such whose bottom is similar to the neighbouring lake. It is found in vast abundance in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> lakes on the summits of the Lapland <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, and is almost the only fish that is met with in any plenty in those regions; where it would be wonderful how they subsisted, had not <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> supplied them with innumerable larva of the gnat kind; these are food to the fish, who in their turn are a support to the migratory Laplanders in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>-voyages to the distant lakes. In such excursions those vacant people find a luxurious and ready repast in these fish, which they dress and eat without the addition of sauces; for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> render useless the inventions of epicurism. There are but few lakes in our <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> that produce this fish; and even those not in any abundance. It is found in Winander <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">Mere</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>; in Llyn Quellyn, near the foot of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SNOWDON">Snowdon</a>; and, before the discovery of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, in those of Llynberis; but the mineral streams have entirely destroyed the fish in the last lakes. In Scotland it is found in Loch Inch, and other neighbouring lakes, and is said to go into the Spey to spawn. "The largest and most beautiful we ever received (says Mr Pennant) were taken in Winender Mere, and were communicated by the Rev. Mr Farrish of Carlisle, with an account of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. He sent five specimens; two under the name of the cafe charr, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>; another he called the galt charr, i.e. a charr which had not spawned the preceding season, and on that account is reckoned to be in the greatest perfection. The two others were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a>, the red charr, the silver or gilt charr, the carpia lacus benacti, RAII Syn. pifc. 66. which last are in Westmoreland distinguished by the epithet red, by reason of the flesh assuming a higher colour than the other when dressed. "The umbla <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>, or cafe charr, spawns about Michaelmas, and chiefly in the river Brathy, which uniting with another called the Rowthay, about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> above the lake, they both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into it together. The Brathy has a black, rocky bottom; the bottom of the Rowthay is a bright sand, and into this the charr are never observed to enter. Some of them, however, spawn in the lake; but always in such parts of it which are stony, and resemble the channel of the Brathy. They are supposed to be in the highest perfection about May, and continue so all the summer; yet are rarely caught after April. When they are spawning..." spawning in the river they will take a bait, but at no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; being <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> taken, as well as the other species, in what they call <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-nets, which are in length about 24 fathoms, and about 5 where broadest.—The season which the other species spawn in is from the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> to the end of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. They are never known to ascend the rivers, but always in those parts of the lake which are springy, where the bottom is smooth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, and the water warmest. The fishermen judge of this warmth, by observing that the water seldom freezes in the places where they spawn except in intense frosts, and then the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICE">ice</a> is thinner than in other parts of the lake. They are taken in greatest plenty from the end of September to the end of November; at other times they are hardly to be met with. This species is much more esteemed for the table than the other, and is very delicate when potted. The length of the red char to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> in its tail, was 12 inches; its biggest circumference almost 7. The first dorsal fin was five inches and three quarters from the tip of its nose, and consisted of 12 branched rays, the first of which was short, the fifth the longest; the fat fin was very small. Each of the five fish had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> nostrils, and small teeth in the jaws, roof of the mouth, and on the tongue.—The jaws of the sea-char are perfectly even; on the contrary, those of the red-char were unequal, the upper jaw being the broadest, and the teeth hung over the lower, as might be perceived on passing the finger over them.—The gelt or barren char, was rather more slender than the others, as being without spawn. The back was of a gloomy dusky blue; the sides silvery, mixed with blue, spotted with pale red; the sides of the belly were of a pale red, the bottom white. The tails of each bifurcated.” 7. The thymalus, or grayling, haunts clear and rapid streams, and particularly those that flow through mountainous countries. It is found in the rivers of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>; in some of those of the north; in the Tame near <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUDLOW">Ludlow</a>; in the Lugg, and other streams near Leominster; and in the river near Christchurch, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>. It is also very common in Lapland: the inhabitants make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the guts of this fish instead of rennet, to make the cheese which they get from the milk of the rein deer. It is a voracious fish, rises freely to the fly, and will very eagerly take a bait. It is a very swift swimmer, and disappears like the transient pallage of a shadow, from whence we believe it derived the name of umbra. Effugiensque oculos celestis levis umbra natatu. Auson. The umbra swift escapes the quickest eye. Thymalus and thymus, are names bestowed on it on account of the imaginary scent, compared by some to that of thyme; but we never could perceive any particular smell. It is a fish of an elegant form; less deep than that of a trout; the largest we ever heard of was taken near Ludlow, which was about half a yard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and weighed four pounds six ounces; but this was a very rare instance. The irides are silvery, tinged with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; the teeth very minute, seated in the jaws and the roof of the mouth, but none on the tongue: the head is dusky; the covers of the gills of a gloomy green: the back and sides of a fine silvery grey; but when the fish is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> taken, varied slightly with blue and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>: the side-line is straight: the scales are large, and the lower edges dusky, forming straight rows from head to tail: the tail is much forked. 8. The eperlanus, or smelt, inhabits the seas of the northern parts of Europe, and probably never is found so far south as the Mediterranean: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> is one of the French rivers which receive it; but whether it is found south of that, we have not at present authority to say. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we can depend on the observations of navigators, who generally have too much to think of to attend to the minutiae of natural history, these fish are taken in the straits of Magellan, and of a most surprising size, some measuring 20 inches in length, and 8 in circumference. They inhabit the seas that wash these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> the whole year, and never go very remote from shore, except when they ascend the rivers. It is remarked in certain rivers, that they appear a long time before they spawn, being taken in great abundance in November, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, and January, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, but in others not till February; and in March and April they spawn; after which they all return to the salt water, and are not seen in the rivers till the next season. It has been observed, that they never come into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a> as long as there is any snow-water in the river. These fish vary greatly in size; but the largest we ever heard of was 13 inches long, and weighed half a pound. They have a very particular scent, from whence is derived one of their English names, smelt, i.e. smell it. That of sparling, which is used in Wales and the north of England, is taken from the French sperlan. There is a wonderful disagreement in the opinion of people in respect to the scent of this fish: some assert it flavours of the violet; the Germans, for a very different reason, distinguish it by the elegant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of flinchfish. —Smelts are often sold in the streets of London split and dried. They are called dried sparlings; and are recommended as a relish to a glass of wine in the morning. It is a fish of a very beautiful form and colour; the head is transparent, and the skin in general so thin, that with a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> the blood may be observed to circulate. The irides are silvery; the pupil of a full black; the under jaw is the longest: in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the upper jaw are four large teeth; those in the sides of both are small; in the roof of the mouth are two rows of teeth; on the tongue two others of large teeth. The scales are small, and readily drop off; the tail consists of 19 rays, and is forked. The colour of the back is whitish, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of green, beneath which it is varied with blue, and then succeeds a beautiful gloa of a silvery hue. 9. The lavaretus, or gwiniad, is an inhabitant of several of the lakes of the alpine parts of Europe. It is found in those of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, Savoy, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; of Norway, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, Lapland, and Scotland; in those of Ireland, and of Cumberland; and in Wales, in that of Llyngeid, near Bala, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERIONETHSHIRE">Merionethshire</a>. It is the same with the ferra of the lake of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>; the chelly of Hulie-water; the pollen of Lough Neagh; and the vangis and juvengis of Loch Mubon. The Scots have a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, that it was first introduced there by the beauteous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, their unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Stuart; and as in her time the Scots <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> was much Frenchified, it seems likely that the name was derived from the French vendoise, a “dace,” to which a slight observer might be tempted to compare it, from the whiteness of its scales. The British name gwiniad, or whitling, was bestowed upon it for the same reason. It is a gregarious fish, and approaches the shores in vast shoals in spring and in summer; which proves in many places a blessed relief to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> of inland countries, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> as the annual return of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> is to those who inhabit the coasts. Between 7000 and 8000 have been taken at one draught. The gwiniad is a fish of an insipid <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and must be eaten soon, for it will not keep long; those that choose to preserve them do it with salt. They die very soon after they are taken. Their spawning season in Llynegid is in December. The largest gwiniad we ever heard of weighed between three and four pounds: the head is small, smooth, and of a dusky hue: the eyes very large; the pupil of a deep blue: the nose blunt at the end; the jaws of equal length: the mouth small and toothless: the branchiostegal rays <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a>: the covers of the gills silvery, powdered with black. The back is a little arched, and slightly carinated: the colour, as far as the lateral line, is glossed with deep blue and purple; but towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> assumes a silvery cast, tinged with gold; beneath which those colours entirely prevail. The tail is very much forked: the scales are large, and adhere <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the body.

SALON

Pages 623-623
or Saloon, in architecture, a lofty, spacious sort of hall, vaulted at top, and usually comprehending two stories, with two ranges of windows. The salon is a grand room in the middle of a building, or at the head of a gallery, &c. Its faces, or sides, are all to have a symmetry with each other; and as it usually takes up the height of two stories, its ceiling, Daviler observes, should be with a moderate sweep. The salon is a state-room much used in the palaces in Italy; and from thence the mode came to us. Ambassadors, and other great visitors, are usually received in the salon. It is sometimes built square, sometimes round or oval, sometimes octagonal, as at Marly, and sometimes in other forms.

SALONICHI

Pages 623-623

formerly called Thessalonica, a seaport town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, with an archbishop's see. It is <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, and rich, being about 10 miles in circumference. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade, carried on principally by the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> and Jews, the former of which have 30 churches, and the latter as many synagogues; the Turks also have a few mosques. It is surrounded with walls, flanked with towers, and defended on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-side by a citadel, and near the harbour with three forts. It was taken from the Venetians by the Turks in 1431. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> merchandise is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. It is seated at the bottom of a gulph of the same name, partly on the top, and partly on the side of a hill, near the river Vardar. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23. 13. N. Lat. 40. 41.

SALSES

Pages 623-623

a very strong castle of France, in Roussillon, on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>. It was taken from the Spaniards by the French in 1642; and is seated on a lake of the same name, among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, 10 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Perignan. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 0. N. Lat. 43. 35.

SALSETTA

Pages 623-623

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the East-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, near the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on this side the Ganges, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Decan. It is 25 miles in length, and 12 in breadth; and is very fertile in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, fruit, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes. It belongs to the Portuguese, and the Jesuits possess the best <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of it. It has a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many villages and churches; but no town, except an old one called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORA">Cora</a>, hewn out of the side of a rock, which is extremely <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>. It is near a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in length, and has many antique figures and columns, curiously carved in the rock; at present it has no inhabitants but wild beasts and birds of prey. They have no trade, except in dried fish, because it is so near <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>, being only separated from it by a channel half a mile over, which is fordable at low <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 72. 15. N. Lat. 19. 0.

SALSOLA

Pages 623-624

Glass-wort; a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the pentandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The kali, which grows naturally in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> marshes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parts of England. It is an annual plant, which rises above five <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> six inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, sending out many side branches, which spread on every side, garnished with short awl-shaped leaves; which are fleshy, and terminate in acute spines. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are produced from the side of the branches, to which they fit <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, and are encompassed by short prickly leaves; they are small, and of an herbaceous <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The seeds are wrapped up in the empalement of the flower, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> in autumn; soon after which, the plant decays. 2. The tragus grows naturally on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> shores of the south of France, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. This is also an annual plant, which sends out many diffused stalks, garnished with linear leaves an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, ending with sharp spines. The flowers come out from the side of the stalks in the same manner as those of the former; their empalements are blunt, and not so closely encompassed with leaves as those of the other. 3. The soda, rises with herbaceous stalks near three feet high, spreading wide. The leaves on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> stalk, and those on the lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the branches, are long, slender, and have no spines; those on the upper part of the stalk and branches are slender, short, and crooked. At the base of the leaves are produced the flowers, which are small, and hardly perceptible; the empalement of the flower afterwards encompasses the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a>, which contains one coiled seed. 4. The vermiculata grows naturally in Spain. This hath shrubby perennial stalks, which rise three or four feet high, sending out many side-branches, garnished with fleshy, oval, acute-pointed leaves, coming out in clusters from the side of the branches; they are hoary, and have stiff prickles. The flowers are produced from between the leaves toward the ends of the branches; they are so small as scarce to be discerned, unless they are closely viewed. The seeds are like those of the other kinds. 5. The rosetacea grows naturally in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. This is an annual plant, whose stalks are herbaceous, and seldom rise more than five or six inches high. The leaves are awl-shaped, ending in acute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; the empalements of the flowers spread open; the flowers are small, and of a rosy colour, but soon fade; the seeds are like those of the other sorts. All the sorts of glass-wort are sometimes promiscuously. SAL curiously used for making the sal alkali, but it is the third sort which is esteemed best for this purpose. The manner of making it is as follows: Having dug a trench near the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, they <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> laths across it, on which they lay the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> in heaps, and, having made a fire below, the liquor, which runs out of the herbs, drops to the bottom, which at length thickening becomes sal alkali, which is partly of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and partly of an ash-colour, very sharp and corrosive, and of a saltish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. This, when thoroughly hardened, becomes like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and is then called sode or sod. It is transported from thence to different countries for making of glaas.

SALTIER

Pages 631-631

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> ordinances defined p. 3595, and represented in Plate CXLVII. This says G. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEIGH">Leigh</a>, in his Accedence of Arm. 70. was anciently made of the height of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and driven full of pins, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of which was to fell walls, &c. Upton says it was an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> to catch wild beasts, whence he derives this word from saltus, i.e. "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>," The French call this ordinary sautoir, from sauter "to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>;" because it may have been used by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to leap over walls of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, which in former times were but low; but some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> authors think it is borne in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of St Andrew's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALTPETRE">SALTPETRE</a>. See Nitre.

SALTSBURG

Pages 631-632

an archbishopric of Germany, in the circle of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, bounded on the east by Styria and the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Tyrol, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Bavaria, and on the south by the duchy of Carinthia and the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIXEN">Brixen</a>. It is said to be about 100 miles from east to west, and upwards of 60 from north to south. With respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, it is very mountainous; yielding, however, excellent pasturage, and, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of that, abounding in cattle, and horses remarkable for their mettle and hardiness. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is particularly noted for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> it produces, and its strong pastures and cattle. Here are also considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> calaminaris, with quarries of marble, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> hot-bath. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Salza, the Inn, the Ens, and Muer; which, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and other streams, are well stored with fish. The peasants here are all allowed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of arms, and trained to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> duty. There are no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> in the country, and most of the lands belong to the clergy. The states consist of the prelates, the cities, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. Notwithstanding this country is under the power of a Popish ecclesiastic, and the violent, arbitrary, and oppressive manner in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> have always been treated, great numbers of them still remained in it till the year 1732, when no less than 30,000 of them withdrew from it, dispersing themselves in the several Protestant states of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and some of them were even sent from Great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> to the American colonies. Besides <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALZBURG">Salzburg</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> wares, and all sorts of arms and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of coarse cloth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> here. The archbishop has many and great prerogatives: he is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the empire, and perpetual legate of the holy see in Germany, of which he is also <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a>. He has the first <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the diet of this circle, and next to the electors in that of the empire, in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of princes, in which he and the archduke of Austria preside by turns. No <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> lies from him, either in civil <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> causes, but to the pope alone; and he is entitled to wear the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>. He has also the nomination to several bishoprics; and the canonates that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> vacant in the months in which the popes, by virtue of the concordat, are allowed to nominate, are all in his gift. His suffragans are the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of Freisingen, Ratibon, Brixen, Gurk, Chiemsee, Seckau, and Lavant; and of these, the four last are nominated, and even confirmed by him, and not by the pope. At the diet of the empire, his envoy takes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of all the princes that are present, under the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a>. His revenue is said to amount to near 200,000l. a-year, a great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of it arising from the salt-works. He is able to raise 25,000 men; but keeps in constant pay, besides his guards, only one regiment, consisting of 1000 men. His <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> is very magnificent; and he has his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> great officers, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> colleges. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> consists of 24 canons, who must be all noble, but are obliged only to four months residence. At his accession to the see, the archbishop must pay 100,000 crowns to Rome for the pall. There is an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> here, instituted in 1711, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of St Rupert, who was the first bishop of Salzburg about the beginning of the eighth century. Salzburg, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a German archbishopric of the same name, and which takes its own from the river Salza, on which it stands, and over which it has a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. It is well fortified, and the residence of the archbishop. The castle here is very strong, and as strongly garrisoned, and well provided with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and warlike stores. The archbishop's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is magnificent; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> before it is a fountain, esteemed the largest and grandest in Germany. The stables are very lofty; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the horses usually kept by the archbishop, is said to be upwards of 200. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, of which one part stands on a steep rock, is well built, but the streets are narrow and badly paved. Besides the abovementioned, there are two other lately palaces belonging to the archbishop, one of which is called the Neubau, and the other Marienbella. The latter of these has a very beautiful garden; and the number of trees in the orangery is so great, that Mr Keyser tells us, 20,000 oranges have been gathered from them in one year. The river Salza runs <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by the walls of this garden. There are a great many other fine structures in the city, public and private, such as palaces, monasteries, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and churches. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> dedicated to St Rupert, (the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> of Bavaria, and a Scotsman by birth,) all the altars are of marble of different kinds, and one of the organs has above 3200 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>. The winter and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> riding-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> here are noble structures. The university was founded in 1620, and committed to the SALVAGE <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, a reward allowed by the civil and statute <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, for the saving of ships or goods from the danger of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, pirates, or enemies.—Where any ship is in danger of being stranded, or driven on shore, justices of the peace are to command the constables to assemble as many persons as are necessary to preserve it; and, on its being preserved by their means, the persons assisting therein shall, in 30 days after, be paid a reasonable reward for their salvage; otherwise the ship or goods shall remain in the custody of the officers of the customs as a security for the same. SALVATOR ROSA. See Rosa.

SALUTATION

Pages 632-632

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of saluting, greeting, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> paying respect and reverence to any one. There is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety in the forms of salutation. The Orientals salute by uncovering their feet, laying their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on their breasts, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> we salute by uncovering the head, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> the body, &c. The pope makes no reverence to any mortal except the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, to whom he stoops a very little when he permits him to kiss his lips.

SALUTE

Pages 632-633

in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, a testimony of deference <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> homage rendered by the ships of one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> to another, or by ships of the same nation to a superior or equal. This <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> is variously performed, according to the circumstances, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, or situation, of the parties. It consists in firing a certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cannon, or volleys of small arms; in striking the colours or topsails; or in one or more general shouts of the whole ship's crew, mounted on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> or rigging for that purpose. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> regulations with regard to salutes in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> navy are as follow: "When a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>-officer salutes the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> and commander-in-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the fleet, he is to give him fifteen guns; but when captains salute him, they are to give him seventeen guns. The admiral and commander-in-chief of the fleet is to return two guns less to flag-officers, and four less to captains. Flag-officers saluting their superior or senior officer, are to give him thirteen guns. Flag-officers are to return an equal number of guns to flag-officers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> their flags on the same mast, and two guns less to the rest, as also to captains." "When a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> salutes an admiral of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or blue, he is to give him fifteen guns; but to vice and rear admirals, thirteen guns. When a flag-officer is saluted by two or more of his majesty's ships, he is not to return the salute till all have finished, and then to do it with such a reasonable number of guns as he shall judge proper. "In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of the meeting of two squadrons, the two chiefs only are to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> salutes. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> single ships meet a squadron consisting of more than one flag, the principal flag only is to be saluted. No salutes shall be repeated by the same ships, unless there has been a separation of six months at least. "None of his majesty's ships of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, commanded only by captains, shall give or receive salutes from one another, in whatsoever <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world they meet. "A flag-officer commanding in chief shall be saluted, upon his first hoisting his flag, by all the ships present, with such a number of guns as is allowed by the first, third, or fifth <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. "When any of his majesty's ships shall meet with any ship or ships belonging to any foreign <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or state, within his majesty's seas (which extend to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINISTERRE">Finisterre</a>), it is expected, that the said foreign ships do strike their top-tail, and take in their flag, in acknowledgement of his majesty's sovereignty in those seas; and if any shall refuse or offer to resist, it is enjoined to all flag-officers and commanders to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> their utmost endeavours to compel them thereto, and not suffer any dishonour to be done to his majesty, and if any of his majesty's subjects shall so much forget their duty, as to omit striking their top-tail in passing by his majesty's ships, the name of the ship and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and from whence, and whither bound, together with affidavits of the fact, are to be sent up to the secretary of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, in order to their being proceeded against in the admiralty <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>. And it is to be observed, that in his majesty's seas, his majesty's ships are in no ways to strike to any; and that in other parts, no ship of his majesty's is to strike her flag or top-tail to any foreigner, unless such foreign ship shall have first struck, or at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> strike her flag or top-tail to his majesty's ship. "The flag-officers and commanders of his majesty's ships are to be careful to maintain his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> upon all occasions, giving protection to his subjects, and endeavouring, what in them lies, to secure and encourage them in their lawful <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; and they are not to injure, in any manner, the subjects of his majesty's friends and allies. "If a foreign admiral meets with any of his majesty's ships, and salutes them, he shall receive <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a> for gun. If he be a vice-admiral, the admiral shall answer with two guns less. If a rear-admiral, the admiral and vice-admiral shall return two less. But if the ship be commanded by a captain only, the flag-officer shall give two guns less, and captains an equal number. "When any of his majesty's ships come to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> in a foreign port or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, within cannon-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> of its forts, the captain may salute the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with such a number of guns as have been customary, upon good assurance of having the like number returned, but not otherwise. But if the ship bears a flag, the flag- officer shall first carefully inform himself how flags of like rank, belonging to other crowned heads, have given or returned salutes, and to insist upon the same terms of respect. "It is allowed to the commanders of his majesty's ships in foreign parts, to salute the persons of any admirals commanders in chief, or captains of ships of war of foreign nations, and foreign noblemen or strangers of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, as also the factories of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s subjects, coming on board to visit the ship; and the number of guns is left to the commander, as shall be suitable to the occasion and the quality of the persons visiting; but he is nevertheless to remain accountable for any excesses in the abuse of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. If the ship visited be in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with other ships of war, the captain is not to make use of the civilities allowed in the preceding articles but with leave and consent of the commander in chief or the senior captain. "Merchant-ships, whether foreigners or belonging to his majesty's subjects, saluting the admiral of the fleet, shall be answered by six guns less; when they salute any other flag-ships, they shall be answered by four guns less; and if they salute men of war commanded by captains, they shall be answered by two guns less. If several merchant-ships salute in company, no return is to be made, till all have finished, and then by such a number of guns as shall be thought proper; but though the merchant-ships should answer, there shall be no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> return. "None of his majesty's ships of war shall salute any of his majesty's forts or castles in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, on any pretence whatsoever."

SALUZZO

Pages 633-633

called by the French Saluces, a town and castle of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a marquisate of the same name, with a bishop's see. It is situated on an eminence at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> near the river Po, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18. 27. N. Lat. 44. 35. It is subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>. Saluzzo, the marquisate of, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Piedmont in Italy, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Dauphiny and the province of the four valleys, on the east by those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVIGLIANO">Savigliano</a> and Fossano, on the south by that of Cona and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Nice, and on the west by Barcelonetta. It was ceded to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy in 1601.

SALVIA

Pages 632-632

sage; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the diandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The officinalis, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sage, which is cultivated in gardens, of which there are the following varieties: 1. The common green sage. 2. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMWOOD">wormwood</a> sage. 3. The green sage, with a variegated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>. 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> sage. 5. The red sage with a variegated leaf; these are accidental variations, and therefore are not enumerated as species. The common sage grows naturally in the southern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, but is here cultivated in gardens for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; but that variety with red or blackish leaves, is the most common in the British gardens; and the wormwood sage is in greater plenty here than the common green-leaved sage, which is but in few gardens. 2. The tomentosa, generally titled balsamic sage by the gardeners. The stalks of this do not grow up upright as those of the common sage; they are very hairy, and divide into several branches, which are garnished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> heart-shaped woolly leaves standing upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> foot-stalks; they are sawed on their edges, and their upper surfaces are rough; the leaves, which are upon the flower-stalks, are <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> and oval, standing upon shorter foot-stalks, and are very slightly sawed on their edges; they grow in whorled spikes toward the top of the branches; the whorls are pretty far distant, but few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> in each; they are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> blue, about the size of those of the common sort. This sage is preferred to all the others for making <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEA">tea</a>. 3. The auriculata, common sage of virtue, which is also well known in the gardens and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>. The leaves of this is narrower than those of the common sort; they are hoary, and some of them are indented on their edges towards the base, which indentures have the appearance of ears. The spikes of flowers are longer than those of the two former sorts, and the whorls are generally naked, having no leaves between them. The flowers are smaller, and of a deeper blue than those of common red sage. 4. The pomifera, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>-shaped oval entire leaves, grow naturally in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. This hath a shrubby stalk, which rises four or five feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, dividing into several branches. The flowers grow in spikes at the end of the branches; they are of a pale blue <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and have obtuse empalements. The branches of this sage have often punctures made in them by insects, at which places grow large protuberances as big as apples, in the same manner as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a> upon an oak, and the rough balls on the briar. All the sorts of sage may be propagated by seeds, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they can be procured; but, as some of them do not perfect their seeds in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and most of the sorts, but especially the common kinds for use, are easily propagated by slips, it is not worth while to raise them from seeds.

SALVIANUS

Pages 632-632

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> father of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, who flourished in the 5th century, and was well skilled in the sciences. It is said he lived in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINENCE">continence</a> with his wife Palladia, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she had been his sister; and that he was so afflicted at the wickedness of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that he was called the Jeremiah of the 5th century. He acquired such reputation for his piety and learning, that he was named the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. He wrote a Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>; another on Avarice; and some epistles, of which Baluze has given an excellent edition; that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONRAD">Conrad</a> Ritterhufius, in 2 vols octavo, is also esteemed.

SAMARCAND

Pages 633-633
or Samarqand, an ancient and famous town of Asia, capital of the kingdom of the same name in the country of the Uzbek Tartars, with a castle and a famous university. The houses are built with stones, and it carries on a trade in excellent fruits. It is pleasantly seated near the river Sogde, a branch of the Amu, E. Long. 69. 0. N. Lat. 39. 50. This town was the capital of the kingdom of Sogdia in the time of Alexander the Great, when it was called Maracanda. It was afterwards the capital of the empire of Tamerlane the Great. In the time of Jenkiz Khan it was forced to yield to the arms of that cruel conqueror; by whom the garrison, amounting to 30,000 men, were butchered; 30,000 of the inhabitants, with their wives and children, were presented to his generals; the rest were permitted to live in the city, on paying a tribute of 300,000 dinars or crowns of gold.

SAMARIA

Pages 633-635

(anc. geogr.) one of three larger Cisjordan districts, situated in the middle between Galilee to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and Judea to the south, beginning Samaria at the village Ginnæa, in the Campus Magnus, and ending at the toparchy called Acrobatena, (Josephus). Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> differing in nothing from that of Judæa; both equally hilly and champain, both equally fertile in corn and fruit, (id.) Called the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Samaria and Ephraim, (<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>); comprising the ten tribes, and consequently all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the north of Judea and east and west of Jordan. Samaria, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the kingdom <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> country of that name; anciently called Schomron, from Semer, the owner of the hill; the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of the kings of Israel, from Omri, who built the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to its destruction, and the Assyrian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, under Hosea the last <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICAH">Micah</a>, Sulp. Severus.) It soon after rose from its ruins, being restored by the Cuthæans, who thence took the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a>; said to be a very strong city under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MACCABEES">Maccabees</a>, but entirely destroyed by John Hyrcanus, (Josephus), and again restored by Gabinius, prefect of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; till at length it was enlarged and adorned by Herod, and called Sebaste, that is, Augusta, in compass twenty stadia, (Josephus). Samaritans, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> among the Jews, still subsisting in some parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, under the same name. Its origin was in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Rehoboam, under whose reign the people of Israel were divided into two distinct kingdoms, that of Judah and that of Israel; when the capital of the latter being Samaria, the Israelites obtained the name of Samaritans. They were anciently guilty of idolatry, and the Rabbins pretend, that they worshipped the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a dove on mount Gerizim; but the present Samaritans, who are but few in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, are far from being idolaters. They celebrate the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PASSOVER">passover</a> every year, on the fourteenth <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, on Mount Gerizim, and begin that feast with the sacrifice appointed for that purpose in Exodus: they keep the Sabbath with all the rigour with which it is enjoined in the book of Exodus, none of them stirred off doors but to the synagogue. They sacrifice nowhere but on mount Gerizim: they observe the feasts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a>, tabernacles, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>, &c. and never defer circumcision beyond the eighth day: they never marry their nieces as the Jews do; have but one wife; and in fine, do nothing but what is commanded in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Sambucus, elder; a genus of the trigynia order, belonging to the pentandra clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The nigra, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> blackelder-tree, rises with a tree-stem, branching numerously into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> spreading head, twenty or thirty feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; pinnated leaves, of two or three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of oval lobes and an odd one; and large, five-parted umbels of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> towards the ends of the branches, succeeded by bunches of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and other different coloured berries, in the varieties, which are—Common black-berried elder-tree—White-berried elder—Green-berried elder—Laciniated, or parsley-leaved elder, having the folioles much lacinuated, so as to resemble parsley-leaves—<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>-striped-leaved elder—Silver-striped elder—Silver-dusted elder. 2. The racemosæ, racemosæ <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>-berried elder, rises with atree-like stem, branching ten or twelve feet high, having reddish-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> branches and buds; pinnated leaves of six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> oval deeply-sawed lobes; and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, oval, ra- Sambucus cemous clusters of whitish-green flowers, succeeded by oval clusters of red-berries. This is a resident of the mountainous parts of the south of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and is retained in our gardens as a flowering shrub, having a peculiar singularity in its oval clustered flowers and berries. 3. The Canadensis, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> shrubby elder, rises with a shrubby stem, branching eight or ten feet high, having reddish shoots; somewhat bipinnated leaves, often ternate below, the other composed of five, seven, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> oval lobes; and towards the ends of the branches, cymose quinquepartite umbels of flowers, succeeded by blackish-red berries. All the sorts of elder are of the deciduous tribe, very hardy, and grow freely any where; are generally free shooters, but particularly the common elder and varieties, which make remarkably strong, jointed shoots, of several feet in length, in one season; and they flower mostly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, except the racemosæ elder, which generally begins flowering in April; and the branches being large, spreading, and very abundant, are exceedingly conspicuous; but they emit a most disagreeable odour. The flowers are succeeded in the midst of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, by large bunches of ripe berries in autumn, which, although very unpalatable to eat, are in high estimation for making that well known cordial liquor called elder wine, particularly the common black-berried elder.
