The merit of the elder in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a> may be both for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and ornament, especially in large grounds. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAMOGITIA">Samogitia</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, bounded on the north by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>, on the east by Lithuania, on the west by the Baltic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, and on the south by Regal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, being about 175 miles in length and 125 in breadth. It is full of forests and very high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which feed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of cattle, and produce a large <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. There are also very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> horses, in high esteem. The inhabitants are clownish, but honest; and they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not allow a young woman to go out in the night, without a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and two bells at her girdle. Rof-senna and Wormia are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> places. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAMOIEDA">Samoieda</a>, a country of the Russian empire, between Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a> and Archangel, lying along the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> as far as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. The inhabitants are a rude people, that they can hardly pretend to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, except in their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> and figure: they have little understanding; and in many things resemble <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, for they will eat carrion of every kind. They travel on the snow on sledges, drawn with an animal like a rein-deer, but with the horns of a stag. Those who have seen them affirm, that no people on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> make such shocking figures: their stature is short; their shoulders and faces are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, with flat broad noses, great blubber hanging lips, and staring eyes; their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> is dark, their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and as black as pitch, and they have very little beards; and it is said that all the Samoied women have black nipples. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they have any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> at all, it is idolatry, though there has been some attempts of late to convert them. Their huts are made of birch bark sewed together, which is laid upon stakes set in the ground, and at the top is a hole to let out the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>; the fire is made in the middle, and both men and women <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> naked round them all night. They have little regard to the nearness of kin, and take as many wives as they can keep; their only employment is hunting and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>.

SAMIAN EARTH

Pages 635-635

in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>, the name of two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a> used in medicine, viz. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> kind, called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> collyrium sanium, being astringent, and therefore good in diarrhoeas, dysenteries, and haemorrhagies; they also used it externally in inflammations of all kinds. 2. The brownish-white kind, called after sanium, by Dioscorides; this also stands recommended as an astringent.

SAMOS

Pages 635-635

(anc. geogr.), an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> at no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from the promontory Mycale, on the continent of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and opposite to Ephesus; the distance only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> stadia, (Strabo); a free island, in compass eighty-seven miles, (Pliny); <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> one hundred, (Ididorus): with a cognominal town, (<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Horace); famous for the worship and a temple of Juno, with a noted <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Strabo, Tacitus); and hence their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> exhibited a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>, (Athenaeus): The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, who, to avoid the oppression of tyrants, retired to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> of freedom. Samos, tho' not so happy in producing wine, which Strabo wonders at, all the adjoining <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> yielding a generous sort, yet abounding in all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The Vafa Samia, among earthen <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, were held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> repute. Samii, the people, (Ovid).—The island is now in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Turks. It is about 32 miles in length, and 22 in breadth, and extremely fertile. The inhabitants live at their ease, their <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a> by the Turks being moderate. The women are very nasty and ugly, and they never shift above once a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. They are clothed in the Turkish manner, except a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> coat, and their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> hanging <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> their backs, with plates of silver or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>-tin fastened to the ends. They have abundance of melons, lentils, kidney-beans, and excellent mukadine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>. They have <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> figs, four times as big as the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sort, but not so well tasted. Their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a> is very fine, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and wax admirable; besides which, their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> are excellent: they have <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, and most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is of a rusty <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>: they have also <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMERY">emery</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are of white marble. The inhabitants are about 12,000, who are almost all Greeks; and the monks and priests occupy most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island. They have a bishop who resides at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORA">Cora</a>.

SAMSON

Pages 635-635

one of the judges of Israel, memorable for his supernatural strength, his victories over the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>, and his tragic end, as related in the book of Judges. Samson's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">Post</a>, a sort of pillar erected in a ship's hold, between the lower deck and the keelson, under the edge of a hatchway, and furnished with several notches that serve as steps to mount <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> descend, as occasion requires. This post, being firmly driven into its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, not only serves to support the beam and fortify the vessel in that place, but also to prevent the cargo or materials contained in the hold, from shifting to the opposite side, by the rolling of the ship in a turbulent and heavy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Books of SAMUEL, two canonical books of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, as being usually ascribed to the prophet Samuel. The books of Samuel, and the books of Kings, are a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the reigns of the kings of Israel and Judah; for which reason the books of Samuel are likewise styled the first and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> books of Kings. Since the first 24 chapters contain all that relates to the History of Samuel, and the latter <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the first book and all the second include the relation of events that happened after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that prophet, it has been supposed that Samuel was author only of the first 24 chapters, and that the prophets Gad and Nathan finished the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The first book of Samuel comprehends the transactions under the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELI">Eli</a> and Samuel, and under <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a> the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>; and also the acts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> while he lived under Saul; and is supposed to contain the space of 101 years. The second book contains the history of about 40 years, and is wholly spent in relating the transactions of David's reign.

SANCHONIATHON

Pages 635-635

a Phoenician historiographer, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Gideon the Israelitish judge, who wrote <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> books of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Phoenicia; we have some fragments of it in Porphyry de Abstinentia, and in Eusebius. Mr Dodwell thinks it all counterfeit.

SANCROFT

Pages 635-635

archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, was born at Fressingfield in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, in 1616; and admitted into Emanuel <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, in 1633. In 1642, he was elected a fellow; and, for refusing to take the covenant, was ejected from his fellowship. In 1660, he was chosen one of the university preachers; and in 1663, was nominated to the deanery of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>. In 1664, he was installed <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of St Paul's. In this station he set himself with unrestrained diligence to repair the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, till the fire of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1666 employed his thoughts on the more noble undertaking of rebuilding it, toward which he gave 1400l. He also rebuilt the deanery, and improved the revenue of it. In 1668, he was admitted archdeacon of Canterbury, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s presentation. In 1677, being now prolocutor of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>, he was unexpectedly advanced to the archbishopric of Canterbury. In 1678, he was committed to the tower, with six other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, for presenting a petition to the king against <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>. Upon king James II.'s withdrawing himself, he concurred with the lords in a declaration to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> for a free <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and due indulgence to the protestant dissenters. But when that prince and his consort were declared king and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> refusing to take the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> to their majesties, he was suspended and deprived. He lived in a very private manner, till he died in 1693. His learning, integrity, and piety, made him an exalted ornament of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He published a volume in 12mo, intitled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> Politics, taken from Machiavel, Borgia, and other choice authors; Familiar Letters to Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a>, an 8vo pamphlet; and three of his sermons were printed together after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.

SANCTIFICATION

Pages 635-636

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of sanctifying, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> rendering a thing holy. The reformed divines define sanctification to be an act of God's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, by which a person's desires and affections are alienated from the world; and by which he is made to die to sin, and to live to righteousness; or in other words, to feel an abhorrence horrence of all vice, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and virtue.

SANCTION

Pages 636-636

the authority given to a judicial <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, by which it becomes legal and authentic.

SANCTORIUS

Pages 636-636

a most ingenious and learned physician, professor in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, in the beginning of the 17th century. He contrived a kind of statical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, by means of which, after estimating the aliments received, and the sensible discharges, he was enabled to determine with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> exactness, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of insensible perspiration, as well as what kind of victuals and drink increased <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> diminished it. On these experiments he erected a curious system, which he published under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of De medicina fluida; of which we have an English translation by Dr Quincy. Sanctorius published several other treatises, which shewed great abilities and learning.

SANCTUARY

Pages 636-636

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, is also used for that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the church in which the altar is placed, encompassed with a rail <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> balustrade.

SAND

Pages 636-636

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a genus of fossils, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are, that they are found in minute concretions; forming together a kind of powder, the genuine particles of which are all of a tendency to one determinate shape, and appear regular though more <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> less complete concretions; not to be dissolved or disunited by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or formed into a coherent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> by means of it, but retaining their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in it; transparent, vitrifiable by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and not dissoluble in nor effervescing with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>. Sands are subject to be variously blended, both with homogene and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> substances, as that of talc, &c. and hence, as well as from their various colours, are subdivided into, 1. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a> sands, whether pure or mixed with other arenaceous or heterogeneous particles; of all which there are several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, differing no less in the fineness of their particles, than in the different degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, from a bright and shining white, to a brownish, yellowish, greenish, &c. white. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> and reddish sands, both pure and impure. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> sands, whether pure or mixed, are also very numerous. 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> sands, distinguished in the same manner. 5. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> sands, whereof there are only two species, viz. a fine shining greyish-black sand, and another of a fine shining reddish-black colour. 6. The green kind; of which there is only one known species, viz. a coarse variegated dusky green sand, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>. Sand is of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the glass-manufacture; the white <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> sand being employed for making of the white glass, and a coarse greenish-looking sand for the green glass. In <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, it seems to be the office of sand to make unctuous earths fertile, and fit to support vegetables, &c. For <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> alone, we find, is liable to coalesce, and gather into a hard coherent mass, as appears in clay; and being thus embodied, and as it were glued together, is no way disposed to nourish vegetables. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> such earth be mixed with sand, its pores are thereby kept open, and the earth itself loosed, so as thus to give room for the juices to ascend, and for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> to be nourished thereby. A vegetable planted only in sand, or in a fat glebe, or in earth, receives little growth or increase; but a mixture of both renders the mass fertile. In effect, earth is in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> made organic by means of sand; pores and spaces, something analogous to vessels, being thereby maintained, by which the juices may be conveyed, prepared, digested, circulated, and at length discharged. Common sand is, therefore, a very good addition, by way of manure, to all sorts of clay-lands; it warms them, and makes them more open and loose.

SAND-BAGS

Pages 636-636

in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, are bags filled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> sand, holding each about a cubic foot; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is to raise parapets in haste, or to repair what is beaten <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>.

SANDAL

Pages 636-636

in antiquity, a rich kind of slipper worn on the feet by the Greek and Roman ladies, made of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other precious stuff; consisting of a sole, with an hollow at one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> to embrace the ankle, but leaving the upper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the foot bare. Sandal, is also used for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a> or slipper worn by the pope and other Roman prelates when they officiate. It is also the name of a sort of slipper worn by several congregations of reformed monks. This last consists of no more than a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> leathern sole, fastened with latches or buckles, all the rest of the foot being left bare. The capuchins wear sandals; the recollets, clogs; the former are of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and the latter of wood.

SANDARACH

Pages 636-637

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a very beautiful native fossil, though too often confounded with the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> factitious <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> arsenic, and with the red <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> formed by melting the common <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORPIMENT">orpiment</a>. It is a pure substance, of a very even and regular structure, is throughout of that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> which our dyers <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-scarlet, and is considerably transparent even in the thickest pieces. But though, with respect to colour, it has the advantage of cinabar while in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, it is vastly inferior to it when both are reduced to powder. It is moderately hard, and remarkably heavy; and, when exposed to a moderate <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, melts and flows like <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> set on fire, it burns very briskly. It is found in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; and is sold to the painters, who find it a very fine and valuable red: but its virtues <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> qualities in medicine, are no more ascertained at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> than those of the yellow orpiment. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">Gum</a>-Sandarach, is a dry and hard resin, usually met with in loose granules, of the bigness of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, a hori- horfe-bean, or larger; of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> whitish yellow colour, transparent, and of a resinous smell, brittle, very inflammable, of an acid and aromatic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and diffusing a very pleasant smell when <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>. It is produced from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the juniper. It flows only from these trees in hot countries; but the natives promote its discharge by making incisions in the bark. Sandarach is esteemed good in diarrhoeas, and in hemorrhagies. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>-makers make a kind of varnish of it, by dissolving it in oil of turpentine or linseed, or in spirit of wine. SANDERS. See SAUNDERS.

SANDIVER

Pages 637-637

a whitish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, continually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> up from the metal, as it is called, whereof glass is made; and, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> on its surface, is skimmed off. Sandiver is also plentifully thrown out in the eruptions of volcanos; some of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and others tinged bluish <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> yellowish. Sandiver is said to be detergent, and good for foulnesses of the skin. It is also used by gilders of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>.

SANDIX

Pages 637-637

a kind of minium, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, made of cerule, but much inferior to the true minium.

SANDWICH

Pages 637-637

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, one of the cinque ports, and which has the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of an earldom. It consists of about 1500 houses, most of them old, and built with wood, though there are a few new ones built with brick and flints. It has three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> narrow streets paved, and thirty <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-street <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> alleys, with about 6000 inhabitants, but no particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a>. The town is walled round, and also fortified with ditches and ramparts; but the walls are much decayed, on account of the harbour being so choked up with sand that a ship of 100 tons burthen cannot get in. E. Long. 1° 20'. N. Lat. 51° 20'. SANDWICH <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, one of those lately discovered in the South <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, lying near <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol16.html#article-NEW_IRELAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. No particulars concerning it are known, but that it is inhabited by woolly-headed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>.

SANDYS

Pages 637-637
brother of the foregoing Sir Edwin, and youngest son of archbishop Sandys, was born in 1577. He was a most accomplished gentleman; travelled over several parts of Europe and the East; and published a relation of his journey in folio, in 1615. He made an elegant translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses; and composed some poetical pieces of his own, that were greatly admired in the times of Sanguification, their being written. He also paraphrased the Psalms; and has left behind him a Translation, with Notes, of one Sacred Drama written originally by Grotius, under the title of Christus Patiens; on which, and Adamus Exul, and Maenius, is founded Lauder's impudent charge of plagiarism against our immortal Milton. Our author became one of the privy chamber to Charles I, and died in 1643.

SANGUIFICATION

Pages 637-637

in the animal economy, the conversion of the chyle into true blood. See BLOOD.

SANGUISORBA

Pages 637-637

greater wild burnet; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the tetrandria class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is the officinalis, with oval spikes. This grows naturally in moist meadows in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The stalks rise from two to three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, branching towards the top; and are terminated by thick oval spikes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of a greyish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which are divided into four segments almost to the bottom. These are succeeded by four <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> cornered seeds. The leaves of this plant are composed of five <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of lobes placed along a midrib, terminated by an odd one. These are heart-shaped, deeply sawed on their edges, and a little downy on their under-sides. The cultivation of this plant has been greatly recommended as food to cattle. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a>, n° 47—49.

SANGUNARIA

Pages 637-637

blood-root; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the polyandria class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is only one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz., the canadensis, a native of the northern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, where it grows plentifully in the woods; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, before the leaves of the trees come out, the surface of the ground is in many places covered with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which have some resemblance to our wood <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANEMONE">anemone</a>; but they have short naked pedicels, each supporting one flower at top. Some of these flowers <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have 10 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> 12 petals, so that they appear to have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> range of leaves, which has occasioned their being termed double flowers; but this is only accidental, the same roots in different years producing different flowers. The plant can bear the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but should be placed in a loose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and sheltered situation, not too much exposed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. It is propagated by the roots; which may be taken up and parted, in September, every other year. The Indians paint themselves <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> with the juice of these plants.

SANHEDRIM

Pages 637-638
or SANHEDRIN, among the Jews, the great council of the nation, consisting of 70 senators, taken partly from among the priests and levites, and partly out of the inferior judges, who formed what was called the lesser sanhedrim. The room they met in was a rotunda, half of which was built without the temple, and half within. The nasi, or president of the sanhedrim, sat upon a throne, with his deputy on his right-hand, his sub-deputy on his left, and the other senators ranged in order on each side. The authority of this council was very extensive; for they decided such causes as were brought before them by way of appeal from the inferior courts; and the king, the high priest, and prophets, were under the jurisdiction of this tribunal. They had the right of judging in capital cases, and sentence of death might not be pronounced in any other place; for which which reason the Jews were forced to quit this hall, when the power of life and death was taken out of their hands, 40 years before the destruction of the temple, and three years before the death of Christ. There were several inferior sanhedrins in Palestine, each of which consisted of 23 persons; all these depended on the great sanhedrin of Jerusalem.

SANICULA

Pages 638-638

*sanicle*, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> *self-heal*; a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the pentandria class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. the europaea, found in many parts both of Scotland and England. This plant was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> celebrated for its healing virtues, both internally and externally; but is now totally disregarded.

SANIDIUM

Pages 638-638

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of a genus of foliis of the clas of the felenitae, but neither of the rhomboidal nor columnar kinds, nor any other way distinguishable by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; being made up of several plain flat plates.

SANIES

Pages 638-638

in medicine, a serous putrid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, issuing from wounds. It differs from pus, which is thicker and whiter.

SANNAZARIUS

Pages 638-638

in Latin *Adius Cinzenii Sannazarius*, a celebrated Latin and Italian poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> in 1458. He by his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> ingratiated himself into the favour of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Frederic; and, when that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was dethroned, attended him into France, where he staid with him till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1504. Sannazarius then returned into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he applied himself to polite literature, and particularly to Latin and Italian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. His gay and facetious humour made him sought for by all companies; but he was so afflicted at the news that Philibert prince of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, general of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, had demolished his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, that it threw him into an illness, of which he died in 1530. It is said, that being informed a few days before his death, that the prince of Orange was killed in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, he cried out, "I shall die contented, since <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> has punished this barbarous enemy of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>." He wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Italian and Latin poems; among those in Latin, his *De Partu Virginis*, and Eclogues, are chiefly esteemed; and the most celebrated of his Italian pieces is his *<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>*.

SANTA CRUZ

Pages 638-638

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Barbary, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, with a harbour and a fort. The Moors took it from the Portuguese in 1536. It is seated at the extremity of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Aguer. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 55. N. Lat. 36. 30. **Santa Cruz de la Sierra**, a town of South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a province of that name in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, and in the audience of Los-Charcas, with a bishop's see. It is seated at the foot of a mountain, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounding in good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, on the river Guayp. W. Long. 59. 35. S. Lat. 20. 40. **<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SANTA_FE">Santa Fe</a> de Bogota**, a town of South America, and capital of New <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, with an archbishop's see, a supreme <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and an university. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGDALENA">Magdalena</a>, in a plentiful country, abounding in corn, cattle, and fruit, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, 360 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>. W. Long. 60. 5. N. Lat. 3. 58.

SANTAREN

Pages 638-638

a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a>, seated on a mountain near the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TA">Ta</a>- jo, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> very fertile in wheat, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. They get in their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> here two months after they have sown their corn. It was taken from the Moors in 1447. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 45. N. Lat. 39. 12.

SANTEN

Pages 638-638

a town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>. It has a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, wherein is an image of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, which they pretend performs a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. Here the fine walks begin that run as far as Wefel, from which it is five miles distant to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 33. N. Lat. 51. 38.

SANTERRE

Pages 638-638

a small territory of France, in Picardy; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Cambresis, on the east by Vermandois, on the west by Amienois, and on the south by the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOMME">Somme</a>. It is very fertile, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERONNE">Peronne</a>.

SANTEUIL

Pages 638-639
or rather **Santeul**, (John Baptist de), in Latin *Santolius Victorinus*, an excellent Latin poet, was born at Paris in 1630. Having finished his studies in Lewis the Great's college, he applied himself entirely to poetry, and celebrated in his verse the praises of several great men; by which he acquired universal applause. He enriched Paris with a great number of inscriptions, which are to be seen on the public fountains, and the monuments consecrated to posterity. At length, some new hymns being to be composed for the Breviary of Paris, Claude Santeuil his brother, and M. Boffuet, persuaded him to undertake that work; and he succeeded in it with the greatest applause. On which the order of Clugny desiring him to compose some for their Breviary, he complied with their request; and that order, out of gratitude, granted him letters of filiation, with an annual pension. Santeuil was cared for by all the learned men of his time; and had for his admirers the two princes of Condé, the father and son, from whom he frequently received favours. Lewis XIV. also gave him a proof of his esteem, by bestowing a pension upon him. He attended the duke of Bourbon to Dijon, when that prince went thither in order to hold the estates of Burgundy; and died there in 1697, as he was preparing to return to Paris. Besides his Latin hymns, he wrote a great number of Latin poems, which have all the fire and marks of genius discoverable in the works of great poets. To Santeuil we are indebted for many fine church-hymns, as above mentioned. Santeuil read the verses he made for the inhabitants of heaven with all the agitations of a demoniac. Despreaux said he was the devil whom God compelled to praise saints. He was among the number of poets whose genius was as impetuous as his muse was decent. La Bruyere has painted the character of this singular and truly original poet in the most lively colours. "Image a man of great facility of temper, complaisant and docile, in an instant violent, choleric, passionate, and capricious. A man simple, credulous, playful, volatile, puerile; in a word, a child in grey hairs: but let him collect himself, or rather call forth his interior genius, I venture to say, without his knowledge or privacy, what fallies! what elevation! what images! what latinity! Do you speak of one and the same person, you will ask? Yes, of the same; of Theodas, and of him alone. He shrieks, he jumps, he rolls upon the..." Santillane, the ground, he roars, he storms; and in the midst of Santolina, this tempest, a flame issues that shines, that rejoices. Without a figure, he rattles like a fool, and thinks like a wise man. He utters truths in a ridiculous way; and, in an idiotic manner, rational and sensible things. It is astonishing to find good sense disclose itself from the bottom of buffoonery, accompanied with grimaces and contortions. What shall I say more? He does and he says better than he knows. There are like two souls that are unacquainted with each other, which have each their turn and separate functions. A feature would be wanting in this extraordinary portrait, if I omitted saying, that he has at once an insatiable thirst for praise, ready to throw himself at the mercy of the critics, and at the bottom so docile as to profit by their censure. I begin to persuade myself, that I have been drawing the portraits of two different persons: it would not be impossible to find a third in Theodas; for he is a good man, a pleasant man, an excellent man. This poet ought not to be confounded with Claude de Santeuil, his brother, a learned ecclesiastic, who also wrote several hymns in the Paris Breviary under the name of Santolus Maglioranus, a name given him from his having lived a long time in the seminary of St Magliore at Paris, in quality of secular ecclesiastic. He was esteemed not only for his poetical abilities, but also for his profound erudition and his exemplary piety. He died at Paris in 1684, aged 57. He wrote several other pieces of poetry, besides his hymns, which are printed with his brother's works.

SANTILLANE

Pages 639-639

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASTURIAS">Asturias</a>, of which it is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. It is seated on the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, 55 miles east of Oviedo, and 200 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 33'. N. Lat. 43° 30'.

SANTOLINA

Pages 639-639

LAVENDER-COTTON; a genus of the order of polygamia aequalis, belonging to the syngenesia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The chamæcyparissus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> Lavender-cotton, which has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> known in the English gardens; it was formerly titled abrotanum femina, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> fowternwood, and by the corruption of words was called brotany by the market-people: it grows naturally in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and the warm parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. This hath a ligneous stalk, dividing into many branches, garnished with slender hoary leaves, that are four ways indented, and have a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> strong odour when handled. The branches are terminated by a single flower, composed of many hermaphrodite florets, which are filiform, cut into five parts at the top, of a sulphur <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and are included in one common calyx empalement, having no borders or rays. These are succeeded by small, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, striated seeds, which are separated by scaly chaff, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> in the empalement; the plants <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> a dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and a sheltered situation. 2. The villosa, with woolly leaves, has a shrubby stalk, which branches out like the former, but the plants seldom grow so tall. The branches are garnished very closely below with leaves shaped like those of the other sort, but shorter, thicker, and whiter; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are much larger, and the brims of the florets are more reflexed; they are of a deeper sulphur colour than the other. It grows naturally in Spain. 3. The decumbens, with linear leaves, is of lower stature than either of the former, seldom rising more than 15 or 16 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The branches spread horizontally near the ground, and are garnished with shorter leaves than either of the former, which are hoary and finely indented; the stalks are terminated by single flowers, of a bright <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour, which are larger than those of the first sort. 4. The viridis, with very long linear leaves, rises higher than either of the former. The branches are more diffused; they are slender, smooth, and garnished with very narrow long leaves, which are of a deep green colour, but two ways indented; the stalks are slender, naked towards the top, and terminated by single flowers of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> colour. 5. The rosmarinifolia, with linear entire leaves, hath shrubby stalks, which rise about three feet high, sending out long slender branches, garnished with single linear leaves of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>-green colour. The stalks are terminated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, single, globular flowers, of a pale sulphur colour. 6. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>, with linear obtuse leaves, is somewhat like the fifth; but the branches are shorter, thicker, and closer garnished with leaves, which come out in clusters. The flower-stalks are sparingly disposed, and have leaves to their top; the flowers are small, and of a yellow colour. 7. The chamæmelifolia, with obtuse woolly leaves, hath shrubby stalks, which rise three feet high, garnished with broader leaves than either of the former, whose indentures are looser, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>; they are hoary, and when bruised have an odour like chamomile. The leaves are placed pretty far asunder, and the stalks are garnished with them to the top. The stalks are divided likewise at the top into two or three foot-stalks, each sustaining one pretty large sulphur-coloured flower. All these plants may be cultivated so as to become ornaments to a garden, particularly in small bosquets of ever-green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, where, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are artfully intermixed with other plants of the same growth, and placed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> line, they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> make an agreeable variety; especially if care be taken to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a> them twice in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> to keep them within bounds, otherwise their branches are apt to straggle, and in wet <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> to be borne <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and displaced, which renders them unsightly; but when they are kept in order, their hoary and different-coloured leaves will have a pretty effect in such plantations.—They may be propagated by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> slips or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a> during the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, in a border of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> fresh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, but must be watered and shaded in hot dry weather until they have taken root; after which they will require no farther care but to keep them clean from weeds till autumn, when they should be transplanted where they are designed to remain: but if the ground is not ready by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to receive them, it will be proper to let them remain in the border until spring; for if they are transplanted late in autumn, they are liable to be destroyed by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> in winter.

SANTORINI

Pages 639-640

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Candia, and to the south-west of Naphlio. It is eight miles in length, and near as much in breadth, and almost covered with pumice-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in general must be dry and barren; it is, however, greatly improved by the labour and industry. industry of the inhabitants, who have turned it into a garden. It affords a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of barley, plenty of cotton, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of wine. Fruit is scarce, except figs; and they have neither <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> nor wood. The inhabitants are all Greeks, and are about 10,000 in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. Pyrgos is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town, and there are several little <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages. They have but one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> in the island, for which reason they prefer the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> in cisterns. Though subject to the Turks, they choose their own magistrates. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>., 25° 5'. N. Lat., 39° 10'.

SAONE

Pages 640-640

a considerable river of France, which has its source in mount Vosgue, near Darney; runs thro' the Franche Comte, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, Beaujolais; and falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a> at Lyons. It passes by Gray, Chalons, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACON">Macon</a>.

SAPINDUS

Pages 640-640

the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">SOAP</a>-BERRY TREE; a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the octandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The saponaria with winged leaves, grows naturally in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the West Indies, where it rises with a woody stalk from 20 to 30 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, fending out many branches garnished with winged leaves composed of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of spear-shaped lobes. The midrib has a membranaceous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> leafy border, running on each side from one pair of lobes to the other, which is broadest in the middle between the lobes; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are produced in loose spikes, at the end of the branches; they are small and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, so make no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> appearance. These are succeeded by oval berries as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as middling cherries, sometimes single, at others, two, three, or four are joined together; these have a saponaceous skin or cover, which incloses a very smooth roundish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> of the same form, of a shining <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> when ripe. The skin or pulp which surrounds the nuts, is used in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> to wash <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>; but it is very apt to burn and destroy it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> often used, being of a very acrid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. 2. The rigidus, with rigid acute-winged leaves, grows in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. This hath Saponaria a strong woody stalk, which rises about 20 feet high, fending out many strong ligneous branches, covered with a smooth grey bark, and garnished with winged leaves, composed of many spear-shaped lobes; they are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> green, and sit <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the midrib, which has no border or wing like the other. The end of the branches are divided into two or three foot-stalks, each sustaining a loose spike of flowers like those of the other sort; these are succeeded by roundish berries like those of the former. These plants are propagated by seeds; they must be put into small pots, and plunged into a hot-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of tanner's bark. In five or six weeks the plants <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear, when the glases of the hot-bed should be raised every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> in warm <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, to admit fresh <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> to the plants. In three weeks or a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> after the plants appear, they will be fit to transplant, when they must be shaken out of the pots, and carefully parted, so as not to injure their roots, and each planted into a separate small pot, and plunged into the hot-bed again, observing to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> them from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> until they have taken new root; after which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> they must have free air admitted to them every day when the weather is warm, and will require to be frequently watered.

SAPONARIA

Pages 640-640

Soapwort; a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the decandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is the officinalis, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> soapwort, which grows naturally in many parts of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. It has a creeping root, so that in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> it would fill a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> space of ground. The stalks are about two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and of a purplish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The footstalks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> arise from the wings of the leaves opposite; they sustain four, five, or more purple flowers each; which have generally two small leaves placed under them. The stalk is also terminated by a loose bunch of flowers growing in form of an umbel; they have each a large swelling cylindrical empalement, and five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> obtuse petals, which spread open, of a purple colour. These are succeeded by oval capsules with one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CELL">cell</a> filled with small seeds.—The decoction of this plant is used to cleanse and scour woollen cloths: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people in some countries <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it instead of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> for washing; from whence it had its name.

SAPPERS

Pages 640-640

are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, whose business it is to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> at the saps, and for which they have an extraordinary pay. A brigade of sappers generally consists of eight men, divided equally into two parties; and whilst one of these parties is advancing the sap, the other is furnishing the gabions, fascines, and other necessary implements, who relieve each other alternately.

SAPPHIRE

Pages 640-641

a pellucid gem, which, in its finest state, is extremely beautiful and valuable, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> only to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> in lustre, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>, and price. Its proper <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is a pure blue; in the finest specimens it is of the deepest azure, and in others varies into paleness in shades of all degrees between that and a pure crystal brightness and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, without the least tinge of colour, but with a luster much superior to the crystal. They are distinguished into four sorts, viz. the blue sapphire, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> sapphire, the water sapphire, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> sapphire. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a> known to us by this name is extremely different from the sapphire of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, which was only a semi-opaque <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of a deep blue, veined with white, and spotted with small <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>-coloured spangles, in the form of stars, and was only a more beautiful kind kind of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> lazuli; but our sapphire they have described under the name of beryllus acrodes, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the sky-blue <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERYL">beryl</a>. The finest sapphires in the world are brought from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a>, in the East Indies; where some are found perfectly colourless, and others of all the shades of blue; these are all found in the pebble-form. We have very fine sapphires also, partly pebble, partly crystal-shaped, from Bisnagar, Cononar, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALICUT">Calicut</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ceylon: these also are of all the shades of blue. And in Ceylon there are sometimes found a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> gems, of a mixed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> between the sapphire and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RUBY">ruby</a>. The occidental are from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and many other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; but though these are often very beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, they are greatly inferior, both in lustre and hardness, to the oriental.

SAPPHO

Pages 641-641

a famous poetess of antiquity, who for her excellence in her art has been called the Tenth Muse, was born at Mitylene in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>, about 610 years before Christ. She was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Stesichorus and Alcæus; which last was her countryman, and as some think her suitor. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of this poet, in which he intimates to her his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, is preserved in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, Rhet. lib. i. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 9. together with the fair damsel's answer. ALCÆUS. I fain to Sappho would a wish impart, But fear locks up the secret in my heart. SAPPHO. Thy downcast looks, respect, and timid <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, Too plain the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of thy wish declare; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> lawless, wild, inordinate desire, Did not with thoughts impure thy bosom fire, Thy tongue and eyes, by innocence made bold, Ere now the secret of thy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> had told. M. la Fevre observes, that Sappho was not in her usual good-humour when she gave so <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> an answer to a request, for which, at another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, perhaps she would not have waited.—It has been thought too, that Anacreon was one of her lovers, and his editor Barnes has taken some pains to prove it: but <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not admit this; since, upon inquiry, it will be found that Sappho was probably dead before Anacreon was born. Of the numerous poems this lady wrote, there is nothing remaining but some small fragments, which the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> scholiasts have cited; a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> to Venus, preserved by Dionysius of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>; and an ode to one of her mistresses; which last piece confirms a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> delivered <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from antiquity, that her amorous passion extended even to persons of her own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, and that she was willing to have her mistresses as well as her gallants. Ovid introduces her making a sacrifice to Phaon one of her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> paramours: from which we learn, that Sappho's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for her own sex did not keep her from loving ours. She fell desperately in love with Phaon, and did all she could to win him; but in vain: upon which she threw herself headlong from a rock, and died. It is said, that Sappho could not forbear following Phaon into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, whither he retired that he might not see her; and that during her stay in that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, she probably composed the hymn to Venus, still extant, in which she begs so ardently the assistance of that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>. Her prayers, however, proved ineffectual; Phaon was cruel to the last <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. The unfortunate Sappho was forced to take the dread- ful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>; she went to the promontory Leucas, and threw herself into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The cruelty of Phaon will not surprise us so much, if we reflect, that she was a widow; (for she had been married to a rich <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> in the isle of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANDROS">Andros</a>, by whom she had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, named Cleis;) that she had never been handsome; that she had observed no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> in her passion to both sexes; and that Phaon had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> known all her charms. She was, however, a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and for that alone deserves to be remembered. The Mitylenians had her merit in such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem, that they paid her sovereign honours after her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and stamped their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> with her image. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> afterwards erected a noble statue of Porphyry to her; and in short, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> as well as moderns have done <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. Voisius says, that none of the Greek poets excelled Sappho for sweetness of verse; and that she made Archilochus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of her style, but at the same time took care to soften the severity of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. It must be granted, says Rapin, from what is left us of Sappho, that Longinus had great reason to extol the admirable genius of this woman: for there is in what remains of her something delicate, harmonious, and impassioned to the last degree.

SARABAND

Pages 641-641

a musical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> in the triple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the motions of which are slow and serious. Saraband is also a dance to the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, which usually terminates when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> that beats the time falls; and is otherwise much the same as the minuet. The saraband is said to be originally derived from the Saracens, and is usually danced to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of the guitar <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> cittern.

SARACENS

Pages 641-641

the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>; so called from the word sara, which signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, as the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Arabia is: and this being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Mahomet, his disciples were called Saracens.

SARAGOSSA

Pages 641-642

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> Arragon, with an archbishop's see, an university, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>. It is said to have been built by the Phenicians; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> sent a colony here in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Augustus, whence it had the name of Caesar Augustus, which by corruption has been changed into Saragossa. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, handsome, and well-built town. The streets are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, well paved, and very clean, and the houses from three to six stories <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. It is adorned with many magnificent buildings; and they reckon 17 large churches, and 14 handsome monasteries, not to mention others less considerable. The river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EBRO">Ebro</a> runs across the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, dividing into two; and on its banks is a handsome quay, which serves for a public walk. The Holy-street is the largest, and so broad that it may be taken for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; and here they have their bull-fights: in this street there are several noblemen's families, particularly that of the viceroy. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> are handsome and richly adorned, as well as the churches. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, after the Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; but the finest church is that of Nuestra Signora del Pilar, seated on the side of the Ebro, and is a place of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> in Spain. They tell us the virgin appeared to St James, who was preaching the gospel, and left him her image, with a handsome pillar of jasper; it is still in this church, which they pretend is the first in the world built to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. This image stands on a marble pillar, with a little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> in her arms; but the place is so dark, that it cannot be seen without the assistance of lamps, which are 50 in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and all of silver. There are also chandeliers and balustrades of maffy silver. The ornaments of this image are the richest that can be imagined, her <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> being full of precious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of an inestimable price; in short, there is scarce anything to be seen but <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and jewels, and a vast number of people come in pilgrimage hither. The town-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is a sumptuous structure, adorned with fine columns; in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> are the pictures of all the kings of Arragon; and in a corner of it St George on horseback, with a dragon of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble under him. It is seated in a very large plain, where the Ebro receives two other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; and over it are two bridges, one of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and the other of wood, which last has been thought the most beautiful in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. A victory was obtained here over the French and Spaniards in 1710, but it was abandoned by the allies soon after. It is 97 miles west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TARRAGONA">Tarragona</a>, 137 west of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>, and 150 north-east of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. W. Long. 0° 48'. N. Lat. 41° 47'.

SARCASM

Pages 642-642

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, a keen bitter <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> which has the true point of satire, by which the orator scoffs and insults his enemy: such as that of the Jews to our Saviour; "He saved others, himself he cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a>."

SARCOCELE

Pages 642-642

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, a spurious rupture, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERNIA">hernia</a>, wherein the testicle is considerably tumefied or indurated, like a scirrhus, or much enlarged by a fleshy excrescence, which is frequently attended with acute pains, so as to degenerate at last into a cancerous disposition. See Surgery.

SARCOCOLLA

Pages 642-642

a concrete juice, brought from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, in small whitish-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> grains, with a few of a reddish and sometimes of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> mixed with them; the whitest tears are preferred, as being the freshest: its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is bitter, accompanied with a dull kind of sweetness. This drug dissolves in watery liquors, and appears chiefly to be of the gummy kind, with a small admixture of resinous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. It is principally celebrated for coagulating wounds and ulcers; (whence its name σαρκοξυλον, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>), a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> which neither this nor any other drug has any <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to.

SARCOLOGY

Pages 642-642

is that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of anatomy which treats of the soft parts, viz. the muscles, intestines, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a>, veins, nerves, and fat.

SARCOPHAGUS

Pages 642-642
or Lapis Affinis, in the href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural history of the ancients; a stone much used among the Greeks in their sepultures, and is recorded to have always perfectly consumed the flesh of human bodies, buried in it, in forty days. This property it was much famed for, and all the ancient naturalists mention it. There was another very singular quality also in it, but whether in all, or only in some peculiar pieces of it, is not known; that is, its turning into stone anything that was put into vessels made of it. This is recorded only by Mutianus and Theophrastus, except that Pliny had copied it from these authors, and some of the later writers on these subjects from him. The account Mutianus gives of it is, that it converted into stone the shoes of persons buried in it, as also the utensils which it was in some places customary to bury with the dead, particularly those which the person, while living, most delighted in. The utensils this author mentions, are such as must have been made of very different materials; and hence it appears that this stone had a power of consuming only flesh, but that its petrifying quality extended to substances of very different kinds. Whether ever it really possessed this last quality, has been much doubted; and many, from the seeming improbability of it, have been afraid to record it. What has much encouraged the general disbelief of it is, Mutianus's account of its taking place on substances of very different kinds and textures; but this is no real objection, and the whole account has probably truth in it. Petrifications in those early days might not be distinguished from incrustations of sparry and stony matter on the surfaces of bodies only, as we find they are not with the generality of the world even to this day; the incrustations of spar on mosses and other substances in some of our springs, being at this time called by many petrified mosses, &c. and incrustations like these might easily be formed on substances enclosed in vessels made of this stone, by water passing through its pores, dislodging from the common mass of the stone, and carrying with it particles of such spar as it contained; and afterwards falling in repeated drops on whatever lay in its way, it might again deposit them on such substances in form of incrustations. By this means, things made of every so different matter, which happened to be inclosed, and in the way of the passage of the water, would be equally incrusted with and in appearance turned into stone, without regard to the different configuration of their pores and parts.
