The place from whence the ancients tell us they had this stone was Assos, a city in Lycia, in the neighbourhood of which it was dug; and De Boot informs us, that in that country, and in some parts of the East, there are also stones of this kind, which, if tied to the bodies of living persons, would in the same manner consume their flesh. Hill's Notes on Theophrastus, p. 14.

SARCOTICS

Pages 642-642

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, medicines which are supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> in wounds.

SARDANAPALUS

Pages 642-643

the last <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, whose character is one of the most infamous in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. He is said to have sunk so far in depravity, that, as far as he could, he changed his very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. He cloathed himself as a woman, and spun amidst companies of his concubines. He painted his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and behaved in a more lewd manner than the most lascivious <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARLOT">harlot</a>. In short, he buried himself in the most unbounded sensuality, quite regardless of sex, and the dictates of nature. Having grown odious to all his subjects, a rebellion was formed against him by Arbaces the Mede and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BELSHAZZAR">Belshazzar</a> the Babylonian. They were attended, however, with very bad success at first, be- ing defeated with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> slaughter in three pitched battles. With great difficulty Belesis prevailed upon his men to keep the field only five days longer; when they were joined by the Bactrians, who had come to the assistance of Sardanapalus, but had been prevailed upon to renounce their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to him. With this reinforcement, they twice defeated the troops of Sardanapalus, who shut himself up in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NINEVEH">Nineveh</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of his empire. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> held out for three years; at the end of which, Sardanapalus finding himself unable to hold out any longer, and dreading to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of an enraged enemy, retired into his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of which he caused a vast pile of wood to be raised; and heaping upon it all his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> apparel, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> inclosing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a> and concubines in an apartment within the pile, he set fire to it, and so destroyed himself and all together.

SARDINIA

Pages 643-643

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Mediterranean, bounded by the strait which divides it from Corsica, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; by the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which flows between this island and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, on the east; and by other parts of the Mediterranean sea on the south and west. It is about 140 miles in length, and 60 in breadth. There is a pleasing variety of hills and valleys, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is generally fruitful, and would produce corn, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> in abundance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was manured; but the inhabitants are a slothful <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, and cultivate but a little <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of it. On the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> there is a fishery of anchovies and coral, of which they send <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>. The beeves and sheep are very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, as well as horses. This island was under the dominion of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> till the year 1708; when Sir John Leake, the English <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, reduced it to the obedience of the late <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VI. It was afterwards allotted to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy as an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Sardinia; under whose dominion it still remains. This island is divided into two parts; the one, called Capo-di-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAGLIARI">Cagliari</a>, lies to the south; and the other Capo-di-Lugary, which is seated to the north. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Cagliari the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, Orifatagno, and <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol19.html#article-SASSARI">Sassari</a>. SARDONIUS risus, Sardonian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>. A convulsive involuntary laughter; thus named from the herba sardonia, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of ranunculus, and is said to produce such convulsive motions in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> as resemble those motions which are observed in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> during a fit of laughter. This complaint is sometimes speedily fatal. If the ranunculus happens to be the cause, the cure must be attempted by means of a vomit, and frequent draughts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYDROMEL">hydromel</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>.

SARDIS

Pages 643-643

now called Sardo, is an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and is seated forty miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>. This town was formerly the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Croesus; but is now reduced to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> village, containing nothing but wretched huts. However, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> caravansary, where travellers may commodiously lodge. The inhabitants are generally shepherds, who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> their sheep into the fine pastures of the neighbouring plain. The Turks have a mosque here, which was a Christian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, at the gate of which there are several columns of polished marble. There are a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who are employed in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 28° 5'. N. Lat. 37° 5'.

SARDONYX

Pages 643-643

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a genus of semipellucid gems, of the onyx structure, zoned <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> tabulated, and composed of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the onyx variegated with that of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> Carnelian. See Carnelian and Onyx.

SARGUS

Pages 643-643

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>. See Sparus. SARMENTOSÆ, (from farmentum, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> shoot like that of a vine); the name of the 11th class in Linnæus's Fragments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> method, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which have climbing stems and branches, that like the vine, attach themselves to the bodies in their neighbourhood for the purpose of support. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, p. 1306.

SASHES

Pages 643-643

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> dress, are badges of distinction worn by the officers of most nations, either round their waist, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> over their shoulders. Those for the British <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> are made of crimson <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; for the Imperial army, crimson and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; for the Prussian army, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> silk and silver; the Hanoverians, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> silk; the Portuguese, crimson silk with blue tassels.

SASINE

Pages 643-643
or Seasine. See Law, No cixiv. 15, &c. SASAFRAS. See Laurus.

SATELLITE

Pages 643-643

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, the same with a secondary planet <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>.

SATRAPA

Pages 643-643
or Satrapes, in Persian antiquity, denotes an admiral; but more commonly the governor of a province.

SATTIN

Pages 643-643

a glossy kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stuff, the warp of which is very fine, and stands so as to cover the coarser woof.

SATTINET

Pages 643-643

a slight thin kind of sattin, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> striped, and ordinarily used by the ladies for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> night-gowns.

SATURATION

Pages 643-643

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, is the impregnating an acid with an alkali, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> vice versa, till either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> receive no more, and the mixture will then become neutral.

SATURDAY

Pages 643-643

the seventh and last <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, so called from the idol Seater, worshipped on this day by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Saxons, and thought to be the same as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> of the Latines.

SATUREIA

Pages 643-644

savory; a genus of the gymnospermia order, belonging to the didynamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">Species</a>. 1. The hortensis, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> savory, is an annual plant, which grows naturally in the south of France and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, but is cultivated in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> both for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> and medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. 2. The montana, or winter savory, is a perennial plant growing naturally in the south of France and Italy, but is cultivated in gardens both for culinary and medicinal purposes. Culture. Both kinds are propagated by seeds. Those of the first kind should be sown in the beginning of April upon a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, either where they are to remain, or for transplanting. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the plants are to stand unmoved, they should be sown thinly; but if they are to be transplanted, they may be sown closer. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> species may be sown upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, where the plants <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> will endure the severest winters, though they are often killed by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a> when planted in good ground. The plants will continue several years; but when they are old, the shoots will be short and not so well furnished with leaves: it will therefore be proper to raise a supply of young plants every year. **Ufer.** Summer savory is a very warm pungent aromatic; and affords in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> a subtile essential <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, of a penetrating smell, and very hot acid <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. It yields little of its virtues by infusion to aqueous liquors; rectified spirit extracts the whole of its taste and smell, and elevates nothing in distillation. **SATURN,** in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> of our solar system revolving at the distance of more than 900 millions of miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. See Astronomy. **SATURN,** in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, an appellation given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. **SATURN,** in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> in bazoning the arms of sovereign princes. **SATURN,** one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of the Pagan deities, was the son of Caelus and Terra, and the father of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. He depoised and calumniated his father; and obliged his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Titan to resign his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> to him, on condition of his bringing up none of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> issue, that the succession might at length devolve on him. For this purpose he devoured all the sons he had by his wife Rhea or Cybele: but she bringing forth at one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> Jupiter and Juno, she presented the latter to her husband, and sent the boy to be nursed on mount Ida; when Saturn being informed of her having a son, demanded the child; but in his stead his wife gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> swaddled up like an infant, which he instantly swallowed. Titan finding that Saturn had violated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> he had made with him, put himself at the head of his children, and made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> on his brother, and having made him and Cybele prisoners, confined them in Tartarus: but Jupiter being in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time grown up, raised an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, went to his father's assistance, defeated Titan, and restored Saturn to the throne. Some time after, Saturn being told that Jupiter intended to dethrone him, endeavoured to prevent it; but the latter being informed of his intention, depoised his father, and threw him into Tartarus. But Saturn escaping from thence, fled into Italy, where he was kindly received by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of the country, who associated him to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>: whence Italy obtained the name of **Saturnia Tellus**; as also that of **Latium,** from *latio,* "to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> hid." There Saturn, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and mildness of his government, it is said to have produced the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. **SATURNALIA,** in Roman antiquity, a festival observed about the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the god Saturn, whom Lucan introduces giving an account of the ceremonies observed on this occasion, thus: "During my whole reign, which lasts but for one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, no public business is done; there is nothing but drinking, singing, playing, creating imaginary kings, placing servants with their masters at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, &c. There shall be no disputes, reproaches, &c. but the rich and poor, masters and slaves, shall be equal, &c." On this festival the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> sacrificed bare-headed, contrary to their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> at other sacrifices. **SATURNINE,** an appellation given to persons of a melancholy disposition, as being supposed under the influence of the planet Saturn. **SATYR,** or **Satire,** in matters of literature, a discourse or poem, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> the vices and follies of mankind. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, n° 88. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> satirists among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> are, Horace, Juvenal, and Persius; those among the moderns, are, Regnier and Boileau, in French; and Dryden, Oldham, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>, Pope, Young, &c. among the English. **SATYRIASIS.** See Medicine, n° 466. **SATYRS,** in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>'s retinue, represented with disagreeable faces, their heads armed with short horns, with hairy bodies, and with the feet and legs of goats. They are represented by the poets as having their usual residence in the woods and forests, and as being of a wanton and lustful disposition. Some think the notion of these satyrs might have been derived from the monkeys known at present under the same name. See the article SIMIA.

SAUCISSON

Pages 647-647

is likewise a kind of salcine, longer than the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ones; they serve to raise batteries and to repair breaches. They are also used in making e-paumets, in stopping <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, and in making traverses over a wet ditch, &c.

SAUMUR

Pages 648-648

a considerable town of France, in Anjou, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Saumarois, with an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> castle. Here is an important passage over the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, upon which there is a famous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, o. 2. N. Lat. 47° 15'.

SAUNDERS

Pages 648-648

a kind of wood brought from the East Indies. There are three kinds of it; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>.—The white comes in billets about the thickness of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s leg, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> whitish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. It has been recommended for its medical virtues; but from its total want of smell <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, nothing in this way can be expected.—The yellow kind has a pleasant smell, and a bitterish aromatic taste accompanied with an agreeable pungency. This wood, according to Dr <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, though unnoticed in the present practice, might undoubtedly be applied to many valuable medical purposes. Distilled with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, it yields a fragrant essential <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which thickens in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> into the consistence of a balsam. Digested in pure spirit, it imparts a rich yellow tincture; which being committed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, the spirit arises without bringing over anything considerable of the flavour of the saunders. The residuum contains the virtues of six times its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the wood. Hoffman looks upon the extract as a medicine of similar virtues to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a>, and recommends it as an excellent restorative in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> debilities.—The red kind is brought from the East Indies in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> billets, of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> texture, a dull red, almost blackish colour on the outside, and a deep bright red within. This wood has no manifest smell, and little or no taste; nevertheless it has been recommended as a mild astringent, and corroborant of the nervous system; qualities which belong only to the yellow sort. It is principally employed as a colouring drug; and communicates a deep red to rectified spirit, but scarce to any oil excepting that of lavender.—It is easily distinguished from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>-wood, because the latter readily communicates its colour to water, which saunders <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not.

SAUNDERSON

Pages 648-648

an illustrious professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, was born at Thurleston in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> in 1682. When he was twelve months old, he lost not only his eye-sight, but his very eye-balls, by the small-pox; so that he could retain no more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of vision than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had been born <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>. His father, who was in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>, instructed him in numbers; for which he discovered so uncommon a capacity, that with no more learning than he gained at a private academy, and his own industry, assisted by a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> reader, it was resolved to send him to Cambridge not as a scholar but as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. He accordingly went thither in 1707, and his fame in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> filled the university. The Principia Mathematica, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, and Arithmetica Universalis, of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, were the foundations of his lectures, and afforded him a noble field for the display of his genius; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers came to hear a blind <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> give lectures on optics, discourse on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and colours, explain the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of vision, the effect of glasses.

SAURIN

Pages 649-649

a celebrated protestant minister, was born at Nîmes in 1677. His father, who was a lawyer, retired after the repeal of the edict of Nantz to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, at which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he died; and Saurin quitting his studies, in 1694 made a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>, and procured a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of colours. But when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Savoy concluded a peace with France, he quitted a profession for which he was not calculated, and resumed his studies at Geneva. In 1700, he visited <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and England; in which latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> he staid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough to marry a wife in 1703, and returned to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> in 1705. Here he preached with extraordinary applause, and died in 1730. There are 10 vols of his sermons, besides other works, all greatly esteemed.

SAUVEUR

Pages 650-651

an eminent French mathematician, born at La Fleche in 1653. He was absolutely dumb until he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and even then his organs of speech did not disengage themselves so freely, but that he was ever after obliged to speak with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> deliberation. Mathematica were the only studies he had any relish for, and these he cultivated with extraordinary success; so that he commenced teacher at 20 years of age, and was so soon in vogue, that he had <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> Eugene for his scholar. He was made mathematical professor in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in 1686; and ten years after was admitted a member of the Academy of Sciences. He died in 1716; and his writings, which consist rather of detached papers than of connected treatises, are all inserted in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of of the Academy of Sciences. He was twice married; and by the last wife had a son, who, like himself, was dumb for the first seven years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.

SAVAGE

Pages 644-647

one of the most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> that is to be met with perhaps in all the records of biography, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> countess of Macclesfield, by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">Rivers</a>, according to her own confession; and was born in 1668. This confession of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a> was made in order to procure a separation from her husband the earl of Macclesfield: yet, having obtained this desired end, no sooner was her spurious offspring brought into the world, than, without the dread of shame <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> poverty to excuse her, she discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of disowning him; and, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he lived, treated him with the most unnatural cruelty. She delivered him over to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> woman to educate as her own; and prevented the earl of Rivers from leaving him a legacy of L. 6000, by declaring him dead. She endeavoured to send him secretly to the plantations; but this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> being either laid aside or frustrated, she placed him apprentice with a shoemaker. In this situation, however, he did not long continue: for his nurse dying, he went to take care of the effects of his supposed mother; and found in her boxes some letters which discovered to young Savage of his birth, and the cause of its concealment. From the moment of this discovery it was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> for him to become dissatisfied with his situation as a shoemaker. He now conceived that he had a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to share in the affluence of his real mother; and therefore, he directly, and perhaps indifferently, applied to her, and made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of every art to awaken her tenderness and attract her regard. But in vain did he solicit this unnatural <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>; she avoided him with the utmost precaution, and took <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> to prevent his ever entering the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> on any pretence whatever. Savage was at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> so touched with the discovery of his birth, that he frequently made it his practice to walk before his mother's door in hopes of seeing her by accident; and often did he warmly solicit her to admit him to see her: but all to no purpose; he could neither soften her heart, nor open her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">Mean</a> time, while he was assiduously endeavouring to rouse the affections of a mother in whom all natural affection was extinct, he was destitute of the means of support, and reduced to the miseries of want. We are not told by what means he got rid of his obligation. Savage. gation to the shoemaker, or whether he ever was actually bound to him; but we now find him very differently employed in order to procure a subsistence. In short, the youth had parts, and a strong inclination towards literary pursuits, especially <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. He wrote a poem; and afterwards two plays, Woman's Riddle and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> in a Veil; but the author was allowed no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the profits from the first; and from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> he received no other advantage than the acquaintance of Sir Richard Steele and Mr Wilkes, by whom he was pitied, cared for, and relieved. However, the kindness of his friends not affording him a constant supply, he wrote the tragedy of Sir Thomas Overbury; which not only procured him the esteem of many persons of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, but brought him in 200l. The celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> Hill, Esq; was of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to him in correcting and fitting this piece for the stage and the press; and extended his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> still farther. But Savage was, like many other wits, a bad manager, and was ever in distresses. As fast as his friends raised him out of one difficulty, he sunk into another; and, when he found himself greatly involved, he would ramble about like a vagabond, with scarce a shirt on his back. He was in one of these situations all the time wherein he wrote his tragedy abovementioned; without a lodging, and often without a dinner; so that he used to scribble on scraps of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> picked up by accident, or begged in the shops, which he occasionally stepped into, as thoughts occurred to him, craving the favour of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INK">ink</a>, as it were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> to take a memorandum. Mr Hill also earnestly promoted a subscription to a volume of Miscellanies, by Savage; and likewise furnished part of the poems of which the volume was composed. To this miscellany Savage wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, in which he gives an account of his mother's cruelty, in a very uncommon strain of humour. The profits of his Tragedy and his Miscellanies together, had now, for a time, somewhat raised poor Savage both in circumstances and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>; so that the world just began to behold him with a more favourable eye than formerly, when both his fame and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> were endangered by a most unhappy event. A drunken frolic in which he one night engaged, ended in a fray, and Savage unfortunately killed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, for which he was condemned to be hanged; his friends earnestly solicited the mercy of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, while his mother as earnestly exerted herself to prevent his receiving it. The countess of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol10.html#article-HERTFORD">Hertford</a> at length laid his whole <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Caroline, and Savage obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>. Savage had now lost that tenderness for his mother, which the whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of her cruelty had not been able wholly to remove; and considering her as an implacable enemy, whom nothing but his blood could satisfy, threatened to harass her with lampoons, and to publish a copious narrative of her conduct, unless she consented to allow him a pension. This expedient proved successful; and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Tyrconnel, upon his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of laying aside his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> his mother's cruelty, took him into his family, treated him as an equal, and engaged to allow him a pension of 200l. a-year. This was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> part of Savage's life. He was courted by all who endeavoured to be thought men of genius, and cared for by all who valued themselves upon a refined <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. In this gay <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of his life he published the Temple of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a> and Mirth, on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of lady Tyrconnel from a languishing illness; and The Wanderer, a moral poem, which he dedicated to lord Tyrconnel, in strains of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>; but these praises he in a short time found himself inclined to retract, being discarded by the man on whom they were bestowed. Of this quarrel lord Tyrconnel and Mr Savage affigned very different reasons. Our author's known character pleads too strongly against him; for his conduct was ever such as made all his friends, sooner or later, grow weary of him, and even forced most of them to become his enemies. Being thus once more turned adrift upon the world, Savage, whose passions were very strong, and whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> was very small, became extremely diligent in exposing the faults of lord Tyrconnel. He, moreover, now thought himself at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to take <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> upon his mother.—Accordingly he wrote The Bafard, a poem, remarkable for the vivacity in the beginning, (where he finely enumerates the imaginary advantages of base birth), and for the pathetic conclusion, wherein he recounts the real calamities which he suffered by the crime of his parents.—The reader <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be displeased with a transcript of some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in the opening of the poem, as a specimen of this writer's spirit and manner of versification. Blest be the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a>'s birth! thro' wond'rous ways, He shines eccentric like a comet's blaze. No fickle fruit of faint compliance he; He! (<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>'d in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>'s mint with ecstasy!) He lives to build, not boast a gen'rous <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a>; No tenth transmitter of a foolish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>. He, kindling from within, requires no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, He glories in a bastard's glowing name. —Nature's unbounded son, he stands alone, His heart unbias'd, and his mind his own. —O mother yet no mother!—tis to you My thanks for such distinguisht claims are due. This poem had an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a>; and its appearance happening at the time when his mother was at Bath, many persons there took frequent opportunities of repeating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> from the Bastard in her hearing. This was perhaps the first time that ever she discovered a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of shame, and on this occasion the power of wit was very conspicuous: the wretch who had, without scruple, proclaimed herself an adulteress, and who had first endeavoured to starve her son, then to transport him, and afterwards to hang him, was not able to bear the representation of her own conduct; but fled from reproach, though she felt no pain from guilt; and left Bath with the utmost haste, to shelter herself among the crowds of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Some time after this, Savage formed the resolution of applying to the queen; who having once given him life, he hoped she might farther extend her goodness to him by enabling him to support it.—With this view, he published a poem on her birth-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, which he entitled The Volunteer-Laureat; for which she was pleased to lend him 50l. with an intimation that he might annually expect the same bounty. But this annual allowance was nothing to a man of his strange and singular extravagance. His usual <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was, as soon as he had received his pension, to disappear with it, and secrete himself from his most intimate friends, till every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> of the 50l. was spent; which done, he again appeared, penniless as before: But he would never inform any person where he had been, nor in what manner his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> had been dissipated.—From the reports, however, of some who found means to penetrate his haunts, it would seem that he expended both his time and his cash in the most forlorn and despicable sensuality; particularly in eating and drinking, in which he would indulge in the most unsocial manner, sitting whole days and nights by himself, in obscure hovels of entertainment, over his bottle and trencher, immersed in filth and sloth, with scarce decent apparel; generally wrapped up in a horseman's great coat; and, on the whole, with his very homely countenance, and altogether, exhibiting an object the most disgusting to the sight, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not to some other of the senses. His wit and parts, however, still raised him new friends, as fast as his misbehaviour lost him his old ones. Yet such was his conduct, that occasional relief only furnished the means of occasional excess; and he defeated all attempts made by his friends to fix him in a decent way. He was even reduced so low as to be destitute of a lodging; insomuch that he often passed his nights in those mean hovels that are set open for casual wanderers; sometimes in cellars amidst the riot and filth of the most profligate of the rabble; and not seldom would he walk the streets till he was weary, and then <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, on a bulk, or, in winter, with his associates among the ashes of a glass-house. Yet, amidst all his penury and wretchedness, had this man so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, and so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his own merit, that he ever kept up his spirits, and was always ready to repulse, with scorn and contempt, the least appearance of any slight or indignity towards himself, in the behaviour of his acquaintance; among whom he looked upon none as his superior. He would be treated as an equal, even by persons of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. We have an instance of this preposterous and inconsistent pride, in refusing to wait upon a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who was furious of relieving him when at the lowest ebb of distress, only because the message signified the gentleman's desire to see him at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in the morning. Savage could not bear that any one should presume to prescribe the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of his attendance, and therefore he absolutely rejected the proffered kindness. This life, unhappy as it may be already imagined, was yet rendered more unhappy, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the queen, in 1738; which stroke deprived him of all hopes from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>. His pension was discontinued, and the insolent manner in which he demanded of Sir Robert Walpole to have it restored, for ever cut off this considerable supply; which possibly had been only delayed, and might have been recovered by proper application. His distress now became so great, and so notorious, that a scheme was at length concerted for procuring him a permanent relief. It was proposed that he should retire into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, with an allowance of £50 per annum, on which he was to live privately, in a cheap <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, for ever quitting his town-haunts, and resigning all farther pretensions to fame. This offer he seemed gladly to accept; but his intentions were only to deceive his friends, by retiring for a while, to write another tragedy, and then to return with it to London in order to bring it upon the stage. In 1739, he set out for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWANSEA">Swansea</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> stage-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COACH">coach</a>, and was furnished with 15 guineas to bear the expense of his journey. But, on the 14th day after his departure, his friends and benefactors, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of whom was no other than the great Mr Pope, who expected to hear of his arrival in Wales, were surprised with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from Savage, informing them that he was yet upon the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and could not proceed for want of money. There was no other remedy than a remittance; which was sent him, and by the help of which he was enabled to reach Bristol, from whence he was to proceed to Swansea by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. At Bristol, however, he found an embargo laid upon the shipping; so that he could not immediately obtain a passage. Here, therefore, being obliged to stay for some time, he, with his usual facility, so ingratiated himself with the principal inhabitants, that he was frequently invited to their houses, distinguished at their public entertainments, and treated with a regard that highly gratified his vanity, and therefore easily engaged his affections. At length, with great reluctance, he proceeded to Swansea; where he lived about a year, very much dissatisfied with the diminution of his salary; for he had, in his letters, treated his contributors so insolently, that most of them withdrew their subscriptions. Here he finished his tragedy, and resolved to return with it to London: which was strenuously opposed by his great and constant friend Mr Pope; who propounded that Savage should put this play into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Mr Thomson and Mr <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a> in order that they might fit it for the stage, that his friends should receive the profits it might bring in, and that the author should receive the produce by way of annuity. This kind and prudent scheme was rejected by Savage, with the utmost contempt.—He declared he would not submit his works to any one's correction; and that he would no longer be kept in leading-strings. Accordingly he soon returned to Bristol, in his way to London; but at Bristol, meeting with a repetition of the same kind treatment he had before found there, he was tempted to make a second stay in that opulent <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, for some time. Here he was again not only cared for and treated, but the sum of £50, was raised for him, with which it had been happy if he had immediately departed for London; But he never considered that a frequent repetition of such kindness was not to be expected, and that it was possible to tire out the generosity of his Bristol friends, as he had before tired his friends everywhere else. In short, he remained here, till his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> was no longer welcome. His visits in every family were too often repeated; his wit had lost its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> behaviour grew troublesome. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">Necessity</a> came upon him before he was aware; his money was spent, his clothes were worn out, his appearance was shabby, and his presence was disagreeable at every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. He now began to find every man from home, at whose house he called; and he found it difficult to obtain a dinner. Thus reduced, it would have been prudent in him to have withdrawn from the place; but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and Savage were never acquainted. He staid, in the midst of poverty, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, and contempt, till the mistress of a coffee-house, to whom he owed about eight pounds, arrested him for the debt. He remained for some time, at a great expense, in the house of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s officer, in hopes of of procuring bail; which expense he was enabled to defray, by a present of five guineas from Mr Nash at Bath. No bail, however, was to be found; so that poor Savage was at last lodged in Newgate, a prison so named in Bristol. But it was the fortune of this extraordinary mortal, always to find more friends than he deserved. The keeper of the prison took compassion on him, and greatly softened the rigours of his confinement, by every kind of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>; he supported him at his own table, gave him a commodious room to himself, allowed him to stand at the door of the goal, and even frequently took him into the fields for the benefit of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>: so that, in reality, Savage endured fewer hardships in this place, than he had usually suffered during the greatest part of his life. While he remained in this not intolerable prison, his ingratitude again broke out, in a bitter satire on the city of Bristol; to which he certainly owed great obligations, notwithstanding the circumstances of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a>; which was but the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of an individual, and that attended with no circumstances of injustice or cruelty. This satire he entitled London and Bristol Compared; and in it he abused the inhabitants of the latter, with such a spirit of resentment, that the reader would imagine he had never received any other than the most injurious treatment in that city. When Savage had remained about six months in this hospitable prison, he received a letter from Mr Pope, (who still <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to allow him 20l. a-year) containing a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of very atrocious ingratitude. What were the particulars of this charge, we are not informed; but, from the notorious character of the man, there is reason to fear that Savage was but too justly accused. He, however, solemnly protested his innocence; but he was very unfavourably affected on this occasion. In a few days after, he was seized with a disorder, which at first was not suspected to be dangerous; but, growing daily more languid and dejected, at last a fever seized him; and he expired on the 1st of August 1743, in the 46th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Thus lived, and thus died, Richard Savage, Esq.; leaving behind him a character strangely chequered with vices and good qualities. Of the former we have seen a variety of instances in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of his life; of the latter, his peculiar situation in the world gave him but few opportunities of making any considerable display. He was, however, undoubtedly a man of excellent parts; and, had he received the full benefits of a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and had his natural talents been cultivated to the best advantage, he might have made a respectable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in life. He was happy in an agreeable temper and a lively flow of wit, which made his company much coveted; nor was his judgment both of writings and of men, inferior to his wit; but he was too much a slave to his passions, and his passions were too easily excited. He was warm in his friendships, but implacable in his enmity; and his greatest fault, which is indeed the greatest of all faults, was ingratitude. He seemed to think everything due to his merit, and that he was little obliged to any one for those favours which he thought it their duty to confer on him: it is therefore left to be wondered at, that he never rightly estimated the kindness of his many friends and benefactors, or preserved a grateful and due sense of their generosity towards him. The works of this original writer, after having long lain dispersed in magazines and fugitive publications, have been lately collected and published in an elegant edition, in 2 vols 8vo; to which are prefixed, the admirable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of Savage, written by Dr Samuel Johnson. Savage <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, one of the small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the south <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, lying in S. Lat. 19. W. Long. 169. 37. It is about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues in circuit, of a good height, and has deep water <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to its shores. Its interior parts are supposed to be barren, as there was no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> to be seen upon the coasts; the rocks alone supplying the trees with humidity. The inhabitants are exceedingly warlike and fierce, so that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> Cook could not have any intercourse with them.

SAVANNAH

Pages 647-647

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 101. 20. N. Lat. 32. 0.

SAVARY

Pages 647-647

an eminent French writer on the subject of trade, was born at Done in Anjou, in 1622. Being bred to merchandise, he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in trade until 1653; when he left off the practice, to cultivate the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>. He had married in 1650; and in 1660, when the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> declared a purpose of affixing privileges and persons to such of his subjects as had twelve children alive, Mr Savary was not too rich to put in his claim to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> bounty. He was afterwards admitted of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> for the reformation of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; and the orders which passed in 1670 were drawn up by his instructions and advice. He wrote Le Parfait Négociant, 4to; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AVIS">Avis</a> et Conseils sur les plus importantes matières du Commerce, in 4to. He died in 1690; and out of 17 children whom he had by one wife, left 11. Two of his sons, James and Philemon <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, laboured jointly on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, Dictionnaire Universelle du Commerce, 2 vols folio: this work was begun by James, who was inspector-general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; who called in the assistance of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Philemon Lewis, although a canon of the royal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Maur; and by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> left him to finish it. This work appeared in 1723, and Philemon afterwards added a third supplemental volume to the former. Postlethwayte's English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> of Trade and Commerce is a translation, with considerable improvements, from Savary.

SAVILE

Pages 647-648

SAVILE (Sir George), afterwards marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>, and one of the greatest statesmen of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born about the year 1630; and some time after his return from his travels, was created a peer, in consideration of his own and his father's merits. He was a strenuous opposer of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a>; but proposed such limitations of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>'s authority, as should disable him from doing any harm either in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> state, as the taking out of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> all power in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> matters, the disposal of the public <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and the power of making peace and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and lodging these in the two houses of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. After that bill was rejected in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords, he pressed them, though without success, to proceed to the limitation of the duke's power; and began with moving, that during the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he might be obliged to live five hundred miles out of England. In August 1682, he was created a marquis, and soon after made privy-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. Upon king James's accession, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; but on his refusal to consent to the repeal of the test, he was dismissed from all public employments. In that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the lords which met after king James's withdrawing himself the first time from Whitehall, the marquis was chosen their president; and upon the king's return from Faversham, he was sent, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Shrewsbury and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Delamere, from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, to order his majesty to quit the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Whitehall. In the convention of parliament he was chosen speaker of the house of lords, and strenuously supported the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> for the vacancy of the throne, and the conjunctive sovereignty of the prince and princess; upon whose accession he was again made privy-seal. Yet, in 1683, he quitted the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and became a zealous opposer of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in April 1695. The rev. Mr Grainger observes, that "he was a person of unfeigned principles, and of a lively imagination, which sometimes got the better of his judgment. He would never lose his jest, though it spoiled his argument, or brought his sincerity or even his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> in question. He was deservedly celebrated for his parliamentary talents; and in the famous contest relating to the bill of exclusion, was thought to be a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATCH">match</a> for his uncle <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHAFTESBURY">Shaftesbury</a>. The pieces he has left us show him to have been an ingenious, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not a masterly writer; and his Advice to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">Daughter</a>, contains more good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> in fewer words, than is, perhaps, to be found in any of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> authors." His lordship also wrote, The Anatomy of an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">Equivalent</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> to a Diffrerter; a Rough Draught of a New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">Model</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>; and Maxims of State; all which were printed together in one volume octavo. Since these, were also published under his name the Character of king <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. octavo; the Character of Bishop Burnet; and Historical Observations upon the reigns of Edward I. II. III. and Richard II. with Remarks upon their faithful Counsellors and false Favourites.

SAVIOUR

Pages 648-648

an appellation peculiarly given to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, as being the Messiah and Saviour of the world. See Jesus. Order of St Saviour, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order of the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>, founded by St Bridget, about the year 1345, and so called from its being pretended that our Saviour himself declared its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and rules to the founders.—According to the constitutions, this is principally founded for religious women who pay a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the holy virgin; but there are some monks of the order, to administer the sacrament and spiritual assistance to the nuns.

SAVONIA

Pages 648-649

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, handsome, populous, and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, with two castles, and a bishop's see. It contains several handsome churches and well-built structures. It was taken by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a> in 1746, at which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> it had a capacious harbour; but the people of Genoa, being afraid that it would hurt their own trade, choaked it up. It is seated on the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in a well-cultivated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, abounding in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and all kinds of good fruit. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 8. 14. N. Lat 44. 21.

SAVOY

Pages 649-650

a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> lying between France and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and which takes its name from the Latin Sabaadia, altered afterwards to Saboia, and Sobojia. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was anciently inhabited by the Celtes, whose descendants therein, were subdivided into the Allobroges, Nantuates, Veragri, Seduni, Salassi, Centrones, Garocelli, and some others of inferior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. Of all these the Allobroges were the most considerable. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of these tribes, in which Julius Caesar had made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress, was completed under Augustus. Afterwards this country shared the fate of the rest of the western empire, and was over-run by the northern Barbarians. The Burgundians held it a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but when <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> how it first became a distinct earldom under the present family, is what historians are not agreed about; thus much, however, is certain, that Amadeus I., who lived in the twelfth century, was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of it. In 1416, Amadeus VIII. was created by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Sigismund, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy; and Victor Amadeus first took the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and afterwards of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>. Savoy is bounded to the south by France and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>; to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the lake of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, which separates it from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>; to the west, by France; and to the east, by Piedmont, the Milanese, and Switzerland; its greatest length being about eighty-eight miles, and breadth about seventy-six. As it lies among the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, it is full of lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which in general are very barren: many of the highest of them are perpetually covered with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICE">ice</a> and snow. The summit of those called Montagnes Maudites, "the cursed mountains," are said to be more than two English miles in perpendicular height above the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the lake of Geneva, and the level itself is much higher than the Mediterranean. In some few of the valleys there is corn-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> and pasture, and a good breed of cattle and mules; and along the lake of Geneva, and in two or three other places, a tolerable wine is produced. Mount Senis or Cenis, between Savoy and Piedmont, over which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-way from Geneva to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a> lies, is as high, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not higher, than the Montagnes Maudites; Savoy. Mandites; but of all the mountains of the Alps, the highest is mount Rochemelon, in Piedmont, between Fertiere and Novalese. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> over these mountains are very tedious, disagreeable, and dangerous, especially as huge masses of snow, called by the Italians avalanches, and fragments of rocks, frequently roll <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into them from the impending precipices. The way of travelling is either in sledges, chairs, or on the backs of mules: in some places the path on the brink of the precipices is so narrow, that there is but <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> room for a single person to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. It begins to snow on these mountains <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> about the beginning of October. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, August, and September, many of them yield very fine grass, with a great variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and herbs; and others box-wood, walnuts, chestnuts, and pines. The height and different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of these mountains, their towering summits rising above one another, and covered with snow, the many cataracts or falls of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the noise and rapidity of the river Arc, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROTH">froth</a> and green tincture of its water, the echoes of its numerous streams tumbling from cliff to cliff, form altogether a very romantic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. These mountainous tracts, notwithstanding their height, are not altogether free from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> in summer, and are also much exposed to thick <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, which sometimes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> unexpectedly on them, and continue several days. There are some wolves among the thickets; and they abound with hares, rupicapras or chamois, and marmottes. In the lower parts of Savoy, there are also bears, wild boars, deer, and rabbits; and among the defoliate mountains are found great quantities of rock-crystal. In the glaciers or ice-valleys, between the high mountains, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is extremely <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, even in the months of July and August. The surface of these ice-valleys looks like a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> or lake, which, after being agitated by fierce and contrary winds, has been frozen all at once, interspersed with hideous cracks and chasms. The noise of these cracks, when first made by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the noon-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and reverberated by the surrounding rocks and mountains, is astonishing. The height of the impending mountains is such, that the sun's rays seldom reach the ice-valleys, except a few hours in the middle of summer. The avalanches or snow-balls, which the least concussion of the air <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> occasion, tumble down the mountains with amazing rapidity, continually increasing, and carrying all before them. People have been taken out alive, after being buried several days under them. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, which, on the side of Geneva, separates Savoy from France; the Arve, which has some particles of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> in its sands; the Isere, the Seran, the Siers, and the Arc. There are also a great many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> in this country, which yield plenty of fish, but none of them are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, together with medicinal and reciprocating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people is a corrupt French; but the better sort, and those that live in the great cities, speak as good French as they do in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> itself. In their temper, however, and disposition, the Savoyards resemble the Germans more than the French, retaining still much of the old German honesty and simplicity of manners, which no doubt is partly owing to the poverty and barrenness of the country. To this also, joined to their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONGEVITY">longevity</a> and the fruitfulness of their women, which are the effects of their cheerful disposition, healthy air, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, and sobriety, it is owing that great numbers of them are obliged to go abroad in quest of a livelihood, which they earn, those at least who have no trades, by showing marmottes, cleaning shoes, sweeping <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a>, and the like. It is said, that there are generally about 18,000 of them, young and old, about Paris. In summer they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the streets, and in winter, forty, fifty, or sixty of them lodge together in a room: they are so honest that they may be trusted to any amount. The children are often carried abroad in baskets, before they are able to walk. In many villages of Savoy there is hardly a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> to be seen throughout the year, excepting a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> or two. Those that have families generally set out and return about the same season, when their wives commonly lie-in, and they never fail to bring home some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their small earnings. Some of them are such consummate masters of economy, that they set up shops and make fortunes, and others return home with a competency for the rest of their days. An old man is often dispatched with letters, little presents, and some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, from the younger sort, to their parents and relations, and brings back with him fresh colonies, letters, messages, and news. The cultivation of their grounds, and the reaping and gathering in of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> and vintage, are generally left to the women and children: but all this is to be understood of the mountainous parts of Savoy. Great numbers of the mountaineers of both sexes are said to be lame and deformed; and they are much subject to a kind of wens, which grow about their throats, and very much disfigure them, especially the women; but that is the only inconvenience they feel from them. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of Savoy, and the other dominions of the king of Sardinia, labour under great hardships and restrictions, unheard of in other countries, which we have not room here to particularize. A minute account of them will be found in Mr Keyler's Travels. In short, the king has left neither <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, power, nor much <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, to any but himself and the clergy, whose overgrown wealth he has also greatly curtailed. No other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is professed or tolerated in Savoy but that of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome. The decrees, however, of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a> are not admitted; nor are the churches asylums for malefactors. This duchy is divided into those of Chablais, Genevois, and Savoy Proper, the counties of Tarantaile and Maurienne, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> of Faucigny.

SAXE

Pages 651-651
natural Son of Frederic Augustus II., king of Poland, by Aurora countess of Konigsmarck, was born at Dresden in 1696. He discovered an early genius for warlike exercises, neglecting every study but that of war. He cultivated no foreign language but French, as if he had foreseen that France would one day become his country, in which he would rise to the highest military honours. He accompanied the king his father in all his Polish campaigns, and began to serve in the allied army in the Netherlands in 1708, when he was no more than twelve years old, and gave pregnant proofs of an enterprising genius. He afterwards served in the war against the Swedes in Pomerania, and was made colonel of a regiment of horse. He entered into the imperial service in 1717, and made several campaigns in Hungary against the Turks; in which he behaved with the greatest bravery, and thereby attracted the regard of prince Eugene of Savoy, the most illustrious captain of his time. In 1720, he visited the court of France, where he obtained a brevet of camp-marshal from the duke of Orleans, then regent of that kingdom. Two years after, he purchased the colonelcy of the regiment of Spar; and gradually rose in military honours, from the rank of colonel to that of marshal-general. While the count was residing in France, the states of Courland, foreseeing that their duchy would one day be without a head, duke Ferdinand, the last male of the family of Kettler, being valetudinary, and likely to die without issue, were prevailed on, by foreign influence, to choose the count to be their sovereign. The minute of election was signed by the states of Mittaw, the capital of Courland, on the 5th of July 1726. But this election having been vigourously opposed by the court of Russia, and also by the republic of Poland, upon both of which the duchy was dependent, he could never make good his pretensions; so that, upon the death of duke Ferdinand in 1736, count Biron, a gentleman of Danish extraction, in the service of Russia, was preferred before him. When a war broke out in Germany, upon the death of the late king of Poland, our count's father, he attended the duke of Berwick commander in chief of the French army sent into that country, and behaved with unparalleled bravery. When troubles broke out in the same quarter upon the death of the late emperor Charles VI. he was employed in the French army sent into the empire to support the pretensions of the elector of Bavaria; and had no inconsiderable hand in storming Prague: by means of which he acquired the confidence and esteem of that unfortunate prince. When an invasion of Great Britain was projected by the court of France in the beginning of 1744, in favour of Charles-Edward the pretender's eldest son, he was appointed to command the French troops to be employed on that occasion.
