Both the young pretender and the count had come to Dunkirk in order to proceed upon the intended expedition; but the design was frustrated by a furious storm and the vigilance of the British fleet. France having, soon after that event, declared war against Great Britain, he was appointed commander in chief of the French army in the Netherlands, and promoted to the rank of a marshal of France. In this high station he had full room to display his great abilities. Success crowned all his enterprises; and every town he invested was obliged to submit to his victorious arms. During the course of the war, he beat the allies in several battles, and made himself master of the whole Austrian Netherlands, with a good part of Dutch Brabant. Such eminent services procured him an act of naturalization by the king of France, in April 1746; in January following, he was raised to the rank of marshal-general, an office which had been vacant for many years; and in January 1748, he was constituted governor-general of the Netherlands, with a large revenue annexed. After the treaty of peace at Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748, marshal Saxe, covered with glory and loaded with the king's bounties, retired to Chambord in France, where he spent his time in various employments and amusements. But being seized with a fever on the 21st of November 1750, he died on the 30th of that month. His corpse was interred on the 8th of February following, with great funeral pomp, in the church of St Thomas's at Straßburg. All France lamented his death. The king was at the charge of his funeral, and expressed the greatest concern for the loss of a man who had raised the glory of his arms to the highest pitch. By his will, which is dated at Paris, March 1, 1748, he directed that "his body should be buried in lime, if that could be done; that in a short time nothing more of him might remain in the world, but his memory among his friends." This direction, however, was not complied with; for his corpse was embalmed, and put into a leaden coffin, which was inclosed in another of copper, and this covered with one of wood bound about with iron. His heart was put into a silver-gilt box, and his entrails into another coffin. He was bred a Protestant of the Lutheran persuasion, under the eye of the countess his mother; and no worldly consideration could ever induce him to change his religion. He had unhappily, like his royal father, early engaged in a series of amorous adventures; and several natural children were the fruits of his vagrant amours. Though he had been prevailed on by his mother, to marry Victoria countess of Lobin, a lady of distinguished birth and beauty, by whom he had a child or two, who died in their infancy; yet, a coldness having arisen between them, the marriage was dissolved, on account of adultery committed by the count, with a design to procure a divorce; and he never afterwards married. The marshal was a man of middling stature, but of a robust constitution and extraordinary strength. To an aspect noble, sweet, and martial, he joined the interior qualities of a most excellent heart. Affable, and affected with the misfortunes of others, he was great and generous, even more than his fortune would

SAXIFRAGA

Pages 651-652

SAXIFRACE; a genus of the di- gynia order, belonging to the decandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are 38 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable are, 1. The granulata, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> saxifrage, which grows naturally in the meadows in many parts of England. The roots of this plant are like grains of corn, of a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> without; from which arise kidney- shaped hairy leaves, standing upon pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> foot- stalks. The stalks are thick, a foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, hairy, and furrowed: these branch out from the bottom, and have a few small leaves like those below, which fit <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the stalk: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> terminate the stalk, growing in small clusters; they have five white petals, including ten stamens and the two styles. There is a variety of this with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> flowers, which is very ornamental. 2. The pyramidalis, with a pyramidal stalk, grows na- turally on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. The leaves are tongue-shaped, gathered into heads, rounded at their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, and have cartilaginous and sawed borders. The stalk rises two feet and a half high, branching out near the ground, forming a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> to the top. The flowers have five white wedge-shaped petals, and ten stamens, placed circularly the length of the tube, terminated by roundish purple summits. When these plants are strong, they produce very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pyramids of flowers, which make a fine appearance. 3. The punctata, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, or none-so-pretty, grows naturally on the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, and also in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty on a mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> called Mangerton, in the coun- ty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KERRY">Kerry</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. The roots of this are per- ennial; the leaves are <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, oval, and placed cir- cularly at bottom. They have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, flat, furrowed foot-stalks, and are deeply crenated at their edges, which are white. The stalk rises a foot high, is of a purple colour, stiff, slender, and hairy. It extends out from the side on the upper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> several short foot- stalks, which are terminated by white flowers spotted with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>. 4. The oppositiflora, grows naturally on the Alps, Pyrenees, and Helvetian mountains; it is also found pretty plentifully growing upon Ingleborough hill in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SNOWDON">Snowdon</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and some other places. It is a perennial plant, with stalks trailing up- on the ground, and are seldom more than two inches long, garnished with small oval leaves standing oppo- site, which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> over one another like the scales of fish; they are of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> green colour, and have a resem- blance of heath. The flowers are produced at the end of the branches, of a deep blue; so make a pretty appearance during their continuance, which is great part of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> and the beginning of April. All these species are easily propagated by offsets, or by parting their roots.

SAXONY

Pages 652-654

the name of two circles of the German empire, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same. The lower circle is bounded to the south by the circle of Upper Saxony, and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of that of the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>; to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the duchy of Sleswick, be- longing to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, and the Baltic; to the west, by the circle of Westphalia and the north <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and to the east, by the circle of Upper Saxony. The states belonging to it are the dukes and princes of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a> and Bremen, Zell, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRUBENHAGEN">Grubenhagen</a>, Cal- enburg, Wolfenbuttle, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HALBERSTADT">Halberstadt</a>, Mecklenburg- Schwerin, Mecklenburg-Güstrow, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>-Glückstadt, Holstein-Gottorf, Hildesheim, Saxe-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUENBURG">Lauenburg</a>; the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUBECK">Lubeck</a>; the principalities of Schwerin, Ratzeburg, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLANKENBURG">Blankenburg</a>, Raneau; the imperial cities of Lubeck, Gotzlar, Mühlhausen, Nordhausen, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAM">Ham</a>- burgh, and Bremen. The dukes of Bremen and Magdeburg are alternately directors and summoning princes; but, ever since the year 1682, the diets, which used generally to be held at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUNEBURG">Luneburg</a>, have been discontinued. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the empire, which, by a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the empire in 1681, was settled at 40,000 men, this circle was to furnish 1322 horsemen and 2707 foot; and of the 300,000 florins granted to the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> in 1707, its quota was 31,271 florins; both which assessments are the same with those of Upper Saxony, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, Swab- ia, and Westphalia. This circle, at present, nomi- nates only two assessors in the chamber-judiciary of the empire, of one of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Brunswick- Luneburg has the nomination, who must be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>- ian, and is the ninth in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The inhabitants of this circle are almost all Lutherans. The circle of Upper Saxony is bounded by that of Franconia, the Upper Rhine, and Lower Saxony; and also by the Baltic sea, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, Lu- fatia, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>. It is of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and con- tains the following states, viz. the electors of Saxony and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>; Saxe-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIMAR">Weimar</a>, Saxe-Eisenach, Saxe- Coburg, Saxe-Gotha, Saxe-Altenburg, Saxe-Quer- furt, the Hither and Farther Pomerania, Camin, An- halt, Quiltenburg, Gernrode, Walkenried, Schwarz- burg, Sonderhausen, Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt, Manf- feld, Stolberg, Barby, the counts of Reussen, and the counts of Schonberg. No diets have been held in this circle since the year 1683. The elector of Saxony has always been the sole summoning <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of it. Most of the inhabitants profess the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. When the whole empire fur- nishes 40,000 men, the quota of this circle is 1322 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and 2707 foot. Of the 300,000 florins <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>- ed by the empire in 1707, it contributed only 31,271 florins, 28 kruizters, being rated no higher than those of Westphalia, Lower Saxony, Swabia, and Burgundy, though it is much larger. Agreeable to a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and regulation in 1654, this circle no- minates now only two assessors of the chamber-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The electorate consists of the duchy of Saxony, the greatest part of the margravate of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEISSEN">Meissen</a>, a part of the Vogtland, and the northern half of the landgraviate of Thuringia. The Lusatias also, and a part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Henneberg, belong to it, but are no part of this circle. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the electoral dominions lying in this circle is in general exceeding rich and fruitful, yielding corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> in abundance, to- gether with hops, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, aniseed, wild saffron, wood; and in some places woad, wine, coals, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> clay, terra sigillata, fullers-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, lime shiver, various sorts of beautiful marble, serpentine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and almost all the different <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of precious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Sulphur also, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, vitriol, sand, and free-stone, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>, turf, cinnabar, quicksilver, anti- mony, mony, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BISMUTH">bismuth</a>, arsenic, cobalt, and other minerals, are found in it. This country, besides the above <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, contains likewise valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, tin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; and abounds in many places with horned cattle, sheep, horses, and venison. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> by which it is watered, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, the Schwerze-Elster, the Mulde, the Saale, the Unstrut, the Weiße-Elster, and the Pleisse. These rivers, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and rivulets, abound in fish; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a>-Elster are found beautiful pearls. This electorate is extremely well cultivated and inhabited, and is said to include about 250 great and small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, upwards of 5000 villages, 196 <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> manors, and near as many royal castles, besides private estates and commanderies. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> diets here consist of three classes. The first is composed of the prelates, the counts, and lords, and the two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Leipzig and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WITTENBERG">Wittenberg</a>. To the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> belong the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> in general, immediate or mediate, that is, such as stand immediately under the sief-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> or the aulic judicatories, and such as are immediately under the jurisdiction of the amtmann. The third class is formed of the towns in general. The general provincial diets are ordinarily held every six years; but there are others, called selection diets, which are convened <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> every two years. We would here observe, that not only these diets, but those in most of the other states of Germany, are at present extremely insignificant and unimportant, retaining little more than the shadow of their former power and privileges; for even the petty princes, though they depend upon their more potent neighbours, and must be very careful not to give them any umbrage, are almost as <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> in their respective territories as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> seignior himself. As to religion, it was in this country that the reformation took its rise in the 16th century, to which it hath ever since adhered, according to the doctrines of Luther. The two late electors, when they embraced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> in order to qualify themselves to be elected kings of Poland, gave the most solemn assurances to their people, that they would inviolably maintain the established religion and its professors in the full and free enjoyment of all their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, privileges, and prerogatives whatsoever, in regard to churches, worship, ceremonies, usages, universities, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, benefices, incomes, profits, jurisdictions, and immunities. The electoral families still continue <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, though they have lost the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Poland, for which they at first embraced Popery. With respect to ecclesiastical matters, the country is divided into parishes, and these again into spiritual inspections and consistories, all subordinate to the ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> and upper consistory of Dresden, in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> and Leipzig the Calvinists and Roman Catholics enjoy the free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their religion. Learning flourishes in this electorate; in which, besides the free-schools and gymnasia in most of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> towns, are the two celebrated universities of Wittenberg and Leipzig, in the last of which are also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> for the liberal arts and the German <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, with bookellers and printers of the greatest eminence. A great variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are also carried on in this country. The principal are those of fine and coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, thread, fine <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, fine glasses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a>; porcelain, equal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not inferior, to that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; iron, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> wares; manufactures of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; gloves, caps, Saxony. Saxony. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>; in which, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions mentioned above, together with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, an important foreign <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is carried on. A great addition has been made since the year 1718 to the electoral territories, by the extinction of the collateral branches of Zeitz, Merseburg, and Weißenfels, whose dominions devolved to the elder electoral branch, descended from the margraves of Meissen. The first of these, who was elector of Saxony, was Frederic the Warlike, about the beginning of the 13th century. This elector styles himself <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Saxony, Juliers, Cleve, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERG">Berg</a>, as also of Engern and Westphalia, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-marshal and elector of the Holy Roman empire, landgrave in Thuringia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARGRAVE">margrave</a> of Meissen, and of Upper and Lower <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUSATIA">Lusatia</a>, burgrave of Magdeburg, princely <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Henneberg, count of La Mark, Ravenberg, Barby, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANAU">Hanau</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Ravenstein. Among the electors he is reckoned the sixth, as great-marshal of the empire, of which he is also <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, during an interregnum, in all places not subject to the vicariate of the count palatine of the Rhine. He is moreover sole director of the circle; and in the vacancy of the see of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, claims the directorium at the diet of the empire. His matricular affluence, on account of the electorate, is 1984 florins, besides what he pays for other districts and territories. To the chamber-courts he contributes, each <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, the sum of 1545 rix-dollars, together with 83 rix-dollars and 62 kruizers on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Mansfeld. In this electorate, subordinate to the privy-council, are various colleges for the departments of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, foreign affairs, the finances, fiefs, mines, <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>, and ecclesiastical affairs, together with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tribunals and courts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, to which appeals <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> from the inferior. The revenues of this elector are as considerable as those of any prince in the empire, if we except those of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. They arise from the ordinary and extraordinary subsidies of the states; his own demesnes, consisting of 72 bailiwicks; the impost on beer, and the fine porcelain of the country; tenths of corn, fruit, wine, &c. his own silver mines, and the tenths of those that belong to particulars: all which, added together, bring in an yearly revenue of betwixt 700,000 l., and 800,000 l.; yet the electorate is at present deeply in debt. The regular troops commonly amount to 20,000 men, exclusive of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> of the ban, the arrriere-ban, and the body of miners and hunters, who are obliged in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of war to bear arms. The whole electorate is divided into circles. The electoral circle, or the duchy of Saxony, is bounded by the circles of Meissen, Leipzig, and Thuringia, the principality of Anhalt, the mark of Brandenburg, and Lusatia. The principality of Anhalt lies across it, and divides it into two parts. Its greatest length and breadth is computed at about 40 miles; but tho' it is watered by the Elbe, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Elster, and the Mulde, it is not very fruitful, the soil for the most part consisting of sand. It contains 24 towns, three boroughs, betwixt 400 and 500 villages, 164 noblemen's estates, 11 superintendencies, three inspections, under one consistory, and 11 prefectures or districts. The present duchy of Saxony is not to be confounded with the old; for the latter was of a much greater extent, and contained in it those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tracts anciently called... Saxony, called Eastphalia, Engern, and Westphalia, of which the electoral circle was no part, but was taken by Albert the Bear, margrave of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALZWEDEL">Salzwedel</a>, from the Veneti. His son Bernard obtaining the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of duke of Saxony from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Frederic I., the name of duchy was given to this country; and the electoral dignity having been afterwards annexed to the duchy, it acquired thereby also the name of the electoral circle. The country of Saxony is remarkable for being the mother of the present English <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; but concerning the Saxons themselves, previous to that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, we have very few particulars. The Saxons (says Mr. Whitaker) have been derived by our historians from very different parts of the globe; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, the north of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and the forests of Germany. And their appellation has been equally referred to very different causes; the name of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> progenitor, the plundering disposition of their Asiatic fathers, and the short hooked weapons of their warriors. But the real origin of the Saxons, and the genuine derivation of their name, seem clearly to be these. In the earlier period of the Gallic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the Celtæ of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> crossed the Rhine in considerable numbers, and planted various colonies in the regions beyond it. Thus the Volcae Tectosages settled on one side of the Hercynian forest and about the banks of the Neckar, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELVETII">Helvetii</a> upon another and about the Rhine, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, the Boii beyond both, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENONES">Senones</a> in the heart of Germany. Thus also we see the Treviri, the Nervii, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUEVI">Suevi</a>, and the Marcomanni, the Quadi, the Venedi, and others, in that country; all plainly betrayed to be Gallic nations by the Gallic appellations which they bear, and all together possessing the greatest part of it. And, even as late as the conclusion of the first century, we find one nation on the eastern side of this great continent actually speaking the language of Gaul, and another upon the northern using a dialect nearly related to the British. But as all the various tribes of the Germans are considered by Strabo to be ῥαγοι ταχαινει, or genuine Gauls in their origin; so those particularly that lived immediately beyond the Rhine, and are asserted by Tacitus to be indubitably native Germans, are expressly denominated ῥαγοι, or Gauls, by Diodorus, and as expressly declared by Dio to have been distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> appellation of Celtæ from the earliest period. And the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> line of nations, which extended along the ocean, and reached to the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>, was all known to the learned in the days of Diodorus, by the same significant appellation of ῥαγοι, or Gauls. Of these, the most noted were the Si-Cambri and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CIMBRI">Cimbri</a>; the former being seated near the channel of the Rhine, and the latter inhabiting the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a>. And the denominations of both declare their original; and show them to have been derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> stock of the Celtæ, and to be of the same Celtic kindred with the Cimbri of our own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, and the Cymbri or Cambrians of our own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. The Cimbri are accordingly denominated Celtæ by Strabo and Apian. And they are equally asserted to be Gauls by Diodorus; to be the descendants of that nation which sacked the city of Rome, plundered the temple of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>, and subdued a great part of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and some of Asia. Immediately to the south of these were the Saxons, and extended from the isthmus of the Chersonesus to Saxony; the current of the Elbe. And they were equally Scabiosa, Celtic in their origin as their neighbours. They were denominated Ambrones as well as Saxons; and, as such, are included by Tacitus under the general appellation of Cimbri, and comprehended in Plutarch under the equal one of Celto-Scythe. And the name of Ambrones appears particularly to have been Gallic; being common to the Saxons beyond the Elbe, and the Ligurians in Cisalpine Gaul; as both found to their surprise, on the irruption of the former into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> with the Cimbri. And, what is equally surprising, and has been equally unnoticed by the critics, the Welsh distinguish England by the name of Lloegyr or Ligguria, even to the present moment. In that irruption these Saxons, Ambrones, or Ligurians, composed a body of more than 30,000 men, and were principally concerned in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> to pieces the large armies of Manlius and Caepio. Nor is the appellation of Saxons less Celtic than the other. It was originally the same with the Belgic Sueiones of Gaul; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of that tribe being now intitled Soifons by the French, and the name of the Saxons pronounced Sui-fen by the Welsh, Safen by the Scotch, and Safenach or Saxenach by the Irish. And the Sueiones or Saxones of Gaul derived their own appellation from the position of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> on a river, the stream at Soifons being now denominated the Aisne, and formerly the Axon; Uelf-on or Axon importing only waters or a river, and S-uff-on or S-ax-on the waters or the river. The Sueiones, therefore, are actually denominated the Ueffones by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>; and the Saxones are actually intitled the Axones by Lucan. These, with their brethren and allies the Cimbri, having been more formidable enemies to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, than the Samnites, Carthaginians, Spaniards, Gauls, or Parthians, in the second century applied themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, and became nearly as terrible by sea. They soon made themselves known to the inhabitants of the British isles, by their piracies in the northern channels, and were denominated by them Lochlyn or Lochlynach; loch lyn signifying the people of the wave, and the D being quiescent in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>. They took possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORKNEY_ISLANDS">Orkney <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, which were then merely large shoals of sand, uncovered with woods, and overgrown with rushes; and they landed in the north of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and ravaged the country. Before the middle of the third century they made a second <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> upon the latter, disembarked a considerable body of men, and desigued the absolute subjection of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Before the conclusion of it, they carried their naval operations to the south, infested the British channel with their little vessels, and made frequent descents upon the coasts. And in the fourth and fifth centuries, acting in conjunction with the Picts of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALEDONIA">Caledonia</a> and the Scots of Ireland, they ravaged all the eastern and south-eastern shores of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, began the formal conquest of the country, and finally settled their victorious soldiery in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> and the houes of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>.

SCABIOSA

Pages 654-655

scabious; a genus of the monogy- Scævola, belonging to the tetrandria class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The arvensis, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>-scarious, grows naturally in many places of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. It hath a strong, thick, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> root, sending out many branching stalks, which rise to the height of three feet; the lower leaves are sometimes almost entire, and at others they are cut into many segments almost to the midrib. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are produced upon naked footstalks at the end of the branches; they are of a purple <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and have a faint odour. 2. The succisa, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>'s bit, grows naturally in woods and moist places. This has a short tap-root, the end of which appears as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was bitten or cut off, whence the plant has taken its name. The leaves are oval and spear-shaped, and smooth; the stalks are single, about two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, garnished with two leaves at each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>; they generally send out two short foot-stalks from their upper joint, standing opposite, which are terminated by purple flowers.—Both these have been recommended as aperient, sudorific, and expectorant; but the present practice has no dependence on them. SCÆVOLA (Marius), the celebrated Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, famous in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> for having singly opposed Porfenna <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Etruria, and his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, upon a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> at Rome, till it was cut <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; after which he flung himself into the Tiber, and swam to the Roman army on the opposite shore, 507 B.C.

SCAFFOLD

Pages 655-655

also denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> raised in the manner of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, for the more commodious viewing any show <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>: it is also used for a little stage raised in some public <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, whereon to behed criminals.

SCALADO

Pages 655-655
or SCALADE, in the art of war, a furious assault made on the wall or rampart of a city, or other fortified place, by means of ladders, without carrying on works in form, to secure the men.

SCALE

Pages 655-655

in music, sometimes denominated a gamut, a diagram, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, an order, a diapason. It consists of the regular gradations of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, by which a composer <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> performer, whether in rising or descending, may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from any given tune to another. These gradations are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>. When this order is repeated, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is consonantaneous with the lowest note of the first; the second of the former with the second of the latter; and so through the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a>. The second order, therefore, is justly deemed only a repetition of the first. For this reason the scale, among the moderns, is sometimes limited to an octave; at other times extended to the compass of any particular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. It likewise frequently includes all the practical gradations of musical sound, or the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of octaves employed in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> or execution, arranged in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order.

SCALENE

Pages 655-655
or Scalene Triangle, scalenum, in geometry, a triangle whose sides and angles are unequal. See Geometry.

SCALIGER

Pages 655-656

a learned critic, poet, physician, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>; was born at the castle of Ripa, in the territories of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a> in 1484; and is said to have been descended from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> princes of Verona, though this is not mentioned in the letters of naturalization he obtained in France in 1528. He learned the first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the Latin tongue in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and in his 12th year was presented to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximilian, who made him one of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>. He served that emperor 17 years, and gave signal proofs of his valour and conduct in several expeditions. He was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a> in April 1512, in which he had the misfortune to lose his father Benedict Scaliger, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Titus; on which his mother died with grief: when being reduced to necessitous circumstances, he entered into the order of the Franciscans, and applied himself to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>; but soon after changing his mind with respect to his becoming a monk, he took arms again, and served in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>. At which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> a physician persuaded him to study physic, which he did at his leisure-hours, and also learned Greek; but at last the gout determined him, at forty years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, to abandon a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He soon after settled at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGEN">Agen</a>, where he married, and began to apply himself seriously to his studies. He learned first the French tongue, which he spoke perfectly in three months; and then made himself <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the Gascon, Italian, Spanish, German, Hungarian, and Slavonian: but the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> object of his studies was polite literature. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">Mean</a> while he supported his family by the practice of physic. He did not publish any of his works till he was 47 years of age; when he soon gained a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> name in the republic of letters. He had a graceful person, and a strong <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, even in his old age, that he dictated to his son two hundred verses which he had composed the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> before, and retained without <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> them <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. He was so charitable, that his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was as it were an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and sick; and he had such an aversion to lying, that he would have no correspondence with those who were subject to that vice; but on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, he had much vanity, and a satirical spirit, which created him many enemies. He died of a retention of urine in 1558. He wrote in Latin, 1. A Treatise on the Art of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>. 2. Exercitations against Carden: these works are much esteemed. 3. Commentaries on <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Animals, and on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>. 4. Some Treatises on Physics. 5. Letters, Orations, Poems, and other works, in Latin. Scaliger (<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Julius), one of the most learned critics and writers of his time: he was the son of the former, and was born at Agen in France in 1540. He studied in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Bordeaux; after which his father took him under his own care, and employed him in transcribing his poems; by which means he obtained such a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for poetry, that before he was 17 years old, he wrote a tragedy upon the subject of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OEDIPUS">Oedipus</a>, in which he introduced all the poetical ornaments of style and sentiment. His father dying in 1558, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> the year following, with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to apply himself to the Greek tongue. For this purpose he he for two months attended the lectures of Turnebus; but finding that in the usual course he should be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time in gaining his point, he shut himself up in his closet, and by constant application for two years gained a perfect knowledge of the Greek tongue. After which he applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, which he learned by himself with great facility. He made no less progress in the sciences; and his writings procured him the reputation of one of the greatest men of that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> any other age. He embraced the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> at 22 years of age. In 1563, he attached himself to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Caffeignier de la Roch Pozay, whom he attended in several journeys; and in 1593, was invited to accept of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of honorary professor of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, which he complied with. He died of a dropy in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> in 1609. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>; was never married; and was so <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> a student, that he often spent whole days in his study without eating: and though his circumstances were always very narrow, he constantly refused the presents that were offered him. He published many works; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are: 1. Notes on Seneca's Tragedies, on Varro, Aufonius, Pompeius Feltus, &c. 2. His Latin Poems. 3. A Treatise de Emendatione Temporum. 4. Eusebius's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a> with Notes. 5. Canones Ifagogici; and many other works. The collections intitled Scaligariana, were collected from his conversations by one of his friends; and being ranged into alphabetical order, were published by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Vossius.

SCALLOP

Pages 656-656

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>. See PECTEN. In the highlands of Scotland, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> teacallop shell is made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for the skimming of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. In old times, it had a more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; being admitted into the halls of heroes, and was the cup of their fertility when the tribe assembled in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of their chieftain.

SCALPEL

Pages 656-656

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> used in anatomical dissections and operations in surgery. SCALPER <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> SCALPING <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">IRON</a>, a surgeon's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used for scraping foul carious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>.

SCALPING

Pages 656-656

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, in practice among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> warriors, of taking off the tops of the scalps of the enemies' skulls with their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> on. They preserve them as trophies of their victories, and are rewarded by their chiefs according to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of scalps they bring in.

SCALPRA DENTALIA

Pages 656-656

instruments used by the surgeons to take off those <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, livid, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> crusts which infest the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and not only loose and destroy them, but taint the breath.

SCAMMONY

Pages 656-656

a concreted vegetable juice of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of convolvulus, partly of the resin, and partly of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a> kind. See CONVOLVULUS. The best scammony comes from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> spongy masses, easily friable, of a shining ash-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> verging to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; when powdered, of a light grey <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> whitish colour: an inferior sort is brought from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, in more <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> ponderous pieces, of a darker colour, and full of sand and other impurities. This juice is chiefly of the resinous kind; rectified spirit dissolves six ounces out of five, the remainder is a mucilaginous substance mixed with dross; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>-spirit totally dissolves it, the impurities only being left. It has a faint unpleasant smell, and a bitterish, somewhat acrimonious, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Scammony is an efficacious and strong purgative. Some have condemned it as unsafe, and laid sundry ill Scammony qualities to its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which is, that its operation is uncertain, a full dose proving sometimes ineffectual, whilst at others a much smaller one occasions dangerous hypercataractes. This <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, however, is owing entirely to the different circumstances of the patient, and not to any ill <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> or irregularity of operation of the medicine: where the intestines are lined with an excessive load of mucus, the scammony passes through without exerting itself upon them; where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> mucus is deficient, a small dose of this or any other resinous cathartic, irritates and inflames. Many have endeavoured to abate the force of this drug, and correct its imaginary virulence, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> it to the fume of sulphur, dissolving it in acid juices, and the like; but this could do no more than destroy as it were a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the medicine, without making any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the rest. Scammony in substance, judiciously managed, stands not in need of any corrector; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> triturated with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> or with almonds, it becomes sufficiently safe and mild in operation. It may likewise be conveniently dissolved by trituration, in a strong decoction of liquorice; and then poured off from the faeces; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WURTEMBERG">Wurtemberg</a> assures us, that by this treatment it becomes mildly purgative, without being attended with gripes, or other inconveniences; and that it likewise proves inoffensive to the palate. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> dose of scammony is from three to twelve grains.

SCANDALUM MAGNATUM

Pages 656-656

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is a defamatory speech <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to the injury of a person of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; for which a writ that bears the same name is granted for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of damages.

SCANDERBEG

Pages 656-656

the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of George Castrion <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, dependent on the Ottoman empire. He was delivered up with his three elder brothers as hostages, by their father, to Amurath II. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of the Turks, who poisoned his brothers, but spared him on account of his youth, being likewise pleased with his juvenile <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and amiable person. In a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he became one of the most renowned generals of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and revolting from Amurath, he joined Hunniade Corvin, a most formidable enemy to the Ottoman power. He defeated the sultan's <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, took Amurath's secretary prisoner, obliged him to sign and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> an order to the governor of Croia, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Albania, to deliver up the citadel and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> to the bearer of that order, in the name of the sultan. With this forged order he repaired to Croia; and thus recovered the throne of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, and maintained the independency of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> against the numerous armies of Amurath and his successor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAHOMMED">Mahommed</a> II. who was obliged to make peace with this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERO">hero</a> in 1461. He then went to the assistance of Ferdinand of Arragon, at the request of Pope Pius II. and by his assistance Ferdinand gained a complete victory over his enemy the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Anjou. Scanderbeg died in 1467. SCANDEROON. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRETTA">Alexandretta</a>.

SCANDINAVIA

Pages 656-658

a general name for the countries of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, anciently under the dominion of one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. The inhabitants of these countries, in former times, were excessively addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>. From their earliest years they applied themselves to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, and accustomed them- We are informed that Harold, surnamed Blue-tooth, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Denmark who lived in the beginning of the ninth century, had founded on the coasts of Pomerania a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> named Jolin <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Jomsburg. To this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he sent a colony of young Danes, bestowing the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> on a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> called Palnatok. In this colony it was forbidden to mention the word fear, even in the most imminent dangers. No citizen of Jomsburg was to yield to any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of enemies however <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. The sight of inevitable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was not to be taken as an excuse for showing the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>. And this legislature really appears to have eradicated from the minds of most of the youths bred up under him, all traces of that sentiment so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and so universal, which makes men think on their destruction with horror. Nothing can show this better than a single fact in their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, which deserves to have place here for its singularity. Some of them having made an irruption into the territories of a powerful Norwegian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, named Haquin, were overcome in spite of the obstinacy of their resistance; and the most distinguished among them being made prisoners, were, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of those times, condemned to death. The news of this, far from afflicting them, was on the contrary received with joy. The first who was led to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> was content to say, without changing countenance, and without expressing the least sign of fear, "Why should not the same happen to me as did to my father? He died, and so must I." A warrior, named Thorchill, who was to cut off the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, having asked him what he felt at the sight of death, he answered, "that he remembered too well the laws of Jomsburg, to utter any words that denoted fear." The third, in reply to the same question, said, "he rejoiced to die with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, and that he preferred such a death to an infamous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> like that of Thorchill's." The fourth made an answer much longer and more extraordinary. "I suffer with a good heart; and the present <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> is to me very agreeable. I only beg of you," added he, addressing himself to Thorchill, "to be very quick in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off my head; for it is a question often debated by us at Jomsburg, whether one retains any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> after being beheaded. I <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> therefore grasp this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> in my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, after my head is cut off, I strike it towards you, it will show I have not lost all sense; if I let it drop, it will be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the contrary. Make haste therefore, and decide the dispute." Thorchill, adds the historian, cut off his head in a most expeditious manner; but the knife, as might be expected, dropt from his hand. The fifth showed the same tranquility, and died rallying and jeering his enemies. The sixth begged of Thorchill, that he might not be led to punishment like a sheep: "Strike the blow in my <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>," said he, "I will sit still without shrinking; and take notice whether I once wink my eyes, or betray one sign of fear in my countenance. For we inhabitants of Jomsburg are used to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> ourselves in trials of this sort, so as to meet the stroke of death without once moving." He kept his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> before all the spectators, and received the blow without betraying the least sign of fear, or so much as winking with his eyes. The seventh, says the historian, was a very beautiful young <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, in the flower of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, as fine as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, floated in curls and ringlets on his shoulders. Thorchill asked him what he thought thought of death? I receive it willingly, said he, since I have fulfilled the greatest duty of life, and have seen all those put to death whom I would not survive. I only beg of you one favour, not to let my hair be touched by a slave, or stained with my blood." Neither was this intrepidity peculiar to the inhabitants of Jomsburgh; it was the general character of all the Scandinavians, of which we shall only give this further instance. A warrior, having been thrown upon his back in wrestling with his enemy, and the latter finding himself without his arms, the vanquished person promised to wait, without changing his posture, till his antagonist fetched a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> to kill him; and he faithfully kept his word.—To die with his arms in his hand was the ardent wish of every free man; and the pleasing idea which they had of this kind of death led them to dread such as proceeded from old age and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. The history of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Scandinavia is full of instances of this way of thinking. The warriors who found themselves lingering in disease, often availed themselves of their few remaining moments to shake off life, by a way that they supposed to be more glorious. Some of them would be carried into a field of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, that they might die in the engagement. Others flew themselves: many procured this melancholy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to be performed by their friends, who considered it as a most sacred duty. "There is, on a mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>," says the author of an old Icelandic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>, "a rock so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, that no animal can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the top and live. Here men betake themselves when they are afflicted and unhappy. From this place all our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, even without waiting for sickness, have departed into Edin. It is useless, therefore, to give ourselves up to groans and complaints, or to put our relations to needless expenses, since we can easily follow the example of our fathers, who have all gone by the way of this rock."—When all these methods failed, and at last when Christianity had banished such barbarous practices, the disconsolate heroes consoled themselves by putting on complete armour as soon as they found their end approaching.

SCANDIX

Pages 658-658

Shepherd's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEEDLE">Needle</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Venus-comb; a genus of the dignia order, belonging to the pentandra clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is the odorata with angular furrowed seeds. It is a native of Germany; and has a very thick perennial root, composed of many fibres, of a sweet aromatic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> like aniseed, from which come forth many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> leaves that branch out somewhat like those of fern, from whence it is named fæuet-fem. The stalks grow four or five feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, are fistulous and hairy; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are disposed in an umbel at the top of the stalk, are of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and have a sweet aromatic scent.—This species is easily propagated by seeds, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> permitted to scatter, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> supply an abundance of young plants, that may be put into any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the garden, and require no care.

SCANNING

Pages 658-658

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, the measuring of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> by feet, in order to see whether <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> not the quantities be duly observed. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> is chiefly used in Greek and Latin verses. Thus an hexameter verse is scanned by resolving it into six feet; a pentameter, by resolving it into five feet, &c.

SCAPE-GOAT

Pages 658-658

in the Jewish antiquities, the goat which was set <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of solemn <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a>. For the ceremonies on this occasion, see Levit. xvi. 5. 6. &c. Some say, that a piece of scarlet cloth, in form of a tongue, was tied on the forehead of the scape-goat. Hofsm. Lex. Univ. in voc. Lingua. Many have been the disputes among the interpreters, concerning the meaning of the word scape-goat; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> rather of azazel, for which scape-goat is put in our version of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>. Spencer is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that azazel is a proper name, signifying the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> or evil daemon. See his reasons in his book De leg. Hebr. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a>. Dissert. viii. Among other things, he observes, that the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Jews used to substitute the name Samaïl for Azazel, and many of them have ventured to affirm, that at the feast of expiation they were obliged to offer a gift to Samaïl to obtain his favour. Thus also the goat, sent into the wilderness to Azazel, was understood to be a gift or oblation. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> have been of the same opinion. But Spencer thinks that the genuine reasons of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> were, 1. That the goat, loaded with the sins of the people, and sent to Azazel, might be a symbolical representation of the miserable condition of sinners. 2. God sent the goat thus loaded to the evil demons, to show that they were impure, thereby to deter the people from any conversation or familiarity with them. 3. That the goat sent to Azazel, sufficiently expiating all evils, the Israelites might the more willingly abstain from the expiatory sacrifices of the Gentiles.

SCAPULAR

Pages 658-660
or Scapulary, a part of the habit of several religious orders in the church of Rome, worn over the gown as a badge of peculiar veneration for the Blest Virgin. It consists of two narrow slips or breadths of cloth covering the back and the breast, and hanging down to the feet.—The devotees of the scapulary celebrate its festival on the 10th of July. SCARABÆUS, the Beetle, in zoology, a genus of insects of the coleoptera order: the antennae of the beetles are of a clavated figure, and fiddle longitudinally; and their legs are frequently dentated. There are 87 species; all, however, concurring in one common formation of having cases to their wings, which are the more necessary to those insects, as they often live under the surface of the earth, in holes, which they dig out by their own industry. The cases prevent the various injuries their real wings might sustain by rubbing or crushing against the sides of their abode. These, though they do not assist flight, yet keep the internal wings clean and even, and produce a loud buzzing noise when the animal rises in the air. If we examine the formation of all animals of the beetle kind, we shall find, as in shell-fish, that their bones are placed externally, and their muscles within. These muscles are formed very much like those of quadrupeds; and are ended with such surprising strength, that, bulk for bulk, they are a thousand times stronger than those of a man. The strength of these muscles is of use in digging the animal's subterraneous abode, whither it most frequently returns, even after it becomes a winged insect capable of flying. Besides the difference which results from the shape and colour of these animals, the size also makes a considerable one; some beetles being not larger than the head of a pin; while others, such as the elephant beetle, are as big as one's fist. But the greatest difference among them is, that some are produced in a month, and in a single season go through all the stages of their existence; while others take near four years to their production, and live as winged insects a year more. The may-bug, or dorr-beetle, as some call it, has, like all the rest, a pair of cases to its wings, which are of a reddish brown colour, sprinkled with a whitish dust, which easily comes off. In some years their necks are seen covered with a red plate, and in others with a black; these, however, are distinct forms, and their difference is by no means accidental. The fore-legs are very short, and the better calculated for burrowing in the ground, where this insect makes its retreat. It is well known for its evening buzz, to children; but still more formidably introduced to the acquaintance of the husbandman and gardener, for in some seasons it has been found to swarm in such numbers as to eat up every vegetable production. The two sexes in the may-bug are easily distinguished from each other, by the superior length of the tufts, at the end of the horns, in the male. They begin to copulate in summer, and at that season they are seen joined together for a considerable time. The female being impregnated, quickly falls to boring a hole into the ground, where to deposit her burden. This is generally about half a foot deep; and in it she places her eggs, which are of an oblong shape, with great regularity, one by the other. They are of a bright yellow colour, and noway wrapped up in a common covering, as some have imagined. When the female is lightened of her burden, she again ascends from her hole, to live, as before, upon leaves and vegetables, to buzz in the summer evening, and to lie hid among the branches of trees in the heat of the day. In about three months after these eggs have been thus deposited in the earth, the contained insect begins to break its shell, and a small grub or maggot crawls forth, and feeds upon the roots of whatever vegetable it happens to be nearest. All substances, of this kind, seem equally grateful; yet it is probable the mother insect has a choice among what kind of vegetables she shall deposit her young. In this manner these voracious creatures continue in the worm state for more than three years, devouring the roots of every plant they approach, and making their way under ground in quest of food with great dispatch and facility. At length they grow to above the size of a walnut, being a great thick white maggot with a red head, which is seen most frequently in new turned earth, and which is so eagerly sought after by birds of every species. When largest, they are found an inch and an half long, of a whitish yellow colour; with a body consisting of twelve segments or joints, on each side of which there are nine breathing holes, and three red feet. The head is larger in proportion to the body, of a reddish colour, with a pincer before, and a semicircular lip, with which it cuts the roots of plants and sucks out their moisture. As this insect lives entirely under ground, it has no occasion for Scarabaeus eyes, and accordingly it is found to have none; but is furnished with two feelers, which, like the crutch of a blind man, serve to direct its motions. Such is the form of this animal, that lives for years in the worm state under ground, still voracious, and every year changing its skin. It is not till the end of the fourth year, that this extraordinary insect prepares to emerge from its subterraneous abode, and even this is not effected but by a tedious preparation. About the latter end of autumn, the grub begins to perceive the approaches of its transformation: it then buries itself deeper and deeper in the earth, sometimes six feet beneath the surface; and there forms itself a capacious apartment, the walls of which it renders very smooth and shining, by the excretions of its body. Its abode being thus formed, it begins soon after to shorten itself, to swell, and to burst its last skin in order to assume the form of a chrysalis. This, in the beginning, appears of a yellowish colour, which heightens by degrees, till at last it is seen nearly red. Its exterior form plainly discovers all the vestiges of the future winged insect, all the fore parts being distinctly seen; while, behind, the animal seems as if wrapped in swaddling cloths. The young may-bug continues in this state for about three months longer; and it is not till the beginning of January that the aurelia divests itself of all its impediments, and becomes a winged insect completely formed. Yet still the animal is far from attaining its natural strength, health, and appetite. It undergoes a kind of infant imbecility; and unlike most other insects, that the instant they become flies are arrived at their state of full perfection, the may-bug continues feeble and sickly. Its colour is much brighter than in the perfect animal; all its parts are soft; and its voracious nature seems for a while to have entirely forsaken it. As the animal is very often found in this state, it is supposed, by those unacquainted with its real history, that the old ones, of the former season, have buried themselves for the winter, in order to revisit the sun the ensuing summer. But the fact is, the old one never survives the season; but dies, like all the other winged tribe of insects, from the severity of cold in winter. About the latter end of May, these insects, after having lived for four years under ground, burst from the earth when the first mild evening invites them abroad. They are at that time seen rising from their long imprisonment, from living only upon roots, and imbibing only the moisture of the earth, to visit the mildness of the summer air, to choose the sweetest vegetables for their banquet, and to drink the dew of the evening. Wherever an attentive observer then walks abroad, he will see them bursting up before him in his pathway, like ghosts on a theatre. He will see every part of the earth, that had its surface beaten into hardness, perforated by their egression. When the season is favourable for them, they are seen by myriads buzzing along, hitting against every object that intercepts their flight. The mid-day sun, however, seems too powerful for their constitutions: they then lurk under the leaves and branches of some shady tree; but the willow seems particularly their most Scarabaeus, favourite food; there they lurk in clusters, and seldom quit the tree till they have devoured all its verdure. In those seasons which are favourable to their propagation, they are seen in an evening as thick as flakes of snow, and hitting against every object with a sort of capricious blindness. Their duration, however, is but short, as they never survive the season. They begin to join shortly after they have been let loose from their prison; and when the female is impregnated, she cautiously bores a hole in the ground, with an instrument fitted for that purpose which she is furnished with at the tail; and there deposits her eggs, generally to the number of three score. If the leaflon and the soil be adapted to their propagation, these soon multiply as already described, and go through the various stages of their contemptible existence. This insect, however, in its worm state, though prejudicial to man, makes one of the chief repasts of the feathered tribe, and is generally the first nourishment with which they supply their young. Rooks are particularly fond of these worms, and devour them in great numbers. The inhabitants of the county of Norfolk, some time since, went into the practice of destroying their rookeries; but in proportion as they destroyed one plague, they were pestered with a greater; and these insects multiplied in such an amazing abundance, as to destroy not only the verdure of the fields, but even the roots of vegetables not yet shot forth. One farm in particular was so injured by them in the year 1751, that the occupier was not able to pay his rent; and the landlord was not only content to lose his income for that year, but also gave money for the support of the farmer and his family. In Ireland they suffered so much by these insects, that they came to a resolution of setting fire to a wood, of some extent, to prevent their mischievous propagation. The scarabaeus carnifex, which the Americans call the tumble-dung, particularly demands our attention; it is all over of a dusky black, rounder than those animals are generally found to be, and so strong, though not much larger than the common black beetle, that if one of them be put under a brass candlestick, it will cause it to move backwards and forwards, as if it were by an invisible hand, to the admiration of those who are not accustomed to the sight: but this strength is given it for much more useful purposes than those of exciting human curiosity; for there is no creature more laborious, either in seeking subsistence, or providing a proper retreat for its young. They are endowed with sagacity to discover subsistence by their excellent smelling, which directs them in flights to excrement just fallen from man or beast, on which they instantly drop, and fall unanimously to work in forming round balls or pellets thereof, in the middle of which they lay an egg. These pellets, in September, they convey three feet deep in the earth, where they lie till the approach of spring, when the eggs are hatched and burst their nests, and the insects find their way out of the earth. They assist each other with indefatigable industry in rolling these globular pellets to the place where they are to be buried. This they are to perform with the tail foremost, by raising up their hinder part, and shoving along the ball with their hind-feet.
