They are always accompanied with other beetles of a larger size, and of a more elegant structure and colour. The breast of this is covered with a shield of a crimson colour, and shining like metal; the head is of the like colour, mixed with green; and on the crown of the head stands a shining black horn, bending backwards. These are called the kings of the beetles; but for what reason is uncertain, since they partake of the same dirty drudgery with the rest. The elephant-beetle is the largest of this kind hitherto known; and is found in South-America, particularly in Guinea and Surinam, as well as about the river Oronooko. It is of a black colour; and the whole body is covered with a very hard shell, full as thick and as strong as that of a small crab. Its length, from the hinder part to the eyes, is almost four inches; and from the same part to the end of the proboscis or trunk, four inches and three quarters. The transverse diameter of the body is two inches and a quarter; and the breadth of each elytron, or case for the wings, is an inch and three tenths. The antennae or feelers are quite horny; for which reason the proboscis or trunk is moveable at its insertion into the head, and seems to supply the place of feelers; the horns are eight-tenths of an inch long, and terminate in points. The proboscis is an inch and a quarter long, and turns upwards; making a crooked line, terminating in two horns, each of which is near a quarter of an inch long; but they are not perforated at the end like the proboscis of other insects. About four tenths of an inch above the head, or that side next the body, is a prominence, or small horn; which, if the rest of the trunk were away, would cause this part to resemble the horn of a rhinoceros. There is indeed a beetle so called; but then the horns or trunk has no fork at the end, though the lower horn resembles this. The feet are all forked at the end, but not like lobsters claws. See Plate CCLVII.

SCARDONNA

Pages 660-660

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, seated on the eastern banks of the river Cherca, with a bishop's see. It has been taken and retaken several times by the Turks and Venetians; and the last ruined the fortifications and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> buildings in 1537; but they have been since put in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17. 25. N. Lat. 43. 55.

SCARIFICATION

Pages 660-660

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, the operation of making several incisions in the skin by means of lances <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other instruments, particularly the cupping <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. See Surgery.

SCARLET

Pages 660-661

a beautiful bright <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-colours, minium mixed with a little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a> produces a good scarlet; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a flower in a print is to be painted a scarlet colour, the lights as well as the shades should be covered with minium, and the shaded parts finished with carmine, which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> produce an admirable scarlet. **Scarlet-Fever.** See Medicines, no 337—339. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCARP">Scarp</a>,** in fortification, is the interior talus <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> slope of the ditch next the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, at the foot of the rampart. **Scarp,** in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, the scarf which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> commanders wear for ornament. It is borne somewhat like a battoon finister, but is broader than it, and is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> out to the edges of the field, whereas the battoon is cut off at each end. **Scarpanto,** an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, and one of the Sporades, lying to the S.W. of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, and to the N.E. of that of Candia. It is about 22 miles in length, and 8 in breadth; and there are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. It abounds in cattle and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a>; and there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, quarries of marble, with several good harbours. The Turks are masters of it, but the inhabitants are Greeks. **Scarpe,** a river of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, which has its source near Aubigny in Artois, where it washes <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARRAS">Arras</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOUAY">Douay</a>; after which it runs on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> and Hainault, passing by St Amand, and a little after falls into the Scheld. **Scarron (Paul),** an eminent comic, or rather <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a>, French writer, was the son of Paul Scarron a counsellor in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1610. He was deformed, and of very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> manners; yet his father designed him for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> state. He went to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> when he was four and twenty; but returned <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> as licentious as he went, and so continued till by a terrible stroke he was deprived of all power to indulge vicious appetites. He was at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a> where he was a canon; but retiring from thence, at a carnival season, into a damp and fenny situation, a torpor suddenly seized him, and he lost the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>. The physicians attempted in vain to restore them; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> Scarron, at 27 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, had no movements left him but those of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and tongue. Melancholy and terrible as his condition was, his comical and burlesque humour never forsook him; he was continually talking and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> in this strain; and his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> became the rendezvous of all the men of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a>. Afterwards a fresh misfortune overtook him: his father, who had hitherto supplied his wants, incurred the displeasure of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> Richelieu, and was banished. Scarron, deprived of his resources, presented an humble request to Richelieu; which was so humorously drawn, that the minister could not forbear laughing. What the effect would have been, cannot be said, since both Richelieu and his father died soon after: however, it is reckoned among his best pieces. This extraordinary person at length conceived thoughts of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>; and in 1654, was actually married to Mademoiselle d'Aubigné, afterwards the most celebrated Madam de <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAINTENON">Maintenon</a>, who lodged near him, and who was about 16 years of age. This lady, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for Scarron, if she had any, must have been quite intellectual, had wit and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and served to increase the good <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> which frequented his house: she also restrained him in his buffooneries, making him more reserved and decent. Scarron died in 1660, and his jesting humour did not die before him. Within a few minutes of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, when his acquaintance were about him all in tears: "Ah! my friends, (said he), you will never cry for me so much as I have made you laugh." He wrote many books both prose and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; but his Comical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROMANCE">Romance</a> is almost the only one which continued to be liked by persons of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; and this was foretold by Boileau. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">Scene</a>,** in its primary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denoted a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, or the place where dramatic pieces and other public shows were exhibited; for it does not appear that the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets were at all acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> way of changing the scenes in the different parts of the play, in order to raise the idea of the persons represented by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> being in different places. The original scene for acting of plays was as simple as the representations themselves: it consisted only of a plain plot of ground proper for the occasion, which was in some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> shaded by the neighbouring trees, whose branches were made to meet together, and their vacancies supplied with boards, ricks, and the like; and to complete the shelter, these were sometimes covered with skins, and sometimes with only the branches of other trees newly cut <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and full of leaves. Afterwards more <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> scenes, or sceneries, representations were introduced, and paintings used instead of the objects themselves. Scenes were then of three sorts: tragic, comic, and satyrical. The tragic scene represented stately magnificent edifices, with decorations of pillars, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and other things suitable to the palaces of kings; the comic exhibited private houses with balconies and windows, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> buildings; and the satyrical was the representation of groves, mountains, dens, and other rural appearances; and these decorations either turned on pivots, or slid along grooves, as those in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>. To keep <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, the scene should never be shifted from place to place in the course of the play: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were pretty severe in this respect, particularly Terence, in some of whose plays the scene never shifts at all, but the whole is transacted at the door of some old <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s house, whether with inimitable art he occasionally brings the actors. The French are pretty strict with respect to this rule; but the English pay very little regard to it. Scene is also a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of a dramatic poem. Thus plays are divided into acts, and acts are again subdivided into scenes; in which sense the scene is properly the persons present at or concerned in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> on the stage at such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>: whenever, therefore, a new <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> appears, or an old one disappears, the action is changed into other hands; and therefore a new scene then commences. It is one of the laws of the stage, that the scenes be well connected; that is, that one succeed another in such a manner as that the stage be never quite empty till the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>. **Scenography,** (from the Greek, σκηνή, scene, and γραφειν, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>), in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, a representation of a body on a perspective <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>; or a description thereof in all its dimensions, such as it appears to the eye. See Perspective. **Scepter,** a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, or battoon, borne by kings on solemn occasions, as an ensign of command and authority. See Regalia. **Scepticism,**

SCEPTICISM

Pages 661-662

the doctrines and opinions of the sceptics: whose distinguishing tenet was, that all things are uncertain and incomprehensible; and that the mind is never to assent to any thing, but to remain in perpetual doubt and suspense. This doctrine was also called Pyrrhonism, from the name of its author. See the article PYRRHONISM and SCEPTICS.

SCEPTICS

Pages 662-662

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, founded by Pyrrho, whose distinguishing tenet was, That all things are uncertain and incomprehensible; consequently traries are equally true; and that the mind is never to assent to any thing, but to keep up an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> hesitancy <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> indifference. See SCEPTICISM.—The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> skeptic, in its original Greek, σκεπτικός, properly signifies considerative, and inquisitive; or, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> who is ever weighing reasons on one side and the other, without ever deciding between them: it is formed from the verb σκεπτόμαι, I consider, look about, deliberate. Laertius notes, that the followers of Pyrrho had various denominations. From their manner, they were called Pyrrhonians. From their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOGMA">dogma</a>, aporetic, that is, doubters, of ἀνοίγω, to doubt; From their suspension and hesitation, ἐπιστηλί, of ἐπιστηλή, to stay, to keep back; And from their never getting beyond the search of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, zetetic, seekers. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> refutes the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> principle of the sceptics thus: When you say that all things are incomprehensible, do you comprehend or conceive that they are thus incomprehensible, or do you not? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> you do, then something is comprehensible; if you do not, there is no reason we should believe you, since you do not comprehend your own assertion.

SCHAFFHAUSEN

Pages 662-662

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, handsome, and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of the same name, with a castle in the form of a citadel. It is well built, with fine large streets, and adorned with several fountains; and the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the houses are painted on the outside. It is well fortified, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is the largest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in Switzerland; besides which, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINSTER">minster</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> adjoining thereto, the arsenal, the town-houle, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> clock (which shows the course of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> with their eclipses), and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, are well worth the observation of a traveller. That river is of great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to the inhabitants, with regard to trade. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 51'. N. Lat. 47° 39'.

SCHIRAS

Pages 662-662

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and famous town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Parsistan. It is 3 miles in length from east to west, but not so much in breadth. It is seated at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west end of a spacious plain surrounded with very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hills, under one of which the town stands. The houles are built of bricks dried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; the roofs are flat and terraced. There are 15 handsome mosques, tiled with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of a bluish green <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and lined within with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> polished marble. There are many large and beautiful gardens, surrounded with walls of fourteen feet high, and four thick. They contain various kinds of very fine trees, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> almost of every kind, besides various beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. The wines of Schiras are not only the best in Persia, but, as some think, in the whole world. The women are much addicted to gallantry, and it is called an earthly paradise by some. The ruins of the famous Persepolis are 30 miles to the north-east of this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 56° 0'. N. Lat. 29° 36'.

SCHISM

Pages 662-662

(from the Greek, σχίσμα, cliff, fissure), in the general, signifies <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> separation; but is chiefly used in speaking of separations happening thro' diversity of opinions, among people of the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Thus we say the schism of the ten tribes of Judah and Benjamin, the schism of the Persians from the Turks and other Mahometans, &c. Among <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> authors, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> schism of the West, is that which happened in the times of Clement VII. and Urban VI. which divided the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> for 40 or 50 years, and was at length ended by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of Martin V. at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>. The Romanists <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> 34 schisms in their church.—They below the name English schism on the reformation of religion in this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Those of the church of England again apply the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> schism to the separation of the non-conformists, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">presbyterians</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">independents</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">anabaptists</a>, for a further reformation.

SCHOENOBATES

Pages 662-662

(from the Greek, σχοῖνος, a rope; and βάνα, I walk), a name which the Greeks gave to their rope-dancers: by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> called funambuli. See ROPE-DANCER and FUNAMBULUS.

SCHOLASTIC

Pages 662-663

something belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. See SCHOOL. Scholastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a>, is that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of divinity which clears and discusses questions by reason and arguments; in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands, in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, opposed to positive divinity, which is founded on the authority of fathers, councils, &c. The school-divinity is now fallen into the last contempt; and is scarce regarded anywhere but in some of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, where they are still by their charters obliged to teach it.

SCHOLIAST

Pages 663-663
or Commentator, a grammarian who writes scholia, that is, notes, glosses, &c. upon ancient authors who have written in the learned languages. See the next article.

SCHOLIUM

Pages 663-663

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, annotation, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> remark, occasionally made on some passage, proposition, or the like. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> is much used in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, where, after demonstrating a proposition, it is customary to point out how it might be done some other way, or to give some advice or precaution in order to prevent mistakes, or add some particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> or application thereof.

SCHOMBERG

Pages 663-663

of an illustrious German family: He served first under Frederic-Henry, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>; then under <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. who made him marshal of France, though a Protestant. France lost him by the revocation of the edict of Nantes in 1685, when he retired to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. His merit raised him to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANDEE">grandee</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. At the revolution, he came to England with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> William; and, for his signal services at that era, he was made an English duke, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> also voted him 100,000l. In 1689, he was made commander in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the king's forces in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; and in 1690, he was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOYNE">Boyne</a>, by the French refugees of his own <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, by a fatal mistake, in the 82nd year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

SCHOOL

Pages 663-663

a public <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, wherein the languages, humanities, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other arts, are taught. Thus we say, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> school, a school of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, &c.—The word is formed from the Latin, schola, which, according to Du Cange, signifies <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> and correction; he adds, that it was anciently used, in the general, for all places where several persons met together, either to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a>, or do any other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Accordingly, there were schola palatinae, being the several posts wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s guards were placed; schola scutariorum, schola gentilium, &c. At length the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> passed also to civil magistrates; and accordingly in the code, we meet with schola chartulariorum, schola agentium, &c.; and even to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, as schola cantorum, schola sacerdotum, &c.

SCHREVELIUS

Pages 663-663

a laborious Dutch critic and writer, who has given the public some editions of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors more elegant than correct: his Greek Lexicon is esteemed the best of all his works. He died in 1667.

SCHULTENS

Pages 663-663

professor of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> and of the Eastern languages at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, and one of the most learned men of the 18th century, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a>, where he studied till the year 1706, and from thence <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his studies at Leyden and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>. Schultens at length applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of Arabic books, both printed and in manuscript; in which he made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress. A short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, he became minister of Wassenar; and, two years after, professor of the Eastern tongues at Franeker. At length he was invited to Leyden, where he taught Hebrew and the Eastern languages with extraordinary reputation till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1750. He wrote many learned works; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOB">Job</a>, 2 vols 4to. 2. A Commentary on the Proverbs. 3. Vetus regia via Hebraizandii. 4. Animadverfiones philologicae & criticae <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> varia loca Veteris Testamenti. 6. An excellent Hebrew <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, &c. Schultens discovered in all his works <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> criticism, and much learning and erudition. He maintained against Goussit and Driessen, that in order to have a perfect knowledge of Hebrew, it is necessary to join with it, not only the Chaldee and Syriac, but more particularly the Arabic.

SCHURMAN

Pages 663-663

a most extraordinary German lady. Her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> genius discovered itself at six years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, when she cut all sorts of figures in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> with her scissors, without a pattern. At eight, she learned, in a few days, to draw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> in a very agreeable manner. At ten, she took but three hours to learn <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>. Afterwards she was taught music, vocal and instrumental; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, and engraving; in all of which she succeeded admirably. She excelled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a>-painting, and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> portraits upon glass with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Greek, and Latin, were so familiar to her, that the most learned men were astonished at it. She spoke French, Italian, and English, fluently. Her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, in almost all languages, was so imitable, that the curious preserved specimens of it in their cabinets. At length, all this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of learning and uncommon penetration could not protect her from falling into the errors of Labadie, the famous French enthusiast, who had been banished France for his extravagant tenets and conduct. To this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> she entirely attached herself, and accompanied him wherever he went; and even attended him in his last illness, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTENA">Altena</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>. Her works, consisting of De vita humanae termino, and Disputatio de ingenti multebris <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> doctrinam et meliores literae aptitudine, and her Letters to her learned correspondents, were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1648; but enlarged in the edition of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, 1562, in 12mo, under the following <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a>: A. M. Schurman Opulcula Hebraea, Graeca, Latina, Gallica, Prosaica et Metrica. She published likewise at Altena, in Latin, A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">Defence</a> of her <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to Labadie, while she was with him in 1673; not worth <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a>. She was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> in 1607, but resided chiefly in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and died in Friesland in 1678.

SCHWARTENBURG

Pages 664-664

a town and castle of Germany, and circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, in the landgrave of Thuringia, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name belonging to a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Saxony. It is seated on the river Schwartz, 20 miles south-east of Erford, and 35 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Cullembach. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 27. N. Lat. 50. 45.

SCHWARTS

Pages 663-664

an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>-painter, born at Ingolstadt in 1550, who was distinguished by the appellation of the German Raphael. He learned the first principles of the art in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but finished his studies at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; when he not only made the works of Titian his models, but had SCI Schwarteburg had the advantage of receiving some personal instructions from that illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. His performances were soon in the highest esteem; as his manner of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> was very different from what the Germans had been accustomed to before that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>: he was, therefore, invited by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and appointed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> painter. He died in 1594; and his most <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> works, as well in fresco as in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, are in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Munich, and in the churches and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>.

SCHWARTZEMBERG

Pages 664-664

a town of Germany, in the circle of Franconia, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a principality of the same name. The castle is seated on the river Lec, 5 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Nurembeg, and 20 east of Wurtsburg, subject to its own <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 27. N. Lat. 49. 43.

SCHWEIDNITZ

Pages 664-664

a strong town of Germany, in Silecia, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the same name, with a castle. It is the handsomest town of Silecia, next to Breslaw. The streets are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> fine, and the houses well built. The fortifications are not very considerable; the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is turned into a convent. All the magistrates are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>; but most of the inhabitants are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, who have a church without the town, as also a public school and bells. It is seated on an eminence on the river Weifritz, 27 miles south-east of Lignitz, and 22 southwest of Breslaw. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. 48. N. Lat. 50. 46.

SCHWEINFURT

Pages 664-664

a very strong, free, and imperial town of Germany, in Franconia, with a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, where the senators meet, who are 12 in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. The environs are rich in cattle, corn, and wine; and the inhabitants are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, but not very rich. However, they carry on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trade in woollen and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, goose-quills, and feathers. It is seated on the river Main, 27 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Wurtzburg, and 22 west of Bamberg. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 25. N. Lat. 50. 4.

SCHWINBURG

Pages 664-664

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, on the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Fionia, over-against the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Arroa and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGELAND">Langeland</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 55. N. Lat. 55. 8.

SCHWITZ

Pages 664-664
or Switz, a canton of Swisserland, which gives name to them all. It is bounded on the west by the lake of the four cantons, on the south by the canton of Uri, on the east by that Glaris, and on the north by those of Zurich and Zug. Its principal riches consist in cattle, and the capital town is of the same name. This is a large, handsome place, seated near the lake of the four cantons, in a pleasant country among the mountains. E. Long. 8. 41. N. Lat. 47. 2.

SCIENA

Pages 664-664

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of thoracici. The membrane of the gills has six rays; the opercula and whole head are scaly. There are five <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>.

SCIENCE

Pages 664-664

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, denotes any doctrine, deduced from self-evident principles. Sciences may be properly divided as follows. 1. The knowledge of things, their constitutions, properties, and operations: this, in a little more enlarged <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, may be called science, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy; the end of which is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. See NATURAL PHILOSOPHY, and PHYSICS.—2. The skill of rightly applying these powers, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>: the most considerable under this head is ethics, which is the seeking out those rules and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> actions that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, and the means to practise them, (see <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">MORAL PHILOSOPHY</a>); and the next is mechanics, or the application of the powers of natural agents to the uses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, (see MECHANICS.)—3. The doctrine of signs, semiotics; the most usual of which being words, it is aptly enough termed logic. See LOGIC. This, says Mr Locke, seems to be the most general, as well as natural, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the objects of our understanding. For a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> can employ his thoughts about nothing but either the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of things themselves for the discovery of truth; or about the things in his own power, which are his actions, for the attainment of his own ends; or the signs the mind makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of both in the one and the other, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> ordering of them for its clearer information. All which three, viz., things as they are in themselves knowable, actions as they depend on us in order to happiness, and the right use of signs in order to knowledge, being toto caelo different, they seem to be the three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> provinces of the intellectual world, wholly separate and distinct one from another.

SCILLA

Pages 664-665

the squill; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the hexandria class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is the maritima, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-onion, whose roots are used in medicine. Of this there are two sorts, one with a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, and the other with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> root; which are supposed to be accidental varieties, but the white are generally preferred for medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. The roots are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, somewhat oval-shaped, composed of many coats lying over each other like onions; and at the bottom come out several fibres. From the middle of the root arise several shining leaves, which continue green all the winter, and decay in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. Then the flower-stalk comes out, which rises two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and is naked half-way, terminating in a pyramidal thyrse of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which are white, composed of six petals, which spread open like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a>. This grows naturally on the sea-shores, and in the ditches, where the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> naturally flows with the tide, in most of the warm parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, so cannot be propagated in gardens; the frosts in winter always destroying the roots, and for want of salt-water they do not thrive in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. Sometimes the roots which are bought for use put forth their stems and produce flowers, as they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the druggists shops.—This root is very nauseous to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, intensely bitter, and so acrimonious that it ulcerates the skin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> much handled. Taken internally, it powerfully stimulates the solids, and promotes urine, sweat, and expectoration. If the dose is considerable, it proves emetic, and sometimes purgative. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> use of this medicine is where the phlegm is abundant with mucous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and the lungs are oppressed by tenacious phlegm. It has been recommended in hydropic <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, Scilly. cases, taken in powder, from four to ten grains in a dose, mixed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of nitre. The most commodious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of exhibiting this root is as a bolus or pill. Liquid forms are too disagreeable to most people; though this may be remedied in some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> by the addition of some aromatic distilled waters. It yields the whole of its virtues to aqueous and vinous menstrua, and likewise to vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>.

SCILLY

Pages 665-668
or SULLEY, a cluster of small islands and rocks, situated in the Atlantic Ocean, in W. Long. 7°. N. Lat. 50°. These islands were first called Galiterides, or the Tin Isles, from their being rich in that metal. The common opinion is, that this is a Greek appellation; which in the most obvious sense is true: But as the Phoenicians were familiar with the metal, and with the country that produced it, before the Greeks knew anything of either, it is very likely they introduced the names of both from their own language. Strabo says these islands were ten in number, lying close together, of which only one was uninhabited; the people led an erratic life, lived upon the produce of their cattle, wore an under-garment which reached down to their ankles, and over that another, both of the same colour, which was black, girt round a little below the breast with a girdle, and walked with staves in their hands. The riches of these islands were tin and lead, which, with the skins of their cattle, they exchanged with foreign merchants, that is, the Phoenicians from Carthage, for earthen-ware, salt, and utensils made of brass. An author of great or greater antiquity, seems to include a part at least of Cornwall amongst these islands; or rather he suggests, that they were not perfect islands except at full sea, but that at ebb the inhabitants passed from one to another upon the sands, and that they even transported their tin in large square blocks upon carriages from one island to another. He farther takes notice, that such as inhabited about Belerium, (the Land's End), were in their conversation with strangers remarkably civil and courteous. Other ancient writers style these islands Hesperides, from their western situation, and Ogygianides, asserting that the land was extremely fertile, as well as full of mines; and that the people, though very brave, were entirely addicted to commerce, and boldly passed the seas in their leather boats. The Romans were exceedingly desirous of having a share in this commerce, which the Phoenicians as carefully laboured to prevent, by concealing their navigation to these islands as much as it was in their power. At length, however, the Romans prevailed; and Publius Crassus coming thither, was so well pleased with the industry and manners of the people, that he taught them various improvements, as well in working their mines, which till that time were but shallow, as in carrying their own merchandise to different markets. There is no room to doubt that they followed the fate of the rest of Britain, and particularly of Cornwall, in becoming subject to the Roman empire. We find them called in the itinerary of Antoninus, Sigdelos; by Sulpitius, Silenus; and by Solinus they are termed Silures. All we know of them during this period is, that their tin trade continued, and that sometimes state-prisoners were exiled, or, to use the Roman phrase, relegated hither as well as to other islands. When the legions were withdrawn, and Britain with its dependencies left in the power of the natives, there is no reason to question that these islands shared the same lot with the rest. As to the appellation which from this period prevailed, the ordinary way of writing it is Silly; in records we commonly find it spelt Silly, Silley, or Sulley; but we are told the old British appellation was Sulloc, or Syllac, which signifies rocks consecrated to the sun. We have not the least notice of any thing that regards them from the fifth to the tenth century. It is, however, with much appearance of truth, conjectured, that some time within this space they were in a great measure destroyed by an earthquake, attended with a sinking of the earth, by which most of their lowlands, and of course the greatest part of their improvements, were covered by the sea, and those rich mines of tin, which had rendered them so famous, swallowed up in the deep. They have a tradition in Cornwall, that a very extensive tract of country called the Llomefn, in the old Cornish Lethboulo, supposed to lie between that country and Scilly, was lost in that manner; and there are many concurrent circumstances which render this probable. In reference to these islands the case is still stronger; for at low ebb their stone-inclosures are still visible from almost all the isles, and thereby afford an ocular demonstration that they were formerly of far greater extent, and that in remoter ages their inhabitants must have been very numerous, and at the same time very industrious. This sufficiently proves the fact, that by such an earthquake they were destroyed; and that it happened at some period of time within those limits that have been assigned, appears from our hearing nothing more of their tin trade, and from our having no notice of it at all in any of our ancient chronicles, which, if it had fallen out later, from their known attention to extraordinary events, must certainly have happened. It is generally supposed, and with great appearance of truth, that king Athelstan, after having overcome a very powerful confederacy formed against him, and having reduced Exeter, and driven the Britons beyond the river Tamar, which he made the boundary of their Cornish dominions, passed over into these islands, (then surely in a better state than now, or they would not have been objects of his vengeance), and reduced them likewise. History does not inform us that the Danes ever fixed themselves in these islands; but as their method of fortifying is very well known, it has been conjectured that the Giant's Castle in the isle of St Mary was erected by them; and indeed, if we consider the convenient situation of these islands, and the trade of piracy which that nation carried on, there seems to be nothing improbable in that conjecture. It is more certain that there were churches erected in these isles, and that there were in them also many monks and hermits, before the conquest. The fertility of the islands is much insisted upon in all the accounts; and it is expressly said of St Mary's, that it bears exceeding good corn, insomuch that if men did but cast corn where swine had rooted, it would come up. There is mention made of a breed of wild swine, and the inhabitants had great plenty of fowl and fish. But notwithstanding the fertility of the country, and the many commodities that men had or might might have there, it was nevertheless but thinly peopled; and the reason assigned is, because they were liable to be frequently spoiled by French or Spanish pirates. In Leland's time one Mr Davers of Wilshire, and Mr Whittington of Gloucestershire, were proprietors of Scilly, and drew from thence, in rents and commodities, about forty merks a-year. The inhabitants at that juncture, and long before, appear to have carried on a small trade in dried fish and other fish to Brittany, with which they purchased salt, canvases, and other necessaries. This seems to be the remains of a very old kind of commerce, since for many ages the people of that country, those of the Scilly isles, and the people of Cornwall, looked upon themselves as countrymen, being in truth no other than remnants of the ancient Britons, who, when driven out by the Saxons, took refuge in those islands, and in that part of France which had before been called Armorica, and from hence styled Bretagne, Brittany, or Little Britain, and the people Bretons. This in all probability was a great relief to these who dwelt in those isles; who, during the long civil war between the houses of York and Lancaster, had their intercourse with England so much interrupted, that if it had not been for this commerce with their neighbours on the French coast, they might have been driven to the last distress. The Scilly, or Silly islands, lie due west from the Lizard about seventeen leagues; west and by south from the old Land's End, nearest Mount's Bay, at the distance of ten leagues; and from the western Land's End, they lie west-south-west, at the distance of something more than nine leagues. There are five of them inhabited; and that called Samson has one family in it. The largest of these is St Mary's, which lies in the north latitude of 49 degrees 55 minutes, and in the longitude of 6 degrees 40 minutes west from Greenwich. It is two miles and a half in length, about one and a half in breadth, and between nine and ten miles in compass. On the west side there projects an isthmus. Beyond this there is a peninsula, which is very high; and upon which stands Star Castle, built in 1593, with some outworks and batteries. On these there are upwards of three score pieces of cannon mounted; and for the defence of which there is a garrison of an entire company, with a master-gunner and six other gunners. In the magazine there are arms for 300 islanders, who, when summoned, are bound to march into the fortress. Underneath the castle barracks and lines, stands Hugh Town, very improperly built, as lying so low as to be subject to inundations. A mile within land stands Church Town, so denominated from their place of worship; it consists of a few houses only, with a court-house. About two furlongs east of this lies the Old Town, where there are more houses, and some of them very convenient dwellings. The number of inhabitants in this island is about 6 or 700; and it produces to the lord proprietor 300l. per annum. Trescoaw lies directly north from St Mary's, at the distance of two miles. It was formerly styled St Nicholas's island; and was at least as large as St Mary's, though at present about half the size. The remains of the abbey are yet visible, the situation well chosen, with a fine basin of fresh water before it, half a mile long and a furlong wide, with an ever-green bank high enough to keep out the sea, and serving at once to preserve the pond and shelter the abbey. In this pond there are most excellent eels, and the lands lying round it are by far the best in those islands. There are about half a score stone houses, with a church, which are called Dolphin Town; an old castle built in the reign of Henry VIII. called Oliver's Castle; and a new block-house, raised out of the ruins of that castle, which is of far greater use. This island is particularly noted for producing plenty of the finest samphire, and the only tin works that are now visible are found here. There are upon it at present about 40 families, who are very industrious, and spin more wool than in St Mary's. Its annual value is computed at 80l. a year. A mile to the east of Trescoaw, and about two miles from the most northern part of St Mary's, lies the isle of St Martin's, not much inferior in size to that of Trescoaw. It very plainly appears to have been formerly extremely well cultivated; notwithstanding which it was entirely deserted, till within somewhat less than a century ago, that Mr Thomas Ekines, a considerable merchant, engaged some people to settle there. He likewise caused to be erected a hollow tower twenty feet in height, with a spire of as many feet more; which being neatly covered with lime, serves as a daymark for directing ships crossing the channel or coming into Scilly. St Martin's produces some corn, affords the best pasture in those islands, nourishes a great number of sheep, and has upon it 17 families, who pretend to have the secret of burning the best kelp, and are extremely attached to their own island. As a proof of this it is observable, that though some of the inhabitants rent lands in St Mary's, yet they continue to reside here, going thither only occasionally. St Agnes, which is also called the Light-house Island, lies near three miles south-west of St Mary's; and is, though a very little, a very well cultivated island, fruitful in corn and grass. The only inconvenience to which the people who live in it are subject, is the want of good water, as their capital advantage consists in having several good coves or small ports, where boats may lie with safety; which, however, are not much used. The light-house is the principal ornament and great support of the island, which stands on the most elevated ground, built with stone from the foundation to the lanthorn, which is fifty-one feet high, the gallery four, the lath-lights eleven feet and a half high, three feet two inches wide, and fifteen in number. The floor of the lanthorn is of brick, upon which stands a substantial iron grate, square, barred on every side, with one great chimney in the canopy-roof, and several lesser ones to let out the smoke, and a large pair of smith's bellows are so fixed as to be easily used whenever there is occasion. Upon the whole, it is a noble and commodious structure; and being plastered white, is a useful day-mark to all ships coming from the southward. The keeper of this light-house has a salary from the Trinity-house at Deptford of 40l. a-year, with a dwelling-house and ground for a garden. His assistant has 20l. a-year. It is supplied with coals by an annual ship; and the carriage of these coals from the sea-side to the light-house is looked on as a considerable benefit to the poor inhabitants. They have a neat neat little church, built by the Godolphin family. There are at present 50 households in the island, which yield the proprietor 40l. a year. Breher, or, as pronounced, Bryer island, lies north-west of St Mary's, and to the west of Trefcau, to which, when the sea is very low, they sometimes pass over the sand. It is very mountainous, abounds with sea and land fowls, excellent samphire, and a great variety of medical herbs. There are at present thirteen families, who have a pretty church, and pay 30l. a-year to the proprietor. South from hence, and west from Trefcau, stands the island of Samson, in which there is not above one family, who subsist chiefly by the making of kelp. To the westward of these there lie four islands, which contain in the whole 360 acres of meadow and arable land. The eastern islets, so denominated from their position in respect to St Mary's, contain 123 acres; and there are also seven other rocky and scattered islands, that have each a little land of some use; and besides these, innumerable rocks on every side, among which we must reckon Scilly, now nothing more than a large, ill-shaped, craggy, inaccessible island, lying the farthest north-west of any of them, and consequently the nearest to the continent. The air of these islands is equally mild and pure; their winters are seldom subject to frost or snow. When the former happens, it lasts not long; and the latter never lies upon the ground. The heat of their summers is much abated by sea-breezes. They are indeed frequently incommoded by sea-fogs, but then these are not unwholesome. Agues are rare, and fevers more so. The most fatal distemper is the small-pox; yet those who live temperately survive commonly to a great age, and are remarkably free from diseases. The soil is very good, and produces grain of all sorts, (except wheat, of which they had anciently plenty), in large quantities. They still grow a little wheat, but the bread made of it is unpleasant. They eat, for this reason, chiefly what is made of barley; and of this they have such abundance, that though they use it both for bread and beer, they have more than suffices for their own consumption. Potatoes is a new improvement; and they prosper to such a degree, that in some places they have two crops in a year. Roots of all sorts, pulse, and salads, grow well; dwarf fruit-trees, gooseberries, currants, raspberries, and everything of that kind, under proper shelter, thrive exceedingly; but they have no trees, though formerly they had elder; and porthleik, i.e. the harbour of willows, proves they had these likewise; and with a little care, no doubt, great improvements might be made. The ranunculus, anemone, and most kinds of flowers, are successfully cultivated in their gardens. They have wild fowl of all sorts, from the swan to the snipe; and a particular kind called the hedge-chicken, which is not inferior to the ortolan: tame fowl, pufins, and rabbits, in great numbers. Their black cattle are generally small, but very well tasted, though they feed upon ore-weed. Their horses are little, but strong and lively. They have also large flocks of fine sheep, whose fleeces are tolerably good and their flesh excellent. There are no venomous creatures in these islands. We must now pass to the sea, which is of more consequence to these isles than that small portion of land which is distributed amongst them. St Mary's Scilly harbour is very safe and capacious, having that island on the south; the eastern islands, with that of St Martin, on the east; Trefcau, Breher, and Samson, to the north; St Agnes and several small islets to the west. Ships ride here in three to five fathom water, with good anchorage. Into and out of this harbour there are four inlets, viz. Broad Sound, Smith's Sound, St Mary's Sound, and Crow Sound: so that hardly any wind can blow with which a ship of 150 tons cannot safely sail through one or other of them, Crow Sound only excepted, where they cannot pass at low water, but at high there is from 16 to 24 feet in this passage. Besides these there are two other harbours; one called New Gryney, which lies between Breher and Trefcau, where ships of 300 tons may ride securely. The other is called Old Gryney, and lies between Trefcau, St Helen's, and Theou, for smaller ships. The former is guarded by the batteries at Oliver's Castle; the latter by the Blockhouse, on the eastern side of Trefcau, called Dover. Small coasters bound to the northward have more convenient outlets from these little harbours than from St Mary's, where, at the west end of Hugh Town, there is a fine pier built by the present earl of Godolphin, 430 feet long, 20 feet wide in the narrowest part, and 23 feet in height, with 16 feet of water at a spring, and 10 at a neap tide; so that under the shelter of this pier vessels of 150 tons may lie securely, not only close to the quay, but all along the strand of the town. In this harbour, and in all the little coves of the several isles, prodigious quantities of mackerel may be caught in their season; also soal, turbot, and plaice, remarkably good in their kind. Ling, which from its being a thicker fish, mellower, and better fed, is very justly preferred to any caught nearer our own coasts. Salmon, cod, pollock, are in great plenty, and pilchards in vast abundance. To these we may add the alga marina, fucus, or ore-weed, which serves to feed both their small and great cattle, manures their lands, is burned into kelp, is of use in physic, is sometimes preserved, sometimes pickled, and is in many other respects very beneficial to the inhabitants of whom we are next to speak. The people of Scilly in general are robust, handsome, active, hardy, industrious, generous, and good-natured; speak the English language with great propriety; have strong natural parts, (though for want of a good school they have little education), as appears by their dexterity in the several employments to which they are bred. They cultivate most of their lands as well as can be expected under their present circumstances. They are bred from their infancy to the management of their boats, in which they excel; are good fishermen, and excellent pilots. Their women are admirable housewives, spin their own wool, weave it into coarse cloth, and knit stockings. They have no timber of their own growth, and not much from England; yet they have many joiners and cabinet-makers, who, out of the fine woods which they obtain from captains of ships who put in here, make all kinds of domestic furniture in a very neat manner. They are free from the land-tax, malt-tax, and excise; and being furnished with plenty of liquors from the vessels which are driven into their roads for refreshment, for necessary repairs, or to wait for a fair wind, in return for provisions and other conveniences; this, with what little fish they can cure, makes the best part of their trade, if we except their help, which has been a growing manufacture for these fourscore years, and produces at present about 500l. per annum. The right honourable the earl of Godolphin is styled proprietor of Scilly, in virtue of letters-patent granted to the late earl, then lord Godolphin, dated the 25th of July 1698, for the term of 89 years, to be computed from the end and expiration of a term of 50 years, granted to Francis Godolphin, Esq.; by king Charles I.; that is, from the year 1709 to 1758, when his lease determines. In virtue of this royal grant, his lordship is the sole owner of all lands, houles, and tenements; claims all the tithes, not only of the fruits of the earth, but of fish taken at sea and landed upon those premises; harbour-duties paid by ships; and one moiety of the wrecks, the other belonging to the admiralty. There is only one ecclesiastical person upon the islands, who resides at St Mary's, and visits the other inhabited islands once a-year. But divine service is performed, and sermons preached, or rather read, every Sunday in the churches of those islands, by an honest layman appointed for that purpose; and there are likewise church-wardens and overseers, regularly chosen in every parish. As to the civil government, it is administered by what is called the Court of Twelve; in which the commander-in-chief, the proprietor's agent, and the chaplain, have their seats in virtue of their offices; the other nine are chosen by the people. These decide, or rather compromise, all differences; and punish small offences by fines, whippings, and the ducking-stool: as to greater enormities, we may conclude they have not been hitherto known; since except, for the soldiers, there is no prison in the islands. But in case of capital offences, the criminals may be transported to and brought to justice in the county of Cornwall. The great importance of these islands arises from their advantageous situation, as looking equally into St George's Channel, which divides Great Britain from Ireland, and the English Channel, which separates Britain from France. For this reason, most ships bound from the southward arrive to make the Scilly islands, in order to steer their course with greater certainty. It is very convenient also for vessels to take shelter amongst them; which prevents their being driven to Milford Haven, nay sometimes into some port in Ireland, if the wind is strong at east; or, if it blows hard at north-west, from being forced back into some of the Cornish harbours, or even on the French coasts. If the wind should not be very high, yet if unfavourable or unsteady, as between the channels often happens, it is better to put into Scilly, than to beat about at sea in bad weather. The intercourse between these two channels is another motive why ships come in here, as choosing rather to wait in safety for a wind, than to run the hazard of being blown out of their course; and therefore a strong gale at east seldom fails of bringing thirty or forty vessels, and frequently a larger number into Scilly; not more to their own satisfaction than to that of the inhabitants. Ships homeward-bound from America often touch there, from the desire of making the first land in their power, and for the sake of refreshment. Some or other of these reasons have an influence on foreign ships, as well as our own; and afford the natives an opportunity of showing their wonderful dexterity, in conducting them safely into St Mary's harbour, and, when the wind serves, thro' their sounds. Upon firing a gun and making a waft, a boat immediately puts off from the nearest islands, with several pilots on board; and having with amazing activity dropped one of them into every ship, till only two men are left in the boat, these return again to land, as the wind and other circumstances direct, in one of their little coves. In time of war, the importance of these islands is still more conspicuous; and it is highly probable, that they afforded the allies a place for assembling their fleet, when the Britons, Danes, Scots, and Irish, sailed under the command of Anlaff, to attack king Athelstan; which convinced him of the necessity of adding them to his dominions. Upon the like principle, Henry VIII., when upon bad terms with his neighbours, caused an old fortres to be repaired; and queen Elizabeth, who had more to fear, directed the construction of a castle, which, in part at least, still remains. But the most singular instance of the detriment that might arise from these islands falling into other hands than our own happened in 1651, when Sir John Greenville took shelter in them with the remains of the Cornish cavaliers. For the depredations committed by his frigates soon made it evident that Scilly was the key of the English commerce; and the clamours of the merchants upon rose so high, that the parliament were forced to send a fleet of fifty sail, with a great body of land-forces on board, under Sir George Aylfe and admiral Blake, who with great difficulty, and no inconsiderable loss, made themselves masters of Trefcau and Brehar; where they erected those lines and fortifications near the remains of the old fortres that are called Oliver's Castle. But at length, finding that little was to be done in that way, they chose to grant Sir John Grenville a most honourable capitulation, as the surest means to recover places of such consequence: with which the parliament were very little satisfied, till Mr Blake gave them his reasons; which appeared to be so well founded, that they directed the articles he had concluded to be punctually carried into execution.

SCIO

Pages 668-669

one of the most beautiful, pleasant, and celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the Archipelago, near to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>, to the south of Meteina, and to the northeast of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>. It is 32 miles in length, and 15 in breadth; a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and yet pleasant enough, there being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of various kinds growing in the fields, such as oranges, citrons, olives, mulberries, and pomegranates. There is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of pleasant wine, which they export to the neighbouring islands; but their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> trade is in silks. They have also a small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, cheese, figs, and mastic. The women are better bred than in other parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>; though the dress is odd, yet it is very neat. The partridges are tame, being sent every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> into the fields to get their living, and in the evening are called back with a whistle. The town called Scio is large, pleasant, and the best built of any in the Levant, the houles being beautiful and commodious, some of which are terraced, and others covered with tiles. The streets are paved with flint-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; and Scipio and the Venetians, while they had it in their possession, made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many alterations for the better. The castle is an old citadel built by the Genoese, in which the Turks have a garrison of 1400 men. The harbour of Scio is the rendezvous of all shipping that goes to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> comes from Constantinople, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> hold a fleet of fourscore vessels. They reckon there are 10,000 Turks, 100,000 Greeks, and 10,000 Latins, on this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. The Turks took it from the Venetians in 1695. Scio is a bishop's see, and is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-side, 47 miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, and 210 south-west of Constantinople.

SCIOPIUS

Pages 669-669

one of the most formidable critics of the 17th century, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a> in 1576, and studied at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBERG">Amberg</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a>, and afterwards at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTDORF">Altdorf</a>; where he made such a rapid progress, that at 16 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> he published some critical works which rendered him admired. In 1599, he abjured the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and embraced that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>; notwithstanding which he was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enemy of the Jesuits, and was extremely satirical upon them in several books; while on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> he wrote with the utmost fury also against the Protestant party, and even persuaded the Catholic princes to extirpate them by the most languishing methods. He particularly vented his rage against <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Scaliger, Caiusbou, and Du Plessis Mornai. He even attacked James I. of England; nor did he spare the person of Henry IV. of France, in his book intitled Ecclesiastica, which was burnt in France by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the hangman. In short, Sciopius, having drawn upon himself universal hatred, and being justly apprehensive of some attempt upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, sought for shelter at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, where he died in 1649. He was undoubtedly a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of great abilities; and his application to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, the multitude of his writings, his fire and eloquence, would have justly ranked him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in the republic of letters, had his moderation been equal to his learning.

SCIPIO

Pages 669-669

a renowned Roman general, surnamed Africanus, for his conquests in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His other signal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> exploits were, his taking the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of New <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> in a single <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; his complete victory over <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>, the famous Carthaginian general; the defeat of Syphax <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>, and of Antiochus in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. He was as eminent for his chastity, and his generous behaviour to his prisoners, as for his valour. He died 180 B.C. aged about 51. Scipio (Lucius Cornelius), his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, surnamed Asiaticus, for his complete victory over Antiochus at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNESIA">Magnesia</a>, in which Antiochus lost 50,000 infantry, and 4000 cavalry. A triumph, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Asiaticus, were the rewards of his valour. Yet his ungrateful countrymen accused him, as well as his brother, of peculation; for which he was fined; but the public <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of his effects proved the falsehood of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>; for they did not produce the amount of the fine. He flourished about 190 B.C. Scipio (Publius Emilianus), was the son of Paulus Emilius; but being adopted by Scipio Africanus, he was called Scipio Africanus junior. He showed himself worthy his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a>, following the footsteps of Scipio Africanus, whom he equaled in military fame and public virtues. His <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> victories were the conquest of Carthage and Numantia; yet these signal services to his country could not protect him from an untimely fate. He was strangled in his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMVIRI">Decemviri</a>, who dreaded his popularity, 129 B.C. aged 56.

SCIRO

Pages 669-669

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, to the west of Mytilene, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Nigropont, and to the south-east of Sciati. It is 15 miles in length, and 8 in breadth. It is a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. The vines make the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the island, and the wine is excellent; nor do the natives want wood. There is but one village; and that is built on a rock, which runs up like a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-loaf, and is 10 miles from the harbour of St George. The inhabitants are all Greeks, the eadi being the only Turk among them.

SCIRRHUS

Pages 669-669

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a> and medicine, a hard tumour of any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body, void of pain, arising, as is supposed, from the inspissation and induration of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> contained in a gland, though it may also appear in any other part of the body, especially in the fat; being one of the ways in which an inflammation terminates. These tumours are exceedingly apt to degenerate into cancers.

SCIURUS

Pages 669-671

the squirrel; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> belonging to the order of glires. It has two fore-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> in each jaw, the superior ones shaped like wedges, and the inferior ones compressed. There are 11 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable are, 1.
