The vulgaris, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> squirrel, with ears terminated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> tufts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, lively, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> eyes; head, body, legs, and tail, of a bright reddish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and belly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; hair on each side the tail lies flat. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, it changes in winter into grey. In Russia, it is sometimes found black. In many parts of England there is a beautiful variety, with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>-white tails.—This species inhabits <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, the northern and the temperate parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; and a variety is even found as far south as the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Ceylon. It is a neat, lively, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> animal; lives always in woods; in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> is seen purposed from tree to tree by the males, feigning an escape from their embraces; makes its nest of moss and dried leaves, between the fork of two branches; brings three or four young at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; has two holes to its nest; stops up that on the side the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows, as Pliny justly remarks; lays in a hoard of winter provision, such as nuts, acorns, &c.; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, feeds on buds and young shoots; is particularly fond of those of fir, and the young cones; sits up to eat, and uses its fore-feet as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; covers itself with its tail; leaps to a surprising distance; when disposed to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> a river, a piece of bark is its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, its tail the sail. 2. The cinereus, or grey squirrel, with plain ears; plate hair of a dull grey <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, mixed with black, and of CCLXTI ten tinged with dirty <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; belly and insides of the figs; legs white; tail long, bushy, grey, and striped with black; size of a half-grown rabbit.—Inhabits the woods of Northern Asia, North America, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>. They are very numerous in North America, do incredible damage to the plantations of maize, run up the stalks and eat the young ears. Descend in vast flocks from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and join those that inhabit the lower parts; are prohibited by the provinces, and a reward of three-pence per head given for every one that is killed. killed; such a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> was destroyed one year, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a> alone paid in rewards 8000l. of its currency. Make their nests in hollow trees, with moss, fir, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, &c. Feed on maize in the season, and on pine-cones, acorns, and malt of all kinds: form holes under ground, and there deposit a large stock of winter provision. Descend from the trees, and visit their magazines when in want of meat; are particularly busy at the approach of bad <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; during the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> season keep in their nests for several days together; seldom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> from tree to tree, only run up and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the bodies; their hoards often destroyed by swine; when their magazines are covered with deep snow, the squirrels often perish for want of food; are not easily <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, nimbly changing their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> when they see the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a> levelled; have the actions of the common squirrel; are easily tamed; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is esteemed very delicate. Their furs, which are imported under the name of petit-gris, are valuable, and used as linings to cloaks. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NIGER">niger</a>, or black squirrel, with plain ears; sometimes wholly black, but often marked with white on the nose, the neck, or end of the tail; the tail shorter than that of the former; the body equal. It inhabits the north of Asia, North America, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>; breeds and associates in separate troops; is equally numerous with the former; commits as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ravages among the maize; makes its nest in the same manner; and forms, like them, magazines for winter food. The finest are taken near the lake <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAIKAL">Baikal</a>, and about Barguzinfskofortrog, upon the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGARA">Angara</a>, in the district of Nertchinsk, which are the best in all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>; these continue black the whole year, the others grow rusty in summer.—There is a variety with plain ears; coarse fur mixed with dirty white and black; throat and inside of the legs and thighs black; tail much shorter than those of squirrels usually are; of a dull yellow colour, mixed with black; body of the size of the grey squirrel. It inhabits <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>; the planters call it the cat squirrel. 4. The flavus, or fair squirrel, with the body and tail of a flaxen colour; of a very small size, with plain round ears, and rounded tail. Inhabits the woods near Amadabad, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Guzurat, in great abundance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a> from tree to tree. Linnæus says it is an inhabitant of South America. 5. The striatus, or ground squirrel, with plain ears; ridge of the back marked with a black streak; each side with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> yellow stripe, bounded above and below with a line of black; head, body, and tail, of a reddish brown; the tail the darkest; breast and belly white; nose and feet pale-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>; eyes full.—Inhabits the north of Asia, but found in the greatest abundance in the forests of North America. They never run up trees except they are pursued and find no other means of escaping; they burrow, and form their habitations underground, with two entrances, that they may get access to the one in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> the other is stopped up. Their retreats are formed with great skill, in form of a long gallery, with branches on each side, each of which terminates in an enlarged chamber, as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> to store their winter provision in; in one they lodge the acorns, in another the maize, in a third the hickory nuts, and in the last their favourite food the chinquapin chestnut. They very seldom stir out during winter, at least as long as their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> last; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that fails, they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> dig into cellars where apples are kept, or barns where maize is stored, and do a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of mischief; but at that time the cat destroys great numbers, and is as great an enemy to them as to mice. During the maize <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>, these squirrels are very busy in biting off the ears, and filling their mouths so full with the corn, that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> are quite distended. It is observable, that they give great preference to certain food; for if, after filling their mouths with rye, they happen to meet with wheat, they fling away the first, that they may indulge in the last. They are very wild, bite severely, and are scarcely ever tamed; the skins are of little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, but are sometimes brought over to line cloaks. 6. The glis, or fat squirrel, with thin naked ears; body covered with soft ash-coloured hair; belly whitish; tail full of long hair; from nose to tail, near six inches; tail, four and a half; thicker in the body than the common squirrel.—Inhabits France and the south of Europe; lives in trees, and leaps from bough to bough; feeds on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and acorns; lodges in the hollows of trees; remains in a torpid state during winter, and grows very fat. It was esteemed a great delicacy by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who had their ghiraria, places constructed to keep and feed them in. 7. The fagitta, or failing squirrel, with a small round head, cleft upper lip; small blunt ears, two small warts at the utmost corner of each eye, with hairs growing out of them; neck short; four toes on the fore feet; and instead of a thumb, a slender bone two inches and a half long, lodged under the lateral membrane, serving to stretch it out; from thence to the hind legs extends the membrane, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and a continuation of the skin of the sides and belly; there are five toes on the hind feet; and on all the toes, sharp compressed bent claws; the tail is covered with long hairs disposed horizontally: colour of the head, body, and tail, a bright <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>; in some parts inclining to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>; breast and belly of a yellowish white; length from nose to tail, eighteen inches; tail, fifteen.—Inhabits <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, and others of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; leaps from tree to tree as if it flew; will catch hold of the boughs with its tail. Nieuhoff, p. 354, describes this under the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> cat, and says the back is black. 8. The volans, or flying squirrel, with round naked ears, black eyes, and a lateral membrane from the fore to the hind legs; tail with long hairs disposed horizontally, longest in the middle; colour above, a brownish ash; beneath, white tinged with yellow; much less than the common squirrel. Inhabits <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, Lapland, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, Russia, North America, and New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; lives in hollow trees; sleeps in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; during the night is very lively; is gregarious, numbers being found in one tree; leaps from bough to bough some times at the distance of ten yards; this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> has improperly been called flying, for the animal cannot go in any other <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> than forward; and even then cannot keep an even line, but flinks considerably before it can reach the place it aims at; sensible of this, the squirrel mounts the higher in proportion to the distance it wishes to reach; when it would leap, it stretches out the fore legs, and extending the membranes becomes specifically <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than it would otherwise be; and thus is enabled to spring further than other squirrels that have not this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>. When numbers leap at a time, they seem like leaves blown Sclavonia blown off by the wind. Their food the same as the other squirrels. They are easily tamed: bring three or four young at a time. See fig. 3, 4, the one representing the animal in what is called a flying, the other in a sitting posture.

SCLAVONIA

Pages 671-671

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAVA">Sava</a>, the Drave, and the Danube. It is divided into five counties, viz. Poegra, Zabrab, Creis, Waradten, Zreim, and Walpon; and belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. It was formerly called a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and is very narrow, not being above 75 miles in breadth; but it is 300 in length, from the frontiers of Austria to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a>. The eastern <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> is called Ratzia, and the inhabitants Ratzian. These, from a particular notion, are of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Sclavonia is the mother of four others, namely, those of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, and Russia.

SCLEROTICS

Pages 671-671

medicines proper to harden and consolidate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of the parts to which they are applied; as purflain, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEEK">leek</a>, fleawort, garden nightshade, &c.

SCOLOPAX

Pages 671-672

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of grallae. The back is cylindrical, obtuse, and longer than the head; the nostrils are linear; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> is covered; and the feet have four toes. There are 18 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the following are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>. 1. The arquata, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> curlew, frequents our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coasts and marshes in the winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flocks, walking on the open lands; feeding on shells, frogs, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>, and other marine insects. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> they retire to the mountainous and unfrequented parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> and breed. Their eggs are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> olive <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, marked with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> but distinct spots of pale <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is very <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and fishy, notwithstanding an old English proverb in its favour. Curlews differ much in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and size; some weighing 37 ounces, others not 22; the length of the largest to the tip of the tail, 25 inches; the breadth, three feet five inches; the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; the head, neck, and coverts of the wings, are of a pale brown; the middle of each feather <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and belly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, marked with narrow <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; the back is white, spotted with a few black stripes; the quill-feathers are black, but the inner webs spotted with white; the tail is white, tinged with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, and beautifully barred with black; the legs are long, strong, and of a blueish grey colour; the bottoms of the toes flat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, to enable it to walk on the soft mud, in search of food. 2. The phasopus, or whimbrel, is much less frequent on our shores than the curlew; but its haunts, food, and general appearance, are much the same. It is observed to visit the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPALDING">Spalding</a> (where it is called the curlew knot) in vast flocks in April, but continues there no longer than May; nor is it seen there any other time of year: it seems at that season to be on its passage to its breeding <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which Mr Pennant suspects to be among the Highlands of Scotland. The specific <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is the size; this never exceeding the weight of 12 ounces. 3. The rusticola, or woodcock, during summer inhabits the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, Polish <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, and the northern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>: they all retire from those countries the beginning of winter, as soon as the frosts commence; which force them into milder climates, where the ground is open, and adapted to their manner of feeding. They live on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> and insects, which they search for with their long bills in soft ground and moist woods. Woodcocks generally arrive here in flocks, taking advantage of the night or a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MIST">mist</a>: they soon separate; but before they return to their native haunts, pair. They feed and fly by night; beginning their flight in the evening, and return the same way or through the same glades to their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> retreat. They leave England the latter end of February, or beginning of March; not but they have been known to continue here accidentally.—These birds appear in Scotland first on the eastern coasts, and make their progress from east to west. They do not arrive in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BREADALBANE">Breadalbane</a>, a central <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, till the beginning or middle of November; nor the coasts of Nether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORN">Lorn</a>, or of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROSS_SHIRE">Ross-shire</a>, till <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>: they are very rare in the remote <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>, or in the Orkneys. A few stragglers now and then arrive there. They are equally scarce in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAITHNESS">Caithness</a>.—Our species of woodcock is unknown in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>: but a kind is found that has the general appearance of it; but is scarce half the size, and wants the bars on the breast and belly. The weight of the woodcock is usually about 12 ounces; the length near 14 inches; and the breadth, 26; the bill is three inches long, dusky towards the end, reddish at the base; tongue slender, long, sharp, and hard at the point; the eyes large, and placed near the top of the head, that they may not be injured when the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> thrusts its bill into the ground; from the bill to the eyes is a black line; the fore-head is a reddish ash colour; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of the head, the hind part of the neck, the back, the coverts of the wings, and the scapulars, are prettily barred with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> red, black and grey; but on the head the black predominates: the quill-feathers are dusky, indented with red marks. The chin is of a pale <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; the whole under side of the body is of a dirty white, marked with numerous transverse lines of a dusky colour. The tail consists of 12 feathers, dusky or black on the one web, and marked with red on the other; the tips above are ash-coloured, below white; which, when <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> on the ground was in vogue, was the sign the fowler discovered the birds by. The legs and toes are livid; the latter divided almost to their very origin, having only a very small web between the middle and interior toes; as those of the two species of snipes found in England. 4. The argocephala, or godwit, weighs 12 ounces and a half; the length is 16 inches; the breadth 27; the bill is four inches long, turns up a little, black at the end, the rest a pale purple; from the bill to the eye is a broad white stroke; the feathers of the head, neck, and back, are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> reddish brown, marked in the middle with a dusky spot; the belly and vent feathers white, the tail regularly barred with black and white. The six first quill-feathers are black their interior edges of a reddish brown; the legs in some are dusky, in others of a greyish blue; which perhaps may be owing to different ages; the exterior toe is connected as far as the first <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> of the middle toe with a strong <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a> membrane. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> is distinguished from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> by some black lines on the breast and throat; which in the female are wanting. These birds are taken in the fens, in the same season and in the same manner with the ruffs and reeves; and when fattened <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRINGA">Tringa</a> are are esteemed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> delicacy, and sell for half a crown or five shillings a piece. A flake of the same species is placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NET">net</a>. They appear in small flocks on our coasts in September, and continue with us the whole winter; they walk on the open sands like the curlew, and feed on insects. 5. The gullot, or greenshank, is in length to the end of the tail, 14 inches; to that of the toes, 20; its breadth, 25. The bill is two inches and a half long; the upper mandible black, strait, and very slender; the lower reflects a little upwards; the head and upper part of the neck are ash-coloured, marked with small dusky lines pointing <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; over each passes a white line; the coverts, the scapulars, and upper part of the back, are of a brownish ash colour; the quill-feathers dusky, but the inner webs speckled with white; the breast, belly, thighs, and lower part of the back, are white; the tail is white, marked with undulated dusky bars; the inner coverts of the wings finely crossed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> and treble rows of a dusky colour. It is a bird of an elegant shape, and small weight in proportion to its dimensions, weighing only six ounces. The legs are very long and slender, and bare above two inches higher than the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. The exterior toe is united to the middle toe, as far as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> joint, by a strong membrane which borders their sides to the very end. These birds appear on the English coasts and wet grounds in the winter-time in but small numbers. 6. The calidris, or red-shank, is found on most of our shores; in the winter-time it conceals itself in the gutters, and is generally found single or at most in pairs. It breeds in the fens and marshes; and flies round its nest when disturbed, making a noise like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPWING">lapwing</a>. It lays four eggs, whitish tinged with olive, marked with irregular spots of black chiefly on the thicker end. It weighs five ounces and a half; the length is 12 inches, the breadth 21; the bill near two inches long, red at the base, black towards the point. The head, hind part of the neck, and scapulars, are of a dusky ash colour, obscurely spotted with black; the back is white, sprinkled with black spots; the tail elegantly barred with black and white; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, under side of the neck, and upper part of the breast, are white, streaked downward with dusky lines; the belly white; the exterior webs of the quill-feathers are dusky; the legs long and of fine bright <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> colour; the utmost toe connected to the middle toe by a small membrane; the inmost by another still smaller. 7. The gallinago, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> snipe, weighs four ounces; the length, to the end of the tail, is near 12 inches; the breadth about 14; the bill is three inches long, of a dusky colour, flat at the end, and often rough like shagrin above and below. The head is divided lengthwise with two black lines; and three of red, one of the last passing over the middle of the head, and one above each eye; between the bill and the eyes is a dusky line; the chin is white; the neck is varied with brown and red. The scapulars are beautifully striped lengthwise with black and yellow: the quill-feathers are dusky; but the edge of the first is white, as are the tips of the secondary feathers: the quill-feathers next the back are barred with black and pale red; the breast and belly are white; the coverts of the tail are long, and almost cover it; they are of a reddish brown colour. The tail consists of 14 feathers, black on their lower part, then crossed with a broad <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of deep Scopula-orange, another narrow one of black; and the ends white, or pale orange. The vent feathers are of a dull yellow; the legs pale green; the toes divided to their origin. In the winter-time snipes are very frequent in all our marshy and wet grounds, where they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> concealed in the rushes, &c. In summer they disperse to different parts, and are found in the midst of our highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> as well as of our low moors; their nest is made of dried grass; they lay four eggs of a dirty olive colour, marked with dusky spots; their young are so often found in England, that we doubt whether they ever entirely leave this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. When they are disturbed much, particularly in the breeding season, they soar to a vast height, making a singular bleating noise; and when they descend, dart down with vast rapidity; it is also amusing to observe the cock (while his mate sits on her eggs) poise himself on her wings, making sometimes a whistling and sometimes a drumming noise. Their food is the same with that of the woodcock; their flight very irregular and swift, and attended with a shrill scream. They are most universal birds, found in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the globe, and in all climates.

SCOLOPENDRA

Pages 672-672

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of aptera. The feet are very numerous, being as many on each side as there are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> in the body; the antennae are fetaceous; there are two jointed pappi, and the body is depressed.—These insects are very formidable and noxious in the warm countries, where they grow to the length of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a yard <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> more, though in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> they seldom grow above an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. The scolopendra is also called the centipede from its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of feet. In the east Indies it grows to six inches in length, and as thick as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s finger: it consists of many joints; and from each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> proceeds a leg on each side: they are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and seem to have no eyes; but there are two feelers on the head, with which they find out the way they are to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>: the head is very round, with two small sharp <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, with which they inflict wounds that are very painful and dangerous. A sailor that was bit by one on board a ship felt excruciating pain, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was supposed to be in danger; but by the application of roasted onions to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, he recovered. The bite of the scolopendra mortifans in Jamaica is said to be as poisonous as the sting of a scorpion. Some of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> live in holes in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; others under <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and among rotten wood; so that the removing of these is exceedingly dangerous in the countries where the scolopendra breed.—These insects, like the scorpion, are supposed to be produced perfect from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, and to undergo no changes after their first <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a>. They are found of all sizes; which is a sufficient reason for believing that they preserve their first appearance through the whole of their existence. It is probable, however, that, like most of this class, they often change their skins; but of this we have no certain information.

SCOMBER

Pages 672-675

the Mackerel, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of thoracici. The head is smooth and compressed, and there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> rays in the gill-membrane. There are ten <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>;—of which the most remarkable are the following. 1. The scomber, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> mackerel, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> fish of passage that visits our shores in vast shoals. It is less useful than other species of gregarious fish, being very tender, and unfit for carriage; not but that it may be preserved by pickling and salting, a method, we believe, practised only in Cornwall, where it proves a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> relief to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> during winter. It was a fish greatly esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, because it furnished the precious garum, a sort of pickle that gave a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> relish to their sauces; and was besides used medicinally. It was drawn from different kinds of fish, but that made from the mackerel had the preference: the best was made at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>, vast quantities of mackerel being taken near an adjacent <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a>, called from that circumstance Scombraria; and the garum, prepared by a certain <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, bore a high price, and was distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of garum sociorum. This fish is easily taken by a bait; but the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> is during a fresh <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALE">gale</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, which is thence called a mackerel gale. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> the eyes of mackerel are almost covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILM">film</a>; during which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> they are half <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>. This film grows in winter, and is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> the beginning of summer. It is not often that it exceeds two pounds in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, yet there have been instances of some that weighed upwards of five. The nose is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> and sharp-pointed; the eyes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; the jaws of an equal length; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> small, but numerous. The form of this fish is very elegant. The body is a little compressed on the sides; towards the tail it grows very slender, and a little angular. It is a most beautiful fish when alive; for nothing can equal the brilliancy of its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> impairs, but does not wholly obliterate. 2. The thunnus, or tunny, was a fish well known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>: it made a considerable branch of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; the time of its arrival into the Mediterranean from the ocean was observed, and stations for taking them were established in places it most frequented. There are still very considerable tunny <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, as well as several other parts of the Mediterranean; where they are cured, and make a great article of provision in the adjacent kingdoms. They are caught in nets, and amazing quantities are taken; for they come in vast shoals, keeping along the shores. They frequent our coasts, but not in shoals like the tunnies of the Mediterranean. They are not uncommon in the lochs on the western coast of Scotland; where they come in pursuit of herrings; and often during night strike into the nets, and do considerable damage. When the fishermen draw them up in the morning, the tunny rises at the same time towards the surface, ready to catch the fish that drop out. On perceiving it, a strong hook baited with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> and fastened to a rope, is instantly flung out, which the tunny seldom fails to take. As soon as hooked, it loses all spirit; and after a very little resistance submits to its fate. It is dragged to the shore and cut up, either to be sold fresh to people who carry it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, or is preserved salted in large casks. The pieces, when fresh look exactly like raw beef; but when boiled turn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, and have something of the flavour of salmon. One that was taken when Mr Pennant was at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERARY">Inverary</a> in 1769, weighed 460 pounds. The fish was fe- Ven feet ten inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; the greatest circumference five feet seven; the least near the tail one foot six. The body was round and thick, and grew suddenly very slender towards the tail, and near that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> was angular. The irides were of a plain green: the teeth very minute. The tail was in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>; and two feet seven inches between tip and tip. The skin on the back was smooth, very thick, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. On the belly the scales were visible. The colour of the sides and belly was silvery, tinged with cerulean and pale purple: near the tail marbled with grey. They are known on the coast of Scotland by the name of mackerelfish: Mackerel, from being of that genus; and sture, from the Danish, stor "great."

SCONE

Pages 675-675

a town of Scotland, remarkable for being the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the kings were anciently crowned. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 10. N. Lat. 56. 28. Here was once an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, which was burnt by the reformers at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUNDEE">Dundee</a>. The present <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> was begun by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Gowrie; but was completed by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Murray of Gofpatrie, the favourite of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> James VI. to whom that monarch had granted it; and the new possessor in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to his benefactor put up the king's arms in several parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. It is built around two courts. The dining room is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and handsome; and has an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, but magnificent chimney-piece, and the king's arms with this motto: Nobis hæc invicta miserunt centum <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a> proavis. Beneath are the Murray arms. In the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> room is some good old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, with an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>. In a small <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>-chamber is a medley scripture-piece in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, with a border of animals, pretty well done, the work of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> during her confinement in Loch Leven Castle; but the house in general is in a manner unfurnished. The gallery is about 155 feet long, the top arched, divided into compartments filled with paintings in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-colours. The pieces represented are various kinds of huntings; that of Nimrod, and king James and his train, appear in every piece. Till the destruction of the abbey, the kings of Scotland were crowned here, sitting in the famous wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> which Edward I. transported to Westminster Abbey, to the great mortification of the Scots, who looked upon it as a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALLADIUM">palladium</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. before the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a> was crowned in the present chapel. The old pretender resided for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> at Scone in 1715; and his son paid it a visit in 1745. SCOPE <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> SCUPPER HOLES, in a ship, are holes made through the sides, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the deck, to carry off the water that comes from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>.

SCORIA

Pages 675-675
or DROSS, among metallurgists, is the recrystallization of metals in fusion; or, more determinately speaking, is that mass which is produced by melting metals and ores: when cold, it is brittle, and not dissoluble in water, being properly a kind of glass.

SCORIFICATION

Pages 675-675

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METALLURGY">metallurgy</a>, is the art of reducing a body, either entirely <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, into scoria. SCORPÆNA, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of thoracici. The head is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and sharp;

SCORPIO

Pages 675-678

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of aptera. It has eight feet, besides two frontal claws; the eyes are eight in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, three on each side of the thorax, and two on the back. It has two claw-shaped palpi, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> jointed tail, with a pointed weapon at the extremity; it has likewise two combs situated betwixt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>. There are six <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, all natives of southern climates. Of all the classes of noxious insects the scorpion is the most terrible, whose shape is hideous, whose size among the insects is enormous, and whose sting is generally fatal. Happy for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, the scorpion is entirely a stranger among us! In several parts of the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> it is but too well known, though it seldom grows above four inches long; but in the warm tropical climates, it is seen a foot in length, and in every respect as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as a lobster, which it somewhat resembles in shape. There have been enumerated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> different kinds of this dangerous insect, including species and varieties, chiefly distinguished by their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>: there being scorpions <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, and ash coloured; others that are the colour of rusty <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, green, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> yellow, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, claret colour, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and grey. There are four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> parts distinguishable in this animal; the head, the breast, the belly, and the tail. The scorpion's head seems, as it were, jointed to the breast; in the middle of which are seen two eyes; and a little more forward, two eyes more, placed in the fore <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the head: those eyes are so small, that they are scarcely perceptible; and it is probable the animal has but little occasion for seeing. The mouth is furnished with two jaws; the undermost is divided into two, and the parts notched into each other, which serve the animal as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and with which it breaks its food, and thrusts it into its mouth: these the scorpion can at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> pull back into its mouth, so that no part of them can be seen. On each side of the head are two arms, each composed of four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>; the last of which is large, with strong muscles, and made in the manner of a lobster's claw. Below the breast are eight articulated legs, each divided into five joints; the two hindmost of which are each provided with two crooked claws, and here and there covered with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. The belly is divided into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> little rings; from the lowest of which is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a tail, composed of six joints, which are brittle, and formed like little globes, the last being armed with a crooked sting. This is that fatal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> which renders this insect so formidable: it is long, pointed, hard, and hollow; it is pierced near the base by two small holes, through which, when the animal stings, it ejects a drop of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, which is white, caustic, and fatal. The reservoir in which this poison is kept, is in a small bladder near the tail, into which the venom is distilled by a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this bladder be greatly pressed, the venom <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be seen issuing out through the two holes above-mentioned; so that it appears, that when the animal stings, the bladder is pressed, and the venom issues through the two apertures into the wound. There are few animals more formidable, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> more truly mischievous, than the scorpion. As it takes refuge in a small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and is generally found sheltering in houses, so it cannot be otherwise than that it must frequently sting those among whom it resides. In some of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and in France, in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, it is one of the greatest pests that torments mankind: but its malignity in Europe is trifling, when compared to what the natives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and the east are known to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. In Batavia, where they grow twelve inches long, there is no removing any piece of furniture, without the utmost danger of being stung by them. Bosman assures us, that along the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">Coast</a> they are often found larger than a lobster; and that their sting is inevitable fatal. In Europe, however, they are by no means so large, so venomous, or so numerous. The general size of this animal does not exceed two or three inches; and its sting is very seldom found to be fatal. Maupertius, who made several experiments on the scorpion of Languedoc, found it by no means so invariably dangerous as had till then been represented. He provoked one of them to sting a dog, in three places of the belly, where the animal was without hair. In about an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> animal seemed greatly swollen, and became very sick: he then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> up whatever he had in his bowels; and for about three hours continued vomiting a whitish liquid. The belly was always greatly swollen when the animal began to vomit; but this operation afterwards seemed to abate the swelling; which alternately swelled, and was thus emptied, for three hours successively. The poor animal after this fell into convulsions, bit the ground, dragged himself along upon his fore-feet, and at last died, five hours after being bitten. He was not partially swollen round the place which was bitten, as is usual after the sting of a wasp or a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEE">bee</a>; but his whole body was inflated, and there only appeared a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> spot on the places where he had been stung. Some days after, however, the same experiment was tried upon another dog, and even with more aggravated cruelty: yet the dog seemed no way affected by the wounds; but, howling a little when he received them, continued alert and well after them; and soon after was set at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, without showing the smallest symptoms of pain. So far was this poor creature from being terrified at the experiment, that he left his own <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, to come to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, where he had received more plentiful entertainment. The same experiment was tried by fresh scorpions upon seven other dogs, and upon three hens; but not the smallest deadly symptom was seen to ensue. From hence it appears, that many circumstances, which are utterly unknown, must contribute to give efficacy to the scorpion's venom. Whether its food, long fasting, the season, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the vessels it wounds, or its state of maturity, contribute to or retard its malignity, is yet to be ascertained by succeeding experiment. In the trials made by our philosopher, he employed scorpions of both sexes, newly caught, and seemingly vigorous and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>. The success of this experiment may serve to shew, that many of those boasted antidotes which are given for the cure of the scorpion's sting, owe their success rather to accident than their own efficacy. They only happened to cure when their sting was no way dangerous; but in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of actual malignity, they might probably be utterly unserviceable. The scorpion of the tropical climates being much larger than the former, is probably much more venomous. Helbigius, however, who resided for many years in the east, affirms us, that he was often hung by the scorpion, and never received any material injury from the wound: a painful tumour generally ensued; but he always cured it by rubbing the part with a piece of iron or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, as he had seen the Indians practice before him, until the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> became insensible. Seba, Moore, and Bofman, however, give a very different account of the scorpion's malignity; and assert, that, unless speedily relieved, the wound becomes fatal. It is certain, that no animal in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> seems endowed with such an irascible nature. They have often been seen, when taken and put into a place of security, to exert all their rage against the sides of the glass-vessel that contained them. They will attempt to sting a stick, when put near them; and attack a mouse or a frog, while those animals are far from offering any injury. Maupertius put three scorpions and a mouse into the same vessel together, and they soon stung the little animal in different places. The mouse, thus assaulted, stood for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> upon the defensive, and at last killed them all, one after another. He tried this experiment, in order to see whether the mouse, after it had killed, would eat the scorpions; but the little quadruped seemed satisfied with the victory, and even survived the severity of the wounds it had received. Wolkamer tried the courage of the scorpion against the large spider and inclosed several of both kinds in glass vessels for that purpose. The success of this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> was very remarkable. The spider at first used all its efforts to immesh the scorpion in its web, which it immediately began <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>; but the scorpion refused itself from the danger, by stinging its adversary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>: it soon after cut off, with its claws, all the legs of the spider, and then sucked all the internal parts at its leisure.—If the scorpion's skin had not been so hard, Wolkamer is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the spider would have obtained the victory; for he had often seen one of these spiders destroy a toad. The fierce spirit of this animal is equally dangerous to its own species; for scorpions are the cruellest enemies to each other. Maupertius put about 100 of them together in the same glass; and they scarce come into contact when they began to exert all their rage in mutual destruction: there was nothing to be seen but one universal carnage, without any distinction of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; so that in a few days there remained only 14, which had killed and devoured all the rest. But their unnatural malignity is still more apparent in their cruelty to their offspring. He inclosed a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> scorpion, big with young, in a glass vessel, and she was seen to devour them as fast as they were excluded: there was but one only of the number that escaped the general destruction, by taking refuge on the back of its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>; and this soon after revenged the cause of its brethren, by killing the old one in its turn. Such is the terrible and unrelenting nature of this insect, which neither the bonds of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> nor of nature can reclaim: it is even asserted, that, when driven to an extremity, the scorpion will often destroy itself. The following experiment was ineffectually tried by Maupertius: "But," says Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDSMITH">Goldsmith</a>, "I am so well assured of it by many eye-witnesses, who have seen it both in Italy and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, that I have no doubt remaining of its veracity. A scorpion, newly caught, is placed in the midst of a circle of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, and thus an egrets prevented on every side: the scorpion, as I am assured, runs for about a minute round the circle, in hopes of escaping; but finding that impossible, it stings itself on the back of the head; and in this manner the undaunted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUICIDE">suicide</a> instantly expires." It is happy for mankind that these animals are thus destructive to each other; since otherwise they would multiply in so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> as to render some countries uninhabitable. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> and female of this insect are very easily distinguishable; the male being smaller and less hairy. The female brings forth her young alive, and perfect in their kind. Redi having bought a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of scorpions, selected the females, which, by their size and roughness, were easily distinguishable from the rest, and putting them in separate glass vessels, he kept them for some days without food. In about five days one of them brought forth 38 young ones, well-shaped, and of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>-white colour, which changed every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> more and more into a dark rusty hue. Another female, in a different vessel, brought forth 27 of the same colour; and the day following the young ones seemed all fixed to the back and belly of the female. For near a fortnight all these continued alive and well: but afterwards some of them died daily; until, in about a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, they all died except two. Were it worth the trouble, these animals might be kept living as long as curiosity should think proper. Their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> food is <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> and insects; and upon a proper supply of these, their lives might be lengthened to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. How long that may be, we are not told; but if we may argue from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, it cannot be less than seven or eight years; and perhaps, in the larger kind, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. As they have somewhat the form of the lobster, so they resemble that animal in casting their shell, or more properly their skin; since it is softer by far than the covering of the lobster, and set with hairs, which grow from it in great abundance, particularly at the joinings. The young <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the womb of the parent, each covered up in its own membrane, to the number of 40 or 50, and united to each other by an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> thread, so as to exhibit altogether the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPLET">chaplet</a>. Such is the manner in which the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> scorpion produces its young: but there is a scorpion of America, produced from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, in the manner of the spider. The eggs are no longer than pins <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; and they are deposited in a web, which they spin from their bodies, and carry about with them, till they are hatched. As soon as the young ones are excluded from the shell, they get upon the back of the parent, who turns her tail over them, and defends them with her sting. It seems probable, therefore, that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> produces that unnatural disposition in the scorpion which induces it to destroy its young; since, at liberty, it is found to protect them with such unceasing affluency. Scorpiurus, Caterpillars; a genus of decandria order, belonging to the diadelphia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are four species, the most remarkable of which is the vermiculata, a native of Italy and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It is an annual plant, with trailing herbaceous stalks, which at each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> have a spatula-shaped <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> with a long foot-stalk. From the wings of the leaves come out the foot-stalks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which sustain at the top one yellow butterfly flower, succeeded by a thick twisted pod having the size and appearance of a larger caterpillar, from whence it had this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. This has long been preferred in the gardens of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, more on account of its odd shape than for any great <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. It is propagated by sowing the seeds on a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and when the plants come up, they must be kept free from weeds and thinned, so that there may be a foot distance between them. Sorzonerà, Viper-grass; a genus of the polygamia squamosa order, belonging to the syngenesia class of plants.—The most remarkable species is the hispanica or common scorzonera, which is cultivated in the gardens of this country, both for culinary and medicinal purposes. The root is carrot-shaped, about the thickness of a finger, covered with a dark brown skin, is white within, and has a milky juice. The stalk rises three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, is smooth, branching at the top, and garnished with a few narrow leaves, whose base half embrace the stalk. The flowers are of a bright yellow colour, and terminate the stalks in scaly empalements composed of many narrow tongue-shaped hermaphrodite florets lying imbricated over each other like the scales of fish, and are of a bright yellow colour. After these are decayed, the germen, which sits in the common empalements, turns to oblong cornered seeds, having a roundish <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of feathery <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> at the top. This plant is propagated by seeds; and must be carefully thinned and kept free from weeds, otherwise the plants will be weak. The roots of scorzonera were formerly much celebrated for their alexipharmic virtues, and for throwing out the small-pox; but have now almost entirely lost their character; however, as they abound with an acrid juice they may sometimes be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for strengthening the viscera, and promoting the fluid secretions.

SCOT

Pages 678-678

a customary contribution laid upon all subjects, according to their abilities. Whoever were assessed to any contribution, though not by equal proportions, were said to pay feet and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>. Scot (Michael) of Balwirie, a learned Scottish author of the 13th century. This singular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> made the tour of France and Germany; and was received with some distinction at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Frederic II. Having travelled enough to gratify his curiosity <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> his vanity, he returned to Scotland, and gave himself up to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>. He was skilled in languages; and, considering the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived, was no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> proficient in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and medicine. He translated into Latin from the Arabic, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of animals by the celebrated physician <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AVICENNA">Avicenna</a>. He published the whole works of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, with notes, and affected much to reason on the principles of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. He wrote a book concerning The secrets of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, in which he treats of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, phyllognomy, and the signs by which we judge of the temperaments of men and women. We have also a tract of his On the nature of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. He here speaks of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> operation, as it is termed by alchemists, and is exceedingly folicious about the projected powder or the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER_S_STONE">philosopher's <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. He likewise published what he calls Menfa philosophica, a treatise replete with astrology and chiromancy. He was much admired in his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and was even suspected of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>; and had Roger <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> and Cornelius Agrippa for his panegyrists. Scot (Reginald), a judicious writer in the 16th century, was the younger son of Sir John Scot of Scot's-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, near Smeethe in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>. He studied at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HART">Hart</a>-hall in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; after which he retired to Smeethe, where he lived a studious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and died in 1599. He published, The perfect <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of a Hop-garden; and a book intitled, The discovery of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">witchcraft</a>; in which he showed that all the relations concerning magicians and witches are chimerical. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> was not only censured by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> James I. in his Demonology, but by several eminent divines; and all the copies of it that could be found were burnt.

SCOTAL

Pages 678-678
or SCOTALE, is where any officer of a forest keeps an ale-house within the forest, by colour of his office causing people come to his house, and there spend their money for fear of his displeasure. We find it mentioned in the charter of the forest, cap. 8. "Nullus foresterius faciat Scotallas, vel garbas colligat, vel aliquam collectam faciat," &c. Manwood, 216.—The word is compounded of feet and ale, and by transposition of the words is otherwise called alefoot.

SCOTIA

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a semicircular cavity <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> channel between the tores in the bases of columns.

SCOTISTS

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of school-divines and philosophers, thus called from their founder J. Duns Scotus, a Scottish cordelier, who maintained the immaculate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of the virgin, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> that she was born without original sin, in opposition to Thomas Aquinas and the Thomists.

Scotland then produced. The first essay of his arms by sea was in favour of his kinsman John king of Denmark. This prince was brother to Margaret queen of

Scotland, and had given orders for a formidable invasion of the Scotch borders. He complained that James had usurped his title of Defender of the Faith, to which he had added the word Christian, implying that Henry was an infidel: but the kings of

Pages 792-811

Scotland. Aration of the house of Guise had involved that nation in troubles and distress. Its credit was greatly diminished, and its treasury was nearly exhausted. Persecutions, and the spirit of Calvinism, produced commotions and conspiracies; and amidst domestic and dangerous intrigues and struggles,

SCOTLAND

Pages 810-829

Scotland, duke of Rothesay, earl of Carrick, lord of the Isles, and baron of Renfrew. Amidst the scenes of joy displayed on this occasion, the king showed his folly more than he had done before. As Elizabeth did not mean to acknowledge him in his sovereign capacity, it was neither consistent with the dignity of the queen, nor his own, that he should be present at the baptism. He did not indeed present himself either at the ceremony or the entertainments and masquerades with which it was accompanied. At this juncture, however, though he had often kept at a greater distance before, he took up his residence at Stirling, as if he had meant to offend the queen, and to expose their quarrels to the world. Du Croc, who was inclined to be favourable to him, was struck with the impropriety of his behaviour, that he affected to have instructions from France to avoid all intercourse with him; and when the king proposed to pay him a visit, he took the liberty to inform him, that there were two passages in his chamber; and that if his majesty should enter by the one, he should be constrained to go out by the other. While he resided at Stirling, the king chiefly confined himself to his chamber. His strange behaviour to the queen did not give the public any favourable idea of him; and as the earl of Murray and his faction took care to augment the general odium, no court was paid to him by foreign ambassadors. His situation, therefore, was exceedingly uncomfortable; but though he must have been conscious of his imprudence and folly, he did not alter his conduct. In a sudden humour he left Stirling, and proceeded to Glasgow. Here he fell sick, with such symptoms as seemed to indicate poison. He was tormented with violent pains, and his body was all covered over with putrefaction of a bluish colour; so that his death was daily expected. Mary did not repay his coldness to her by negligence. She set out immediately for Glasgow, and waited on him with all the affluence of an affectionate wife until he recovered; after which she returned with him to Edinburgh; and as the low situation of the palace of Holyroodhouse was thought to render it unhealthy, the king was lodged in a house which had been appointed for the superior of the church, called St Mary's in

SCOTLAND

Pages 828-847

Scotland. It was therefore her pleasure to allow the affairs of

SCOTLAND

Pages 846-864

Scotland. The counsellors of Elizabeth were now in possession of all the evidence they could expect in this important business. Norfolk was admonished to prepare for his trial; and bishop Lefly perceived, that though he might escape with his life, he would never more be permitted to reside in England, and to act there as the ambassador, the minister, and the friend of the queen of Scots. The defeat of the duke of Norfolk's conspiracy was a blow to Mary which she could never recover. Her most faithful friends were languishing in prisons upon her account; she had no longer the counsels of the bishop of Ross; and the Spanish ambassador, who had entered into her concerns with an unscrupulous cordiality had been ordered to withdraw from England. The trial and condemnation of Norfolk soon followed, and plunged her into the most calamitous distresses. The massacre of the Protestants at Paris in 1572 proved also extremely detrimental to her. It was interpreted to be a consequence of the confederacy which had been formed at Bayonne for the extermination of the reformed. The Protestants were everywhere transported with rage against the Papists. Elizabeth prepared herself against an attack from the Roman-Catholic powers; and was haunted with the notion that they meant to invade her kingdom, and to give it to the queen of Scots. Her ambassador at Paris, Sir Francis Walsingham, augmented her apprehensions and terror. He compared her weakness with the strength of her enemies, and assured her that if they should possess themselves of Scotland, she would soon cease to be a queen. He represented Mary as the great cause of the perils that threatened her personal safety and the tranquility of her kingdom; and as violent diseases required violent remedies, he scurried not to counsel her to unite Scotland to her dominions, and to put to death a rival whose life was inconsistent with her security. The more bigoted Protestants of Scotland differed not very widely in their sentiments from Sir Francis Walsingham; while those of them who were more moderate, were still more attached to their religion than to Mary; and amidst the indignation and horror into which the subjects of Scotland were thrown by the sanguinary outrages of Charles IX. and Catherine de Medicis, they surveyed the sufferings of their sovereign with a diminished sympathy. This year the regent, finding himself beset with difficulties which he could not overcome, and the affairs of the nation involved in confusion from which he could not extricate them, died of melancholy, and was succeeded by the earl of Morton. During the regency of the earl of Marre, a remarkable innovation took place, in the church, which deserves to be particularly explained, being no less than the introduction of Episcopacy instead of the Presbyterian form of worship. While the earl of Lennox was regent, the archbishop of St Andrews was put to death, on account of his being supposed to have had a concern in the death of the earl of Murray; after which the earl of Morton procured a grant of the temporalities of that see. Out of these he allotted a stipend to Mr John Douglas, a Protestant clergyman, who took upon him the title of archbishop. This violence excited censure and murmurs. In the language of the times, it was pronounced to be a profanation of the kirk, and a high contempt of God; and it underwent the scrutiny of the ministry in applications and complaints to the regent. The matter was doubtless of too much importance to be overlooked; and a commission of privy-counsellors and clergymen was appointed in the name of the king to inquire into it, and to reform and improve the policy of the church. This commission, upon the part of the privy-council, consisted of the earl of Morton, the lord Ruthven, Robert abbot of Dunfermline, Mr James Macgill, Sir John Balfour, and Colin Campbell of Glenorchie; and upon the part of the church there were named John Erskine of Dun, and Mr John Winram, Mr Hay, Mr Lindsay, Mr Pont, and Mr John Craig. There were long consultations and debates; and the influence and management of the earl of Morton directed their determinations. It was resolved, that till the majority of the king, or till the wisdom of the three estates should be consulted, the titles of archbishop and bishop should continue as in the times which preceded the reformation; and that a chapter of learned ministers should be annexed to every metropolitan or cathedral seat. It was determined, that the fees as they became vacant should be given to those of the Protestant ministry who were most eminent for their qualifications; that the archbishops and bishops should exercise no higher jurisdiction than what was permitted to superintendents; and that they should be subject to the control of the general assemblies of the church. It was agreed, that all abbots, priors, and other inferior prelates presented to benefices, should be examined by the bishop or superintendent of the diocese or precinct where the preferment was situated; and that their fitness to represent the church in parliament should be duly inquired into. It was judged that the king and the regent should recommend qualified persons to vacant bishoprics, and that the elections of them should be made by the chapters of the respective cathedrals. It was ordered, that all benefices with cure under prelacies, should only be disposed of to officiating ministers; that every minister should receive ordination from the bishop of the diocese, or the superintendent of the province; and that the bishops and superintendents, upon the ordination of ministers, should exact an oath from them to recognize the authority of the king, and to pay canonical obedience to their ordinary in all things that were lawful. By these artful regulations the earl of Morton did not mean solely to consult his own capacity or that of the nobles. The exaltation of the Protestant church to be one of the three estates was a consequence of them; and the clergy being the strenuous enemies of Mary, he might by their means secure a decided influence in parliament. The earl of Marre, as regent, giving his sanction to the proceedings of the commission, they were carried into practice. The delusive expectation of wealth, which this revival of Episcopacy held out to the ministry, was flattering to them; and they bore with tolerable patience this severe blow that was struck against the religious policy of Geneva. Mr John Douglas was desired to give a specimen of his gifts in preaching; and his election took effect; notwithstanding the opposition that was made to it by John Knox and other ecclesiastics, who stood up for Scotland. The rules and forms which had been established at the reformation. He was inaugurated in his office by the bishop of Cathness, Mr John Spotwood superintendent of Lothian, and Mr David Lindsay, who violating the book of discipline, communicated to him his character and admission by the imposition of hands. This was a singular triumph to Episcopacy; and the exaltation of Douglas included other peculiarities remarkable and offensive.
